en.abaisser: Formed in Old French from the prefix ~a-~ (“to, toward”, from Latin ~ad-~) and the verb ~baisser~ (“to lower”), so literally “to bring down toward.” The base ~baisser~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~, built on Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low”). The sense is both physical and moral: ~abaisser~ means to lower a thing, such as a lever or a bridge, and also to humble someone, in the reflexive ~s'abaisser~ (“to demean oneself”). The ~a-~ prefix is no longer productive in French, and ~abaisser~ is one of the verbs that preserve it.
en.abandonner:
Attested around 1100, ~abandonner~ is a denominal verb built on the Old French noun ~bandon~, drawn from the phrase ~mettre à bandon~, “to put at bandon.” ~Bandon~ meant “power, jurisdiction, discretion,” and derives from ~ban~, a term of Frankish origin (*~ban~ / *~bannan~, “proclamation, command, the authority to summon”). To place something ~à bandon~ was to leave it open to anyone's power or will — at the disposal of all. The Frankish ~ban~ is cognate with English ~ban~ and German ~Bann~.

The logic of the meaning is quietly elegant: if a thing is surrendered to everyone's discretion, its owner has, in effect, let it go — and so “to put at the disposal of all” became simply “to abandon, to forsake.” The reflexive ~s'abandonner~ kept a softer trace of the original, “to give oneself over” to an emotion or a person. English borrowed the verb as ~abandon~, and the old noun survives fossilised in the French adverbial phrase ~à l'abandon~, “left untended, in neglect.” From the same Frankish ~ban~ French also holds ~bannir~ (“to banish”), ~banal~ (originally “belonging to the lord's ~ban~,” shared by all), and ~banlieue~.
en.abattre:
From Vulgar Latin *~abbattere~, formed from the prefix ~a-~ (from ~ad-~, “to, down”) and ~battere~, the popular form of Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, strike”). It is cognate with Italian ~abbattere~, Spanish ~abatir~, and Occitan ~abatre~. The origin of ~battuere~ itself is uncertain: rare in literary Latin, it is thought to be a borrowing, perhaps from Gaulish or Germanic, and may be onomatopoeic; Welsh ~bathu~ (“to beat”) is cited as a relative.

The prefix adds a downward force to “beat”: to ~abattre~ is to strike down — to fell a tree, slaughter an animal, demolish a wall, or, figuratively, to dishearten (~être abattu~, “to be dejected”). The same ~battuere~ underlies a busy French family: ~battre~, ~combattre~, ~rabattre~, ~débattre~, plus the nouns ~abattoir~, ~abattage~, and ~abattement~. The English doublets ~battle~, ~beat~, and ~batter~ come from the same uncertain Latin verb, carried across the Channel by the Normans.
en.abolir: Borrowed from Latin ~abolēre~ (“to destroy, to efface, to put an end to”). The Latin verb described wiping something out so that no trace remained, and French kept that sense of annulling a law, a custom or a practice. The verb entered French with the ending ~-ir~, though the Latin infinitive ended in ~-ēre~. Its family includes ~abolition~ and ~abolitionniste~, the name of the movement that sought to abolish slavery.
en.abonder:
Inherited as Old French ~abonder~ from Latin ~abundāre~ (“to overflow, to be abundant”), a formation on ~ab-~ (“away from”) and ~undāre~ (“to rise in waves, to flow”), from ~unda~ (“wave”). The picture is a flood: water that surges up and spills over its banks. Latin ~abundāre~ also gave Italian ~abbondare~, Spanish ~abundar~ and English ~abound~, and its adjective gave French ~abondant~ and English ~abundant~.

In French the image of overflowing softened into plenty: a place that ~abonde~ in something is rich in it. A telling idiom is ~abonder dans le sens de quelqu'un~, “to agree wholeheartedly with someone.” The root ~unda~ lives on in ~onde~ (“wave”), ~inonder~ (“to flood”) and ~ondulation~, and the same prefixed pattern gave ~redonder~ and ~redondant~ (from Latin ~redundāre~) and ~surabonder~ (“to superabound”).
en.abonner:
The verb rests on an old French word for a limit. French Wiktionary derives ~abonner~ from Old French ~aboner~ (“to set boundaries,” and figuratively “to fix a limit”), itself from ~bone~ (“boundary marker, limit”). English Wiktionary describes the same formation as ~a-~ + ~borne~ (“boundary”). That noun goes back to Old French ~bodne~ and, before it, to Early Medieval Latin ~bodina~, a word whose ultimate origin is unknown. One proposal links it to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰudʰmḗn~ (“bottom, base”), with a possible relative in Proto-Celtic *~bundos~, but this is a conjecture, not a settled descent.

The oldest sense is physical: to mark out with boundaries, and then figuratively to fix a limit. The modern meaning “to subscribe” is a plausible next step, since a subscription is an arrangement fixed in advance, for a set term or a set sum, but the sources do not document that step, so it should be read as likely rather than proven. The same noun gave French ~borne~ (a boundary stone, as in the kilometer marker) and ~borner~ (“to limit”), and the verb gave ~abonnement~ and ~abonné~. A verb that began with marking limits thus came to serve magazines and streaming plans.
en.aborder:
A French formation, ~a-~ (“to, toward,” from Latin ~ad~) + ~border~ (“to skirt, to come alongside the edge”), attested from 1306. ~border~ derives from ~bord~ (“edge, side; ship's plank, ship's side”), a borrowing from Frankish *~bord~, from Proto-Germanic *~burdą~ (“board, plank”). This is cognate with English ~board~ and German ~Bord~ — the same word that gives the nautical English ~aboard~.

The nautical scene is the key: to ~aborder~ a ship was to bring one's own ~bord~ up against another's — to come alongside, whether to dock, to board, or to attack. From this concrete “draw up to the side” grew the modern figurative senses: to ~aborder~ a person is to approach and accost them, and to ~aborder un sujet~ is to “tackle” or “take up” a topic, as if steering one's vessel toward its shore. The Germanic ~bord~ proved a rich import, seeding ~bord~, ~border~, ~bordure~, ~abordage~, ~abordable~, ~babord~ (“port side”), and ~tribord~ (“starboard”).
en.aboutir:
Unlike most verbs in this app, ~aboutir~ has no single Latin ancestor: it was built inside French itself, first attested around 1319. It is a parasynthetic derivative of the noun ~bout~ (“end, tip”), framed by the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad~, “to, toward”) and the second-group verbal suffix ~-ir~ — literally “to bring to an end / to a point.” The noun ~bout~ is itself a deverbal of Old French ~bouter~ (“to push, to strike”), borrowed from Frankish *~bōtan~ (“to push, beat”), of Proto-Germanic stock *~bautaną~ (“to beat”). Through that Germanic root it is cousin to English ~beat~ and to the ~butt~ of a goat.

The metaphor inside ~aboutir~ is a journey reaching its far ~bout~. Concretely, a street or pipe can ~aboutir~ somewhere — physically come out at that point; abstractly, an effort, a negotiation, or a project ~aboutit~ when it finally arrives at its result, hence “to succeed.” The negative ~ne pas aboutir~ is the everyday way to say a plan “came to nothing.” The same humble noun ~bout~ seeds a wide family: ~embout~ (“tip, nozzle”), ~about~ (a carpenter's butt-joint), ~rebouter~ (“to set a bone”), and the bone-setter ~rebouteux~ — all turning, like ~aboutir~, on the idea of an end pushed up against something.
en.abriter:
A denominal verb (attested 1489) from ~abri~ (“shelter”), which replaced an older verb ~abrier~ (“to cover, to shelter”). The deeper origin is debated: ~abrier~ is often linked to Late Latin ~aprīcārī~ (“to bask, to keep warm in the sun”), from ~aprīcus~ (“sunny, exposed to the sun”); some etymologists instead propose a Frankish source. Cognate, on the Latin account, with Italian ~aprico~ (“sunny”).

If the Latin derivation holds, the word's history is charming: a shelter was first a sunny spot, a warm nook where one came to bask, and only later the general idea of cover against wind, rain, or danger. The semantic slide runs from “warmth” to “protection.” ~Abriter~ supplanted ~abrier~ entirely, surfaced as a gardening term in the eighteenth century (sheltering tender plants), then broadened to its modern range — to shelter a person, to house an institution, even figuratively to harbour a secret. From ~abri~ French also keeps ~abribus~ (a bus shelter) and the reflexive ~s'abriter~, “to take cover.”
en.abroger:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~abrogāre~ (“to repeal a law, to annul”), made of ~ab-~ (“away from”) and ~rogāre~ (“to ask, to propose”). The Latin verb ~rogāre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to stretch out, to direct”), the same root that gave Latin ~rex~ (“king”, literally “the one who directs”), as well as English ~right~ and German ~recht~. French has taken many words from ~rogāre~ and its compounds: ~interroger~, ~déroger~, ~proroger~, ~arroger~, ~prérogative~ and ~rogatoire~. English ~abrogate~ comes straight from the same Latin verb, and Latin ~abrogāre~ has a family of sibling compounds that French has also kept in its legal vocabulary.

The verb carries the mechanics of Roman lawmaking. A law was a ~rogatio~, a bill that a magistrate put to the people, as if asking for their assent. To repeal it, one proposed a counter-measure, hence ~abrogāre~, “to undo by a counter-vote”. Its Latin siblings each named a different kind of legislative surgery: ~derogāre~ to repeal in part, ~subrogāre~ to substitute one provision for another, ~obrogāre~ to modify by a new provision. The legal vocabulary of French has kept them, and ~abroger~ still names the formal cancellation of a law, a decree or a custom. A word of the Roman assembly thus lives on in every statute book that is amended.
en.abréger:
From Old French ~abregier~, inherited from Late Latin ~abbreviāre~ (“to shorten”), a verb built on the adjective ~brevis~ (“short”) with the prefix ~ab-~, a form of ~ad-~ (“to”). The sense is thus “to make short.” The same Latin verb entered French a second time as a learned borrowing, ~abrévier~, now obsolete, so ~abréger~ and ~abrévier~ are doublets. English did the same: ~abbreviate~ came straight from Latin, while ~abridge~ came through Old French ~abregier~, the very verb that became ~abréger~.

The Latin adjective ~brevis~ is the source of ~bref~ and ~brève~ in French, and the noun ~brièveté~ belongs to the same family. The learned noun ~abréviation~ keeps the Latin shape more plainly than ~abréger~ does. Such pairs, one worn down by speech and one close to the Latin, are common in French vocabulary. In use, ~abréger~ spans cutting a text, a stay or a word. Note that the g of the stem takes an e before a and o, as in ~nous abrégeons~, to keep its soft sound.
en.absorber:
From Latin ~absorbēre~ (“to swallow up, suck in”), from ~ab-~ (“away, from”) + ~sorbēre~ (“to suck in, swallow”). ~Sorbēre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~sorβeō~ and to PIE *~srebʰ-~ (“to sip, slurp”), an iterative *~srobʰéyeti~. The Romance descendants of the simple verb survive — Spanish ~sorber~, Italian ~sorbire~ — and English took the rare verb ~sorb~ from the Latin.

The picture is of drinking something entirely down and away: ~ab-~ adds the sense of carrying off, so to ~absorber~ is to draw a liquid, a light, a sound, or a shock completely into oneself until it is gone from view. French extended this readily to the figurative — a task or a passion can ~absorber~ a person, swallowing up their attention. Relatives in French include ~absorption~, ~absorbant~, and the medical ~résorber~. A tempting cognate to flag and reject: ~sorbet~ looks related but is not — it comes by a separate path from Arabic ~شَرْبَة~ (~šarba~, “a drink”) through Turkish and Italian, and the resemblance to ~sorbēre~ is mere coincidence.
en.abstenir:
From Old French ~abstenir~, borrowed from Latin ~abstinēre~ (“to hold back, to keep away”), formed from ~abs-~ (“away from”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). French reshaped the Latin infinitive on the model of ~tenir~, so the verb conjugates like it. Related forms in other languages include Italian ~astenere~ and Spanish ~abstener~, and English ~abstain~, which was borrowed through Old French ~abstenir~ itself.

Etymologically, to ~abstenir~ is to hold oneself away from something, and the verb is almost always reflexive: ~s'abstenir de voter~ means to refrain from voting. The sense of voluntary restraint, whether from food, drink or action, was present in Latin and remains the core of the French verb. It gave the nouns ~abstinence~ and ~abstention~ and the adjective ~abstinent~. The verb also lives in a large family descended from ~tenēre~, including ~tenir~, ~contenir~, ~retenir~, ~soutenir~ and ~maintenir~. Each pairs the same “hold” with a different prefix, and ~abstenir~ is the one that holds itself aloof.
en.abuser: From the noun ~abus~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. French ~abus~ comes from Latin ~abūsus~ (“a using up, misuse”), from the verb ~abūtī~ (“to use up, to use wrongly”). The verb has two main senses, “to mislead” and “to misuse or overdo” (~abuser de~ something). Both rest on the idea of using a thing in a way it was never meant for, whether someone's trust or a substance.
en.abîmer: Formed from the noun ~abîme~ (“abyss”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. ~Abîme~ is inherited from Old French ~abisme~, from a Late Latin form *~abīsmus~, an altered version of Latin ~abyssus~, which borrowed Greek ~ábussos~ (“bottomless pit”). It is a doublet of ~abysse~. The verb first meant to cast into an abyss, to engulf or ruin, and the sense weakened over time to the everyday “to damage, to spoil”, while the reflexive form can still mean to sink or be lost in something. A damaged object is thus, figuratively, one sent down into the abyss.
en.accentuer:
Attested from the 12th century, from Medieval Latin ~accentuāre~, derived from Latin ~accentus~ (“accent, tone of voice”). ~Accentus~ is built from ~ad-~ (“to”) + ~cantus~ (“song”), from ~canere~ / ~canō~ (“to sing”), and is itself a calque of Ancient Greek ~prosōidía~ (“a song sung to music; the tone of a syllable”) — ~prós~ (“to”) + ~ōidḗ~ (“song”) — the Greek term the Romans were translating piece for piece. ~Canere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”), cognate with English ~chant~ and ~cantor~, and, through the Germanic line, English ~hen~ and German ~Hahn~ (“rooster”), the singers of the farmyard.

The buried metaphor is lovely: an ~accent~ was understood as the “song” added to a syllable, its pitch or stress — speech as melody. From ~accentus~ the verb ~accentuer~ came to mean “to mark with an accent,” then more broadly “to stress, to emphasize, to make more pronounced.” The same Latin family gives French ~accent~, ~chant~, ~chanter~, ~cantique~, ~incantation~, and ~chantre~ — all of them, at root, about singing.
en.accepter:
From Latin ~acceptare~ (“to receive willingly, to take regularly”), the frequentative of ~accipere~ (“to receive, to take to oneself”), which is itself ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”). The verb ~capere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, to seize”), and through the Germanic branch is a true cognate of English ~have~ and ~heave~. Italian ~accettare~ and Spanish ~aceptar~ are the Romance siblings; English ~accept~ is a borrowing from the same Latin stem.

Because ~acceptare~ is a frequentative, its built-in nuance is repeated or habitual taking — not a single grab but a settled willingness to receive. That shade of consent is what French kept: to accept is to receive something offered, and by extension to agree or to tolerate. The base ~capere~ is one of the most fertile roots in French, surfacing in ~capter~, ~capturer~, ~captif~, ~recevoir~ and ~concevoir~ (through ~capere~'s combining form ~-cipere~), and in ~capable~ and ~capacité~. Latin ~acceptare~ also gave the noun ~acceptation~ and, in commerce, the ~acceptation~ of a bill — a creditor's formal “taking” of a draft.
en.accoler:
~Accoler~ is built on ~col~ (“neck”) with the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-er~. It appears in Old French, where it meant “to throw one's arms around someone's neck,” and so “to embrace.” English Wiktionary only records it as inherited from Old French ~acoler~. The base ~col~ is inherited from Latin ~collum~ (“neck”), and ~col~ is a doublet of ~cou~, the ordinary modern word for the neck. The Latin noun also gave Italian ~collo~ and Spanish ~cuello~, and English ~collar~ comes from the Latin derivative ~collāre~.

The meaning faded over time. Where Old French spoke of necks and arms, modern ~accoler~ means “to place side by side” or “to join,” with no body in sight. By one account, the weakening toward “bring together” was helped by ~coller~ (“to stick”), though the source states this only as a possibility. The older sense lives on in ~accolade~, which means both an embrace and the ceremonial tap or embrace of a knighting, and which English borrowed as ~accolade~. In writing, ~accolade~ also names the curly bracket that joins lines together, a visual form of ~accoler~.
en.accommoder:
From Latin ~accommodāre~ (“to fit to, to adapt”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~commodāre~, a verb built on ~commodus~ (“fitting, suitable”). That adjective is a compound of ~com-~ (“with”) and ~modus~ (“measure”), so something ~commodus~ is in full measure, exactly right for its purpose. The root ~modus~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~med-~ (“to measure, to take appropriate measures”), which also gave English ~mete~. Italian ~accomodare~, Spanish ~acomodar~ and English ~accommodate~ are relatives of the French verb.

The central idea is making one thing fit another. French ~accommoder~ therefore covers adapting something to circumstances, reconciling people (an older use) and, in the kitchen, preparing or dressing food: accommoder les restes is to turn leftovers into a decent meal. The reflexive ~s'accommoder de~ means to make do with, and the adjective ~accommodant~ describes someone easy to deal with. The same ~modus~ gives ~mode~, ~modèle~, ~modeste~, ~modérer~, ~commode~ and ~commodité~.
en.accompagner:
From Old French ~acompaignier~, derived from ~compaing~ / ~compagnon~ (“companion”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”). ~Compagnon~ comes from Late Latin ~companio~ (accusative ~companionem~), literally ~cum~ (“with”) + ~panis~ (“bread”) — “one with whom you share bread.” The Latin word was likely a calque of Gothic ~gahlaiba~ (~ga-~ “with” + ~hlaifs~ “loaf”), a fellow soldier of the same mess. Cognate with Spanish ~compañero~ and, via Old French, English ~company~.

So ~accompagner~ means, at root, to go alongside someone as a bread-sharer — to keep company. From there the sense fanned out: to escort, to go with, to add to (« accompagner un plat d'un vin »), and in music to support a soloist with a secondary part. The bread is still visible across the family: the same ~companio~ gave the Old French nominative ~compain~, which became the familiar modern ~copain~ (“buddy, pal”), and the collective ~compagnie~ (“company,” military, theatrical, or commercial). Few everyday words wear their convivial origin so plainly: to accompany someone is, etymologically, to break bread with them.
en.accomplir:
From Old French ~complir~, ~acomplir~, from Latin ~complēre~ (“to fill up, fill out, complete”) reinforced by the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”). ~Complēre~ itself is ~com-~ (“together, completely”) plus the bound verb ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). That root is enormously productive: it gives Latin ~plēnus~ (“full”), and is cognate with Greek ~plērēs~ (“full”), English ~full~, and English ~plenty~ (the last borrowed from the same Latin family).

The sense path runs from filling to finishing: to fill out a task is to complete it, and to complete it fully is to accomplish it — the prefix ~ad-~ adding a sense of carrying through to the end. Latin built a whole series on ~plēre~ by swapping prefixes — ~implēre~ (“to fill in”), ~explēre~ (“to fill out”), ~replēre~ (“to refill”) — and French inherited the lot. From the same root come French ~plein~, ~complet~, ~remplir~, ~accomplissement~, ~complément~, ~plénitude~, and even ~plus~ (from ~plūs~, “more,” the same idea of fullness).
en.accorder:
From Vulgar/Late Latin ~accordare~ (“to bring into agreement”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~cor~, genitive ~cordis~ (“heart”), with the verbal ending ~-are~. Latin ~cor~ comes from Proto-Italic *~kord~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱerd-~ (“heart”). The same root gave Greek ~kardia~ (“heart”), English ~heart~, and German ~Herz~, while the Latin compound surfaces as Italian ~accordare~ and Spanish ~acordar~.

Literally, ~accorder~ means “to bring heart to heart” — to make two hearts beat as one. From this image flow its modern senses: to make things agree (grammatical agreement, ~l'accord du participe~), to tune an instrument so its strings are in harmony, and, by extension, “to grant” a request, as though granting it from the heart. The noun ~accord~ (“agreement, chord”) was borrowed into English as ~accord~ and, musically, lies behind ~chord~. The same *~ḱerd-~ heart underlies a striking family of French words: ~courage~ (from ~cor~, the seat of feeling), ~cordial~, ~concorde~ and ~discorde~, ~record~ (originally “to call back to the heart, to remember”), and even ~croire~ (from ~credere~, “to put one's heart in”).
en.accoucher: Formed from ~coucher~ (“to lay down”) with the prefix ~a-~, from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). The base ~coucher~ comes from Old French ~couchier~ and Latin ~collocare~ (“to place, to lay in position”), built on ~locus~ (“place”). At the end of the twelfth century ~accoucher~ simply meant “to lie down”. The specialized sense came later: a woman who ~accouche~ is one who takes to her bed, so the verb moved from lying down to giving birth.
en.accourcir: An archaic verb meaning “to shorten,” taken from Old French ~acorcier~. English Wiktionary describes its structure as ~a-~ + ~court~ + ~-ir~, “to make short.” The adjective ~court~ comes from Latin ~curtus~ (“cut short”), which English borrowed as ~curt~. Modern French has largely replaced ~accourcir~ with ~raccourcir~, built on the same stem with a further prefix.
en.accrocher:
~accrocher~ is a French formation, built on the noun ~croc~ (“hook, fang”) with the prefix ~a-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~ — literally “to put on a hook.” The noun ~croc~ comes, by fr.Wiktionary’s account, from Frankish *~krok~ (“hook”), reflected in Medieval Latin ~croccus~; the late borrowing explains the preserved final ~c~. The Germanic word is cognate with English ~crook~ and ~crooked~ and with Norwegian ~krok~, all from a common Germanic source meaning a bend or hook.

From the concrete act of hanging something on a hook, ~accrocher~ spread in every direction a hook suggests: to catch, to snag, to bump (two cars that ~s’accrochent~), to cling (s’~accrocher~ à un espoir), and, in modern slang, to grab someone’s attention or to hit it off. The same ~croc~ root gives French ~crochet~ (“hook, crochet-needle”), ~accroc~ (“a snag, a tear, a hitch”), and the verb ~décrocher~ (“to unhook,” and figuratively to land a job or pick up the phone) — a whole small vocabulary of hooking and unhooking grown from one Frankish hook.
en.accroître:
From Middle French ~accroistre~, from Old French ~acroistre~ (“to grow, to increase”), from Latin ~accrēscere~ (“to grow larger, to increase”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and the verb ~crēscere~ (“to grow”). The Latin verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ker-~ (“to grow, to nourish”). The same root gave Latin ~creāre~ (“to bring forth, create”) and the divine name ~Cerēs~, goddess of grain. Through Latin it is cognate with English ~accrue~, ~crescent~, ~increase~, and even ~croissant~, the “growing” crescent-shaped pastry.

In Latin, ~crēscere~ described organic growth — plants, children, the moon waxing — and the prefixed ~accrēscere~ sharpened this to growth added onto something already there. Old French ~acroistre~ kept that nuance, and modern ~accroître~ still means to augment a quantity or intensity rather than merely to enlarge in size. A memorable quirk of its conjugation is the circumflex inherited from a vanished ~s~ (~accroistre~ → ~accroître~), and the past participle ~accru~ that distinguishes it from ~cru~. The root *~ker-~ flowered into a wide French family: ~croître~ itself, ~croissance~ (“growth”), ~accroissement~ (“increase”), ~recrue~ and ~recrutement~ (a “recruit” being fresh growth for an army), ~concret~, ~créer~, and ~croissant~ — all branches of the same idea of swelling and coming into being.
en.accréditer: The sources differ. French Wiktionary derives it in French from ~crédit~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the suffix ~-er~, literally “to give credit to.” English Wiktionary instead sees a borrowing from Spanish ~acreditar~. Either way the base idea is credit, and ~crédit~ came into French from Italian ~credito~, from Latin ~crēditum~, the supine of ~crēdere~ (“to believe”). To ~accréditer~ is to make credible: to give an ambassador or a journalist official recognition, or to lend weight to a rumor or a theory.
en.accueillir:
From Old French ~acoillir~, ~acueillir~ (“to receive, to gather, to attack”), from Vulgar Latin *~accolligere~, formed from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus Latin ~colligere~ (“to gather, to collect”). ~Colligere~ is itself ~con-~ (“together”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”), which descends from PIE *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, to gather”) — the root that also gave Greek ~légein~ (“to pick out, to say”) and Latin ~lēx~ (“law”). Cognate with Italian ~accogliere~ and Spanish ~acoger~.

The base verb ~cueillir~ means “to pick, to gather” (flowers, fruit); add the directional ~ad-~ and the picture becomes “to gather someone toward oneself,” to take them in — hence “to welcome, to receive.” Old French ~acoillir~ could even mean “to set upon, to assail,” another way of moving toward someone, a sense now long gone. Modern ~accueillir~ has settled on hospitality, and yields the warm noun ~accueil~ (“welcome, reception”). From the same *~leǵ-~ root French keeps ~cueillir~, ~recueillir~ (“to collect, to gather up”), ~collecte~, ~lire~ (“to read,” via ~legere~), ~légende~, and ~élire~ (“to elect, to pick out”).
en.accumuler:
French ~accumuler~ was borrowed from Latin ~accumulare~ (“to heap up”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~cumulare~ (“to pile”), itself from the noun ~cumulus~ (“heap, mound”). ~cumulus~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱuh₁mós~ (“heap”), built on the root *~ḱewh₁-~ (“to swell”). That swelling root links it to Ancient Greek ~κῦμα~ (“swell, wave”). The learned borrowing displaced an earlier, popularly evolved Old French ~acombler~, which had reached the same sense by an unbroken oral descent.

The metaphor sits right in the etymon: to ~accumuler~ is to let things swell into a heap, as a ~cumulus~ cloud swells into a puffy mound in the sky. French keeps a rich progeny from the root — ~accumulation~, ~accumulateur~ (“accumulator, storage battery”), and the prefixed ~suraccumuler~ (“to over-accumulate”), ~bioaccumuler~, and ~désaccumuler~ — while the simple ~cumul~ (“the holding of several offices or sums together”) and the meteorological ~cumulus~ stand beside them. English ~accumulate~ and ~cumulus~ were taken from the very same Latin words, so the “heaping” image crosses neatly into both languages.
en.accuser:
From Latin ~accūsāre~ (“to call to account, to bring a charge against”), itself built on ~ad-~ (“toward, with regard to”) and the noun ~causa~ (“cause, lawsuit, legal case”) — so that to ~accuser~ someone was literally to bring a ~causa~ against them, to summon them to a legal reckoning. The same ~causa~ underlies ~excuser~ (“to clear of a charge,” from ~ex-~ + ~causa~) and, through Old French, English ~cause~ and ~accuse~. Italian ~accusare~ and Spanish ~acusar~ are direct cognates.

Latin ~causa~ also gives the grammatical term ~accusatif~ (the accusative case), through a chain of translation errors: Greek grammarians called it the case of the thing affected, but the Latin ~accūsātīvus~ misread the Greek as relating to ~accusation~. Modern French derivatives clustering around ~causa~ include ~accusation~, ~accusateur~, ~accusatoire~, and ~inaccusable~, alongside ~cause~, ~causer~, and ~à cause de~. The origin of ~causa~ itself before Latin is obscure and not securely reconstructed, so its prehistory is best left open. What is certain is the courtroom flavor at the root of ~accuser~: the word never simply meant to blame, but to lay a formal charge — and in French it still carries that weight of summoning someone to answer.
en.accéder:
From Latin ~accedere~ (“to approach, to draw near to”), formed from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~ac-~ before c) and the verb ~cedere~ (“to go, to move, to withdraw, to yield”). ~Cedere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~kezdō~; its deeper origin is disputed, perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to go away, to yield.” Through Latin compounds the verb fathered a whole English series — ~cede~, ~access~, ~recede~, ~precede~, and ~succeed~.

The Latin sense was physical: to ~accedere~ was to step toward something, to approach it. French kept that motion but turned it into reaching and entering: to ~accéder~ to a place is to get to it, and the noun ~accès~ is the way in. From there grew the figurative senses — to ~accéder à~ a request is to “come around” to it, to grant it; to ~accéder~ to a throne or an office is to attain it. The root ~cedere~ runs through a broad French family: ~céder~ (“to yield”), ~accès~, ~succéder~, ~procéder~, ~précéder~, ~excéder~, and the nouns ~succès~ and ~procédure~. To gain access, then, is simply to have walked all the way up to the door.
en.accélérer:
From Latin ~accelerare~ (“to hasten, to do more quickly”), formed from the prefix ~ad-~ (assimilated to ~ac-~) and ~celerare~ (“to quicken”), a verb on the adjective ~celer~ (“swift, rapid”). ~celer~ is traced to Proto-Indo-European *~kel-~ (“to drive, to set in motion”) and is probably cognate with Ancient Greek ~κέλλω~ (“to drive on”) and ~κέλης~ (“a runner, a swift horse”). The prefix ~ad-~ adds a sense of motion toward, so the Latin meant to drive a thing forward faster.

The word kept its plain meaning across the centuries — to make something go faster — but the modern world handed it a vehicle: to ~accélérer~ now first calls to mind pressing the pedal of a car. Figuratively French uses it for hastening a process, a reform, a heartbeat. From the same ~celer~ root French keeps the adjective ~célère~ (rare, “swift”) and the noun ~célérité~ (“celerity, speed”), the latter also the physicists' word for the speed of a wave. The everyday ~accélérateur~ (“accelerator”) and ~accélération~ round out a small family in which the ancient sense of swift driving still presses forward.
en.acharner: Built from ~a-~, Old French ~charn~ (“flesh”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The original sense was to give a hunting animal, a dog above all, a taste for flesh in order to excite it, hence “to incite, to sic.” The reflexive ~s'acharner~ then came to mean attacking something with fury. ~Charn~ is the Old French ancestor of modern ~chair~, from Latin ~carnem~ (“flesh, meat”), the accusative of ~carō~. French ~carne~ is a doublet of ~chair~, from the same Latin word.
en.acheminer: Formed from the prefix ~a-~, the noun ~chemin~ (“road, path”) and the ending ~-er~, so it means “to set on the road” and then “to send toward a destination.” The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), and it joins the ending ~-er~ to build the verb around the noun, a pattern called parasynthesis. ~Chemin~ descends from Old French ~chemin~ and from Late Latin ~cammīnus~, a word that sources trace to Gaulish, so it is one of the rare Celtic survivors in French. The verb ~acheminer~ is used for mail, goods and troops that are forwarded on their way.
en.acheter:
From Old French ~achater~ (“to buy”), from Vulgar Latin *~accaptāre~, a reinforced form built with ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) on Latin ~captāre~ (“to seek to seize, chase after”). ~captāre~ is the frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take, seize, hold”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp”). Through that root ~acheter~ is a distant cousin of English ~have~ and ~heave~, and of the borrowed ~capable~, ~captive~, and ~capture~. The Latin verb of buying proper, ~emere~, did not survive into French here.

The semantic path is one of narrowing: from “to grasp at, try to take” to “to obtain” and finally to the specific “to obtain in exchange for money” — to buy. This mirrors what happened to ~emere~ itself, which began meaning “to take” before specializing into “to buy” in Classical Latin. The pronunciation traveled too: medieval ~achater~ smoothed into modern ~acheter~. From the same ~capere~ family, French keeps a remarkable crowd of words — ~captif~, ~capable~, ~capter~, ~recevoir~ (through ~recipere~), and ~chasser~ (through *~captiāre~) — so that buying, capturing, and hunting are all, at the deepest level, manners of grasping.
en.achever:
From Old French ~achever~ (“to bring to a head, complete”), a derivative formed with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) on ~chief~ (“head, end”), the Old French outcome of Latin ~caput~ (“head”). The verb belongs to the phrase ~venir a chief~ (“to come to a head, to bring to an end”). ~Caput~ descends from Proto-Italic *~kaput~ and Proto-Indo-European *~kaput~, and is a true cognate of English ~head~ and German ~Haupt~.

The core image is reaching the head or top of something: to achieve a task is to bring it to its culminating point, its ~chief~ end. From this grew the darker sense “to finish off,” to deal the death-blow that brings a wounded creature to its final point — French still says ~achever une bête~. English borrowed the verb as ~achieve~, where the sense drifted toward attaining success rather than merely ending. The same ~caput~ runs through a remarkable French family: ~chef~ (“head, leader, chef”), ~chief~'s modern reflex; ~chevet~ (“bedhead”); ~achèvement~ (“completion”); ~capitaine~; ~chapitre~; and ~cap~ (“headland”), each preserving the head as the foremost or culminating part.
en.acquitter:
From Old French ~acquiter~, inherited from Medieval Latin ~acquitāre~ (also written ~adquietāre~, “to pay a debt”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~quitare~ (“to set free”). That verb comes from Late Latin ~quietāre~ (“to set at rest”), from Latin ~quiētus~ (“at rest”). French Wiktionary describes the verb as ~ad-~ joined to ~quitte~ (“free of debt”), which belongs to the same family. To ~acquitter~ a debt is, at bottom, to bring it to rest. English took the family more than once: ~quit~ is a cousin by way of Old French, ~quiet~ is a more learned cousin from the same Latin ~quiētus~, and ~acquit~ borrowed the French verb itself.

The sense moved from settling accounts to settling obligations. The verb first meant to pay what one owed, hence ~acquitter une dette~ (“to pay off a debt”). Payment frees the debtor, so the meaning widened to releasing someone from any charge: a court that ~acquitte~ a defendant declares him ~quitte~ of the accusation. The reflexive ~s'acquitter de~ means to discharge a duty or a debt. Related French words include ~quitte~, ~quittance~ (“receipt”), ~acquit~ (“receipt, discharge,” as in ~par acquit de conscience~, “to set one's conscience at rest”) and ~acquittement~. ~Quitter~ (“to leave”) is also a relative, from the older sense “to release.”
en.acquérir:
From Latin ~acquirere~ (Vulgar Latin ~acquaerere~), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask for”). Old French had the inherited form ~acquerre~ (attested 1148); the modern ~acquérir~, reshaped on the model of other ~-ir~ verbs, appears around 1370. Cognate with Italian ~acquisire~ and Spanish ~adquirir~, and — through ~quaerere~ — with English ~acquire~, ~quest~, and ~query~.

The force of ~ad-~ turns a simple “seeking” into a seeking that attains its object: to ~acquérir~ is to seek something all the way to getting it. The supine ~acquisitum~ gave the noun ~acquisition~ and the past participle ~acquis~, which doubles as a noun meaning the knowledge or advantages one has gained. The bare root verb survives in French as the archaic ~quérir~ (“to fetch, to go seek”), still felt in ~aller quérir~. The same ~quaerere~ branches widely: ~conquérir~ (“to seek thoroughly, to win”), ~requérir~ (“to seek back, to demand”), ~enquérir~, and ~quérable~. Strikingly, Spanish let ~quaerere~ drift from seeking to wanting and then to loving — ~querer~ — while French kept the harder, more acquisitive edge of the original.
en.acter:
~Acter~ is a denominal verb, coined directly on the noun ~acte~, which French took from Latin ~āctum~ (“a thing done; the written record of a proceeding”), the neuter past participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, to lead, to carry through, to do”). ~Agere~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~agō~ to PIE *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”), a root that surfaces again in Ancient Greek ~ágō~ (“I lead”). Latin ~āctum~ is the source of the noun in nearly every European language — Italian ~atto~, Spanish ~acto~, English ~act~ — and its plural ~ācta~, “the things done,” was the Roman name for official minutes, which is exactly the sense French ~acte~ preserves in legal usage. So ~acter~ does not mean “to act” in the English sense at all: it means to put something into the ~ācta~, to enter it in the record.

The verb's history is not quite settled, and the TLFi says so. A stray thirteenth-century attestation, glossed “to date documents properly,” appears in the chronicle of Philippe Mouskès, and the verb turns up again in the Encyclopédie of 1751; but the dictionary cautions that modern ~acter~ may instead be an independent creation of court clerks, extracted from the fixed phrase ~prendre acte~ (“to take note”) in just the way ~contacter~ was later extracted from ~prendre contact~. Medieval Latin ~actare~ (“to decide”) is invoked as well. For centuries the word stayed inside the courtroom, and that is where the Académie française still endorses it — ~acter une clause, une décision~ — while objecting both to the construction ~acter de~, built by false analogy with ~prendre acte de~, and to the verb's recent spread into emphatic everyday speech in place of ~enregistrer~ or ~reconnaître~. Canadian French has a separate anglicism, ~acter~ meaning to play a role. Kin: ~agir~, ~agent~, ~action~, ~agile~, ~ambigu~, ~exiger~.
en.actionner: Formed in French from ~action~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun ~action~ comes from Latin ~actio~, itself drawn from the verb ~agere~ (“to do, to drive”). The suffix turns the noun into a verb: ~actionner~ is to put something into action, as when one operates a lever or a mechanism. In law the verb took a second sense, to bring a lawsuit against someone, which fits the older legal meaning of ~action~ as a right to sue.
en.activer:
Attested from the 15th century, ~activer~ is a French formation built on the adjective ~actif~ (“active”) plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~Actif~ descends from Latin ~āctīvus~ (“active, practical”), a derivative of ~āctus~, the past participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do, to act”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to lead”). Through this root it is cognate with English ~act~, ~agent~, and ~agile~, with Greek ~ágein~ (“to lead, to drive”), and — surprisingly — with English ~ambassador~, by way of a long Celtic-Latin detour.

To ~activer~ is literally to render ~actif~, to set something in motion or speed it up. In everyday French it long meant chiefly “to hurry, to get a move on” — ~activer le pas~, “to quicken one's step,” or the colloquial reflexive ~s'activer~, “to bustle about.” The age of machines and screens then handed it a new technical life: one now ~active~ a switch, an account, a feature, or an alarm. The prolific ~agere~ feeds a wide French family alongside ~activer~: ~agir~, ~action~, ~acte~, ~agent~, ~agiter~, ~exiger~, and ~rédiger~ — every one of them a form of doing or driving.
en.actualiser: Formed from the adjective ~actuel~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make A”: to make something current or real. The stem loses its ending and becomes ~actual-~ before the suffix. The base ~actuel~ was borrowed from Latin ~actuālis~ (“active, practical”), itself from Latin ~āctus~ (“act, doing”). The suffix goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which carried Greek verbs into Latin. So ~actualiser~ is a French formation on a Latin base, and it is the verb behind the everyday sense “to update”.
en.adapter:
From Latin ~adaptare~ (“to fit to, to adjust”), made of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~aptare~ (“to fit, to make ready”), a frequentative of ~apere~ (“to fasten, to attach”). The participle ~aptus~ (“fitted, suitable”) gave French ~apte~ and English ~apt~; the whole family rests on PIE *~h₂ep-~ (“to join, to fit”). Cognate with Italian ~adattare~ and Spanish ~adaptar~, and the source, through French, of English ~adapt~.

The underlying image is mechanical — making one thing fit snugly onto another — and the verb kept it: to fit a part to a machine, then, by extension, to adjust oneself to circumstances, and in the arts to turn a novel into a film. The reflexive « s'adapter » (“to adapt oneself”) makes the organism, not the object, do the fitting. The same root *~h₂ep-~ produced a surprisingly varied family: ~apte~ and ~aptitude~ (“fitness, ability”), ~inapte~, and — through a learned Latin pun on “fitting a posture” — ~attitude~, borrowed from Italian ~attitudine~, itself from Latin ~aptitudo~. To adapt is, at heart, to fit.
en.additionner: Formed in French from the noun ~addition~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so it is a denominal verb. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~additio~, from ~addere~ (“to add, to place near”), itself ~ad-~ (“toward”) + ~dare~ (“to give”). The arithmetical sense is recorded in Medieval Latin in the twelfth century and appears in French in the fifteenth. ~Additionner~ means to add numbers together, and by extension to add one thing to another.
en.adhérer:
A late borrowing from Latin ~adhaerēre~ (“to stick to, to be fixed to”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~haerēre~ (“to stick, to cling, to hang on”). French ~adhérer~ is the learned doublet of an older, now-lost ~aherdre~ (from Old French ~aerdre~), which descended by ordinary speech rather than scholarly borrowing. The origin of ~haerēre~ itself is genuinely uncertain: it is traditionally traced to PIE *~gʰays-~ (“to stick, to be fixed”), but Wiktionary flags real difficulties — an unexplained vowel and a wide semantic gap with the proposed cognates such as Lithuanian ~gaišti~ (“to linger”).

The core image is sticking fast — glue, a label, a clinging vine. French ~adhérer~ runs from the physical (a stamp ~adhère~) to the social: to join a party or sign up to an idea (~adhérer à une thèse~). The same Latin ~haerēre~ gives ~adhésion~, ~adhésif~, ~cohérent~, ~inhérent~, and ~hésiter~ (literally “to stick, to be stuck” over a choice).
en.adjoindre:
From Latin ~adjungere~ (“to join to, attach”), which appears in Old French around 1190 as ~ajoindre~. The Latin verb compounds the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) with ~jungere~ (“to join, yoke”). ~jungere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~yewg-~ (“to join, yoke”), a root cognate with English ~yoke~, Sanskrit ~yoga~ (a “yoking” of body and mind), and Greek ~zeugma~ — all built on the image of fastening two things into one.

French reshaped ~ajoindre~ into ~adjoindre~ under the pull of the Latin spelling, and the verb means to attach a person or thing to another, to associate it alongside. That association survives most visibly in the noun ~adjoint~ (“deputy, assistant”), literally one “joined to” a superior. The *~yewg-~ root, by way of ~jungere~, gives French a large family: ~joindre~, ~jonction~, ~conjoint~, ~disjoindre~, and ~joug~ (“yoke”) itself, every one of them a joining or a yoking.
en.admettre:
French ~admettre~ comes from Latin ~admittere~ (“to let in, to grant access, to allow”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”). The form was remodeled on French ~mettre~, which itself descends from ~mittere~. The deeper origin of ~mittere~ is debated; the most accepted reconstruction traces it through Proto-Italic *~meitō~ to a Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, to remove”), with a meaning that drifted from “to exchange” to “to let go, to send.” Italian ~ammettere~ and Spanish ~admitir~ are its Romance kin, and English borrowed the learned ~admit~ from the same Latin verb.

The Latin sense, “to let in,” is still the spine of the French word. Concretely ~admettre~ means “to allow entry” — to admit someone to a club, a school, a hospital. From “to let in” the meaning broadened to intellectual acceptance: to admit a hypothesis as true, to grant a point in argument, and finally to confess (~admettre une erreur~, “to admit a mistake”), the most reluctant kind of letting-in. The root ~mittere~ runs through a huge French family by way of ~mettre~ and its many compounds: ~mettre~ itself, ~admettre~, ~permettre~, ~promettre~, ~commettre~, ~soumettre~, plus the learned ~admission~, ~mission~, ~message~, and ~transmettre~. To admit, etymologically, is simply to let something — or someone, or some truth — come in.
en.administrer:
From Latin ~administrāre~ (“to manage, to serve, to carry out”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~ministrāre~ (“to serve, to attend”), the verb of ~minister~ (“servant, attendant”). ~minister~ is itself transparent: it joins ~minus~ (“less”) with a comparative suffix, from Proto-Italic *~minosteros~ and ultimately PIE *~mei-~ (“small, less”). It was deliberately patterned against its mirror-twin ~magister~ (“master”), built the same way on ~magis~ (“more”): the ~minister~ is the lesser man, the ~magister~ the greater. Cognate with English ~minister~ and ~administer~, Italian ~ministro~, Spanish ~ministro~.

So at its root, to ~administer~ is to do the work of the lesser one — to serve. The word carried a strong ecclesiastical charge: the ~minister~ of God served by delegation on earth, and to ~administrer~ a sacrament was to dispense it on higher authority. From church to court the model spread, and princes borrowed the vocabulary to ~administrer~ their domains — hence the modern senses of governing, managing, and dispensing (one still ~administers~ a remedy or an oath). The same ~minister~ underlies French ~ministre~, ~ministère~, and ~administration~; the buried ~minus~ surfaces again in ~moins~, ~minus~, ~mineur~, and ~diminuer~. The greater-lesser pair endures: every ~ministre~ is, etymologically, somebody's servant.
en.admirer:
~Admirer~, attested from 1360, comes from Latin ~admirari~, compounded of the prefix ~ad-~ (« toward ») and ~mirari~ (« to wonder at, to marvel »). The deponent ~mirari~ rests on the adjective ~mirus~ (« remarkable, astonishing »), which English Wiktionary traces through Proto-Italic *~smeiros~ to PIE *~sméyros~ (« smiling »), from the root *~(s)mey-~ (« to laugh, to be glad »). If that derivation holds, wonder and a smile share an ancestor. Italian ~ammirare~ and Spanish ~admirar~ are Romance kin; English borrowed ~admire~ from the French.

The original force was « to be astonished at », tinged with surprise as much as approval — a shade still felt in the ironic French use, where to ~admirer~ someone's nerve is hardly praise. Over time the warmer sense, regarding something beautiful with pleasure, took the lead. The same ~mirari~ / ~mirus~ family gave French ~miracle~, ~mirage~, ~mirer~, ~se mirer~, and ~miroir~ — and, by the contested *~(s)mey-~ link, the English ~smile~ would be a distant cousin of the mirror you ~admire~ yourself in.
en.adonner: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *~addonāre~, which is formed from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and the Latin verb ~donāre~ (“to give”), the source of ~donner~ and of ~don~ (“gift”). Only English Wiktionary supplies this origin; French Wiktionary gives none. The verb has been used mainly in the reflexive, ~s'adonner à~, “to give oneself over to” a pursuit, a habit or a vice. The sense is thus a literal giving of oneself, which has since drifted toward habit and passion.
en.adopter:
From Latin ~adoptāre~ (“to choose for oneself, to take by selection, to adopt”), compounded from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~optāre~ (“to choose, to wish, to desire”). The origin of ~optāre~ is debated, but it is plausibly traced through Proto-Italic *~opeje-~ to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to choose, to grasp,” perhaps the same that gave Hittite ~ēpzi~ (“seizes, takes”). The Latin verb is the direct source of Italian ~adottare~ and Spanish ~adoptar~, and of English ~adopt~.

The literal force is « choisir vers soi » — to choose someone toward oneself — which is exactly the original legal meaning: to take a child as one's own son or daughter, with full civil rights. Roman adoptio was a solemn juridical act, and the word kept that formal flavor before broadening. From the legal sense French extended ~adopter~ to informal taking-in of a child, then figuratively to embracing an opinion, voting a law (« adopter un texte »), and finally to taking up a style, a method, or a stray animal — all variations on deliberate choosing. From the same ~optāre~ French inherited ~opter~ (“to opt”) and ~option~, and from the related ~coöptāre~ (~com-~ + ~optāre~) the verb ~coopter~ (“to co-opt”).
en.adorer:
From Latin ~adōrāre~ (“to address a prayer to, to worship”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and the verb ~ōrāre~ (“to speak formally, to plead, to pray”). To ~adōrāre~ was thus literally “to speak toward,” to direct ritual words at a god. ~Ōrāre~ is traditionally tied to ~ōs~, ~ōris~ (“mouth”), from a Proto-Indo-European root for the mouth, the speaking aperture. Cognate, through ~ōrāre~, with English ~oration~ and ~orator~.

The original gesture was sacred and verbal: one ~adored~ a deity by uttering a formula toward it, the spoken prayer at the core of the act. Roman worship even kept a bodily echo — bringing the hand to the mouth in reverence. The religious sense survives intact (one ~adore~ God), but French wore the word down to everyday hyperbole, so that one may now ~adorer~ chocolate or a film with no thought of altars. From the same ~ōrāre~ French inherits ~oraison~, ~orateur~, ~oral~, and ~adoration~, while the ~ad-~ of approach recurs across countless verbs of turning-toward.
en.adosser: Formed in French from ~a-~, ~dos~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to set the back against.” The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”) and here marks placing something onto a surface, so ~adosser~ is to put a back to a wall, and ~s'adosser~ is to lean one's back against something. The base ~dos~ comes from Old French, from Latin ~dorsum~ through a popular form ~dossum~; Italian ~dosso~ preserves the same Vulgar Latin shape. A building is likewise said to be ~adossé~ to a hillside or to a neighboring wall.
en.adoucir: Inherited from Old French ~adoucir~ (also ~adolcir~), which was built from ~dolz~ and ~douz~ (“sweet”), from Latin ~dulcis~ (“sweet”). By surface analysis, the verb is the prefix ~a-~ (“toward”), the adjective ~doux~ and the second-conjugation ending ~-ir~, with the sense “to make sweet, to make gentler.” It is used both literally (to sweeten a drink) and figuratively (to soften a manner, a climate or a pain). Compare ~adoucir~ with ~attendrir~ and ~assouplir~, which are built the same way.
en.adresser:
From Old French ~adrecier~ (twelfth century), composed of the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) and ~dresser~ (“to straighten, to set up, to direct”). ~dresser~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~directiare~ (“to make straight”), built on Latin ~directus~ (“straight, direct”), the past participle of ~dirigere~ (~dis-~ + ~regere~, “to guide straight”). ~regere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~reg-~ (“to move in a straight line, to direct”). Through this root ~adresser~ is cognate with English ~address~, ~direct~, and ~dress~, all sharing the Vulgar Latin *~directiare~.

In Old French through the seventeenth century, ~adresser~ meant “to straighten, to set upright, to direct.” The modern senses unfold naturally from that core: to direct a letter toward someone is to ~adresser~ it; to direct words at a person is to ~adresser la parole~ to them. The English noun ~address~ — first the act of directing, later the destination written on an envelope — followed the same path. From the root *~reg-~ French drew a broad family: ~droit~ (“straight, right,” from ~directus~), ~diriger~ (“to direct”), ~dresser~ itself, ~redresser~ (“to set straight again”), and ~adresse~ in both its senses, the postal address and the “skill” of one who does things rightly.
en.advenir:
Modern French ~advenir~ goes back to Latin ~advenīre~ (“to arrive, to come to”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). Its exact route is not entirely settled. French Wiktionary describes it as a reworking of Old French ~avenir~, while English Wiktionary says it is inherited from Middle French ~advenir~ and may be a re-Latinization of that Old French form, with the ~d~ restored from the Latin spelling. English Wiktionary also links it to the archaic ~aveindre~ (“to take something from where it lies”), a doublet which it derives from a Vulgar Latin *~advenĭre~ or explains as influenced by ~atteindre~. Either way, the verb continues the Latin ~advenīre~ rather than being built in French from a prefix and a base.

Two outcomes of the same Latin verb therefore sit side by side in French. The Old French form ~avenir~ survives as a noun meaning “future”, while the learned spelling ~advenir~ remained as a verb meaning “to happen, to occur”. The restored ~d~ is the visible trace of the Latin spelling ~advenīre~. The sources do not agree on whether the verb is a reworking of the Old French form or an inheritance through Middle French, and the paragraph above therefore leaves that question open. What the two Wiktionaries share is the Latin starting point, ~advenīre~, and the fact that the learned spelling with ~d~ is a later feature rather than the original Old French shape. English Wiktionary adds the doublet ~aveindre~, a reminder that the older family of this verb had more than one outcome.
en.affaiblir:
Recorded from the early twelfth century, ~affaiblir~ is built on ~faiblir~ (“to grow weak”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”), giving a causative sense: to render weak. The heart of the word is the adjective ~faible~ (“weak”), Old French ~foible~ / ~feble~, which descends — surprisingly — from Latin ~flēbilis~ (“lamentable, worthy of being wept over”), itself from ~flēre~ (“to weep”). The same ~flēbilis~ gives English the learned ~feeble~, borrowed through Old French.

The semantic journey is striking and well attested: a thing ~flēbilis~ was something to cry about, pitiable; from “pitiable” the sense drifted to “lacking strength, frail,” and the original tears dropped away entirely. So a French speaker who calls a signal, an argument, or an old man ~faible~ is using, at the root, a word that once meant “tear-jerking” — weakness named for the weeping it provokes. To ~affaiblir~ is then to push something toward that pitiable state. The family includes ~faible~, ~faiblir~, ~faiblesse~ (“weakness”), and ~affaiblissement~ (“weakening, decline”) — all carrying, far below the surface, the memory of ~flēre~, “to weep.”
en.affecter:
From Latin ~affectare~ (“to strive after, to aim at, to pursue eagerly”), a frequentative of ~afficere~ (“to act upon, to influence, to affect”), itself from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~af-~) and ~facere~ (“to do, to make”). ~Facere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, to put, to make”). Cognate, through ~facere~, with Italian ~affettare~ and Spanish ~afectar~, and — through the root *~dʰeh₁-~ — with English ~do~ and ~deed~ and with Greek ~títhēmi~ (“I place”).

The Latin frequentative ~affectare~ meant “to keep doing toward,” hence “to strive after” and, with a darkening twist, “to pursue with a show one does not feel.” That second branch gave French ~affecter~ its sense “to feign,” as in affecting a calm one lacks. The other branch, from ~afficere~, gave “to affect, to move” and “to assign, to allocate.” The root *~dʰeh₁-~ is colossal: through ~facere~ it underlies ~faire~, ~défaire~, ~affaire~, ~facile~, ~fait~, and the suffix ~-fier~; through related forms it yields English ~fact~, ~factory~, and ~fashion~. To affecter a feeling is, at bottom, to ~make~ a face that does the feeling for you.
en.afficher:
From Old French ~aficher~, from Vulgar Latin *~affigicare~, a frequentative reshaping of Latin ~affigere~ (“to fasten to, to fix upon”), itself ~ad-~ (“to, onto”) plus ~figere~ (“to fix, to drive in, to plant”). ~figere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, to set up”). Cognate with Italian ~affiggere~ and Spanish ~afijar~, and — through ~figere~ — with English ~affix~ and ~fix~.

The sense is concrete and physical: to ~afficher~ was first to pin or nail something up against a wall, and only by extension to post a notice, then to display or flaunt anything at all — one can now ~afficher~ a price, an opinion, or a smug confidence. The doublet ~ficher~ shares the same source and the same idea of driving in (a stake, a card into a file), giving the noun ~fiche~, a slip or filing card, and the curt ~fichu~. From ~affigere~ directly come the nouns ~affiche~ (a poster) and ~affichage~ (posting or, today, a screen display). The PIE root *~dʰeygʷ-~, “to stick,” also surfaces far afield in the Germanic words for an earthwork — English ~dike~ and ~ditch~ — a heap of fixed, planted earth.
en.affilier: Borrowed from Latin ~affiliāre~ (also written ~adfiliāre~), “to adopt as a son,” formed from ~ad~ (“to”) and ~filius~ (“son”). The verb began as the act of taking a stranger into a family. French kept that image and moved it to institutions: to affiliate someone is to attach them to a society, a party or an organization as though they belonged to its household. The same Latin ~filius~ gave French ~fils~, its feminine ~filia~ gave ~fille~, and English ~affiliate~ is the sibling of the French verb.
en.affiner: Formed in French from ~a-~ + ~fin~ + ~-er~, a verb built in one step by adding a prefix and an ending at once, meaning “to make fine or pure.” The doubled f in the spelling is a trace of Latin ~ad-~, whose d assimilated to the next consonant. The adjective ~fin~ is traced to Latin ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, end”): from the idea of the utmost point it came to mean “perfect, pure, delicate,” a sense attested in Old French around 1100. The verb ~finir~ comes from the same Latin noun.
en.affirmer:
From Latin ~affirmare~ (“to make firm, to assert”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~firmare~ (“to strengthen, to make firm”), itself from ~firmus~ (“strong, steadfast, stable”). ~firmus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fermos~ and ultimately to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, to support”). Through that root it is cognate with Sanskrit ~dhárati~ (“he holds”) and, through ~firmus~ directly, with English ~firm~ and ~farm~ and with Italian ~fermare~ and Spanish ~afirmar~.

The metaphor inside the word is concrete: to ~affirmer~ something is to make it ~firm~, to stand it up so it will not topple. Latin ~affirmare~ already carried this sense in legal and philosophical contexts — to assert as solid truth — and the verb entered French in the thirteenth century with that meaning intact. From the same root *~dʰer-~ and its Latin offshoot ~firmus~ French inherited a large family: ~ferme~ (“firm”), ~fermer~ (“to close,” by way of making fast), ~affermir~ (“to strengthen”), ~firmament~ (the “fixed” vault of heaven), and the noun ~affirmation~. The doublet ~fermer~ and ~affirmer~ is striking — one shut a door, the other shored up a claim, yet both rest on the idea of making something hold fast.
en.affoler: Formed from the old adjective ~fol~ (“mad”), the earlier form of modern ~fou~, with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. No verb *~foler~ stands behind it, so prefix and suffix came on together, and the ~f~ was doubled in spelling, a trace of the Latin ~ad-~ behind ~a-~. ~Affoler~ means to make someone mad, and so to throw them into a panic. Today the past participle ~affolé~ (“panicked”) is much more common than the infinitive.
en.affranchir: Formed in Old French on the model of ~franchir~: the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~) added to ~franc~ (“free”) and the ending ~-ir~. The adjective ~franc~ comes from Late Latin ~Francus~ (“a Frank”), the Germanic people's name having come to mean “free”, and is cognate with English ~frank~. Where ~franchir~ drifted toward “to clear an obstacle”, ~affranchir~ kept the literal sense of “to set free”: a master ~affranchit~ a slave, and a state ~affranchit~ a colony. Its other familiar sense, to pay the postage on a letter, treats the stamp as a release from the charge.
en.affronter:
From Old French ~afronter~ (“to strike on the forehead, to face, to defy”), formed with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, against”) on ~front~, from Latin ~frōns~, accusative ~frontem~ (“forehead, brow, front”). The underlying notion is ~ad frontem~, “to the forehead, face to face.” Cognate, through the same Latin noun, with Italian ~affrontare~, Spanish ~afrontar~, and English ~affront~ and ~front~.

The original sense was startlingly physical: to ~afronter~ someone was to strike them on the brow — to slap the face, the seat of one's dignity. From that blow grew two branches. One led to the noun ~affront~, an insult delivered “to the face,” preserving the sense of injured honor. The other softened the violence into mere confrontation: ~affronter~ now means to face, to brave, to stand up to a danger or an opponent. The forehead, in Latin thought, was where feelings showed and pride resided, which is why an attack ~ad frontem~ struck at honor itself. The same ~frōns~ gave French ~front~ (“forehead, front,” military and meteorological alike), ~frontière~ (“border,” the “front” edge of a land), ~affronter~, ~confronter~ (“to confront,” literally to set brow against brow), and ~effronté~ (“brazen,” one who has rubbed the shame off their forehead).
en.agacer:
The favored account, found in both Wiktionaries, runs from Old French ~aacier~ back to a Vulgar Latin verb *~adacidāre~, formed on Latin ~acidāre~ (“to make sour”), from ~acidus~ (“sour, sharp”). The image is of sourness setting one on edge. Latin ~acidus~ belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂ek-~ (“sharp”), which also yielded Latin ~acer~ and ~acūtus~. The form ~agacer~ arose through a dissimilation of the two ~d~ sounds, and the Old French adjective ~agu~ (“sharp”, modern ~aigu~) is thought to have influenced its meaning. English ~acid~ and ~acute~ are cousins of the same stock.

The origin is not settled, however. The nineteenth-century scholar Diez linked ~agacer~ to Old High German ~hazjan~ (“to chase, to harass”), whence German ~hetzen~, with a Romance ~a-~ that would have turned the initial ~h~ into a ~g~. French Wiktionary mentions this alternative without adopting it. It also separates out a different Old French ~agacier~ (“to cry like a magpie”), which belongs to ~agace~ (“magpie”) and is unrelated. The meaning moved from physical sharpness toward irritation: to ~agacer~ is to annoy, to needle, or, in a lighter register, to tease. The Latin family also gave ~acide~, ~aigre~ and ~aigu~.
en.agencer: From Old French ~agencier~, built on the adjective ~gent~, ~gente~ (“noble, fair, graceful”), which is generally traced to Latin ~genitus~ (“born”), in the sense of well-born. The root idea is making something fair and elegant, and from there the verb settled on its modern sense of arranging parts into a harmonious whole. It has nothing to do with ~agence~ (“agency”), a different word that French borrowed from Italian.
en.aggraver:
French ~aggraver~ continues Latin ~aggravāre~ (“to make heavier”), from ~ad-~ plus ~gravāre~ (“to weigh down”), built on ~gravis~ (“heavy”). The adjective is ancient: it reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~gʷréh₂us~ (“heavy”), whose offspring make a striking set — Sanskrit ~gurú~ (“heavy,” hence “weighty with authority”: the source of the modern word guru), Ancient Greek ~barús~ (“heavy,” hiding in ~baromètre~ and ~baryton~, the “deep-weighted” voice), and Gothic ~kaurus~. English ~aggravate~ is the same Latin verb in learned dress. The French word is old as well: a form ~agravet~ already appears in the eleventh-century Vie de saint Alexis, of a man borne down by illness.

Medieval French actually preferred ~agrever~, an altered form showing Vulgar Latin *~grevis~, whose vowel is usually explained by the pull of its opposite ~levis~ (“light”) — heavy and light leaning on each other; only in the fourteenth century was the verb straightened back toward Latin as ~aggraver~. The older line never died: it survives in ~grever~ (“to burden,” as taxes do), in the noun ~grief~, and in ~grièvement~, the adverb French still requires for serious wounds — ~grièvement blessé~ — while ~gravement~ serves everywhere else: two adverbs, one root, parted by a medieval vowel. Beside them stand ~grave~ and ~gravité~, where physics meets seriousness. The semantic core never moved: to aggravate a penalty, a wound or a quarrel is to add weight to it — a circonstance aggravante is, literally, a circumstance thrown onto the scale.
en.agir:
French ~agir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~agere~ (“to drive, to set in motion, to do, to act”), adopted directly into the language in the fifteenth century rather than inherited through the slow erosion of Vulgar Latin. The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to lead”). Its cognates are spectacularly far-flung: Greek ~ágein~ (“to lead, to drive”), Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“he drives”), and, through the same root, English ~act~ and ~agent~. Because it entered French as a bookish import, ~agir~ kept the clean, unworn shape of its Latin model, unlike the battered everyday verbs that descend by oral tradition.

The Latin sense was concrete and forceful — to drive cattle, to push something forward — and from that physical pushing came the abstract idea of doing and behaving. French ~agir~ carries both the general sense (“to act”) and, reflexively in ~il s'agit de~, the impersonal “it is a question of.” The same root *~h₂eǵ-~ seeds a huge family in French: ~agile~ (“nimble,” literally easily driven), ~agent~, ~action~, ~agiter~, ~ambigu~ (from “driving both ways”), and even ~examen~, originally the tongue of a balance that drives toward the true weight. A single image of setting things in motion thus underlies words for nimbleness, lawsuits, anxiety, and judgment alike.
en.agiter:
~Agiter~ was borrowed in the thirteenth century from Latin ~agitāre~, “to set in vigorous motion, to drive about,” the frequentative of ~agere~, “to drive (a herd), to do”: where ~agere~ drives once, ~agitāre~ drives again and again — harried cattle, tossed seas, hounded men. ~Agere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~, “to drive,” with cognates in Greek ~ágō~ (“I lead”) and Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“drives”). Italian ~agitare~, Spanish ~agitar~ and English ~agitate~ are all takings from the same Latin verb. French has scarcely moved the meaning: ~Agiter avant emploi~, says the medicine bottle — shake before use — and the harried herd is still faintly there.

Latin already used ~agitāre~ for minds and assemblies as well as herds — to turn a matter over, to debate it — and French inherited the full span: attested from the thirteenth century in the sense “to shake about,” the verb served, by the late sixteenth century, to ~agiter une question~ — to toss a question about — troubled minds from 1580 on, then turned political under the Revolution, breeding the ~agitateur~. The family of ~agere~ is among the largest in French — ~agir~, ~acte~, ~action~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~agenda~ (“things to be done”) — but its best secret is ~cogiter~: Latin ~cōgitāre~, “to think,” is ~con-~ + ~agitāre~, to shake together. When Descartes wrote cogito, he was — etymologically — declaring his mind a shaken bottle; every deep thought is, by this old verb’s lights, an inner agitation.
en.agrandir:
Attested around 1280, formed from the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) and the verb ~grandir~ (“to grow”), itself built on ~grand~ (“large, great”), from Latin ~grandis~ (“large, full-grown”). The origin of ~grandis~ is genuinely uncertain: it goes back to Proto-Italic *~grandis~ of unclear source, and the older guesses linking it to a PIE root for “to swell” were rejected by De Vaan on phonetic grounds — so we leave the deeper ancestor open. Italian and Spanish ~grande~ share the same Latin word.

Where ~grandir~ describes growing of itself, the prefix ~a-~ makes ~agrandir~ transitive and causal: to make larger, to enlarge — a house, a photograph, an empire. English borrowed the parallel ~aggrandize~ through French. The native French family is compact and transparent: ~agrandissement~ (“enlargement”), ~agrandisseur~ (the photographic “enlarger”), ~grandeur~ (“greatness, size”), and ~grandir~ itself. The whole group turns on a single idea, bigness, with the prefix supplying only the push from within outward — the move from a thing growing to a hand that makes it grow.
en.agresser:
From Latin ~aggressus~, the past participle of ~aggredī~ (“to approach, to attack”), built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~gradī~ (“to step”). The Latin root ~gradī~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to step”), and is also the source of English ~grade~, ~progress~ and ~ingredient~. A first French verb ~agresser~ existed from the Latin form but fell out of use in the sixteenth century, so the modern verb is in effect a second coinage on the same Latin source.

The modern verb was probably remade on ~agressif~ and ~agression~, on the pattern of pairs like ~collectif~ and ~collecter~, ~exécutif~ and ~exécuter~, or ~régressif~ and ~régresser~. Dictionaries did not welcome it: Trévise in 1771 called it old-fashioned, and Quillet in 1965 dismissed it as a “barbarous neologism.” Despite the purists it settled into everyday French as the natural verb for assault, as in ~se faire agresser~ (“to be attacked”). The notion of “stepping toward” is still visible in ~agression~ and ~agressif~, and the same Latin ~gradī~ gave ~grade~ and ~gradation~ as well.
en.agréer:
Formed from the noun ~gré~ (“liking, will, pleasure”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to”) and the ending ~-er~ — built on the phrase ~à gré~, “to one's liking.” The noun ~gré~ comes from Latin ~grātum~, the neuter of ~grātus~ (“pleasing, welcome, thankful”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷrātos~, from PIE *~gʷerH-~ (“to welcome, to praise”). Through that root it is cognate with Sanskrit ~gṛṇā́ti~ (“he praises”) and the Latin family of ~grātia~ and ~grātus~.

To ~agréer~ is therefore to take to one's liking — to accept favorably, to approve. The older intransitive use, “to please” (as in a thing that ~agrée~ to someone), preserves the original flavor of ~à gré~ most clearly. The same ~gré~ runs through a wide family: ~agréable~ (“pleasant”), ~agrément~ (“consent; charm”), ~gré~ itself in ~bon gré, mal gré~, ~malgré~ (“despite,” literally “ill-will”), and ~maugréer~ (“to grumble”). Latin ~grātus~ further yields ~grâce~, ~gratitude~, ~gratuit~, and agréger is unrelated — but ~ingrat~ (“ungrateful”) shares the root.
en.agrémenter: Formed on ~agrément~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~agrément~ comes from ~agréer~ (“to accept, to approve”) plus the noun-forming suffix ~-ment~, and it was already used in Old French. It means pleasure, charm or approval. To ~agrémenter~ something is therefore to give it ~agrément~, that is, to brighten it with a pleasing touch: a dish with herbs, a story with anecdotes, a room with flowers.
en.aider:
From Old French ~aidier~, from Latin ~adiūtāre~ (“to help, to assist”), a frequentative of ~adiuvāre~ (“to help”), itself the prefix ~ad-~ (“toward”) joined to ~iuvāre~ (“to help, to please, to delight”). The frequentative form, suggesting help given again and again, is the one that won out across the Romance languages: ~adiūtāre~ yielded Italian ~aiutare~, Spanish ~ayudar~, Portuguese ~ajudar~, and French ~aider~, and, through Old French, English ~aid~.

Latin offered two verbs of helping, and French chose the more emphatic. ~Iuvāre~ alone could mean simply “to help” but also “to delight,” a shade preserved in the impersonal ~iuvat~ (“it is pleasing”); the prefixed, intensified ~adiūtāre~ pushed the meaning firmly toward active assistance. From the same Latin family French draws ~aide~ (both the action and the helper), ~aidant~, ~entraide~ (“mutual aid”), and the learned doublet ~adjuvant~ — a substance that “helps along” a medicine or vaccine — together with ~adjudant~, a military rank, both pointing straight back to ~adiuvāre~ and ~iuvāre~.
en.ailler: Formed from the noun ~ail~ (“garlic”) with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to flavour with garlic,” as in ~ailler un gigot~. The noun comes from Old French, inherited from Latin ~allium~ (“garlic”). It is a cooking verb of the same shape as ~poivrer~ or ~saler~: a seasoning noun turned into the act of adding it.
en.aimer:
From Middle French ~aimer~, refashioned by analogy with the stressed conjugated forms ~(j')aime~, ~(tu) aimes~, from Old French ~amer~, from Latin ~amāre~ (“to love”), from Proto-Italic *~amā-~. The deeper root is debated, but it is often linked to PIE *~am-~, a nursery word seen in *~amma~ (“mother”), a child's term of affection. Cognate with Italian ~amare~, Spanish/Portuguese ~amar~, and Catalan ~amar~; from the same Latin stock English borrowed ~amateur~ (“lover” of an art) and ~amorous~.

The split between Old French ~amer~ and modern ~aimer~ is a tidy lesson in sound change: a stressed Latin ~a~ diphthongized while an unstressed ~a~ did not, so the conjugation once alternated between ~aime~ (stressed) and ~amons~ (unstressed). Middle French leveled the paradigm in favor of the ~aim-~ stem, leaving ~aimer~. The root ~amāre~ blossomed into one of French's richest emotional families: ~amour~, ~amant~ (“lover”), ~amoureux~, ~amitié~ (“friendship,” via ~amīcus~, “friend”), ~aimable~ (the source of English ~amiable~), and ~amateur~. Even the verb's range — from mild liking to passionate love — mirrors that of its Latin parent, which covered every shade of affection.
en.ajouter:
French ~ajouter~ comes from Old French ~ajoster~ (“to bring together, to put side by side”), built ultimately on the Latin preposition and adverb ~juxtā~ (“near, beside”). The Old French verb reflects a Vulgar Latin *~adjuxtāre~, formed with the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) on ~juxtā~ — literally “to set next to.” The base ~juxtā~ itself derives from the Proto-Indo-European root *~yewg-~ (“to join, to yoke”), the same root behind Latin ~iungere~ (“to join”) and ~iugum~ (“yoke”), and behind English ~yoke~ and ~join~.

The meaning slid naturally from physical placement to arithmetic and rhetorical addition: to put one thing beside another is, in the end, to add it. Along the way Old French ~ajoster~ also meant “to bring into agreement, to fit together,” a sense that survives in its doublet ~ajuster~ (“to adjust, to fit”), relatinized straight from ~juxtā~ and kept distinct from ~ajouter~ in modern usage — one adds, the other fits. From the same ~juxtā~ French has the learned adjective ~juxtaposé~ and the noun ~juxtaposition~, while the deeper *~yewg-~ root surfaces in ~joindre~, ~jonction~, and ~conjuguer~ — fittingly, the very act of joining a verb to its endings.
en.ajuster:
Derived from French ~juste~ (“just, exact, fitting”) with the prefix ~a-~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~juste~ descends from Latin ~iūstus~ (“lawful, right”), from ~iūs~ (“law, right”), and ultimately from Old Latin ~iovestos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂yew-~, a root tied to sacred law and binding formulas. Through the same Latin ~iūstus~, French is cousin to English ~just~ and ~justice~.

The verb began life meaning “to make exact, to bring to a right measure,” and the modern senses — to adjust, fit, tune, tweak — all keep that idea of bringing something into proper alignment. Speakers sometimes feel ~ajuster~ as if it meant “to bring close together,” associating it with ~joindre~, but the sources derive it cleanly from ~juste~, not from ~iungere~. The same ~iūstus~ family yields French ~justesse~, ~justice~, ~ajustement~, and the English borrowing ~adjust~ — which reached English through this very Old French verb, so the two languages share the word almost intact.
en.alarmer: Formed from the noun ~alarme~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~all'arme~ (“to arms”), a battle cry that soldiers shouted to call the camp to defend itself or to attack, and which fused into a single word. French ~alerte~ comes from a similar Italian phrase, ~all'erta~ (“on the lookout”). The noun first meant the call to arms or a signal of danger, and the verb followed: ~alarmer~ is to sound the alarm, and then to fill someone with sudden fear or anxiety, as in ~s'alarmer~ (“to become worried”). The ending ~-er~ turns the noun into a first-conjugation verb.
en.alerter: Formed from the noun ~alerte~ (“alarm, warning”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to carry out” what the noun names: to sound an alert. The origin of ~alerte~ is debated. One account derives it from Old French ~a l'herte~ (“on guard”). Another treats it as borrowed from Italian ~all'erta~ (“on the lookout”), from ~erta~ (“lookout, height”), a word tied to Latin ~ērigere~ (“to raise up”), so that the phrase first meant standing on a height to watch. Either way, the noun began as a call to stay on guard, and the verb ~alerter~ turned that call into an action.
en.aligner:
From Old French ~alignier~ (12th century), formed from ~à~ (“to”) + ~ligne~ (“line”) — literally to bring things ~to a line~. ~Ligne~ comes from Latin ~linea~ (“linen thread, line”), the feminine of ~lineus~ (“flaxen”), from ~linum~ (“flax”). The link is concrete: a builder's straight line was a stretched flax thread. ~Linum~ is matched across Indo-European by Ancient Greek ~linon~ and shows up, through Latin, in English ~line~, ~linen~, and ~lining~.

The core meaning has stayed put for nine centuries: to set things on the same straight line. From troops dressed in a row the verb spread to figures lined up in a column, words set in order, and — in the reflexive ~s'aligner sur~ — to falling into step with a policy or a standard. French slang gave it a sharper edge too: to ~aligner~ someone can mean to tell them off or to make them pay up. Modern relatives include the nouns ~alignement~ and ~ligne~ itself, the compounds ~réaligner~ and ~désaligner~, and — from the same Latin ~linum~ — ~lin~ (“flax, linen”), ~linge~, and ~lignée~.
en.alimenter:
Attested from the 14th century, ~alimenter~ is a French formation built on the noun ~aliment~ (“food, nourishment”) plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~Aliment~ comes from Latin ~alimentum~ (“nourishment”), a derivative of ~alere~ (“to nourish, to feed, to rear”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂el-~ (“to nourish, to grow”). Through that root it is cousin to a surprising crowd: Latin ~altus~ (“high,” literally “grown tall”), English ~old~ (originally “grown up”) and ~adult~, and even — via a Germanic branch of the same root — English ~ale~.

The metaphor inside ~alimenter~ is feeding, and it has spread well beyond the table.
