One still ~alimente~ a person or an animal, but one also ~alimente~ a fire with wood, a town with water, a bank account with deposits, and — figuratively — a quarrel, a rumor, or a debate, keeping it fed and alive. The Latin ~alere~ left a rich table of French words: ~aliment~, ~alimentaire~, ~alimentation~, the adjective ~adulte~ (“one who has finished growing”), and ~coalition~ (literally “a growing together”). The very word ~élément~, through Latin ~elementum~, has sometimes been traced to the same nourishing root — a fittingly elemental kinship.
en.allaiter:
From Old French ~alaitier~, from Late Latin ~allactāre~ (“to suckle, to feed with one's milk”), a verb made from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~lactāre~ (“to give milk, to suck”), itself built on Latin ~lac~ (“milk”). The ~d~ of ~ad-~ merged with the following ~l~, giving the double ~l~ of ~allactāre~. Modern French speakers can also read the verb as ~a-~ + ~lait~ + ~-er~, a surface analysis that matches the sense: to give the child ~lait~. English Wiktionary notes that analysis, though the Late Latin source comes first.

The Latin noun ~lac~ gave French ~lait~ by regular change, and Greek ~gála~ (“milk”) is a probable relative, a link visible in English ~galaxy~, the “milky” band of the Milky Way. In French the family is large: ~laitier~, ~laitage~, ~laiteux~, ~lactation~ and ~lactose~ all trace to ~lac~. The verb ~allaiter~ stayed narrowly attached to nursing a baby, and it now covers feeding a newborn at the breast and, by extension, animals feeding their young.
en.aller:
~Aller~ is one of the most famous suppletive verbs in French, stitched together from three unrelated Latin sources. The present forms in ~v-~ (~vais~, ~vas~, ~va~, ~vont~) come from Latin ~vādere~ (“to go, to advance”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weh₂dʰ-~ (“to go forward, to wade”), the same root that gives English ~wade~. The future and conditional in ~ir-~ (~irai~, ~irais~) descend from Latin ~īre~ (“to go”), from PIE *~h₁ey-~. The infinitive ~aller~ itself, with its ~all-~ forms, has a debated origin.

For the third stem, scholars hesitate. The traditional guess derives it from Latin ~ambulāre~ (“to walk”), but the sound changes are hard to defend. A phonetically cleaner hypothesis traces it to a Vulgar Latin *~allāre~, drawn from ~allātum~, the orphaned supine of ~afferō~ (“to bring”). French Wiktionary calls the matter genuinely uncertain, so its ancestry is best left open. The result is a single everyday verb whose “I go,” “I will go,” and “to go” each look toward a different Latin word — a living museum of how Romance speakers rebuilt the idea of motion from spare parts, the future tense reaching back to one verb while the present strode off from another.
en.allier:
French ~allier~ descends from Latin ~alligare~ (“to bind to, tie to”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~al-~) and the verb ~ligare~ (“to bind, tie”). ~Ligare~ traces back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). The same ~alligare~ surfaces elsewhere in Romance — Italian ~allegare~, Spanish ~aliar~ — and, by way of Anglo-Norman, gave English its own ~ally~ and even ~alloy~, a true semantic twin of the metallurgical sense.

The binding image splits neatly in two. When people or states are “tied together,” ~allier~ means to ally; the noun ~alliance~ covers political pacts and the wedding ring alike. When metals are “bound together,” ~allier~ means to alloy, giving the noun ~alliage~. French even reborrowed the same Latin verb in learned form as ~alléguer~ (“to allege,” to bind in a citation), so that ~allier~ and ~alléguer~ are doublets from one source. The wider *~leyǵ-~ family is vast: through ~ligare~ come ~lier~ (“to tie”), ~lien~ (“bond, link”), ~ligament~, ~liasse~ (“bundle of papers”), and ~liage~; through the prefixed ~ob-~ form come ~obliger~ and ~obligation~ — every one of them, at root, a knot.
en.allonger:
Formed in French from the adjective ~long~ with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, replacing Old French ~alongier~. ~Long~ comes from Latin ~longus~ (“long”), from Proto-Italic *~dlongos~, from PIE *~dlongʰos~. Through that root it is cognate with Proto-Germanic *~langaz~, the source of English ~long~ and German ~lang~.

The verb means literally “to make long(er)” — to stretch a hem, to extend a deadline. From there French drew two vivid uses: to ~allonger~ the legs is to stretch out and lie down, and ~allonger~ a sauce is to thin it by adding liquid, making it go further. The ~longus~ family fills the language: ~long~, ~longueur~, ~longer~ (“to run alongside”), ~rallonger~, ~allongement~, and ~prolonger~. English shares the inheritance directly through ~long~ and ~length~.
en.allouer: From Latin ~allocāre~, made of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~locāre~ (“to place, to put”), itself from ~locus~ (“place”). To allot something is thus to put it in a place, to assign it to someone. English ~allow~ is generally thought to come from the same Old French verb, which is usually held to have merged two Latin sources, ~allocāre~ and ~allaudāre~ (“to praise”). The doubled l in French is the usual trace of ~ad-~ assimilating to the next consonant. The learned English cousin ~allocate~ comes straight from medieval Latin.
en.allumer:
Inherited from Old French ~alumer~ (around 1100), from Vulgar Latin *~alluminare~, an assimilated form of *~adluminare~, from ~ad-~ (“to”) + a base tied to ~lumen~ (“light”) and ~luminare~ (“to light”). Cognate with Italian ~alluminare~ and the Spanish ~alumbrar~; through ~lumen~ it is kin to English ~illuminate~ and ~luminous~. The exact internal shape of the Latin form — built on the noun ~lumen~ or on a verb ~luminare~ — is reconstructed rather than directly attested, so it carries the usual asterisk of a Vulgar-Latin form.

The sense ran from “to give light to” to “to kindle, to set alight” — to light a lamp, a fire, a candle. Modern French extended it naturally to switching on electric light and devices (« allumer la lumière », « allumer la télé »), and figuratively to kindling a passion or, in slang, to provoke or seduce someone. From the same ~lumen~ French keeps a bright family: ~lumière~ (“light”), ~lumineux~, ~illuminer~, ~allumage~ (“ignition”), and the little ~allumette~ (“match”), the small stick made for the very act of kindling. The opposite ~éteindre~ took over “to put out,” but ~allumer~ kept the whole field of bringing light into being.
en.alléger:
From Old French ~aleger~ (“to lighten, to relieve”), from Late Latin ~alleviāre~ (“to lighten a load”), a compound of ~ad-~ and ~leviāre~, itself built on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”). ~levis~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~leɣʷis~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light in weight”), which also yields Sanskrit ~laghú~, Ancient Greek ~elaphrós~ and, by way of Germanic, English ~light~ and German ~leicht~ — so the French verb and the English adjective rest, at a great remove, on one and the same ancient word for weightlessness. The classical verb ~levāre~ (“to lift, to relieve”), also formed on ~levis~, is the source of French ~lever~, so lightening and lifting are the same gesture at the root. Spanish ~aliviar~ continues the same Late Latin verb, and English took it up in learned dress as ~alleviate~.

The earliest French uses are at once very concrete and very legal: in early twelfth-century Anglo-Norman the verb meant to clear someone of an accusation, while a twelfth-century maritime sense was to lighten a ship by taking off cargo; by 1165 the pronominal form meant to grow less heavy, and by 1177 the verb could ease bodily pain. Modern French keeps the whole range — ~alléger un fardeau~, ~alléger un texte~, ~alléger une peine~ — and the food industry annexed it in ~allégé~, said of yogurt or butter. The same family gave French ~léger~, ~allégement~ and ~soulager~, whose Late Latin source *~subleviāre~ differs only in its prefix. A curiosity: the noun ~allégeance~ has two lives, the old one, “relief”, derived from ~alléger~ and archaic since the end of the eighteenth century, and the modern political one, “loyalty”, which the CNRTL treats as a separate entry borrowed from English and unrelated to lightness. The verb also carries a live spelling hesitation: the future is traditionally written ~allégera~, but the 1990 rectifications recommend ~allègera~, and both forms are current.
en.alléguer:
French ~alléguer~ is a borrowing from Latin ~allēgāre~ (“to dispatch, to send for, to cite”), built on ~ad-~ (“toward,” assimilated to ~al-~) and ~lēgāre~ (“to send as a deputy, to appoint, to bequeath”). The Latin verb ~lēgāre~ is itself a derivative of ~lēx~ (“law”), since sending someone with a commission or leaving a legacy were legal acts. Spanish ~alegar~ and Italian ~allegare~ are close counterparts.

The sense path runs from “send” to “bring forward as a plea”: ~alléguer~ is to cite a fact or an excuse, often as a pretext. Many French words come from the same ~lēgāre~ and ~lēx~ roots: ~léguer~ (“to bequeath”), ~légal~, ~délégué~, ~légat~, ~collègue~ and ~loi~. A near-twin to avoid is ~alléger~ (“to lighten”), which comes from Latin ~alleviare~ and has no relation despite the similar look.
en.alourdir: Built in French from the adjective ~lourd~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, meaning “to make or become heavy.” The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). The origin of ~lourd~ itself is debated: French Wiktionary gives Latin ~lūridus~ (“pale yellow, livid”), while English Wiktionary favors Late Latin ~lurdus~, probably from ~lūridus~ and possibly influenced by a Frankish word for “clumsy.” French Wiktionary notes that ~alourdir~ was rare until the seventeenth century, when ~grever~ was the usual verb for weighing something down.
en.alterner: From Latin ~alternāre~, “to do by turns,” a verb built on ~alternus~ (“one after the other, in turn”), which comes from ~alter~ (“the other of two”). That small word also gave French ~autre~, so ~alterner~ and ~autre~ are distant cousins, one learned and the other inherited. Italian ~alternare~ and English ~alternate~ come from the same Latin verb. The idea at the core is strict: each of two things yields to the other in turn, and not merely a vague variety.
en.altérer:
From Latin ~alterāre~ (“to change, to make different”), a verb formed on ~alter~ (“the other, a second one”). That adjective is traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂el-~ (“beyond, other”), the same root as Latin ~alius~ (“other”) and English ~else~. The Latin verb gave Italian and Spanish ~alterare~ and ~alterar~, and English ~alter~ reached English through French. Inside French, the inherited descendant of ~alter~ is ~autre~, so ~altérer~ and ~autre~ are learned and popular offspring of one word.

In modern French, ~altérer~ most often means to change something for the worse: to impair, to distort, to spoil. One speaks of a document or a truth that is altered, a food that is spoiled, a color that fades. A distinct sense is “to make thirsty,” as in a throat that is ~altéré~. The family includes ~altération~, ~inaltérable~ (“unalterable”), ~altérité~ (“otherness”) and, through the same Latin ~alter~, ~alterner~ and ~alternatif~.
en.amasser: French ~amasser~ is inherited from Old French ~amasser~, and it can be analysed as the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”) plus ~masse~ (“lump, heap”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to gather into a heap.” French Wiktionary names the verb ~masser~ as the base, but that verb, “to massage,” is a much later word of debated origin, so the noun ~masse~ is the more natural base. The noun comes from Latin ~massa~ (“lump, dough”), a word the Romans took from Greek ~mâza~ (“barley cake, kneaded lump”).
en.amender:
From Old French ~amender~, from Latin ~ēmendāre~ (“to free from faults, to correct, to improve”), formed from ~ex~ (“out of”) and ~mendum~ (“a fault, a blemish”). The Old French form replaced the initial ~e-~ with ~a-~. The Latin verb therefore means, literally, to take the faults out of something. English inherited the same word twice over: ~amend~ comes from the Old French verb, and the learned form ~emend~ comes straight from Latin. English ~mend~ is a shortened form of ~amend~, so a humble repair and a constitutional change are variants of one word.

French ~amender~ kept the sense of correcting and improving. It is used for soil, which a farmer amends with lime or compost, for a person who reforms himself, and for a text of law, which a legislator amends by revising it. The noun ~amendement~ names both a legislative revision and a soil conditioner. The word ~amende~ (“fine”) also belongs to this family. Related words are ~amendable~, ~amendement~ and ~amende~, with the learned English cousins ~emendation~ and ~amendment~.
en.amener:
A French formation, ~a-~ (“to, toward,” from Latin ~ad~) + ~mener~ (“to lead, to conduct”), attested from around the tenth century. ~mener~ comes from Late Latin ~minare~ (“to drive animals”), a striking shift from Classical Latin ~minari~ (“to threaten”). The Romance cognate is Italian ~menare~; the underlying ~minari~ also gives French ~menacer~ (“to threaten”).

The semantic story is vivid: a Roman drover urged his beasts along with shouts and threats, so ~minari~ (“to threaten”) slid into ~minare~ (“to drive a herd”), and thence to the neutral “to lead, to conduct.” With the directional prefix ~a-~, ~amener~ means to lead a person or animal toward the speaker — to ~bring~ someone — as against ~emmener~ (with ~en-~), to lead them away. The contrast with ~apporter~ (for objects one carries) preserves the verb's animate, on-foot origin: properly one ~amène~ a guest but ~apporte~ a gift. From the same ~mener~ French built ~emmener~, ~ramener~, ~promener~, ~mener~ a life or a dance, and the menacing ~menacer~.
en.amorcer: ~Amorcer~ is formed from the noun ~amorce~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to bait, to prime, to set something going. The noun descends from Old French ~amorse~ (“bait”), a substantivized participle of ~amordre~, a compound of ~mordre~ (“to bite”), so an ~amorce~ is literally “a thing to bite at.” ~Mordre~ itself comes from Latin ~mordēre~. From the angler's lure, the sense passed to the small charge that sets off a larger one and then to starting anything, such as a conversation, a movement or a pump.
en.amortir:
From Old French ~amortir~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~admortīre~, a verb built with the prefix ~ad-~ (“to”) on the Latin word for death, ~mors~ (genitive ~mortis~). English Wiktionary instead derives it from the adjective ~mortuus~ (“dead”), but both bases lead to the same Proto-Indo-European root, *~mer-~ (“to die”). That root also gave English ~murder~ and, through Latin, ~mortal~. The Vulgar Latin verb is a reconstruction that stands behind the Old French form, not a word found in surviving Latin texts.

The earliest sense was violent: to kill, or to die. It softened to “make as if dead,” then to “extinguish,” and finally to the figurative “lessen the force or ardor of something.” That last sense is the living one, since to ~amortir~ a blow, a fall or a noise is to deaden it, hence ~amortisseur~ (“shock absorber”). Finance borrowed the image too: to ~amortir~ a debt is to wear it down toward nothing, and English ~amortize~ comes from the same French verb. Other French words from the root include ~mort~, ~mortel~ and ~amortissement~.
en.amplifier:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~amplificāre~ (“to enlarge, to widen”), made of ~amplus~ (“large, ample”) and the combining form ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”). The adjective ~amplus~ has no secure origin beyond Latin. The verbal half is better known: ~facere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place”), which also lies behind English ~do~ and German ~tun~. Because French is a learned borrower here, it kept the Latin shape and never reduced it, whereas the native descendant of ~facere~ is ~faire~. Spanish ~amplificar~ and Italian ~amplificare~ are parallel borrowings, and English ~amplify~ reached English through Old French.

The Latin verb was at home in rhetoric: ~amplificāre~ meant to enlarge a subject by development and emphasis, and from there to exaggerate. French kept the plain sense of making larger, then used it for sounds and signals, with the electronic ~amplificateur~ of the twentieth century and the familiar clipped ~ampli~. The ending ~-fier~ is the regular French form of Latin ~-ficāre~ and marks a whole series of learned verbs: ~clarifier~, ~simplifier~, ~magnifier~, ~purifier~, ~justifier~. The other descendants of ~amplus~ are ~ample~, ~ampleur~ and ~amplitude~. So an amplifier is, etymologically, a device that “makes ample”.
en.amputer: ~Amputer~ is borrowed from Latin ~amputāre~ (“to cut around, to prune”), formed from ~ambi-~ (“around”) and ~putāre~ (“to prune, to trim”). That last verb also came to mean “to reckon,” as accounts were trimmed clean, and it stands behind French ~compter~, ~imputer~ and ~disputer~. A verb of gardeners, cutting away a branch, thus became a verb of surgeons, cutting away a limb.
en.amuser:
Formed in the 12th century from the Old French verb ~muser~ (“to dawdle, to idle, to muse”) with the prefix ~a-~. The origin of ~muser~ is debated: one attractive theory links it to ~mus~ (“muzzle, snout”), so that ~muser~ would mean “to stand with one’s muzzle in the air,” gaping idly; others point to Medieval Latin ~musare~ or to a Germanic source meaning “leisure.” English ~muse~ and ~amuse~ are both borrowed from these French verbs.

The key to ~amuser~ is its older sense, which survives in the related amuser of trickery: to ~amuser~ someone first meant “to make them waste time, to distract, to keep them idly occupied” — even to deceive by diversion, as a feint ~amuse~ an enemy. Only later did idle distraction soften into pleasant distraction, giving the modern sense “to entertain, to amuse.” The reflexive ~s'amuser~ (“to have a good time, to enjoy oneself”) follows the same path. Traces of the old idea linger in ~amusette~ (“a trifle, a pastime”) and the wonderfully literal ~amuse-bouche~ or ~amuse-gueule~ (“appetiser,” something to “amuse the mouth” while one waits), as well as in the noun ~amusement~.
en.améliorer:
Modern French ~améliorer~ is a learned reshaping of Old French ~ameillorer~ (« to make better »), a verb built on ~meillor~, the older form of ~meilleur~ (“better”). The base goes back to Latin ~melior~ (“better”), the comparative of ~bonus~ (“good”), from Proto-Italic *~meljōs~ and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~mel-~ (“strong, great”) — so the original sense was less “better” than “stronger.” Latin ~melior~ is cognate, through that root, with ~multus~ (“much”) and with Ancient Greek ~mála~ (“very”). In the Romance languages the comparative survived directly: Italian ~migliore~ and Spanish ~mejor~ are the everyday words for “better.”

The older verb ~ameillorer~, attested by the twelfth century, would by sound-law have given a modern *~améliorer~ with a different spelling; instead scholars in the late Middle Ages refashioned it on the Latin ~melior~, restoring the ~-lior-~ that ordinary phonetic wear had worn away — the modern form is therefore half-inherited, half-relatinized. From the same family French keeps ~meilleur~ itself, the noun ~amélioration~, and the rarer ~mélioratif~ (a word that makes a meaning “better” or more favorable), all turning on the idea of betterment that began as raw strength.
en.aménager:
Derived from ~ménager~ (“to manage, arrange, use sparingly”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”). ~Ménager~ comes from ~ménage~ (“household”), itself the deverbal of Old French ~manoir~ (“to dwell, remain”), from Latin ~manere~ (“to stay, remain”). ~Manere~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to remain, stay”) and is cognate with Ancient Greek ~μένω~ (“I remain”) and, through Latin borrowings, with English ~remain~ and ~mansion~.

The chain is wonderfully domestic: ~manere~ “to stay” gave the place where one stays, the ~ménage~ or household, then ~ménager~ “to run a household, to manage carefully,” and finally ~aménager~ “to arrange a space, to fit out, to lay out.” To ~aménager~ a room is to organize and equip it; in modern usage it extends to landscaping and town planning (~aménagement du territoire~, “regional planning”). The same root ~manere~ scatters across French in ~maison~ (“house,” from ~mansio~, “a staying”), ~demeurer~ (“to dwell”), ~manoir~ (“manor”), ~permanent~, and ~rester~ — a whole vocabulary of staying put, all rooted in the idea of remaining.
en.analyser:
Derived from the noun ~analyse~ (“analysis”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~Analyse~ entered French in the 16th century from Ancient Greek ~ἀνάλυσις~ (“a dissolving, a loosening-up”), a noun built on ~ἀναλύω~ (“to unloose, dissolve, resolve into parts”), from ~ἀνά~ (“up, throughout”) + ~λύω~ (“to loosen, untie, release”). The verb ~λύω~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~lewh₁-~ (“to cut off, separate, set free”), cognate with Latin ~luō~ (“to atone, pay off”) and with English ~loose~.

The image at the heart of the word is undoing a knot: to analyze is to ~loosen~ a tangle back into its separate threads, the reverse of ~synthèse~, which binds them together. Greek philosophers used ~ἀνάλυσις~ for working a problem backward to its first principles; mathematicians and chemists later borrowed it for resolving a whole into its elements. The same ~λύω~ underlies a learned family in French: ~analyse~ and ~analytique~, but also ~catalyse~ (a “loosening-down” that frees a reaction), ~paralysie~ (a “loosening beside,” a slackening of the limbs), ~dialyse~, and ~électrolyse~ — each, etymologically, a kind of releasing or dissolving.
en.ancrer:
~ancrer~ is a denominal of ~ancre~ (“anchor”), as old as French seafaring narrative itself: around 1160–1170, in the Tristan romance of Thomas of England, a ship lies in port ~ancree~. The noun descends from Latin ~ancora~, itself most likely borrowed from Greek ~ἄγκυρα~ (~ánkura~). There the certainty ends: by the traditional account the Greek word is connected to ~ἄγκος~ (~ánkos~, “bend, hollow”) and to a PIE root *~h₂enk-~ (“to bend”) — the anchor as “the crooked one,” a bent hook — but Beekes suspects a pre-Greek loanword, so that seductive image must be taken as a hypothesis, not a fact. The Latin word travelled far beyond Romance: Old English borrowed it as ~ancor~, whence English ~anchor~; German has ~Anker~; Italian ~ancora~ and Spanish ~ancla~ carry it on.

What is striking about ~ancrer~ is how early and how completely it slipped its moorings. By 1397 builders spoke of pillars ~ancrez~ with good Spanish iron — the anchor turned architectural tie, still visible in the iron ~ancres~ on old façades. By 1470 a devotional text could wish a person's will ~ancrée~ in the divine will: the figurative sense — fixed deep, immovable — was in place before Columbus ever sailed. Modern French leans hard on that figure: opinions, habits and traditions are ~ancrées~; ~ancrage~ names both a ship's mooring and a politician's local base; ~désancrer~ undoes them. A verb born on the water thus spends most of its modern life ashore, fastening convictions rather than hulls — while the sailor's literal sense survives alongside, in ~jeter l'ancre~ and ~lever l'ancre~.
en.animer:
From Latin ~animāre~ (“to give breath to, to bring to life”), from ~anima~ (“breath, air, life, soul”), which goes back through Proto-Italic to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂enh₁-~ (“to breathe”). The same root produced Latin ~animus~ (“mind, spirit, courage”) and Greek ~ánemos~ (“wind”). Cognates of the verb survive across the Romance languages: Italian ~animare~, Spanish and Portuguese ~animar~, and Occitan ~animar~.

The etymological core is breath as the sign of life: to ~animer~ something is literally to breathe a soul into it. From there the meaning fanned out — to enliven, to stir up, to lead and energize a group. Modern French keeps all these layers: an ~animateur~ may host a television show or run children's activities at a summer camp, while in film and computing ~animer~ means to make drawings appear to move, giving rise to ~animation~ and the borrowed ~anime~. The contrast between ~animé~ (“lively, animated”) and ~inanimé~ (“lifeless, inanimate”) preserves the original sense exactly. The prefixed ~ranimer~ and ~réanimer~ mean to revive — the latter is the ordinary medical term for resuscitation, an intensive-care ~service de réanimation~ being, etymologically, a place for breathing life back in. The same breath-root underlies ~animal~, ~unanime~, and ~magnanime~.
en.annexer: Formed from the noun ~annexe~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to make into an annex”, to attach. The noun is borrowed from Latin ~annexus~ (“tied to, attached”), the past participle of ~annectere~ (“to bind to”), made of ~ad-~ and ~nectere~ (“to tie”). The same Latin verb ~nectere~ stands behind ~connecter~ and ~connexion~. The political sense of ~annexer~, to attach a territory to another state, grew out of this plain idea of binding one thing to another. English ~annex~ is cognate.
en.annoncer:
From Latin ~adnūntiāre~ (also written ~annūntiāre~), “to report, to make known,” from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~nūntiāre~ (“to announce”), a verb built on the noun ~nūntius~ (“messenger; message”). The deeper origin of ~nūntius~ is debated; one well-supported account ties it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~newH-~ (“to shout, to call out”), seen in Old Irish ~núall~ (“a loud cry”). The Romance siblings include Italian ~annunciare~ and Spanish ~anunciar~.

The heart of the word is the messenger: to ~annoncer~ is to bring word, to proclaim, and reflexively ~s'annoncer~ is for something to give early signs of itself (a storm, a good year). The same ~nūntius~ underlies a striking family in French: ~annonce~ (“announcement, advertisement”), ~dénoncer~ (“to denounce,” literally to report against), ~prononcer~ and ~énoncer~, and the ecclesiastical ~nonce~, the pope's ambassador — a messenger in the most literal sense. English drew ~announce~, ~denounce~, ~pronounce~, and ~nuncio~ from the same Latin spring.
en.annoter: Borrowed from Latin ~adnotāre~ (“to note down, to mark”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~notāre~ (“to mark, to note”), itself from the noun ~nota~ (“mark, sign”). In French the ~d~ of ~ad-~ assimilated to the following ~n~, giving ~an-~. To ~annoter~ is therefore to add marks or notes to a text, and the family includes ~note~, ~noter~ and ~annotation~.
en.annuler:
From Old French ~anuler~ (attested around 1250), borrowed from Late Latin ~adnullare~ (“to bring to nothing, to consider as null”), formed from ~ad-~ and the stem of ~nullus~ (“none, not any”). ~nullus~ is itself a contraction of ~ne~ (“not”) and ~ullus~ (“any”), a diminutive of ~unus~ (“one”), from Proto-Italic *~oinos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~óynos~ (“one”). Through that distant root the verb is kin to English ~one~ and ~unit~, and the borrowing surfaces in English ~annul~.

The Latin word meant to treat something as worthless or to reduce it to nothing; French narrowed it toward the legal and administrative act of rendering an act, contract, or marriage void. The everyday sense “to call off” (a meeting, a trip) is a modern extension of the same idea of voiding. From the same ~nullus~ French keeps the adjective ~nul~ (“null, worthless”), the noun ~nullité~, and the back-formed noun ~annulation~. The bookkeeping that once cancelled a debt and the keystroke that cancels a command both descend from this Latin sense of making a thing count for nothing.
en.anticiper:
From Latin ~anticipāre~ (“to take beforehand, forestall”), a compound of ~ante~ (“before”) and ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from PIE *~kh₂p-~ / *~kap-~ (“to grasp”). The same ~capere~ underlies a swarm of French words — ~capter~, ~captif~, ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~ — and the root is cognate with English ~have~ and ~heave~ and with German ~haben~.

The literal Latin act is seizing in advance: ~anti-cip-āre~, taking a thing before its proper time. That temporal grasp is the whole modern range of the verb — to ~anticiper~ a payment is to make it early, to ~anticiper~ an objection is to meet it before it is raised, to ~anticiper~ the future is to seize it mentally ahead of its arrival. The ~ante~ here is the same “before” that gives ~antérieur~ and ~ancêtre~, while the ~capere~ half quietly powers a vast vocabulary of taking and holding. Around the verb stand ~anticipation~ and ~anticipé~. To anticipate is, very precisely, to lay hold of what has not yet come.
en.anéantir: ~Anéantir~ descends from Old French ~anientir~ (“to reduce to nothing”), a formation with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”), the noun ~néant~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, so the word means “to bring to nothing.” ~Néant~ comes from Old French ~nient~ (attested 1050), whose origin is uncertain; it is probably from a Vulgar Latin phrase such as *~ne gentem~ (“no person, no one”) or, by another suggestion, ~ne entem~ (“not existing”). Italian ~niente~ is a parallel. English Wiktionary compares ~annihiler~, a parallel formation built on Latin ~nihil~ (“nothing”).
en.apaiser:
Old French coined ~apaisier~ — attested in 1160–1174, in Wace — from ~a-~ and ~pais~, the old form of ~paix~ (“peace”): to bring someone to peace. ~pais~ descends from Latin ~pāx~ (accusative ~pācem~), from Proto-Italic *~pāks~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ (“to join, to fasten”), the root also found in Latin ~pangere~ (“to fix, to drive in”) and in ~pactum~ (“agreement”): to Roman eyes peace was not a mood but a thing made fast — a binding accord. English ~appease~ was borrowed straight from the Old French verb, just as English ~peace~ was borrowed from ~pais~ itself.

The best story in this family is the fate of ~apaiser~'s cousin ~payer~: it descends from Latin ~pācāre~ (“to pacify, to appease”), which in medieval use came to mean satisfying — then simply paying — a creditor. To pay, in French, is etymologically to make peace with the person you owe. While ~payer~ drifted into finance, ~apaiser~ — built on the stem ~pais-~ heard in ~paisible~ — kept the gentler work: calming anger, storms, hunger, pain; from its first decades it could quiet things as well as people. From the same fastening root *~peh₂ḱ-~ come ~paix~, ~paisible~, ~pacifique~ and ~pacte~ — and ~payer~, every payment being, at bottom, an appeasement.
en.apercevoir:
Derived from ~percevoir~ (“to perceive, collect”) with the prefix ~a-~, an allomorph of Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”). ~Percevoir~ continues Latin ~percipere~ (“to seize thoroughly, take in, perceive”), a compound of ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and ~capere~ (“to take, seize”). ~Capere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp”). Through the same ~percipere~, English has ~perceive~, and through ~capere~ a vast cognate family.

The metaphor is mental grasping: to perceive is to take something in fully, and ~apercevoir~, with its directional ~a-~, adds the nuance of catching sight of, of perception suddenly directed at an object — “to glimpse, to catch sight of.” The reflexive ~s'apercevoir de~ moved further inward, to “to realize, to become aware,” the moment one mentally seizes a fact. The root ~capere~ seeds an enormous French vocabulary — ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~, ~décevoir~, ~capter~, ~captif~, ~capable~ — all turning on the idea of taking or holding. Historically ~apercevoir~ was often spelled ~appercevoir~ with a doubled consonant, before French standardized the single ~p~.
en.aplatir: A parasynthetic formation: the prefix ~a-~ (spelled ~ap-~ before the ~p~, from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”) and the ending ~-ir~ were added to the adjective ~plat~ (“flat”) in one step, giving the sense “to make flat.” No intermediate verb stands behind the base. The adjective ~plat~ came through Old French from Vulgar Latin *~plattus~, itself borrowed from Greek ~platús~ (“broad, flat”), a word that goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “broad, spread out.”
en.apparaître:
From Middle French ~apparoistre~, from Old French ~aparoistre~ (“to show oneself, become visible”), an inchoative reshaping built on Latin ~appārēre~ (“to appear, be visible”), via the Late Latin form ~appārēscere~ (“to come suddenly into view”). ~appārēre~ is ~ad-~ (“toward”) + ~pārēre~ (“to be visible, to obey”). The simple verb gave French ~paraître~, while the prefixed one gave ~apparaître~. Cognate with Italian ~apparire~, Spanish ~aparecer~, and — through Old French — English ~appear~.

The ~-aître~ spelling preserves the old ~s~ of ~apparoistre~ as a circumflex: the verb was written ~apparoître~ until 1835, then ~apparaître~, and since the 1990 reforms ~apparaitre~ is also allowed. The inchoative suffix ~-ēscere~ marked a beginning, so ~appārēscere~ meant not merely “to be visible” but “to start being visible,” which suits a thing that suddenly swims into sight — the nuance that still separates ~apparaître~ from a flat statement of presence. The root ~pārēre~ left a wide family in French: the present participle ~apparēns~ underlies ~apparent~, the noun ~appāritiō~ underlies ~apparition~, and the same verb survives in the old legal ~comparaître~ (“to appear in court”) and in ~transparaître~ (“to show through”).
en.apparenter:
~Apparenter~ is attested around 1165, in Gautier d'Arras, meaning “to treat as a relative”; it is a French formation — ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”) + ~parent~ + ~-er~ — literally, to draw someone into the circle of kin. ~Parent~ descends from Latin ~parentem~ (“father or mother; ancestor”), tied to ~parere~ (“to bring forth, to give birth”), from Proto-Italic *~parjō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~perh₃-~ (“to produce, to procure”). Italian ~apparentare~ and Spanish ~emparentar~ are exact parallels, and English ~parent~ came over from the French word. Other offspring stay close to the birthing sense: Latin ~partus~ (“birth”) and ~parturire~ (“to be in labour”) stand behind French ~parturition~.

For centuries the verb spoke of marriage: by 1636 ~apparenter~ means “to ally by marriage,” and someone ~bien apparenté~ had rich or powerful relatives. Modern French loosened blood into likeness: the dominant use is pronominal, ~s'apparenter à~, said of things sharing a nature — a novel that ~s'apparente~ to a confession. Twentieth-century politics added one more twist: under the French electoral law of 1951, party lists could formally ally and pool their votes, an arrangement called ~apparentement~ — kinship by ballot box. The most vivid relative lurks in the terrarium: Latin ~vipera~, source of French ~vipère~, is by the standard account a contraction of ~vivipara~, “she who bears her young alive” (~vivus~ + ~parere~) — the viper, that improbable mother, is etymologically a ~parent~ too.
en.appartenir:
From Old French ~apartenir~, from Late Latin ~appertinere~ (also ~appertĭnere~), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~pertinere~ (“to pertain, to reach to, to belong”). ~pertinere~ is itself ~per-~ (“through”) plus ~tenere~ (“to hold”), which descends from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~appartenere~ and Spanish ~pertenecer~, and — through *~ten-~ — with English ~thin~ and ~tenant~.

The semantic path is vivid: ~tenere~ means to hold, ~pertinere~ to hold all the way through to something, hence to reach it, concern it, pertain to it; and ~appartenir~ adds ~ad-~ to direct that reaching toward an owner — what belongs to someone is what reaches and attaches to them. The PIE root *~ten-~, “to stretch,” yielded “hold” through the notion of keeping something taut, and it underlies a large French family: ~tenir~, ~contenir~, ~retenir~, ~maintenir~, ~obtenir~, and the nouns ~tenue~ and ~contenu~. The pronominal ~s'appartenir~, “to belong to oneself,” preserves the older flavor of the verb, used of a person free and answerable to no one — a fine reminder that to belong is, at root, to be held.
en.appauvrir: Built around the adjective ~pauvre~ (“poor”) with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, a pattern that yields “to make poor.” French Wiktionary lists Old French ~apovrir~, while English Wiktionary gives ~empoverir~ with a different prefix, so the verb is old either way. The base ~pauvre~ comes from Latin ~pauper~ (“poor”) through Old French ~povre~, and ~pauper~ is traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~peh₂w-~ (“few, small”). The learned spelling ~pauvre~ appeared in Middle French, and ~povre~ remained the usual form until the sixteenth century. The doubled ~p~ in ~appauvrir~ is a trace of the Latin prefix ~ad-~ taking on the next consonant.
en.appeler:
From Old French ~apeler~ (“to call, name, summon”), from Latin ~appellāre~ (“to address, call upon, name”), a frequentative of ~appellere~ (“to drive toward”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~pellere~ (“to push, drive, beat”), from PIE *~pelh₂-~ (“to drive, push”). Cognate with Italian ~appellare~ and Spanish ~apelar~; through ~pellere~ and its participle ~pulsus~, English has ~appeal~, ~appellation~, ~compel~, ~pulse~, and ~propel~.

The surprise is the maritime metaphor underneath: ~appellere~ literally meant to drive a ship toward land, and from “to drive toward” the figurative ~appellāre~ came to mean to drive your voice toward someone — to address, summon, or name them. French ~appeler~ keeps that whole spread: to call out, to telephone, to name (~comment t'appelles-tu ?~, “what is your name?”), and the legal ~faire appel~ (“to appeal”), where one literally calls upon a higher court. The driving root ~pellere~ scattered widely in French through compounds — ~repousser~, ~pousser~ (via ~pulsāre~), ~propulser~, ~compulsion~, ~impulsion~ — and the verb's own offspring include the noun ~appel~, the reflexive ~s'appeler~ (“to be named”), ~rappeler~ (“to recall, remind”), and ~interpeller~ (“to hail, challenge”).
en.applaudir: Borrowed in the fourteenth century as Middle French ~applaudir~, from Latin ~applaudere~, itself built from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~plaudere~ (“to beat, to strike”). To applaud is thus, literally, to strike one's hands together in someone's direction. The Latin verb ~plaudere~ also gave ~plausible~, which first meant “worthy of applause” before weakening to “believable”, and, through ~explodere~ (“to drive off the stage by clapping”), the ancestor of ~explosion~ and English ~explode~. Italian ~applaudire~ and Spanish ~aplaudir~ are close cousins, and English ~applaud~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.appliquer:
From Latin ~applicāre~ (“to attach to, join, bring into contact”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~Plicāre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~plek-~ (“to plait, fold”), the same root that yielded Greek ~plékein~ (“to braid”) and, through Germanic, English ~fold~ and ~flax~. Romance relatives include Italian ~applicare~ and Spanish ~aplicar~; the doublet ~appliquer~ borrowed straight from Latin sits beside the inherited ~plier~ (“to fold”).

The original image is wonderfully concrete: to fold or lay one thing flat against another, to press them into contact. From “lay against” grew “devote to” — to ~appliquer~ oneself is to fold one’s whole attention onto a task — and the abstract sense of putting a rule, a method, or a remedy into practice (to ~appliquer~ a law). The root *~plek-~ folds its way through a vast French family: ~plier~, ~ployer~, ~pli~, ~simple~, ~double~, ~complexe~, ~compliquer~, ~impliquer~, and ~explication~ — literally an “unfolding.” Even ~plaie~ (“wound”) and the embroidery term ~appliqué~, borrowed back into English for a folded-on ornament, trace to the same humble act of folding.
en.apporter:
From Latin ~apportāre~ (“to carry something to someone”), composed of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”). ~Portāre~ derives from PIE *~per-~ (“to lead across, to pass over”), the same root behind Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor”). Through this root ~apporter~ is cognate with English ~ferry~, ~ford~, and ~fare~, and with Greek ~póros~ (“passage, way”).

Where ~porter~ simply means to carry, the prefix ~ad-~ adds direction: to ~apporter~ is to carry toward a destination or a person, as opposed to ~emporter~ (carry away) or ~rapporter~ (carry back). The root idea of passing across a threshold radiates through French in a large family: ~porter~, ~portail~, ~port~, ~porche~, ~importer~, ~exporter~, ~transporter~, ~rapport~, ~apport~, and ~déporter~. Even the seemingly distant ~opportun~ belongs here — it once described a wind driving a ship toward (~ob~) the ~portus~, the harbor. So ~apporter~, ~importer~, and ~opportun~ all hark back to the act of carrying something across a passage to where it is wanted.
en.apposer: Formed from ~poser~ with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”), but its senses are modelled on Latin ~appōnere~ (“to put to, to place upon”). The base ~poser~ is a verb of mixed ancestry: it comes from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to halt”) but absorbed the meaning “to place” from Latin ~ponere~. So ~apposer~ means “to affix, to put on,” as in ~apposer sa signature~ or ~apposer des scellés~, a formal, administrative sense. The related noun ~apposition~ keeps the old Latin stem.
en.apprendre:
From Latin ~apprehendere~ (“to seize, to grasp, to take hold of”), ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~prehendere~ (“to grasp”). ~Prehendere~ itself is ~prae-~ (“before”) + an old root ~-hendere~ with no surviving simplex, from PIE *~gʰed-~ (“to seize, to grasp”), the very root that gives English ~get~. Old French reduced ~apprehendere~ to ~aprendre~. The fuller Latin form was later re-borrowed directly as a learned doublet, ~appréhender~ (“to apprehend, to dread”), so French keeps both the worn-down popular verb and its scholarly twin. Italian ~apprendere~ and Spanish ~aprender~ are cognates.

The semantic leap is a beautiful one: to learn is to seize knowledge with the mind, just as the hand grasps an object — the same metaphor English makes when it says one “grasps” an idea. From “to take hold of” French ~apprendre~ developed two faces that still coexist: one learns (acquires knowledge oneself) and one teaches (~apprendre quelque chose à quelqu'un~, “to impart knowledge to someone”), the same verb facing in opposite directions. It also means “to find out,” as in ~apprendre une nouvelle~ (“to learn of a piece of news”). From the ~prehendere~ root descend French ~prendre~, ~apprendre~, ~comprendre~ (“to grasp together, to understand”), ~surprendre~ (“to seize from above, to surprise”), ~apprenti~, and ~appréhender~.
en.apprivoiser:
Old French ~aprivoisier~ is traced to a Vulgar Latin form *~apprīvātiāre~, built on Latin ~prīvātus~ (“private, belonging to oneself, not public”), the participle of ~prīvāre~ (“to set apart, to deprive, to free”). The prefix is ~ad-~. Latin ~prīvātus~ is also the source of French ~privé~ and ~privauté~ (“familiarity, a liberty taken”), and of English ~private~, ~privy~ and ~deprive~.

The path of meaning is easy to follow. A creature that is ~privé~ lives within the household, so to ~apprivoiser~ it is, presumably, to make it live there, that is, to tame it. The verb later extended to people and fears: to win over a shy person, a skeptic, or an unfamiliar technology. In Saint-Exupéry's Le Petit Prince the fox gives the verb perhaps its best-known modern meaning, “to create ties.” The adjective ~apprivoisé~ is the opposite of ~sauvage~.
en.approcher:
From Old French ~aprochier~ (“to bring near, to draw near”), from Late Latin ~appropiāre~ (“to come near”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and the adverb ~prope~ (“near”). Latin ~prope~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~prokʷe~, built on *~pro-~ (“forward, in front”). Cognate with Italian ~approcciare~ and, through English borrowing from Old French, with ~approach~ itself.

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: from the start ~aprochier~ meant to reduce the distance between two things, and modern ~approcher~ still does. The Latin adverb ~prope~ is unusually productive in French. Its comparative ~propior~ and superlative ~proximus~ gave ~proche~ (“near”) and the learned family ~proximité~, ~approximatif~, and ~rapprocher~ (“to bring closer together,” with an extra ~re-~). A nice detail is that ~approcher~ and the look-alike ~approprier~ are false relatives: the first rests on ~prope~ (“near”), the second on ~proprius~ (“one's own”), two distinct Latin words that French merely happened to dress in similar clothing. So when you ~approcher~ something, you are etymologically bringing it ~prope~ — near — and nothing more.
en.approfondir:
Formed from the adjective ~profond~ (“deep”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from ~ad-~, triggering the doubled ~p~) and the second-group verbal suffix ~-ir~ marking change of state — so “to make deep, to deepen.” ~Profond~ comes from Latin ~profundus~ (“deep, bottomless”), a compound of ~prō-~ (“forward, before”) and ~fundus~ (“bottom, base”). ~Fundus~ rests on PIE *~bʰudʰmḗn~ (“bottom”), the same root that yields English ~bottom~, German ~Boden~, and Greek ~puthmḗn~ (“bottom of a cup”). To go ~pro-fundus~ is to head toward the bottom.

The French verb runs the metaphor that English shares: from making a hole or channel literally deeper to deepening one's knowledge — ~approfondir~ une question, to probe a matter to its bottom. The abstract sense now dominates entirely. From ~fundus~ French also draws ~fond~ (“bottom, background”), ~fonder~ and ~fondation~ (“to found, foundation” — to set on a base), ~foncer~, and ~tréfonds~ (the deepest depths). The image holds throughout: every act of founding or deepening is a reaching down to the ground, the bottom on which a thing can rest.
en.approprier:
From Latin ~appropriāre~ (“to make one's own”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~proprius~ (“one's own, particular”). Latin ~proprius~ is generally traced to the phrase ~pro privō~, “for the individual,” involving ~prīvus~ (“single, one's own”). Cognate, through ~proprius~, with Italian ~appropriare~, Spanish ~apropiar~, and English ~appropriate~.

To ~approprier~ is to make a thing ~proprius~ — fitting, particular, one's own. Two threads run through its history. The reflexive ~s'approprier~ means to seize something as one's own, to take possession; this is the sense closest to English “appropriate.” But the transitive ~approprier~ kept the older idea of making a thing suitable to a situation — adapting, tailoring, fitting it. The shared ancestor ~proprius~ is one of Latin's most fertile roots in French: it gave ~propre~ (which means both “clean” and “one's own”), ~propriété~ (“property, ownership”), ~propriétaire~ (“owner”), ~approprié~ (“appropriate, suitable”), and ~exproprier~ (“to expropriate”). Note that ~approprier~ and ~approcher~ only look like twins: the former rests on ~proprius~ (“one's own”), the latter on ~prope~ (“near”), two unrelated Latin words.
en.approuver:
From Latin ~approbare~ (“to approve, to assent to”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~probare~ (“to test, to prove, to deem good”), itself from ~probus~ (“good, upright, honest”). ~Probus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~proβwos~ and PIE *~pro-bʰuH-wó-s~ (“being in front, foremost”), from *~pro-~ (“forward”) and *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, to grow”) — the very root of English ~be~ and Latin ~fui~ (“I was”). Sanskrit ~prabhú-~ (“foremost, excellent”) is a cognate. Through ~probare~, English ~prove~, ~probe~, and ~approve~ share this ancestry.

The Latin sense was to find a thing good by testing it, and that testing is buried inside the modern word: to ~approuver~ is to judge worthy after weighing. Old French had ~aprover~, refashioned toward Latin to give ~approuver~. The same ~probus / probare~ family yields French ~prouver~, ~preuve~, ~épreuve~, ~éprouver~, ~probable~, and ~probité~. The thread tying “honest,” “to prove,” and “to approve” is the idea of the upright thing that stands the test — the good being, etymologically, what is foremost and forward-standing.
en.apprécier:
From Late Latin ~appretiare~ (“to set a price to, value”), from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to”) and Latin ~pretium~ (“price, value, worth”). The noun ~pretium~ goes back to a suffixed form of the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to traffic in, sell, exchange”). Cognate with Italian ~apprezzare~ and Spanish ~apreciar~, and — through ~pretium~ — with English ~appreciate~, ~price~, and ~precious~.

The original act was commercial: to ~apprécier~ was to “put a price on” something, to appraise its monetary worth — a sense the verb still keeps in valuation and finance. From assessing value in coin grew the warmer modern sense of esteeming, enjoying, and being grateful for something. A pleasing tangle hangs off this root: from the same ~pretium~ Old French spun ~praise~, ~price~, and ~prize~, three English words that began as one before splitting apart. In French the family includes ~prix~, ~précieux~, ~priser~, ~déprécier~, and ~mépriser~ — this last a “mis-pricing,” to value too low, the very opposite of ~apprécier~.
en.appréhender:
French ~appréhender~ was borrowed from Latin ~apprehendere~ (“to seize, grasp, take hold of”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~prehendere~ (“to grasp”). ~prehendere~ itself breaks down into ~prae-~ (“before”) and *~hendere~ (“to take hold”), from Proto-Italic *~praiɣendō~ and ultimately Proto-Indo-European *~gʰed-~ (“to seize, grasp”). That root is cognate with English ~get~ and ~forget~, and with Ancient Greek ~χανδάνω~ (“to hold, contain”); ~prehendere~ is even a doublet of Latin ~praeda~ (“prey”).

The verb's two modern senses both flow from “seizing.” Physically and legally, to ~appréhender~ a suspect is to lay hands on and arrest him — a hand closing on its object. Mentally, to ~appréhender~ a danger is first to “grasp” it intellectually, and then, by a chilling narrowing, to grasp it as something to dread: the mind seizes the threat in advance. From the same ~prehendere~ French inherited, by the popular route, the everyday ~prendre~ (“to take”) and ~apprendre~ (“to learn,” literally to take hold of knowledge), while the learned line gave ~appréhension~ (both “grasp” and “dread”), ~compréhension~, and ~répréhensible~.
en.apprêter:
French ~apprêter~ is a native formation rather than a direct borrowing: it is ~prêter~ prefixed with ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”), literally “to make ~prêt~ (ready).” The base ~prêter~ comes from Old French ~prester~, from Latin ~praestare~ (“to furnish, provide, place at one's disposal”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) + ~stare~ (“to stand”), on the PIE root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). So an old, very literal image lies beneath: to ~praestare~ was to “stand something before” someone — to set it ready to hand. The form is attested remarkably early; an Old French ~aprestunt~ (“they made ready”) appears around 980.

Meaning followed the “make ready” thread into many trades. To ~apprêter~ a meal is to prepare and dress it; in textiles and leatherwork it means to finish or “prime” a material; in painting, ~l'apprêt~ is the priming coat laid on a canvas before color. Reflexively, ~s'apprêter à~ means “to be about to, to get ready to.” From the same ~praestare~ stock French keeps ~prêt~ (both “ready” and “a loan”), ~prêter~ (“to lend”) — whose sense narrowed from “furnish” to “furnish temporarily” — and ~prestation~ (“a service rendered, a benefit”). Curiously, the everyday ~prêt~ meaning “ready” and ~prêt~ meaning “loan” are the very same word, split by the two destinies of “providing.”
en.appuyer:
From Old French ~apuier~ (also ~apoier~), from Vulgar Latin ~appodiare~ (“to support, prop up”), from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, against”) and Latin ~podium~ (“raised platform, support”). That ~podium~ was borrowed from Greek ~podion~ (“little foot, base of a vase”), a diminutive of ~pous~ (genitive ~podos~, “foot”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ped-~ (“foot”). Cognate with Italian ~appoggiare~, Spanish ~apoyar~, and Portuguese ~apoiar~, and — through *~ped-~ — with English ~foot~ and Latin ~pes~.

The charming detail is the foot hidden at the bottom: a ~podium~ was named by Greek architects who thought a low base beneath a wall or colonnade looked like a little foot to stand on. To ~appuyer~ is thus to set something against such a support, to “prop it on a footing.” From the physical act of pressing or leaning grew the figurative senses of backing a candidate or supporting an argument. The Italian sibling ~appoggiare~ gave music the ~appogiature~, a leaning grace-note. Through ~podium~ and Greek ~pous~ French also holds ~appui~, ~podium~ itself, ~podologue~, and the ~-pode~ of ~antipode~.
en.arbitrer: The sources differ slightly. French Wiktionary treats ~arbitrer~ as formed from the noun ~arbitre~ with the ending ~-er~, while English Wiktionary traces it straight to the Latin deponent verb ~arbitrārī~ (“to judge, to give a verdict”). The noun ~arbitre~ itself comes from Latin ~arbiter~, which meant first a witness or onlooker and then a judge, one whose decision settles a matter. The related Latin ~arbitrium~ (“decision, judgment”) gave ~arbitraire~. The verb is used for settling a dispute, and, in sport, for refereeing a match.
en.arborer:
From Italian ~arborare~ (“to set upright, to raise like a tree, to hoist a mast or flag”), from Latin ~arbor~ (“tree”). The word came into French through the world of ships and standards, where ~arborer~ first meant to raise something tall and straight — a mast, a banner — bolt upright like a tree trunk. Cognate through ~arbor~ with French ~arbre~, Italian ~albero~ (which means both “tree” and “ship's mast”), and Spanish ~árbol~.

From “to hoist a flag” the sense climbed naturally to “to fly one's colors,” then to a brilliant figurative use: to ~arborer~ is to display something with conspicuous pride — to ~sport~ a fine suit, ~arborer~ a wide grin, ~arborer~ a medal or a defiant air. The image of the upright tree never quite leaves: what you ~arborer~ you carry held high for all to see, like a flag run up a mast. The maritime sense persists alongside the figurative one, so a ship still ~arbore~ its national pavilion. From the same ~arbor~ branch French ~arbre~, ~arbuste~, ~arboriculture~, ~arborescent~, and the botanical ~arboretum~ — a whole grove sprung from a single Latin tree.
en.archiver: Formed in French from ~archives~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to put into the archives.” The noun comes from Latin ~archivum~, a variant of ~archium~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ἀρχεῖον~ (~arkheîon~), “magistrate's office, town hall.” In the plural, the Greek and Latin word came to mean the records kept by such an office. The resemblance to French ~arche~ (“chest”), from Latin ~arca~, is only a coincidence. The sense of storing computer files is a modern extension of the original filing of official papers.
en.argenter: Formed from ~argent~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to provide with silver”: to coat a surface with a thin layer of silver or give it a silvery sheen. The noun ~argent~ comes from Latin ~argentum~ (“silver”), a word related to Greek ~argós~ (“white, shining”), so the metal was named for its brightness. French ~argent~ also came to mean money in general, but ~argenter~ keeps the strictly physical sense of silver-plating.
en.argumenter: The sources differ. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~argumentor~ (“to adduce as proof, to argue”), a verb built on ~argumentum~ (“argument”), while English Wiktionary treats it as French ~argument~ plus the ending ~-er~. Either way the root is Latin ~argumentum~, from ~arguere~ (“to make clear, to prove”), and the verb means to put forward reasons for or against something. French ~argument~ comes from the same Latin noun, and English ~argue~ and ~argument~ are cousins.
en.armer:
From Latin ~armāre~ (“to arm, to equip with weapons”), attested in French from the 10th century, derived from ~arma~ (“weapons, tools”). The Latin noun comes from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂er-~ (“to fit, to join”), through a form *~h₂(e)rmos~ (“fitting, that which is fitted together”) — so a weapon was first simply “gear, fitted equipment.” The same root underlies Latin ~ars~ (“art, skill”) and ~artus~ (“joint”), Ancient Greek ~ἀραρίσκω~ (~ararískō~, “to fit together”), and English ~arm~, ~art~, and ~harmony~.

The verb’s history is steeped in the medieval world of war and chivalry. Beyond “to arm,” ~armer~ acquired the feudal sense “to dub a knight” — to ceremonially fit a man out with his weapons and so make him a ~chevalier~. It later spread to any kind of equipping: one ~arme~ a ship (fitting it out for sea), ~arme~ a camera or a trap (setting its mechanism), and ~arme~ concrete with steel rods (~béton armé~, “reinforced concrete”). From the same Latin source come ~arme~ and ~armée~ (“army”), ~armure~ (“armour”), ~armurier~, ~armistice~, and, by a curious route through ~armarium~ (“a cupboard for tools”), the French ~armoire~ (“wardrobe, cabinet”).
en.arpenter: Formed from the noun ~arpent~ and the verb ending ~-er~. An ~arpent~ was an old French land measure, and ~arpenter~ first meant to measure land with it, to survey. The noun comes from Late Latin ~arepennis~ (“surface of a field”), itself from Gaulish *~are-penno-~ (“end, extremity of a field”). The meaning “to stride up and down” is a figurative extension: one walks a space as a surveyor would, covering every length of it with long steps.
en.arracher:
From Old French ~arrachier~, an alteration of ~esrachier~, from Latin ~exradicare~ (« to uproot »), a variant of ~eradicare~, both built on ~radix, radicis~ (« root »). The prefix shift reflects an Old French habit of swapping ~a-~ and ~es-~. ~radix~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wrādīks~ and Proto-Indo-European *~wréh₂ds~ (« root »), cognate with English ~root~, ~wort~, and ~radish~.

So ~arracher~ is etymologically « to pull out by the roots », and the modern verb keeps all the violence of that image: one « tears out » a tooth, « rips up » a plant, « wrenches » a confession from someone, or « snatches » a victory at the last moment. The buried root ~radix~ is everywhere in French once you look — ~racine~ (« root » itself), ~déraciner~ (« to uproot »), ~radical~, ~radis~ (« radish »), and ~éradiquer~ (« to eradicate ») — every one of them turning on the idea of the root that ~arracher~ so forcefully pulls free.
en.arranger:
Attested around 1160 as Old French ~arengier~, formed from ~a-~ and ~rengier~ (modern ~ranger~, “to set in rows”), itself from the noun ~renc~ or ~ranc~ (“row, line, rank” — modern ~rang~), borrowed from Frankish *~hring~ (“ring, circle”), from Proto-Germanic *~hringaz~ (“ring”), generally traced to PIE *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, to bend”). The Germanic word is the very one that survives as English ~ring~ and German ~Ring~. English ~arrange~, ~rank~ and ~range~ were all drawn from this Old French family — and ~derange~ from its negative, ~déranger~.

Inside every tidy arrangement hides a circle of Frankish warriors. Frankish *~hring~ meant “ring,” and in Old French the circle straightened into a line: ~renc~ was a row — above all a row of fighters — and ~arengier~ meant to marshal them; the verb's earliest reflexive use was precisely “to take one's place in battle formation.” Peace then did its slow work. From “put in order,” the verb softened toward accommodation: in the eighteenth century ~s'arranger~ came to mean “to make one's arrangements” (1740), then “to suit” (1747) — whence today's ~ça m'arrange~ — and ~arranger~ even took on “to mend, to patch up” (1768). Modern French lets it stretch from the musician's ~arrangement~ of a song to the soothing ~tout s'arrange~ (“everything works out in the end”) — a long road for a word that began by drawing warriors up in a ring. Its closest French kin are ~rang~, ~rangée~, ~ranger~ and ~déranger~ — etymologically, to disturb is to break ranks.
en.arriver:
From Old French ~ariver~ (“to come to shore, land”), from Vulgar Latin *~arripāre~ (“to touch the shore, come to land”), from the phrase ~ad rīpam~ (“to the shore”), built on ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~rīpa~ (“riverbank, shore”). Cognate with Italian ~arrivare~ and Catalan/Occitan ~arribar~; through the root noun ~rīpa~ it is kin to English ~river~ (via Old French ~rivière~) and to the geological term ~riparian~.

The original notion was wholly nautical: after a long voyage, a ship ~arriva~ when it finally touched the bank. From this image of coming ashore the verb generalized to reaching any destination by any means, then bleached further into the impersonal sense “to happen” — what ~arrive~ is what comes to pass, as in ~il arrive que~ (“it happens that”). The same ~rīpa~ gave French ~rive~ (“bank”), ~rivière~ (“river”), ~riverain~ (“riverside resident”), and the borrowed ~arriviste~ — one who has “arrived” socially by any means, a striver. So a word that once meant simply reaching the riverbank now spans both triumphant arrival and the sheer contingency of events.
en.arrondir: Formed from the prefix ~a-~ and ~rondir~, a verb itself built from ~rond~ (“round”) and the ending ~-ir~. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), and in verbs like this it carries the idea of passing into a state: ~arrondir~ is “to make round.” ~Rond~ goes back to Latin ~rotundus~, a word built on ~rota~ (“wheel”). English Wiktionary analyzes the verb in one step as ~a-~ + ~rond~ + ~-ir~, which amounts to the same thing. The sense later extended from shapes to numbers, so that one ~arrondit~ a sum to the nearest unit.
en.arroser:
From Middle French ~arrouser~, inherited from a Vulgar Latin verb *~arrōsāre~, built on the prefix ~ad-~ (“to”) and Latin ~rōs~ (“dew”). The verb literally meant to bring dew to something. Latin ~rōs~ also lies behind French ~rosée~ (“dew”) and Spanish ~rocío~ (“dew”). A famous disguise of the same word is ~romarin~ (“rosemary”), from Latin ~ros marinus~, “sea dew”; it has nothing to do with roses.

The sense moved from the gentle fall of dew to deliberately watering plants, then to wetting anything with a spray, as in the garden tool ~arrosoir~ (“watering can”) and the noun ~arrosage~. Figurative uses then multiplied. To ~arroser~ a meal or a success is to wash it down with wine, and the same verb can describe sweeping an area with gunfire, or, colloquially, bribing someone with a shower of money.
en.arrêter:
From Middle French ~arrester~, from Old French ~arrester~, ~arester~ (“to stop, to halt, to fix”), from Vulgar Latin *~arrestare~, that is ~ad-~ (“to”) + ~restare~ (“to remain, to stay behind”). ~Restare~ is ~re-~ + ~stare~ (“to stand”), from PIE *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). The literal force was thus “to make remain, to bring to a standstill.” Cognate with Italian ~arrestare~ and Spanish ~arrestar~; through Old French it gave English ~arrest~.

A persistent folk etymology tried to link the word to Germanic ~Rast~ or ~Rest~ (“rest, repose”), but the true ancestor is the Latin “standing” family, not the Germanic “resting” one. From the idea of bringing motion to a halt grew the noun ~arrêt~ — both a “stop” (un arrêt de bus) and, in law, a fixed and binding “decree” or court judgment, something settled and immovable. The verb also means to decide firmly (« arrêter une date ») and to detain a suspect. The same PIE root *~steh₂-~ underlies ~rester~, ~stable~, ~station~, ~constant~, and ~stature~ — a whole vocabulary of standing and staying put.
en.articuler:
From Latin ~articulare~ (“to give joints to, to divide, to pronounce distinctly”), from ~articulus~ (“a little joint, a knuckle”), the diminutive of ~artus~ (“joint, limb”). ~Artus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂er-~ (“to fit, to join together”), the root of an idea of fitting parts into order — cognate with Latin ~ars~ (“art, skill”) and ~arma~ (“arms, gear”), Ancient Greek ~ἄρθρον~ (“joint”), and Sanskrit ~ṛtú~ (“fixed order, season”). To articulate is, etymologically, to set in joints.

The word carries two living senses from that one image. Physically, bones ~articulate~ where they are jointed; mechanically, two parts that pivot are ~articulated~ (an ~articulated~ lorry bends at its joint). Figuratively, to ~articulate~ speech is to break the stream of sound into distinct, well-jointed syllables — and so, to express clearly. From ~articulus~ also come ~article~ (a small jointed part, then a clause, then a piece of writing) and ~articulation~; and from the same root *~h₂er-~ French keeps ~art~, ~arme~, and ~ordre~.
en.aspirer:
~aspirer~ reached Old French by about 1165, from Latin ~aspīrāre~ — ~ad-~ (“toward”) plus ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe, to blow”) — literally “to breathe toward.” In Latin the verb could mean to blow favorably upon — of winds and gods — and hence to strive toward something: aspiration as a wind at your back. The deeper origin of ~spīrāre~ is uncertain; etymologists suspect an imitative formation — the word as a puff of air — and the sometimes-proposed root *~(s)peys-~ (“to blow”) is not asserted with confidence. The Romance siblings are Italian ~aspirare~ and Spanish ~aspirar~; English ~aspire~ arrived through French. From the Latin verb's noun ~spīritus~ (“breath”) French inherited ~esprit~ — mind and wit, in French, are etymologically breath.

French kept the verb's whole respiratory range. It meant “to breathe” by the thirteenth century, “to draw in by breathing” by 1393 — whence, in the age of machines, the ~aspirateur~, a vacuum cleaner that literally inhales the house — and “to long for” (~aspirer à~) from the fourteenth century. In 1529 grammarians added the phonetic sense, and left modern French a small joke: the ~h aspiré~, the “aspirated h” that blocks liaison in “les héros,” has not been aspirated for centuries — no breath survives in it; the name is the fossil of a vanished pronunciation. The family of ~spīrāre~ breathes through the whole language: ~respirer~, ~inspirer~, ~expirer~, ~transpirer~, ~conspirer~ (“to breathe together,” as plotters huddled close), and ~soupirer~, from Latin ~suspīrāre~, the breath drawn from below — a sigh. To aspire, in French as in English, is still to set your breath toward something.
en.assaisonner: Formed in French from the prefix ~a-~, the noun ~saison~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, through an older verb ~saisonner~. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). The first sense was “to arrange according to the season”, in particular for the care of crops (attested in 1371), and some explain it as “to ripen in due time”. Once the verb entered the kitchen, it came to mean “to bring a dish to the right point of taste with ingredients”. The noun ~saison~ comes from Latin ~satiō~ (“sowing”), so seasoning starts in a field.
en.assassiner:
French ~assassiner~ is derived from the noun ~assassin~ with the suffix ~-er~. ~assassin~ was borrowed from Italian ~assassino~, from Medieval Latin ~assassinus~, and ultimately from Arabic ~حشّاشين~ (~ḥaššāšīn~), applied to the Nizari Ismaili sect of the Alamut period. The famous gloss explains the name as “hashish-eaters,” but the sources treat that as a popular, folkloric reading rather than settled fact — the term is also linked to roots meaning “followers of the foundation [of the faith]” — so the “hashish” story should be carried as a colorful hypothesis, not asserted as the established truth.

Whatever the name's real motive, in Italian ~assassino~ came to mean a hired killer, and the verb followed: to ~assassiner~ is to murder, especially by treachery or for a cause. The Romance languages share the word — Italian ~assassino~, Spanish ~asesino~, and the English ~assassin~ borrowed through French and Italian alike — making this one of the rare everyday verbs whose root reaches back to a medieval Near-Eastern sect. French keeps the related ~assassinat~ (“assassination, murder”) and ~assassinable~ in the same grim family.
en.assembler:
From Vulgar Latin *~assimulāre~ (“to bring together, to make alike”), from ~ad-~ (“to, together”) and ~simul~ (“together, at the same time”), beside ~similis~ (“like, similar”). These trace to Proto-Italic *~semalis~ and to PIE *~sem-~ (“one, together”) — the root of oneness. The learned French doublet of this same Latin verb is ~assimiler~, while ~sembler~ (“to seem”) is its inherited, popular form. Cognate, through *~sem-~, with English ~assemble~, ~similar~, ~simultaneous~, and ~same~, and with Greek ~homós~ (“same”).

The core idea is to make things go ~together~ as one. Old French ~assembler~ meant both “to gather, to bring together” and, of armies, “to join battle” — two hosts coming together. The reflexive ~s'assembler~ (“to convene”) gave the noun ~assemblée~, the gathering itself: a French ~Assemblée nationale~ is, etymologically, a putting-of-people-into-one. From the same *~sem-~ root spread French ~sembler~, ~ensemble~ (“together,” literally ~in-simul~), ~assemblage~, ~similaire~, and ~rassembler~. That tiny root for “one” quietly underlies both the act of assembling a machine and the sense that two things merely ~seem~ alike.
en.asseoir:
From Latin ~assidēre~ (also ~adsidēre~), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), meaning “to sit beside, to settle.” ~Sedēre~ comes from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”), one of the most widespread of all roots, cognate with Sanskrit ~sī́dati~, Old Church Slavonic ~sěděti~, and English ~sit~, ~seat~, and ~settle~. The French verb is attested from the tenth century, and its tangled conjugation (~assieds~, ~assoit~, ~asseyait~) preserves traces of the Latin stems in fossilized form.

From the literal sense of placing someone in a seated position, ~asseoir~ developed a rich figurative life centered on the idea of settling something firmly in place. One ~assoit~ a reputation, an argument, or a tax — establishing it on a solid base. The same image runs through architecture and warfare, where a building or a camp is ~assis~ on firm ground. The English noun ~siege~, by way of Old French ~sege~ (“seat”), comes from this same family — a besieging army “sits down” before a city. From the root *~sed-~ descend French ~asseoir~, ~siège~, ~séance~ (“a sitting, a session”), ~résider~, and ~sédentaire~ (“given to sitting”).
en.asservir:
The sources differ on the first step. French Wiktionary derives ~asservir~ from Latin ~adservire~, while English Wiktionary treats it as a French formation, ~a-~ + ~serf~ + ~-ir~, literally “to enserf,” and says it is not directly related to ~servir~ or to the Latin verb ~asservīre~. The two accounts therefore disagree about more than a detail: one makes the verb an inheritance from Latin, the other a native coinage built on the noun ~serf~, the word for a person bound to the land. On the second account, ~a-~ turns that noun into a verb, so that to be ~asservi~ is to be brought into the condition of a ~serf~, and the ending ~-ir~ marks the second conjugation. Since the evidence does not settle the matter, the origin of the verb should be called disputed.

In French, ~asservir~ means “to reduce to servitude,” and it is used of persons and peoples and, figuratively, of anyone made to obey: one can be ~asservi~ to a tyrant, to a habit or to a passion. The related noun ~asservissement~ keeps the same range. Words such as ~serviteur~, ~service~ and ~servitude~ are near in meaning, but English Wiktionary denies a direct link between ~asservir~ and ~servir~, so the resemblance should not be pressed. Whichever account is right, the meaning is clear: the one who is ~asservi~ loses freedom of action, whether to a master or to a compulsion.
en.assigner:
French ~assigner~ goes back, through Old French ~asigner~ (attested by 1160), to Latin ~assignāre~ (“to mark out, allot, assign”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark, to seal”), itself built on ~signum~ (“mark, token, sign”), from Proto-Italic *~seknom~. Latin used the verb above all of land — marking out plots and allotting them to colonists, the surveyor's word before it was the bureaucrat's. Beyond Latin the trail forks, and etymologists keep both paths open: ~signum~ is traced either to PIE *~sek-~ (“to cut”), a sign as a notch cut into wood or stone, or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), a sign as the thing one follows; neither account is settled. Cognates include Italian ~assegnare~, Spanish ~asignar~ and English ~assign~, which English took from the Old French verb.

Its French history is a slow march from land to law. In its earliest attestations it meant to allot someone property as a share; by 1282 it covered earmarking funds for a payment; and in the mid-fourteenth century appeared the judicial sense that dominates today — to summon someone before a court, as in ~assigner en justice~. The family of ~signum~ stocked French with relatives: ~signe~, ~signer~, ~signal~, ~désigner~ and — most charming of all — ~enseigner~ (“to teach”), from Vulgar Latin *~insignāre~, literally to press a mark into someone, as though teaching were the act of stamping signs upon a mind. Etymologically, to assign is simply to set one's mark on something — a parcel of land, a sum of money, or a defendant's court date.
en.assimiler:
French ~assimiler~ was borrowed from Latin ~assimilare~ (also ~adsimilare~), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~similis~ (“like, similar”) — literally “to render alike.” ~similis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~sem-~ (“one, together”), the root of sameness and unity. Through it ~similis~ is cognate with English ~same~ and ~similar~, with Greek ~ὁμαλός~ (“even, level”), and with the family that gave English ~assemble~, where the “together” sense shows plainly.

The semantic core never wandered far from “making alike”: whether the body assimilates food into its own substance, the mind assimilates knowledge, or a people assimilates into a society, each sense is one of incorporation into a likeness. Interestingly, the same Latin ~similis~ took a second, popular path into French as ~assembler~ (“to gather together”), so ~assimiler~ and ~assembler~ are etymological doublets of a sort — one learned, one inherited. From the same root French also holds ~semblable~ (“similar”), ~ressembler~ (“to resemble”), ~sembler~ (“to seem”), ~similaire~, ~simuler~, and ~assimilation~.
en.assister:
From Latin ~assistere~ (“to stand by, to take one's place near”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, to place oneself”). ~sistere~ is a reduplicated formation on ~stare~ (“to stand”), from PIE *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the very root behind the worked example ~ester~. Cognate with Italian ~assistere~ and Spanish ~asistir~, and, through ~assistere~, with English ~assist~.

The literal sense is bodily and spatial: to ~assister~ was to stand beside someone. From that single posture two modern meanings unfolded in opposite directions. Stand beside an event as a bystander and you are merely present — hence ~assister à~ a concert or a meeting, “to attend.” Stand beside a person to lend a hand and you are a helper — hence ~assister~ someone in need, “to aid.” French keeps both senses live, a rare case where one verb means both “to watch” and “to help.” The reduplicated ~sistere~ seeds a whole cohort of French verbs — ~résister~, ~insister~, ~persister~, ~consister~, ~subsister~ — while the parent ~stare~ gives ~stable~, ~station~, ~stade~, and ~rester~. Behind them all stands the same upright PIE *~steh₂-~, and behind ~assister~ in particular, the ~assistant~ who simply stands close by.
en.associer:
From Late Latin ~associāre~ (“to join to, to unite, to take as a companion”), from Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~sociāre~ (“to join, to ally”), itself derived from ~socius~ (“companion, ally, partner”). The noun ~socius~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~sokjos~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”): a ~socius~ was originally “a follower,” one who goes along with another. From that same root flow Latin ~sequī~ (“to follow”) and a great train of its cousins, while ~socius~ itself underlies English ~social~ and ~society~, Italian ~socio~, and Spanish ~socio~.

That the word for “partner” should spring from “follower” is a quiet lesson in how alliances were imagined: to associate with someone was, at root, to fall in behind them. In 13th-century French ~associer~ named the act of allying among companions, and the sense has stayed close to that ever since — to bring people or things into partnership, to link them in the mind. The reflexive ~s'associer~ means to join forces or go into business together. From ~socius~ and its kin French also drew ~société~, ~social~, ~associé~, ~association~, and ~sociable~.
en.assortir:
From Old French, ~assortir~ is a derivative of ~sortir~ in its old sense of “to choose, to allot,” built with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”). The base belongs to the family of ~sorte~ and ~sort~, from Latin ~sortem~, accusative of ~sors~ (“drawing of lots, fate, share”). ~Sors~ derives from Proto-Italic *~sortis~ (“a joining, a row”), from PIE *~ser-~ (“to bind, to put together”), the same root that gave Latin ~serere~ (“to link, to arrange in a row”) and ~seriēs~. Through Old French ~sorte~, this family also yielded English ~sort~ and ~assortment~.

The semantic thread runs from “lot” to “kind” to “a matching set.” A ~sorte~ was originally a portion fallen to someone by lot, then a category of like things; to ~assortir~ was thus to gather things ~of the same sort~, to arrange them so they agree. Hence the modern senses: to match colors or fabrics, to stock a shop with a fitting range of goods (~un magasin bien assorti~), and reflexively ~s'assortir~, for one thing to harmonize with another. The binding sense of PIE *~ser-~ surfaces across French in ~série~, ~insérer~, ~assertion~, and ~dissertation~, while the “lot, fate” branch lives on in ~sort~, ~sortilège~, and ~consorts~ — etymological kin, all, of the well-matched tie and scarf.
en.assouplir: Built in French from the adjective ~souple~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, a typical pattern for “make or become A” (compare ~adoucir~, ~alourdir~). The prefix ~a-~ descends from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), and here it marks the passage into a state. The adjective ~souple~ comes from Old French ~sople~, which English Wiktionary traces to Latin ~supplex~ (“suppliant”), someone bending the knee. So ~assouplir~ is to make flexible, whether a muscle, a rule or a policy. There is no verb *~souplir~ behind it: the prefix and the ending arrive together.
en.assujettir:
From Middle French ~assubiectir~. Only English Wiktionary gives an analysis, and it is a surface one: ~a-~ + ~sujet~ + ~-ir~, with the ~a-~ pointing toward something and the ending turning the noun or adjective into a verb. The base ~sujet~ comes from Latin ~subiectus~ (“placed under, subjected”), the past participle of ~subicere~, built from ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~iacere~ (“to throw”). The verb is thus, at bottom, a word for “throwing under,” that is, putting someone beneath an authority. The Middle French spelling with ~-bi-~ still shows the Latin ~b~ that later French dropped in ~sujet~.

The central sense is political and legal: to subject a people to a ruler, or a person to a duty or a tax, as in ~assujetti à l'impôt~. A second, physical sense, “to fasten firmly, to secure,” also exists, as when one secures a plank or a cable. The family also includes ~assujettissement~, ~sujet~ and ~sujétion~. The Latin root ~iacere~ gave ~jeter~ (“to throw”), ~jet~, ~projet~, ~objet~ and ~adjectif~, which makes ~assujettir~ a distant cousin of every French word that “throws” something somewhere.
en.assumer:
