Borrowed from Latin ~assumere~ (“to take to oneself, take up”), formed from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sumere~ (“to take”). ~Sumere~ itself is a contraction of *~subemere~, that is ~sub-~ (“up from under”) plus ~emere~ (“to take, later to buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, distribute”). The root is cognate with Lithuanian ~imti~ (“to take”) and, through Latin borrowings, with English ~example~ and ~redeem~ (Latin ~redimere~, literally “to take back”).

In classical Latin ~assumere~ meant to take something up for oneself — to adopt, to claim, to take on. French preserved this in the sense of taking on a role or burden: ~assumer ses responsabilités~ (“to shoulder one's responsibilities”). A modern nuance, “to come to terms with, to own,” has grown common — to ~assumer~ one's choices is to accept them without apology. Note that French ~assumer~ has nothing to do with the English false friend “to assume” in the sense of supposing; that meaning split off in English. The ~emere~ root seeds a wide French family: ~exemple~, ~rédemption~, ~prime~ (via ~praemium~), ~prompt~, and the legal ~péremption~ — a scattered descent from a verb that first meant simply “to take.”
en.assurer:
French ~assurer~ comes from Old French ~asseürer~ (“to make safe, to give confidence to”), from Late Latin ~assecūrāre~ (“to render secure”), formed with the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) on Latin ~sēcūrus~ (“safe, free from care”). The adjective ~sēcūrus~ is itself transparent: ~sē-~ (“without, apart from”) plus ~cūra~ (“care, worry”) — so to be secure is, literally, to be “care-free.” Through the Romance line ~assurer~ is cognate with Italian ~assicurare~ and Spanish ~asegurar~; the bare ~sēcūrus~ gave both English ~secure~ and, by a worn-down French route, English ~sure~.

Latin ~sēcūrus~ left two parallel descendants in French: the inherited, phonetically eroded ~sûr~ (“sure, safe” — once spelled ~seür~) and the learned borrowing ~sécurité~ (“security”), a doublet pair from one source. The verb ~assurer~ accordingly fans out across many senses — to make sure, to assert confidently, to provide insurance, to belay a climber on a rope — all turning on the idea of removing care or danger. From the same ~cūra~ root French keeps ~assurance~ (“insurance, confidence”), ~rassurer~ (“to reassure”), ~sûreté~ (“safety”), and ~curer~ — the carefree and the careful alike springing from one Latin worry.
en.attacher:
From Old French ~estachier~ (“to fasten, fix, stake up”), a verb built on ~estache~ (“stake, post”), itself from Frankish *~stakka~ (“stake, post”), from Proto-Germanic *~stakô~, from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)teg-~ (“pole, stick, stake”). The initial vowel later shifted under the influence of the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to”). Cognate with Italian ~staccare~, Spanish ~estaca~ (“stake”), and — through the same Germanic root — with English ~stake~ and ~attach~ itself, which English borrowed back from French.

The earthy origin is a post driven into the ground: to ~attacher~ was first to tether a thing to a stake, and only later to bind, affix, or fasten in general, then figuratively to “attach” someone to a cause or person. The same base gives the perfect antonym ~détacher~ (Old French ~destachier~, “to un-stake, unfasten”), and from that pair English drew both ~attach~ and ~detach~. A surprising relative is ~tâche~ (“task”): many etymologists tie it to the same family, a “task” being originally something one is bound or pledged to do — a duty staked to a person, like an animal tethered to its post.
en.attaquer:
Attested in French from 1549, ~attaquer~ was borrowed from Italian ~attaccare~ (“to attach; to join; to assail”). The Italian verb arose by swapping the prefix of ~staccare~ (“to detach”) for ~a-~, and its tac- element is generally referred to a Germanic source — Frankish *~stakka~ (“stake, post”), the same root that gives English ~stake~. Crucially, ~attaccare~ first meant “to fasten, to attach,” and the military sense grew out of the phrase ~attaccare battaglia~, “to join battle,” literally “to fasten a fight onto” the enemy.

This makes ~attaquer~ an etymological doublet of native French ~attacher~ (“to attach”): the two are the same word, one inherited and one re-imported from Italy, which is why ~s'attaquer à~ and ~s'attacher à~ shadow each other so closely. The combative branch — to fall upon, to assail — eventually overshadowed the “fastening” sense in the borrowed form, leaving ~attacher~ to keep the literal meaning. From the same Germanic stock French also holds ~attache~, ~détacher~, and ~tache~ in some analyses, a small cluster all turning on the idea of pinning one thing fast to another.
en.attarder: Formed from ~tarder~ (“to delay, to be late”) with the prefix ~a-~, which descends from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). ~Tarder~ itself comes from Latin ~tardāre~ (“to slow down, to hinder”). The d of the prefix merged into the following t, giving the double tt, and the two consonants are both dentals. French Wiktionary draws a neat contrast: ~tarder~ describes a state, being late, whereas ~attarder~ describes an action, moving toward lateness, which is why the verb is most often reflexive, as in ~s'attarder~, “to linger.” English Wiktionary adds that it replaced an Old French ~atargier~ from the same source.
en.atteindre:
From Old French ~ataindre~, ~ateindre~ (“to reach, to touch”), from Latin ~attingere~ (“to touch, to reach, to border on”), itself ~ad-~ (“toward”) + ~tangere~ (“to touch”), from Proto-Italic *~tangō~, from PIE *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch”). Cognate with Italian ~attingere~ (“to draw, to obtain”) and, through the same Latin root, with English ~tangent~, ~contact~, and ~intact~.

The core sense was always physical contact, and Latin ~tangere~ already stretched from “to touch” to “to reach” and “to affect.” French inherited and developed this range: one can ~atteindre~ a summit, a target, an age, or — figuratively — be touched by an illness, ~atteint~ d'une maladie. The notion of striking a mark gave the noun ~atteinte~ (“an attack, an impairment, a blow to”), as in « porter atteinte à » (“to undermine, to infringe upon”). The same PIE root *~teh₂g-~ seeded a wide family in French through learned Latin borrowings: ~tangente~, ~contact~, ~contagion~, ~intact~, ~tactile~, and ~contigu~ all preserve, under their abstract meanings, the ancient idea of one thing touching another.
en.atteler:
French ~atteler~ most likely continues a Vulgar Latin verb *~attelare~. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~protelare~ (“to drive on, to carry through”), which probably took the meaning “to harness” under the influence of ~protelum~ (the trace or fastening of a team), and then had its prefix swapped to give *~attelare~. English Wiktionary gives the same chain in brief. The prefix swap is the key point: the ~pro-~ of the Latin verb gave way to ~at-~, the assimilated form of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”).

There is also a rival account. Littré treated ~atteler~ as a verb drawn from the noun ~attelle~, a part of a draft horse's collar to which the traces are fastened, which would reverse the direction of derivation. The Latin explanation is the one the two Wiktionaries favor, though the question is not fully settled. Whatever its path, the verb is about joining animals to a vehicle, and it extends to people: ~s'atteler à une tâche~ is to yoke oneself to a job. Its opposite is ~dételer~, and the harnessed team is the ~attelage~.
en.attendre:
From Old French ~atendre~ (late eleventh century), from Latin ~attendere~ (“to stretch toward, to pay attention”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). ~tendere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, to extend”), through which ~attendre~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~teínō~ (“to stretch”), with Sanskrit ~tan-~ (“to stretch”), and with English ~thin~ and ~tend~. The underlying image is concrete: to attend is to stretch one's mind toward something.

In Latin, ~attendere~ literally meant to stretch (one's attention) in a direction — to heed. French inherited that sense, still visible in the old reflexive ~s'attendre à~ (“to expect”), but the everyday meaning drifted: someone whose attention is fixed on an awaited thing is, in effect, waiting for it, and so ~attendre~ became the ordinary verb “to wait.” English ~attend~ kept the original “pay attention” sense, making the two a neat false-friend pair. The root ~tendere~ produced a large French family: ~tendre~, ~étendre~, ~entendre~, ~prétendre~, ~tension~, ~intention~, ~tente~, and ~attention~ itself — all turning, one way or another, on the idea of stretching.
en.atterrir: A parasynthetic formation: ~a-~ + ~terre~ + ~-ir~, with the prefix and the ending added around the noun at once, since there is no verb of the form ~terrir~ underneath. The ~a-~ is Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), here with a doubled consonant as in many such verbs, and ~terre~ comes from Latin ~terra~, from a Proto-Indo-European root *~ters-~ (“dry”). The verb first belonged to sailing, “to make landfall, to reach the shore,” and was later applied to aircraft. It has a neighbor in ~atterrer~ (“to knock to the ground,” and so “to dismay”), a different verb of similar shape.
en.attester:
Borrowed from Latin ~attestari~ (“to bear witness to”), from ~ad-~ (“toward”) + ~testari~ (“to testify”), the verb of ~testis~ (“witness”). By the accepted account ~testis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~tri-st-i-~, literally a “third party standing by” — from *~tréyes~ (“three”) + *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the impartial third person who stands beside two disputants and observes. Cognate with Italian ~attestare~ and Spanish ~atestar~, and — through the same ~testis~ — with English ~attest~, ~testify~, and ~testament~.

So at the root of ~attester~ stands a vivid courtroom image: the neutral bystander, the third one present, whose standing-there makes a fact official. The verb means to certify that something is true, to vouch for it, and by extension to provide evidence of it — « les fouilles attestent une occupation ancienne ». Around it cluster ~attestation~ (a written certificate) and ~attestataire~. The same ~testis~ gave French a broad family: ~témoin~ (“witness,” by a worn-down path) and ~témoigner~, plus the learned ~testament~, ~protester~ (“to declare publicly”), ~contester~, and ~détester~ — all turning on the act of calling something to witness.
en.attirer:
Attested from the thirteenth century, ~attirer~ is formed from the verb ~tirer~ (“to pull, to draw”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”), so the word means to draw something toward oneself. ~Tirer~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~tīrāre~, whose ultimate origin is genuinely uncertain — one much-cited hypothesis derives it from a shortening of Old French ~martirer~ (“to make a martyr of, to torture”), from ~martyrium~, on the idea of drawing out and tormenting, but this remains disputed. Cognate with Italian ~tirare~ and Spanish ~tirar~.

In Old French ~atirer~ first meant “to arrange, to put in order, to adorn,” a sense English borrowed and still keeps in ~attire~ (“to dress, clothing”) — a surprising sibling of the everyday French verb. Only later did the pull of ~tirer~ reassert itself, giving the dominant modern meaning of attracting, whether a magnet drawing iron or a spectacle drawing a crowd. From ~tirer~ French keeps a busy family — ~tirage~, ~tiroir~ (“drawer,” a thing that is pulled), ~retirer~, ~soutirer~, ~étirer~, and the marksman's ~tireur~ — every one of them a kind of pulling.
en.attiser:
From Old French ~atisier~, from Vulgar Latin *~attītiāre~, a verb derived from Latin ~tītiō~ (“firebrand, burning log”). The initial ~at-~ of the Vulgar Latin form reflects the prefix ~ad-~ assimilated to the consonant that follows. Cognates survive in Italian ~attizzare~ and Spanish ~atizar~, both “to poke a fire.” The Latin noun itself also lives on in French as ~tison~ (“ember, half-burnt log”), and from it come ~tisonner~ (“to poke the fire”) and ~tisonnier~ (“poker”).

The original action was concrete: to stir the embers so the fire burns brighter. In French, ~attiser le feu~ remains an everyday phrase. The verb is also used figuratively, since a feeling can be fanned like a fire, and French speaks of ~attiser la haine~, ~attiser les tensions~ or ~attiser la curiosité~. The word thus keeps a small domestic scene, a hearth and a stick, behind its modern political and emotional uses.
en.attraper:
From Old French ~atraper~, a derivative of ~trappe~ (“trap, snare”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”): literally “to catch in a trap.” ~Trappe~ comes from Old Low Frankish *~trappa~ (“snare, step”), a Germanic word also at the root of Medieval Latin ~trappa~. Its Germanic relatives include Dutch ~trap~ (“step, staircase”), German ~Treppe~ (“staircase”), and — keeping the “snare” sense — English ~trap~, which makes the English and French words cognate at the source.

The sense began at the snare and spread outward by metaphor. To ~attraper~ is to catch what flees or eludes: an animal, a thief, a passing bus, a few words overheard. From the idea of catching by surprise grew “to deceive, to take in” (one is ~attrapé~ by a ruse), preserved in ~attrape~ (“a trick, a hoax”) and the shop-window ~attrape-nigaud~ (“a booby trap for fools”). It even catches the involuntary — ~attraper un rhume~, to “catch” a cold. The Germanic ~trappa~ seeded a wide French field: ~trappe~ (a trapdoor), ~trappeur~ (the fur-trapper, re-borrowed from English ~trapper~), ~chausse-trappe~ (a caltrop or pitfall), and ~attrape-tout~ — all descendants of a Frankish word for a snare underfoot.
en.attribuer:
From Latin ~attribuere~ (“to assign, to allot, to add to”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~at-~) and the verb ~tribuere~ (“to grant, to allot, to divide”). ~tribuere~ is a denominative of ~tribus~ (“a tribe,” one of the divisions of the Roman people), so that to allot something was, originally, to distribute it among the tribes. Through this root ~attribuer~ is cognate with English ~attribute~, ~tribute~, ~contribute~, ~distribute~, and ~tribe~ itself.

The political-administrative origin still shows: ~attribuer~ is to apportion a share, a credit, a role, a cause — to assign a prize, attribute a painting to a master, ascribe a motive. The reflexive ~s'attribuer~ means to claim something for oneself. French carries the whole Latin family forward: ~attribut~ (“an attribute, a grammatical predicate”), ~attribution~ (“an allocation, a remit”), ~contribuer~ and ~contribution~, ~distribuer~ and ~distribution~, ~rétribuer~ (“to pay, to remunerate”), and ~tribu~ (“a tribe”). The notion of a ~tribut~ (“tribute”) — a payment apportioned to a ruler — and that of a ~tribunal~ (the platform of the ~tribus~) sit in the same etymological neighborhood, all turning on the idea of dividing and assigning shares.
en.atténuer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~attenuāre~ (“to make thin, to weaken”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and the verb ~tenuāre~, itself built on the adjective ~tenuis~ (“thin, slender”). The adjective goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”): something stretched becomes thin. The same root gave Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch”) and the Germanic words for thinness, English ~thin~ and German ~dünn~. English ~attenuate~ is a direct borrowing from the same Latin verb.

In French, ~atténuer~ has the general sense of lessening the force of something: to soften a pain, to tone down a color, to mitigate a fault or a blow. The legal phrase ~circonstances atténuantes~ (“mitigating circumstances”) rests on this sense, as does the rhetorical ~atténuation~, which softens a statement. Learned relatives from the same Latin family include ~ténu~ (“very thin, slight”) and ~extenuer~. The verb also has a technical life in optics, acoustics and electronics, where a signal is weakened as it travels.
en.augmenter:
From Latin ~augmentāre~ (“to increase”), a late verb built on ~augmentum~ (“an increase, growth”), itself from ~augēre~ (“to increase, to enlarge”). ~Augēre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~augeō~ and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂ewg-~ (“to grow, to increase”). The root spread widely: English ~eke~ (“to eke out”), Ancient Greek ~αὐξάνω~ (auxánō, “to grow”), Lithuanian ~áugti~ (“to grow”), and, through Latin, English ~augment~, ~author~, and ~auction~ — the last literally a sale by increasing bids.

The Latin ~augēre~ already carried the idea of making something greater, and ~augmentāre~ simply intensified it; French kept the plain sense “to make or become larger.” The same fertile root yields a surprising spread in French: ~augmenter~ and ~augmentation~, of course, but also ~auteur~ and ~autoriser~ (an ~auctor~ being one who makes a thing grow), ~auguste~ and the name ~Auguste~ (“the venerable, the one who increases”), and even ~auxiliaire~ — an auxiliary being help that augments one's own forces. What began as the simple notion of growth thus branched into authority, majesty, and aid.
en.authentifier: Formed in French from ~authentique~ + ~-ifier~, with the ending of the adjective dropped. ~Authentique~ comes from Latin ~authenticus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~authentikós~ (“genuine, original”). The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), and builds verbs meaning “to make or render so”. ~Authentifier~ therefore means “to make authentic”, that is, to certify that a document, a signature or a user is genuine. Coinages in ~-ifier~ are still productive in learned and technical French, and this is one of them.
en.automatiser: Formed from the noun ~automate~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to turn into an automaton” or “to equip with one”: to make a process run by itself. The base ~automate~ comes from Latin ~automatus~ (“self-moving”) and, through the neuter noun ~automatum~, from Ancient Greek ~αὐτόματος~ (“self-moving, self-willed”). The stem loses its final ~-e~ before the suffix. A Greek word for a thing that moves of its own accord thus ended up, after a long trip through Latin, as a verb for a modern industrial and computing task.
en.autoriser:
From Medieval Latin ~auctorizare~ (“to give authority to, to confirm”), from Latin ~auctor~ (“originator, author, guarantor”), itself from ~augere~ (“to increase, to make grow”) + the agent suffix ~-tor~. ~augere~ rests on Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to increase”), the source also of English ~author~, ~augment~, and ~auction~. The Old French intermediary was ~actoriser~, and ~autoriser~ stands as a doublet of ~octroyer~ (“to grant”), the popular outcome of the same Latin verb.

An ~auctor~ was originally one who “causes to grow” — who augments, vouches for, sets a thing on foot: a founder, a backer, a source of trust. To ~autoriser~ was thus to lend something the weight of such a guarantor, to make it valid and warranted; from this came both “to authorize, to permit” and the sense of conferring ~autorité~. The thread back to “growth” is invisible in modern usage yet binds a surprising kin: ~auteur~, ~autorité~, ~augmenter~, ~auguste~, ~enchère~ (“auction,” via ~auctio~), and even ~août~ (“August,” the month of ~Augustus~, “the increased, the venerable”).
en.avaler: Formed from the adverb ~aval~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The adverb ~aval~ means “downward, downstream” and is explained as ~à val~, from ~à~ (Latin ~ad~, “to”) + ~val~ (from Latin ~vallis~, “valley”), the opposite of ~amont~. Another account, in English Wiktionary, sees it as a shortening of ~à valoir~. The verb first meant to send or go down, and from that came the sense of letting food slide down the throat. Figuratively, one ~avale~ an insult or a story, meaning one accepts it. The financial noun ~aval~ (“a guarantee”) is a different word, which French Wiktionary derives from Italian ~avallo~.
en.avancer:
From Old French ~avancier~ (also ~avancir~), from Vulgar Latin *~abantiare~, a verb built on Late Latin ~abante~ (“before, in front”), itself a fusion of ~ab~ (“from”) and ~ante~ (“before”). ~Ante~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂énti~ (“in front, before”), which also gives Greek ~antí~ (“opposite, against”) and is cognate with English ~answer~ (originally a “swearing against”). The whole formation means, roughly, “to put forward, to move to the front.”

A charming etymological mishap haunts this word. Speakers came to feel that the ~a-~ of ~avancer~ was the ordinary prefix ~a-~, and that the rest was a stem ~vant~ — so when they wanted a noun for what lies ahead, they coined ~avant~ by clipping off that imagined prefix, even though the ~a~ was part of the root all along. The same false cut produced ~avantage~. Meanwhile ~avancer~ kept widening: from spatial movement forward it reached time (to advance a date), money (to advance a sum), and argument (to advance a claim). Kin in French include ~avant~, ~avance~, ~avantage~, ~avancement~, and ~devancer~.
en.aventurer: Formed from ~aventure~ + the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put to the hazard of adventure”. ~Aventure~ comes from Vulgar Latin ~adventūra~, literally “things about to happen”, a neuter plural of the future participle of Latin ~advenīre~ (“to arrive, to happen”) that was reinterpreted as a feminine singular. In Old French the noun meant “fate, chance”, and that fatalistic sense survives only in ~bonne aventure~. The verb therefore means to risk, to hazard, to launch into an uncertain undertaking, and its pronominal form means “to venture” somewhere.
en.avertir:
From Old French ~avertir~, from a Vulgar Latin *~advertire~ reshaping Latin ~advertere~ (« to turn toward, to direct toward »), from ~ad-~ (« toward ») and ~vertere~ (« to turn »). ~vertere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~wertō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (« to turn »), cognate with English ~worth~ (via Proto-Germanic *~werþaną~, « to become »), Sanskrit ~vartate~ (« it turns »), and Russian ~vertétʹ~ (« to rotate »).

The sense « to warn » grew naturally out of « to turn toward ». By the late twelfth century the verb meant « to turn, to divert »; by around 1250 it had become « to turn someone's attention toward something », that is « to inform, to warn ». English ~avert~ keeps the older, literal sense — to turn danger aside — beside French's warning sense. The same root *~wert-~ is enormously productive in French: ~vers~, ~verser~, ~divertir~, ~convertir~, ~inverser~, and ~adversaire~ all turn on the idea of turning.
en.aviser: The sources describe it in two ways. One derives Old French ~aviser~ from the noun ~avis~ (“opinion, advice”); the other analyzes it as ~a-~ + ~viser~. The second analysis rests on ~viser~, from Latin ~vīsāre~ (“to look at attentively”), a frequentative built on ~vīsere~, itself from ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), the root also behind English ~wit~ and ~wise~. The prefix ~a-~ is Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”) by way of Old French. Either way, the sense moved from looking at something to noticing it, and then to warning or informing someone.
en.avoir:
From Old French ~avoir~ (also ~aveir~), from Latin ~habēre~ (“to have, hold, possess”), from Proto-Italic *~habēō~, generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~gʰh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, to take, to hold”). Its Romance siblings are everywhere everyday verbs: Italian ~avere~, Spanish ~haber~, Portuguese ~haver~, Romanian ~avea~. Tempting as it looks, English ~have~ is not in fact a cognate — the resemblance is a coincidence, that verb belonging to a separate Germanic family.

Latin ~habēre~ began with the concrete sense “to hold,” then widened to “to possess.” In Romance, ~avoir~ went a step further and became an auxiliary, the engine of the compound past: ~j'ai mangé~ is literally “I have eaten,” a possession of the completed act. From the impersonal ~il y a~ (“there is, there are”) French even built an existential out of mere having. The same root threads through a rich family of borrowed and inherited words: ~habit~ (a way of “holding” oneself, hence both costume and custom), ~habitude~, ~habiter~ (“to dwell”), ~exhiber~, ~prohiber~, and, through the compound ~dēbēre~ (~dē-~ + ~habēre~, “to hold away from”), the verb ~devoir~ itself. To have, to owe, to dwell — all are ways of holding.

The same auxiliary turn happened on the far side of the linguistic frontier. German ~haben~ likewise became the engine of a compound past: ~ich habe gesungen~ (“I have sung”) mirrors ~j'ai chanté~ exactly. Yet here lies a fine irony — ~haben~ and ~avoir~ are not cognates at all. Despite their near-identical look and identical meaning, German ~haben~ descends from a different Proto-Indo-European root (*~keh₂p-~, “to grasp,” the source also of Latin ~capiō~ and so of French ~capter~, ~captif~, and ~accepter~), while ~avoir~ comes from *~gʰh₁bʰ-~. Two unrelated “have” verbs were independently pressed into the very same grammatical service. That convergence is a hallmark of the Western European ~Sprachbund~ — a zone where neighboring but unrelated languages, through centuries of contact, grow shared structures: the definite article, the relative pronoun, and precisely this split between ~être~ and ~avoir~ (German ~sein~ and ~haben~) as the two auxiliaries of the past (~je suis allé~ / ~j'ai mangé~ beside ~ich bin gegangen~ / ~ich habe gegessen~). These traits feel inevitable to a European but are unusual among the world's languages. That grammar, no less than vocabulary, can be borrowed across a frontier is the quiet lesson of ~avoir~.
en.avouer:
From Old French ~avoer~ (“to acknowledge, recognize, accept as one's own — especially to recognize as a protector or lord”), from Latin ~advocare~ (“to call to oneself, summon”), built from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~vocare~ (“to call”). Some authorities note an alternate influence from ~advotare~ (related to ~votum~, “a vow”), paralleling ~dévouer~ from ~devotare~. The verb is kin to Italian ~avvocare~ and to the English borrowing ~avow~.

The medieval sense was feudal and legal: to ~avouer~ a lord was publicly to acknowledge him as one's protector, and to ~avouer~ a deed was to claim and own it. From “acknowledging as one's own,” the meaning slid toward acknowledging a fact about oneself — and so to the modern sense “to confess, admit,” often something one would rather not (~avouer un crime~, ~avouer sa défaite~). The same ~vocare~ runs through a large French family: ~avocat~ (“lawyer,” the advocate “called to” a case), ~vouer~ and ~dévouer~, ~évoquer~, ~invoquer~, ~provoquer~, ~convoquer~, and ~vocation~. A confession, in this old light, is the act of calling a truth toward yourself and owning it before others.
en.avérer:
From Medieval Latin or a Vulgar Latin *~adverare~, built on ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus the adjective ~verus~ (“true”). ~Verus~ is inherited through Proto-Italic *~wēros~ from Proto-Indo-European *~weh₁ros~ (“true, trustworthy”) — the same root that, through Germanic, gives German ~wahr~ (“true”) and, through Old French ~verai~, the English adverb ~very~, which once meant “truly.”

The original sense was juridical: to ~avérer~ a fact was to establish it as true, to prove or verify it, and Old and Middle French used it transitively in just that way. Modern French has largely shifted to the reflexive ~s'avérer~ (“to prove to be, to turn out”) — a thing ~s'avère~ exact, or false, or impossible. This produces a famous purist's quibble: since the verb already contains “true,” the common phrase ~s'avérer faux~ (“to prove false”) is, taken literally, a small contradiction (“to prove-true to be false”), though usage has long since accepted it. From the same ~verus~ French keeps ~vrai~ (its popular descendant), ~vérité~ (“truth”), ~vérifier~ (“to verify”), and ~véridique~ (“truthful”).
en.axer:
Denominal verb from the noun ~axe~ (“axis, axle”) + ~-er~. ~Axe~ descends from Latin ~axis~ (“axle, pivot, axis”), from Proto-Italic *~aksis~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eḱs-~ (“axis, axle”). The root is widely attested: it gives Ancient Greek ~áxōn~, Sanskrit ~ákṣa~ (“axle”), Lithuanian ~ašis~, and — through the inherited Germanic line — English ~axle~, while English ~axis~ is a later direct loan from Latin.

The noun ~axe~ first named the physical axle of a wheel and the geometric or astronomical axis around which things turn. From this pivot-line the verb ~axer~ developed its modern abstract meaning: “to align on an axis,” hence figuratively “to center, to focus on.” One says ~axer un débat sur~ (“to center a debate on”) a question — orienting it along a single line. Words from the same ~axis~ root include ~axe~, ~axial~, axiome (in fact unrelated, from Greek), and the technical ~désaxer~ (“to throw off axis, to unbalance”). The image stays remarkably constant: everything in this family turns on, or is arranged along, a single defining line.
en.aérer: Formed in French from Latin ~āēr~ (“air”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The Latin noun is itself the Greek word for air taken over, and it is also the source of French ~air~. To ~aérer~ is to let air into a room, a garment or a text, and the figurative sense of loosening up a dense page or schedule follows naturally from it.
en.bafouer:
The origin of ~bafouer~ is uncertain, and the sources offer several rival accounts. French Wiktionary lists four. In the first, it takes its shape from Old French ~baffe~, ~beffe~ or ~buffe~ (words of mockery) with the phonetic influence of ~fou~ (“mad”). Old Occitan ~bafar~ and Italian ~beffare~, both “to mock,” come from kindred nouns ~bafa~ and ~beffa~. In the second, it is an alteration, after ~battre~ and ~fou~, of Middle French ~beffer~ (“to trick, to fool”). In the third, it was built like ~bavoler~ from ~bas~ and ~fouer~ (“to tread”), meaning to trample down. In the fourth, it is a separate word: Middle French ~bafouer~ meant to tie up with a rope, from ~baffe~ (“bundle”). English Wiktionary gives yet another account, an expressive formation on an interjection of disdain made by blowing air through pouted lips, comparable to Catalan ~baf~ (“puff”).

The sense “to treat with derision, to outrage” is cited from Montaigne's Essais, while the rope sense is cited earlier, from Rabelais's Gargantua in 1534. From scorn came the modern sense of flouting, usually of something that deserves respect, as in ~bafouer la loi~ or ~bafouer les droits de l'homme~. The adjective ~bafoué~ describes one whose dignity has been ignored. Whichever theory is right, the word keeps a hint of the mocking gesture. The Italian noun ~beffa~, a practical joke, shows the same family of mockery on the other side of the Alps.
en.baigner:
From Old French ~baignier~, earlier ~bagner~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~baneare~, a reshaped form of Late Latin ~balneāre~ (“to bathe”), from Latin ~balneum~ (“a bath”). The popular Latin form lost its ~l~, which explains why the Romance verbs look alike: Occitan ~banhar~, Catalan ~banyar~, Italian ~bagnare~, Spanish ~bañar~ and Portuguese ~banhar~ are all cognates. The French spelling ~baigner~ is probably a later remodeling after ~bain~ (“a bath”), the noun that comes from the same Latin ~balneum~. By this account, the ~i~ was added to the verb to match its noun, since the older ~bagner~ lacked it.

The verb began as “to give a bath to” and “to take a bath,” and it kept that concrete meaning. It then widened to anything immersed or washed by water: a river or sea ~baigne~ (“washes”) a shore, a face is ~baigné de larmes~ (“bathed in tears”), and a room can be ~baignée de lumière~ (“bathed in light”). The reflexive ~se baigner~ is the usual verb for going for a swim. Derivatives include ~baignoire~ (“bathtub”), ~baigneur~ (“bather”, also a baby doll) and ~baignade~ (“a swim, a bathing place”).
en.baiser:
Inherited from Old French ~baisier~ and Middle French ~baiser~, from Latin ~bāsiāre~ (“to kiss”), a verb made on the noun ~bāsium~ (“a kiss”). French Wiktionary says ~bāsiāre~ first named the kiss given to respected people, such as one's father, and that it gradually pushed out two older Latin words, ~suāvium~ (“a lover's kiss”) and ~osculum~ (literally a “little mouth”). Italian ~baciare~, Spanish ~besar~ and Portuguese ~beijar~ are its sisters.

The sense shift is the striking part. The sexual meaning, now dominant and vulgar, is attested from the twelfth century, and English Wiktionary describes it as arising by euphemism before becoming the main sense of the verb. The noun ~baiser~ (“a kiss”) was then derived from the verb, and it stayed innocent. As a result, speakers today say ~embrasser~ for kissing in everyday speech, and the verb ~baiser~ in its original sense survives mainly in literary or fixed uses, such as the noun ~baisemain~ (“a kiss on the hand”). Few French words have changed register so far from their Latin starting point.
en.baisser:
From Middle French, from Old French ~baissier~ (eleventh century, “to lower”), from Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~ (“to make low”), a verb derived from Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low, base, short”). The same ~bassus~ gave French the adjective ~bas~, Italian ~basso~ and Spanish ~bajo~, and, through musical Italian, English ~bass~ — the lowest voice. *~Bassiāre~ thus means, transparently, “to bring low.”

The verb has stayed close to its literal sense throughout: to lower a thing physically — to ~baisser~ the eyes, the head, a curtain, a window — and from there to turn down (a volume, a price) and to decline (the sun lowers, prices fall, strength wanes). The reflexive ~se baisser~ means to stoop or bend down. From the same ~bas~ family come ~abaisser~ (“to lower, to humble”), ~rabaisser~ (“to belittle”), ~baisse~ (“a fall, a drop”), ~soubassement~ (“a base, a footing”), and the bas-relief of sculpture, ~bas-relief~, a carving that stands only slightly proud of its background. The whole cluster turns on a single idea: lowness, and the act of bringing down toward it.
en.balader: Formed from the noun ~ballade~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary explains the leap from poem to walk by the constant wandering of troubadours, jugglers and other travelling performers, an account that is plausible but not documented in detail. ~Ballade~ comes from Old Occitan ~ballada~ (“dance song”), the text being inseparable from the music, from ~balar~ (“to dance”), itself from Late Latin ~ballare~, which may be connected to Greek ~ballízō~. So ~balader~ first meant to carry about or lead around, and then to stroll, mostly in the reflexive ~se balader~ (“to go for a walk”).
en.balancer: Formed on ~balance~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~balance~ is inherited through Old French from Vulgar Latin ~bilancia~ and Latin ~bilanx~, a compound of ~bi-~ (“twice”) and ~lanx~ (“plate, pan”): a balance with two pans. The same Latin word gave French ~bilan~ (“balance sheet”). To ~balancer~ is to move like the pans of a scale, rocking back and forth, and so to swing, sway, or weigh one thing against another. In informal French the verb also means “to throw” or “to toss out.”
en.balayer: Formed from ~balai~ (“broom”), a verb meaning “to use a broom.” The sources differ slightly on the ending: one simply adds ~-er~ to the noun, while fr.Wiktionary notes that some senses may instead come from the verb ~baler~ with the ending ~-ayer~, or at least that ~baler~ and ~balancer~ influenced how the meaning developed. The ~y~ of ~balayer~ is a feature of the ending and not a sign of an older Latin root. The core sense is the physical one, to sweep, and French extends it to anything cleared away in a broad stroke, such as doubts or opponents.
en.baliser: Formed from the noun ~balise~ (“beacon, marker”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The navigational noun was borrowed from Portuguese ~baliza~, and the French entry also lists a separate homonym ~balise~ tied to ~balisier~, a plant, which is not the source of this verb. To ~baliser~ is to mark a channel, a path or a runway with beacons or markers, and the sense can be extended to marking out a course of action.
en.bander:
The origin of ~bander~ is not settled in the sources. English Wiktionary gives a Germanic descent: Middle French ~bander~, from Old French ~bander~ (also spelled ~bender~), from Frankish *~bandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bandijaną~. English ~bend~ is a cognate, and the whole Germanic family revolves around a band or bond that is tied and drawn tight. French Wiktionary lists two accounts side by side. One goes back to Old High German ~binda~ (“to bind”), which is again Germanic. The other, introduced with “probably,” goes back to Occitan ~bandar~ (“to make tipsy, to exasperate”). The sources do not say which account covers which sense of the modern verb, so the Germanic descent is the better documented, and the Occitan one remains a proposal.

The modern verb has two main groups of senses. One is “to bind with a band,” as in ~bander une plaie~ (“to bandage a wound”) or ~bander les yeux~ (“to blindfold”). The other is “to stretch tight,” as in ~bander un arc~ (“to draw a bow”) or ~bander ses muscles~ (“to tense one's muscles”). The step from tying to tightening is a natural one, since a band that is tied is drawn taut. These senses sit beside the related words ~bande~ (“strip, band”), ~bandeau~ (“headband”) and ~bandage~, though this entry does not claim that every sense of ~bander~ comes from a single source. Where the origin is debated, the safest summary is that a Germanic word for binding is the best-attested ancestor.
en.bannir:
French ~bannir~ is first attested around 1100. It comes from Old French ~bannir~ (also ~banir~), borrowed from Frankish *~bannijan~, a West Germanic verb. Behind it lies Proto-Germanic *~bannijaną~ (“to banish, to forbid”), formed on the noun *~bannaz~ or *~banną~ (“prohibition, curse, order, banishment”), which French Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to speak, to say”). So the verb began as a Germanic word of proclamation, passed to the Gallo-Romans through the Franks. The cognates are Germanic: German ~Bann~ and English ~ban~ belong to the same family.

The Germanic word meant an official proclamation, a command backed by authority, and it is not far from there to “banishment,” a sentence pronounced aloud. French kept both ends. In feudal law, the lord's ~ban~ was his right to command and to compel, which is why ~banal~ first described what was subject to that ban, such as the communal oven, before it came to mean “commonplace.” The Italian verb ~bandire~ gave ~bandito~, hence French ~bandit~, an outlaw originally one who had been proclaimed outside the law. And ~abandonner~ comes from the expression ~à bandon~, “at someone's disposal,” built on the same ~ban~.
en.baptiser:
From Latin ~baptizo~ (“to wash, baptize”), itself from Ancient Greek ~baptízō~ (“to plunge, dip, immerse”), a frequentative of ~báptō~ (“to dip, dye”). The image at the root is wholly physical: total immersion in water. Christian Latin took this Greek verb and narrowed it to the rite of baptism, and French inherited the religious sense.

The original “dipping” survives in a surprising cousin: the dyeing sense of Greek ~báptō~ gives English ~baptistery~ and, distantly, the deep-blue pigment-trade word behind ~baptism~ imagery. In French the family is liturgical and rich: ~baptême~, ~baptistère~, ~baptismal~, ~anabaptiste~, ~rebaptiser~, ~débaptiser~. The verb also drifted playfully into everyday French — to ~baptiser~ a ship is to name it, and slang once used ~baptiser le vin~ for watering it down, a wink at the immersion buried in the word. From a Greek term for plunging into water came a vocabulary of naming, blessing, and christening.
en.barrer: Formed in French from ~barre~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, “to close or block with a bar.” The noun ~barre~ comes from Old French ~barre~ (“beam, bar, barrier”), from Vulgar Latin *~barra~, whose origin is uncertain. French Wiktionary derives it from Gaulish *~barros~. English Wiktionary offers two rival accounts: a Frankish or Germanic source, or a Celtic one related to Breton ~barri~ (“branch”). The ending ~-er~ is the usual way of turning a noun into a verb.
en.basculer: From Old French ~baculer~ (“to strike the backside against the ground”), built from ~bas~ (“low”), ~cul~ (“backside”) and the verb ending ~-er~; the sense is said to be to bump someone's bottom down. Both parts are old: ~bas~ from Late Latin ~bassus~, ~cul~ from Latin ~cūlus~. The modern spelling with a pronounced ~s~ shows the influence of the noun ~bascule~ (“seesaw”), which steered the verb toward tipping or swinging over like a balance, and then to figurative shifts from one state to another.
en.baser:
From the noun ~base~ with the suffix ~-er~ (15th century). The noun ~base~ comes, through Old French, from Latin ~basis~ (“pedestal, foundation”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βάσις~ (“a step, that on which one stands”). The Greek noun belongs to the verb ~βαίνω~ (“to go, to walk, to step”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to go, to come”). Through that same root, ~base~ is distantly cognate with English ~come~ and Latin ~venire~ (“to come”).

The path of meaning is wonderfully concrete: a ~βάσις~ was first the act of stepping, then the thing one steps onto — a pedestal — and finally any foundation or supporting surface. From that physical sense the verb ~baser~ generalized to the abstract “to found, to ground,” as in an argument ~basé sur~ the evidence. The same Greek-Latin family yields a rich harvest in modern French: ~base~ in all its senses, ~basique~, ~baside~, and ~soubassement~ (“understructure”). English ~basis~, ~base~, and ~basement~ descend along the same line, making the French verb a near twin of an everyday English word.
en.battre:
From Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, to strike, to thrash”), a verb almost certainly borrowed from Gaulish: native Latin words rarely begin with ~b-~, and the Celtic cousins are clear — Welsh ~bathu~ (“to coin money, to strike”), Old Breton ~bat~, and Irish ~bath~. The ultimate source is often traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰewh₂-~ (“to strike”). Rare in classical literature but vigorous in spoken Latin, ~battuere~ flourished in the Romance languages: Italian ~battere~ and Spanish ~batir~ are its direct heirs, and English ~batter~, ~battle~, and ~battalion~ all reach back to it through French.

The word's most charming offshoot is Late Latin ~battuālia~ (“the beatings”), the name for the practice combats of gladiators and soldiers; this became Old French ~bataille~ and English ~battle~ — so every battle is, etymologically, a drill in striking. ~Battre~ stayed earthily concrete in French: to beat eggs, beat a drum, beat a rival, beat a path. From it spread a wide family — ~battement~, ~bataille~, ~batterie~ (whether of guns, of a kitchen, or of a drum kit), ~combattre~, ~débattre~, ~abattre~, and ~rabattre~. Even a heated ~débat~ is, at root, two sides beating at each other. A modest verb for hitting things turns out to underlie much of the vocabulary of conflict.
en.baver: ~Baver~ is formed from the noun ~bave~ (“drool, saliva”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is probably imitative, from a Vulgar Latin *~baba~ built on the baby-babble sound ~bab~, a root also seen in Spanish and Portuguese ~baba~. French Wiktionary mentions an alternative, a Gaulish word *~baua~ (“mud”). The verb means “to drool,” and it gave idioms such as ~en baver~, “to have a hard time,” and ~baver sur~, “to slander.”
en.bayer:
French ~bayer~ (“to gape”) is the surviving spelling of Old French ~beer~, which English Wiktionary derives from Early Medieval Latin ~batāre~ (“to gape”). French Wiktionary treats ~bayer~ more simply as a variant of ~bâiller~ (“to yawn”), which belongs to the same family of words about open mouths. The two verbs thus tell one story from two angles: a mouth that falls open, whether from sleepiness or wonder.

The old verb ~beer~ gave modern French several words that sound nothing like ~bayer~. Its participle survives in ~béant~ (“gaping, wide open”) and in the fixed phrase ~bouche bée~ (“open-mouthed, astonished”). The Occitan cousin of the same Latin root, ~badar~, produced ~badaud~ (“gawker, idle onlooker”), a person who stands gaping at whatever passes. As for ~bayer~ itself, it is nearly restricted today to a single idiom, ~bayer aux corneilles~ (“to stare vacantly into the air, literally to gape at crows”), and to its older sense in ~bayer à~ (“to long for”). The verb has largely given way to ~bâiller~, a fossil in a phrase about daydreaming.
en.bercer:
The origin is debated. French Wiktionary treats ~bercer~ as a verb formed on Old French ~bers~ (“cradle”). English Wiktionary gives a different chain: Middle French, then Old French ~bercier~ (“to rock”), then a Vulgar Latin form *~bertiāre~, reaching Latin through Gaulish, from a Proto-Celtic root *~berta-~ (“to shake”) related to *~bereti~ (“to carry”). The two accounts agree that the word belongs to Old French and that its core idea is a rocking motion.

Whatever its source, ~bercer~ means to rock a child in a cradle, and from there it extends to soothe and lull. The figurative sense is the most familiar: ~bercer quelqu'un d'illusions~ is to lull someone with false hopes, and ~se bercer d'illusions~ is to feed oneself on them. Related words include ~berceau~ (“cradle”), ~berceuse~ (“lullaby”) and ~bercement~ (“rocking”).
en.beurrer: ~Beurrer~ is a denominal verb: ~beurre~ (“butter”) plus the ending ~-er~, “to spread with butter.” The noun comes from Old French ~burre~, from Latin ~būtȳrum~, which borrowed Greek βούτυρον, literally “cow-cheese.” The modern form ~beurre~ is a regional variant, from the east or the west of the langue d'oïl, that replaced ~burre~ by the sixteenth century. English ~butter~ is a cousin loan from the same Latin and Greek word, so the two languages share one Mediterranean ancestor for the spread.
en.blanchir:
From Old French ~blanchir~, from Vulgar Latin *~blancīre~, a verb built on Frankish *~blank~ (“shining, white”). French Wiktionary simply treats it as formed from ~blanc~; the two accounts agree, since ~blanc~ itself comes from the same Frankish word. The Franks' *~blank~ pushed aside Latin ~albus~ in Gaul, which survives only in a few remnants such as ~aube~ (“dawn”) and ~albâtre~. Italian ~bianco~ and Spanish ~blanco~ are siblings of ~blanc~, and English ~blank~ was borrowed from French ~blanc~.

The meaning of ~blanchir~ spread outward from “to make white.” One can ~blanchir~ linen, walls with lime, or vegetables by plunging them briefly into boiling water, and English ~blanch~ was borrowed from this French verb. Hair turns white with age, hence the idiom ~blanchi sous le harnais~, “grown grey under the harness,” of someone who has aged in a long career. A defendant is ~blanchi~ when cleared of suspicion, and money is ~blanchi~ when its criminal origin is hidden. The family includes ~blanchisserie~, ~blanchiment~ and ~blanchâtre~.
en.blesser:
From Old French ~blecier~ (“to bruise, to injure”), from Gallo-Romance *~blettiare~ (“to make bruised, to make soft like overripe fruit”). The ultimate source is Germanic: Frankish, from Proto-West Germanic *~blaitijan~ (“to bruise, to make discoloured”), a factitive verb formed on *~blait~ (“pale, livid, discoloured”) with the causative suffix *~-jan~. The same Germanic root surfaces in Old English ~blātian~ (“to grow pale”).

The original image was vivid and physical: to ~blesser~ was to mark flesh with the dull, discoloured patch of a bruise — the very softness an apple shows when it turns ~blet~ (“overripe, bruised”), a French word from the same Germanic family. Over time the verb shifted from this narrow sense of bruising toward the general meanings “to wound” and “to injure,” whether by blade, bullet, or accident. By extension it also came to mean “to hurt” emotionally: harsh words can ~blesser~ as surely as a weapon, and one speaks of ~amour-propre blessé~ (“wounded pride”). Related French words include the noun ~blessure~ (“wound, injury”) and the participle ~blessé~ used as a noun for a casualty or injured person.
en.bloguer:
~bloguer~ offers one of the shortest etymological chains in French. It is formed on the noun ~blog~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~, and ~blog~ was borrowed from English at the turn of the millennium — French dictionaries date the noun to 1999 and the verb to the years just after. English ~blog~ is itself a clipping of ~weblog~, a compound of ~web~ and ~log~; that ~log~ is the sailor’s word, the ship’s record named for the piece of wood once trailed overboard to gauge a vessel’s speed. ~weblog~ was coined in 1997 by Jorn Barger; ~blog~ was cut out of it on 23 May 1999 by Peter Merholz, who divided ~weblog~ in the wrong place — as though it read ~we blog~ — and so made a verb visible inside a noun. The joke stuck, and the derivative ~blog~ all but buried ~weblog~.

The verb’s real story is orthographic. French had to decide how to write an English monosyllable in a language where ~g~ before ~e~ or ~i~ is soft: ~bloger~ would rhyme with ~loger~. The solution is the digraph ~gu-~, already used by ~blaguer~ and ~naviguer~, which keeps the hard sound through the whole paradigm — ~nous bloguons~, ~en bloguant~. In 2006 the Office québécois de la langue française said so explicitly, recommending ~bloguer~ and judging ~blogger~, ~bloger~ and ~blogguer~ poorly adapted to French morphology; Quebec also prefers the noun ~blogue~ to ~blog~. France largely kept ~blog~ for the noun while adopting the same ~-guer~ verb, so a French sentence can now pair ~blog~ with ~bloguer~ — a visible seam left by two different answers to the same question. The family that grew up around it is wholly French in shape: ~blogueur~, ~blogosphère~, ~blogage~ and the playful ~blogouiller~.
en.bloquer:
French ~bloquer~ is a denominal verb, coined in the fifteenth century from the noun ~bloc~ (“block, log”) — or its military relative ~blocus~. The noun ~bloc~ is not Latin at all: Old French ~bloc~ was taken from Middle Dutch ~blok~ (“tree-trunk”), from Proto-Germanic *~blukką~ (“beam, log”), traced by many to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰelǵ-~ (“plank, beam”). The same Germanic word gave English ~block~ and German ~Block~, so ~bloquer~ and to ~block~ are, satisfyingly, the very same word doing the same job in two languages.

The semantics follow the wood. To set a ~bloc~ in a doorway is to jam it shut, and from that ~bloquer~ generalized to stopping, jamming, or barricading anything — a road, a door, an account, a salary, a negotiation, or, in football, an opponent. French also distinguishes the borrowed Dutch ~blokken~ (“to cram, to swot”) in some dialects, but the mainstream verb is wholly about obstruction. From the same block of wood come ~blocage~ (“blocking, a mental block”), ~débloquer~ (“to unblock, to release funds”), ~blocus~ (“blockade”), and the borrowed-back ~blockhaus~ — a whole family piled up, log upon log, from one Germanic ~bloc~.
en.boire:
From Old French ~boivre~ (also ~beivre~, ~bevvre~), from Latin ~bibere~ (“to drink”). The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~pibō~, a reduplicated form whose initial ~p~ voiced to ~b~, and ultimately to the Proto-Indo-European root *~peh₃-~ (“to drink”). The kinship is spectacular: Sanskrit ~píbati~, Ancient Greek ~πῑ́νω~ (~pī́nō~), and Proto-Slavic *~piti~ all descend from the same root, as does — through a sister formation — Latin ~pōtiō~, source of English ~potion~.

The phonetic history is a small drama. The Old French stem ~bev-~ underwent labialization, passing through ~beuv-~ to ~buv-~, which is why the modern verb shifts shape across its conjugation: ~je bois~ but ~nous buvons~, ~ils boivent~ but ~je buvais~. The older ~beuv-~ form fossilized in ~beuverie~ (“drinking bout”). The same root waters a whole field of French words: ~boisson~, ~breuvage~, ~buvable~, ~buvette~, ~buveur~, and ~pourboire~ (literally “for drinking,” a tip). The everyday act named here is, etymologically, one of humanity's oldest spoken words.
en.boiter:
From the root of Old French ~boiteux~ (“lame, limping”), ultimately tied to ~boîte~ in its old anatomical sense of the socket or cavity of a joint. The TLFi traces a derivational chain through the attested ~boistoier~ (1358) and ~boister~ (1539), the latter form supplanting the older one before settling into the modern ~boiter~. Old French and Walloon used ~boîte~ for the hollow of an articulation, so to deboiter a limb was to knock it out of its socket and to ~boiter~ was to walk on a joint that no longer sat right.

The deeper origin of ~boîte~ itself is debated, so etymologists hedge the ultimate source; what is well documented is the joint-socket image at the heart of the word. The picture is vivid: a limp framed not as weakness but as a bone riding loose in its housing. The same family gives modern French ~déboîter~, said both of a dislocated shoulder and of a car pulling out of its lane, and ~emboîter~, to fit one thing snugly into another — every one of them turning on the idea of a part seated, or unseated, in its socket.
en.bombarder: Formed from the noun ~bombarde~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Middle French ~bombarde~, which named an early cannon or mortar, a catapult, and also a bassoon-like wind instrument. It goes back to Latin ~bombus~ (“buzzing, booming”), a word imitating a deep sound. To ~bombarder~ was first to fire a bombard at a target, then to shell with any projectile, and figuratively to bombard someone with questions.
en.bondir:
From Old French ~bondir~, earlier ~bundir~ (“to resound, to echo”), from Vulgar Latin *~bombitīre~, a variant of *~bombitāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~bombīre~ (“to buzz, to hum”). Behind it stands ~bombus~ (“the buzzing of bees, a booming noise”), a sound-imitating word that Latin borrowed from Greek ~bómbos~. The same Latin noun came through Italian ~bomba~ into French ~bombe~ and English ~bomb~, so a leaping verb and an explosive share an ancestor that began as a deep hum.

The odd part is the meaning. In the thirteenth century ~bondir~ shifted from “to resound” to “to jump, to spring.” French Wiktionary explains the change as a shift of register: the auditory impression of sounds rising and falling gave way to a visual impression of the same rhythm, as with a ball that bounces and rebounds. Modern French uses ~bondir~ for a leap, for a start of surprise, and figuratively for anger or joy, as when someone leaps in indignation. Its family includes the noun ~bond~ (“leap”), ~rebondir~ (“to bounce back, to take a new turn”), ~rebond~ and ~bondissant~.
en.border:
Denominal verb from the noun ~bord~ (“edge, ship's side”), attested by 1170, formed with ~-er~. The noun is a borrowing from Frankish *~bord~ (“plank, side of a ship”), from Proto-Germanic *~burdą~ (“board, plank, edge”). It is therefore cognate with English ~board~, German ~Bord~, and Dutch ~boord~ — all reflexes of the same Germanic word. The deeper Indo-European source of *~burdą~ is uncertain, sometimes tied to a root *~bʰers-~ (“tip, edge”).

The noun ~bord~ first meant the side of a ship — the planking that rose along the hull — before broadening to any edge, brink, or rim. The verb ~border~ thus means “to run along the edge of,” whether a road borders a forest, a lace borders a sleeve, or a sailor handles the lines along the ship's side. From the same maritime ancestor French keeps ~aborder~ (“to come alongside, to approach”), ~déborder~ (“to overflow, to go over the edge”), ~rebord~ (“rim, ledge”), and ~bordure~ (“border, trim”). The everyday English ~aboard~ likewise harks back to being “on the ~bord~.”
en.borner: Formed in French from the noun ~borne~ (a boundary marker, a limit) with the verb ending ~-er~. The verb first means to mark the limits of something, to fix its boundaries: one ~borne~ a field with boundary stones. From there it took the figurative sense “to confine within limits”, as in ~se borner à~ (“to limit oneself to”). The adjective ~borné~ turned that image on the mind itself, describing someone whose outlook is narrow, as if hemmed in by markers.
en.bosser: ~Bosser~ is a slang verb first attested in 1878, probably formed from ~bosse~ (“bump, hump”) plus ~-er~, though the path from “bump” to “work” is uncertain. Sources offer three guesses: that workers bent their backs, forming a hump; that raising an anchor on a ship was the typical hard labor; or that it began as artisans' cant from the sense “to emboss.” French Wiktionary also suggests the English ~boss~ as a base. ~Bosse~ itself comes from Old French ~boce~, which English Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~bottja~.
en.boucher:
From Old French ~bousche~ (“a bundle, a handful of straw, a faggot”), itself from Vulgar Latin *~bosca~ (“brushwood, a bundle of twigs”). The noun is attested in 1461 in the sense “a bundle of hemp,” and by the fourteenth century through its derivative ~bouchon~. The same Vulgar Latin word underlies French ~bois~ and ~bosquet~, and Italian ~bosco~ and Spanish ~bosque~ (“woods”) are its cognates. Despite appearances, the verb has nothing to do with ~bouche~ (“mouth”).

The link between a wisp of straw and plugging a hole is easy to picture: the verb seems to have meant “to stop up with a wisp of straw,” and then simply “to stop up.” From the same noun, ~bouchon~ became the word for a cork or stopper, and ~boucher~ now covers corks, pipes, noses (~se boucher le nez~), views and arteries. The figurative adjective ~bouché~ means “blocked,” and in everyday speech “dim-witted.” ~Déboucher~ is the opposite: to uncork or to emerge into the open. Note that ~boucher~ the noun (“butcher”) is another word entirely, from Old French ~bouchier~, a derivative of ~bouc~ (“he-goat”).
en.boucler: A denominal verb from the fourteenth century, formed from ~boucle~ plus ~-er~: first “to fasten with a buckle,” then “to curl hair into loops,” and in many figurative senses “to close, to wrap up” (finishing a file, shutting a door, locking someone up). The noun is inherited from Latin ~buccula~, the cheek strap of a helmet, a diminutive of ~bucca~ (“cheek, mouth”). The Old French noun also gave English ~buckle~, so the two words are cousins.
en.bouffer: Inherited from Old French ~bouffer~ (“to puff up”), which comes from a Medieval Latin ~buffa~ that seems to imitate the sound and look of puffed-out cheeks. The original idea was inflation: swelling the cheeks or something else with air. The familiar informal sense “to eat” came later, plausibly from the image of cheeks stuffed with food, although the evidence gives only the “puff up” origin and not that step. The noun ~bouffe~ means “food” in the same register, and ~bouffant~ still describes a sleeve or a hairstyle that puffs out.
en.bouger:
From Old French ~bougier~, from Vulgar Latin *~bullicāre~ (“to bubble, seethe, stir”), a frequentative of Latin ~bullīre~ (“to boil, bubble up”). The semantic path is wonderfully concrete: water that boils churns and stirs, and from that ceaseless agitation the sense slid from “to bubble” to “to stir” to simply “to move.” The same root surfaces in Catalan ~bellugar~ and, through Latin ~bullīre~, in French ~bouillir~ (“to boil”) and ~bouillon~ (“broth”).

English, fittingly, borrowed the French verb back as ~budge~ — which, like the negative French idiom, lives chiefly in the negative: nothing will budge, ça ne bouge pas. That narrowing to stubbornness is a quiet comedy of the word: a verb born from the violent churn of a boiling pot now most often denotes the refusal to move at all. From a single image of bubbling water, French drew both the rolling boil of the kitchen and the smallest twitch of a body that will not stay still.
en.bouillir:
From Middle French ~bouillir~, from Old French ~boillir~ (“to boil, to burst”), inherited from Latin ~bullīre~ (“to bubble”), itself derived from ~bulla~ (“bubble, knob, stud”). In Italy and Gaul, ~bullīre~ displaced the older Latin verb ~fervēre~ (“to boil”), which survived on the Iberian Peninsula and in Romania: Spanish ~hervir~, Portuguese ~ferver~ and Romanian ~a fierbe~ are its descendants, while Italian has ~bollire~. English ~boil~ is a French loan from the same Old French verb.

The verb is named after what one sees in a boiling pot: ~bulla~ is a bubble, and ~bullīre~ is to produce bubbles. French drew many words from that picture. ~Bulle~ (“bubble”) is the noun itself, ~bouillon~ is the liquid in which things bubble, ~bouillie~ is a thick cooked mash, and the learned ~ébullition~ comes from the Latin compound ~ēbullīre~. The figurative uses followed naturally, as in ~bouillir de colère~ (“to seethe with anger”) and ~bouillant~ (“fiery, hot-headed”).
en.bouler: ~Bouler~ is a verb formed on the noun ~boule~ (“ball”) plus the ending ~-er~, with the sense of swelling or puffing up into a round shape. The origin of ~boule~ is itself debated: it comes from Old French ~bole~ (“knob”), which is traced either to Latin ~bulla~ (“bubble”), making it a doublet of ~bulle~, or to Frankish *~bollā~ (“ball, bun”), making it a doublet of ~bol~.
en.bouleverser:
~bouleverser~ is not inherited Latin but homemade Renaissance French: first recorded in 1557 as ~boulverser~ in the poet Belleau, it welds together ~bouler~ (“to send rolling like a ball,” from ~boule~, from Latin ~bulla~, “bubble, round boss”) and ~verser~ (“to tip over, to overturn,” from Latin ~versāre~, frequentative of ~vertere~, “to turn”). Philologists call it a tautological compound: both halves mean “to knock over,” so the verb says it twice. The halves carry deep roots. ~vertere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”), the root of German ~werden~ (“to become” — a turning-into) and of the English suffix ~-ward~ (“turned toward”); Latin ~bulla~ named anything round and swollen, from a water bubble to the boss on a door.

For its first decades the verb stayed purely physical — walls, fortifications, furniture turned upside down. In 1622 it reached politics — to throw a kingdom into disorder — and with Pascal's Provinciales in the 1650s it crossed into the soul: to trouble someone profoundly. That inner sense conquered the language: today a piece of news bouleverse you long before any furniture falls, and ~bouleversant~ and ~bouleversement~ belong above all to emotion. The parent families thrived on their own. From ~bulla~ French gets ~bulle~ — the soap bubble, but also the papal bull, sealed with a round leaden boss — and ~bulletin~, originally a little sealed note, today the ballot in the box. From ~vertere~ come ~version~, ~vertige~, ~renverser~ and ~univers~ — the universe being, literally, everything “turned into one.” To be bouleversé is, etymologically, to be sent rolling and tipped over — an image French speakers can still feel.
en.bourrer: Both Wiktionaries derive ~bourrer~ from the noun ~bourre~ (“stuffing, padding, wadding”): to stuff a cushion or a pipe is to fill it with stuffing, and the verb then stretched to cramming anything full, up to force-feeding someone. French Wiktionary adds that the verb first appears in the sense of mistreating or roughing someone up, which it links to Old French ~burir~ (“to rush, to charge”, also written ~bourrir~). The sources do not connect these two lines, so the origin of that violent sense should be treated as uncertain. The stuffing image survives in idioms such as ~bourrer le crâne~ (“to fill someone's head with nonsense”).
en.bousculer:
French Wiktionary favors a blend: ~bousculer~ is said to cross Middle French ~bousser~ (“to strike, knock”) with ~culer~ (“to walk backwards”). It rejects the older explanation, an Old French ~bouteculer~ (“to search by turning things over”) built from ~bouter~, ~cul~ and ~-er~. Middle French ~bousser~ was widespread in Lorraine and Franco-Provençal territory, and is said to be borrowed from Middle High German ~bōzen~ (“to strike”), to which regional German ~boßen~ (“to beat”) is related. It corresponds to the French verb ~bouter~ (“to push”). ~Culer~ comes from ~cul~, the French word for the backside.

The account is therefore of a word half Germanic and half French, though the choice between the two origins is a matter of competing proposals, and the blend is the one the source prefers. The sense is compatible with such a blend, striking joined to backing away. The meaning spread from physical jostling to disturbing an order, a schedule or an assumption, as in ~bousculer les habitudes~. Related words include ~bousculade~ (“a crush, a jostling crowd”) and, on the ~cul~ side, ~reculer~ and ~acculer~ (“to back up, to corner”), whose stems ~-culer~ and ~cul~ are the same one that appears here.
en.boycotter: From the English verb ~boycott~, with the French ending ~-er~ added to the borrowed word. English took it from the surname of Captain Charles ~Boycott~, an Irish land agent whom tenants and neighbors shunned in 1880 during a rent dispute. He was cut off from labor, trade and even the post, and his name became a verb for any such organized refusal to deal with someone. French borrowed it soon afterward, first as the noun ~boycott~ and then as the verb ~boycotter~. It is one of the few French verbs named for a single person's misfortune. It now covers politics, trade and elections.
en.brancher:
Modern French ~brancher~ is a denominal verb built directly on the noun ~branche~ (“branch”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~branche~ descends from Late Latin ~branca~ (“paw, claw”), a word the dictionaries flag as of uncertain origin: by one account it goes back to a hypothetical Gaulish *~vranca~, and through it to a Proto-Indo-European *~wronk-~ related to Proto-Balto-Slavic *~ranka~ (“hand, arm”), though the Latin form may also have been colored by ~bracchium~ (“arm”). Cognates of ~branca~ survive across Romance — Italian ~branca~, Occitan and Catalan forms — and German ~Pranke~ (“paw”) was borrowed from the same family.

The path from “paw” to “branch” runs through the image of a limb spreading out from a trunk, and ~brancher~ inherited that branching idea. Its modern senses fan out accordingly: to “branch,” to “connect” one thing to another (as a wire is plugged into a circuit), and colloquially to “turn (someone) on” to a topic. From the same noun French built ~branchage~ (“boughs”), ~embrancher~ and ~embranchement~ (“to join, junction”), ~débrancher~ (“to unplug”), and ~brindille~ stands nearby in the same arboreal field. The English ~branch~ comes, through Old French, from the very same ~branca~.
en.brandir:
French ~brandir~ comes from Old French ~brandir~, formed on ~brand~ (“sword”), which French Wiktionary derives from Germanic ~brand~ (“firebrand, burning log”). English Wiktionary only records the verb as inherited from Middle and Old French. The Germanic word has close cousins: English ~brand~ (originally a burning piece of wood, hence the later sense of a mark burned into skin) and German ~Brand~ (“fire”). Italian ~brando~ (“sword”) is a related word.

The sources do not say how “burning log” came to mean “sword,” and this entry does not guess. French Wiktionary points the reader to ~branler~ (“to shake, to wobble”) and ~brandon~ (“torch, firebrand”) as relatives of the same word. The modern verb ~brandir~ means to wave a weapon, a flag or a document, in a threatening or triumphant way. English borrowed it as ~brandish~, from the stem ~brandiss-~ of the French verb.
en.branler:
French ~branler~ is an old contraction. Middle French ~bransler~ came from Old French ~bransler~ (“to shake, to move”), itself a shortened form of ~brandeler~ (“to wobble”). That verb is built on Old French ~brant~ (“sword blade, big sword”), which French Wiktionary traces to a Germanic ~brand~ (“firebrand”). English Wiktionary gives the route through Vulgar Latin *~brandus~ (“firebrand, flaming sword, sword”), ultimately from Frankish *~brand~ (“sword”), from Proto-Germanic *~brandaz~ (“burning, flash, firebrand, flaming sword”). A Late Latin step *~brandulare~ has sometimes been proposed as the go-between, but English Wiktionary finds it unlikely, since the suffix ~-ulāre~ was no longer productive when the word was borrowed.

The chain of forms points to a weapon: a sword, ~brant~, lies behind ~brandeler~ (“to wobble”) and ~bransler~ (“to shake (a sword at), move”), and the modern verb means “to shake.” The step from ~brandeler~ to ~bransler~ contracts the word, and the spelling later lost its s, giving ~branler~. Related words keep the full root: ~brandir~ (“to brandish”), which English Wiktionary tells us to compare with English ~brandish~, and ~brandon~ (“firebrand”). In very vulgar slang ~branler~ also has a well-known sexual sense, which learners should be wary of.
en.braquer:
The origin of ~braquer~ is uncertain, and the sources do not agree on how firmly to speak. fr.Wiktionary offers, with the hedge “probably,” a Vulgar Latin verb *~brachitāre~ (“to set in motion with the arms”), derived from Latin ~bracchium~ (“arm”), which was itself borrowed from Greek ~brakhíōn~. en.Wiktionary simply says the origin is uncertain, so the Latin link should be read as a proposal and not as settled fact. The Vulgar Latin verb is a reconstruction, never attested in writing. If the proposal is right, the idea behind ~braquer~ is of turning or aiming something by means of the arm.

The meanings fit that picture. ~Braquer~ was first to aim, to point something in a given direction, as one does with a telescope, a camera or a firearm. The motorist’s sense, to turn the steering wheel sharply, comes from the same idea of swinging round, and a ~braquage~ is the turning circle. In slang, to ~braquer~ a bank is to hold it up at gunpoint, and the figurative reflexive ~se braquer~ is to dig in one’s heels, so that a ~braqué~ person has turned all their defenses against you. If the Latin source holds, French ~bras~ (“arm”), ~brasse~, ~embrasser~ (“to embrace”) and ~brassard~ (“armband”) are its relatives.
en.brasser:
From Old French ~bracier~, from ~brace~ (“malt”), which comes from Gaulish ~bracis~, Latinized as ~bracem~ by Pliny. French Wiktionary gives the Vulgar Latin intermediate as *~braciare~. The Gaulish word goes back to Proto-Celtic *~mrakis~ and, by the Wiktionary account, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~merk-~ (“to be soaked”). Celtic cousins are Scottish Gaelic ~braich~ and Welsh ~brag~, and outside Celtic the same root is compared with Latin ~marcēre~ (“to wither, droop”) and Lithuanian ~mer̃kti~ (“to soak”). The original sense is thus close to “to ferment” or “to steep.”

The spelling is a trap. Because the word does not come from ~bras~ (“arm”), the true spelling would be ~bracer~, as it was once written, though ~bras~ influenced the verb in some of its senses. A second account treats ~brasser~ instead as a denominal of ~bras~ or ~brasse~, so the origin is not beyond dispute, although the Gaulish derivation is the one French Wiktionary gives first. French Wiktionary links the root to ~braise~ in the sense of “spent grain” and to ~brai~.
en.braver: Formed from the adjective ~brave~ (“courageous”) with the verb-forming ending ~-er~: “to treat as brave,” hence to challenge or defy, to face a danger boldly. French ~brave~ was probably borrowed from Italian ~bravo~ rather than from Spanish ~bravo~ (“wild”), and the Italian word is itself taken to be a loan from Occitan ~brau~. English ~brave~ and its doublet ~bravo~ come from the same Romance source.
en.breveter: Formed from the noun ~brevet~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: to grant, or to take out, a patent. The noun is usually explained as ~brève~ (a short official letter, from Latin ~brevis~, “short”) plus the diminutive suffix ~-et~, a letter short enough to carry a royal grant or privilege, and the word later came to mean any official certificate. The lexicographer Pihan proposed instead an Arabic origin, from a word for a diploma conferring a right, but the Latin account is the standard one.
en.bricoler: ~Bricoler~ is formed from the noun ~bricole~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun appeared as ~brigole~ and then ~bricole~, borrowed from Italian ~briccola~, a kind of catapult launched by the swing of a beam. By the end of the Middle Ages, the phrase ~mettre en la bricole~ meant “to deceive.” Later, once the catapult had become obsolete as a weapon, ~bricole~ took the sense of an indirect, clever means, and the verb ~bricoler~ grew from that idea: to manage by roundabout, ingenious methods, and so to tinker. The ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~.
en.brider: ~Brider~ is formed from the noun ~bride~ (“bridle, rein”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun came from Old French, which took it from Middle High German ~brīdel~, from Old High German ~brīdil~. A related Old High German form, ~brittil~, gave French ~bretelle~, and the word is cognate with English ~bridle~. The verb first meant “to put a bridle on,” as with a horse, and then “to hold back,” as in ~brider ses émotions~. It is also used in cooking, where a bird is ~bridée~, trussed, before roasting, and in ~yeux bridés~, narrow, tight-drawn eyes.
en.briller:
From Italian ~brillare~ (“to shine; also to beat the wings, to quiver”), borrowed into French around 1559. The Italian word's own origin is genuinely disputed, and the sources hedge: by one account it is a variant of Italian ~prillare~ (“to spin, to whirl”); by another it descends from Latin ~beryllus~ (“beryl,” the gemstone), in the sense “to shine like a beryl.” Littré favored the gemstone, but conceded it fails to explain the older “quiver, dart about” meaning — so the question stays open.

The semantic history is the surprising part. In its earliest French life ~briller~ did not mean “to shine” at all: it meant to be restless, to dart and quiver — a sense now obsolete except in old hunting language for an agitated dog. The luminous meaning, today the only one, seems to have grown out of that trembling motion, the way a flickering, jittering light scintillates (compare the link between English ~flick~ and ~flicker~). From the bright sense comes the whole modern family — ~brillant~ (“brilliant, shiny”), ~brillance~, ~briller de mille feux~ — and the wry idiom ~briller par son absence~ (“to be conspicuous by one's absence”).
en.briser:
From Old French ~brisier~, from Late Latin ~brisāre~ (“to crush, press”), widely held to be of Gaulish origin, from a Celtic *~brissu~ (“to shatter, break”). The Celtic connection is supported by cognates such as Irish ~bris~ (“to break”) and Breton ~bresk~ (“fragile”), ~brien~ (“crumbs”) and ~bruzun~ (“fragments”). The verb is thus one of the Gaulish substrate words that survived the Roman conquest beneath the Latin of Gaul.

Notably, ~briser~ displaced the older Old French ~fraindre~ (from Latin ~frangere~, “to break”), which has otherwise left only learned derivatives like ~fraction~ and ~fragment~. From the concrete sense of smashing, ~briser~ grew a rich figurative life: ~briser la glace~ (“to break the ice”), ~briser le cœur~ (“to break someone's heart”), and the cry of a wrecked spirit. Its descendants name the things that break or break things — ~brisure~, ~débris~, ~brisant~ (a breaker, a reef), and the compounds ~brise-glace~ (“icebreaker”) and ~brise-lame~ (“breakwater”).
en.broder:
From Old French ~brosder~ (later ~broder~), a word of Germanic origin. French Wiktionary derives it from Old Low Franconian *~brosdôn~, which it analyzes as ~borst~ (“bristle”) combined with *~brordôn~ (“to embroider”). It points to German ~Borste~ (“bristle”) and to Old Saxon ~brordôn~ (“to embroider, decorate”) and ~brord~ (“needle”). English Wiktionary gives a simpler line, a Proto-Germanic verb *~bruzdōną~ passing into Old French, without the compound. The two accounts agree on a Germanic source but differ on how it was built. Either way, ~broder~ is a Germanic loan hiding behind a French shape, with no Latin ancestor.

In French the verb meant to decorate cloth with needle and thread, and ~broder~ still does. From that came a figure: ~broder une histoire~ means to embellish a tale with invented detail, as thread embellishes plain fabric. The family includes ~broderie~ (“embroidery”), ~brodeur~ and ~brodeuse~ (“embroiderer”). The Old Saxon word for “needle” suits the craft well, but the sources do not say how the Frankish word came to mean needlework.
en.bronzer: ~Bronzer~ is formed from ~bronze~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~bronzo~, the alloy of copper and tin. The verb first meant “to give the colour or finish of bronze,” as when a statue or an object is coated or tinted to look like it. From there came the sense of turning the skin the same warm brown, so that ~bronzer~ today usually means “to tan,” as one does in the sun.
en.brosser: Formed from the noun ~brosse~ (“brush”) and the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary adds that in Old French ~brosse~ also meant “brushwood, undergrowth,” and it uses this to explain an older sense of ~brosser~, “to dash through thick woods,” and the colloquial ~tu peux te brosser~, “you can go without” (literally, “you can brush yourself”). The everyday sense of brushing clothes, hair or teeth is the one that now dominates. The two senses of the noun, the tool and the thicket, are not shown to be connected here, so the ordinary reading remains simply “to work on something with a ~brosse~.”
en.brouiller:
From Old French ~brouiller~, from Vulgar Latin *~brodiculāre~ (French Wiktionary says Gallo-Romance), itself built on *~brodicāre~, from Late Latin ~brodium~ (“broth, stew, mixture”), which was borrowed from Proto-Germanic *~bruþą~ (“stock, broth”). Lombard ~brodigar~ (“to soil, to pollute”) is a comparison offered for the intermediate verb. The Germanic word is also the source of English ~broth~. French Wiktionary places the verb beside ~bruir~ (“to steam”), Old French ~bruller~ (“to burn”) and English ~broil~ and ~brew~, and explains the noun ~brouillard~ (“fog,” properly “vapor”) in the same way. These are comparisons to note, not steps in the chain, which is why the entry does not claim the verb comes from any of them.

A rival explanation, mentioned by Littré, connects the verb with Old Occitan ~bruelhar~ (“to sprout”) and Catalan ~brollar~ (“to gush”). French Wiktionary rejects it, since it cannot account for the three-syllable forms of the word in Old French. The word also left France and came back: Italian borrowed it as ~brogliare~, ~imbrogliare~ and ~sbrogliare~, and French took it back in the form ~imbroglio~. The safest reading is that ~brouiller~ descends from ~brodium~, with ~bruir~, ~broil~ and ~brew~ left as possible relatives. The earliest sense of the verb is not given in the evidence.
en.broyer:
French ~broyer~ is a Germanic word in Romance clothing. English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French ~broier~ and Old French ~breier~ (“to break”) to Frankish *~brekan~ (“to break”), from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰreg-~ (“to break”). French Wiktionary adds an intermediate step, a Vulgar Latin *~brecāre~ that Romance speakers fashioned from the Frankish verb. The cognates are plentiful: English ~break~, German ~brechen~, Old English ~brecan~, Spanish ~bregar~ (“to toil, to deal with”) and Italian ~sbrigare~ (“to sort out”).

The Old French verb meant simply “to break,” and French later narrowed it to breaking something into very small pieces, which is to say crushing or grinding. ~Broyer~ now covers the mortar and pestle, the mill and the industrial crusher, with the nouns ~broyeur~ (“grinder”) and ~broyage~ (“grinding”). The figurative idiom ~broyer du noir~ (“to brood”) literally grinds black, an image of the mind working over dark thoughts. The English cousin ~break~, from the same Germanic root, keeps the broad original sense.
en.brunir: The verb already existed in Old French, where ~brunir~ meant “to polish, make brown”, and it descends from Middle French.
