It is a derivative of the adjective ~brun~ with the verb ending ~-ir~. The adjective comes from Late Latin ~brūnus~, borrowed from Frankish *~brūn~ (“brown, shiny”), from Proto-Germanic *~brūnaz~, which is cognate with English ~brown~ and German ~braun~. That old double sense, brown and gleaming, explains why ~brunir~ means both “to tan” and “to burnish metal”. English ~burnish~ comes from a variant of the same Old French verb.
en.brûler:
Attested as Old French ~bruller~ (around 1120), later ~brusler~, then modern ~brûler~ — the circumflex marking the lost ~s~. The deeper origin is genuinely debated. The favoured account makes it an intensified form of Old French ~usler~ (“to scorch”), from Latin ~ustulāre~ (“to singe, scorch slightly”), a diminutive of ~ūrere~ (“to burn”). But several sources may have contributed and the matter is unsettled: a Frankish element *~brōjan~ (“to scald, sear”, source of Old French ~bruir~), the Latin participles ~ambustus~ and ~combustus~, and a Gaulish cognate of Old Irish ~bruth~ (“burning heat”) have each been proposed as shaping the ~br-~. Italian ~bruciare~ is comparably murky.

Whatever its tangle of roots, ~brûler~ settled as the ordinary French word for burning, literal and figurative. It heats idiom richly: ~brûler les étapes~ (“to skip the stages,” rush ahead), ~brûler la politesse~ (to leave abruptly), ~brûler ses vaisseaux~ (to burn one's boats). From it French built ~brûlure~ (“a burn”), ~brûlant~ (“burning, scalding”), ~brûleur~, and the blunt phrase ~à brûle-pourpoint~ (“point-blank”). The competing etymologies make the verb itself a small monument to how messily a common word can be assembled.
en.buter: From Old French ~buter~ (“to push, to strike”), a variant of ~bouter~ (“to push”). The sense “to bump into, to come up against” (~buter contre~) continues that old idea of pushing. The slang sense “to kill” is tied by French Wiktionary to the noun ~but~ (“goal, target”), though the sources do not detail the steps. The verb is related to ~bouter~ and to words such as ~butée~ (“abutment, stop”), ~rebuter~ and ~débouter~.
en.butter: ~Butter~ is formed from ~butte~ (“mound”) with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Butte~ is itself recorded as a variant, the feminine form, of ~but~ (“aim, target”). The verb is used in gardening: to ~butter~ potatoes or leeks is to heap earth up around the base of the plants in a little mound. The ending ~-er~ is the usual first-conjugation ending, the descendant of Latin ~-are~, here turning a noun into a verb meaning “to provide with” or “to work with” that noun.
en.bâtir:
From Old French ~bastir~ (“to baste, to interweave”), from Old Low Frankish *~bastjan~ (“to assemble, to interlace fibers”), from a Proto-Germanic root meaning bast, the fibrous inner bark used for tying and weaving. The word is cognate with German ~Bast~ and Dutch ~bast~ (“bast, inner bark”). The circumflex of ~bâtir~ marks a lost ~s~ that the older spelling ~bastir~ still showed.

The development is a small lesson in how houses were once made. From the sense “to weave, to lash together with bast,” the word moved to “to make a fence of stakes interwoven with branches,” the wattle of early construction, and from there simply to “to build, to erect.” French thus reached its grand modern verb — ~bâtir~ une maison, une cathédrale, une fortune — from a humble word for tying plant fibers together. (The competing guess that linked it to ~bât~, “packsaddle,” or ~bâton~, “stick,” is rejected by the TLFi.) The Frankish origin left a compact French family: ~bâtiment~ (“building”), ~bâtisse~ (“edifice”), ~bâtisseur~ (“builder”), and ~rebâtir~ (“to rebuild”) — all standing on a foundation of woven bast. The older sewing sense survives separately in ~bâtir~ meaning “to tack, to baste” cloth.
en.bénir:
From Old French ~beneïr~, inherited from Latin ~benedīcere~, a compound of ~bene~ (“well”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say”), so literally “to speak well of.” Latin ~dīcere~ is the everyday verb of speaking that gave French ~dire~. Its sister ~maledīcere~ (“to speak ill of”) gave ~maudire~, which makes ~bénir~ and ~maudire~ a matched pair of blessing and cursing. The Latin verb lived on across the Romance languages: Italian ~benedire~ and Spanish ~bendecir~ are its cognates, and English ~benediction~ is a learned borrowing from the related Latin noun ~benedictio~.

The meaning stayed close to the Latin, in a religious setting: a priest or a parent calls down divine favor on someone or something. Figuratively, one ~bénit~ a person or a day for which one is grateful, as in the phrase “je bénis le jour où…”. French keeps two participles. ~Béni~ is the ordinary one, while ~bénit~ survives only for things consecrated by a priest, as in ~eau bénite~ (“holy water”) and ~pain bénit~ (“consecrated bread”). The family is still large: ~bénédiction~ and ~bénédicité~ (the prayer before a meal, from Latin ~benedicite~, “bless ye”) come straight from the Latin, and the given name ~Benoît~ descends from Latin ~Benedictus~ (“blessed”).
en.bénéficier:
From the noun ~bénéfice~, itself from Latin ~beneficium~ (“a kindness, favor, service”); the verb mirrors Medieval Latin ~beneficiāre~ (“to grant a benefice to”). ~Beneficium~ is built from ~bene~ (“well”) and a combining form of ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), so it means literally “a thing well done.” ~Facere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, put, place”), shared with English ~do~ and ~deed~ and with Greek ~títhēmi~ (“I place”). Romance kin include Italian ~beneficiare~ and Spanish ~beneficiar~.

The Latin word named an act of generosity, a good turn done for another. In the Middle Ages the Church narrowed ~beneficium~ to a very specific gift: a ~bénéfice~ became an endowed ecclesiastical post and the income that came with it — a clergyman’s living. From that benefit-as-income the word broadened back out to commercial profit and, in the verb ~bénéficier~, to the general sense “to enjoy, to profit from” an advantage. The ~bene-~ element survives in ~bénir~ (“to bless”), ~bénévole~ (“volunteer,” literally “well-wishing”), and ~bienfait~ (“good deed”); the ~facere~ element seeds a teeming family — ~faire~, ~défaire~, ~parfait~, ~bienfaiteur~, and the everyday ~bénéfice~ itself.
en.cacher:
From Old French ~cachier~ (also ~quachier~), from Vulgar Latin *~coacticare~ (“to compress, to press together”), a frequentative formed on Latin ~coactare~ (“to constrain, to force”), itself from ~cogere~ (“to drive together, to compel,” from ~co-~ + ~agere~, “to drive”). Through ~cogere~ the verb is cognate with Italian ~quattare~ and with the French doublet ~cacher~ beside the learned ~coaguler~.

The original idea was purely physical: to press or squeeze something down. The path to “to hide” runs through that pressing — what is pressed flat or tucked away is concealed — and the sense “to hide” stayed comparatively rare until the 16th century, when ~cacher~ rose to displace older rivals for concealment such as ~musser~, ~esconser~, and ~repondre~. The pressing sense survives in the cousin ~écacher~ (“to crush, to flatten”). From the same Latin ~cogere~ family French keeps ~cachette~ (“hiding place”), ~cache~, ~cache-cache~ (the game “hide-and-seek”), ~cachot~ (“dungeon”), and ~cachotterie~ (“a small secret”) — a whole nest of words for hiding spun out of an ancient verb meaning, of all things, “to squeeze.”
en.cadrer:
French ~cadrer~ goes back to Latin ~quadrāre~ (“to make square, to fit, to agree”), from ~quadrus~ (“square”), a relative of ~quattuor~ (“four”), from the Proto-Indo-European word *~kʷetwóres~ (“four”). The sources describe it in two ways: one calls it a borrowing from Latin, the other a verb built on ~cadre~ (“frame”). The two views are compatible, since ~cadre~ itself reached French from Italian ~quadro~, from Latin ~quadrum~ (“square”). Italian ~quadrare~ and Spanish ~cuadrar~ are parallel descendants of ~quadrāre~, and ~carrer~ is a doublet of ~cadrer~: the same Latin verb arriving by another route.

The earliest idea is geometric: to ~cadrer~ is to square one thing to another so that the two line up. From there French drew the figurative sense “to agree with, to be consistent”, as in cela cadre avec ce que je sais (“that fits what I know”). The sense “to frame” a photograph or a shot is a second development, probably drawn from the noun ~cadre~, and it likely explains why speakers now feel the verb as derived from ~cadre~. The family also includes ~carré~ (“square”), ~carreau~, ~équarrir~ and ~quadrature~.
en.calculer:
From Latin ~calculāre~ (“to reckon, compute”), from ~calculus~, the diminutive of ~calx~ (“limestone, pebble”). A ~calculus~ was a small stone — and specifically the little counters that Romans pushed along the grooves of an ~abacus~ to do sums. To calculate was, literally, to move pebbles. ~Calx~ is perhaps borrowed from Greek ~khálix~ (“gravel, small stone”), though the connection is uncertain. Italian ~calcolare~ and Spanish ~calcular~ share the root.

The charm of this etymology is how it fossilizes an ancient counting board inside a word for abstract arithmetic: every calculation still carries, etymologically, a handful of pebbles. The same ~calculus~ gives medicine its sense of a “stone” formed in the body — a kidney ~calculus~ — and gives mathematics the ~calculus~ of Newton and Leibniz, the supreme reckoning. French keeps ~calcul~ (both “calculation” and the medical “stone”), ~calculer~, ~calculateur~, and ~calculatrice~. From the parent ~calx~ in its limestone sense also descend ~chaux~ (“lime”) and ~calcaire~ (“limestone, calcareous”), so the humble pebble underlies both arithmetic and the white cliffs of chalk.
en.caler:
French has more than one verb ~caler~, of two different origins, and the senses asked about belong to the second. The older ~caler~ (attested around 1165, “to lower a sail”) comes from Old Occitan ~calar~ (“to lower”), traced to Ancient Greek ~khaláō~ (“to slacken, lower the mast”); the TLFi notes this sense is unattested in Latin and survives directly from the Greek in the Mediterranean nautical world. From “lower the sails” it drifted figuratively to “to yield, back down,” and to an engine that ~cale~ — stalls and dies.

The ~caler~ of “to wedge, to jam, to immobilize” is a separate, denominal verb built on the noun ~cale~ (“wedge, chock”). The deeper origin of that ~cale~ is uncertain: en.Wiktionary derives the wedge-sense ~cale~ — by one account — from German ~Keil~ (“wedge”), a hypothesis worth flagging rather than asserting. From wedging an object steady the verb took its everyday meanings: to chock a wheel, to prop something firm, to ~se caler~ comfortably in an armchair, and colloquially to be ~calé~ — well-fixed, hence “clued-up, expert.” Relatives include ~décaler~, ~recaler~, and the noun ~calage~.
en.calmer: Formed from the noun ~calme~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, although English Wiktionary also allows that the verb may be borrowed directly from Italian ~calmare~. The noun comes, by one account, from Occitan ~cauma~ (“heat, calm”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~kaûma~ (“heat”). English Wiktionary instead prefers a path through Italian ~calma~, or possibly an Iberian language, from the same Greek word. Either way, the root meant scorching heat before it meant stillness. The older Occitan verb ~caumar~ gave French ~chômer~ (“to stop working”) as a doublet of ~calmer~, and ~chômer~ is the earlier of the two in French.
en.calquer: A borrowing from Italian ~calcare~ (“to press, to tread”), from Latin ~calcāre~ (“to tread”). The sense developed from pressing on a drawing to transfer it onto another sheet, which is “tracing,” and then to any close copying: one ~calque~ a model, an attitude, a plan. The noun ~calque~ is linked to the verb, but the sources disagree about which came first: French sources derive the noun from Italian ~calco~, while English Wiktionary derives it from ~calquer~. Either way, both lead to the same Latin ~calcāre~. The same Latin verb also gave French ~inculquer~, “to stamp in.”
en.camer: Formed from the noun ~came~ and the ending ~-er~, so “to dope oneself,” most often in the pronominal form ~se camer~. The noun ~came~ is a clipping of ~camelote~ (“junk, shoddy goods”) according to both Wiktionaries, which then took the slang sense of “drug.” It is unrelated to the homonym ~came~ (“cam of a wheel”), borrowed from Germanic. The underlying idea is that of cheap stuff, which is exactly what the slang word first suggested.
en.camper: The origin is uncertain, and the one source available gives two accounts. By one, ~camper~ is simply a verb formed on the noun ~camp~. By the other, it is a Latinising reworking, based on Latin ~campus~ (“field”), of Old French ~champier~ (“to range over the fields, to camp”), a verb that also produced ~champer~; in that case ~camper~ may be the Picard form of that older word. Either way the root is ~campus~, the Latin “field,” and the sense is that of settling on open ground. French also uses ~camper~ figuratively, as in ~camper sur ses positions~ (“to stand one's ground”).
en.canaliser: Formed from the noun ~canal~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to provide with”). The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~canālis~ (“pipe, channel”), and it is a doublet of ~chenal~, the form of the same Latin word that was inherited and worn down in speech. To ~canaliser~ is first to provide a river with canals or to put it into a channel, then, figuratively, to direct energy, anger or a crowd along a single path.
en.caner: ~Caner~ is formed from ~cane~ with the ending ~-er~, from the expression ~faire la cane~, literally “to act like a duck,” which was used of someone who ducks out or backs down. The sense “to die” is slang that grew from the same verb. The origin of ~cane~ itself is explained in two ways. French Wiktionary treats it as a back-formation from ~canard~ with the suffix dropped, while English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French and Old French to a Germanic word for “boat,” Middle Low German ~kane~, whose cognates include German ~Kahn~. The sources disagree here.
en.cantonner: Formed in French from the noun ~canton~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense “to station troops in a district”, then “to confine to a limited area”. The noun ~canton~ comes from Old Occitan ~canton~ (“corner, canton”), which was adopted from a northern Italian form ~cantone~ (“edge, corner”), ultimately built on a Latin ~cant-~ (“rim”) with an augmentative ending. By one proposal that French Wiktionary mentions, the Italian word may have a Gaulish source meaning “circle”. A soldier ~cantonné~ is posted to his corner of the map.
en.capitaliser: Formed in French from ~capital~ and the suffix ~-iser~, with the sense “to turn into capital, to accumulate.” The base ~capital~ comes from Latin ~capitālis~ (“of the head”), from ~caput~ (“head”). In the financial sense, French Wiktionary suggests it is either the adjective used as a noun or a borrowing, by way of Lombard bankers, from Italian ~capitale~ (thirteenth century), the “main sum” on which interest accrues. The word ~capital~ is also the learned doublet of Old French ~chatel~, which survives in ~cheptel~ (“livestock”): the “head” of wealth became both money and cattle.
en.capter:
Borrowed in the 15th century from Latin ~captāre~ (“to try to seize, to grasp at, to angle for”), the frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Italic *~kapjō~, from PIE *~kh₂pyéti~, root *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”) — the root that also gave English ~heave~ and German ~heben~. Latin capere spread through Romance: Italian ~capire~ came to mean “to understand” (to grasp!), Spanish ~caber~ “to fit.” French, meanwhile, had already inherited the family twice in popular form before borrowing capter from the books: Vulgar Latin *~captiāre~ became ~chasser~ (“to hunt”) — and, through Norman ~cachier~ and Old French ~chacier~, the English doublets ~catch~ and ~chase~ — while *~accaptare~ became ~acheter~ (“to buy”): hunting, catching, chasing and shopping, all one verb of seizing.

In Latin, ~captāre~ was the verb of hunters, anglers — and flatterers. Orators practiced the ~captātiō benevolentiae~, the ritual “capture of the audience's goodwill”; Horace mocked Rome's legacy-hunters, whose art was ~captāre testāmenta~, “to angle for wills” — and French law still calls inheritance-grabbing by undue influence ~captation~. Hence the verb's first French sense, to win by insinuation (15th century): for centuries capter kept a faintly sinister air. Engineering redeemed it: from 1863 one collects the waters of a spring (~capter une source~); the 20th century added radio — ~capter une station~, ~capter des ondes~ — then attention itself, ~capter l'attention~. Familiar French has even rejoined Italian capire: ~tu captes ?~ — “you get it?” The wider family: ~captif~, ~captiver~, ~capture~, ~capable~, plus the great verbs in ~-cevoir~ — ~recevoir~, ~percevoir~, ~concevoir~, ~décevoir~ — from Latin compounds of capere in ~-cipere~.
en.capturer:
A relatively recent and learned formation: ~capturer~ is derived inside French from the noun ~capture~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~Capture~ in turn comes from Latin ~captūra~ (“a catching, a taking”), a noun built on ~captus~, the past participle of ~capere~ (“to seize, take”). That verb descends from Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ and from PIE *~keh₂p-~ (“to seize, grasp”). Through this root Latin ~capere~ is cognate with English ~have~ and ~heave~ (both from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~) and with Ancient Greek ~κάπτω~ (~káptō~, “to gulp down”).

French long expressed “to catch” with native verbs like ~prendre~ and ~saisir~; ~capturer~ entered later as a more technical, deliberate word — to capture a fugitive, a fortress, an animal, an image. Because it was built on the noun rather than inherited directly, it carries the clean Latin stem ~capt-~ rather than a worn-down popular form. The same ~capere~ seeds a vast family in French: ~captif~, ~captiver~, ~captivité~, ~capable~, ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~, ~capacité~, and ~occuper~. English drew from the same well with ~captive~, ~capture~, and ~capable~.
en.caractériser:
From the noun ~caractère~ plus the suffix ~-iser~. ~Caractère~ comes from Latin ~character~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~χαρακτήρ~ (~kharaktḗr~), an “engraved mark, stamp, distinctive impression,” derived from ~χαράσσω~ (~kharássō~, “to engrave, scratch, sharpen”). Originally the word named both the engraver's tool and the mark it cut — a stamped sign that set one thing apart from another. The suffix ~-iser~ descends from Latin ~-izāre~, from Greek ~-ίζειν~ (~-ízein~), the ending behind English ~-ize~.

The semantic arc is elegant: a physical ~mark~ engraved on metal or wax became the figurative “stamp” of a personality, then the sum of traits defining a person, and finally any distinguishing feature at all. To ~caractériser~ is thus to identify the mark that sets something apart — to pin down its defining trait. The Greek root left French a sizeable family: ~caractère~, ~caractéristique~, ~caractérisation~, and ~caractériel~. English ~character~, ~characteristic~, and ~characterize~ are the exact cousins, and even the typographic ~character~ on a screen preserves the original sense of an engraved, distinctive sign.
en.caresser: Borrowed from Italian ~carezzare~ (“to cherish”), and also analyzable in French as the noun ~caresse~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~caresse~ was itself borrowed from Italian ~carezza~, which belongs to the family of ~caro~ (“dear”). The sense is thus “to treat as dear”: from cherishing, the verb came to mean touching or stroking tenderly, and by extension “to toy with” an idea or a hope. The ending ~-er~ is the usual first-conjugation ending, from Latin ~-are~.
en.carrer:
From Latin ~quadrāre~ (“to make square, to fit”), attested in French from the twelfth century. The Latin verb comes from ~quadrus~ (“square”), itself from ~quattuor~ (“four”), and so from the PIE numeral *~kʷetwóres~ (“four”). Through that root ~carrer~ is a distant cognate of English ~four~, Ancient Greek ~téssares~ and Sanskrit ~catur~ — and a near relative of every learned ~quadr-~ word in French. A separate, regional ~carrer~ meaning “to put, to place” is, by one account, borrowed from Occitan ~carrar~.

The literal sense is geometric — to ~carrer~ a stone or a number is to square it — but the verb's liveliest life is reflexive. ~Se carrer~ once meant to walk squarely, with a broad and self-important bearing, and came to mean to settle oneself comfortably and squarely into a chair. From the same Latin root descend ~carré~ (“square”), ~carreau~ (“tile, pane”), ~carrefour~ (“crossroads,” a place where four ways meet), ~équarrir~ and the borrowed ~quadrant~.
en.cartographier:
~cartographier~ is a young verb built on an old word: it derives from ~cartographie~ (~carte~ plus the suffix ~-graphie~, from Greek ~gráphein~, “to write”), and is first recorded in 1906. ~carte~ itself was borrowed from Latin ~charta~ (“a sheet of papyrus prepared for writing,” hence “a written document”), which Latin had taken from Ancient Greek ~χάρτης~ (~khártēs~). The same Latin word reached French twice: through its diminutive ~chartula~ came ~charte~, attested in the eleventh century, so ~carte~ and ~charte~ are doublets. Italian ~carta~ and Spanish ~carta~ continue the same noun, and Old French ~carte~ gave English both ~chart~ and ~card~.

The Greek source is a dead end for etymologists: ~khártēs~ was long derived from ~kharássō~ (“to scratch, to inscribe”), but Beekes and Chantraine both reject that link and treat the word’s origin as unknown — one proposal makes it a Phoenician borrowing, but the question is unsettled. The French coinage is better documented: ~cartographie~ first appears in 1832 in the hellenizing spelling ~chartographie~, closer to Greek ~khártēs~ than to French ~carte~, and the modern spelling follows in 1838, though the ~ch-~ form was still being recorded in the 1860s. The verb waited nearly seventy years more and arrived only in 1906 — mapping was a discipline long before it was something one simply did. Today ~cartographier~ has slipped its geographic moorings: one maps a genome, a network, a supply chain. From the same Latin ~charta~ modern French keeps ~carte~, ~charte~, ~carton~ and ~cartouche~.
en.cartonner: Formed from ~carton~ (“cardboard”) with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with N”: to cover or bind something with cardboard. ~Carton~ itself was borrowed from Italian ~cartone~, which goes back to Latin ~charta~ (“paper”), the same word that gave English ~chart~ and ~card~ their start. The slang sense “to be a huge hit” is a later figurative extension, and the sources do not spell out its path.
en.caser: Formed in French from ~case~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to put in a compartment, to find a place for.” The sources do not agree about the noun. English Wiktionary says it was borrowed from Latin ~casa~ (“hut, cabin”), with the other senses, including the square of a chessboard or compartment, a semantic loan from Spanish ~casa~, and calls it a doublet of ~chez~. French Wiktionary instead cites English ~case~, which probably concerns another sense of the word. Either way the verb means to slot something into its place, and by extension to find a job or a spouse for someone.
en.casser:
French ~casser~ first appears around 1100 as ~quasser~ “to break into pieces,” taking its modern shape by about 1160. It descends from Latin ~quassāre~ “to shake violently, to shatter,” itself a frequentative — an intensive, repetitive form — of ~quatere~ “to shake.” That verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷet-~ “to shake.” The same Latin source, by way of Old French, gave English ~quash~ “to crush, to annul.” But a second, homophonous Latin verb left its mark too: Late Latin ~cassāre~ “to annul, to make void,” derived from the adjective ~cassus~ “empty, vain.” The two converged so completely in French that one verb came to carry both meanings.

This fusion explains a remarkable split in sense. The ~quassāre~ side gives the physical meanings — to break a glass, and figuratively to wear out or exhaust. The ~cassāre~ side gives the legal one: “to annul, to overturn,” enshrined in the Cour de cassation, France's supreme court, which can quash a lower judgment. So when a verdict is set aside, it is, etymologically, declared empty rather than broken. From the shaking root also descend the rare ~quassation~ and French ~fracasser~ “to smash” and ~concasser~ “to crush,” alongside the everyday ~casse-tête~ “puzzle,” literally a head-breaker.
en.causer:
Modern French ~causer~ conceals two distinct verbs that fell together by sound. The first, “to cause,” was derived around 1275 from the noun ~cause~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~, ~cause~ itself coming from Latin ~causa~ (“cause, reason, lawsuit”). The second, “to chat,” descends directly from Latin ~causari~ (“to plead a case, debate, dispute”), a verb built on that same ~causa~. So both ultimately rest on ~causa~, cognate with Italian ~cosa~ and Spanish ~cosa~ (“thing”) and with the English borrowing ~cause~.

The surprise lies in the second verb's drift. In Latin, ~causari~ belonged to the courtroom: to argue a legal cause. As the centuries passed, the solemn sense of pleading and debating softened into mere talking, then into friendly chatter — so that today ~causer~ most often means simply “to have a chat,” and to ~causer de la pluie et du beau temps~ is to make small talk. From ~causa~ in its “thing” sense Latin also gave Romance its everyday word for an object (Italian ~cosa~), while French preserved the learned ~cause~ alongside ~causerie~ (“an informal talk”), ~causette~, and ~accuser~ (literally to call something to one's cause).
en.cautionner: Formed from ~caution~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to provide a ~caution~ for”: to stand surety for someone, to post bail, and by extension to lend one's backing to a person or an idea. The noun ~caution~ is a borrowing, through Old French, of Latin ~cautiō~ (“caution, precaution”), from ~cautus~, the past participle of ~cavēre~ (“to be on one's guard”). The verb thus rests on a medieval idea: a surety is a guarantee given by someone who has taken care for another.
en.censurer: Formed from the noun ~censure~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is borrowed from Latin ~cēnsūra~, which named the office of the Roman censor, the magistrate who took the census and judged public morals. The verb carries both of its senses today: “to criticise or condemn” and “to cut something from a work before it is published,” the second giving the English ~censor~ as a verb.
en.centraliser: Built in French from ~central~ and the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make central.” The adjective ~central~ is borrowed from Latin ~centrālis~, which belongs to ~centrum~ (“center”), a word Latin took from Greek ~kéntron~ (“a sharp point, a goad”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it remains fully productive in French for verbs meaning “make A.” In French, ~centraliser~ is used especially of gathering power, administration or services into a single center.
en.centrer:
From ~centre~ (“center”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, the noun being from Latin ~centrum~ (“the fixed point of a compass, a center”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κέντρον~ (~kéntron~, “a sharp point, a goad, the stationary leg of a pair of compasses”), from ~κεντέω~ (~kentéō~, “to prick, to goad”), from PIE *~ḱent-~ (“to prick”).

The Greek ~kéntron~ was literally a point that pricks — a goad, a wasp's sting — and then the still leg of a compass jabbed into the page while the other swung the circle. That pivot became the “center.” French ~centrer~ therefore means to bring to the middle, to aim at a target's middle, and in football to cross the ball toward the center. The same prickly root *~ḱent-~ surfaces in ~centre~, ~central~, ~excentrique~, ~concentrer~, and the borrowed insect-name element in ~centrifuge~.
en.cerner:
Inherited from Old French ~cerner~ (“to encircle”), from Latin ~circināre~ (“to make round, to go around in a circle”). The Latin verb is built on ~circinus~, the draftsman's compass or pair of dividers, which belongs to the family of ~circus~ (“ring, circle”). That noun is usually compared with Greek ~kírkos~ (“ring, circle”), but its deeper Proto-Indo-European origin is uncertain. French holds the same family in its other forms: ~cercle~ and ~cirque~, from ~circulus~ and ~circus~, and the learned ~circuit~. Spanish ~cercar~ (“to fence in, to surround”) comes from the closely related Latin ~circāre~, and English ~circle~ and ~circus~ come from the same family. Because ~cerner~ is inherited, centuries of spoken French wore its sounds down, unlike the learned ~circuit~.

In Old French, ~cerner~ meant to encircle. The noun ~cerne~, a ring, is tied to the verb and survives in the rings of a tree trunk and in the dark circles under tired eyes, which is why eyes are said to be ~cernés~. The verb also has a military sense, closing a circle around a town or an enemy force, and a figurative sense that now dominates: to ~cerner~ a problem is to draw a line around it in thought until its edges are clear, and so to understand it. The modern phrase ~cerner une personnalité~ keeps that picture of an investigator going around a subject. The abstract sense of grasping something thus rests on the older picture of a drawn circle.
en.certifier:
~certifier~ comes from Late Latin ~certificāre~, a compound of ~certus~ (“certain, settled, decided”) and ~facere~ (“to make”) — literally “to make certain.” The key is ~certus~, originally the participle of ~cernere~ (“to sift, to separate, then to distinguish, to decide”), from Proto-Italic *~krinō~, from PIE *~krey-~ (“to sieve, to separate”). The same root produced Greek ~krī́nō~ (“I judge, separate”), whence English ~crisis~, ~critic~, and ~criterion~; on the Latin side it gave ~discerner~, ~secret~, and ~crime~. To certify, then, is to make a matter as decided as grain that has passed clean through the sieve.

The metaphor is precise: judgment as a sifting, the sure thing as what is sorted out from doubt. French ~certifier~ means to attest formally — a notary certifies a copy, a school certifies a diploma — and from the family come ~certain~, ~certitude~, ~certificat~, and the adverb ~certes~. English borrowed the whole cluster: ~certain~, ~certify~, ~certificate~. Through the Greek branch of *~krey-~ the very word ~critique~ shares an ancestor with ~certifier~, so that to criticize and to certify both descend, ultimately, from the act of running grain through a sieve.
en.cesser:
From Latin ~cessāre~ (“to delay, to hold back, to leave off, to be idle”), the frequentative of ~cēdere~ (“to go, to withdraw, to yield”), whose past-participle stem ~cess-~ supplies the longer verb. Latin ~cēdere~ comes, through Proto-Italic *~kesd-o-~ (“to go away, to avoid”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱesd-~. Because a frequentative names a repeated or lingering action, ~cessāre~ originally suggested keeping on holding back — hence “to tarry,” and from there “to stop.” Italian ~cessare~ and Spanish ~cesar~ continue the same verb directly.

The semantic drift is gentle: from “withdrawing” to “hanging back” to simply “ceasing.” French kept the literary, slightly formal ring of the word — ~cesser de~ + infinitive, or the elevated ~sans cesse~ (“ceaselessly”), where the bare noun ~cesse~ survives almost only in that fixed phrase. The base verb ~cēdere~ gave French ~céder~ (“to yield”) directly, so ~cesser~ and ~céder~ are doublets sprung from the same Latin root by different paths. The wider family is large and legal-flavored: ~cessation~, ~cession~, ~cessible~, ~incessant~, ~incessamment~, and, through the ~cēdere~ branch, ~accéder~, ~procéder~, ~succéder~. A pleasant surprise: the English ~cease~ and the courtroom ~cease and desist~ rest on the very same Roman idea of stepping back and leaving off.
en.changer:
From Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to exchange, barter”), a variant of Classical ~cambīre~, a word of Gaulish origin tracing to Proto-Celtic *~kambos~ (“bent, crooked”) and the PIE root *~kamb-~ (“to bend, to curve”). The notion of bending underlies that of swapping one thing for its counterpart. ~Changer~ is cognate with Italian ~cambiare~, Spanish ~cambiar~, Occitan ~cambiar~, and Catalan ~canviar~.

The sound history is itself memorable: when Latin ~-bi-~ before a vowel followed a bilabial, it palatalized to ~-ge-~, the same shift that turned ~simium~ into ~singe~ and ~rabia~ into ~rage~ — hence ~cambiāre~ became ~changer~. Borrowed straight from Gaulish into provincial Latin, the verb is a small monument to Celtic survival in everyday French. Its descendants form a busy family: ~change~ (money exchange), ~changement~, ~échanger~, ~rechange~, and ~changeur~. The learned Italian doublet ~cambiare~ also re-entered French finance, yielding ~cambiste~ (“foreign-exchange dealer”) and ~cambisme~ — so a Gaulish word for “bending” still names the people who trade one currency for another.
en.chanter:
French ~chanter~ descends, through Middle and Old French ~chanter~ (with the northern variant ~canter~), from Latin ~cantāre~ (“to sing”). ~Cantāre~ is the frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing, to play, to recite”), so it originally meant something like “to keep singing”; it goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). Cognates dot the family tree: Welsh ~canu~ (“to sing”) is a direct Celtic relative, Old Irish ~canaid~ another, and — more unexpectedly — English ~hen~, the “singer” among fowl, belongs to the same root. Italian ~cantare~ and Spanish ~cantar~ are its Romance twins, and English borrowed the learned ~chant~ from French itself.

The initial Latin c- softened to the French ch- sound in the north, which is why the verb is ~chanter~ and not the Picard ~canter~ — a split still visible in place and family names. The meaning held steady at “to sing,” but French spun off vivid idioms: ~faire chanter quelqu'un~ (“to make someone sing”) means to blackmail, and ~chanter~ in the dismissive ~si ça te chante~ means “if it appeals to you.” The root seeded a tuneful family: ~chant~, ~chanson~ and ~chansonnier~, ~chanteur~ and ~cantatrice~, ~enchanter~ (literally “to sing a spell upon,” from ~incantāre~), ~cantique~, and ~cantate~. To enchant, fittingly, is to sing magic into being.
en.charger:
From Old French ~chargier~ (“to load, to put in a cart”), attested around 1080, from Late Latin *~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled cart, war chariot”). ~Carrus~ was itself borrowed from Gaulish ~karros~, from Proto-Celtic *~karros~ (“wagon”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The same Romance verb survives as Italian ~caricare~, Spanish ~cargar~, and Portuguese ~carregar~.

The core image is concrete: to ~charger~ was first to pile goods onto a cart, and from that load the meaning fanned out — to burden a person, to fill a weapon (a gun is ~chargé~), to entrust someone with a task (~charger quelqu'un de~), and, in the modern age, to charge a battery or load a file. French kept a learned doublet, ~carguer~, a sailor's term for furling a sail. Strikingly, the humble Gaulish cart-word seeded a whole network of French and English vocabulary through that same “to run” root: ~char~, ~chariot~, ~charrette~, ~carrière~ (“career,” originally a racecourse), and the borrowed ~cargo~ and ~charge~ all trace back to the wheels that once rolled across Roman Gaul.
en.charmer: Formed from the noun ~charme~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~. The ~charme~ in question is the one meaning “magic spell,” not the hornbeam tree of the same spelling. It comes from Old French ~charme~, from Latin ~carmen~ (“song, incantation, magic formula”), related to the verb ~canere~ (“to sing”). A charm was thus first a chanted formula, and ~charmer~ meant to put under a spell, to enchant. The sense then softened, as it did in English, from magical bewitching to simply delighting or captivating someone, which is the everyday meaning today. The ending ~-er~ makes the noun a first-conjugation verb.
en.chasser:
~chasser~ comes from Late Latin *~captiāre~, formed on ~captus~ (the past participle of ~capere~, “to take, seize”), from PIE *~kh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). The Romance descendants make a neat family: Italian ~cacciare~, Spanish ~cazar~, Occitan ~caçar~ — all meaning “to hunt” or “to chase.” English borrowed both ends of the development: ~chase~ from the Old French form and, through a different route, ~catch~ from a Norman variant, so that English keeps two verbs where French keeps one. Latin ~capere~ also lies behind English ~have~ and ~heave~ through the Germanic side of the root.

The core idea is repeated, eager seizing — the frequentative force of the *~-tiāre~ formation — which fits both the hunter pursuing game and the act of driving something away. French ~chasser~ accordingly means “to hunt,” “to chase,” and “to drive off”: one can ~chasser~ a deer, ~chasser~ a thought, or be ~chassé~ from a job. From the same stem come ~chasse~ (“the hunt”), ~chasseur~ (“hunter”), ~pourchasser~ (“to pursue relentlessly”), and the borrowed-back dance step ~chassé~. The whole cluster traces, ultimately, to one PIE notion of the closing hand.
en.chauffer:
From Vulgar Latin *~calefare~, a worn-down form of Classical Latin ~calefacere~ (“to make warm, to heat”), a compound of ~calere~ (“to be hot”) and ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~Calere~ goes back to PIE *~ḱelh₁-~ (“to be warm”), seen also in Latin ~calor~ (“heat”) and ~calidus~ (“hot”), Latvian ~silts~ (“warm”), and Welsh ~clyd~ (“cozy, warm”). ~Facere~ rests on PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to make”), the root of English ~do~ and ~deed~. So ~chauffer~ literally carries the meaning “to make hot.”

The phonetic erosion is dramatic: four Latin syllables in ~calefacere~ collapsed to the single stressed core of French ~chauffer~, the ~cal-~ becoming ~chau-~ by regular palatalization. The verb runs from the literal (~chauffer~ de l'eau) to the figurative — ~chauffer~ une salle, to warm up a crowd; ~ça chauffe~, things are heating up. From the same ~calor~ family French has ~chaud~, ~chaleur~, ~échauffer~, ~réchauffer~, and the borrowed ~calorie~ and ~chauffage~. And the ~chauffeur~ — now a driver — was once exactly what the word says: the man who stoked the boiler, the one who made the heat.
en.chausser:
From Old French ~chaucier~, inherited from Latin ~calceāre~ (“to furnish with shoes”), a verb built on ~calceus~ (“shoe”). The change of initial ~ca-~ to ~cha-~ is the regular northern French treatment of Latin ~ca-~. The verb has relatives across the Romance languages: Italian ~calzare~ and Spanish ~calzar~ both mean “to put shoes on” and come from the same Latin verb. Modern French kept the whole family of footwear words close to it, since ~chaussure~, ~chaussette~ and ~chausson~ all grow from the same stem.

The core sense, “to put shoes on someone,” underlies the reflexive ~se chausser~, “to put one's own shoes on,” and the verb extends to anything that goes on the feet, as with ~chausser ses skis~. The verb also describes size and fit: ~chausser du 42~ means “to take a size 42 shoe,” and a shoe can ~chausser~ well or badly. A figurative use exists as well, so that ~chausser ses lunettes~ means “to put on one's glasses,” the shoe image carried over to something worn on the face. The opposite verb ~déchausser~ (“to take shoes off”), and ~rechausser~ (“to put shoes back on”), are built on it with ~dé-~ and ~re-~.
en.chaîner: Formed from the noun ~chaîne~ (“chain”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to bind or link with a chain.” The noun comes from Old French ~chaiene~, from Latin ~catēna~ (“chain”). The circumflex does not mark a lost letter directly: it replaced the silent ~s~ of Middle French ~chaisne~, which itself signaled a long vowel. Latin had its own verb ~catēnāre~, which English Wiktionary invites us to compare, but the French verb is built on the French noun.
en.cheminer: Formed in French from ~chemin~ (“path, road”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so that to ~cheminer~ is to travel along a path, to keep walking steadily. English Wiktionary alternatively traces it to a Vulgar Latin verb *~cammīnāre~. The noun ~chemin~ comes from Late Latin ~cammīnus~, traditionally explained as a borrowing from Gaulish, which is why it has no classical Latin ancestor and replaced the older ~via~. Besides walking, the verb is used of ideas and plans that progress slowly but surely.
en.chercher:
From Old French ~cerchier~ (also ~cercer~, “to travel through, go around”), from Late Latin ~circāre~ (“to go around, traverse”), a verb derived from ~circus~ (“ring, circle”) and the preposition ~circā~ (“around, about”). ~Circus~ comes, through Greek ~kríkos~ / ~kírkos~ (“ring”), from PIE *~sker-~ (“to turn, to bend”). The same Old French ~cerchier~ crossed the Channel and gave English ~search~, which preserves the older form.

~Circāre~ first meant to move in a circuit around something, and the early verb described traversing a region — even moving one's hand about in all directions — before the dominant sense narrowed to “to look for, to seek.” In doing so ~chercher~ displaced the older ~querre~, which survives marginally as ~quérir~. The original idea of going around lingers in the noun ~recherche~ and the agent ~chercheur~, who circles a problem until it yields. From the same root *~sker-~ French keeps ~cirque~, ~cercle~, ~cerceau~, ~circuit~, and ~recherche~ itself — a whole vocabulary of rings and rounds standing behind the everyday act of searching.
en.chevaucher:
From Old French ~chevauchier~, by way of Middle French, from Late Latin ~caballicāre~ (“to ride a horse, to travel on horseback”), a verb built on Latin ~caballus~ (“nag, workhorse”). The same Latin verb gave Italian ~cavalcare~ and Spanish ~cabalgar~, and English has borrowed its descendants as ~cavalcade~. The origin of ~caballus~ itself is uncertain, and some scholars think it was borrowed from a non-Latin language, so the chain is traced only as far as the Latin word.

The humble ~caballus~ is the surprise of the story. Classical Latin used ~equus~ for a horse, and the plain ~caballus~ gradually replaced it in everyday speech, which is why the Romance languages say ~cheval~, ~caballo~ and ~cavallo~. French built a family on it: ~cheval~, ~chevalier~ and ~chevalerie~. The verb ~chevaucher~ meant “to ride on horseback.” Its modern figurative sense is “to overlap”: roof tiles, dates or themes ~se chevauchent~, as though one rode astride the other.
en.chier: Inherited from Latin ~cacāre~ (“to defecate”) by way of Old French and Middle French ~chier~. The initial Latin ~c~ before ~a~ became ~ch~ in northern French, the same change that turned Latin ~canis~ into ~chien~. The Latin verb lives on across the Romance languages, as in Italian ~cacare~ and Spanish ~cagar~. French also has the doublet ~caguer~, borrowed from Occitan ~cagar~, and the regional ~caquer~, along with the nursery word ~caca~. Many familiar vulgar words come from the same family, such as ~chiotte~, ~chiasse~ and ~chiant~, which began as concrete terms and developed figurative senses of annoyance.
en.chiffrer: Formed from the noun ~chiffre~ (“digit, number”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to put into numbers,” then “to encode.” ~Chiffre~ comes from Middle and Old French ~chifre~ and from Medieval Latin ~cifra~ (“zero”), borrowed from Arabic ~ṣifr~ (“empty”). The word entered the West in the Middle Ages together with the concept of zero and the so-called Arabic numerals, and by extension came to name every digit. Zero and cipher share this ancestor: ~chiffre~ is a doublet of ~zéro~. The secret-code sense of ~chiffrer~ follows from the idea of writing in figures instead of letters.
en.choir:
The verb ~choir~ is inherited from Middle French ~cheoir~, from Old French ~cheoir~, which was older ~chedeir~. It goes back to Late Latin (popular Latin) *~cadēre~, a reshaped form of classical Latin ~cadĕre~ (“to fall”). Latin ~cadĕre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~kadō~ and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱh₂d-~ (“to fall”). The Latin verb survives across the Romance languages, for example Italian ~cadere~ and Spanish ~caer~, so French ~choir~ has close siblings throughout the family.

In the Middle Ages ~choir~ was the ordinary verb for falling, until ~tomber~ displaced it. It now survives almost only in the fixed phrase ~laisser choir~ (“to let fall, to drop”) and in a literary past participle. Its family is far larger than the verb itself. The old feminine participle gave ~chute~ (“a fall”). Compounds of the verb gave ~échoir~ (“to fall due”) and ~déchoir~ (“to decline, to fall from rank”), with ~déchéance~ as its noun. Latin ~cadentia~, “a falling,” gave ~chance~, which began as the way dice fall, and Latin learned borrowings gave ~cadence~ and ~décadence~. The word that once meant simply “to fall” now lingers in the language of luck, due dates and downfall.
en.choisir:
French ~choisir~ (attested around 1050) comes from Old French ~coisir~ (“to perceive, to discern, then to select”), borrowed from the Frankish verb *~kausjan~ (“to taste, to test, to try”). This is one of the many Germanic words the Franks left embedded in French. The Frankish form goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵews-~ (“to taste, to choose”), the very same root that gave Latin ~gustāre~ (“to taste”) — so ~choisir~ and ~goûter~ are distant relatives. Through that Germanic branch it is cognate with English ~choose~, German ~kiesen~ (“to choose, elect”), and Dutch ~kiezen~, all sharing the idea of testing a thing before taking it.

The semantic thread is intuitive: one tastes or tries, then discerns, then picks. Old French ~coisir~ first meant “to make out, to catch sight of,” and only gradually settled into the sense “to select,” pushing aside the older verb ~élire~ (from Latin ~ēligere~), which narrowed to formal “electing.” The shift from a verb of perception to a verb of decision mirrors how English ~choose~ itself developed from “taste, test.” From the same Germanic and Indo-European stock, French keeps the noun ~choix~ (“choice”), back-formed from the verb, and — by the Latin route — the gustatory family of ~goût~ and ~déguster~.
en.choquer:
First attested in the 13th century in the Picard form ~chuquier~ (“to clash in combat, to strike”), whence ~choquer~. The origin is obscure — “perhaps Germanic,” says the TLFi. The favored comparison is with Middle Dutch and Middle Low German ~schokken~ (“to strike, jolt, shake”), but every version of the Germanic hypothesis runs into trouble: the Dutch verb is attested only from 1494, and the word's early French territory — almost exclusively Picardy and Wallonia — fits the proposed High German variants badly. The etymology therefore remains genuinely unsettled: a verb of collision whose own pedigree is a collision of hypotheses. English ~shock~ belongs to the same tangle: dictionaries trace it to Middle French ~choquer~ (and its noun ~choc~), to Middle Dutch ~schokken~, or to both at once.

For its first centuries ~choquer~ stayed strictly physical: knights, lances, ships and armies clashed. The figurative sense — to offend, to scandalize, to jar feeling or taste — is attested by 1621 and became the dominant one (warnings still promise images that “may shock”). The deverbal noun ~choc~ followed the same road, from the impact of cavalry charges to emotional and medical states (~état de choc~), and the family grew with ~choquant~ and ~s'entrechoquer~ (“to knock together”). English ~shock~, first of blows and then of feelings, kept pace on the other side of the Channel. As for the unsettled origin, it is better savored than hidden: a verb meaning “to collide” over whose birth the etymologies themselves collide — a borrowing from Middle Dutch, a High German variant, a derivative of an Old High German word for a jolt — with no single account crowned by the TLFi.
en.chromer: Derived from the noun ~chrome~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to plate a metal object with chromium. The noun ~chrome~ is a scientific coinage from Greek ~khrôma~ (“color”), given to the metal because its compounds are so brightly colored. The verb names the process of giving fittings, bumpers and taps their mirror-like finish. Note that French Wiktionary gives only the base, with no further source, so the story of the noun rests on common reference knowledge.
en.chuter: French Wiktionary derives ~chuter~ from the noun ~chute~ (“fall”) with the verb ending ~-er~, with a second, separate verb ~chuter~ (“to hush”) coming from the interjection ~chut~. ~Chute~ is a feminine past participle used as a noun: the old participle ~cheüt~ of ~choir~ (“to fall”), from Vulgar Latin *~cadūta~, built on Latin ~cadere~ (“to fall”). English Wiktionary merges two Old French feminine participles, ~cheüe~ and ~cheoite~. So ~chuter~ is literally “to make a fall,” a verb made from the noun of ~choir~, a verb now almost lost.
en.cibler:
Denominal from the noun ~cible~ (“target”), with the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun is regional in origin: it comes from Swiss German dialect ~Schibe~, corresponding to standard German ~Scheibe~ (“disc, pane, target”), the round board shot at in marksmanship. The form was altered to ~cibe~, and fr.Wiktionary notes that the final ~-l~ may represent a Germanic diminutive — though it flags this with “possibly,” so the suffix is not certain. The word entered French from the German-speaking cantons where target-shooting was a civic sport.

The sense moved from the physical bull's-eye to its figurative uses. In older or familiar speech ~cibler~ could mean to hurl something at someone; today it means to aim at, to single out — a market, an audience, an objective. The marketing and military senses (“une campagne ciblée,” “une frappe ciblée”) are modern. The image is constant across all of them: a single round mark to be hit. Because the root is Germanic rather than Latin, ~cible~ has no Romance cousins in Italian or Spanish, which use ~bersaglio~ and ~blanco~ instead — a small reminder that French borrowed its word for the target from across the Rhine.
en.circonscrire:
French ~circonscrire~ was borrowed from Latin ~circumscrībere~ (“to draw a line around, to limit”), made of ~circum~ (“around”) and ~scrībere~ (“to write, to scratch, to draw”). The Latin verb ~scrībere~ first meant to scratch lines on a surface, long before it meant to write in the modern sense. English ~circumscribe~ is a parallel borrowing of the same Latin verb, and the Romance languages have Italian ~circoscrivere~ and Spanish ~circunscribir~. Its second half is the root of a very large family of words about writing, including English ~scribe~ and ~describe~.

The Latin sense is a geometric one: to trace a circle or outline around something. Figurative use followed, as in English: to confine a thing within bounds, whether a fire, an epidemic or a subject of discussion. In French, ~circonscrire un incendie~ is to keep a fire from spreading, and ~circonscrire un sujet~ is to define its limits. Geometers still speak of a circle ~circonscrit~ to a triangle, one that passes through all its corners. Its conjugation follows ~écrire~ (past participle ~circonscrit~), because the two verbs share the Latin ~scrībere~. The family reaches ~circonscription~ (“district, constituency”), the word for a territory drawn on a map with a boundary line, as well as ~écrire~, ~décrire~ and ~inscrire~.
en.circuler:
From Latin ~circulāri~ (“to form a circle, move in a circle”), from ~circulus~ (“little ring, circle”), the diminutive of ~circus~ (“ring, circle”). ~Circus~ was borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κρίκος~ / ~κίρκος~ (~kríkos~ / ~kírkos~, “ring”), tracing to PIE *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, bend”); through the Germanic side of that turning root stands English ~ring~.

The diminutive matters: a ~circulus~ is a small circle, a hoop, a ring — and to ~circuler~ is to travel that closed loop and return, motion that comes back on itself. From the literal ring the verb opened onto every kind of going-round: blood ~circule~ through the body, money and rumours ~circulent~ through society, and a policeman's ~Circulez!~ orders a crowd to keep moving along. The same ~circulus~ gives ~circulaire~ (both the shape and the letter sent round to many readers) and ~circulation~ (of traffic, blood, currency); the parent ~circus~ survives in ~cirque~, the ring where performers turn. What unites them all is the closed curve of *~(s)ker-~ — the path that bends back to where it began.
en.ciseler: From Old French ~ciseler~, built on ~cisel~, a cutting tool, with the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary glosses ~cisel~ as a pair of scissors or blade, and the word survives in modern French in the plural ~ciseaux~ (“scissors”) and in ~ciseau~ (“chisel”). To ~ciseler~ is to work metal, stone or wood with a chisel, hence to carve or engrave finely; in cooking it means to chop herbs or spices very small, as with a blade. English ~chisel~ is a cognate, borrowed from the Anglo-Norman form of the same Old French word. The sources consulted do not trace ~cisel~ further back, so no Latin source is claimed here.
en.citer:
From Latin ~citare~ (“to set in motion, rouse, summon, call forth”), the frequentative of ~ciēre~ (“to move, stir, call”). The verb was borrowed into French as a learned word. ~ciēre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~keih₁-~ (“to set in motion, to move”), making it cognate with Greek ~kīneîn~ (“to move, set in motion” — the source of ~cinéma~ and ~kinetic~) and with Sanskrit ~cyávate~ (“he stirs himself, sets out”). To cite is, etymologically, to put something or someone into motion.

That original kinetic sense explains the verb’s spread of meanings. To ~citer~ first meant to “summon” — to call a person before a court or to muster troops — and from “calling someone forth” came “calling forth someone’s words,” that is, to quote, and “calling out a name,” to mention. The motion sense stays vivid in the Latin-built relatives French inherited: ~exciter~ (“to excite, stir up,” from ~ex-~ + ~citare~), ~inciter~ (“to incite, urge on”), ~susciter~ (“to arouse, give rise to”), and ~solliciter~. The noun ~citation~ keeps both the courtroom summons and the quoted passage under one roof — two faces of a single act of “calling forth.”
en.claquer:
French ~claquer~ is a sound word. English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French and Old French ~claquer~ (“to clack, clap, clatter”) to Middle Dutch ~klacken~ (“to clack, crack, whack”), then Old Dutch *~klakon~ and Proto-Germanic *~klakōną~ (“to clap, chirp”). French Wiktionary presents it instead as built on the imitative ~clac~, the noise of a sharp, short slap, and notes the kinship with Dutch ~klakken~ and German ~klacken~. The two accounts differ on whether the verb was imitated afresh in French or came in from Dutch, and the evidence does not settle the matter. Either way the meaning stays close to a sharp, dry noise. French Wiktionary adds ~cliquer~ as a close relative.

From the clap, the senses spread. A door, a whip or a set of teeth ~claque~ in the sense of making a sharp noise, and slang stretched the verb to squandering money. The noun ~claque~ means a slap, and also the group of people paid to applaud, a sense English Wiktionary ties to the practice of hiring audience members at the Paris Opera. French Wiktionary links another slang noun to the verb in its sense of spending lavishly. Tap dancing is ~claquettes~, named for the clatter of the shoes. English Wiktionary also lists a separate, homonymous verb built on ~claque~ (“vamp”), a shoe part, which is a different word.
en.clarifier: Borrowed from Latin ~clārificāre~, a compound of ~clārus~ (“clear, bright”) and ~facere~ (“to make”), so “to make clear.” French Wiktionary offers a second reading, that the verb was built in French from ~clair~ plus the suffix ~-ifier~, which comes to the same meaning. ~Clārus~ is also the source of French ~clair~, and English ~clarify~ is the matching verb. The word still serves two worlds: literally, to ~clarifier~ a liquid such as butter or a broth is to make it clear, and figuratively it means to make a situation or an idea easy to understand.
en.classer:
From the noun ~classe~ (“class, category”), with the suffix ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~classis~, a word that originally meant a “summons” or “call to arms” and then the categories of citizens that could be called up — the political-military divisions into which the Roman census sorted the population by wealth. Cognates of the verb include Italian ~classificare~ and Spanish ~clasificar~, and through the noun, English ~class~ and ~classify~.

The semantic journey runs from the muster-roll to the filing cabinet. From the Roman census-classes, ~classe~ generalized into any rank or category, then into the schoolroom ~classe~ and, by extension, the verb ~classer~: to sort, to file, to rank. The military memory lingers in French phrases — a ~classe d'âge~ is a cohort of conscripts, and ~classer une affaire~ is to file a case away, to close it. The noun also spawned ~classique~ (“classical,” first the literature of the top “class” of writers), and the verb gave ~classement~ (a ranking or league table), ~classeur~ (a binder or filing folder), and ~classification~. The prefixed forms ~reclasser~ (to reclassify, or to redeploy a worker) and ~déclasser~ (to downgrade) round out a family all descended from a Roman call to arms.
en.climatiser: Formed in French from ~climat~ and the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, so to ~climatiser~ is to give a space a controlled climate, in other words to air-condition it. The base ~climat~ came into French from Latin ~clima~ (genitive ~climatis~), borrowed from Greek ~klíma~. That Greek word meant the slope of the earth toward the poles, then a zone or region, then its weather. It comes from the verb ~klinein~ (“to lean, to incline”). A climate is thus, at the root, a slant. The shortened colloquial form is ~clim~, and the noun ~climatiseur~ names the machine.
en.cliquer:
Formed in French from the onomatopoeia ~clic~, an imitation of a short, dry sound — the snap of a latch or the tap of a key — to which the verbal ending ~-er~ was added. It belongs to a small family of sound-words that includes ~claquer~ (“to slam, to clack”) and ~clicher~ (which gave ~cliché~, originally a printer's stereotype plate, named for the clicking noise the casting tool made). The pair ~clic~ and ~clac~ even survive together in the expression ~clic-clac~.

For most of its life ~cliquer~ named a faint mechanical noise and was rare. Its fortune was made by the computer mouse: the modern sense “to click” is a calque on English ~click~, itself an independent onomatopoeia of the same kind, so the two languages arrived at nearly identical words by imitating the same sound. From the family come ~cliquet~ (“a pawl, a ratchet”), ~cliqueter~ and ~cliquetis~ (“to jingle / a jingling”), and the borrowed ~cliché~. Few verbs show so clearly how a noise, frozen into a syllable, can be conjugated.
en.clore:
From Old French ~clore~ (early 12th century), from Latin ~claudere~ (“to shut, close, lock”), from Proto-Italic *~klaudō~, from PIE *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg, key”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~κλείς~ (~kleís~, “key, bolt”) and, through Germanic, Old High German ~sliozan~ (“to lock, conclude”); it is also the source, through Latin, of English ~close~, ~clause~, and ~cloister~.

The noun behind it all was essentially a key or bolt — to ~claudere~ was to set the bar across the door. French inherited the verb directly, but ~clore~ led a troubled life: several of its conjugated forms collided with those of ~clouer~ (“to nail”), and it steadily ceded ground to ~fermer~, surviving now mainly in fixed and elevated uses (~clore~ un débat, un compte). Yet the root is everywhere in its descendants: the participle gave ~clos~ and ~clôture~, the prefixed compounds ~enclore~, ~exclure~, ~inclure~, ~conclure~, and ~reclus~, and the learned ~clé~ / ~clef~ preserves the original “key.” A verb in retreat, anchoring a vast and thriving family.
en.clouer: ~Clouer~ is formed from ~clou~ (“nail”) with the verb ending ~-er~, “to fasten with nails.” English Wiktionary adds an alternative: it may instead descend from Late Latin ~clāvāre~, itself from Latin ~clāvus~, compare Italian ~chiavare~ and Catalan ~clavar~. Either way the root is the same, since ~clou~ comes from Latin ~clāvus~ and, through Proto-Italic *~klāwos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kleh₂u-~. The older spelling ~cloer~ is attested in the Life of Saint Giles.
en.clôturer: From the noun ~clôture~ + the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Old French ~closture~, from Late Latin ~clausūra~ (“a closing”), built on ~clausus~, the past participle of ~claudere~ (“to close”). The circumflex of ~clôture~ may come from a crossing with Latin ~claustra~ (“barrier, enclosure”), though that is only a suggestion. The verb first meant to surround with a fence, and then, figuratively, to bring something to a close, as when one ~clôture~ a meeting, a debate or an account. English ~closure~ comes from the same Old French word.
en.cocher: Formed from the noun ~coche~ (“notch”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The ~coche~ in question was originally a stick that people cut notches into to keep a tally, and then the notch itself, so ~cocher~ first meant to notch and then to mark with a stroke, hence to tick a box. The origin of that noun is uncertain. One proposal is Italian ~cocca~ (“notch on an arrow”), a sense also found in the Occitan verb ~encocar~ (“to nock an arrow”). The word is not the same as ~coche~ (“coach”), from Hungarian ~kocsi~, nor as ~coche~ (“sow”), related to ~cochon~. French ~encoche~ (“notch”) belongs to the same family.
en.coder: Either a denominal verb built on ~code~ and the ending ~-er~, or a borrowing of English ~to code~, recorded as a verb from 1815; fr.Wiktionary offers both. French ~code~ comes from Latin ~codex~, a variant of ~caudex~ (“tree trunk”), which came to name books, then books of laws, and finally the body of written laws itself. The sense “secret code” arrived later from English ~code~ (attested in 1808), where French had used ~chiffre~. The computing sense, “to write the code of a program,” dates from 1947.
en.codifier: ~Codifier~ is formed from ~code~ and the suffix ~-ifier~, meaning “to put into a code.” French Wiktionary also allows that it may instead come from English ~codify~, attested in 1800, while English Wiktionary gives Latin ~cōdex~ plus ~-ifier~. ~Code~ comes from Latin ~cōdex~, a variant of ~caudex~ (“tree trunk”), the wooden block from which writing tablets and then books were made. The word named books, then law books in particular, and finally the body of laws they contained. The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”), so ~codifier~ is literally to make into a code.
en.coexister:
Both Wiktionaries agree on the formation: ~co-~ (“together”) + ~exister~, though French Wiktionary adds a Latin model, ~coexsistere~, which French speakers felt as a compound of those two parts. The core is Latin ~exsistere~ (“to step forth, to emerge, to be”), made of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~sistere~ (“to set, to stand”). That last verb is a reduplicated formation on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~, the same root as in English ~stand~.

The sense has therefore moved from “stand forth” to “be there” to “be there together.” Latin ~exsistere~ gave French ~exister~, and the ~co-~ prefix added the idea of sharing the same time or space: nations, species or ideas that ~coexist~, without one replacing the other. A whole family shares the ~sistere~ element: ~persister~, ~résister~, ~subsister~, ~consister~, ~assister~ and ~insister~, as well as ~coexistence~ and ~coexistant~. Seen this way, ~coexister~ is a verb about “standing out” together.
en.cogner: From Old French ~coignier~, inherited from Latin ~cuneāre~ (“to wedge”), a verb built on ~cuneus~ (“wedge”). The same Latin noun gave French ~coin~, which still means “wedge” in some uses and also “corner,” an object that is wedge-shaped. The sense of ~cogner~ moved from driving in a wedge to striking hard, so that one now ~cogne~ a door, a head or a nail. The shift is the obvious one, from the tool to the blow that drives it, though the sources do not narrate it. The verb is familiar and a little colloquial, and it also means “to fight” in slang.
en.cohabiter: Borrowed from Latin ~cohabitāre~ (“to live together”), built from ~co-~ (“with”) and ~habitāre~ (“to dwell”). The Latin verb ~habitāre~ is itself a frequentative of ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”), so to dwell somewhere was, etymologically, to keep holding it. The same ~habitāre~ gave French ~habiter~, which makes ~cohabiter~ a learned relative of an everyday verb: the word was taken whole from Latin, not assembled in French from ~co-~ and ~habiter~.
en.coiffer: Formed from the noun ~coiffe~ (“headdress, cap”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb first meant “to put a cap on.” The noun comes from Late Latin ~cofia~, whose origin is obscure but probably Germanic: English Wiktionary traces it to an Old High German diminutive of ~kuffa~ (“hood, cap”), a relative of English ~cop~ (“top, crest”). The sense then widened from covering the head to dressing the hair, hence the modern meaning “to do someone's hair.” The old spelling ~coeffe~ survived in dictionaries until the eighteenth century.
en.coincer: Formed in French from the noun ~coin~ (“wedge, corner”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is inherited from Old French ~coin~, from Latin ~cuneus~ (“wedge”), which also gave French the learned ~cunéiforme~ (“wedge-shaped”). To ~coincer~ is therefore to fix something with a wedge, so that it jams and cannot move, and by extension to trap a person in a corner or in a tight spot: ~se faire coincer~ is to get caught.
en.collaborer:
Borrowed from Latin ~collaborare~ (“to work together”), from ~com-~ (“with”) + ~laborare~ (“to labor”), the verb of the noun ~labor~ (“toil, work”). The origin of ~labor~ itself is uncertain: one account links it to the verb ~labare~ (“to totter”), imagining a worker swaying under a heavy load, but the linguist De Vaan rejects this without offering a replacement, and other roots have been proposed. So the appealing image of toil as a “tottering under burden” should be flagged as disputed, not assumed. Cognate with Italian ~collaborare~ and Spanish ~colaborar~, and, through the same ~labor~, with English ~labor~ and ~elaborate~.

~Collaborer~ entered French only in the 19th century, a learned re-borrowing rather than an inherited form, which is why it kept its Latin shape so cleanly. Its everyday sense is positive — to work jointly on a shared task — but the 20th century gave it a dark second life: under the Occupation, ~collaborer~ came to mean cooperating with the enemy, spawning the noun ~collaborateur~ and its scornful clipped form ~collabo~. From the same ~labor~ French also keeps ~labeur~ (“hard toil”), ~laborieux~, ~laboratoire~, ~élaborer~, and the older ~labourer~ (“to plough”), the field-work sense of working the land.
en.collecter:
A denominal verb built on the noun ~collecte~ (« a collection, a gathering »), from Latin ~collecta~ (« contribution, levy »), the feminine of the participle ~collectus~. That participle belongs to ~colligere~ (« to gather together »), itself ~com-~ (« together ») + ~legere~ (« to pick, choose, read »), from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (« to collect, gather »). Cognates of the base abound: Italian ~cogliere~, Spanish ~coger~, and — through the same root — English ~collect~, ~legend~, and ~lecture~.

Latin ~legere~ first meant the physical act of « picking up » and only later « reading, » as one gathers letters with the eye; that semantic leap echoes through the whole family. French inherited the popular line in ~cueillir~ (« to pick ») and the learned line in ~collecter~, ~collection~, ~collectif~, ~recueillir~, and ~récolte~ (« harvest »). The same *~leǵ-~ underlies ~lire~ (« to read »), ~légion~, ~élire~ (« to elect »), and ~négliger~ (« to neglect »), literally « not to gather up. »
en.collectionner: ~Collectionner~ is formed from the noun ~collection~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~: to gather things of one kind for pleasure or study. ~Collection~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~collēctiō~ (“a gathering”), from ~colligere~ (“to gather together”), made of ~com-~ and ~legere~ (“to pick, to gather”). The same Latin verb reached French by the popular route as ~cueillir~, so ~collectionner~ and ~cueillir~ are distant cousins.
en.coller:
A denominal verb, formed in French directly from the noun ~colle~ (“glue, paste”). That noun comes from Vulgar Latin *~colla~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κόλλα~ (~kólla~, “glue”). The Greek word is the same one hidden inside English ~collagen~ (literally “glue-producer”) and ~protocol~, and it gives French ~collage~, ~colloïde~, and ~collagène~.

To ~coller~ is first of all to stick or glue one thing to another, but French has let the verb wander into a wealth of figurative and slang senses. Something that fits or works can ~coller~ (~ça colle~, “that works, that’s fine”); a person who clings to you ~colle~; and in everyday speech to ~coller~ someone is to stump them with a hard question — which is exactly why ~une colle~ became student slang for a tough quiz or oral exam, and why a school detention is also ~une colle~ (originally being “stuck” at school). A demanding examiner is even called a ~colleur~. From the same Greek-derived root come ~décoller~ (“to unstick,” and so “to take off” in an aeroplane), ~encoller~, and the noun ~colle~ in all its glue-bound and exam-bound meanings.
en.coloniser: Formed in French from ~colonie~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to turn into, to treat with, to provide with.” French Wiktionary adds that the verb may instead be borrowed from English ~colonize~, attested in 1622, so the exact path is uncertain. The base ~colonie~ goes back to Latin ~colōnia~, a settlement of ~colōnī~, and was used in Middle French from the fourteenth century. English Wiktionary notes that ~colonie~ is a doublet of ~Cologne~, the German city founded as a Roman colony.
en.colorer:
From Latin ~colorare~ (“to color, to give color to”), the verb formed on ~color~ (“color, hue, outward appearance”). The noun descends from Old Latin ~colōs~, from Proto-Italic *~kelōs~, from PIE *~ḱel-~ (“to cover, to conceal”) with the suffix *~-ōs~. Color, then, was first what covers a thing — its surface, its outward show. From that same root *~ḱel-~ come, through Latin, ~conceal~ and ~cell~ (a hidden chamber), and through Germanic, English ~hall~, ~hell~ (the covered-over place), ~hull~, and ~helmet~ — all things that cover or hide.

The link between “color” and “concealment” is the skin of appearances: the hue is the cover laid over the substance. French keeps ~colorer~ for giving or taking on color, often figuratively (a story ~coloré~ by emotion), and distinguishes it from ~colorier~, the later verb for filling in a drawing with crayons. Both descend from ~color~, alongside ~coloris~, ~coloration~, ~décolorer~, and ~incolore~. The borrowed cognate ~couleur~ travelled the popular route from the same ~color~. The étymon's quiet lesson is that color was understood as a veil — the visible covering through which we read what lies beneath.
en.combattre:
A French compound of the prefix ~com-~ (a form of ~con-~, here “with, against”) and the verb ~battre~ (“to beat, to strike”) — literally, to beat against one another. French ~battre~ descends from Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, to strike”), a word the Romans seem to have borrowed from Gaulish; its further origin is debated, perhaps a Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰat-~ (“to strike”), with a possible Celtic cognate in Welsh ~bathu~ (“to beat, to coin”).

The compound was already in Old French (~combatre~), and its sense has scarcely budged: to fight, to do battle, and figuratively to oppose or strive against (one ~combats~ an idea, a disease, an injustice). The whole ~battuere~ family is a battlefield in itself: from it French draws ~combat~, ~combattant~, ~bataille~ (“battle,” via Late Latin ~battālia~), ~bataillon~, ~débattre~ (“to debate,” to beat back and forth), ~abattre~ (“to fell, to slaughter,” whence ~abattoir~), ~rabattre~, and the simple ~battre~ of beating eggs or hearts. English borrowed much of the same cluster — ~combat~, ~battle~, ~battalion~, ~debate~, ~abattoir~ — all of it ringing with the old sound of blows struck.
en.combiner:
From Late Latin ~combīnāre~ (“to join two by two, to pair”), formed from ~com-~ (“together”) and the distributive numeral ~bīnī~ (“two each, in pairs”). ~Bīnī~ comes from Proto-Italic *~dwiznos~, built on ~bis~ (“twice”) — both ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root for “two,” *~dwóh₁~. Cognate, through that root, with English ~binary~ and ~twin~, with Latin ~duo~, and with the Italian and Spanish doublets ~combinare~ and ~combinar~.

The verb's literal sense — “to set things two by two” — is still visible: to ~combiner~ is to bring elements together so they pair up and work as one. From the same ~bis~ / ~bīnī~ stock French inherited a whole numerical family: ~binaire~, ~combinaison~, ~combinatoire~, and the everyday ~combine~ (a scheme or trick) and ~combinard~ (a schemer). The English ~combine~ is the same Latin verb, borrowed; in farming, a “combine harvester” is so named because it combines several operations. What began as a precise Roman way of counting in twos thus widened into the general idea of joining, arranging, and contriving — and, less flatteringly, of cooking up a clever ~combine~.
en.combler:
From Latin ~cumulāre~ (“to heap up, pile, accumulate”), a denominative verb from ~cumulus~ (“a heap, mound”). The connection of ~cumulus~ to a PIE source (~perhaps~ *~ḱuh₁mós~) is marked as uncertain in the sources, so the deep root is best left open. The Latin noun ~cumulus~ survives untouched as the meteorologists' name for the heaped, piled-up cloud, and the learned family ~cumuler~ and ~accumuler~ comes straight from the Latin verb.

While those learned doublets kept the literal “heaping,” the inherited popular form ~combler~ traveled further. To heap something to the brim is to fill it completely, so ~combler~ came to mean “to fill up” — a ditch, a gap, a hole (one ~comble une lacune~). From filling to the brim it rose to the figurative sense of satisfying utterly: to ~combler~ someone is to fulfil their every wish, to shower them so fully that nothing is left wanting — ~comblé de bonheur~, “overflowing with happiness.” The noun ~comble~ (“the height, the summit, the very top”) preserves the original image of the heap piled as high as it will go.
en.commander:
From Old French ~comander~ (eleventh century), from Vulgar Latin *~commandare~, an alteration of Latin ~commendare~ (“to entrust, to commit to one's care”), formed from ~com-~ (intensive) + ~mandare~ (“to hand over, to charge with a task”). ~Mandare~ itself is usually traced to ~manus~ (“hand”) + ~dare~ (“to give”) — to “give into the hand.” The Romance cousins are everywhere: Italian ~comandare~, Spanish ~comandar~ and ~mandar~, and, by Norman transmission, English ~command~.

The semantic slide is striking. In classical Latin ~commendare~ leaned toward “to entrust, to recommend,” but in Late Latin and Old French it hardened into “to order, to have authority over”: what you place in someone's hand as a charge becomes what you impose on them as a command. French preserves both faces of the word — ~commander~ a soldier is to give an order, while ~commander~ a meal is to place one's request, the older sense of “committing a task” still visible at the table. Kin from the same root crowd the language: ~commande~, ~commandement~, ~commandant~, ~recommander~, and, directly from ~mandare~, ~mander~, ~mandat~, and ~demander~.
en.commencer:
From Old French ~comencier~ (“to begin”), from Vulgar Latin *~cominitiāre~, from ~com-~ (an intensive of ~cum~, “with, together”) + ~initiāre~ (“to initiate, begin”), from ~initium~ (“a beginning, entrance”), itself from ~inīre~ (“to go in,” ~in-~ + ~īre~, “to go”). Cognate with Italian ~cominciare~, Spanish ~comenzar~, and Portuguese ~começar~; English ~commence~ was borrowed from the Old French verb.

The sense traces back to a literal act of entering: ~initium~ is the going-in, the threshold of a thing, and to ~initiāre~ was to set someone or something on its way — in religion, to admit to the rites (hence English ~initiation~). Vulgar Latin reinforced it with ~com-~ and reshaped it as *~cominitiāre~, simply “to begin.” From the same ~īre~ (“to go,” PIE *~ey-~) French draws a surprising scatter of words once you trace the path — ~initial~, ~initier~, ~initiative~ — and ~īre~ itself underlies ~issue~ (“a going out”) and the future stems of ~aller~. ~Recommencer~ (“to begin again”) layers ~re-~ on top, while the noun ~commencement~ names the start that ~commencer~ performs.
en.commenter:
From Latin ~commentari~ (“to consider thoroughly, to discuss, to interpret”), a deponent verb tied to ~commentus~, past participle of ~comminisci~ (“to contrive, to devise”), formed from ~com-~ (intensive) and a verb on the root of ~mens~ (“mind”). The ultimate source is Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”) — one of the most prolific of all roots. Through it ~commenter~ is kin to English ~mind~, ~mental~, and ~mention~, to Latin ~memini~ (“I remember”), and, more remotely, to a vast family of words about thought and memory.

Latin ~commentari~ meant to think a thing over fully and then to expound it, and that double motion — to ponder, then to explain — survives in French: to ~commenter~ a text is to annotate and interpret it, while to ~commenter~ a match is to provide a running spoken account. The internet sense, leaving a ~commentaire~ under a post, is only the newest layer over this very old idea of remarking upon. From the same ~men-~ root French gathers ~commentaire~, ~mental~, ~mention~, ~réminiscence~, and ~mémoire~ — a whole vocabulary of the thinking mind grown from one syllable.
en.commercer: Formed in French from the noun ~commerce~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~, and attested in Middle French. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~commercium~ (“trade, dealings”), itself built from ~com-~ (“together”) and ~merx~ (“goods, wares”). The verb therefore means, at heart, to deal in wares with others. It is intransitive and now somewhat literary: one ~commerce~ with someone, in the old sense of keeping company or doing business with them, whereas modern speech prefers ~faire du commerce~. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary one for turning a noun into a first-conjugation verb.
en.commercialiser:
Derived from the adjective ~commercial~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, which forms verbs of “making into” something. ~Commercial~ rests on ~commerce~, borrowed from Latin ~commercium~ (“trade, traffic in goods”), from ~com-~ (“together”) + ~merx~ (“merchandise, wares”). The ultimate origin of ~merx~ is uncertain: De Vaan suspects an Etruscan source, linking it to the god-name ~Mercurius~, while more recent proposals reconstruct an Indo-European root — none of these accounts is settled. The same ~merx~ family gave English ~merchant~, ~commerce~, and ~market~.

~Commercialiser~ is a 19th- and 20th-century coinage, born when economies needed a word for turning a thing into an object of trade — bringing a product to market, putting it on sale. It can carry a faint pejorative edge, the sense of cheapening something by making it for profit, as when one speaks of having « commercialisé » a holiday or a tradition.
