In everyday French, the verb weakened to “to annoy, to upset” (~ça me contrarie~), often of a mild frustration.
en.contraster: The sources disagree slightly. French Wiktionary derives the verb from the noun ~contraste~, which was borrowed from Italian ~contrasto~, itself drawn from ~contrastare~ and ultimately Latin ~contrā~ + ~stāre~ (“to stand against”). English Wiktionary instead derives the verb directly from Latin ~contrāstāre~ (“to resist, to withstand”). Both routes end at the same Latin pair: ~contrā~ (“against”) and ~stāre~ (“to stand”). To ~contraster~ is thus to stand opposite something, and so to differ sharply from it. The noun ~contraste~ is the more familiar half of the pair.
en.contredire:
~Contredire~ was inherited from Old French ~contredire~, which was itself borrowed from Latin ~contrādīcere~ (“to speak against”), built from ~contrā~ (“against”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say”). French today analyzes it as ~contre-~ + ~dire~. The Latin verb ~dīcere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”): to say is, at root, to point something out. The same root gave Greek ~deíknymi~ (“I show”), German ~zeigen~ (“to show”) and English ~teach~, as well as French ~dicter~ and ~dictionnaire~.

One feature of ~contredire~ is the second-person plural of the present indicative. The simple verb ~dire~ has ~vous dites~, but ~contredire~ follows ~dédire~, ~interdire~, ~médire~ and ~prédire~ and keeps the regular ending: ~vous contredisez~. The meaning has barely moved since Latin: to say the opposite of what another person says, then to be at odds with a fact, and, reflexively, with oneself. The old noun ~contredit~ survives in the fixed phrase ~sans contredit~ (“beyond dispute”), while ~contradiction~ and ~contradictoire~ are the later learned forms, and English ~contradict~ was borrowed directly from the Latin verb.
en.contrer: A nineteenth-century coinage, formed from the preposition ~contre~ (“against”) plus the verb ending ~-er~: to oppose, to block, to counter. The preposition is inherited from Latin ~contra~ (“opposite, against”), and its first written appearance with a final ~e~, as ~cuntre~, dates from about 1100. The verb is thus a young word built on a very old one, a pattern that French uses freely whenever a preposition needs to become an action.
en.contribuer:
From Latin ~contribuere~ (“to bring together, contribute, give as a share”), from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~tribuere~ (“to allot, assign, grant”). The verb ~tribuere~ derives from ~tribus~, the “tribe,” so its core sense was to “distribute among the tribes”; ~tribus~ is often connected to the Proto-Indo-European numeral root *~trey-~ (“three”), pointing to an archaic threefold division of the Roman people. Cognate with Italian ~contribuire~ and Spanish ~contribuir~, and — through ~tribuere~ — with English ~contribute~, ~distribute~, and ~tribute~.

The political origin is the memorable detail: long before it meant “to help,” ~contribuere~ described carving a populace up by tribe and assigning each its share of duties and taxes. From that fiscal sense — paying one's portion into a common pot — grew the modern meaning of voluntarily giving toward a shared end, whether money, effort, or an article. The same ~tribus~ underlies a wide French family: ~tribu~ itself, ~tribut~ (“tribute, levy”), ~attribuer~, ~distribuer~, ~rétribuer~, and ~tribun~, the Roman magistrate who was originally the head of a tribe. The noun ~contribution~ preserves the old tax sense in expressions referring to public levies.
en.controverser: Formed in French from ~controverse~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to debate, to dispute.” The noun ~controverse~ was borrowed from Latin ~controversia~, from ~controversus~ (“turned the other way”), itself built from ~contrā~ (“against”) and ~versus~ (“turned”), the participle of ~vertere~. A controversy is thus, literally, a matter on which people face opposite directions. The English evidence adds that the noun passed through Old French ~controversie~ and Middle French ~controverse~. The verb is much rarer than the noun.
en.contrôler:
From Old French ~contrerole~ / ~contre-rolle~, a clerk's “counter-roll”: a duplicate register kept alongside the original to verify it. The word joins ~contre-~ (“against, counter,” from Latin ~contra~) and ~rôle~ (“roll, scroll of parchment,” from Latin ~rotulus~, “little wheel,” diminutive of ~rota~, “wheel”). To ~contrôler~ an account was thus to check it against its mirror-copy. In the nineteenth century the sense of “mastery, command” was reinforced by English ~control~ — itself borrowed from this very French word centuries earlier and sent home with a new meaning.

The semantic arc runs from bookkeeping to power. The original act — comparing one register against another — generalized into “to verify, to inspect,” which is still the dominant French sense: a ticket ~contrôleur~ checks, a ~contrôle~ is an inspection or a roadside check, false. From the English re-import came the further idea of holding something in one's grip, of steering it. The ~rotulus~ branch flourished elsewhere too: French ~rôle~ kept its theatrical and administrative life (an actor's part was once literally the scroll bearing the lines), and ~rouleau~, ~enrôler~, and ~contrôle~ all descend from the humble Latin ~rota~, the turning wheel.
en.convaincre:
From Latin ~convincere~ (“to refute, to prove conclusively, to convict”), formed from the prefix ~con-~ (an intensive use of ~cum~, “with, completely”) and ~vincere~ (“to conquer, to defeat”). ~Vincere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~winkō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~weik-~ (“to overcome, to fight”), reached through a nasal-infixed form *~wi-n-k-~. Cognate, through ~vincere~, with Italian ~vincere~ and Spanish ~vencer~ (“to win”), and with the borrowed English doublet ~convince~.

The Latin sense was forensic: to ~convincere~ someone was to defeat them decisively in argument, and so to prove them guilty or in error. French kept the verb close to this combative origin — to ~convaincre~ is, etymologically, to vanquish another's resistance with reasons until they yield. The same root *~weik-~ runs through a large family of French and English words built on ~vincere~: ~vaincre~ (“to defeat”), ~invincible~, ~victoire~, convaincre's near-twin ~convaincu~, and the legal ~conviction~. The Latin past participle ~convictus~ even gave English ~convict~, preserving the courtroom flavor that French ~convaincre~ has largely traded for the gentler work of persuasion.
en.convenir:
From Latin ~convenire~ (“to come together, to assemble, to agree”), a compound of ~con-~ (“with, together”) and ~venire~ (“to come”). ~venire~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷeniō~ and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”). Cognate with Italian ~convenire~ and Spanish ~convenir~, and — through the same PIE root — with English ~come~ and Latin-derived ~convene~.

The literal sense, “to come together,” fans out beautifully in modern French. When people come together they reach accord, hence ~convenir~ “to agree, to admit”; when a thing comes together well with a situation it fits, hence “to suit, to be convenient.” The same gathering image gives ~couvent~ (a convent, those who have come together) and ~convention~ (an agreement reached in common). The PIE root *~gʷem-~ is among the most fertile in the language, underlying through ~venire~ a whole battery of French verbs — ~venir~, ~devenir~, ~revenir~, ~prévenir~, ~parvenir~, ~survenir~ — and, via the supine ~ventum~, the nouns ~avenue~ and ~événement~. The everyday ~ça me convient~ thus carries, fossilized within it, the ancient picture of two paths meeting.
en.converger: ~Converger~ is borrowed from Latin ~convergere~, formed from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~vergere~ (“to bend, to incline”). The picture is of lines or paths that lean toward one another until they meet at a point. French first used it for geometry and optics, where rays and lines converge, and then figuratively for opinions, efforts or interests that draw together. Its mirror image is ~diverger~, which bends apart instead. English ~converge~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.convertir:
From Latin ~convertere~ (“to turn around, transform”), a compound of the prefix ~con-~ (“together, completely”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~Vertere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wertō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”). The root is widespread: it gives Sanskrit ~vártate~ (“turns”), and through Proto-Germanic *~werþaną~ (“to become”) the English ~-ward~ and ~worth~ and German ~werden~ — the link between turning and coming-to-be.

The Latin verb of physical turning broadened into many figurative directions, all kept in French. ~Convertir~ can mean to transform one substance into another, to exchange currency or property, to turn someone toward a new faith — the religious sense that made the ~converti~ — or to change an opinion. The same root *~wert-~ underlies a vast French family: ~conversion~, ~convertisseur~, ~divertir~, ~inverser~, ~pervertir~, ~revers~, and ~verser~. Across all of them runs the single image at the heart of ~vertere~: a turning, whether of an object, a currency, a soul, or a mind.
en.convier:
From Old French ~cunveer~ and ~cunvier~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~convitāre~ (“to invite”), attested in Medieval Latin as ~convitare~. The shape of this verb is probably explained as a cross between Latin ~invītāre~ (“to invite”) and ~convivium~ (“a banquet, a feast together”), a noun built from ~con-~ (“together”) and the root of ~vīvere~ (“to live”). The origin is thus a blend rather than a plain derivation, and it stays a hypothesis. The verb has relatives elsewhere in Romance: Italian ~convitare~ and Portuguese ~convidar~ (and Spanish ~convidar~) follow the same Vulgar Latin form.

If the blend is right, ~convier~ carried from the start the idea of an invitation to share a table. In modern French it keeps a formal, slightly literary tone: one ~convie~ guests to a ceremony or ~convie~ someone to reflect (~convier à la réflexion~), where ordinary speech would say ~inviter~. The two words are rivals from the same Latin source ~invītāre~, if the blend is right, but ~inviter~ is the plain everyday verb. The family also includes ~convive~ (“a guest at table”), from Latin ~convīva~, and ~convivial~ and ~convivialité~, which preserve the shared-meal image.
en.convoiter:
From Old French ~convoitier~, an altered form of the older ~coveitier~ and ~covoitier~; the ~con-~ spelling arose by analogy with the prefix ~con-~. The sources differ on the step before that. English Wiktionary posits a Vulgar Latin verb *~cupidietāre~, built on *~cupidietās~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~cupiditās~ (“desire, greed”) on the model of words like ~medietās~. French Wiktionary instead starts from Latin ~cupiō~ (“to desire”), whose frequentative *~cupitāre~ in Late Latin would have given the Old French verb, and it adds that a passage through the noun ~cupiditās~ is conceivable. Both accounts meet at the same Latin root, ~cupere~. English ~covet~ is the same word borrowed from Old French, and ~cupidity~ and ~Cupid~ belong to the same Latin family.

The French account leans on a general habit of the spoken language: Latin verbs were often replaced by their frequentatives, built on the supine, as with ~habiter~, ~bouger~ and ~exploiter~. The consonants tell their own story. The Latin ~p~ between vowels became ~v~ in French, the same change that turned Latin ~cūpa~ into ~cuve~. The meaning, by contrast, stayed remarkably steady: ~convoiter~ is to desire what belongs to someone else or lies out of reach, with an edge of greed. Its family includes ~convoitise~ (“covetousness”) and the learned ~cupidité~, a reminder that two words from one root can arrive by different roads, one worn down by the people and one lifted straight from Latin.
en.convoquer:
From Latin ~convocāre~ (“to call together, assemble”), from ~con-~ (“together”) plus ~vocāre~ (“to call”). ~vocāre~ rests on ~vōx~ (“voice”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wekʷ-~ (“to speak, utter”). Cognate, through that root, with English ~voice~ and ~vocal~ and with Sanskrit ~वाच्~ (~vāc~, “speech”).

The image is exact: to ~convoquer~ is to use the voice to gather people in one place. French keeps this in its formal registers — a court ~convoquer~ a witness, a director ~convoquer~ the staff, an assembly is ~convoquée~ into session. From the same ~vocāre~ / ~vōx~ stem French drew a large family: appeler's learned twin ~invoquer~, plus ~évoquer~, ~provoquer~, ~révoquer~, ~vocation~, ~vocal~, and ~voix~ itself. Every ~convocation~ is, at heart, a calling-together by voice.
en.coopérer:
From Latin ~cooperari~ (“to work together”), formed from ~co-~, the form of ~cum-~ (“with”) before a vowel, and ~operari~ (“to work, to labor”). The Latin verb ~operari~ is built on ~opus~ (“work, task”), the same root as French ~œuvre~, and English ~cooperate~ and Italian ~cooperare~ descend from the same Latin verb. French ~coopérer~ keeps the learned stem ~opér-~, unlike the popular verb ~ouvrer~, which also comes from ~operari~ but followed the ordinary sound changes of inherited words.

The idea of joint labor has hardly moved since Latin: to ~coopérer~ is still to work with others toward a shared end. The family around it is large. ~Opérer~ and ~opération~ come from ~operari~ and ~opus~ by learned routes, and ~coopération~ and ~coopératif~ share the prefix. The Latin plural of ~opus~, ~opera~ (“works”), came through Italian as ~opéra~, so an opera is, etymologically, a collection of works.
en.coordonner:
~Coordonner~ is ~ordonner~ (“to order, arrange”) prefixed with ~co-~ (Latin ~cum~, “with, together”), the whole meaning “to arrange things together.” ~Ordonner~ descends from Latin ~ordinare~, from ~ōrdō~ (“row, rank, order”), from Proto-Italic *~ordō~, from PIE *~h₂er-~ (“to fit together”) — the same root that gave Latin ~artus~ (“joint”) and, through it, English ~art~ and ~article~.

The oldest image under ~ōrdō~ is weaving: a row of threads fitted side by side on the loom, things set in their proper place. ~Coordonner~ adds the togetherness of ~cum~, so that to coordinate is to fit several ordered series into one working whole — exactly what the grammatical sense preserves, where ~coordonner~ links clauses of equal rank by a conjonction de ~coordination~. The verb is learned and relatively late, and French smoothed its vowels to align it with ~ordonner~ rather than keep a stiffer *coordiner. Around it cluster ~coordination~, ~coordinateur~, and ~coordonnée~ (the mathematician's “coordinate,” a number that fixes a point's place in an ordered grid). To coordinate is, etymologically, to fit ranks together.
en.copier:
From Medieval Latin ~copiare~ (“to copy out, transcribe”), derived from Classical Latin ~copia~ (“abundance, plenty”), which also gave French ~copie~. ~copia~ is itself a compound of ~co-~ (“with, together”) and ~ops~ (“wealth, resources”), the latter from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, produce”). Through that root ~copia~ is cognate with English ~copious~ and ~cornucopia~ — the “horn of plenty.”

The semantic leap from “abundance” to “copy” happened in the medieval scriptorium: to copy a text by hand was, literally, to make it abundant, to multiply the available exemplars. From ~copia~'s sense of plenty, ~copiare~ took on the new meaning of reproducing, and modern French ~copier~ runs from faithful transcription to imitation and, in the classroom, to cheating off a neighbor. English borrowed the word through Old French as ~copy~, shifting it firmly toward “duplicate.” The same ~copia~ underlies French ~copie~, ~copieux~ (“copious, ample”), and ~photocopie~.
en.correspondre:
French ~correspondre~ comes from Medieval Latin ~correspondēre~, formed from ~respondēre~ (“to answer, to respond”) with the prefix ~con-~ / ~cor-~ (“with, together”). ~Respondēre~ is itself ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~spondēre~ (“to pledge, to promise solemnly”), from Proto-Italic *~spondeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~spend-~ (“to perform a rite, to make an offering”). The Greek cognates ~spéndō~ (“to pour a libation”) and ~spondḗ~ (“libation, solemn truce”) preserve the religious flavour; through the same Latin verb English gained ~respond~, ~sponsor~, and ~spouse~.

The literal idea is mutual pledging: to ~correspondre~ is etymologically “to pledge back together,” one party answering another in kind. From this came two great branches. The first is the abstract sense “to match, to agree, to be in harmony” — colours that ~correspondent~ to one another. The second is the sense “to exchange letters,” reciprocal answering carried on at a distance, which gave the noun ~correspondance~ and, by a charming extension, the ~correspondance~ one makes between two metro lines. The buried root surfaces across French in ~répondre~, ~époux~ and ~épouse~ (a spouse is one solemnly pledged), ~répons~, and ~spontané~. A solemn libation poured to seal an oath has become, in the end, a postcard.
en.corriger:
From Latin ~corrigere~ (“to set straight, reform, amend”), a compound of ~cum~ (“with, together”) — reduced to ~cor-~ before ~r~ — and ~regere~ (“to direct, guide, rule”). ~Regere~ descends from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct, make right”), one of the most productive roots in the language, source also of Latin ~rēx~ (“king”) and ~rēctus~ (“straight, right”). Through that root ~corriger~ is cognate with English ~right~ and German ~recht~, and with Italian ~correggere~ and Spanish ~corregir~. The literal Latin image is concrete: to “straighten thoroughly,” to bring a crooked thing back into line.

That spatial metaphor — making the bent straight — underlies every modern sense. To correct an error is to straighten what has gone awry; to correct a pupil or a fault is to guide conduct back onto the right path. French preserved the schoolroom sense of marking and grading work, ~corriger une copie~, alongside the moral one of ~se corriger~ (“to mend one's ways”). From the same root *~h₃reǵ-~ French draws a wide family: ~diriger~, ~régir~, ~règle~, ~droit~ (from ~dīrēctus~), ~roi~, and ~correct~ itself, the learned doublet of the past participle. The crooked line made straight runs quietly through them all.
en.corrompre:
Taken into Old French from Latin ~corrumpere~ (“to break totally, to destroy, to spoil”), formed from the intensive prefix ~com-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~rumpere~ (“to break”). English Wiktionary notes that the French verb was reshaped on ~rompre~, the inherited descendant of ~rumpere~, so ~corrompre~ looks and conjugates like its simple verb. English ~corrupt~ was borrowed from the Latin past participle ~corruptus~, and ~rupture~, ~erupt~ and ~interrupt~ come from the same ~rumpere~.

Latin already used ~corrumpere~ for more than physical breaking. It meant to spoil, to taint, to seduce, and to bribe a witness or a judge, and French kept the whole range. In modern French the verb covers moral depravity (~corrompre la jeunesse~), bribery (~corrompre un fonctionnaire~), and, more rarely, physical decay. The idea is always one of something whole being broken. The noun ~corruption~ gives the political scandal its name, ~corrupteur~ is the briber, and the adjective ~incorruptible~ was famously used of Robespierre. The family also includes ~rompre~, ~rupture~, ~interrompre~ and ~irruption~.
en.corréler: ~Corréler~ is a back-formation from ~corrélation~, which French borrowed from Late Latin ~correlātiō~, built on ~con-~ (“together”) and ~relātiō~ (“a bringing back, a relation”). The verb was made by stripping the noun's ending and adding the infinitive ending ~-er~, the reverse of the usual order in which a verb gives a noun. It means “to put two things in relation, to establish a statistical link between them,” and it is used above all in science and statistics, where one variable is ~corrélée~ with another.
en.corser: Both Wiktionaries derive ~corser~ from ~corps~ (“body”) plus ~-er~, with fr.Wiktionary specifying the old spelling ~cors~. The idea is to give something body: to make a drink, a sauce or a dish stronger, fuller, more highly flavored, and by extension to make a story or a situation more intense. ~Corps~ itself comes from Latin ~corpus~. The reflexive ~se corser~ is the common modern use: when a plot or a problem ~se corse~, it thickens and gets harder. The suffix ~-er~ is the usual one for building a verb from a noun.
en.coter:
Modern French ~coter~ is a denominal verb, drawn from the noun ~cote~. That noun was borrowed from Medieval Latin ~quota~ (clipped from ~quota pars~, “the share due from each person”), the feminine of Latin ~quotus~ (“which in order? what number?”), itself built on ~quot~ (“how many”). The chain reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European interrogative stem *~kʷo-~, the same pronominal root behind Latin ~quis~ and ~quod~. Through ~quota~, the noun ~cote~ is an etymological doublet of the international word ~quota~ and a cousin of English ~quote~, which passed through Medieval Latin ~quotare~ (“to mark off by numbers”).

From the bookkeeper's ~quota pars~ — each person's numbered share on a tax roll — ~cote~ branched into a surprising spread of senses: a figure marked on a plan (a dimension), a price quoted on the exchange, a horse's odds, a library shelfmark, and a grade given to a pupil's work. The verb ~coter~ inherited this whole range, so that today one may ~coter~ a security, a drawing, or an essay. The same numbering instinct lives on in ~quote-part~ (“share, portion”), ~quotient~, ~quotidien~ (literally “however many days there are,” hence “daily”), and ~quorum~ — all heirs of that small Latin question ~quot~, “how many?”
en.cotiser: Formed from the noun ~cote~ with the suffix ~-iser~. ~Cote~ is from Old French ~quote~, itself from Medieval Latin ~quota~, built on Latin ~quotus~ (“how many?”), the same source as ~quota~ and the French ~quote-part~ (“share”). The verb first meant to fix each person's share of a sum, then to pay one's share, which is how ~cotiser~ now means “to pay dues or contributions,” as in ~cotiser à la Sécurité sociale~. In the reflexive, ~se cotiser~ is to chip in together.
en.coucher:
From Old French ~couchier~ (also ~colchier~), from Latin ~collocare~ (“to place, lay in position”), formed from the prefix ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~locare~ (“to place”), itself derived from ~locus~ (“place”). Old Latin had ~stlocus~, traditionally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~stel-~ (“to put, place”), though that derivation is now treated cautiously. Latin ~collocare~ also gave Spanish ~colgar~ and Italian ~coricare~, and, through learned borrowing, English ~collocate~.

In Latin ~collocare~ meant to set something carefully in its place — to arrange, to position, even to invest money or marry off a daughter (placing her well). French ~coucher~ specialized toward one kind of placing: laying a body down, hence “to put to bed,” “to lie down,” and reflexively ~se coucher~ (“to go to bed”). From the horizontal it spread to the sun that ~se couche~ (“sets”), to writing something down (~coucher par écrit~, “to put in writing”), and to the noun ~couche~ (“a layer”). Beside it stands the learned doublet ~colloquer~ and the broad ~locus~ family — ~lieu~, ~local~, ~localiser~, ~louer~ (“to rent,” from ~locare~) — all built on the idea of a place.
en.coudre:
From Middle French ~coudre~, from Old French ~coudre~ or ~cosdre~, from Vulgar Latin *~cōsere~, an altered form of Classical Latin ~cōnsuere~ (“to sew together”), itself built on ~suere~ (“to sew”). The original Old French infinitive was *~cosre~, and a ~d~ slipped in as a gliding sound between the ~s~ and the ~r~. The ~s~ then went silent, and dropped from the spelling early on. The ~d~ of present forms such as ~je couds~ is analogical, since the expected form would have been ~je cous~. English ~sew~ is a distant cousin of Latin ~suere~, and the same family gave ~suture~.

Latin ~cōnsuere~ meant to sew pieces together, so the verb has meant “to join with a thread” from the start. The past participle ~cousu~ comes from Latin ~cōnsūtus~, and several words kept the Latin stem: ~couture~ (“sewing, a seam”), ~couturier~, ~couturière~ and ~recoudre~ (“to sew back”). French also uses ~coudre~ figuratively, in ~cousu de fil blanc~ (“sewn with white thread”), said of a ruse that is too obvious to fool anyone. The noun ~coudre~ (“hazel”) is a separate word, an altered form of Latin ~corylus~.
en.couler:
From Latin ~cōlāre~ (“to strain, filter, purify”), derived from the noun ~cōlum~ (“a strainer, sieve”). The filtering sense is the original one, still faintly audible in the old phrase ~couler le lait~ (“to strain the milk”). The Romance descendants keep close: Italian ~colare~, Spanish ~colar~, Portuguese ~coar~ — all about passing a liquid through a cloth or sieve. This ~cōlō~ is etymologically distinct from the Latin ~colō~ meaning “to cultivate.”

From straining, the meaning slid naturally to the liquid's own movement — to flow, to trickle, to run — and then, of a boat letting water through, to sink. So the same verb that strains milk also sends a ship to the bottom: ~couler~ un navire. The figurative reach is wide, from ~couler des jours heureux~ (“to spend happy days,” days that flow by) to a reputation one ~coule~. Its family is large: ~coulée~, ~coulis~, ~coulant~, ~couloir~ (a corridor, a channel for passage), ~découler~ (“to follow, ensue”) and ~écouler~.
en.couper:
From Old French ~colper~, ~couper~ (eleventh century), derived from the noun ~colp~ (modern ~coup~, “a blow”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~: to ~couper~ is literally to “separate with a blow.” The noun goes back through Vulgar Latin ~colpus~ to Late Latin ~colaphus~, itself borrowed from Greek ~kólaphos~ (“a blow on the cheek, a slap”). Cognates of the noun include Italian ~colpo~ and Spanish ~golpe~, both meaning “blow, strike.”

The striking thing — fitting for a word born of a slap — is how far the meaning travelled from violence. In Old French the sense had already moved from “to strike” to “to cut,” cutting being the result of a blow with a blade, and the original Greek “box on the ear” faded entirely. From there ~couper~ spread into a huge range of idioms: ~couper l'eau~ (to cut off the water), ~couper la parole~ (to interrupt), ~couper les ponts~ (to break off relations), and from 1610 the wine-merchant's ~couper~, to dilute or blend a wine with water or another vintage. Modern French keeps a rich family around the noun ~coup~ — ~coupe~ (a cut, and a cup or trophy), ~coupon~, ~découper~ (to cut out), ~couperet~ (the cleaver, and the guillotine's blade) — all ultimately a single Greek slap.
en.coupler:
French ~coupler~ comes from Latin ~cōpulāre~ (“to join together, to bind”), a verb built on ~cōpula~ (“bond, tie, link”). Latin ~cōpula~ is generally explained as ~co-~ (“together”) plus a root meaning “to fasten.” The Latin verb reached French twice. The popular, inherited form gave ~coupler~, while a later learned borrowing gave the doublet ~copuler~, whose sense of sexual union is now the only one it keeps. The noun ~couple~ and the grammatical term ~copule~ come from the same source, and English ~couple~ and ~copula~ are cousins, ~couple~ having come through Old French.

The verb’s meaning has always centered on joining two things so that they work together. In French it covers coupling railway carriages, linking devices or circuits, pairing animals, and, figuratively, combining two elements. The two doublets show how a single Latin word can split by register: ~coupler~ stayed technical and everyday, while ~copuler~ was borrowed later for the biological sense and remains learned. The family also includes ~couple~, ~accoupler~, ~découpler~, ~copule~ and ~copulation~, all built on the image of a tie between two partners.
en.courber:
From Latin ~curvāre~ (“to bend, to make crooked”), from the adjective ~curvus~ (“bent”). French Wiktionary notes that in Vulgar Latin the verb became *~curbare~, with the ~v~ hardening to ~b~, a shift that is frequent in Romance speech. That is the form French inherited, and it explains the ~b~ in ~courber~ against the ~v~ of the learned relatives. English ~curve~ belongs to the same Latin family.

The literal sense is to bend something straight into an arc: a branch under fruit, a back under a load. The figurative uses followed naturally, as in ~courber l'échine~ (“to bow one's back, to submit”) and ~se courber~ (“to stoop, to bow down”), and in the old idea of ~courber la tête~ (“to bow the head”). The family includes ~courbe~ (“curve”), ~courbure~ (“curvature”), ~recourber~ (“to bend back”) and ~incurver~ (“to curve inward”), the last borrowed back from the Latin ~curvus~ family in learned form.
en.courir:
From Old French ~courre~, ~corre~ (“to run”), from Latin ~currere~ (“to run, to hasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The infinitive ~courir~ is an analogical reshaping that, from the fourteenth century onward, displaced the older ~courre~ on the model of other verbs. Cognate, through ~currere~, with Italian ~correre~ and Spanish ~correr~, and — through the same PIE root *~ḱers-~ — with English ~horse~ and ~hurry~ and with the Latin-borrowed ~current~ and ~career~.

The old form ~courre~ has not vanished entirely: it survives, fossilized, in the hunting term ~chasse à courre~ (“hunting with hounds on horseback”), a phrase that still uses the medieval infinitive. ~Currere~ is one of Latin's most mobile roots, and French is full of its offspring: ~course~, ~coureur~, ~courrier~ (originally a “runner” who carried messages), ~courant~, ~concourir~, ~parcourir~, ~secourir~, and ~recourir~. The English ~courier~, ~course~, ~current~, ~occur~, and ~excursion~ all descend from the same running root, as does ~corridor~ — etymologically a “running-place.” Few Latin verbs have sprinted so far through the vocabulary of its daughter languages.
en.courser: Formed in French from ~course~ and the first-group ending ~-er~. The noun ~course~ is itself derived from ~cours~, with influence from Italian ~corsa~, and ~cours~ goes back to Latin ~cursus~ (“a running, course”), from ~currō~ (“to run”). So the verb belongs to the large family of Latin ~currere~, which also gave ~courir~, ~concours~ and ~recours~. ~Courser~ is a familiar word meaning “to chase after someone,” as in ~courser quelqu'un~: it turns the run of the noun back into an action, a pursuit at full speed.
en.couver:
Inherited from Latin ~cubāre~ (“to lie down, to recline”). fr.Wiktionary adds that the Latin verb was used in the sense of ~incubāre~ (“to lie upon”), the source of English ~incubate~ and French ~incuber~, and that the figurative sense of a fire smoldering under the ashes comes from the same ~cubāre~ taken as “to lie.” Hatching is the image: a hen lies on her eggs. Italian ~covare~ also comes from ~cubāre~, and the Latin family includes ~cubiculum~ (“bedroom”, the source of English ~cubicle~) and ~concumbere~, from which French ~concubine~ ultimately derives, as does ~succomber~ through ~succumbere~ (“to lie down under”).

In French, ~couver~ first meant what a hen does, that is, to sit on eggs to hatch them, with the noun ~couvée~ (“brood”) and ~couveuse~ (“incubator”) as its products. The idea of tender, patient sitting then spread to people: one ~couve~ a child, meaning one over-protects it, or ~couve~ someone with the eyes, meaning gazes at them with longing. It also took a darker turn. An illness, a plot or a resentment can ~couver~, that is, develop in silence before breaking out, in the same way as a fire that smolders under cold ash. Do not confuse it with ~couvrir~ (“to cover”) and ~couvercle~ (“lid”), which come from Latin ~cooperīre~ and merely look alike.
en.couvrir:
From Old French ~covrir~, from Latin ~cooperire~ (“to cover wholly, to cover over”), a compound of ~co-~ (an intensive form of ~cum~, “with, together”) and ~operire~ (“to close, to cover”). ~operire~ comes from a Proto-Indo-European compound *~op-wer-yo-~, joining *~op-~ (“over”) with the root *~wer-~ (“to cover, to shut”). ~couvrir~ is cognate with Italian ~coprire~ and Spanish ~cubrir~, and — through Old French ~covert~ — with English ~cover~ and ~covert~.

A neat irony hides in the family. The same root *~wer-~ produced a near-mirror verb, ~aperire~ (“to open, to uncover”), from *~ap-wer-yo-~: change the prefix from “over” to “off, away” and covering becomes uncovering. That ~aperire~ gave French ~ouvrir~ (“to open”) and English ~overt~ and ~aperture~ — so ~couvrir~ and ~ouvrir~, perfect opposites in meaning, are siblings built on one root. From ~cooperire~ French drew a rich harvest: ~couvert~ (“covered,” also a table setting and shelter), ~couverture~ (“blanket, cover”), ~couvercle~ (“lid”), ~découvrir~ (“to uncover, to discover”), and the vivid compounds ~couvre-chef~ (“headgear”) and ~couvre-feu~ (literally “cover-fire,” the medieval ~curfew~).
en.coûter:
From Middle French ~couster~, from Old French ~couster~, from Latin ~constāre~ (“to stand firm, to stand together,” and so “to be fixed at a price, to cost”), the infinitive of ~cōnstō~. The verb is built from the intensive prefix ~com-~ and ~stāre~ (“to stand”), the same root that gives English ~stand~ and ~stay~. Italian ~costare~ and Spanish ~costar~ are its everyday cousins, and English ~cost~ is borrowed, through Old French, from the very same source.

The semantic leap from “to stand” to “to cost” runs through the idea of a price at which something is fixed or settled: what a thing ~constat~ is what it firmly “stands at.” Old French ~couster~ kept this commercial sense, and modern French extended it figuratively — an effort, a sacrifice, or a mistake can ~coûter~ dearly without any money changing hands, as in the proverb ~coûte que coûte~ (“cost what it may, at all costs”). From the same Latin ~stāre~ descend a broad family of French words, including ~constant~, ~coût~ (the noun “cost”), ~constance~, and — through ~constāre~ itself — ~contraster~ and ~contraste~, where things are made to “stand against” one another.
en.cracher:
The origin is debated. French Wiktionary derives it from an imitative syllable ~crac~, present in both the Romance and the Germanic worlds. English Wiktionary gives Old French ~crachier~ (“to eject from the mouth”), from Vulgar Latin *~craccare~, also imitative, and says it may have come by way of Frankish *~hrākijan~ or *~hrakkjan~. Cognates support the Germanic route: Old High German ~hrahhan~ (“to spew, spit”), Old English ~hrǣċan~ (“to retch, cough up, spit”) and Old Norse ~hrǽkja~ (“to hawk, spit”). They descend from Proto-Germanic *~hrēkijaną~ (“to spit, retch”), itself perhaps related to a sound-word *~krakōn~ (“to make a cracking sound”). So the verb may be pure sound-imitation or a loan from the Franks, or a blend of the two.

Whatever its source, the verb has stayed close to the physical act. Its family includes ~crachat~ (“spit, spittle”) and ~crachoir~ (“spittoon”). French Wiktionary also offers a hedged explanation for the expression ~tout craché~, said of a striking likeness: it may come from a comparison between a ~crachat~ and a drop of water, in the manner of the phrase for two people alike as two drops of water. The sources only offer this as a possibility, so it is best held lightly. Figuratively, ~cracher~ can also mean to hand something out with disdain or to pay up reluctantly.
en.craindre:
From Old French ~criembre~, ~creindre~ (attested as early as the ninth-century ~Cantilène de sainte Eulalie~), later reshaped to ~craindre~ on the model of other ~-aindre~ verbs like ~plaindre~ and ~fraindre~. The source is Gallo-Roman *~cremere~, an alteration of Latin *~tremere~ (“to tremble, to quake”) under the influence of a Gaulish form related to ~critos~ (“trembling, shudder”). The Latin verb descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~trem-~ (“to tremble”), cognate with Greek ~trémō~ (“I tremble”) and Italian ~tremare~. English ~tremble~ and ~tremor~ belong to the same family.

The shift from “to tremble” to “to fear” is intuitive: dread makes the body shake, so the physical tremor lent its name to the emotion. The Celtic colouring of the initial ~cr-~ is a rare visible trace of Gaulish on a Latin verb, a substrate fingerprint left as Latin settled over Gaul. From the same ~trem-~ root, but borrowed by the learned route, French also possesses ~trembler~ (through Late Latin ~tremulāre~), ~trémousser~ (“to wriggle”), ~tremblement~ (“trembling, earthquake”), and ~trémolo~. So the homely ~craindre~ and the literary ~trembler~ are, beneath their very different shapes, two reflexes of a single ancient shudder.
en.craquer:
Modern French ~craquer~ (1544) is built on the onomatopoeia ~crac~, an imitation of a sharp snapping sound. The deeper origin is genuinely debated: French sources such as the TLFi treat the word as a native echoic formation, while other accounts derive it instead from a Germanic verb — Middle Dutch ~kraken~ (“to crack, crackle”), traced back to Frankish *~krakōn~ and ultimately to an imitative Proto-Indo-European *~gerg-~ (“to caw, shout”). The two stories are hard to separate precisely because the sound itself is so naturally imitative that several languages coined near-identical words independently. By either account, English ~crack~ (from Old English ~cracian~) belongs to the same echoic family.

From the literal noise of something snapping, ~craquer~ branched widely. The figurative sense “to threaten ruin, to give way” is attested from 1718 — a structure, a nerve, or a resolve that ~craque~ is one about to break. Slang lent it “to die” and, later, “to crack under pressure” or even “to fall for” someone. The petroleum and computing senses (1967 onward) were re-modeled on English ~crack~. The same root cluster gives French ~craquement~ (“a cracking sound”), craquer’s noun ~craque~ (“a tall tale”), and ~craquelure~, the fine web of cracks prized on old varnished paintings.
en.creuser:
A denominal verb from the noun and adjective ~creux~ (« hollow »), attested as a noun (« cavity ») around 1121 and as an adjective around 1180. The origin of ~creux~ is of disputed origin: the dictionaries reconstruct a Late Latin *~crosus~ (« hollow »), which they call « probably » the source, while noting it « perhaps » rests on a Celtic, that is Gaulish, base. The Latin etymon is itself unattested, and the sources frankly label the whole « of uncertain origin. »

From « to make hollow, » ~creuser~ broadened to « to dig » in the ordinary sense — a well, a ditch, a tunnel — and then to the figurative « to dig into, » as one ~creuse~ a question to its depths, or « creuser l'écart » to widen a gap in a race or a score. The hollow also gnaws: « ça me ~creuse~ » means hunger is digging at the stomach. Modern kin of the base include the noun ~creux~ itself, ~creuset~ (« crucible, » a hollow vessel), and the past participle ~creusé~ used as a noun for a dug-out hollow. Cognates appear in Old Occitan ~cros~ and northern Italian dialects, confirming the Gallo-Romance spread even as the deepest source stays unproven.
en.crever:
From Old French ~crever~, inherited from Latin ~crepāre~ (“to rattle, to creak, to crack”). The Latin verb imitates a sharp noise, and its first sense was about sound. Italian ~crepare~ and Romanian ~crăpa~ come from the same Latin verb, and, like French, both reached the informal sense of “to die.” The learned side of the family gives French ~crépiter~, “to crackle,” borrowed from a Latin verb built on ~crepāre~. In French, the original idea of something bursting with a crack was extended from the noise to the break itself.

French Wiktionary traces the development as a slide from “to burst,” in the sense of a loud crack, to “to split” (compare the noun ~crevée~, a slash in a garment), and finally to “to die.” It notes that figurative speech shows the same drift in laughter, where ~éclater de rire~, ~se fendre la gueule~ and ~mourir de rire~ all point to something bursting open. Today ~crever~ covers a tire that bursts (~crevaison~), a balloon that pops, hunger or work that wears one out, and, in blunt registers, dying. From the verb come ~crevasse~ (a split in ice or earth) and ~crevé~ (“exhausted”).
en.crier:
From Old French ~crier~ (also ~crider~), attested by about 980, from Vulgar Latin *~critare~, a reduction of Latin ~quiritare~ (“to cry out, wail, shriek”); compare Old Occitan ~cridar~. The origin of ~quiritare~ is disputed: De Vaan accepts the ancient idea that it meant to call upon the ~Quirites~, the Roman citizens, for help; others derive it from ~queror~ (“to complain”), though the phonetics are hard to trace, or treat it as onomatopoeic. A comparison with Frankish *~krītan~ (“to cry out”) has also been noted. The sources leave the matter open.

Whatever its source, the verb has always named the raising of the voice — in alarm, in pain, in protest, in proclamation. French keeps the full range, from a child's cry to a vendor crying his wares. From the same stem come ~cri~ (“cry, shout”), ~criard~ (“shrill, garish”), ~crieur~ (“crier, hawker”), ~criailler~ (“to squawk”), and the prefixed ~s'écrier~ (“to exclaim”). If the disputed Quirites story is right, then every French ~cri~ faintly echoes an ancient Roman shouting for his fellow citizens.
en.cristalliser: Formed from ~cristal~ and the suffix ~-iser~, “to make into”, so ~cristalliser~ means to turn into crystals. ~Cristal~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~crystallus~ (“ice”, then “rock crystal”), which comes from Greek ~krústallos~ (“ice”), a derivative of ~krúos~ (“frost”). The name reflects an ancient notion that clear quartz was ice frozen hard. The verb passed from chemistry and mineralogy to figures of speech: an opinion, a plan or a feeling ~cristallise~ when it hardens into a definite form.
en.critiquer:
A denominal verb, recorded in 1546, built on the noun and adjective ~critique~, borrowed from Latin ~criticus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~κριτικός~ (~kritikós~, “able to discern or judge”), from ~κριτής~ (~kritḗs~, “a judge”), from the verb ~κρίνω~ (~krínō~, “to separate, sift, decide, judge”). That verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~krey-~ (“to sieve, separate, distinguish”). Through Latin ~cernere~ and ~crīmen~ the same root reaches English ~certain~, ~crime~, ~discern~, and ~crisis~.

The buried image is a sieve: to judge is to sift, separating the sound from the unsound. A ~critique~ in Greek and early French was first one who discerns and evaluates — a literary or medical judge — and ~critiquer~ began neutrally as “to examine and appraise.” Only later did the pejorative tilt set in, so that today ~critiquer~ leans toward finding fault. French keeps the whole spread from this root: ~critique~ (both “a critic” and “a review”), ~critère~ (“criterion,” a means of sifting), ~crise~ (“crisis,” a decisive turning point), and ~hypocrite~ — etymologically one who answers from under a mask, judging in disguise.
en.croire:
From Middle French ~croire~, from Old French ~creire~, ~croire~, from Latin ~crēdere~ (“to entrust as a loan; to trust, to have confidence in”). The Latin verb continues a Proto-Indo-European compound *~ḱred-dʰeh₁-~, literally “to place one's heart,” fusing *~ḱred-~ (the oblique stem of “heart”) with *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, set, place”). The same archaic compound surfaces far afield: Sanskrit ~śrad-dhā~ (“faith, trust”) and Old Irish ~creitid~ (“believes”) preserve the identical heart-placing image.

The earliest Latin sense was concrete and commercial — to ~crēdere~ was to entrust money to someone, to extend credit, trusting they would repay. From this lending of trust grew the sense “to have confidence,” and during the Christian era the strong religious meaning “to believe, to hold as an article of faith” developed and came to dominate. The metaphor at the bottom — belief as setting one's heart on something — is one of the oldest in Indo-European. From ~crēdere~ French inherited or borrowed a rich set: ~croyance~, ~croyant~, ~crédit~, ~crédible~, ~créance~, ~crédule~, and the liturgical ~credo~ (Latin for “I believe”).
en.croiser:
A denominal verb, derived from the noun ~croix~ (“cross”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. ~Croix~ descends from Latin ~crux~ (genitive ~crucis~, “stake, cross”), the instrument on which the condemned were impaled or crucified. The same ~crux~ gave Italian ~croce~, Spanish ~cruz~, and — by way of Old Norse and Old Irish ~cros~ — English ~cross~ itself.

The ultimate origin of Latin ~crux~ is uncertain and best left open. The French verb means, fundamentally, “to put in the form of a cross”: one ~croise~ one's arms, two roads ~se croisent~ (intersect), and two travellers ~se croisent~ when their paths cross going opposite ways. From ~croix~ the language built a rich field: ~croisement~ (“crossing, intersection,” and in biology “crossbreeding”), ~croisière~ (“cruise,” a ship originally “crossing” to and fro on patrol), ~croisé~ (“crusader,” one who took the cross), and ~croisade~ (“crusade”). Through Latin ~crux~ the same root reaches English ~crucial~, ~crucify~, ~crusade~, and ~cruise~ — every one of them shaped, literally or figuratively, like a cross.
en.croquer:
The origin of ~croquer~ is not settled, and the sources offer two accounts. French Wiktionary treats it as imitative, from the onomatopoeia ~croc~, the dry sound of something hard breaking under the teeth, related to ~cric~ and ~crac~. English Wiktionary instead derives it from Middle French ~croquer~ and Old French ~crokier~ (“to slap, to hit”), and says it is probably a variant of the verb that became modern ~craquer~ (“to crack, to crunch”). The two accounts are compatible in spirit, since both link the verb to a family of sound-imitating words, but they disagree on whether the starting point is the sound itself or an older verb of striking.

Whatever its source, the verb's meanings are easy to follow. ~Croquer~ can describe the crunch of something hard under the teeth, hence ~croquer~ (“to eat with a crunch”) and the adjective ~croquant~ (“crunchy”). It also reaches consuming money, ~croquer sa fortune~ (“to squander one's wealth”), and drawing a quick outline, whence ~croquis~ (“sketch”). The sources do not trace how these senses grew from one another. Related words include ~croquette~, ~croque-monsieur~ and ~croque-mort~, and the sound-word family also contains ~craquer~.
en.croître:
From Middle French ~croistre~, from Old French ~creistre~ (“to grow, prosper”), from Latin ~crescere~ (“to grow”), an inchoative verb (“to begin to grow”) built on the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱer-~ (“to grow, become bigger”) — the same root that gave Latin ~creare~ (“to create”) and the grain-goddess ~Ceres~. It is the everyday cousin of Italian ~crescere~ and Spanish ~crecer~.

Through Latin ~crescere~ and Old French ~creistre~, an astonishing crowd of English words shares this ancestry: ~crescent~ (“the growing moon”), ~increase~, ~accrue~, ~recruit~ (a fresh “growth” of soldiers), ~crew~, and — via ~concrescere~ “to grow together” — ~concrete~. In French the family is just as wide: ~croissance~ (“growth”), ~croissant~ (“growing,” hence the crescent-shaped pastry), ~accroître~ and ~décroître~, and ~crû~ (a wine's “growth,” its vineyard of origin). The inchoative ~-sc-~ that marks ~crescere~ as “entering into growth” is the very element that, worn down, gives French verbs like ~croître~ their distinctive look.
en.crypter: A back-formation: French Wiktionary says ~crypter~ arose from ~encrypter~ by dropping the prefix ~en-~. The longer verb rests on the root ~crypt-~, which French took from Greek ~kruptós~ (“hidden”), the same root as in ~crypte~, ~cryptographie~ and ~cryptogramme~. To ~crypter~ a message is therefore, at root, to hide it. Many language authorities prefer ~chiffrer~ for this sense, but ~crypter~ is common in everyday French about files, messages and television signals.
en.créditer: Formed from the noun ~crédit~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~credito~, from Latin ~crēditum~, the supine of ~crēdere~ (“to believe, to trust”). Credit is thus literally the belief that a borrower will repay. To ~créditer~ an account is to enter a sum in it, extending that trust or the amount owed to it.
en.créer:
From Old French ~creer~, from Latin ~creāre~ (“to bring forth, to produce, to beget”). The verb belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱer-~ (“to grow, to nourish”), and its oldest Latin sense was close to “to make grow.” That same root stands behind ~crēscere~ (“to grow, to arise”) and behind ~Cerēs~, the Roman goddess of grain and agriculture — so to “create” is etymologically to cause to flourish. Cognate verbs survive as Italian ~creare~ and Spanish ~crear~, and the family entered English as ~create~ and ~creature~.

In classical Latin ~creāre~ already covered both the divine act of bringing the world into being and the civic act of electing or appointing a magistrate, who was “created” by the people's vote. French ~créer~ inherited chiefly the productive, originating sense — to bring something new into existence — while keeping a foothold in officialdom, as when a post or a title is “created.” From the same Latin verb and the broader root come a rich family of French words, among them ~création~, ~créature~, ~créateur~, ~créatif~, and, through ~crēscere~, ~croître~ (“to grow”) and ~croissant~ (“growing; crescent; croissant”). The English ~recruit~, a fresh “growth” of new soldiers, springs from the same image of growing.
en.crémer: Two unrelated verbs share this spelling. The one glossed “to add cream” is formed from ~crème~ and the ending ~-er~. The other is a learned borrowing from Latin ~cremāre~ (“to burn”), and it is a doublet of ~cramer~: the same Latin verb reached French both by the learned road, as ~crémer~, and by the popular road, as ~cramer~ (compare slang ~cramé~, “burnt”). This second verb is the root of ~crémation~ and ~crématoire~, and of English ~cremate~. The cream sense is French-internal, while the burning sense goes back to Latin.
en.cueillir:
From Old French ~coillir~, inherited from Latin ~colligere~ (“to gather, to collect”), itself ~con-~ (“together”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick”). The modern spelling needs explaining. In Old French the stressed forms of the verb, such as ~cueil~, had a diphthong from an open Latin vowel, as in Old French ~cuer~, which became ~cœur~. The infinitive took its stem from those stressed forms, and its ending ~-ir~ was a later analogical reshaping, partly on the past form ~coilli~. The original infinitives, ~cueudre~, ~cueildre~ and ~cueldre~, fell out of use. ~Cueillir~ is a doublet of the learned ~colliger~, which took the same Latin verb straight from the book. English ~collect~ comes from the same Latin source, and the root of ~legere~ also lies behind ~lire~, ~élire~ and ~lecture~.

The Latin verb meant to gather things together, and French narrowed it to picking flowers and fruit, though the broader sense survives in ~accueillir~ (“to welcome”, literally to gather someone to oneself) and ~recueillir~ (“to collect”, also “to gather in thought”). The noun ~cueillette~ names the harvest of wild or garden produce. The verb has a famous conjugation, with its ~-e~ endings in the present (~je cueille~) and the future ~cueillerai~. Behind the whole family stands a Proto-Indo-European sense of gathering, preserved as well in Greek ~légein~ and in English ~legend~, literally “what is to be read”.
en.cuire:
From Gallo-Romance *~cocere~, a reshaping of Late Latin ~cocere~, itself an alteration of Classical Latin ~coquere~ (“to cook”). The earlier Latin form was *~quoquō~, dissimilated from Proto-Italic *~kʷekʷō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~pekʷ-~ (“to cook, to ripen”). The root is widespread: it gives Ancient Greek ~πέσσω~ (~péssō~, “to cook, to digest”), Sanskrit ~pácati~ (“he cooks”), and survives faintly in English ~cook~ (a Latin borrowing).

The verb has always covered both the cook’s fire and nature’s slow heat: one can ~cuire~ a meal, but fruit and grain also ~cuire~ as they ripen under the sun, faithful to the root’s double sense of “cook” and “ripen.” French extends ~cuire~ to the sting of pain — a wound or sunburned skin can ~cuire~ (“to smart, to burn”) — and to bitter experience, as in the warning ~il vous en cuira~ (“you’ll regret it, you’ll pay for it”). The same Latin ~coquere~ left a trail of French words: ~cuisine~ and ~cuisinier~, ~cuit~ and ~biscuit~ (“twice-cooked”), ~cuisson~, the archaic ~queux~ (“cook”), and ~cocotte~ (“a small cooking pot”).
en.cuisiner:
~cuisiner~ is simply ~cuisine~ plus the verb ending ~-er~ — and it is attested as far back as the thirteenth-century Chanson d'Antioche. ~cuisine~ descends from Late Latin ~coquīna~ (“kitchen”), from classical ~coquere~ (“to cook; to ripen”). That verb's history holds a small phonetic marvel: Proto-Indo-European *~pekʷ-~ (“to cook, to ripen”) should have given Latin a p-initial verb, but the first consonant assimilated to the second, *~kʷekʷō~, yielding ~coquō~ — in Latin, even the word bubbles. The root's relatives span the family: Sanskrit ~pácati~ and Greek ~péssō~ (“cooks, ripens”), Italian ~cucina~, Spanish ~cocina~ — and English ~kitchen~ with German ~Küche~, both from a very early Germanic borrowing of ~coquīna~: the Anglo-Saxon kitchen is a Latin room.

In French the root cooked up a whole pantry: ~cuire~ and ~cuisson~, ~biscuit~ (literally “twice-cooked,” the hard bread of soldiers and sailors), ~charcuterie~ (from ~chair cuite~, “cooked flesh”), and ~précoce~, from Latin ~praecox~ — “early-ripening,” that is, “cooked ahead of time.” The most surprising descendant took the long way home: Latin ~praecoqua~, “early-ripening peaches,” passed into Greek, then into Arabic as ~al-barqūq~, then through Iberia into French as ~abricot~ — the apricot is etymologically the “precocious” fruit, a Latin word that toured the Mediterranean for a millennium. As for ~cuisiner~ itself, it long meant simply “to do the cooking”; in the nineteenth century it turned figurative, and by 1881 ~cuisiner quelqu'un~ meant to interrogate someone relentlessly — the very metaphor English found in “to grill.”
en.culminer: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ~culmināre~ (“to crown, to bring to a peak”), a verb formed on Latin ~culmen~ (“top, summit, ridge”). The French verb keeps the image of a summit: a career, a crisis or a story ~culmine~ when it reaches its highest point, and the expression ~point culminant~ names that peak. English ~culminate~ is a parallel borrowing from the same Latin verb, so the two languages share both the word and the picture of reaching the top.
en.cultiver:
Attested 1119 as a learned reshaping of Old French ~coutiver~, refashioned on Latin ~cultus~ (“tillage, cultivation, worship”) and more precisely on a reconstructed *~cultivus~ derived from ~cultiō~ (“cultivation”). The whole family rests on Latin ~colere~ (“to till, to tend, to inhabit, to worship”), from Proto-Italic *~kʷelō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷelh₁-~ (“to turn, to move around, and so to dwell”). Cognate, through that root, with English ~wheel~ and with Ancient Greek ~télos~ (“end, purpose”).

The semantic arc is remarkable: a root meaning “to turn / revolve” drifted to “to dwell where one turns about,” then to “to till the ground one dwells on,” and finally to “to tend and revere” — which is why ~colere~ fathered at once ~cultiver~ (the field), ~culture~ (the mind), ~colon~ and ~colonie~ (settlers who inhabit), and ~culte~ (worship). To ~cultiver~ a garden, a talent, or a friendship is the same gesture under three guises: patient tending. French even keeps coining on this stem — playful forms like ~culturer~ show the suffixation is still alive.
en.cumuler:
Borrowed in 1354, in Bersuire's translation of Livy, from Latin ~cumulāre~ (“to heap up, to pile high”), from ~cumulus~ (“heap, pile”), a noun sometimes traced — the evidence is admittedly thin — to PIE *~ḱewh₁-~ (“to swell”), which would make it distant kin to Greek ~κῦμα~ (“swell, wave”). The Latin verb had in fact already entered French once before, by inheritance rather than borrowing: worn down by a millennium of speech, ~cumulāre~ had become ~combler~ (“to fill to the brim, to fulfill”) and ~cumulus~ had become ~comble~ — so ~cumuler~ and ~combler~ are doublets, the learned and the popular face of a single verb. Spanish shows the same split between popular ~colmar~ and learned ~acumular~; English ~accumulate~ and ~cumulative~ complete the family portrait.

The borrowed twin took the paperwork. Where ~combler~ stayed warm and concrete — one fills a gap, showers someone with joy — ~cumuler~ specialized in administration: by 1690 it meant joining several legal claims together, and by 1784 holding several positions at once, the sense behind the very French debate over the ~cumul des mandats~, a politician's stacking of elected offices. The parent noun meanwhile had a second, airier career: in 1803 the Englishman Luke Howard, father of cloud classification, chose ~cumulus~ to name the puffy heaped cloud of fair weather, and French adopted it in turn — every summer sky is, etymologically, piled high. As for ~comble~, it gave French the attic (~les combles~, the space heaped under the roof), the phrase ~de fond en comble~ (“from top to bottom”) and the cry ~c'est un comble !~ — “that's the last straw,” literally the point where the measure overflows.
en.céder:
Borrowed from Latin ~cedere~ (“to go, walk, withdraw, yield”). The traditional analysis, going back to Pokorny, reconstructs ~cedere~ from an element *~ce-~ plus the root of ~sedere~ (“to sit”), giving a sense like “to go away by stepping aside.” The verb is cognate with the family seen in Ancient Greek ~ὁδός~ (“road, way”) and shares the broad Indo-European notion of going. From the idea of giving up one's place came the sense of conceding.

In Latin ~cedere~ first meant simply to move or walk, then to withdraw and so to give way; affairs were said to ~cedere~ well or badly, to “go” well or badly. French ~céder~ kept the yielding sense: to cede territory, to give up, to give in (~céder à la tentation~, “to yield to temptation”), and also to break or collapse under strain — a rope or a dam that ~cède~. Latin contrasted yielding with standing firm (~obstare~, ~resistere~). The same root threads through a large legal and motional French vocabulary: ~cession~, ~accéder~, ~procéder~, ~succéder~, ~précéder~, ~recéder~, and ~incessible~ — each preserving the original image of going, stepping, and giving way.
en.célébrer:
From Latin ~celebrāre~ (“to frequent, to throng, to solemnize, to praise”), derived from the adjective ~celeber~ (“crowded, populous, much-frequented”). The further origin of ~celeber~ is uncertain and best left unguessed, but the Latin verb is the clear and well-attested source of French ~célébrer~, English ~celebrate~, Italian ~celebrare~, and Spanish ~celebrar~.

The surprise is in that root adjective: ~celeber~ first meant simply “crowded” — a place thick with people. A spot that drew throngs was busy, then renowned, then famous, and a ceremony that drew throngs was a grand public occasion. So ~celebrāre~ slid from “to attend in great numbers” to “to mark with solemn pomp” and finally “to honor, to extol.” Both modern strands survive in French: one ~célèbre~ a mass or a marriage (the solemn, ritual sense) and one ~célèbre~ a victory or a hero (the festive, praising sense). From the same ~celeber~ come ~célèbre~ (“famous”) and ~célébrité~ (“fame, a celebrity”) — and the thread back to the beginning is plain, for to be a celebrity is, etymologically, to be surrounded by a crowd.
en.côtoyer: Derived from the noun ~côte~ with the verb suffix ~-oyer~, and inherited from Old French ~costoier~. The noun ~côte~ comes from Latin ~costa~ (“rib, side”) and had the senses of “rib,” “slope” and “coast.” The suffix ~-oyer~ often gives the sense of continued action or of acting along or by means of something, as in ~tutoyer~. So ~côtoyer~ meant literally “to go along the side (or the coast),” as when a ship hugs the shore. The figurative sense “to rub shoulders with, to associate with” grew from that image of moving alongside.
en.danser:
From Old French ~dancier~ (twelfth century), a verb of the langue d'oïl whose ultimate origin is genuinely uncertain. The leading account makes it Frankish, but the sources offer two competing Germanic etymons and flag a difficulty with each. By one hypothesis it descends from Frankish *~dintjan~ (compare Dutch ~deinzen~, « to move about, draw back »), though the expected vowel would be /i/, not the /a/ of ~danser~; by another it goes back to Frankish *~dansōn~ (« to draw, drag »), picturing the dance as a stately, gliding step. Neither is settled.

French ~danser~ was a triumphant export: it spread far beyond its home, giving English ~dance~, and standing beside Spanish ~danzar~ and Italian ~danzare~ (which borrowed it alongside their native ~bailar~ and ~ballare~, from a different root *~ball-~). Modern kin of the verb include ~danse~, ~danseur~, ~danseuse~, and ~dancing~. A vivid old idiom, « faire ~danser~ les écus, » meant to make coins « dance » out of a purse — a turn of phrase sometimes cited in support of the « drag, pull » hypothesis, though that origin remains unproven.
en.dater:
A fourteenth-century formation from the noun ~date~, with the suffix ~-er~. ~date~ comes from Latin ~data~, the feminine past participle of ~dare~ (“to give”), lifted from the formula ~data littera~ (“letter given”) — the phrase Roman and medieval scribes wrote before the place and day a document was issued, as in ~data Romae~ (“given at Rome”). ~dare~ descends from PIE *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~datare~ and Spanish ~datar~, and, through ~data~, with English ~date~.

So the very notion of a calendar “date” is fossilized inside a giving: a letter was “given” on such a day, and the participle naming the act of giving slid over to name the day itself. To ~dater~ a document is to record that moment of issue; from there the verb grew the intransitive sense “to be old-fashioned,” as in ~ça date~ — a thing so plainly of its time that it betrays its age. The same ~dare~ root runs deep in French through ~donner~, ~don~, ~dose~, and learned ~data~; and ~dater~ itself anchors a tidy family — ~datation~, ~datable~, ~antidater~, and ~postdater~ — every one of them still quietly turning on the idea of something “given” at a fixed point in time.
en.demander:
From Old French ~demander~ (attested around 980), from Latin ~dēmandāre~ (“to entrust, to commit; to charge with”), built from ~dē-~ (“fully, away”) and ~mandāre~ (“to commit to one's charge, to order”). ~mandāre~ itself is transparently ~manus~ (“hand”) plus a verb of giving, so its literal sense is “to put into someone's hand” — to entrust. ~manus~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~man-~ / *~meh₂-~ (“hand”). Cognate verbs survive as Italian ~domandare~ and Spanish ~demandar~, and the ~mandāre~ family entered English as ~mandate~, ~command~, ~commend~, and the legal ~demand~.

The semantic shift from “to entrust, to commit” toward “to ask, to request” happened within Latin and Romance: charging someone with a task slid into requesting something of them. French ~demander~ therefore lost the heavy sense of “entrust” and became the everyday verb for “to ask” — a question, a favour, a price. English ~demand~ kept a more forceful, insistent tone, which is why the French ~demander~ is a notorious false friend: ~je vous demande~ is a polite “I ask you,” not “I demand of you.” From ~manus~ and ~mandāre~ come a broad French family, including ~commander~ (“to order”), ~recommander~ (“to recommend”), ~mandat~ (“mandate; warrant”), and ~mander~ (“to summon”).
en.demeurer:
From Old French ~demorer~, ~demourer~ (“to delay, to remain, to dwell”), from Latin ~demorari~ (“to linger, to tarry, to stay”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ and the deponent verb ~morari~ (“to delay, to tarry”), itself from the noun ~mora~ (“a delay, a pause”). Cognate with Italian ~dimorare~ (“to dwell, to reside”), Spanish ~morar~ (“to dwell”) and Portuguese ~morar~ (“to live, to reside”), all reflexes of the same family.

The Latin sense was strictly temporal — to be held up, to be delayed — and that meaning survived early on: the medieval expression ~sans demeurer~ meant “without delay.” But a thing that lingers in a place comes to belong there, and so ~demeurer~ drifted from “to tarry” toward “to remain” and finally “to dwell, to reside,” the meaning the verb still carries when one asks where someone ~demeure~. French preserves both threads: the residential one in the noun ~demeure~ (“a dwelling”), and the old temporal one in the legal locution ~mettre en demeure~ (“to serve formal notice,” literally to put someone in a state of delay or default) and in the adverb ~désormais~, whose buried ~-mais~ goes back to the same ~mora~. The participle ~demeurant~ even works as a connective, ~au demeurant~ meaning “for the rest, moreover.”
en.descendre:
From Latin ~dēscendere~ (“to climb down, to go down”), a compound of the prefix ~dē-~ (“down from”) and ~scandere~ (“to climb, to mount”). ~Scandere~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~skend-~ (“to leap up, to climb”), so the Latin verb is, literally, a “climbing-down” — a downward motion expressed, paradoxically, by a verb of ascent. The root shows up across Latin in ~ascendere~ (“to climb up”) and ~trānscendere~ (“to climb across”), and survives in English borrowings such as ~ascend~, ~descend~, and ~transcend~.

Attested in French from the eleventh century, ~descendre~ kept its plain sense of moving from a higher point to a lower one. By the eighteenth century it had acquired a figurative use — “to derive one's origin from,” as one ~descends~ from an ancestor — turning a movement through space into a movement through generations, down the branches of a family tree. The same root *~skend-~ underlies the noun ~descendant~ (“offspring”) and ~descente~ (“a going down, a raid”). The wider Latin family of ~scandere~ also reached French in the learned word ~scander~ (“to scan verse”), where the climbing sense survives in the metrical “stepping” through a line of poetry.
en.desservir:
From ~des-~ (a privative prefix, from Latin ~dis-~) + ~servir~ (« to serve »), the latter from Latin ~servire~ (« to serve »), a verb derived from ~servus~ (« slave, servant ») whose own deeper origin the dictionaries call uncertain, perhaps from Proto-Italic *~serwos~. The prefix points two ways at once, which is why ~desservir~ carries strikingly different meanings under one spelling.

In its plain sense the ~des-~ « undoes » the serving: to ~desservir~ a table is to clear away the dishes, the reverse of « servir. » Figuratively it sours into « to do a disservice, » to harm someone's cause — « cette remarque l'a ~desservi~ » (« that remark worked against him »). Yet a third, positive sense developed in the language of duty and route: a priest ~dessert~ a parish (« serves » a village church), and a bus or train line ~dessert~ a town (« provides service to » it). The shared family runs through ~service~, ~serviteur~, ~serveur~, ~servile~, and ~asservir~ (« to enslave »); ~desservir~ alone manages to mean both « to serve a place » and « to do a bad turn. »
en.dessiner:
From Latin ~designare~ (“to mark out, to designate, to trace”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ and the verb ~signare~ (“to mark with a sign”), itself from ~signum~ (“a sign, a mark”). The route into French was indirect: the Italian ~disegnare~ — which had specialized toward the sense “to draw” — reshaped the older French word, giving the modern ~dessiner~. The very same Latin ~designare~ also descends straight into French as ~désigner~ (“to designate, to point out”), so ~dessiner~ and ~désigner~ are a doublet. English ~design~ and ~designate~, Spanish ~diseñar~, and Portuguese ~desenhar~ belong to the same family.

The split is telling. Latin ~designare~ meant to mark something out — and that single act forks two ways: you can mark a thing in order to point to it (whence ~désigner~) or mark lines on a surface to depict it (whence ~dessiner~). The noun ~dessin~ (“a drawing”) and ~dessein~ (“a design, an intention”) were long spelled alike and only later prised apart, preserving in French the old kinship between drawing a figure and forming a plan. Through ~signum~, ~dessiner~ is also cousin to ~signe~, ~signal~, ~signer~, ~signature~, ~enseigne~ (“a shop sign”), and ~enseigner~ (“to teach,” literally to mark out for someone).
en.destiner:
From Latin ~destinare~ (“to make fast, fix, establish, resolve upon”), formed from the prefix ~de-~ and an element ~-stinare~ connected to ~stare~ (“to stand”). It thus belongs to the great family of the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), through a nasal-infixed derivative meaning roughly “to make stand firm.” The same root and the same ~-stinare~ element appear in Latin ~obstinare~ (“to stand firm against”), which gives French ~obstiner~, and at a deeper level it links ~destiner~ to Greek ~histēmi~ (“I cause to stand”) and to English ~stand~.

The metaphor is striking: to destine something is to make it ~stand fixed~, to settle it firmly in place for a purpose — fate as a thing nailed down in advance. Latin ~destinare~ ran from the concrete (“to fasten, to fix a target”) to the abstract (“to resolve, to set apart for”), and French kept the “set apart for a purpose” sense in ~destiner quelqu'un à une carrière~. The past-participle noun ~destinata~ underlies the idea of a fixed endpoint, surfacing in ~destination~ and ~destinée~, while the abstract noun gives ~destin~ (“fate, that which is fixed”). The same *~steh₂-~ root, so prolific in French, also yields ~stable~, ~constant~, ~obstiner~, and a host of words built on standing firm.
en.devancer: Derived from ~devant~ (“in front”), on the pattern of ~avancer~, whose own ancestry is Latin ~ab ante~ (“from before”). The verb means “to get in front of”: to outstrip someone, and by extension to anticipate a move or a wish before it is expressed. The idea of being in front is present in the base, so the sense has stayed close to its literal image.
en.devenir:
From Latin ~dēvenīre~ (“to come down to, to arrive at, to fall into a state”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“down, from”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”), the source of French ~venir~. Latin ~venīre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”), one of the most productive verbal roots in the family. Through that root ~devenir~ is cognate with Italian ~divenire~ and Spanish ~devenir~, and, more distantly, with English ~come~ and German ~kommen~, which spring from the same PIE source.

The metaphor at the heart of the word is motion turned into transformation: to ~devenir~ something is, etymologically, to ~come~ to it, to arrive at a new state as one arrives at a place. Latin already used ~dēvenīre~ for falling into a condition, and French generalized it into the ordinary verb of becoming. The root *~gʷem-~ seeded a remarkable crowd of French words through ~venīre~ and its Latin relatives: ~venir~, ~avenir~ (“future,” literally what is “to come”), ~revenir~, ~convenir~, ~prévenir~, ~aventure~, ~revenu~, and ~souvenir~ — the last a memory that, etymologically, “comes up from below” into the mind.
en.deviner:
From Latin ~divinare~ (“to foresee, to prophesy, to be inspired by a god”), from ~divinus~ (“of a god, divine”), from ~divus~ (“god, deity”), from Proto-Italic *~deiwos~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deywós~ (“god, celestial being”), itself a derivative of *~dyew-~ (“the bright sky, daylight”). This is one of the great roots: it also gives Latin ~deus~ and ~Jupiter~, Greek ~Zeus~, Sanskrit ~deva~, and the divinity in French ~dieu~. The same family fed Italian ~indovinare~ and Spanish ~adivinar~.

The semantic shift is striking. ~divinare~ first meant to know things by divine inspiration — the prophet's gift of seeing the hidden. As that solemn sense secularized, ~deviner~ slid all the way down to the everyday “to guess,” the small daily act of foreseeing without proof. A pleasing detail lurks in the root: *~dyew-~ originally pointed at the shining daytime sky, so the “god” of ~divinare~ was, at the very bottom, a luminous one — and the diviner's insight is, etymologically, a kind of light. The family persists in ~devin~ (“soothsayer”), ~devinette~ (“riddle”), and the learned ~divination~ and ~divin~.
en.devoir:
From Old French ~devoir~ (also ~deveir~), from Latin ~dēbēre~ (“to owe, to be bound to”). The Latin verb is a contraction of *~dēhibēre~, from ~dē-~ (“from, away”) plus ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”) — literally “to hold away from someone,” that is, to keep what is theirs and so to owe it. Through ~habēre~ it shares the root of ~avoir~. Romance cousins include Spanish ~deber~ and Italian ~dovere~, both meaning “to owe” and “must.”

The meaning traveled a clean path: from “to hold something belonging to another” (to owe), to the felt pressure of that obligation (“to be bound to”), to a pure modal of necessity (“must, ought”). French ~devoir~ carries all three at once — ~je te dois cent euros~ (I owe you), ~je dois partir~ (I must leave) — and, like ~pouvoir~, it froze into a noun: ~le devoir~ (“duty”), and in the plural ~les devoirs~ (“homework”). From the same Latin ~dēbēre~ and its noun ~dēbitum~ come ~dette~ (“debt”), the learned doublet ~débit~, and ~débiteur~; and English borrowed ~debt~, ~debit~, and — by way of the Old French phrase “to put in devoir” — ~endeavour~.
en.diagnostiquer:
French ~diagnostiquer~ is a denominal verb, built on the noun ~diagnostic~ with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary adds that the family goes back to Ancient Greek ~diagignṓskein~ (“to examine thoroughly”), a verb that joins ~dia-~ (“through, apart”) to ~gignṓskein~ (“to know”). English Wiktionary gives only the French step, ~diagnostic~ plus ~-er~, so the two accounts fit together: the Greek verb stands behind the noun, and the French verb is a derivation from it. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary first-conjugation ending, from Latin ~-are~, which French uses to turn a noun into a verb of doing or applying what the noun names.

The Greek sense was that of examining something thoroughly, and the French noun ~diagnostic~ keeps that idea: it names the identification of an illness from its signs. The verb ~diagnostiquer~ is the act itself, so a physician ~diagnostique~ a disease from its symptoms. Because the verb is built on the noun and not borrowed whole from Greek, it belongs to French derivation, like ~torturer~ or ~alerter~, and its ending is that of any regular verb in ~-er~. The long Greek history sits behind the noun, while the verb itself is a plain French formation.
en.dialoguer: A denominal verb formed from ~dialogue~ plus ~-er~, meaning “to hold a dialogue,” and by extension “to negotiate, to talk things through.” The noun came through Latin ~dialogus~ from Ancient Greek ~διάλογος~ (“conversation, discourse”), itself built on ~διά~ (“through, between”) and ~λόγος~ (“speech”). French did not follow the Greek pattern of derivatives in ~-logie~ or ~-logique~ here. It applied its own Latin-style suffixes to the borrowed noun instead, which is how ~dialoguer~ and ~dialogal~ came about.
en.diffuser:
A 15th-century formation, built on the adjective ~diffus~ (“diffuse, spread out”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, created to render the Latin verb ~diffundere~ (“to pour out, to spread”). That verb is ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) plus ~fundere~ (“to pour”), whose past participle ~diffusus~ gave ~diffus~. ~Fundere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰewd-~, an extension of *~ǵʰew-~ (“to pour”), cognate with Ancient Greek ~χέω~ (~kheō~, “I pour”) and Gothic ~giutan~ (“to pour”).

The image is liquid: ~diffundere~ meant to pour a fluid so that it spreads in every direction, and ~diffuser~ kept that sense of even, outward spreading — of light, heat, or a scent through a room. From there it took on “to circulate, to disseminate,” and in the twentieth century became the standard word for broadcasting by radio and television. French built a whole series of verbs on ~fundere~ for pouring in different directions: ~infuser~ (to pour in), ~perfuser~ (to pour through), ~transfuser~ (to pour across), and ~confus~ — literally “poured together,” hence muddled. The noun ~diffusion~ shares the same source.
en.différencier:
A variant of older ~différentier~, from Late Latin ~differentiare~, from ~differentia~ (“difference, distinction”). ~Differentia~ is built on ~differre~ (“to carry apart, to differ”), itself ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). The verb ~ferre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”), one of the most widely attested of all roots — cognate with English ~bear~, Ancient Greek ~φέρω~ (“I carry”), and Sanskrit ~भरति~ (~bharati~, “he carries”). To differentiate is, at root, to carry two things apart from each other.

The Romance languages keep the verb almost unchanged: Spanish and Portuguese ~diferenciar~, Catalan ~diferenciar~. From the general sense of telling things apart, mathematics borrowed a precise one — to ~differentiate~ a function, computing how it changes over an infinitesimal increment. French relatives include ~différence~, ~différent~, ~différer~ (which forks into “to differ” and “to defer”), ~différenciation~, and ~indifférent~. The root *~bʰer-~ alone fans out across ~conférer~, ~préférer~, ~transférer~, ~offrir~, and ~souffrir~ — each a different way of carrying or bearing.
en.différer:
From Latin ~differre~ (« to carry apart, to scatter, to postpone, to be unlike »), a compound of ~dis-~ (« apart ») and ~ferre~ (« to carry, to bear »). ~ferre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (« to bear, to carry »), one of the most widely attested roots of the family. Through that root it is cognate with English ~bear~, Ancient Greek ~φέρω~ (« I carry »), and Sanskrit ~bʰarati~ (« he carries »).

The two modern French senses both fall straight out of « to carry apart ». Things carried apart in time are put off — hence « to defer, to postpone »; things carried apart in nature are unalike — hence « to differ ». English inherited the very same split in the doublet ~defer~ and ~differ~. The prolific root *~bʰer-~ surfaces across French in ~conférer~, ~préférer~, ~offrir~, ~souffrir~, and the noun ~différence~, all carrying, in their Latin bones, the idea of bearing something from one place to another.
en.digérer:
Learned borrowing from Latin ~digerere~ (“to carry apart, to scatter, to dissolve, to digest”), built from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~gerere~ (“to carry, to bear”). Because French took it directly from written Latin, it kept a Latin look and never went through the everyday sound changes of Old French. English ~digest~ comes from the participle of the same Latin verb, and Italian ~digerire~ and Spanish ~digerir~ are its Romance counterparts.

The Latin verb first meant to carry things off in different directions, hence to spread out, arrange or separate. Physicians and writers then applied it to what the body does with food, dividing and dissolving it into parts that can be absorbed, and that sense became the dominant one. French also stretched it figuratively: it can mean to absorb a piece of information, or to swallow an insult or a defeat. The same family includes ~digestion~ and ~indigeste~, and the simple verb ~gerere~ lies behind ~gérer~ and ~suggérer~, while its participle ~gestus~ gave ~geste~.
en.diluer: Borrowed from Latin ~dīluō~, “to wash away, to dissolve, to dilute,” built from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~luō~ (“to wash, to bathe”).
