To ~diluer~ a liquid is therefore to wash its strength away by adding water. The same Latin pair gave ~dīluvium~ (“flood”), source of French ~déluge~, and Latin ~abluere~ gave French ~ablution~. The figurative sense, to weaken an idea, an argument or a shareholding by spreading it thinner, is a later extension of the physical meaning.
en.diminuer:
French ~diminuer~ comes from Latin ~dēminuere~ (“to make smaller, to lessen”), formed from ~dē-~ (“down, from”) plus ~minuere~ (“to make small, to reduce”). The simple verb ~minuere~ rests on the adjective stem of ~minor~ / ~minus~ (“less”), and the whole family traces to a Proto-Indo-European root *~mey-~ (“small, to lessen”). That root is widespread: Gothic ~mins~ (“less”), Ancient Greek ~minúthō~ (“to diminish”), and Sanskrit ~minā́ti~ (“to lessen, to damage”) are all cousins, as is English ~minor~, borrowed from Latin. Italian ~diminuire~ and Spanish ~disminuir~ are its Romance siblings.

The classical sense, “to break into smaller pieces, to reduce,” narrowed cleanly into the modern “to decrease.” A delightful surprise lies in the relatives: the past participle ~minūtus~ (“made small”) gave French ~menu~ — both the adjective (“slender, fine,” as in ~menu peuple~, “the small folk”) and the noun ~menu~, originally a “detailed,” i.e. finely itemized, list, which English then borrowed back for restaurant cards. The same ~minūtus~ also produced ~minute~ (the time unit, a “small” division of the hour). Around this root cluster French ~diminution~, ~diminutif~, ~moindre~ (the irregular comparative, straight from ~minor~), ~mince~ (“thin”), and the learned ~minimum~ and ~minuscule~. To diminish, etymologically, is simply to make ever more ~menu~.
en.diplômer:
A denominal verb coined in 1841 from the noun ~diplôme~. That noun comes from Latin ~diploma~ (“an official document, license”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~díplōma~, literally “a thing folded in two,” from ~diplóos~ (“double, twofold”) via the verb ~diplóō~ (“to double, fold over”). The Greek word itself joins ~dís~ (“twice”) to the root ~-plóos~ (“-fold”).

The image at the bottom of the word is wonderfully concrete: a ~diplôme~ was a sheet of paper folded once over, the form Roman authorities used for a permit or a grant of privilege. From “folded document” the sense narrowed to the certificate awarded for completed study, and ~diplômer~ means to confer such a certificate — hence ~diplômé~, “holding a degree, qualified.” The ~-plóos~ root that gives “fold” runs through a learned family in French: ~diplôme~, ~diplomate~ (one entrusted with folded credentials), and the mathematical ~triple~ and ~multiple~ share the same fold-counting idea.
en.dire:
From Old and Middle French ~dire~, from Vulgar Latin *~dīgere~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~dīcere~ (“to say, to pronounce, to express in words”). The popular form *~dīgere~ arose by analogy with verbs in ~-gere~ whose past participles ended in ~-ctum~, a pattern ~dīcere~ shared (its participle ~dictum~). The verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~deikō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”). Through that root ~dire~ is cognate with English ~token~ and ~teach~, and with German ~zeigen~ (“to show”).

The leap from “to show” to “to say” is the heart of the story: to speak was first to point something out, to indicate it in words. That older sense of pointing survives all around the Latin family — in ~doigt~ (“finger,” from ~digitus~), in ~indiquer~, and in ~index~. From ~dīcere~ itself French inherited a crowd of words: ~dit~ (“said, saying”), the prefixed ~prédire~ (“to foretell”), ~contredire~ (“to contradict”), ~interdire~ (“to forbid,” literally “to say between”), and ~maudire~ (“to curse,” from ~maledīcere~, “to speak ill”). The learned ~diction~, ~dictée~, and ~verdict~ (“a true saying”) carry the original Latin ~dict-~ stem unworn.
en.diriger:
A learned fourteenth-century borrowing from Latin ~dirigere~ (“to set straight, align, guide”), formed from the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~regere~ (“to guide, rule, keep straight”). ~Regere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reg-~ (“to move in a straight line, to direct”), one of the great roots of kingship and rightness. Through it ~diriger~ is cognate with English ~right~ and German ~recht~, and with Latin ~rex~ (“king,” the one who keeps the realm straight).

The governing image is the straight line. To direct is to set something on a straight course, whether a road, a gaze, an enterprise, or an orchestra; the reflexive ~se diriger vers~ (“to head toward”) keeps the literal sense of taking a straight bearing. The past participle of ~regere~ was ~rectus~ (“straight, right”), which gave French ~droit~ — so ~diriger~ and ~droit~ are cousins under the skin. Because French borrowed ~dirigere~ directly from Latin rather than inheriting it through the spoken chain, it kept its bookish shape. From the same *~h₃reg-~ root come a broad family: ~direct~, ~direction~, ~directeur~, ~dresser~, ~adresse~, ~régir~, ~règle~, and ~roi~.
en.discerner:
French ~discerner~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~discernere~ (“to separate, to set apart”), formed from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~cernere~ (“to sift, to separate, to decide”). Like many learned verbs, it was fitted into the regular first conjugation in ~-er~. The Latin verb ~cernere~ is related to Ancient Greek ~krínein~ (“to separate, to judge”), which gave ~crise~ and ~critique~ by way of Greek and Latin.

The Latin image is of a sieve: to ~discernere~ was to sift grain from chaff, then to tell one thing from another, and finally to see clearly. French kept the mental sense almost exclusively. To ~discerner~ is to make out a shape in the fog or a motive behind a gesture, and the noun ~discernement~ names good judgment itself. The root ~cernere~ left many descendants in French through its relatives: ~certain~ (originally “decided, settled”), ~décret~ and ~décréter~, ~secret~ (“set apart”) and ~concerner~ (“to sift together,” hence “to relate to”).
en.discuter:
From Latin ~discutere~ (“to strike apart, to shatter, to break up by shaking”), compounded from ~dis-~ (“apart, asunder”) and ~quatere~ (“to shake, to strike”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷēt-~ (“to shake”). That root also yielded the frequentative ~quassāre~ (“to shatter”), source of English ~quash~, and is cognate with German ~schütteln~ (“to shake”). Italian preserves the verb almost unchanged as ~discutere~.

The original sense was strikingly physical — to dash to pieces, to make something fly apart by shaking it. Late Latin already shifted ~discutere~ toward the figurative: to “shake apart” a question meant to examine it, to break a matter down into its elements. From there the modern senses follow naturally — to debate, to thrash out, and in everyday French simply to chat (« discuter avec un ami »). The image is a good one to remember: a discussion is, etymologically, a controlled shattering of a topic into examinable fragments. The same root underlies a cluster of French words sharing the idea of striking or shaking — ~discussion~, ~indiscutable~, ~percuter~ (“to strike, to collide”), ~percussion~, and ~secouer~ (“to shake”), the last descending from Latin ~succutere~.
en.disparaître:
First attested in 1509, ~disparaître~ was formed in French from the verb ~paraître~ (“to appear, seem”) with the prefix ~dis-~ (expressing reversal or removal), modeled on the Latin ~dispārēre~ (“to vanish”). That Latin verb had already produced an Old French ~disparoir~ (“to disappear”), but the older form was ousted by the new compound built on ~paraître~. The base ~paraître~ itself comes, through Old French ~paroistre~, from Vulgar Latin *~pārēscere~, an inchoative of Latin ~pārēre~ (“to come into view, to appear, to obey”). Spanish ~desaparecer~ and Italian ~disparire~ / ~sparire~ are its Romance counterparts; English ~disappear~ is a parallel ~dis-~ formation on ~appear~.

The key word is the prefix. Where ~paraître~ presents something to view and ~apparaître~ brings it forth, ~dis-~ undoes the showing: ~disparaître~ is, etymologically, “to un-appear.” Latin ~pārēre~ also carried the sense “to obey” — a servant who “appears” at command — which is why the same root gives French ~apparaître~, ~apparition~, ~apparent~, and the noun ~apparence~, alongside the more surprising ~parer~ in some of its uses. The whole family circles the act of becoming, or ceasing to be, visible. A neat detail: French rebuilt this verb from native parts in the Renaissance rather than simply inheriting the worn-down ~disparoir~, choosing transparency of form over the older sound-changed shape.
en.dispenser:
From Latin ~dispensare~, a frequentative of ~dispendere~ (“to weigh out, pay out”), itself ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to pay”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to weigh”). Because the Romans weighed out coin and goods, ~pendere~ meant both “to weigh” and “to pay” — a sense preserved in English ~pension~ and, through related ~pendere~ “to hang,” in ~pendant~ and ~ponder~.

The original picture is a steward literally weighing out portions to distribute them; from “to weigh out, to deal out in measure” came “to dispense, to administer,” and then the legal sense “to release someone from an obligation” — to ~dispenser~ a person from a duty is to measure out an exemption. French kept the family ~dispense~ (“exemption”), ~dispensaire~ (“dispensary”), and ~indispensable~, literally “that cannot be dispensed with.” The same root *~(s)pend-~ underlies ~dépenser~, ~suspendre~, ~peser~, and ~pensée~ — for to think was, figuratively, to weigh.
en.disperser:
From Latin ~dispersus~, the past participle of ~dispergere~ (“to scatter, spread abroad”), itself ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) + ~spargere~ (“to scatter, strew, sprinkle”). The base verb ~spargere~ gives Italian ~spargere~ and underlies English ~sparse~ and ~aspersion~; the prefix ~dis-~ survives across the Romance languages. The deep root of ~spargere~ is debated: it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European *~sperh₂g-~ linked to words for crackling and roaring, but de Vaan and Schrijver prefer a g-extension of *~sper-~ (“to scatter, strew”), tied to Ancient Greek ~speírō~ (“to sow”).

The Latin sense — flinging things in every direction — passed almost unchanged into French: to ~disperser~ a crowd, a fortune, or a fog is to send its parts flying apart. The same Latin family seeds a cluster of French words: ~dispersion~, éparpiller being a separate formation, but ~asperger~ (“to sprinkle”) and the liturgical ~aspersion~ both rest on ~spargere~, as does ~épars~ (“scattered, sparse”). What unites them is the image of a hand casting seed or water broadcast over a field — the literal gesture of sowing, generalized to anything strewn too thin to gather back.
en.disposer:
From Latin ~dispōnere~ (“to set out, to arrange in different places”), from the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place”). ~Pōnere~ is itself widely analyzed as an old compound of *~po-~ (“off, away”) and ~sinere~ (“to leave, to let”), with the past participle ~positus~. In its French form, ~disposer~ joined the great ~-poser~ family, where the descendants of ~pōnere~ blended with those of Late Latin *~pausāre~ (“to cease, to set down”).

The sense is one of placing things apart in good order: to ~disposer~ is to arrange, to lay out, to organize, and reflexively ~se disposer à~ is to get ready to act. From “having things arranged to one's liking” came the idiom ~disposer de~ (“to have at one's disposal”). The ~pōnere~ family blossomed into a regiment of French verbs — ~poser~, ~composer~, ~proposer~, ~exposer~, ~imposer~, ~déposer~ — plus nouns like ~position~, ~disposition~, and ~dépôt~. Curiously, ~disponible~ (“available”) preserves the original Latin ~n~ that ~disposer~ itself has lost, a small fossil of ~dispōnere~ hiding inside the modern word.
en.disputer:
From Latin ~disputāre~, from ~dis-~ (“apart, asunder”) plus ~putāre~ (“to reckon, consider, think — originally to clean, prune”). The literal image is striking: ~putāre~ first meant to lop and clean a tree of its excess branches, and ~disputāre~ to prune an argument apart, clearing away the dead wood to reckon up what is sound. The deeper Proto-Indo-European root of ~putāre~ is uncertain, so its first sense is reconstructed cautiously, but the pruning-then-reckoning development is well attested in Latin.

The French verb appears in the 12th century meaning to debate or discuss; only from the 17th century does it drift toward today's dominant sense of quarreling or vying for something — a familiar slide from reasoned argument to plain argument. The same ~putāre~ underlies a remarkable spread of French words: ~computer~ ideas became to ~compter~ and ~conter~, and the root yields ~réputer~ (and ~réputation~), ~amputer~, ~imputer~, and ~député~ (one reckoned off, delegated). A single verb for cleaning a tree thus branched into counting, calculating, reputation, and the noisy art of the dispute.
en.dissimuler:
French ~dissimuler~ was borrowed around 1355 from Latin ~dissimulāre~ (“to conceal, to pretend that something is not”), formed from ~dis-~ (apart, negation) and ~simulāre~ (“to feign, to make like”), itself from ~similis~ (“similar, alike”). Behind ~similis~ lie Proto-Italic *~semalis~ and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~sem-~ (“one, together”), which also yields English ~same~: to simulate is to make one thing pass for “the same” as another. The Romance family kept the verb — Italian ~dissimulare~, Spanish ~disimular~ — and English took ~dissemble~ as well as the more learned ~dissimulate~ from the same Latin source.

Classical rhetoric drew a neat line between the twins: ~simulāre~ is to pretend that something is — to display what does not exist — while ~dissimulāre~ is to pretend that something is not — to hide what does. French preserved the pair as ~simuler~ and ~dissimuler~: the con artist simulates riches and dissimulates debts. The verb's most famous hour is the Latin maxim “Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit regnare” (“he who cannot dissemble cannot reign”), traditionally said to have been the device of Louis XI, the arch-schemer among French kings — though historians note that the attribution itself is uncertain, the maxim having also been credited to medieval emperors. The root *~sem-~ spread far beyond deception: ~sembler~, ~ressembler~, ~assembler~, ~ensemble~, ~similaire~ and ~simultané~ all descend from it — a whole vocabulary of likeness and togetherness, within which dissimuler is the art of using resemblance to hide.
en.dissiper:
Borrowed from Latin ~dissipāre~ (“to scatter, to disperse, to squander”). The Latin verb is usually analysed as ~dis-~ (“apart”) plus an archaic verb ~supāre~ (“to throw”), so that to ~dissiper~ is, at bottom, to throw things in all directions. Both Wiktionaries trace it directly to Latin. English ~dissipate~ and Italian ~dissipare~ are borrowings of the same Latin verb, and Spanish ~disipar~ is the same word again in a Spanish dress.

The sense moved from the physical to the abstract. The Latin verb covered scattering a crowd or an army, and also wasting money by throwing it away. French kept both strands: ~dissiper~ means to make clouds, fog, fears or doubts vanish, and in an older use, to squander a fortune. The reflexive form adds a schoolroom sense, since a ~dissipé~ pupil is one whose attention has scattered and who cannot stay quiet. The family includes ~dissipation~, ~dissipateur~ (“spendthrift”), and ~dissipé~. The scattering image is the thread through all of them.
en.dissocier: Borrowed from Latin ~dissociāre~ (“to separate, to disunite”), built from the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~sociāre~ (“to join, to ally”), itself from ~socius~ (“companion, ally”). The verb is thus the exact opposite of ~associer~, which pairs ~ad-~ with the same ~sociāre~. In French the sense is to pull apart things that had been joined, such as ideas, people or chemical compounds. The family includes ~société~, ~social~ and ~sociable~.
en.dissoudre:
From Old French — the Sermons of Saint Bernard (late 12th century) already use the participle ~dissoluz~ — with medieval forms like ~dessoudre~ later reshaped on the model of ~absoudre~; from Latin ~dissolvere~ (“to loosen apart, undo, break up”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~solvere~ (“to loosen, untie, release — and to pay”). ~solvere~ goes back to ~se-~ (“away”) + ~luere~, from PIE *~lewh₁-~ (“to loosen”), the root of Greek ~lúō~ (“I loosen, I undo”) and — through Old Norse — of English ~loose~. Cognate with Italian ~dissolvere~, Spanish ~disolver~ and English ~dissolve~.

Latin ~solvere~ led a double life: to untie, and to pay — paying being how one unties oneself from a debt, a sense French keeps in ~solvable~ and ~insolvable~ (able, or unable, to pay). The whole French family is about undoing bonds: ~absoudre~ unties the sinner, ~résoudre~ untangles the problem, a ~solution~ is at once what dissolves and what unknots a difficulty, with ~soluble~, ~solvant~ and ~dissolution~ alongside. A ~dissolu~ person is literally someone come untied — morals loosened. The Greek twin ~lúō~ produced ~analyse~ (etymologically a loosening up into parts) and ~paralysie~ (a loosening of the limbs at one side). And French presidents wield the same chemistry as sugar cubes: dissolving the Assemblée nationale and dissolving sugar are one gesture — undoing what held together. The participle offers a last curiosity: masculine ~dissous~ against feminine ~dissoute~, with the spelling ~dissout~ admitted by the 1990 rectifications.
en.dissuader:
French ~dissuader~ was borrowed from Latin ~dissuādēre~ (“to advise against”), made of ~dis-~ (“apart, away”) and ~suādēre~ (“to advise, to urge”). The Latin verb ~suādēre~ is related to the adjective ~suāvis~ (“sweet, pleasant”), and both go back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~swād-~ (“sweet, pleasant”). Its cognate in English is ~sweet~, inherited through Germanic, while ~suave~ and ~persuade~ are borrowings from the Latin family. English ~dissuade~ was taken from the same Latin verb, as were Italian ~dissuadere~ and Spanish ~disuadir~.

The original idea behind ~suādēre~ is a pleasant one: to advise someone is to make a course of action seem sweet to them. Persuasion, in this picture, is a sweetening of the will. The prefix ~dis-~ turns that around, so that ~dissuader~ means to talk someone out of something, to turn them away from a plan. Its mirror verb is ~persuader~ (“to convince”), built with the prefix ~per-~ (“thoroughly”), and the pair ~persuader~ and ~dissuader~ is a neat illustration of how the same root can push in opposite directions. Other French words from the same Latin root include ~suave~ (“smooth, gentle”), ~persuasion~, ~dissuasion~ and ~dissuasif~ (“deterrent”), the last of which became common in the vocabulary of strategy, in the phrase ~force de dissuasion~ (“deterrent force”).
en.distiller: A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēstillāre~ (“to trickle down, to distil”), built from the prefix ~dē-~ (“down”) and the verb ~stillāre~, which comes from ~stilla~ (“drop”). The word therefore pictures liquid falling drop by drop, which is exactly what happens at the end of a still. The same ~stilla~ lies behind ~instiller~ (“to put in drop by drop”). English ~distil~ and Spanish ~destilar~ have parallel histories. The verb later specialised in the technique of vaporising a liquid and condensing it again, giving ~distillation~, ~distillateur~ and ~distillerie~.
en.distinguer:
From Latin ~distinguere~ (“to separate, to mark off, to distinguish”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~stinguere~ (“to prick, to mark with points”). ~Stinguere~ rests on a Proto-Italic *~stengʷō~, from a Proto-Indo-European root *~steygʷ-~ broadly associated with sharp points and pricking. Through that family the word is connected to English ~stick~, ~sting~, and ~stigma~, and to Greek ~stízō~ (“to tattoo, to prick”). The image at the bottom is concrete: to distinguish was to set things apart by pricking marks between them.

From that literal marking-off the verb climbed to the mental act of telling one thing from another, and then to the social sense in ~distingué~, “distinguished, set apart by excellence” — the same gesture of marking out, now applied to merit. A neat in-house relative is ~éteindre~ (“to extinguish”), from Latin ~exstinguere~: the prick-and-mark root, with a different prefix, came to mean snuffing a flame, perhaps via the idea of pricking it out. French keeps the learned line in ~distinct~, ~distinction~, ~distinctement~, and ~indistinct~, all sharpened, etymologically, to a point.
en.distraire:
Borrowed from Latin ~distrahere~ (“to pull apart, to pull in different directions”), formed from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag”). The verb was fitted into the pattern of the native French verb ~traire~ (“to milk”), and so it conjugates like it (~je distrais~, ~nous distrayons~). ~Traire~ itself continues a Vulgar Latin variant of ~trahere~, so the two verbs are cousins brought together again. Italian ~distrarre~, Spanish ~distraer~ and English ~distract~ are relatives of the same Latin verb.

The Latin picture of something torn in two directions survives in the legal and financial sense of ~distraire~, to take a part away from a whole or divert funds. The mental sense followed: to pull attention away, hence ~distrait~ (“absent-minded”), and then, more pleasantly, to take someone's mind off worries, hence “to amuse.” That is the sense of ~se distraire~ (“to amuse oneself”) and of ~distraction~. The root ~trahere~ also gave ~traction~, ~attraction~, ~extraire~, ~soustraire~, ~abstraire~, ~trait~ and ~portrait~.
en.distribuer:
From Latin ~distribuere~ (“to deal out, divide, apportion”), a compound of the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart, individually”) and the verb ~tribuere~ (“to assign, grant, allot”). That verb is itself drawn from ~tribus~, a “tribe” or division of the Roman people: to ~tribuere~ was originally to allot something among the tribes. French borrowed ~distribuer~ as a learned word directly from Latin, which is why it shows none of the wear of a verb passed down through Old French speech. Through ~tribuere~ it is cognate with English ~distribute~, ~tribute~, ~attribute~, and ~contribute~.

The semantic core is division followed by sharing out. From the civic act of apportioning duties among the Roman ~tribus~, ~distribuere~ generalized to any dividing-and-dealing-out: of goods, of letters, of roles in a play. Modern French ~distribuer~ covers handing out cards, delivering mail, and casting actors (~la distribution~ d'un film is its cast). The root ~tribus~ proved remarkably fertile: French inherited ~tribu~ (“tribe”) itself, ~tribut~ (“tribute”), ~attribuer~ (“to attribute”), ~contribuer~ (“to contribute”), ~rétribuer~ (“to remunerate”), and ~tributaire~ (“tributary”). It even survives in the unexpected ~tribunal~ and ~tribun~, since a ~tribunus~ was originally the head of a tribe — so the courtroom and the postal carrier share, distantly, the same ancestral division of Rome's people.
en.diversifier:
From Medieval Latin ~diversificare~, attested in the 13th century, a compound of Latin ~diversus~ (“diverse, turned different ways”) and ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~diversus~ is the past participle of ~divertere~ (~dis-~ + ~vertere~, “to turn aside”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wert-~ (“to turn”). Through ~vertere~ it is kin to the English words ~divert~, ~version~, and ~verse~, all of which preserve the idea of a turning.

The literal force of ~diversificare~ was “to make turned-apart,” that is, to make things branch off in different directions — exactly the modern senses “to diversify” and “to broaden.” The image is concrete: things diverge by being turned away from one another. From the same ancestor ~vertere~ French inherited a sprawling family — ~divers~, ~diversité~, ~divertir~ (“to divert, amuse”), ~convertir~, ~inverser~, and ~version~ — while ~facere~ supplies the “-fier” of countless verbs like ~simplifier~ and ~modifier~.
en.divertir:
From Latin ~dīvertere~ (“to turn aside, to turn away”), built from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). Latin ~vertere~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to turn,” which also underlies German ~werden~ (“to become,” originally “to turn into”). Italian ~divertire~ and Spanish ~divertir~ continue the same Latin verb, and English ~divert~ was borrowed from it, so the four languages share both the form and the original image of turning something off its course.

The original meaning of French ~divertir~ was exactly that, and it survives in the legal and financial sense: to ~divertir~ funds is to turn them away from their proper use, that is, to misappropriate them. The now dominant meaning came by a short step. To turn someone’s attention away from their cares is to amuse them, and the reflexive ~se divertir~ came to mean “to enjoy oneself.” From it come ~divertissement~ (“entertainment,” and in music a light interlude) and the adjective ~divertissant~. The Latin family around ~vertere~ is large in French, with ~vers~, ~version~, ~convertir~, ~pervertir~ and ~avertir~, and even ~divorce~, which comes from the Latin ~dīvortium~, a variant of ~dīvertium~, the “turning away” of one spouse from the other.
en.diviser:
From Latin ~dīvidere~ (“to force apart, to separate, to distribute, to share out”). The verb is an assimilated ~dis-~ (“apart”) prefixed to a root *~videre~ meaning “to separate,” which de Vaan traces to a Proto-Indo-European *~(d)widʰ-~ (“to separate, to divide in two”). This root is unrelated to ~vidēre~ “to see”; it is, however, the same one behind Latin ~viduus~ (“bereft, void”) and so behind ~vidua~ (“widow”) — division and widowhood share an idea of being set apart. Italian ~dividere~ and Spanish ~dividir~ are cognates, as is English ~divide~.

French actually inherited this verb twice. The popular, orally transmitted form became ~deviser~ (originally “to divide up,” later “to chat, to converse” — talk that goes back and forth, portioned out between speakers), while the learned, book-borrowed form gave ~diviser~, keeping the plain mathematical and physical sense of separating into parts. From the same source come ~division~, ~diviseur~, ~divisible~, ~divisibilité~, and ~divisionnaire~, plus, through ~vidua~, the surprising relatives ~veuf~ and ~veuve~ (“widower, widow”) and ~divorce~ — all turning on the ancient image of two things pulled asunder.
en.divorcer: Formed from the noun ~divorce~ with the first-group ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~dīvortium~ (“separation, divorce”), from the verb ~dīvortere~, a variant of ~dīvertere~ (“to turn aside, to separate from”). The Latin picture is of two paths turning away from each other, which fits the idea of a marriage coming apart. English ~divorce~ comes from the same Latin word through French. The verb ~divorcer~ is therefore a French creation on a Latin noun, not a verb inherited from Latin.
en.divulguer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~dīvulgāre~ (“to spread among the people, to make public”), built from ~dī-~, a form of ~dis-~ (“in all directions”), and ~vulgāre~ (“to make common, to publish”). ~Vulgāre~ comes from ~vulgus~ (“the common people, the crowd”), which also gave French ~vulgaire~ and the ~Vulgate~, the “common” Latin Bible. Italian ~divulgare~, Spanish ~divulgar~ and English ~divulge~ are learned borrowings of the same Latin verb. In Latin the sense was neutral, simply broadcasting; in modern French ~divulguer~ is used above all for revealing what was meant to stay hidden, such as a secret or a name.
en.documenter: Formed in French from the noun ~document~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to support with documents, to supply with evidence.” The noun ~document~ is a borrowing from Latin ~documentum~ (“lesson, example, proof”), derived from the verb ~docēre~ (“to teach, to show”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way French turns a noun into a first-group verb. The reflexive ~se documenter~ (“to research a subject, to gather information”) is common, while ~documenter~ itself also covers recording a process in writing.
en.domicilier: Formed from the noun ~domicile~ with the ordinary verb ending ~-er~ (English Wiktionary writes the ending as ~-ier~, but it is the same verbal ending). The verb means “to give a legal residence to someone or something,” and ~être domicilié~ is “to reside, to be registered at an address.” The noun ~domicile~ is a borrowing of Latin ~domicilium~ (“dwelling”), itself derived from ~domus~ (“house”), the root behind ~domestique~ and ~dôme~.
en.dominer:
From Latin ~dominārī~ (“to be master, to rule, to reign”), a verb derived from ~dominus~ (“master, lord of the household”), which in turn comes from ~domus~ (“house, home”). The chain reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dem-~ (“house, household; to build”). The same ~dominus~ underlies Italian ~dominare~ and Spanish ~dominar~, while ~domus~ shows up across the family in Greek ~domos~ (“house”) and, by a Germanic detour, in English ~timber~ (originally “building material”).

The striking thing is how authority grew out of the home: the ~dominus~ was first simply the head of a ~domus~, the master of a household, and his domestic command broadened into mastery, rule, and at last sheer ascendancy. To ~dominer~ now ranges from a sovereign ruling a realm to a peak ~dominating~ a valley below — physical and figurative supremacy alike. The same root flowered into a large French family: ~maison~ (from ~mansiō~), ~domestique~, ~domicile~, ~domaine~, ~dame~ (from ~domina~), ~madame~, ~dominical~, and the borrowed ~dôme~, all gathered, ultimately, around the idea of the house and its lord.
en.donner:
From Old French ~doner~, from Latin ~dōnāre~ (“to give as a gift, to bestow”), itself built on the noun ~dōnum~ (“gift”). Both go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”), by way of *~deh₃nom~ (“gift”). Through that root ~donner~ is cognate with Spanish ~donar~ and Italian ~donare~, with Sanskrit ~dā~ (“to give”), and with Greek ~dōron~ (“gift,” as in the name Theodore, “gift of god”).

A quiet upset lies behind the everyday verb. Classical Latin had two words here: plain ~dăre~ (“to give”) and ~dōnāre~ (“to make a gift of”). In Gaul, ~dăre~ was driven out early and almost completely, so French took its ordinary “give” from the more ceremonious ~dōnāre~ — where Spanish and Italian kept ~dăre~ alive in ~dar~ and ~dare~. From the same root French keeps ~don~ (“gift”), ~donateur~ (“donor”), ~donation~, and ~pardonner~ (“to forgive,” literally “to give thoroughly”), while the learned ~dose~ and ~anecdote~ reach back through Greek to the very same *~deh₃-~. The gift, in French, swallowed the verb of plain giving whole.
en.doper: Borrowed from English ~to dope~ (“to drug”). English ~dope~ is itself usually traced to Dutch ~doop~ (“dipping sauce”), and its senses moved from a thick liquid to a narcotic and then to the act of drugging, notably racehorses and later athletes. French took the verb up in that sporting sense, and it then spread to ~se doper~ (“to take performance-enhancing drugs”) and to the figurative “to boost, to stimulate,” as in ~doper les ventes~ (“to boost sales”).
en.dorer:
From Latin ~deaurāre~ (“to gild, cover with gold”), from ~de-~ (here intensive) plus ~aurum~ (“gold”), from Proto-Italic *~auzom~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ews-~ (“to shine, glow; dawn”) — the same root that gave Latin ~aurōra~ (“dawn”). Cognate Romance reflexes include Italian ~dorare~ and Spanish ~dorar~; the noun ~aurum~ itself survives in French ~or~ (“gold”) and in English borrowings like ~auriferous~.

The metaphor is bright and old: gold was the metal of the glowing dawn. From “to cover with gold” French ~dorer~ broadened to any warm golden colouring — sunlight that ~dore~ the wheat, an egg-wash that gilds a pastry crust. The figurative idiom ~dorer la pilule~ (“to gild the pill”) means to sweeten unwelcome news, the way an apothecary once coated a bitter pill in gold leaf. From the same ~aurum~ root French keeps ~doré~, ~dorure~, ~orfèvre~ (“goldsmith”), and ~oriflamme~; ~aurore~ (“dawn”) preserves, intact, the original Indo-European image of shining light.
en.dormir:
From Middle French ~dormir~, from Old French ~dormir~ (attested around 1100), from Latin ~dormīre~ (“to sleep”), from Proto-Italic *~dormiō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~drem-~ (“to sleep”). Cognate, through the Latin verb, with Italian ~dormire~, Spanish and Portuguese ~dormir~, and Catalan ~dormir~; through the PIE root, with Old Church Slavonic ~drěmati~ (“to doze”) and Sanskrit ~drāti~ (“sleeps”).

Unusually for a common verb, the meaning never wandered: ~dormir~ has meant simply “to sleep” for two thousand years, with idiomatic extensions like ~dormir comme une souche~ (“to sleep like a log”) and ~qui dort dîne~ (“he who sleeps, dines”). The Latin root proved richly generative. From ~dormīre~ and its relatives French drew ~dormeur~ (“sleeper”), ~dormant~ (“sleeping, dormant,” as in ~eau dormante~, “still water”), ~endormir~ (“to put to sleep”), ~rendormir~ (“to send back to sleep”), and ~dortoir~ (“dormitory”). English borrowed many of the same: ~dormant~, ~dormitory~, and even ~dormouse~, the “sleeping mouse.” The architectural ~dormer~ window, too, descends from this root — once a window for a sleeping-room.
en.doser: Formed from the noun ~dose~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so ~doser~ means “to measure out a dose.” The noun ~dose~ is a learned borrowing of Latin ~dosis~, which Latin took from Ancient Greek ~dósis~ (“a giving, a gift”). Related to it through the same family of “giving” is ~dot~ (“dowry”). From medicine the verb spread to cooking and chemistry, and then to the figurative use of weighing one's words or efforts.
en.doter:
From Latin ~dotare~ (“to endow, to provide with a dowry”), a denominative verb built on the noun ~dos~, stem ~dot-~ (“dowry, marriage portion”). That noun goes back to Proto-Italic *~dōtis~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Through that root ~doter~ is cognate with a remarkable spread of words: Ancient Greek ~dōron~ (“gift”) and ~dosis~ (“a giving, a dose”), Latin ~donare~ (“to give”), and the English borrowings ~donate~, ~dose~, and even ~date~ (from the Roman dating formula “given on such a day”).

The verb began in the law of marriage: to ~doter~ a daughter was to settle a dowry on her, the property she brought to the household. From that contractual core the sense widened generously. To ~doter~ came to mean to furnish or equip with any advantage — funds, talents, qualities — so that today a region may be ~doté~ with resources, a person ~doté~ with charm, a school ~doté~ of a new library. French keeps the original noun ~dot~ (“dowry”) alongside the derived ~dotation~ (“endowment, allocation”). The same *~deh₃-~ root, entering French through learned Latin, also yields ~donner~, ~don~, ~donation~, ~dose~, and ~anecdote~ (Greek for something “not given out,” i.e. unpublished).
en.doubler:
French ~doubler~ comes from the adjective ~double~, from Latin ~duplus~ (“twofold”), with the verb continuing Late Latin ~duplāre~ (“to double”). ~Duplus~ is ~duo~ (“two”) plus ~-plus~ (“-fold”): the first from Proto-Indo-European *~dwóh₁~ (“two”), the second from the root *~pleḱ-~ (“to fold, weave”). It is cognate with English ~double~ and ~duo~, with Ancient Greek ~diplóos~ (“twofold”), and, through the same fold-element, with English ~ply~ and ~-fold~.

The core sense is “to make twofold,” but ~doubler~ has fanned out remarkably. To line a coat is to ~doubler~ it — to give it a second, inner layer (hence ~doublure~, “lining,” and also a stand-in or understudy). On the road, to ~doubler~ a car is to overtake it, briefly running two abreast. In cinema, to ~doubler~ a film is to dub it, laying a second voice over the first. Each sense is a literal doubling. The family also gives ~redoubler~ (“to redouble; to repeat a school year”) and ~dédoubler~ (“to split in two”).
en.douer:
From Old French ~doer~ (twelfth century), from Latin ~dōtāre~ (“to provide with a dowry, to endow”), a derivative of ~dōs~, genitive ~dōtis~ (“dowry”), from Proto-Italic *~dōtis~, from PIE *~déh₃tis~ (“gift, act of giving”), built on the root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — the root of Latin ~dare~ (“to give”) and ~dōnum~ (“gift”). Cognate with Italian ~dotare~ and Spanish ~dotar~; English ~endow~ comes straight from Anglo-Norman ~endouer~, built on this very French verb.

At first ~douer~ meant exactly what its Latin parent meant: to settle a dowry on a bride (late twelfth century). By about 1210 it had taken the figurative leap that defines it today: nature, heaven or fortune endows someone with a quality. Modern French has all but retired the active verb, which lives on chiefly in the participle ~doué~ — to be gifted at mathematics is, etymologically, to have received one's talent as a dowry from nature. French in fact owns the Latin verb twice: ~douer~ is the form worn smooth by a millennium of speech, while ~doter~ was borrowed back from books — a classic popular/learned doublet, the two now divided by use, one endowing institutions with funds, the other persons with gifts. The noun behind them was given to French twice as well: Latin ~dōs~ produced ~dot~ (“dowry”), while the same PIE *~déh₃tis~, travelling through Greek ~δόσις~ (“a giving”), produced ~dose~ — a dowry and a dose are, etymologically, one and the same “gift.” The wider family of *~deh₃-~ includes ~donner~, ~don~, ~donation~ and ~pardonner~.
en.douter:
Attested in Old French from around 980, from Latin ~dubitāre~ (“to waver, hesitate, doubt”), a frequentative connected to ~dubius~ (“doubtful, uncertain”) and ultimately to ~duo~ (“two”). The image at the heart of doubt is being pulled between two ways: to doubt is to hover between two possibilities, unable to commit. Italian ~dubitare~ and Spanish ~dudar~ carry the same Latin root, and English ~doubt~ borrowed it through French.

The earliest French sense was not intellectual uncertainty but fear: in Old French ~douter~ meant “to dread, to fear” — to be of two minds before a danger. This sense survives intact in the compound ~redouter~ (“to dread”). Over time the verb shifted from fearing to questioning, from apprehension to mere uncertainty. The reflexive ~se douter de~ then swung almost to the opposite — “to suspect, to surmise,” to be fairly sure of something. The silent ~b~ in English ~doubt~ was reinserted by scholars to mirror Latin ~dubitāre~; French spelling never restored it. From the same root come ~doute~, ~douteux~, ~indubitable~, and ~dubitatif~.
en.drainer: The sources differ slightly on the route. French Wiktionary sees a derivative of the noun ~drain~ plus the suffix ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb, while English Wiktionary calls it a straight borrowing from the English verb ~drain~. Either way the root is English: French ~drain~ (“channel for carrying off water”) was itself borrowed from English ~drain~. The English word thus crossed the Channel, and the French verb ~drainer~ means to drain off a liquid, whether water from soil or, figuratively, money, talent or traffic. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default for new verbs.
en.dresser:
From Late Latin *~directiāre~ (“to straighten, to set upright”), a verb built on Latin ~directus~ (“straight, direct”), the past participle of ~dīrigere~ (“to lay straight, to direct”). That verb combines ~dis-~ with ~regere~ (“to rule, to keep straight”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to make right”) — the root behind English ~right~ and ~royal~. French ~direct~, ~droit~, ~adresse~, and ~dresser~ are all doublets descending from this single Latin family.

The core idea is “to make straight, to set up vertically,” and French ~dresser~ fans out from it impressively. One ~dresse~ a tent, a ladder, or a statue (raises it upright), ~dresse~ a table (sets it), ~dresse~ a list or a report (draws it up), and ~dresse~ the dishes on a plate (arranges them) — the source of culinary ~dressage~ (“plating”). Applied to animals and people, ~dresser~ means “to train, to break in, to tame,” straightening behaviour into obedience; a trained horse undergoes ~dressage~, the term now used in English for the equestrian discipline. Related French words include ~dressage~, ~redresser~ (“to straighten again, to set right”), ~adresse~ (both “address” and “skill”), and ~dresseur~ (“animal trainer”).
en.durcir: ~Durcir~ means “to become hard” or “to make hard,” and its source is the Latin inchoative verb ~dūrēscere~ (“to harden”), formed on the adjective ~dūrus~ (“hard”). The sources differ on the route. French Wiktionary derives ~durcir~ directly from Latin ~dūrēscere~, while English Wiktionary treats it as a back-formation from ~endurcir~, itself based on the Latin verb. Either way Latin ~dūrēscere~ stands behind it. The adjective ~dūrus~ lives on in French ~dur~, and the verb in the figurative uses of ~durcir~: an argument, a tone or a conflict can harden, not only a material.
en.durer:
From Latin ~durare~ (“to harden, to endure, to last”), attested in French from the 11th century. ~Durare~ derives from the adjective ~durus~ (“hard”), whose deeper Indo-European origin is debated — one account ties it to a root meaning “long” (compare Ancient Greek ~dērós~, “long-lasting,” and Sanskrit ~dūrá~, “far”), another to *~deru-~ (“hard, firm,” as of wood). Whichever holds, the link between hardness and persistence is plain: what is hard endures. Romance kept the verb in Italian ~durare~ and Spanish ~durar~.

Latin ~durare~ already spanned the physical and the temporal — to make hard, but also to hold out and to last — and French settled firmly on the temporal: to ~durer~ is to go on in time, to last. A storm, a friendship, or a battery can ~durer~. The hardness sense lives on in the sibling adjective ~dur~ (“hard, tough”) and its kin ~durcir~ (“to harden”), ~dureté~ (“hardness”), and ~endurer~ (“to endure”). The time sense surfaces in ~durée~ (“duration”) and the preposition ~durant~ (“during”), which began life as a present participle of ~durer~ — “while X is lasting.”
en.dynamiser: Formed in French from the adjective ~dynamique~ with the verb suffix ~-iser~, which replaces the ending ~-ique~ ; the suffix means “to make A”, so ~dynamiser~ is to make something dynamic, to energize it. The adjective ~dynamique~ is a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ~dynamikós~ (“powerful, effective”), derived from ~dýnamis~ (“power”). The suffix ~-iser~ itself comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and is fully productive in modern French in technical and journalistic registers, as in ~moderniser~ and ~automatiser~. The same Greek ~dýnamis~ is behind ~dynamite~ and ~dynamo~.
en.débarquer:
Formed from the noun ~barque~ (« small boat »), with the prefix ~dé-~ (« off, from ») and the suffix ~-er~, by parasynthetic derivation — that is, prefix and suffix were added at once to the noun. ~barque~ comes from Late Latin ~barca~, traced through Latin ~bāris~ to Ancient Greek ~βᾶρις~ (« Egyptian river-boat »), which is itself, by most accounts, of Egyptian origin — a faint memory of Nile barges riding in the word.

Built on « boat », ~débarquer~ means literally « to take off the boat » and so « to unload » cargo, then « to disembark », to get off the ship. From there it lightened into everyday and slang uses: to « turn up » unexpectedly (« il a débarqué chez moi »), or, of a person abruptly dismissed, to be « kicked out » of a job. Its mirror-twin ~embarquer~ (« to embark, to load aboard ») is built the same way on ~barque~, and the pair frames the whole voyage — going aboard and stepping back ashore.
en.débarrasser:
French ~débarrasser~ pairs the privative prefix ~dé-~ (“un-, away”) with ~barrasser~, the family of ~embarrasser~ (“to hinder, encumber”) and ~embarras~ (“obstruction”). These rest on the noun ~barre~ (“bar”), itself from Vulgar Latin *~barra~, a word of disputed origin: by one account it goes back to Old Frankish *~bara~ (“bar, beam, barrier”), and ultimately to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰerH-~ (“to strike, pierce”); an alternative ties it instead to a Celtic source related to Breton ~barri~ (“branch, twig”). The Iberian languages developed the verb in parallel — Spanish ~embarazar~, Portuguese ~embaraçar~ — and French ~débarrasser~ appears to echo a Spanish ~desembarazar~.

The underlying picture is concrete: a ~barre~ is a bar laid across a way, and to ~embarrasser~ is to clutter that way with obstacles, while to ~débarrasser~ is to clear the bars away. The reflexive ~se débarrasser de~ (“to rid oneself of”) keeps that sense of shedding an encumbrance. From *~barra~ French also drew ~barre~, ~barrière~ (“barrier”), ~barreau~, ~barrage~, ~débarras~ (“lumber-room, riddance”), and the borrowed English ~bar~, ~barrier~, and ~embarrass~ — the last carrying the same Romance figure of a path obstructed.
en.débattre:
From Old French ~debatre~ (“to fight, struggle, quarrel, discuss,” attested around 1050), from ~de-~ + ~batre~ (“to beat”), which gave modern ~battre~. ~Battre~ descends through Middle French from Latin ~battere~, a Vulgar form of Classical ~battuere~ (“to beat, strike”). That Latin verb is itself a puzzle: it was rare in literary Latin, and sources flag its origin as uncertain — ~perhaps~ borrowed from Gaulish or Germanic, and ultimately onomatopoeic. The Romance cousins line up neatly: Italian ~dibattere~, Spanish ~debatir~, Catalan ~debatre~.

The development is vivid. The ~de-~ here is intensive, and ~débattre~ began as a thoroughly physical word — to thrash about, to fight, to wrangle. From the body the sense rose to the voice: a ~débat~ (first attested as a verbal form ~debat~ around 1050) became a verbal struggle, an argument made with words rather than blows. The reflexive ~se débattre~ kept the old muscular meaning, “to thrash about, to struggle.” From the same ~battre~ come ~bataille~, ~combat~, ~abattre~, ~rabattre~, and the borrowed-back English doublets ~battle~, ~batter~, and ~debate~.
en.débiter: The sources give two origins for two senses. The older sense “to cut up” (timber, meat) is explained as ~dé-~ + ~bitte~ + ~-er~, literally “to make into pieces”. ~Bitte~ is a nautical term borrowed from Old Norse ~biti~ (“beam”), from a root meaning “to split”, *~bʰeyd-~. The commercial sense “to sell steadily, to turn out in quantity”, and its figurative use for reciting at length, is explained as ~débit~ + ~-er~. ~Débit~ comes from Latin ~debitum~ (“debt”), the neuter participle of ~dēbēre~ (“to owe”), which is why ~débit~ also names the debit side of an account.
en.débloquer: ~Débloquer~ is ~dé-~ + ~bloquer~, with ~dé-~ reversing the action of the base: to undo a blockage, to free what was jammed, and by extension to release funds or lift a freeze. The base ~bloquer~ comes from the noun ~bloc~ (“log, block”), an Old French loan from Middle Dutch ~blok~ (“tree trunk”), so the family is Germanic despite its French look, and English ~block~ is the same word. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and is one of the most productive prefixes of French, as in ~défaire~ and ~déplier~.
en.déborder: Formed from ~dé-~, the noun ~bord~ (“edge”) and the ending ~-er~; French Wiktionary parses it instead as ~dé-~ on the verb ~border~, which comes to the same thing. Here ~dé-~ expresses going beyond or away from: to ~déborder~ is to pass over the edge, hence to overflow, and in the military sense to outflank. The noun ~bord~ is a Frankish borrowing and is cognate with English ~board~. Hence ~débordé~, “swamped” with work. Spanish and Catalan ~desbordar~ are cognate, built the same way.
en.déboucher:
~Déboucher~ is ~dé-~ + ~boucher~ (“to stop up”), attested as ~debochier~ in the thirteenth century — and, against all appearances, the family has nothing to do with ~bouche~, “mouth.” The verb ~boucher~ was drawn from Old French ~bousche~, “wisp of straw, bundle of brushwood”: to stop a hole was, concretely, to stuff it with straw. ~Bousche~ continues a Vulgar Latin *~bosca~, “brushwood,” of the same family as ~bois~ (“wood”), with kin in Italian ~bosco~ and Spanish ~bosque~ (“forest”). So the corkscrew’s verb descends from underbrush: what you remove when you unblock is, etymologically, a fistful of twigs. The same ~bousche~ produced ~bouchon~ — first a twist of straw, then the cork it became, and in today’s French also a traffic jam: cars stoppered in the road like wine in the neck of a bottle.

Then comes the twist. Alongside “unblock, uncork,” French uses the same verb for “to emerge, to open onto”: a street, a river, a line of reasoning débouche somewhere. Lexicographers split here: the TLFi files this intransitive use (attested in the seventeenth century) as a second verb, built this time on ~bouche~ — the mouth of a street, of a river — while other dictionaries fold every sense into one formation on ~boucher~. Either way the irony stands: a family that owes nothing to the mouth ended up borrowing it, or at least leaning on it. The offspring map both senses: ~débouché~, “outlet, opening, career prospect,” belongs to the mouth side; ~reboucher~ (“to stop up again”) to the straw side; and ~embouchure~ — the river’s mouth, the trumpet’s mouthpiece — though built directly on ~bouche~, shows how readily French lets openings speak.
en.débuter:
A French formation (16th century) from the noun ~but~ (“a goal, a target, an aim”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~but~ is of debated origin: it may be a variant of ~bout~ (“an end, a tip”), or come from Old Norse ~butr~ (“a log, a block”), perhaps as the wooden mark one aimed at. Either way, ~débuter~ literally means to move away from the ~but~ — the term comes from games of bowls and target sports, where to ~débuter~ was to make the opening throw that knocks a ball off its mark.

From that opening cast the verb generalized to “to make a first move, to begin,” and especially to begin a public career: an actor, a singer, or a politician ~débute~ when first appearing before the public. French borrowed this sense out again as the noun ~début~ (“a beginning, a first appearance”), which English then took as ~debut~ along with ~debutante~ (a young woman making her ~début~ in society). The opposite end of the same game survives in ~buter~ (“to strike against, to stumble”) and the related ~butoir~ (“a buffer, a stop”), all circling the original notion of the mark struck at the start of play.
en.décaler: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~caler~, in its sense of wedging or immobilizing. That ~caler~ is built on the noun ~cale~ (“wedge”), whose deeper origin is uncertain; by one account it comes from German ~Keil~ (“wedge”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), usually reverses the action of its base, so to ~décaler~ is to take away the wedge and knock something out of its fixed position. The sense then widened to moving anything by one notch, whether an object, a schedule or a date.
en.décentraliser: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~centraliser~, not from ~central~ directly. The prefix, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), here reverses the base verb. ~Centraliser~ is itself ~central~ plus the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make A”), and ~central~ comes from Latin ~centrālis~, the adjective of ~centrum~ (“center”). To ~décentraliser~ is therefore to undo a centralization, that is, to shift powers away from the center.
en.décerner:
~Décerner~ was borrowed around 1247 from Latin ~dēcernere~, “to decide, to decree”: ~dē-~ + ~cernere~, “to sift, to separate, to distinguish — and hence to decide.” ~Cernere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~krey-~, “to sieve,” one of the great mental metaphors of the family: its Greek cognate ~krínō~, “to separate, to judge,” underlies ~crise~, ~critique~ and ~critère~, while English ~riddle~ — the coarse sieve, not the puzzle — sifts on the Germanic side. Within Latin the same root yielded ~crībrum~, “sieve” (French ~crible~), ~certus~, “settled, certain” (French ~certain~), and ~crīmen~, originally the charge brought to judgment (French ~crime~). To decide, in this family, is always to shake the grain until one thing alone is left in the mesh.

In Rome, ~dēcernere~ was the Senate’s verb: it decreed wars, honors, triumphs. French first used ~décerner~ for solemn pronouncements — around 1247 “to declare,” by 1548 “to confer by decree” — and the judicial thread survives intact in ~décerner un mandat d'arrêt~, “to issue an arrest warrant.” But everyday modern French reserves the verb almost entirely for glory: one décerne prizes, medals, diplomas, palms. A jury awarding the Prix Goncourt performs, verb and gesture, the old senatorial decree of a triumph. From the participle of the same Latin verb, ~dēcrētum~, come French ~décret~ and English ~decree~; ~discerner~ and ~concerner~ keep other compounds of ~cernere~ alive. The semantic chain is tidy: sift, then decide, then decree, then bestow — every prize ceremony is the last pass of a very old sieve.
en.décevoir:
From Old French ~decevoir~ (also ~deceveir~), from Latin ~dēcipere~, compounded from ~de-~ plus ~capere~ (“to take, seize, catch”). The root verb ~capere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (also reconstructed *~kap-~, “to grasp, seize”), the same root behind English ~have~ and ~heave~ and German ~haben~. The literal Latin sense is vivid: ~dēcipere~ meant “to catch out, ensnare, take in” — and so, to deceive. Spanish ~decebir~ is largely archaic, but English ~deceive~ comes by the very same path.

Here the French semantic history is the surprise. Old French ~decevoir~ meant exactly “to deceive, beguile,” matching the Latin and matching its English twin. Over centuries French softened the word: from actively tricking someone to merely failing their hopes, so that modern ~décevoir~ means “to disappoint.” The old harsh sense has migrated entirely to ~tromper~. The buried “catching” survives in the noun family — ~déception~ (now “disappointment,” once “deception”), ~déçu~ (“disappointed”), ~décevant~ (“disappointing”) — and the same ~capere~ root feeds ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~, and ~percevoir~, a whole network of French verbs built on the idea of taking in.
en.décharger: Formed from ~charger~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base. English Wiktionary adds that the pair already existed in Old French as ~deschargier~, from Late Latin ~discarricāre~, so the prefixed verb is older than French itself. The base ~charger~ goes back to Late Latin ~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), from Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled wagon”), a word of Gaulish origin. To ~décharger~ is therefore, first, to unload a cart, and from there to relieve someone of a burden, to fire off a weapon, or to clear a defendant.
en.déchirer:
From Old French ~escirer~, which became ~descirer~ and then Middle French ~deschirer~ as the prefix ~es-~ was replaced by ~dé-~. The verb itself is Germanic: it comes from Frankish *~skeran~ (“to shear, cut”), from Proto-Germanic *~skeraną~ (“to shear, shave, cut”). Cognates are easy to find in the Germanic languages: Old English ~scieran~, whence English ~shear~, and German ~scheren~. Dutch ~scheuren~ (“to tear”) is a near relative.

The French verb moved from cutting to tearing: where the Germanic root describes a clean cut of wool or hair, ~déchirer~ is to rip cloth, paper or flesh apart. The figurative uses came easily, since a heart, a country or a silence can all be torn: hence ~déchirant~ (“heartbreaking”) and ~déchirure~ (“a tear, a rip”). Modern slang turned it around again, so that something that ~déchire~ is spectacular. The verb is a reminder of how many everyday French words came from the speech of the Franks, who ruled Gaul after the Romans.
en.décider:
From Latin ~dēcīdere~ (“to cut off, settle, decide a question”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike, to fell”). ~Caedere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~kaidō~, from PIE *~kh₂eyd-~ (“to cut, to hew”). The image is concrete and decisive: to decide is to cut a difficulty off at a stroke. Through the same root ~décider~ is related to English ~caesura~ and to the whole ~-cide~ family of words.

Where our deliberations feel like weighing, the Roman metaphor was a blade severing the tangle of a dispute — a resolution reached by cutting rather than by pondering. From the root ~caedere~ French inherited a sharp-edged vocabulary: ~concis~ (literally “cut short”), ~précis~ (“cut off in front,” hence “exact”), ~incisif~, ~circoncision~, and the murderous ~-cide~ suffix in ~homicide~, ~suicide~, and ~insecticide~ (an ~insecte~ being itself “cut into” segments, though from a different root). ~Décider~ thus shares its ancestry with both the surgeon's precision and the killer's blow — every decision a small, clean cut through uncertainty.
en.déclarer:
From Latin ~declarare~ (“to make clear, to announce, to reveal”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ (here intensive, “thoroughly”) and ~clarare~ (“to make bright or clear”), a verb formed on the adjective ~clarus~ (“clear, bright, distinct”). ~Clarus~ descends from Proto-Italic and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, to cry out”) — the same root behind Latin ~calare~ (“to proclaim”) and ~clamare~ (“to shout”). Italian ~dichiarare~ and Spanish ~declarar~ are the Romance siblings, and English ~declare~ is a borrowing from the same French stem.

The metaphor is light: to ~déclarer~ is to bring something out of obscurity into the open, to make it bright and plain to all. From this came the formal senses of announcing officially — declaring war, declaring one's love, declaring goods at customs, declaring income to the tax office. French ~déclaration~ carries the same weight, as in the ~Déclaration des droits de l'homme~. The underlying ~clarus~ seeds a luminous family in French: ~clair~, ~clarté~, ~clairière~ (a clearing where light enters the forest), ~clairvoyant~, ~éclairer~, and ~clarifier~ — all turning on the idea of brightness made manifest.
en.déclencher:
~Déclencher~ is built on ~clenche~ (“latch, door-lever”) with the prefix ~dé-~, the literal sense being to lift the latch off its catch. ~Clenche~ comes from Old Frankish *~klinka~ (“latch”), a Germanic word; it belongs with German ~Klinke~ (“handle, latch”) and Swedish ~klinka~, the family resting on a Germanic base imitating the click of the mechanism.

The picture is mechanical and precise: a ~clenche~ is the pivoting bar that holds a door shut, and to ~déclencher~ it is to disengage that bar so the door — or any restrained thing — springs free. From a smith's term for a latch, French abstracted one of its most useful modern verbs: one now triggers an alarm, an offensive, a chemical reaction, a crisis. The opposite move kept its own prefix in ~enclencher~ (“to engage, set in motion”), where the latch is pushed home rather than released. Around the same root cluster ~déclenchement~ (“triggering”), ~déclencheur~ (“the trigger, the shutter-release of a camera”), and ~redéclencher~. The everyday abstraction “to set off” still hides a small medieval door-catch clicking open.
en.décliner:
From Latin ~dēclīnāre~ (“to bend aside, to turn away, to inflect”), from ~dē-~ (“away, down”) and ~clīnāre~ (“to lean, to bend”). The verb ~clīnāre~ rests on PIE *~ḱley-~ (“to lean, to incline”), one of the most widely reflected roots in the family: it gives Greek ~klínein~ (“to lean”), English ~lean~, German ~lehnen~, and, through Latin, English ~incline~ and ~decline~. Romance descendants run parallel in Italian ~declinare~, Spanish ~declinar~ and Portuguese ~declinar~.

The core image is of bending or sloping away from an upright, central position. From that single picture Latin already drew several branches: the grammarian’s “to decline” a noun (to bend its endings through the cases), the astronomer’s declination, and the everyday “to turn aside” or “to slope downward.” French inherited the whole spread, so that ~décliner~ can mean to refuse (“to turn away” an offer), to weaken or wane (the sun, one’s health, a day declining toward evening), and to set out in series — to ~décliner~ one’s identity, or a brand to ~décliner~ a product in several versions. The shared thread is departure from a high or central state. French keeps ~déclin~ (“decline”), ~déclinaison~ (“declension”) and ~déclinable~.
en.décoder: Formed from ~coder~ (“to encode”) and the reversing prefix ~dé-~, so that ~décoder~ means to undo a coding and read the original message. The base verb is either built on ~code~ or borrowed from English ~to code~, and the noun ~code~ comes from Latin ~codex~, a variant of ~caudex~ (“tree trunk”), which came to name wooden-tablet books, then law books, then the body of laws itself. The sense “secret code” reached French later from English. ~Décoder~ then applies to ciphers, television signals, and by extension to interpreting any hard-to-read message or behavior.
en.décoller: Two verbs share this spelling. The commoner one is formed from ~dé-~ (reversal) and ~coller~ (“to stick,” from ~colle~, “glue”), so it means to unstick. An aircraft that “comes unstuck” from the ground ~décolle~, which is the sense of “taking off.” The second verb is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dēcollāre~ (“to behead”), built on ~collum~ (“neck”), the same word that gave French ~cou~. This older verb survives mostly in the literary ~décollation~ (“beheading”) and the noun ~décolleté~ (“low-cut neckline”).
en.décomposer: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ (reversal, “undoing”) and ~composer~, so “to undo a composition, to break something into its parts.” The base ~composer~ comes from Latin ~componere~ (“to put together”, from ~com-~ + ~ponere~) but was reshaped in Old French on ~poser~, which explains its odd form. ~Décomposer~ has a literal sense, such as splitting a compound or a number into its elements, and a physical one: matter that rots is said to ~se décomposer~. By extension, a face ~décomposé~ is one drawn with shock or grief, as though its features had fallen apart.
en.décompresser: Borrowed from English ~to decompress~, which French Wiktionary breaks down with the prefixes ~dé-~ and ~con-~ and the verb ~presser~ (“to press”): in other words, “to undo the pressing together.” The first sense was technical, to release pressure on a gas, a diver or a computer file. French then took up the figurative, informal sense “to relax, to unwind,” treating stress as a pressure that can be released. The verb is therefore a recent import dressed in entirely Latin parts, which French speakers can read at once.
en.déconcentrer: Formed in French from ~concentrer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which undoes the base: to ~déconcentrer~ is to scatter what had been gathered. The sense “to distract” applies to attention (a noise ~déconcentre~ a student), while the administrative sense “to devolve” applies to power, handed from a central authority to local offices. The base ~concentrer~ was coined in 17th-century French from ~centrer~ with ~con-~ (“together”), on ~centre~, from Latin ~centrum~, borrowed from Greek ~kéntron~ (“sharp point, compass pivot”).
en.déconnecter: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~connecter~. The prefix, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), here reverses the base verb: to undo a connection. The base ~connecter~ is attested from around 1780 and comes from Latin ~conectere~ (“to bind together”), built from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~nectere~ (“to bind, to tie”). So ~déconnecter~ literally means to untie what was tied together, first said of wires and circuits and later of anyone logging off a network. The reflexive ~se déconnecter~ now means “to log out,” and, by extension, “to switch off mentally.”
en.déconner: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~con~ and the ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary notes that only the first sense follows this formation. The figurative senses (to talk nonsense, to joke around, to mess up) were modeled on ~délirer~ and have no direct etymological link to it. The noun ~con~ comes from Latin ~cunnus~ (“sheath, by analogy the vulva”), which is why the word was long vulgar. English Wiktionary glosses the verb literally as “to pull out of the ~con~.”
en.déconseiller: Formed from ~conseiller~ (“to advise”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to advise against rather than to advise. ~Conseiller~ is inherited from Old French ~conseilier~, from Latin ~cōnsiliārī~ (“to take counsel”), built on ~cōnsilium~ (“counsel, deliberation”), a word that probably began as a “calling together” (~con-~ plus a root related to ~calāre~, “to call”). The same Latin noun gave Italian ~consiglio~, Spanish ~consejo~ and, through Old French, English ~counsel~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and is one of the most productive prefixes in French.
en.décorer:
From Latin ~decorāre~ (“to adorn, beautify”), from ~decus~ / ~decor~ (“grace, ornament, seemliness”), from Proto-Italic *~dekos~, from PIE *~deḱ-~ (“to take, to accept, to be fitting”). The same root reaches widely: through Latin ~decēre~ (“to be becoming”) come ~décent~ and ~dignité~, and the root is cognate with Ancient Greek ~δοκεῖν~ (~dokeîn~, “to seem, think fit”).

The key is that ~decus~ did not mean ornament for its own sake but what is fitting — beauty as propriety. To ~decorate~ was to give a thing the adornment proper to it, which is why the very same notion sits inside ~décent~ (“suitable”) and inside ~décorer~ in its honorific sense: to ~décorer~ a soldier is to confer the distinction his conduct merits, not to prettify him. From this root spread ~décor~, ~décoration~, ~décoratif~, ~décorateur~, and, by the ~decēre~ branch, the whole family of fitness and worth. Decoration, in the word's bones, is less about glitter than about giving each thing its due grace.
en.décortiquer:
From Latin ~dēcorticāre~ (“to strip off bark”), formed from ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~cortex~ (“bark, rind”), whose stem ~cortic-~ shows in the verb. French took it in as a learned word, while its relative ~écorcher~ (“to skin, to flay”), from a Latin verb ~excorticāre~ built in the same way, came down by the popular route. English ~decorticate~ and ~cortex~ come from the same Latin words.

The literal sense is to remove bark or husk: ~décortiquer~ is what one does to shrimp, nuts, rice or grain, and the verb also serves for stripping a tree. By a short step it became figurative: to ~décortiquer~ a text, a speech or a problem is to peel back its outer layer and examine what lies underneath. In anatomy the same Latin ~cortex~ survives in ~cortex~ and ~cortical~, so the brain's outer layer is named for bark.
en.découler:
From the prefix ~dé-~ (here marking downward motion or origin) and ~couler~ (“to flow, to run”). ~Couler~ comes from Latin ~colare~ (“to filter, to strain”), from the noun ~colum~ (“sieve, strainer”). The Romance descendants of ~colare~ keep the watery sense throughout: Italian ~colare~, Spanish ~colar~, Portuguese ~coar~. The original picture is liquid passing through a filter — and from straining, the French verb shifted to the broader idea of flowing freely.

~Découler~ is literally water trickling down a slope, drop running after drop. From that physical image French built an abstract one: a conclusion ~follows from~ a premise the way a stream descends from its source — naturally, by gravity, without a break in the chain. The flowing sense is also why ~couler~ can mean a boat sinking (going under the water) and time passing. Relatives include ~écouler~ (“to flow out; to sell off”), ~couloir~ (“corridor,” a channel things run along), ~coulis~ and ~coulée~, and ~colander~ in English, borrowed from the same Latin ~colum~.
en.découper:
Formed from ~couper~ (“to cut”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (here marking division into pieces). ~Couper~ derives from the noun ~coup~ (“a blow”): to cut was “to separate with a blow.” ~Coup~ runs back through Old French ~colp~ and Late Latin *~colpus~ to Latin ~colaphus~ (“a blow with the fist, a box on the ear”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κόλαφος~ (~kólaphos~, “a cuff, a slap”).

The striking image survives the etymology: the oldest cutting was done by chopping, a blow that parts the thing struck. ~Découper~ specializes this into “to cut up” — to carve a roast, to chop vegetables, to cut shapes out of paper. The ~coup~ family is one of the most productive in French: ~coup~, ~couper~, ~coupure~, ~coupon~, ~découpage~, ~entrecouper~, and ~recouper~. The English ~coup~, ~coupon~, and ~coupé~ are all later borrowings from this same French stock.
en.décourager: From Old French ~descouragier~, built from the prefix ~des-~ (the ancestor of ~dé-~) and ~corage~, the ancestor of modern ~courage~. In Old French ~corage~ meant the heart, in the sense of spirit and feeling, from Latin ~cor~ (“heart”). To ~décourager~ is therefore, quite literally, to take the heart out of someone. The prefix ~dé-~ marks that removal. Middle French ~descourager~ was also borrowed by English as ~discourage~. The opposite verb, ~encourager~, puts the heart back in.
en.découvrir:
French ~découvrir~ is a transparent compound: the prefix ~dé-~ (“un-, reversal”) joined to ~couvrir~ (“to cover”), descending through Old French ~descovrir~ from Late Latin ~discooperīre~. The base ~couvrir~ comes from Latin ~cooperīre~ (“to cover over”), an intensive ~co(m)-~ plus ~operīre~ (“to close, to cover”), which rests on a Proto-Indo-European compound of *~op-~ (“over”) and the root *~wer-~ (“to cover, to enclose”). Curiously, the very same *~wer-~ root, with a different prefix, gives Latin ~aperīre~ (“to open, to uncover”) — so covering and uncovering are etymological twins.

The word's literal sense is simply “to uncover”: to remove the ~couverture~ from something. From taking the lid off came the figurative leap to “to find out, to reveal, to discover” — to uncover a truth, a land, a secret. English ~discover~ took exactly the same path from the same Late Latin source. The family is broad in French: ~couvrir~, ~couverture~ (“cover, blanket”), ~couvert~ (a place setting, what is “covered”), ~recouvrir~, and the nouns of finding, ~découverte~ (“a discovery”) and ~découvreur~. The age of exploration is, etymologically, an age of lifting lids — every ~découverte~ a veil pulled back.
en.décrire:
From Latin ~describere~ (“to copy off, to sketch, to describe”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ (“down, off”) and ~scribere~ (“to write”). French refashioned the verb on the model of ~écrire~, giving ~décrire~. ~scribere~ originally meant “to scratch or carve marks,” from the Proto-Indo-European root *~skribʰ-~, an extended form of *~sker-~ (“to cut”). Through this root ~décrire~ is cognate with English ~scribe~ and ~script~, and — by an early Latin loan into Germanic — with English ~shrive~ and German ~schreiben~ (“to write”).

The buried image is one of cutting: the earliest writing was incised into wood, clay, or stone, and ~scribere~ named that scratching. In ~describere~ the prefix ~de-~ adds the idea of tracing something off or sketching it out, point by point — which is just what a description does, drawing a verbal outline of its subject. The same root left French a dense cluster of ~-crire~ verbs, each with its prefix: ~écrire~ (“to write”), ~inscrire~ (“to inscribe”), ~prescrire~ (“to prescribe”), ~souscrire~ (“to subscribe”), and ~transcrire~ (“to transcribe”), alongside the nouns ~description~, ~écriture~, and ~scribe~ itself.
en.décrocher:
From the prefix ~dé-~ (“un-, away”) and the now-archaic verb ~crocher~ (“to hook”), derived from the noun ~croc~ (“hook”). ~Croc~ came through Old French from Frankish *~krōk~ (“hook”) — or, by an alternative account the sources allow, from Old Norse ~krókr~ (“hook, bend”) — both leading back to Proto-Germanic *~krōkaz~. The word is therefore a Germanic import into a Romance language, and it is cognate with English ~crook~ and ~crooked~, which carry the same notion of something bent.

Literally ~décrocher~ means to lift a thing off its hook: a coat, a painting, a telephone receiver — French still says ~décrocher~ for picking up a ringing phone. From there the senses fan out figuratively: to ~land~ a prize or a job (to unhook it from where it hung, just out of reach), and, in aviation, for a wing to ~stall~ — to lose its grip on the air. Relatives include ~accrocher~ (“to hang up, to snag”), ~raccrocher~ (“to hang up the phone”), ~décrochage~ (“stalling; dropping out”), ~décrochement~, and the ~crochet~ (“little hook”) used for needlework.
en.décroître:
The origin is debated. French Wiktionary derives ~décroître~ from Latin ~decrēscere~ (“to grow less”), while English Wiktionary says it comes either from ~dé-~ + ~croître~ or from Old French ~descreistre~, and that it perhaps corresponds to the Latin verb but is more likely an internal French formation. Either way the Latin model is ~dē-~ (“down, away”) + ~crēscere~ (“to grow”), an inchoative verb from the root of ~creāre~, itself from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱerh₃-~ (“to grow”). Italian ~decrescere~ and Spanish ~decrecer~ are the Latin verb inherited, and English ~decrease~ came from the Old French form.

The meaning is the mirror of ~croître~: where a thing grew, it now shrinks, as with daylight after midsummer or a river after a flood. The noun ~décrue~ names exactly that fall of floodwater. In recent decades ~décroissance~ has also become the name of an economic movement that argues for “degrowth.” The family of the root is rich: ~croissant~ (the pastry takes its name from the crescent moon, literally “the growing one”), ~accroître~, ~croissance~, and ~créer~.
en.décréter: Formed from the noun ~décret~ and the ending ~-er~. ~Décret~ comes from Old French ~decré~ and ~decret~, borrowed from Latin ~dēcrētum~ (“decision, ordinance”), the past participle of ~dēcernere~ (“to decide”). That Latin verb joined ~dē-~ and ~cernere~ (“to sift, to separate, to judge”), the same ~cernere~ behind ~discerner~ and ~certain~. To ~décréter~ is therefore to issue a decree, and by extension to declare something with the weight of an order.
en.décéder:
From Latin ~dēcēdere~ (“to go away, to withdraw, to depart”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“away, from”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, to yield, to withdraw”). ~Cēdere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~kezdō~ and, by one reconstruction, to a Proto-Indo-European *~ḱesd-~ (“to go away, to drive off”); the deeper history is disputed. Through ~cēdere~ it is cognate with Italian ~cedere~, Spanish ~ceder~, and English ~cede~, ~concede~, and ~cease~.

The Latin ~dēcēdere~ was at first wholly neutral — “to withdraw, to step aside, to depart” — and only by gentle euphemism came to mean “to depart this life,” to die. French kept exactly this softened sense: ~décéder~ is the formal, administrative, and respectful word for dying, the verb of death certificates and obituaries, where the blunt ~mourir~ would jar. Its companion noun is ~décès~, from Latin ~dēcessus~ (“a departure”), and one who has died is ~décédé~. From the same ~cēdere~ French gathered a large family of measured movements: ~céder~, ~accéder~, ~procéder~, ~succéder~, ~précéder~, ~excéder~, and the nouns ~accès~, ~succès~, and ~procès~ — each a kind of going, yielding, or coming-to.
en.dédicacer: ~Dédicacer~ is derived from the noun ~dédicace~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Dédicace~ comes from Latin ~dēdicātiō~ (“consecration, inauguration”). The verb appears once in the 15th century in its religious sense, to consecrate a place, and only becomes common in the 19th century with its present meaning: to inscribe a book or a photograph to someone, hence to autograph it.
en.dédier:
Borrowed from Latin ~dedicare~ (“to proclaim, to consecrate, to dedicate”), a compound of ~de-~ (“completely, solemnly”) and ~dicare~ (“to proclaim, to set apart”), a durative variant of ~dicere~ (“to say,” the ancestor of French ~dire~). The chain reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to point out, to show”). It is cognate with English ~dedicate~, with Greek ~deíknumi~ (“to show”), and with Latin ~digitus~ (“finger,” the pointing thing) and ~index~.

The earliest sense was religious: to ~dedicate~ a temple was to point it out solemnly to a god, to declare it his. From that consecration the verb softened into the familiar “to dedicate a book to someone,” the modern offering of a work in another's honor. French keeps both the learned and the popular line: ~dédier~ for the solemn dedication, the noun ~dédicace~, and the back-formed ~dédicacer~ (“to autograph,” to sign a copy). Through the same root *~deyḱ-~ run a surprising company of words — ~dire~ and ~diction~, ~index~ and ~indiquer~ — all turning, at bottom, on the simple act of pointing and saying so.
en.déduire:
From Latin ~deducere~ (“to lead down, to draw away, to derive”), the prefix ~de-~ (“down, away from”) joined to ~ducere~ (“to lead, to draw”). ~Ducere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~doukō~ and PIE *~dewk-~ (“to draw, to pull”). The same root, through Proto-Germanic, gives English ~tow~ (“to pull”) and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”) and ~Herzog~ (“duke,” literally an “army-leader”).

The two English glosses sit side by side in the Latin: ~deducere~ meant both to lead something physically away (whence “to deduct,” to take an amount off) and to draw a conclusion out of premises (whence “to deduce,” to derive logically). French keeps the whole leading family from ~ducere~: ~conduire~ (“to drive, to lead”), ~produire~ (“to bring forth”), ~réduire~ (“to lead back, to reduce”), ~traduire~ (“to lead across,” hence to translate), and the learned ~duc~ (“duke”) and ~conduit~. To deduce, in this old image, is to lead a thought downward and outward to its necessary end.
en.défaire:
Formed from ~faire~ (“to do, to make”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (from Latin ~dis-~, denoting reversal or separation), so literally “to un-make.” The base ~faire~ descends from Latin ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, to put, to make”) — the same vast root behind English ~do~ and ~deed~ and German ~tun~. ~Dé-~ + ~faire~ thus negates the act: it returns a thing to the state it was in before the making.

From that single idea the senses fan out: to empty a container, to unfasten clothing, to untie a knot, to cancel an arrangement, to dissolve a bond. The military sense “to defeat, to rout” is the same gesture writ large — to undo an enemy's array, to break their order. English ~defeat~ travelled the very same path, from Old French ~desfait~. The proverb ~faire et défaire, c'est toujours travailler~ (“to make and unmake is still to work”) catches the verb's spirit. Kindred forms include ~défait~ (“undone; defeated”), ~défaite~ (“defeat”), and the reflexive ~se défaire de~ (“to get rid of”).
en.défavoriser: Formed from ~favoriser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, ~défavoriser~ means “to put at a disadvantage, to treat less favorably,” the reversal of ~favoriser~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here marks the opposite of the base verb. The base ~favoriser~ comes from ~faveur~, from Latin ~favor~, a noun built on the verb ~favēre~ (“to be favorable to”). Latin ~favēre~ began as a religious word, used in the formula ~favēre linguīs~, a call to hold one's tongue during a rite. The disadvantaged, in a sense, are those from whom favor has been withheld.
en.défendre:
From Latin ~defendere~ (“to ward off, to repel, to defend”), attested in French around 1100.
