The verb is ~de-~ (“away”) plus *~fendere~ (“to strike, to thrust”), a root preserved only in compounds and traced to Proto-Indo-European *~gʷʰen-~ (“to strike, to kill”). Its twin compound is ~offendere~ (“to strike against, to offend”), and the pair survive together in English ~defend~ and ~offend~. The same PIE root lies, far back, behind a wide scatter of striking-words across the family.

The original idea was martial: to ~defendere~ was to strike a blow away from someone, to fend off an attacker — English keeps the bare core in ~fend~ and ~fender~. From “to keep harm away” the French verb branched in two directions. One is the familiar “to protect, to defend.” The other, surprising to learners, is “to forbid”: ~défendre~ à quelqu'un de faire quelque chose means to bar them from it — to ward off an action rather than a foe. So the same verb both shields and prohibits. Related French words include ~défense~ (which means both “defence” and “prohibition,” and also an elephant's tusk) and ~offenser~.
en.défier:
~Défier~ is explained as ~dé-~ + ~fier~ (“to trust, to entrust”), with the influence of Latin ~diffīdere~ (“to distrust”), itself made of ~dis-~ and ~fīdere~ (“to trust”). The French base ~fier~ continues Vulgar Latin *~fīdāre~, a verb drawn from ~fidus~ (“faithful”) and related to ~fidēs~ (“trust, faith”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeydʰ-~ (“to trust, to persuade”). English ~defy~ borrowed the French verb, while English ~faith~ comes from Latin ~fidēs~ by way of Old French. So the verb contains the idea of trust twice over, once in its base and once in the Latin verb that colored it.

The sense “to challenge” is the surprising part. In medieval usage the verb first meant to withdraw one's pledged faith, as when a vassal formally broke his bond with his lord or an enemy declared war. A formal challenge to combat followed, and from there came the modern senses “to challenge, to dare, to defy”. The reflexive ~se défier de~ keeps the older meaning of mistrust, so the verb holds two opposite attitudes, boldness toward someone and distrust of them, both springing from a trust that has been broken. Its relatives include ~confier~, ~méfier~, ~défiance~, ~confiance~, ~fidèle~ and ~foi~.
en.défiler:
~défiler~ is built from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~filer~ (“to spin thread, to run in a line”), with the related noun ~file~ (“a rank, a single line of people”); both ~filer~ and ~file~ rest on Latin ~filum~ (“thread”). The word thus straddles two images. On one reading ~dé-~ + ~filer~ means literally “to unthread,” to pull the thread out of something — the sense alive in ~se défiler~ (“to slip away, to wriggle out”), as a thread slides free of the needle.

On the other reading, the one behind “to parade,” the unit is ~file~: to ~défiler~ is to move past in a single column, the way troops march one rank behind another, each soldier a bead on a thread. From this come the military ~défilé~ (a narrow pass through which a column must thread itself in file) and the civilian ~défilé~ — a procession, and by extension a fashion show, where models walk the runway in succession. The shared Latin ~filum~ unites a wide French family: ~fil~, ~file~, ~filer~, ~filet~, ~enfiler~ (“to thread, to string together”), and ~profil~ — all turning on the single idea of a thread, literal or marched.
en.définir:
From Old French ~diffinir~, ~definir~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~dēfīnīre~ (“to bound, to limit, to determine precisely”), built from the prefix ~dē-~ and the verb ~fīnīre~ (“to finish, to set bounds”), itself from ~fīnis~ (“a boundary, a limit, an end”). The Old French scribes favored the spelling ~diffinir~, with ~dis-~ becoming ~dif-~ before the ~f~, partly to keep the word distinct from the classical sense of ~dēfīnīre~. Through ~fīnis~ the verb is kin to Italian ~definire~, Spanish ~definir~, and English ~define~ and ~finish~. The deeper origin of ~fīnis~ is uncertain, though it is often tentatively linked to ~fīgere~ (“to fix, to fasten”), as if a limit were a stake driven into the ground.

The Latin ~dēfīnīre~ meant literally “to mark off within boundaries,” and that spatial image still lives inside the abstract modern sense: to ~définir~ a word is to fence in its meaning, to say where it ends and where it does not. The verb entered French in the 13th century as a scholarly term and kept its precise, intellectual flavor. From the same ~fīnis~ family French inherited a wide harvest of words, among them ~fin~, ~finir~, ~final~, ~définition~, ~définitif~, ~indéfini~, and ~confiner~ — all turning, in one way or another, on the idea of a border or an end.
en.déformer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēformāre~ (“to disfigure, to misshape”), built from ~dē-~ (“away, down”) and ~formāre~ (“to shape”), which comes from ~forma~ (“shape”). Because French already had ~former~, the verb can also be read on the surface as ~dé-~ + ~former~, a literal “un-shaping.” That reading suits the meaning well: to ~déformer~ something is to pull it out of its proper shape, whether a piece of metal, a face, or, figuratively, a fact or a quotation. The same Latin noun gives ~forme~, ~formation~ and ~difforme~.
en.déférer:
French ~déférer~ comes from Latin ~dēferre~, a compound of ~dē-~ (“down, away”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). The simple verb ~ferre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (“to carry”), the same root behind English ~bear~, German ~gebären~ and Greek ~phérein~. French borrowed ~dēferre~ as a learned verb rather than inheriting it through speech. English has taken the same Latin verb as ~defer~ in the sense of yielding to someone's wishes.

The Latin verb meant literally to carry down or carry away, and from there to bring something before someone: to report a matter, to hand over an honor, to lay a case before an authority. French kept two main uses. The legal one is to refer a person or a case to a court, as in ~déférer un accusé à la justice~. The courteous one is to yield to another's opinion or authority, ~déférer à l'avis de quelqu'un~, which gave the noun ~déférence~ (“deference, respect”) and the adjective ~déférent~. The root ~ferre~ is among the most productive in French vocabulary. It also gave ~référer~, ~conférer~, ~transférer~, ~préférer~, ~différer~ and ~offrir~, all rooted in the idea of carrying.
en.dégager:
Modern French ~dégager~ is built from the verb ~gager~ (“to pledge, to pawn”) with the privative prefix ~dé-~, which reverses an action. Its earliest attested form, ~desguagier~ (1174–76), meant quite literally “to redeem something pledged” — to recover from a pawnbroker the ~gage~ one had deposited as security. That noun ~gage~ was no Latin inheritance but a Frankish loan, *~waddi~ “pledge, deposit,” from Proto-Germanic *~wadi~ and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~wedʰ-~ “to pledge, to redeem a pledge.” The same Germanic root surfaces in Dutch ~wedde~ “salary” and German ~Wette~ “a bet,” and, by a parallel borrowing into English through Norman French, in ~wage~. English ~wed~ descends from the same source: to marry was once to pledge oneself, the bridal vow being literally a pledge.

From the concrete medieval sense of buying back a pledge, ~dégager~ drifted toward abstraction. By around 1180 it could mean “to set free, to release,” and by the mid-thirteenth century “to clear away, to strip of a covering.” A pledge, once recovered, leaves one unencumbered — hence the modern senses of freeing, clearing, and emitting (a gas, a scent). The same Frankish family enriched French with ~gageure~ “a wager” and ~engager~ “to commit, to involve,” while ~dégagement~ names the very act of disengaging — the precise reversal of putting something in pledge.
en.dégrader:
From Late Latin ~degradāre~ (“to demote, strip of rank”), attested in French from 1174, built from ~de-~ (“down from”) + ~gradus~ (“step, rank, degree”). ~Gradus~ comes from ~gradī~ / ~gradior~ (“to step, walk”), from Proto-Italic *~graðus~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to walk, stride”). The root is cognate with English ~grade~, ~gradual~, and ~degree~ (itself ~de-~ + ~gradus~ via French ~degré~).

The literal sense is to make someone “step down” a rank — a ceremonial demotion, as a knight or officer was formally stripped of insignia. From this social ~dégrader~ the verb extended along a second axis to physical deterioration: a façade, a colour, an environment can ~se dégrader~, sliding step by step down toward ruin. Both senses share the picture of descending a graded scale. The same ~gradus~ root gives French ~grade~, ~degré~, ~graduel~, ~gradation~, ~progrès~ (“a stepping forward”), ~régresser~, and ~dégradé~ — the last a painter's and hairdresser's term for a smooth gradient, the very deterioration of one tone into the next made beautiful.
en.déguiser: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~guise~ (“manner, way”) and the verb ending ~-er~, via Old French ~desguiser~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and here it points toward changing one's usual manner. ~Guise~ comes from Old French ~guise~ and Frankish *~wīsa~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsǭ~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~ (“to see”). English ~wise~ (as in ~likewise~) and German ~Weise~ are cognates. Hence ~déguiser~ originally means “to alter one's way of appearing,” and later “to disguise.”
en.déguster:
French ~déguster~ comes from Latin ~degustare~ (“to taste, to sample”), formed from the prefix ~de-~ and ~gustare~ (“to taste”), itself from ~gustus~ (“a tasting, a taste”). That noun descends from Proto-Italic *~gustus~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ǵéwstus~ (“taste”), from the root *~ǵews-~ (“to taste, to choose”). The same root produced English ~choose~ and ~gusto~, German ~kiesen~ (“to choose”), and, through Latin, Spanish ~gustar~ and Italian ~gustare~. The everyday French noun ~goût~ (“taste”) is the worn-down heir of ~gustus~.

The Indo-European root joined tasting and choosing, as if to taste were already to judge — the same instinct preserved in English ~gusto~, “hearty enjoyment.” French ~déguster~ kept the careful, appreciative side of that idea: not merely to eat but to savor attentively, to assess a wine or a dish. From the family come ~goût~, ~goûter~, ~dégustation~, ~ragoût~ (“stew,” literally something that restores the appetite), and ~dégoût~ (“disgust”), where the prefix flips savor into its opposite. A ~dégustateur~ is a professional taster whose whole craft is built on this Latin verb.
en.dégénérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēgenerāre~ (“to depart from one's kind, to fall below one's ancestors”), formed from ~dē-~ (“away from”) and ~genus~ (“birth, race, kind”). Latin ~genus~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget”), the same root that gave English ~kin~. English ~degenerate~ is borrowed from the Latin verb, and the Latin noun ~genus~ is the source of French ~genre~ and of the English word ~genus~ in biology.

The Latin idea was literally one of lineage: a person or animal who ~degenerates~ no longer matches the quality of the ancestors. French kept this moral and biological sense, as when a breed or a family ~dégénère~, and then extended it to decline in general. In medicine, a tissue or a disease ~dégénère~ when it worsens, and the adjective ~dégénératif~ describes such conditions. In everyday speech, a situation or a discussion ~dégénère~ when it turns bad, often with ~en~, as in ~dégénérer en bagarre~ (“to degenerate into a brawl”). The same Latin root appears in ~génération~ and ~général~, a reminder that “kind” and “begetting” share a source.
en.déjanter: Formed from ~dé-~, the noun ~jante~ (“wheel rim”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The original transitive sense was technical: to remove the rims, the wooden circles forming the edge of a wheel. That sense fell out of use, and the verb was formed afresh in 1945 in cycling for a tyre that comes off its rim. The informal sense “to go crazy” is a figurative extension of “to come off the rim.” The noun ~jante~ is inherited from Old French, from a Vulgar Latin *~gambita~ or *~cambita~, borrowed from Gaulish *~cambitā~, a derivative of Proto-Celtic *~kambos~ (“curved”).
en.déjouer: Formed in French from ~dé-~ and ~jouer~ (“to play”). The prefix marks reversal or negation: to ~déjouer~ a plan is to counter what another has played, whence “to foil, to thwart.” The base ~jouer~ comes from Old French ~joer~, from Latin ~iocāre~ (“to joke”), from ~iocus~ (“joke, game”), which also gave English ~joke~. Latin ~iocāre~ broadened from jesting to all play and displaced the classical verb ~lūdere~ as the everyday word for playing.
en.délaisser: Formed in French from ~laisser~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base descends from Latin ~laxāre~ (“to loosen, to let go”), built on ~laxus~ (“slack”), the root that also gave English ~lax~ and ~slack~; Old French ~laissier~ already meant “to leave, to allow, to abandon.” Here ~dé-~ does not simply undo ~laisser~. It adds the idea of leaving away from oneself, so that ~délaisser~ means “to forsake, to abandon, to neglect,” a heavier act than merely leaving something behind.
en.délibérer:
Borrowed from Latin ~dēlīberāre~ (“to weigh, to ponder”), which is generally analyzed as ~dē-~ plus ~lībrāre~ (“to weigh”), from ~lībra~ (“scale, balance”). Deliberating was thus, in the image, weighing a question on a pair of scales. Italian ~deliberare~, Spanish ~deliberar~ and English ~deliberate~ are cognates, all learned descendants of the same Latin verb. The Latin noun ~lībra~ also gave French ~livre~ (the unit of weight, not the book) and, with ~aequus~ (“equal”), ~équilibre~. The Latin source also gave the English zodiac sign ~Libra~.

The French verb kept the idea of careful weighing, first in the mind of one person, then in councils, juries and assemblies, where ~délibérer~ means to discuss before deciding. In law, the court ~délibère~ out of the public eye before giving its judgment, and a case held back for decision is said to be ~en délibéré~. Related words are ~délibération~, ~délibéré~ (“deliberate, considered”) and ~délibérément~. One trap deserves a warning: ~délibérer~ is unrelated to ~libérer~ (“to free”), which comes from Latin ~līberāre~ and ~līber~ (“free”), so the two share spelling but not ancestry.
en.délimiter:
French took ~délimiter~ from Latin ~dēlīmitāre~ (“to mark out the boundaries of”). The Latin verb joined the prefix ~dē-~ (“completely, off”) to ~līmitāre~ (“to bound, to set limits to”), itself a verb built on the noun ~līmes~, genitive ~līmitis~ (“boundary, path between fields, frontier”). Modern French can still analyze it as ~dé-~ + ~limiter~, but the verb arrived already formed from Latin. Italian ~delimitare~ and Spanish ~delimitar~ have the same shape, and English ~delimit~ came the same learned route.

In Roman usage ~līmes~ was first the strip of ground left between two fields, then the boundary line of a property, and finally the fortified frontier of the empire. ~Délimiter~ keeps that concrete picture: to trace the border of a territory, a field or a zone. French then stretched it to abstract borders, such as delimiting a subject, a role or a responsibility. The family is large: ~limite~ (borrowed from ~līmes~), ~limiter~, ~illimité~ and ~limitrophe~ (“bordering”) all belong to it.
en.délivrer:
Attested from the 11th century, from Late Latin ~dēlīberāre~ (“to set free”), built on ~līberāre~ (“to set at liberty”), itself from the adjective ~līber~ (“free”). ~Līber~ descends from Proto-Italic *~louðeros~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lewdʰeros~ (“free,” originally “belonging to the people”), making it a distant cognate of Greek ~eleútheros~ (“free”) and German ~Leute~ (“people”).

Note that this Late Latin ~dēlīberāre~ (“to free”) is a different word from Classical Latin ~dēlīberāre~ (“to weigh, deliberate”), which gave French ~délibérer~ — the two are etymological twins that diverged. ~Délivrer~ kept the sense of releasing: freeing a captive, relieving someone of a burden, and, in the obstetric sense, delivering a mother of her child. The “handing over” sense of English ~deliver~ developed in the parallel Old French chain and survives in French ~livrer~ (“to hand over, deliver goods”) and the noun ~livraison~. From the root ~līber~ French draws ~liberté~, ~libérer~, ~libéral~, and ~délivrance~ — the whole vocabulary of freedom radiating from a single Latin adjective meaning simply “free.”
en.délocaliser: Built on ~localiser~ (“to fix in a place”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the idea. French Wiktionary instead parses it as ~dé-~ + ~local~ + ~-iser~, the same pieces in a different order. The adjective ~local~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~locālis~, from Latin ~locus~ (“place”), and ~-iser~ is the suffix that makes verbs meaning “to render” or “to turn into”. So ~délocaliser~ means literally to take something out of its place. In modern French it usually describes a company moving production or services abroad to cut costs, and more loosely detaching anything from its original location.
en.déléguer:
~Déléguer~ comes from Latin ~delegare~ (« to send away on a commission, to assign, to entrust »), made of ~de-~ and the first-conjugation verb ~legare~ (« to depute, to commission, to bequeath »). This ~legare~ is a denominal from ~lex~, ~legis~ (« law, formal motion »): to ~legare~ was to bind someone or something by a formal legal act. It must be kept apart from the third-conjugation ~legere~ (« to gather, to read »), a different verb despite the shared spelling. Italian ~delegare~, Spanish ~delegar~, and English ~delegate~ all descend from the same Latin source.

The legal core still shows: to ~déléguer~ is to hand over authority or a task by formal commission — a power, a vote, a representative sent in one's stead. From ~legare~ French also keeps ~léguer~ (« to bequeath ») and ~legs~ (« a legacy »), and from the noun ~lex~ a broad family of law-words: ~légal~, ~législation~, ~loyal~, and the ~délégué~ who carries another's mandate. English ~legacy~, ~legate~, and ~delegate~ belong to the same lineage.
en.démanteler: ~Démanteler~ is built on ~mantel~, the Old French form (10th century) of ~manteau~ (“cloak”), with the prefix ~dé-~, which here means removal. It appeared in the 16th century in the sense of tearing down a fortress's walls, as if stripping the cloak from it. The French source gives a second account: the verb may have been formed from ~emmanteler~ by swapping ~em-~ for ~dé-~. By the 19th century it had broadened to mean pulling down or breaking up in general.
en.démarcher: The sources analyze it differently. French Wiktionary derives it from ~marcher~ with the prefix ~dé-~, while English Wiktionary derives it from the noun ~démarche~ (“step taken, approach”) plus ~-er~; since ~démarche~ itself comes from the same verb, both lead back to ~marcher~. The sense is “to canvass,” meaning to go from door to door or client to client. As for ~marcher~, it comes from Old French ~marchier~ (“to trample”), probably from Frankish *~markôn~ (“to mark, to press with the foot”), though a rival theory from Latin ~marcus~ (“hammer”) has never been ruled out.
en.démarquer: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~marquer~ (“to mark”), so it means “to remove a mark.” The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ and reverses the action of its base. ~Marquer~ goes back to a Germanic noun *~marka~ (“boundary, sign set at a limit”) of Frankish origin, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~merǵ-~ (“boundary, edge”); English ~mark~ and German ~Mark~ are cognates. A label or a brand is a mark, and ~démarquer~ takes it away, which is why the verb is used for taking a mark off merchandise or for copying a work while hiding its source.
en.démarrer:
From a syncope of older French ~désamarrer~ (“to cast off moorings”), formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (reversal) and ~amarrer~ (“to moor, to make fast”), a nautical term borrowed from Dutch ~aanmarren~ (“to tie, to fasten”). ~démarrer~ thus began life on the water, with ~amarre~ (“a mooring rope”) and ~amarrer~ as its close relatives in French.

The original picture is purely maritime: to ~démarrer~ was to untie a ship from the quay so it could leave port. Once the lines were loosed, the vessel got under way — and it is that moment of getting under way, of breaking from rest into motion, that the verb kept as its core when it drifted ashore. By extension ~démarrer~ came to mean starting a car or an engine, launching a business, or kicking off any undertaking, and in cycling slang a rider who ~démarre~ suddenly accelerates away from the pack. The same idea of casting off survives in the everyday opposite ~amarrer~ and in the noun ~démarrage~ (“startup, getaway”). It is a quietly vivid metaphor: every time a French driver starts the engine, the language remembers a sailor slipping the ropes and pulling away from the dock.
en.dématérialiser: ~Dématérialiser~ is best read as the prefix ~dé-~, here meaning removal, added to ~matérialiser~, itself formed from ~matériel~ plus ~-iser~. French Wiktionary parses it in one go from ~matériel~ with both affixes, which comes to the same thing. ~Matériel~ comes from Late Latin ~māteriālis~, from ~māteria~ (“wood, substance”), which in turn derives from ~māter~ (“mother”). The verb means to strip something of its physical form, as with paperless documents.
en.démentir: Formed in French from ~mentir~ (“to lie”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here cancels what the base does: to ~démentir~ a claim is to give it the lie, to deny or disprove it, and by extension to be at odds with something, as when the facts contradict a rumor. The base ~mentir~ comes from Old French and from Vulgar Latin *~mentīre~, a regularized form of Latin ~mentīrī~ (“to lie”), built on ~mēns~ (“mind”), so that lying is, etymologically, an invention of the mind. The English cognate of that root is ~mind~.
en.démissionner: Formed in French from ~démission~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~démission~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dimissio~ (“release, dismissal”), taken in to serve as the abstract noun for the verb ~démettre~. The ending ~-er~ turns the noun into a verb meaning “to give one's démission,” that is, to resign from a post.
en.démocratiser:
Formed in French from ~démocratie~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~. The base word goes back to Greek ~dēmokratía~, a compound of ~dêmos~ (“the people”) and ~krátos~ (“power, rule”), so “rule by the people.” The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Greek ~-ízein~ through Late Latin ~-izare~, and it is the standard French tool for turning a noun or adjective into “to make X” or “to behave like X.” English has the exact parallel ~democratize~, built the same way.

The verb first appeared in Middle French with the intransitive sense “to live under a democracy.” The modern political sense, “to make something democratic” or “to open it to everyone,” developed later, and it now applies to anything from institutions to luxury goods or technology. Because the base is Greek, the family is rich in learned words: ~démocrate~, ~démocratique~, ~démocratie~, and, from the same ~-cratie~ element, ~aristocratie~ and ~autocratie~, plus ~démagogue~ and ~démographie~ from the ~dêmos~ element.
en.démolir:
Borrowed from Latin ~dēmōlīrī~ (“to demolish, to pull down”), a deponent verb made of ~dē-~ (“down, undo”) and ~mōlīrī~ (“to set in motion, to build, to heave”). Latin ~mōlīrī~ comes from the noun ~mōlēs~ (“a massive structure, a heavy mass”). The Latin infinitive in ~-īrī~ was reshaped in French as a regular ~-ir~ verb of the second group, hence ~nous démolissons~. English ~demolish~ was borrowed from the French verb.

The prefix ~dē-~ makes the meaning an exact reversal: since ~mōlīrī~ could mean to erect a great structure, ~démolir~ is to un-build it. French kept the literal sense of tearing down a building, and then extended it to wrecking a theory, a reputation or an opponent, and in familiar speech to hurting someone badly. The root ~mōlēs~ left several other French words: ~môle~ (“a breakwater, a jetty”), and ~molécule~, coined in modern Latin as a diminutive of ~mōlēs~, a “little mass.”
en.démonter: From the prefix ~dé-~ + ~monter~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and reverses the action of the base. The verb ~monter~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~montāre~ (“to go up”), built on Latin ~mons~ (“mountain”). Since ~monter~ also means “to assemble” (one ~monte~ a machine, a tent or a shelf), ~démonter~ undoes that assembly: it means to take apart or dismantle. It also keeps the older sense of ~monter~ as “to ride,” which gives the sense of unseating a rider, and, figuratively, of throwing someone off balance, as in the common ~ne pas se démonter~, “to keep one's composure.”
en.démontrer:
From Latin ~dēmonstrāre~ (“to point out, show clearly, prove”), a compound of the prefix ~dē-~ (here intensive, “fully”) and ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show”). ~Mōnstrāre~ derives from ~mōnstrum~ (“a portent, a sign from the gods”), itself from ~monēre~ (“to warn, remind”), tracing back to the PIE root *~men-~ (“to think”). So at bottom “to demonstrate” means to make the mind take notice. Cognate with Italian ~dimostrare~ and Spanish ~demostrar~, and — borrowed — with English ~demonstrate~; the plainer French ~montrer~ shares the same ~mōnstrāre~ ancestor.

The Latin verb already split between simply showing and rigorously proving, and French kept ~démontrer~ on the side of proof: where ~montrer~ merely displays, ~démontrer~ establishes by argument. Mathematics adopted it wholesale, and the classroom flourish ~ce qu'il fallait démontrer~ (“which was to be proved”) still closes a proof, abbreviated ~CQFD~. The frightening cousin ~mōnstrum~ — a divine warning made flesh — gave French ~monstre~, so the family yokes the rational demonstration to the prodigy. From the same root *~men-~ come ~mention~, ~admonester~, and ~mémoire~ all keep the ancient sense of the mind remembering and being warned.
en.démunir: Derived from ~munir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to ~démunir~ someone is to take away what they were equipped with. The base ~munir~ comes from Latin ~mūnīre~ (“to fortify, to defend”), built on ~moenia~ (“city walls”). It first meant to fortify a place, and from the late sixteenth century it broadened to “to supply, to provide with what is needed.” The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and here marks removal, so the verb means “to deprive of means or resources.” It appears above all in the participle ~démuni~ (“destitute, at a loss”) and in the reflexive ~se démunir de~ (“to part with”).
en.dénaturer: Inherited from Old French ~desnaturer~, which can be analysed as ~dé-~ + ~nature~ + ~-er~. The noun ~nature~ comes from Latin ~nātūra~ (“birth, natural character, the course of things”), itself from ~nascor~ (“to be born”). The prefix ~dé-~ (from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”) expresses removal, so ~dénaturer~ is to strip something of its natural character. From there the verb took two paths: the physical one, to alter a substance so that it can no longer be used as it was (denatured alcohol), and the figurative one, to distort or misrepresent a fact, a text or someone's words.
en.dénombrer:
From Latin ~dīnumerāre~ (“to count, to enumerate”), built from ~dī-~, a form of ~dis-~ (“apart”), and ~numerāre~ (“to count”), which comes from ~numerus~ (“number”). The simple verb ~nombrer~ comes from the same ~numerāre~. In the noun, the Latin ~numerum~ was reduced in Old French to ~nomre~, and a ~b~ appeared between the ~m~ and the ~r~ to ease the pronunciation, which gave ~nombre~. English ~number~ was borrowed from the French form.

The noun ~dénombrement~ was used for a census, a head count of a population or an army. The Latin family has other branches in French: ~numéro~ and ~numéral~ are learned borrowings, ~énumérer~ is another verb built on ~numerāre~, and ~innombrable~ (“countless”) is the adjective that denies it. The English ~enumerate~ and ~numeral~ belong to this same family.
en.dénommer:
First attested around 1170 as ~denonmer~, borrowed from Latin ~dēnōmināre~ (“to name, to designate”), from ~dē-~ (here an intensifier) and ~nōmināre~ (“to name”), the verb of ~nōmen~ (“name”). ~nōmen~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~nōmn̥~ and to PIE *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”) — one of the most widely preserved roots in the family. Its cognates are everywhere: English ~name~ and ~noun~ (both doublets), Greek ~ónoma~, German ~Name~, Sanskrit ~nā́man~. The sense “to assign a name to” settled in by about 1250.

The ~dē-~ here does not subtract, as it does in ~défaire~; it reinforces, giving ~dénommer~ the flavor of naming explicitly or designating by name. That precise nuance survives in administrative and grammatical French — a ~dénomination~ is an official designation, and the ~dénominateur~ of a fraction is, literally, the number that “names” the parts. From the same ~nōmen~ descend French ~nom~, ~nommer~, ~renommée~ (“fame,” the “re-naming” people give you), ~pronom~, and the learned ~nominal~ and ~nominer~. The PIE root threads through English ~nominate~, ~ignominy~, and ~misnomer~ — a sprawling clan all turning on the simple act of giving a thing its name.
en.dénoncer:
From Old French ~denoncier~ (also ~denuntier~), from Latin ~dēnūntiāre~ (“to announce, to proclaim, to give formal notice”), a compound of ~dē-~ (here intensive) and ~nūntiāre~ (“to report, to bring news”), itself from ~nūntius~ (“messenger, message”). The origin of ~nūntius~ is uncertain; De Vaan tentatively traces it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~newH-~ (“to shout, to cry out”), fitting the herald who proclaims aloud. The Latin verb is cognate with Italian ~denunziare~ and Spanish ~denunciar~, and shares its second element with English ~announce~ and ~pronounce~.

In Latin and Old French the verb was neutral: simply “to make something known officially,” especially a treaty, a declaration of war, or a legal notice. Over time the sense darkened. To “give formal notice” against a person slid toward “to accuse, to inform on,” and modern French ~dénoncer~ now carries a strongly negative charge — to betray a wrongdoer to the authorities, or to publicly condemn an injustice. The older neutral meaning lingers only in formal registers, as when a state ~dénonce~ a treaty (declares it void). From the same ~nūntius~ stem come French ~annoncer~, ~prononcer~, ~énoncer~, and the noun ~nonce~ (a papal envoy — a messenger still).
en.dénuer:
French ~dénuer~ is inherited from Latin ~dēnūdāre~ (“to strip bare”), which was built on ~nūdus~ (“naked”). It reached French through an altered Latin form ~disnūdāre~, which gave Old French ~desnuer~, whose ~s~ later vanished. Spanish ~desnudar~ is its direct cousin, and French also later borrowed the Latin verb a second time as the learned doublet ~dénuder~.

The verb began as a physical act, to strip someone or something bare. In modern French that concrete sense has largely passed to ~dénuder~, while ~dénuer~ survives mostly in the figurative sense of depriving, leaving someone without something. Its past participle is far commoner than the verb itself, in phrases like ~dénué de sens~ (“devoid of meaning”) or ~dénué de scrupules~ (“unscrupulous”). The underlying Latin adjective ~nūdus~ also gave French ~nu~ (“naked”) and, through learned borrowing, English ~nude~. Behind the abstract complaint that an argument is ~dénué de fondement~ lies, then, an image of something stripped to nothing.
en.départir:
From Middle French ~departir~, from Old French ~departir~, from Late Latin ~departīre~, built from Latin ~de-~ and ~partiō~ (“to divide, to share”), a verb based on ~pars~ (“part”). Both Wiktionaries also allow a simpler analysis as ~dé-~ plus ~partir~, so the two accounts coexist. English ~depart~ was borrowed from the same Old French verb. The Latin ~partiō~ also gave ~partir~ itself, whose modern sense “to leave” grew out of the older sense “to divide, to separate.”

The old meaning of ~départir~ was “to divide up, to distribute,” and from there “to separate, to leave.” Once ~partir~ had taken over the sense of leaving, ~départir~ was left with a narrow literary role. It survives mainly in the reflexive ~se départir de~ (“to give up, to depart from”), nearly always in the negative, as in ~ne pas se départir de son calme~ (“not to lose one's composure”), and in the formal sense “to allot,” as in a power or a task allotted to someone. The noun ~départ~ (“departure”) and the verb ~répartir~ (“to distribute”) belong to the same family as ~part~, ~partie~ and ~partition~.
en.dépasser:
A French compound of the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~passer~ (“to pass”), the ~dé-~ here marking the idea of going beyond or past a limit. ~Passer~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~passare~, a verb derived from the Latin noun ~passus~ (“a step, a pace”). That noun is itself the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread, to stretch out”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). Cognates of ~passer~ are everywhere in Romance — Spanish ~pasar~, Italian ~passare~ — and English borrowed both ~pass~ and ~pace~ from the same source.

The underlying image is the stride: a ~passus~ was the distance covered by a step, so ~passer~ first meant to move step by step from one place to another, to go past. ~Dépasser~ sharpens this into “to go beyond” — to overtake a car, to exceed a limit, to surpass a rival, or even, figuratively, for a problem to be beyond someone (cela me ~dépasse~). The prefix ~dé-~ adds the sense of moving clear past a mark. From the same ~passer~ French built ~passage~, ~passant~, ~passerelle~, ~surpasser~, ~trépasser~ (“to pass away, to die”), and ~repasser~ (“to pass again,” hence “to iron”).
en.dépeindre:
~Dépeindre~ is explained in two compatible ways. French Wiktionary treats it as borrowed from Latin ~dēpingere~ (“to paint, to depict, to describe”), reshaped on the model of ~peindre~, while English Wiktionary simply analyses it as ~dé-~ + ~peindre~. Either way, the Latin ancestor ~pingere~ (“to paint”) lies behind the base. It descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~peyḱ-~ (“to mark, to colour”). In Latin, ~dēpingere~ meant both to paint something and to describe it.

That double meaning is what French kept. Modern ~dépeindre~ usually means to describe vividly, as though painting with words (~dépeindre la situation~). The family of ~pingere~ gave French ~peinture~ and ~peintre~ (through Latin ~pictūra~ and ~pictor~), as well as ~pigment~. The verb is irregular like ~peindre~ (~il dépeint~). A rarer sense, “to strip off paint,” reads ~dé-~ as the French prefix of removal, which is how the English analysis ~dé-~ + ~peindre~ would naturally be taken.
en.dépendre:
From Latin ~dependere~ (“to hang down, to hang from”), formed from the prefix ~de-~ (“down, from”) and the verb ~pendere~ (“to hang”), from Proto-Italic *~pendēō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to pull, to draw”). Cognate forms include English ~pendant~, ~suspend~, and ~pendulum~, all sharing the image of something stretched and hanging.

French ~dépendre~ carries two senses that are really one. The concrete meaning — to ~dépendre~ a picture is to take it down off its hook — preserves the literal Latin “to hang from.” The abstract meaning grew by metaphor: that which hangs from something else relies on it, is suspended from it, and so to ~dépendre de~ someone is to “depend on” them, to hang from their support. The same root *~(s)pend-~ spread through a remarkable family, because in Latin ~pendere~ also meant “to weigh” and “to pay” — money was once weighed out. From it French inherited ~suspendre~, ~pendre~, ~pension~, ~dépense~, ~pendule~, and ~appendice~, while the “weighing” branch gave ~peser~ and, through Spanish, the ~peso~. The English ~pound~ and even ~spider~ (the “spinner,” a stretcher of thread) belong to the same ancient web.
en.dépenser:
Attested from the 12th century, derived from the noun ~dépense~ (“expenditure”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. ~dépense~ comes from Latin ~dispensa~, the substantivized neuter past participle of ~dispendere~ (“to weigh out in distributing, hence to pay out”), ~dis-~ + ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to pay”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to weigh”). The Latin noun ~dispendium~ already meant “cost, expense.”

The metaphor at the root is unmistakably mercantile: to spend was to weigh out portions of one's wealth, coin by coin, just as a steward weighed out rations. From money the verb spread to spending time, effort, or energy — one ~dépense~ one's strength as one ~dépense~ one's savings. Sharing the same ancestor ~pendere~ and the root *~(s)pend-~ are ~dispenser~, ~peser~ (“to weigh”), ~suspendre~, ~pension~, and ~pensée~ — a whole family in which weighing, paying, and pondering are one act.
en.déplacer:
A French formation, ~déplacer~ is built from the verb ~placer~ (“to place”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses or undoes an action — to ~déplacer~ is literally to un-place, to take a thing from where it was set. ~Placer~ derives from ~place~, from Old French ~place~, from Latin ~platea~ (“broad street, open square, courtyard”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~πλατεῖα~ (~plateîa~, “broad way”), the feminine of “broad,” from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleth₂-~ (“to spread out, to be flat”). Cognate with Italian ~piazza~, Spanish ~plaza~, and German ~Platz~.

The surprise is that the everyday French ~place~ began as a width: a ~platea~ was a wide thoroughfare, named for its flatness and breadth, and only later did the word narrow to a “spot” where a thing or person belongs. ~Placer~ assigns that spot; ~dé-~ revokes it. The same flat-and-broad root spread across French into ~place~, ~plat~, ~plateau~, ~plaine~, ~plan~, ~esplanade~, and ~remplacer~ (“to re-place, to replace”). Thus to ~déplacer~ furniture, a meeting, or oneself is, at root, to lift it off its flat appointed ground and set it elsewhere.
en.déplaire: Built on ~plaire~ with the prefix ~dé-~ as a reversal: what ~plaire~ does, ~déplaire~ undoes, “to displease.” The French verb follows Latin ~displicēre~ (“to displease”), which was ~dis-~ plus ~placēre~ (“to please”), and ~dé-~ is the French outcome of ~dis-~ by way of Old French ~des-~. The Latin ~placēre~ is also behind Italian ~piacere~, Spanish ~placer~ and English ~please~, so the verb is a clear mirror image of a very old and widespread one.
en.déplier: ~Déplier~ is ~dé-~ + ~plier~, the prefix reversing the action of the base: to unfold what had been folded. The base ~plier~ continues Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to weave”), the same root as Greek ~plékō~ (“I weave”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The verb ~déployer~, from the same Latin root, is a near relative, so a map unfolded and an army deployed share one ancestor.
en.déplorer:
French ~déplorer~ (attested in the 12th century) is borrowed from Latin ~deplorare~ (“to weep over, to lament aloud”), formed from the intensifying prefix ~de-~ and the verb ~plorare~ (“to wail, to cry out, to weep aloud”). ~Plorare~ originally denoted not silent tears but loud, voiced weeping — a cry. Its deeper origin is uncertain; one proposal links it to a PIE *~pleh₃(w)-~ (“to flow”), but the connection is tentative and is best left flagged as such rather than asserted. Latin built a whole family of prefixed ~plorare~ verbs: ~deplorare~, ~implorare~ (“to beg, to cry to”), and ~explorare~ — which began as “to cry out” (perhaps a hunter's shout) before drifting to “to search out, explore.”

The sense traveled from full-throated mourning to the cooler modern range of ~déplorer~: to lament a loss, but also simply to regret or disapprove of something — ~déplorer~ une décision is to deplore it, not to weep over it. The vivid origin survives in the related ~éploré~ (“in tears, tearful”), still close to the literal wailing. From the same ~plorare~ stem French keeps ~implorer~ (“to implore, to beg”) and ~explorer~ (“to explore”), whose tie to weeping is now wholly invisible — a hunter's cry frozen, etymologically, inside every act of exploration.
en.déployer:
From Old French ~desploier~ (“to unfold”), formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (“un-, reversal”) and ~ployer~ (“to bend, to fold”). ~ployer~ — a doublet of modern ~plier~ — descends from Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold, to roll up”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~plek-~ (“to plait, to fold”). The same root gives English ~ply~, ~pleat~, and ~fold~, Greek ~plekein~ (“to plait”), and a whole French cluster including ~plier~, ~pli~, and ~déplier~.

The literal sense is the heart of the word: to deploy is to un-fold. A folded banner, a folded sail, a folded map — ~déployer~ spreads it out flat and open. From this concrete gesture the verb stretched into military language, where troops once tightly packed are unfolded across a field of battle, and then into everyday figurative use: one deploys energy, charm, or arguments, spreading them out for full effect. English ~deploy~ and ~display~ are in fact the same word arriving twice, both from this ~desploier~. The shared root *~plek-~ runs through a remarkably wide family of French words — ~simple~, ~double~, ~complexe~, ~exploit~, ~employer~, and ~appliquer~ among them — all turning, in one way or another, on the idea of folds laid one against another.
en.déporter:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēportāre~ (“to carry away, to convey”), formed from ~dē-~ (“away from”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”). French speakers can still parse it as ~dé-~ plus ~porter~, and English Wiktionary describes that as a surface analysis rather than the real history, since the verb arrived from Latin already formed. ~Portāre~ gave French ~porter~ and, among others, English ~port~ in ~portable~ and ~transport~, which come from related Latin forms.

In Roman law, ~dēportāre~ also meant to banish someone, notably to an island, and the Latin noun ~dēportātiō~ named that punishment. French kept this sense of removal by authority: ~déporter~ is to send a person away from a country or into forced exile or confinement. The word took a grim weight in the twentieth century with mass deportations, and the nouns ~déportation~ and ~déporté~ are now bound to that history. In a milder, physical sense, ~déporter~ also describes a vehicle or a current pushing something off course.
en.déposer:
Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ (“down, away,” from Latin ~de-~) and the verb ~poser~ (“to place, to set”). ~Poser~ has a famously tangled history: in form it continues Late Latin ~pausāre~ (“to halt, to cease,” borrowed from Greek ~pausis~, “a stopping”), seen in early Christian epitaphs such as ~hic pausat in pace~. But in meaning it merged with Latin ~ponere~ (“to put,” past participle ~positus~), so completely that all the French “-poser” verbs took over the senses of ~ponere~ — hence the nouns in ~-position~ rather than ~-pausation~.

With ~dé-~ added, the verb first meant “to set down what one was carrying,” then spread to “to lay aside,” “to entrust” (to ~déposer~ money at a bank), and figuratively “to depose,” to set a ruler down from the throne. The double parentage still shows in the family: from the ~pausāre~ side come ~pause~ and ~repos~ (“rest”), while the ~ponere~ side surfaces in ~déposition~, ~dépôt~, and the cousins ~exposer~, ~imposer~, and ~proposer~ — a whole conjugation built on a verb that, etymologically, means both “to rest” and “to put.”
en.dépouiller:
French ~dépouiller~ is inherited from Middle French ~despouiller~, from Old French ~despoillier~ (attested in the twelfth century), from Latin ~dēspoliāre~, itself built from ~dē-~ (“off”) and ~spoliāre~ (“to strip, to plunder”). The verb ~spoliāre~ comes from the noun ~spolium~, which meant the hide stripped from an animal and, by extension, booty taken from an enemy. Catalan ~despullar~ and Romanian ~despuia~ are close relatives, and English ~spoil~ and ~despoil~ share the same Latin ancestry.

The literal first sense is to skin an animal, to take off its hide. From there the verb widened to stripping a person of clothing or of possessions, and then to any removal of a covering. A later set of senses is more surprising: ~dépouiller~ also means to go through documents. French Wiktionary dates the sense of examining an account to 1690, and ~dépouiller le scrutin~ is to count the ballots. One way to see the link is that the contents of the ballot box or the file are stripped out and laid bare, though the sources do not spell this out. Related words include ~dépouille~ (“hide, remains”), ~dépouillement~, ~spolier~ and ~spoliation~.
en.dépourvoir:
~Dépourvoir~ is built from the privative prefix ~dé-~ (Latin ~dis-~, “apart, away”) on ~pourvoir~ (“to provide, to supply”), which descends from Latin ~prōvidēre~ (“to foresee, to look ahead for, to provide for”). That verb is itself transparent: ~prō-~ (“ahead, in front”) joined to ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Italic *~widēō~ and ultimately from PIE *~weyd-~ (“to see”), one of the most productive roots in the family. Latin ~prōvidēre~ passed into Old French as ~porveoir~, and the earliest French trace of the negative form is the participle ~desporveu~, attested in 1190. The same Latin verb produced Italian ~provvedere~, Spanish ~proveer~, Portuguese ~prover~ and Catalan ~proveir~; crossing the Channel with the Normans, it gave English three words at once — ~provide~, taken from the Latin, alongside ~purvey~ and ~purview~, which came by the softer Anglo-Norman route.

~Dépourvoir~ is the rare negative twin of ~pourvoir~: where one supplies, the other strips bare. It is a defective verb, and spectacularly so. The TLFi records it only in the infinitive and the compound tenses, and adds the deflating remark that its dictionary examples answer to no attested usage at all, more recent dictionaries having dropped the entry altogether. What survives is the participle: ~dépourvu~ (“devoid of, destitute of”), and above all the phrase ~prendre au dépourvu~ (“to catch off guard”) — literally, to catch someone who has not provided ahead. The same root *~weyd-~ runs through the whole French vocabulary of seeing and foreseeing: ~voir~, ~prévoir~, ~évident~, ~providence~. Its best-disguised descendant is ~prudent~, from Latin ~prūdēns~, a worn-down contraction of ~prōvidēns~ (“seeing ahead”): a prudent person is, etymologically, one who saw it coming.
en.déprimer:
~Déprimer~ comes from Latin ~dēprimere~, a compound of ~dē-~ (“down”) and ~premere~ (“to press”), meaning “to press down, to push under.” English has the same verb as ~depress~, and the same Latin ~premere~ stands behind ~press~, ~express~, ~oppress~ and ~repress~. The sense of lowering by pressure is easy to see in the parts: ~dē-~ gives the direction and ~premere~ the force.

In modern French ~déprimer~ is both transitive (“to discourage, to weaken”) and intransitive (“to feel depressed”), and the adjective ~déprimé~ and noun ~dépression~ cover the mood, the weather system and the economic slump alike. The step from a pressed-down surface to a pressed-down spirit is the same picture in French and English: something that weighs on a person's morale. The Latin ~premere~ also gave ~presser~, ~pression~, ~exprimer~, ~opprimer~, ~réprimer~, ~imprimer~ and ~comprimer~, a family built on the gesture of pushing.
en.députer:
From Latin ~deputare~, formed from ~de-~ and ~putare~ (“to reckon, estimate, consider”). ~putare~ began as “to clean, to prune,” a denominative of ~putus~ (“clean”); the shift from trimming to reckoning runs through the idea of cutting away to get a clear account — the same metaphor seen in deciding (Latin ~decidere~, literally “to cut off”). The deeper Proto-Indo-European root of ~putus~ is uncertain and is best left unstated. In Latin ~deputare~ meant “to count off, to assign,” and from that French drew ~députer~: to assign someone, to send them off charged with a duty.

The semantic heart is delegation — to ~députer~ is to appoint a person to act on others' behalf. That sense crystallized in the great nouns of representative government: a ~député~ is one sent to deliberate for those who chose him, and a ~députation~ is a delegation dispatched on a mission. From the same ~putare~ French gathers a wide harvest — ~compter~ and ~conter~ (both from ~computare~), ~réputation~, ~dispute~, and ~amputer~ — a family in which the old senses of pruning and of reckoning still quietly coexist.
en.dépêcher:
From Old French ~despeechier~ (also ~despescher~), built from the prefix ~dés-~ (“undo, remove”) and the stem of ~empeschier~ (“to hinder”), the ancestor of modern ~empêcher~. That Old French verb comes from Late Latin ~impedicāre~ (“to shackle, to entangle”), from ~pedica~ (“a fetter”), from ~pēs~ (“foot”). So ~dépêcher~ literally unshackles: it removes the fetter from the feet.

Etymologically, ~dépêcher~ means to remove obstacles and entanglements in order to get a task done promptly. The noun ~dépêche~ (“a message sent urgently,” then “a telegram”) belongs to the same family, and the reflexive ~se dépêcher~ (“to hurry”) is the commonest use today. The picture is of a traveler or a task freed from its shackles, and ~empêcher~ is the shackle itself.
en.déranger:
From Old French ~ranger~ (earlier ~rengier~, “to arrange in a row”), a denominal verb from ~rang~ (“rank, row”), prefixed with ~dé-~ (Latin ~dis-~, marking reversal). The noun ~rang~ is not Latin at all: it comes from Old French ~renc~, borrowed from Frankish *~hring~ (“ring, circle”), from Proto-Germanic *~hringaz~ (“ring, circle”). It is thus a cognate of English ~ring~ and German ~Ring~ — and, by a curious loop, of English ~rank~, which English borrowed back from French ~rang~.

The semantics are wonderfully concrete. To ~ranger~ is to set things in their proper row; ~déranger~ is to break that order — to pull a thing out of its rank. From this literal “disarrangement” the verb broadened to the figurative “to disturb, to bother,” the sense that now dominates: ~déranger quelqu'un~ is to intrude on someone's peace, not to muddle their furniture. The Germanic “circle” at the root surfaces across the modern family: ~ranger~ (“to tidy”), ~rangée~ (“a row”), and ~rang~ (“rank”) itself. So the everyday apology ~je ne veux pas vous déranger~ rests, etymologically, on the image of not knocking someone out of their ring.
en.dériver:
In the sense “to derive, to originate from,” ~dériver~ comes from Latin ~dērīvāre~, literally “to draw off a watercourse,” from ~dē-~ (“away from”) and ~rīvus~ (“stream, brook”). French sources are emphatic on one point that catches everyone out: despite appearances, the verb descends from ~rīvus~ (the water), not from ~rive~ (“bank, shore,” Latin ~rīpa~). To derive a result is thus to channel it off from its source as one would divert a stream. Italian ~derivare~ and Spanish ~derivar~ carry the same image.

From “draw off water” the verb broadened to “flow from, proceed from,” giving the grammarian's ~dérivé~ (“derivative”) and ~dérivation~. There is, however, a homonym to flag: the nautical ~dériver~, “to drift off course,” which the TLFi traces not to ~rīvus~ at all but to a borrowing influenced by English ~to drive~ (“to push, to drive along”), recorded from the early 16th century — and explicitly not, despite the tempting picture, to ~rive~. The two strands are best kept apart. From ~rīvus~ French also has ~rivière~ (“river”) and ~ru~, and the English doublets ~derive~ and ~rivulet~.
en.dérober:
From Old French ~desrober~ (“to steal, to strip”), formed from ~des-~ and ~rober~ (“to steal”). ~Rober~ itself comes from Late Latin ~raubāre~, borrowed from Frankish *~raubōn~ (“to plunder”), from Proto-Germanic *~raubōną~ (“to rob”). The Germanic verb has cousins elsewhere: English ~rob~ (borrowed through Old French), German ~rauben~, Italian ~rubare~ and Spanish ~robar~. French Wiktionary also gives a second analysis of ~dérober~, as derived from ~robe~, so the sources offer two routes.

The Germanic word for plunder reached French along with the Franks. To ~dérober~ something from sight is to hide it, and ~à la dérobée~ means “furtively”. The reflexive ~se dérober~ means “to slip away, to avoid a duty or a question”, and is also what a horse does when it balks at a jump, giving the noun ~dérobade~.
en.déroger:
From Latin ~dērogāre~, formed from ~dē-~ (“away, down”) and ~rogāre~ (“to ask”). In Roman public law ~rogāre~ meant to put a proposal to the people for a vote, and so ~dērogāre~ meant to repeal part of a law or to take something away from it. The same ~rogāre~ is in several other French verbs: ~interroger~ (“to question”), ~proroger~ (“to extend a term”), ~abroger~ (“to repeal”), and ~arroger~ (“to claim wrongly”). English ~derogate~ and ~derogatory~ come from the Latin as well.

The French verb began as a legal term for partially suspending an existing rule, and from there it grew to mean to depart from a rule or an obligation: ~déroger à la règle~ is to make an exception to it. A curious older use belongs to the social history of France. A nobleman who took up a trade or any occupation judged unworthy of his rank was said to ~déroger~, and risked losing his noble status. The sense of lowering oneself lingers in phrases such as ~déroger à son rang~. The family also has ~dérogation~ (“exemption”) and ~dérogatoire~.
en.dérouler:
From the verb ~rouler~ (“to roll”) with the privative, reversing prefix ~dé-~ (Latin ~dis-~), so literally “to un-roll.” ~Rouler~ comes from Old French ~roeler~, a derivative of ~roele~ (“little wheel”), from Latin ~rotella~, a diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”). ~Rota~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~Hrot-eh₂-~, from the root *~Hret-~ (“to run, to roll”), which also gave German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), Sanskrit ~ratha~ (“chariot”), and Lithuanian ~ratas~ (“wheel”).

The whole word is a small machine of meaning: a wheel (~rota~) turns, so a scroll or carpet ~se déroule~ when its rolled-up length is let out flat. From the literal “unroll” grew the figurative senses “to unfold, to take place over time” — events that ~se déroulent~ like a banner being released. The opposite ~enrouler~ rolls something back up. From the same ~rota~ come a rich family: ~roue~ (“wheel”), ~rouleau~, ~roulette~, ~rotule~ (“kneecap,” the little wheel of the knee), ~rotation~, ~ronde~, and even ~rôle~ — originally a ~rotulus~, a rolled-up sheet of parchment on which an actor's lines were written.
en.désactiver:
French ~désactiver~ is a transparent modern formation: the privative prefix ~dés-~ (Latin ~dis-~, marking removal or reversal) added to ~activer~ (“to activate”). ~Activer~ derives from the adjective ~actif~, from Latin ~activus~, built on ~actus~, the past participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do, to act”). ~Agere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~agō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”), one of the great verbs of the family: it surfaces in Ancient Greek ~ágō~ (“I lead”), in Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“drives”), and, through Latin, in a flood of English words from ~act~ and ~agent~ to ~agile~.

Semantically ~désactiver~ simply reverses ~activer~: to switch off, disable, or render inert a mechanism, an account, a defense system. It is overwhelmingly a word of the technical and digital age — one ~désactive~ an alarm, a button, an option, a virus — and its very modernity shows how a Latin root for “driving cattle” has been press-ganged into the vocabulary of software. The same *~h₂eǵ-~ root, through ~agere~ and its participle ~actus~, underlies a huge French family: ~agir~, ~acte~, ~action~, ~acteur~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~exiger~, and ~rédiger~ — all, at bottom, about setting something in motion.
en.désarmer: Inherited from Old French ~desarmer~, which can be analyzed as ~dés-~ + ~armer~. The prefix ~dés-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here marks reversal: to undo the act of arming. The base ~armer~ comes from Latin ~armāre~, built on ~arma~ (“weapons, tools”), from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to fit together.” The verb means to take weapons from someone, then, by extension, to reduce a country's forces, to defuse a bomb or an alarm, to retire a ship from service, or even to soften an opponent's anger.
en.déserter:
Borrowed from Late Latin ~dēsertāre~ (“to abandon”), from Latin ~dēsertus~ (“abandoned”), the past participle of ~dēserere~ (“to forsake”). That verb is made of ~dē-~ (a prefix of undoing) and ~serere~ (“to join, to link up”), so to forsake is, literally, to undo a bond. Spanish ~desertar~ is a cognate, and English has taken the verb as ~desert~ through French.

The participle ~dēsertus~ also gave French the noun ~désert~ (“abandoned, empty place”) by an older route, so the soldier who flees and the Sahara share an ancestor: a desert is a place left behind. ~Déserter~ first applied to leaving a place, and the military sense of abandoning one's post or army came to dominate, giving ~déserteur~ and ~désertion~. The figurative uses remain alive: ~déserter~ is said of the countryside, a cause or a meeting. The other half of the Latin compound, ~serere~, lives on in ~série~ and ~insérer~.
en.désespérer: ~Désespérer~ is formed from ~espérer~ (“to hope”) and the privative prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the verb: to lose hope. English Wiktionary also notes the Old French form ~desperer~, which shows the word is old. ~Espérer~ goes back to Latin ~spērāre~ (“to hope”), from ~spēs~ (“hope”), and Latin already had ~dēspērāre~, built the same way. English ~despair~ came from the Old French verb. The French verb can be intransitive (“to despair”) or take ~de~ (“to give up hope of something”).
en.désigner:
From Latin ~designare~ (“to mark out, to point out, to designate”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ (“out, off”) and a verb built on ~signum~ (“mark, sign, token, military standard”). The deeper origin of ~signum~ is genuinely disputed: some derive it from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sek-~ (“to cut”), as “something cut or carved out,” while others connect it to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), as the standard one follows. ~désigner~ is cognate with English ~design~ and ~designate~ and with Italian ~designare~, all resting on ~signum~.

The core image in ~designare~ is of marking something out so that it stands apart — pointing to it, singling it out. From this came both the act of indicating (to ~désigner~ a culprit, a successor, a meeting place) and, by a separate route through Italian ~disegno~, the artistic sense of “design” and “drawing.” French actually carries a doublet here: the learned ~désigner~ and the popular ~dessiner~ (“to draw”) both descend from ~designare~, the one keeping the sense of pointing out, the other the sense of tracing a figure. From the same ~signum~ French inherited ~signe~ (“sign”), ~signal~, ~signer~ (“to sign”), ~enseigne~ (“ensign, shop-sign”), and ~insigne~ (“insignia”) — a whole vocabulary of marks and tokens.
en.désirer:
From Latin ~desiderare~ (“to long for, to feel the want of”), which most analyses break down as ~de-~ plus the noun ~sidus~ (genitive ~sideris~, “star, constellation, heavenly body”). The verb passed through Old French ~desirer~ into the modern form. It is the close sibling of ~considerare~ (“to examine attentively”), built on the same stellar noun, and survives in Italian ~desiderare~ and Spanish ~desear~.

The stellar imagery is the memorable part, though its exact logic is debated. One traditional reading places the word in the mouths of augurs or sailors: to scan the night sky for an awaited star and not find it — to note its absence — was to feel ~desiderare~, the ache of something missing, while ~considerare~ was to study the stars present overhead. From “to miss what is absent,” the sense broadened to the general longing of modern ~désirer~. The Latin participle ~desideratum~ survives untranslated in English and French as a thing wished for, and the same ~sidus~ underlies the French family ~sidéral~ (“of the stars”) and ~sidérer~ (“to stun, to dumbfound”), once “to be struck by a baleful star.”
en.désoler:
From Latin ~dēsōlāre~ (“to leave alone, to lay waste, to abandon”), from ~dē-~ (intensive) and ~sōlus~ (“alone, single”). The deeper origin of ~sōlus~ is genuinely unsettled — it is said to have baffled etymologists for generations. One traditional account traces it through Proto-Italic to the reflexive PIE *~swé~ (“oneself”), giving the sense “by oneself”; De Vaan instead proposes a link to *~solh₂-~ (“whole, healthy”), kin to ~salvus~. The sources present these as competing hypotheses, not settled fact. Whatever its root, ~sōlus~ gave Spanish ~solo~, Italian ~solo~ and French ~seul~, and lies behind English ~sole~ and ~solo~.

The earliest French sense was the strong Latin one: to ~désoler~ a country was to devastate and depopulate it, to leave it desolate and alone. From that ruin the meaning softened over time toward the emotional — to lay waste to someone’s spirits, hence “to distress, to grieve.” Today the polite ~désolé~ (“sorry”) is a faded ember of that old devastation; the speaker claims, etymologically, to be laid waste. French keeps the family in ~désolation~ and ~désolant~ (“distressing”), both still tinged with the original sense of emptiness left behind.
en.déstabiliser: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~stabiliser~, meaning “to make unstable”. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here reverses the base. The base ~stabiliser~ is built on ~stable~, from Latin ~stabilis~ (“standing firm”), which comes from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), with the suffix ~-iser~. English ~stand~ shares the same Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~. The verb literally undoes a standing.
en.détacher:
Two French verbs spelled ~détacher~ have run together. The sense here — “to remove spots and stains” — is formed straightforwardly from ~tache~ (“stain, spot”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (marking removal), so that to ~détacher~ a garment is to take the stains out of it. The homonym meaning “to untie, to separate” comes instead from Old French ~destachier~, the ~dé-~ counterpart of ~attacher~ (“to attach”); that family is usually traced to a Frankish or Germanic root for a stake or fastening, the same one behind English ~attach~ and ~detach~ (borrowed from French).

The stain-removing verb keeps to its narrow, useful trade: it belongs to laundering and cleaning, and its derivatives are concrete and modern — ~détachant~ (“stain remover”) and ~détachage~ (“stain removal”), beside the base ~tache~ itself. Its quiet usefulness is a reminder that not every French verb climbs back to Rome; this one is built, late and locally, from a humble native noun. The untying ~détacher~, by contrast, carries the abstract senses of separation, secondment and emotional detachment — a good example of how French spelling can fuse two unrelated histories into a single shape.
en.détailler:
Derived from ~tailler~ (“to cut, carve”) with the prefix ~dé-~. ~tailler~ comes from Old French ~taillier~, from Late Latin ~taliāre~ (“to cut”), from Latin ~talea~ (“a cutting, twig, slip for planting”). Through ~taliāre~, ~tailler~ is cousin to Italian ~tagliare~ and Spanish ~tajar~, and the noun ~taille~ ultimately gave English ~tally~ and ~tailor~ (the cutter of cloth). The prefix ~dé-~ here carries the sense of separation, breaking apart.

To ~détailler~ was first to “cut into pieces” — to divide a whole into its small parts. From dividing physical things grew two important commercial and intellectual senses. Cutting goods into small lots to sell piecemeal gave ~détail~ the meaning “retail” (selling in small quantities, opposed to ~en gros~, “wholesale”); ~vendre au détail~ is to retail. And describing a thing part by part — examining its every small piece — gave the everyday sense “to detail, to recount minutely.” The noun ~détail~ thus carries both ideas at once: a “detail” is a small part cut from the whole, whether of merchandise or of a description. Relatives in modern French include ~tailler~, ~taille~, ~tailleur~, ~détaillant~ (“retailer”), and ~entailler~ (“to notch”).
en.détecter:
~Détecter~ is a 20th-century word (first attested 1929), and its immediate origin is debated. The CNRTL gives two accounts side by side: either it was derived within French from ~détecteur~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~, or it was borrowed from English ~to detect~. Both lead back to the same Latin source: ~dētegere~ (“to uncover, expose”), from ~de-~ (“off, away”) and ~tegere~ (“to cover”), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ (“to cover, roof”), which also gave English ~thatch~ and ~deck~.

The literal Latin image is undressing — pulling the cover off something hidden — and the modern technical sense kept exactly that: a detector strips away concealment to reveal a signal, a flaw, a presence. The English route is plausible because the word arrived precisely with radio and physics vocabulary, where English led; but since French already had ~détecteur~, native back-formation cannot be ruled out, and the sources do not settle it. From the same ~tegere~ come ~protéger~, ~tégument~, and ~toit~ / ~toiture~ (the “cover” overhead), and from the prefixed verb, ~détection~ and ~détective~.
en.détendre:
From Latin ~detendere~ (“to unstretch, slacken, take down”), from ~dē-~ (here reversive, “un-”) plus ~tendere~ (“to stretch, draw tight”). ~tendere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate, through that root, with Ancient Greek ~τείνω~ (“to stretch”), English ~thin~, and German ~dehnen~ (“to stretch”).

If ~tendre~ is to pull taut, ~détendre~ is to let off the tension: one ~détendre~ a bow, a spring, a rope — and then, figuratively, one's nerves, one's mood, the atmosphere of a room. The reflexive ~se détendre~ is the everyday French for “to relax, unwind.” From the same *~ten-~ root French keeps a broad family: ~tendre~, ~étendre~ (“to spread”), ~tension~, ~tendon~, ~attendre~, ~entendre~, and the noun ~détente~ — which travelled into diplomacy as the very word for an easing of strained relations. To ~détendre~ is, at root, to let what was pulled tight go slack.
en.détenir:
From Latin ~detinēre~ (“to hold back, keep occupied, retain”), a compound of ~de-~ (here intensive or “away”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), reshaped in French on the model of the inherited verb ~tenir~. ~Tenēre~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch, draw taut”). The same root surfaces in Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”) and Sanskrit ~tanóti~, and ~tenēre~ itself lives on in Italian ~tenere~ and Spanish ~tener~.

French attests ~détenir~ early — around 1160 in the sense “to seize,” then “to hold someone back, restrain” by 1176, and by 1306 the now-dominant “to hold prisoner.” The trajectory runs from simply holding to holding against someone's will: to detain is to keep a grip on a person or thing that would otherwise slip free, which is why the same verb covers both holding a record and holding an inmate. The link between holding and stretching is the taut rope or sinew one keeps tight; from *~ten-~ French inherits a dense web of words, among them ~tenir~, ~tendre~ (“to stretch”), ~tension~, ~tenace~, ~contenir~, ~maintenir~, and the noun ~détenu~ (“detainee”), the one held fast.
en.déterminer:
From Latin ~determinare~ (“to bound, fix limits to”), from ~de-~ (here intensive) and ~terminare~ (“to limit”), itself from ~terminus~ (“boundary, boundary-stone”). The noun ~terminus~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ter-~ (“peg, post, boundary-marker”), which also gave Greek ~terma~ (“end-point, goal”). Cognate with Italian ~determinare~ and Spanish ~determinar~, and — through ~terminus~ — with English ~determine~, ~term~, and ~terminal~.

The surprise is the boundary-stone at the root: to ~déterminer~ is etymologically to “mark the limits” of a thing, to drive its boundary-posts so that it is fixed and unambiguous. The Romans even worshipped a god ~Terminus~, guardian of boundary-stones, honored at the festival of the ~Terminalia~. From the spatial act of bordering grew the abstract senses of settling a question, fixing a value, and resolving someone to act. The same ~terminus~ underlies a generous French family — ~terme~, ~terminer~, ~terminus~, ~terminal~, ~exterminer~, and ~indéterminé~ — all of them, in the end, about reaching or fixing a limit.
en.détester:
French ~détester~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~detestari~ (“to curse, to denounce, to call down evil upon”), formed from ~de-~ (here “away, down”) and ~testari~ (“to bear witness”), a verb derived from ~testis~ (“a witness”). And ~testis~ hides a small drama: it goes back, by the standard account, to Proto-Italic *~tristos~ and PIE *~tristh₂s~ — literally a “third party standing by,” from *~tréyes~ (“three”) plus *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). A witness was the impartial third person who stood beside the two parties to a dispute. So ~detestari~ first meant to invoke the gods as witnesses against someone — to curse them under solemn testimony.

The heat of that curse cooled, over centuries, into the modern ~détester~: no longer to call down divine judgment, merely to hate or strongly dislike. The original courtroom image is still legible in the verb's cousins, all sharing ~testis~: ~témoin~ (“witness,” via Old French) and ~témoigner~, ~attester~, ~contester~, ~protester~, and ~testament~ — the document by which one “testifies” one's will. To ~détester~ a dish, then, is the faded echo of once standing up, a third party, to swear before the gods against it.
en.détourner:
From Old French ~torner~ (“to turn”), the modern verb being ~tourner~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (Latin ~dis-~, “apart, away”), from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe, to round off”), from ~tornus~ (“a lathe, a turner's tool”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τόρνος~ (~tórnos~, “tool for drawing a circle”), from PIE *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, to turn by twisting”). Cognate, through ~tourner~, with Italian ~tornare~ and Spanish ~tornar~.

The lathe sense is the heart of the family: to turn wood on a spinning tool. From “turn” French built a crowd of words on ~tour~ (“a turn, a lathe”): ~détour~, ~contour~, ~retour~, and the verb ~tourner~ itself. ~Détourner~ adds ~dé-~ to mean “to turn aside,” hence “to divert” a river or a plane, and figuratively “to distract” someone or to embezzle (~détourner des fonds~). The same root *~terh₁-~ surfaces in ~tour~, ~tournoi~, ~tournevis~, and the borrowed ~tornade~.
en.détruire:
From Old French ~destruire~, from Vulgar Latin *~destrugere~, a remodeling of Classical Latin ~destruere~ (“to tear down, to demolish”). The verb joins the prefix ~de-~ (here “un-, reversal”) and ~struere~ (“to pile up, to build”), from Proto-Italic *~strowō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~strew-~ (“to strew, to spread out”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~strew~ and, via the Latin compounds, with ~structure~ and ~construct~.

The etymology is beautifully exact: if ~struere~ is to build by piling up, then ~de-struere~ is to take the pile apart — to un-build. ~Détruire~ is thus the precise opposite of ~construire~ (~con-~ + ~struere~, “to pile together”), its twin and antonym in a single root. The family is tightly knit in French: ~construire~, ~instruire~ (literally “to build into,” hence “to teach”), ~structure~, ~industrie~, and the noun ~destruction~ all rest on the same ~struere~. There is a quiet irony in the shared root: to instruct, to construct, and to destroy are, etymologically, three ways of handling the same heap — building it up into the mind, into a wall, or pulling it back down.
en.détériorer: Borrowed from Late Latin ~deteriorāre~ (“to make worse”), a verb built on the Latin comparative adjective ~deterior~ (“worse, lower in quality”). French took it as a learned word, and it can be transitive, to damage something, or pronominal, as in ~se détériorer~, to decline in condition. English ~deteriorate~ is a borrowing of the same Latin verb.
en.dévaster: ~Dévaster~ is a borrowing from Latin ~dēvastāre~ (“to lay waste completely”), built from ~dē-~, here an intensifier, and ~vastāre~ (“to ravage”). That verb comes from the adjective ~vastus~ (“empty, desolate”), which also gave French ~vaste~ and English ~vast~. English ~devastate~ is a parallel borrowing of the same Latin verb. The idea is of a land stripped until it lies empty.
en.développer:
From Old French ~desveloper~ (attested around 1170 as ~desvoleper~, “to bring out of what envelops it”), formed as the antonym of ~enveloper~ (“to wrap up”) with the separative prefix ~des-~. The shared core ~-veloper~ has an obscure origin that etymologists have never settled: it is also the root of Italian ~viluppo~ (“tangle, bundle”) and its derivative ~sviluppo~ (“development”), but no convincing Latin or Germanic source for the bare stem has won acceptance, so honest dictionaries leave it unexplained. English ~develop~ was borrowed from the French verb.

The image behind ~développer~ is concrete and tactile: to ~unwrap~ a parcel, to peel away a covering and let what was hidden come into the open. From that literal unwrapping the verb extended to “to expand, unfold, set out at length,” then to the modern senses of growing, elaborating an argument, processing photographic film, and — most recently — writing software. The opposite gesture survives intact in ~enveloper~ and in the noun ~enveloppe~. From the same family come ~développement~, ~développeur~, and the adjective ~développable~. The contrast between wrapping and unwrapping still animates the pair: where ~enveloper~ conceals, ~développer~ reveals.
en.déverser: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~verser~ (“to pour”). Here ~dé-~ does not simply undo the base: it adds the idea of pouring something away or out, in quantity. ~Verser~ comes from Late Latin *~versāre~, a repeated-action form of Latin ~vertere~ (“to turn”), because pouring means turning a container over. So ~déverser~ can describe a river emptying into the sea, a truck unloading its cargo, or, figuratively, a stream of insults. The same family gives ~déversoir~, a spillway.
en.dévier:
Borrowed from Latin ~dēviāre~ (“to turn aside from the road”), built from the prefix ~dē-~ (“away from”) and ~via~ (“road, way”). French already had a cousin of its own, Old French ~desvoier~, formed with a different prefix, which survives as ~dévoyer~. Italian ~deviare~ and English ~deviate~ also come from the Latin verb.

The image is literal: to ~dévier~ is to leave the track. French applies it to a vehicle or a river pushed off course, then figuratively to an idea, a policy or a conversation, and in physics and sport to a ray or a ball that is deflected and a blow that is parried. Learned ~dévier~ and inherited ~dévoyer~ show French keeping two versions of one idea: the first is neutral, while the second often carries a moral tinge, as when a young person is led astray. The root ~via~ survives in ~voie~ and in ~envoyer~, literally “to put on the way”.
en.dévoiler:
A French formation of the seventeenth century, built from the prefix ~dé-~ (a privative, “un-, removal of”) plus the verb ~voiler~ (“to veil, to cover with a veil”). ~Voiler~ is itself denominal, from the noun ~voile~, which descends from Latin ~vela~, the plural of ~velum~ (“sail, cloth, covering, curtain”). Through ~velum~ it is kin to English ~veil~ and ~reveal~ and to Spanish ~velo~.

The morphology is wonderfully transparent: where ~voiler~ puts a veil on, ~dé-~ takes it off, so ~dévoiler~ is literally “to un-veil.” The verb runs in step with the concrete and the figurative at once — to ~dévoiler~ a statue at its inauguration, and to ~dévoiler~ a secret, a plot, one's true intentions. Latin ~velum~ is the common ancestor of a small French cluster: the noun ~voile~ (notice that it is masculine, “the veil,” but feminine, “the sail,” the two meanings split by gender), the verbs ~voiler~ and ~révéler~ (from Latin ~revelare~, “to draw back the veil”), and ~vélum~ itself, the awning of an arena. To reveal and to unveil are, at root, the very same gesture.
en.dévorer:
From Latin ~dēvorāre~ (“to swallow down, to devour, to engulf”), a learned borrowing built from ~dē-~ (“down, completely”) and ~vorāre~ (“to swallow, to gulp”). The simple verb ~vorāre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷerh₃-~ (“to swallow”), which also lies behind Greek ~bora~ (“food, meat”) and Sanskrit words for swallowing. Latin ~dēvorāre~ lived on in the Romance languages: Italian has ~divorare~ and Spanish ~devorar~. English ~devour~ came in through French, not from the Latin directly.

The prefix ~dē-~ here is intensive, so the verb means not merely to swallow but to swallow up entirely, and French quickly let that appetite spill over into figurative uses. Flames ~dévorent~ a building, a reader ~dévore~ a novel, a lover ~dévore~ someone with his eyes, and remorse or jealousy ~dévore~ a person from within. The bare Latin verb ~vorāre~ did not survive in French, but it left its mark in learned vocabulary: ~vorace~, ~voracité~, and the family of diet words built on the Latin ending ~-vorus~, among them ~carnivore~, ~herbivore~ and ~omnivore~. So the monster of an appetite and the vegetarian's label share one ancestor.
en.dévouer: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~vouer~, and based on Latin ~dēvovēre~ (“to consecrate by a vow”), through Old French ~devoer~. The Latin verb could mean dedicating something to a god and even doomed someone to the gods below. ~Vouer~ itself goes back to the idea of a solemn promise, linked to Latin ~vōtum~ (“vow”). The French verb lost the darker side. ~Dévouer~ now means to give up, to consecrate, and its reflexive form ~se dévouer~ means to sacrifice oneself for a cause or for others. Related words are ~dévot~, ~dévotion~ and ~vœu~.
en.dîner:
From Old French ~disner~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~disiūnāre~, itself from ~disieiūnāre~ or ~disjejūnāre~ (“to break the fast”). That Latin verb joined ~dis-~ (“undoing”) to Late Latin ~iēiūnāre~ (“to fast”), from Latin ~ieiūnus~ (“fasting”). French ~dîner~ is thus a doublet of ~déjeuner~, which comes from the very same source by a different phonetic route. English borrowed the family from Old French as ~dine~ and ~dinner~.

The circumflex of ~dîner~ is a scar: it stands in for the ~s~ of Old French ~disner~, which fell silent in the Middle Ages. The meaning tells a small story about eating habits. Originally the verb named the first meal of the day, the one that ended the overnight fast. As the main meal drifted later, ~déjeuner~ took over the morning meal, and ~dîner~ followed the main meal toward the evening. The older timetable survives in Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec, where ~dîner~ still means to eat at midday and ~souper~ names the evening meal. French thus keeps, inside one verb, a memory of breaking a fast.
en.effacer:
Attested in the twelfth century, ~effacer~ is a French parasynthetic formation: the noun ~face~ (“face, surface”), from Latin ~facies~ (“appearance, face, surface”), framed by the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out, away”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. It has an Occitan counterpart, ~esfassar~. The literal sense built into the word is striking: to ~effacer~ is, etymologically, to take the face off something — to remove its surface, its outward showing.

From that vivid image — stripping the visible skin from a thing — the verb generalized to making any mark disappear: erasing writing, rubbing out a stain, fading a color. It then climbed into the figurative, where it means to cancel or wipe away (effacer une dette, une faute), to outshine or eclipse (son talent ~efface~ celui des autres), and, reflexively, to withdraw discreetly (s’~effacer~ pour laisser passer quelqu’un).
