The same ~facies~ root spreads through French in ~face~, ~surface~, ~façade~, and ~facette~, so that every time one ~efface~ a word, one is, by the word’s own logic, peeling away a little face.
en.effectuer:
From Latin ~effectuāre~, a verb built on ~effectus~ (“an accomplishment, a result, an effect”), itself the past participle of ~efficere~ (“to bring about, accomplish”). ~Efficere~ is ~ex-~ (“out”) plus a combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”), from Proto-Italic *~fakiō~, from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to set, to place”). Through that same root ~effectuer~ is cognate with English ~do~ and ~deed~ and with German ~tun~.

The Latin ~efficere~ described carrying a thing all the way through to its finished result, and the derived noun ~effectus~ named that result — the modern ~effet~. From this came the learned verb ~effectuer~, which keeps the precise, almost technical flavor of its origin: one ~effectue~ a calculation, a payment, or an experiment, bringing a defined procedure to completion. The PIE root *~dʰeh₁-~ is extraordinarily prolific: ~faire~ itself descends from ~facere~, and the family includes ~effet~, ~affecter~, ~parfait~ (“thoroughly done”), and ~fait~. A surprising relative is ~thème~, which reaches French through Greek from the same root meaning “something set down.”
en.effondrer: Inherited from Old French ~esfondrer~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~exfunderāre~, a verb built on ~fundus~ (“bottom”). The prefix ~ex-~ means “out”, so the picture is of something whose bottom gives way, which is how a floor, a roof or a wall collapses. Catalan ~esfondrar~ is a parallel. The base ~fundus~ also stands behind French ~fond~, ~fonder~ and ~profond~, which shows how many meanings grew from one Latin word for the lowest part of a thing.
en.efforcer:
From Old French ~esforcier~, an intensive formation on ~forcier~ (“to force”) with the prefix ~es-~ (from Latin ~ex-~), matching a Vulgar Latin *~exfortiāre~ (“to put forth one's strength”). Beneath both lies Late Latin ~fortia~ (“strength”) — originally the neuter plural of the adjective ~fortis~ (“strong”), reinterpreted as a feminine noun — the source of French ~force~. ~Fortis~ itself goes back through Old Latin ~forctis~ to Proto-Italic *~forktis~; beyond that the trail forks, scholars hesitating between the PIE roots *~bʰerǵʰ-~ (“to rise, be high”) and *~dʰerǵʰ-~ (“to hold fast, be firm”). Cognate with Italian ~sforzare~ — whose musical imperative ~sforzando~, “forcing” the note, decorates scores the world over — and Spanish ~esforzarse~.

The verb stands at the very dawn of French literature: around 1050, the Vie de saint Alexis, one of the oldest French poems, already uses ~esforcer~ for striving in the service of God. From the beginning it leaned toward the reflexive — force applied to oneself — and modern French confines it there entirely: ~s'efforcer~ exists only with its pronoun, strength turned inward against one's own limits. Its Old French deverbal noun survives as ~effort~, which English borrowed whole. English in fact adopted much of the family: ~force~, ~fort~, ~fortress~, ~effort~ and ~comfort~ — this last from Old French ~conforter~, Late Latin ~confortāre~, literally “to make thoroughly strong”: to comfort someone is, etymologically, to give them back their strength. On the French side stand ~forcer~, ~renforcer~, ~forteresse~, ~fortifier~ and ~réconforter~.
en.effrayer:
French ~effrayer~ comes from Old French ~esfreer~ (also ~esfraer~, ~esfreder~), through Middle French ~effreer~. It is a Germanic word in Latin dress. English Wiktionary derives it from a Vulgar Latin verb *~exfridāre~, built by adding the Latin prefix ~ex-~ to a Frankish *~friþu~ (“security, peace”), from Proto-Germanic *~friþuz~ (“peace”). That noun belongs to the family of *~frijōną~ (“to free; to love”), from Proto-Indo-European *~prāy-~ (“to like, to love”), alongside the variant *~prēy-~. English borrowed the Old French verb as ~affray~. So the chain runs from a Proto-Indo-European root for liking and loving, through Germanic words for peace and security, into Vulgar Latin and Old French.

The Germanic origin deserves a careful reading. Of the two Wiktionaries, only the English one gives the Frankish chain, and it presents the path through *~exfridāre~ as a reconstruction, which is what the asterisk means: the Vulgar Latin verb is not attested but inferred from its descendants. French Wiktionary cites only the Old French forms ~esfreer~, ~esfraer~ and ~esfreder~ and sends the reader to ~effarer~. The variation among those Old French forms is itself worth noticing, since the same verb appeared with several endings before the modern spelling ~effrayer~ settled. Neither source offers a date, so none is given here. The modern verb means “to frighten, to scare.”
en.emballer: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~balle~ (“bundle, packet”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put into a bundle, to pack up.” The prefix ~en-~ is from Latin ~in~ (“in, into”) and here carries its locative sense, with a noun base. As the spelling of the French form shows, ~emballer~ takes ~em-~ before the ~b~, which is only a spelling variant of ~en-~.
en.embarquer:
~Embarquer~ is a parasynthetic derivative of ~barque~ (“boat”), formed at once with the prefix ~en-~ (Latin ~in-~, “into”) and the verbal suffix ~-er~ — literally “to put into a boat.” ~Barque~ comes from Latin ~barca~ (“ship's boat”), and the Romance cousins are everywhere: Italian ~imbarcare~, Spanish and Portuguese ~embarcar~ all match it step for step.

The original act was concrete — loading goods or people aboard a ~barque~ — and from there the verb cast off in every direction. One ~embarque~ passengers, but one also ~s'embarque~ in a marriage, a lawsuit, or a doubtful scheme, the boat becoming a metaphor for any committing venture one can no longer easily leave. French preserves the seafaring caution in the idiom ~s'embarquer~ sans biscuit (“to set out without provisions,” i.e. unprepared), a reminder of voyages where forgetting the ship's biscuit could be fatal. The same ~barque~ underlies ~embarquement~, ~débarquer~ (“to land, disembark”) and ~rembarquer~. Modern slang even lets the police ~embarquer~ a suspect — bundling him aboard the van as one would aboard a hull.
en.embarrasser: Borrowed from Spanish ~embarazar~ (“to hinder, to encumber”). The word entered French as a verb of physical obstruction: to ~embarrasser~ a passage is to clutter or block it, and a person weighed down with luggage is ~embarrassé~. From that concrete sense the meaning moved to the social one: to put someone in an awkward position, to make them uneasy. English ~embarrass~ is a related loan from the same family of words and shows the same movement from “hinder” to “disconcert.”
en.embaucher: The two Wiktionaries explain ~embaucher~ differently. French Wiktionary derives it from ~débaucher~ by swapping the prefix ~dé-~ for ~en-~. English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~en-~ plus ~bauche~ plus the ending ~-er~, a parasynthetic formation; French Wiktionary refers ~bauche~ to ~bauge~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and gives the sense “to bring into”: to embauche someone is to take them on, in contrast with ~débaucher~, to lay them off or lure them away.
en.embellir: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before ~b~), the adjective ~bel~ and the ending ~-ir~. The base is the old form of ~beau~, which survives before a vowel (~bel homme~) and which is not the unit of sound named for Bell. The sense is “to make beautiful,” a typical case where ~en-~ turns an adjective into a verb of change, built together with the second-conjugation ending ~-ir~. Compare ~enrichir~, “to make rich.”
en.embrasser:
From Old French ~embracier~ (attested around 1080), formed from ~en-~ (“in”) + ~brace~/~bras~ (“arm, the two arms”), from Latin ~bracchium~ (“arm, forearm”). ~Bracchium~ was borrowed into Latin from Ancient Greek ~βραχίων~ (~brakhíōn~, “upper arm”). The Romance descendants of the noun are everywhere: Italian ~braccio~, Spanish ~brazo~, French ~bras~. Through Latin ~bracchium~, ~embrasser~ is cognate with English ~brace~ and ~embrace~ and, more distantly, ~bracelet~.

The literal sense is built into the word: ~embrasser~ meant “to take into one's arms,” to enfold. Only later did French let the gesture stand for the lips, so that today ~embrasser~ ordinarily means “to kiss” — a semantic drift from the encircling arms to the meeting of mouths. The older bodily meaning survives in ~s'embrasser~ and in figurative uses: one can ~embrasser~ a cause, a career, or a whole subject “at a glance” (~embrasser du regard~), holding it as if within the arms. From the same ~bras~ come ~brassée~ (“an armful”), ~embrassade~, ~brasser~, and ~bracelet~.
en.embêter: A parasynthetic formation: the prefix ~en-~ and the suffix ~-er~ were added at the same time around the adjective and noun ~bête~, since no *~bêter~ or *~embête~ stands in between. The base ~bête~ comes from Old French ~beste~, probably borrowed in part from Latin ~bēstia~ (“beast”), and the circumflex marks the lost ~s~ of the old spelling. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~, and the suffix ~-er~ from Latin ~-are~. The verb means to bother, annoy or pester someone, and its base shows what the speaker thinks of the person being annoyed.
en.emmener:
Compound of the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~inde~/~in-~, conveying motion away) and ~mener~ (“to lead, conduct”). ~Mener~ descends from Latin ~minare~ (“to drive animals by shouting and threatening”), a Late Latin development of ~minari~ (“to threaten”), which is built on ~minae~ (“threats”). So leading was first a matter of driving livestock forward with menacing cries.

The semantic journey is vivid: from threatening (~minari~), to herding beasts along by threats (~minare~), to simply leading or conducting anyone or anything (~mener~). Adding ~en-~ gives ~emmener~, to lead away, to take someone off with you — distinguished in careful French from ~amener~ (“to bring toward”) and ~ramener~ (“to bring back”): one ~emmène~ a person away to the cinema but ~amène~ them here. The ~minare~/~minari~ family is surprisingly large in French: ~menacer~ (“to threaten”), ~menace~, ~promener~ (“to take for a walk”), ~amener~, ~ramener~, and ~meneur~ (“leader, ringleader”) — a cluster of words whose shared ancestor was the herdsman's threatening shout.
en.emmerder: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before ~m~), the noun ~merde~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~merde~ is inherited from Old French through Latin ~merda~ (“excrement”). The prefix gives the sense “to cover, to supply with,” so the verb means literally “to smother in filth,” and it quickly became the vulgar everyday word for annoying or bothering someone. The pronominal ~s'emmerder~ means “to be bored stiff.”
en.emparer:
From Occitan ~emparar~ (“to protect, defend, lay claim to, seize”), from a Vulgar Latin *~imparare~, which the sources explain as a reshaping of *~imperare~ (“to command, master”) under the influence of ~parare~ (“to prepare, ward off”). It is cognate with Catalan ~emparar~ and connects to the ~parare~ family that also gives ~rempart~ and ~remparer~. In French the verb is attested in a defensive sense in the 14th century and in the possessive sense — “to seize” — by the first half of the 16th.

The two senses sit on a hinge between defense and aggression: to ward off and to take hold are two sides of laying claim to something. Modern French keeps only the reflexive ~s'emparer de~ (“to seize, take possession of”), the defensive meaning having faded. The ~parare~ root is prolific in French — ~parer~, ~séparer~, ~préparer~, ~réparer~, ~apparat~ — and the kindred ~rempart~ still names the very wall behind which one once took shelter.
en.empiler: ~Empiler~ is built from ~pile~ (“a heap of objects laid one on another”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix is spelled ~em-~ before p, but it is the same prefix, here with its locative sense of “putting into”: to empiler is to put things into a pile. The noun ~pile~ comes from Latin ~pila~ (“pillar, column”). The verb is attested in the first quarter of the 13th century, in the Miserere of Renclus de Molliens. French later derived the nouns ~empilage~ and ~empilement~ from it.
en.emplir:
From Old French ~emplir~, inherited from Latin ~implēre~ (“to fill up”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~plēre~ (“to fill”). Late Latin reshaped the verb as *~implīre~, which explains the French ending in ~-ir~. The root is generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”), the source of Latin ~plēnus~ (“full”), of English ~full~, and of German ~voll~. Spanish ~henchir~ is another descendant of ~implēre~, a reminder of how far the same Latin verb could travel.

~Emplir~ is the older verb, and ~remplir~ (~r-~ + ~emplir~, the vowel of ~re-~ dropping before the vowel of the base) took over everyday speech, so that ~emplir~ now sounds literary or elevated, as in a heart filled with joy. The sense of ~remplir~ is “to fill up,” not “to fill again.” The same Latin family gave a whole cluster of French words: ~plein~ (“full”), ~plénitude~, ~complet~ (from ~complētus~, “filled up, finished”), and ~accomplir~, whose “accomplishing” is, at bottom, a filling to the brim.
en.employer:
From Old French ~emploier~, from Latin ~implicare~ (“to fold in, to enfold, to involve”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~plicare~ (“to fold”). ~plicare~ descends from PIE *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). The verb is a doublet of the learned ~impliquer~, borrowed straight from Latin much later, while ~employer~ took the slow popular road through Old French. Cognate with Spanish ~emplear~ and Italian ~impiegare~, and, through ~implicare~, with English ~employ~ and ~imply~.

The semantic journey is a quiet marvel: from “to fold something in” grew the idea of “folding a thing into a task,” hence putting it to use, hence — of a person — giving them work. The same Latin ~implicare~ thus gave French both ~employer~ (to use, to hire) and ~impliquer~ (to involve, to entangle), two faces of one act of folding-in. ~plicare~ seeds a broad family: ~ployer~ and ~plier~ (its native French descendants), ~appliquer~, ~déployer~, ~replier~, and the noun ~pli~ (“a fold, a crease”) all share that root, as do English ~ply~ and ~plait~. From ~employer~ itself come ~emploi~, ~employé~, and ~employeur~ — the worker, after all, being someone “folded into” the work.
en.empoisonner: Built from ~poison~ with the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before ~p~) and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to put poison into”, then “to poison”. The noun ~poison~ is inherited through Old French ~poison~ from Latin ~pōtiōnem~ (“a drink”). It is a doublet of ~potion~, which French borrowed later, straight from Latin. A single Latin word for a drink therefore gave a deadly sense by the popular route and a medicinal or magical one by the learned route. English has the same pair, ~poison~ and ~potion~.
en.emporter:
A French compound: the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~inde~, “from there, away”) joined to the verb ~porter~ (“to carry”), attested already around the year 980 as ~enportet~. The base ~porter~ descends from Latin ~portāre~ (“to carry, to bear”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to lead through, to pass over”), the same root behind Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor”). Italian ~portare~ and Spanish ~portar~ are its siblings, and through the root English gained ~port~ and the kindred ~ford~.

The prefix ~en-~ carries the idea of taking something away with oneself, so ~emporter~ is to carry off — food “to go” is ~à emporter~. From physical carrying the verb won vivid figurative force: a storm or a fever may ~emporter~ a life, and to win a contest is to ~l'emporter~ (literally “to carry it off”). The reflexive ~s'emporter~ means to be carried away by anger, to lose one's temper. From the same ~portāre~ French drew a broad family — ~porter~, ~apporter~, ~rapporter~, ~transporter~, ~importer~, ~exporter~, ~supporter~, and the noun ~portée~ — all pivoting on the act of carrying.
en.empreindre:
French ~empreindre~ comes from Latin ~imprimere~ (“to press into, to imprint”), built from ~in-~ (“in, onto”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). The two Wiktionaries differ slightly in confidence: one gives the Latin verb as the direct source, the other calls the verb inherited, possibly by way of a Vulgar Latin form *~impremere~ that keeps the vowel of ~premere~. Either way, ~empreindre~ is the popular, inherited word, and it has a learned twin. ~Imprimer~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb at a later stage, so the two are doublets. Italian ~imprimere~ and Spanish ~imprimir~ continue the same Latin verb.

The original image is physical: pressing a seal or a die into wax or metal so that it leaves a mark. French kept that picture alive in figurative uses, where a face is ~empreint~ de tristesse (“marked with sadness”) or a style bears the stamp of its author. The noun ~empreinte~, built on the past participle, names the mark itself, from the footprint to the fingerprint and, in our own time, the carbon footprint. Meanwhile ~imprimer~ took over the technical sense of printing on paper. The root ~premere~ also gives ~presser~ (through Latin ~pressāre~), ~pression~ and ~impression~. The verb is conjugated like ~peindre~, hence the odd ~gn~ in ~empreignons~.
en.empresser: ~Empresser~ is formed from the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ~presser~. ~Presser~ comes from Old French ~presser~ (“to oppress, torment”), from Latin ~pressāre~ (“to press hard”), an intensive of ~premere~ (“to press, squeeze”). The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), puts the pressing inside a situation: to be caught up in the crowd, and so to bustle. Today the verb lives almost only in its reflexive form, with the sense of hurrying eagerly or attending zealously to someone, and the participle ~empressé~ describes an attentive, eager person.
en.emprisonner: ~Emprisonner~ is formed from ~en-~ (“in”), ~prison~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: literally, to put into prison. The noun ~prison~ is inherited from Old French ~prison~, which continues Latin ~prēnsiō~, a contracted form of ~prehēnsiō~ (“a seizing, an arrest”), from ~prehendere~ (“to seize, to grasp”). A ~prison~ was therefore first the act of seizing someone, and only later the place where the seized person was kept. The same Latin verb gave French ~prendre~, and English borrowed the French verb as ~imprison~.
en.emprunter:
From Vulgar Latin *~impromutuāre~, reshaped from Classical Latin ~promutuārī~ (“to borrow in advance”), built on ~mutuus~ (“lent, borrowed, reciprocal”). ~mutuus~ derives from the Proto-Indo-European root *~mei-~ (“to change, to exchange”), the same root behind English ~mutual~, French ~muer~ and ~mutuel~, and Latin ~mūtāre~ (“to change”), source of ~muter~ and ~commun~.

The etymology fits the idea perfectly: borrowing is an exchange you promise to reverse, a thing given on the understanding it will change hands back again. From the financial sense of taking a loan, ~emprunter~ broadened to borrowing of every kind — borrowing a book, borrowing words from another language, borrowing a friend's umbrella. Most evocatively, French uses it for roads and paths: one ~emprunte~ a route, a corridor, a staircase — literally “borrowing” the way one travels, as if the road were lent for the duration of the journey. The related noun ~emprunt~ names both a loan and a linguistic loanword. The deep root *~mei-~ thus links the humble act of borrowing to the grand idea of change and exchange that also gives ~mutuel~, ~commun~, and ~migrer~.
en.empêcher:
From Old French ~empeechier~, from Late Latin ~impedicare~ (“to fetter, to entangle, to catch by the feet”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~pedica~ (“a shackle, a foot-fetter”), itself from ~pes~ (genitive ~pedis~, “foot”). ~pes~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ped-~ (“foot”), making ~empêcher~ a distant cousin of English ~foot~, ~pedal~, and ~pedestrian~, and a closer relative of English ~impeach~, which entered through the same Old French verb.

The original picture is vividly physical: to ~empêcher~ someone was to shackle their feet so they could not move — to entangle and hold them fast. From that literal fettering the meaning lifted into the abstract “to prevent, to hinder,” which is all that survives in modern French. Its etymological twin tells a charming story: ~dépêcher~ began as the opposite gesture, “to un-fetter,” to free the feet and so to hurry — whence the reflexive ~se dépêcher~ (“to hurry up”) and the noun ~dépêche~ (a message “sent in haste”). English ~impeach~, by contrast, drifted from “to impede” toward “to accuse,” crossing paths along the way with unrelated Latin ~impetere~. The root *~ped-~ thus underlies an unexpected pair: to be ~empêché~ is to have one's feet tied, while to ~dépêcher~ is to set them free.
en.encadrer:
Formed from the noun ~cadre~ (“frame”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”), so literally “to put into a frame.” ~Cadre~ was borrowed in the 16th century from Italian ~quadro~ (“square, painting”), from Latin ~quadrum~ (“a square”), from ~quadrus~, ultimately from ~quattuor~ (“four”). That numeral goes back to PIE *~kʷetwóres~ (“four”), the same root that yields English ~four~ and ~quarter~, Latin ~quartus~, and Greek ~téssares~. A frame, then, is etymologically a four-cornered thing.

The meaning fanned out from the literal picture-frame to anything that encloses or bounds: to ~encadrer~ a photo, but also to ~encadrer~ troops or staff — to supervise and hold them within structure. From this military and managerial sense French draws ~cadre~ for an executive or officer and ~encadrement~ for supervision. The same ~quadrum~ family gave French ~carré~, ~quadrille~, ~escadre~ and ~escadron~ (a squadron being, originally, a body of soldiers drawn up in a square), and ~cadran~ (a dial, once four-cornered). The whole cluster is built on the number four.
en.encaisser:
Formed within French from ~en-~ + ~caisse~ + ~-er~, literally “to put into a box”. ~caisse~ is not an inherited word: the CNRTL takes it from Old Occitan ~caissa~, attested in the thirteenth century and carried north by trade, itself from Latin ~capsa~ (“box, book-case”), a noun usually connected with ~capere~ (“to take”). French had already inherited ~capsa~ by the regular sound changes as ~châsse~, the chest holding a saint’s relics, so ~caisse~ and ~châsse~ are in effect doublets: the same Latin box, one arriving by evolution and one by import. In Cicero the Latin word named the cylindrical case that held book rolls, and in Pliny a container for fruit, so the sense of a purpose-built receptacle was there from the start. The same etymon gave Italian ~cassa~, Spanish ~caja~ and, through Norman French ~casse~, English ~case~; English ~cash~, originally a money-box, and ~capsule~ belong to the family too.

The sense history is a tidy chain of containers. In 1510 ~encaisser~ meant to pack goods into a crate, and gardeners still ~encaissent~ trees by potting them in wooden boxes. In 1690 the box became specifically the cash box, and to ~encaisser~ was to put money into it; by 1832 the verb had shed the box and simply meant to receive or collect a sum, which is its central modern sense — ~encaisser un chèque~, ~encaisser les recettes~. A third, geographical use appeared in 1791: a river ~encaissée~ between steep slopes is boxed in, and the participle survives in ~une vallée encaissée~. The colloquial sense dates from 1867, with ~encaisser un soufflet~, to take a slap, and it broadened to enduring punishment of any kind and then to ~ne pas pouvoir encaisser quelqu’un~, to be unable to stand someone. The dictionaries record the usage without settling the image behind it: the body imagined as a strongbox absorbing blows, or the blow simply received the way money is. The family includes ~caissier~, ~caisson~, ~encaissement~ and ~tiroir-caisse~.
en.enceindre:
~Enceindre~ matches Latin ~incingere~, “to gird about, to wrap round”: ~in-~ + ~cingere~, “to gird.” The French history has a wrinkle the dictionaries note: the thirteenth century said ~aceindre~ — for the TLFi rather a native compound of ~a-~ and ~ceindre~ — and the form ~enceindre~ (early fourteenth century, first as ~ençaint~) looks like a remodeling of it, the prefix swapped to echo the Latin verb. ~Ceindre~ itself continues ~cingere~, whose deeper ancestry is uncertain: a root *~kenk-~, “to gird, to bind,” has been proposed, but the comparisons remain debated. The kin are clear nearer home: Italian ~cingere~, Spanish ~ceñir~, and a string of English borrowings — ~succinct~, from ~succinctus~, “girded up,” the orator with robes tucked for action; ~precinct~, the space “girded about”; even ~shingles~, the disease, from ~cingulum~, “belt,” for the rash that belts the torso.

~Enceindre~ is the verb of city walls — one girds a town with ramparts — and its participle made the noun ~enceinte~: the ring of fortifications, then any enclosed space, and in today’s French also a loudspeaker, the ~enceinte acoustique~ that boxes sound in. Then there is the adjective ~enceinte~, “pregnant,” from Late Latin ~incincta~ — and here the dictionaries genuinely disagree. Read as the participle of ~incingere~, it means “girded about”: the woman wrapped, encircled. But a tradition as old as Isidore of Seville glosses it the other way — ~incincta, id est sine cinctu~, “that is, without a girdle”: the woman who has loosened her belt. And modern etymologists often suspect the word is really a folk-etymological reshaping of classical ~inciēns~, “pregnant,” an old term tied to the idea of swelling. Girded, ungirded, or neither: the question is still open, and best enjoyed that way. The home family runs from ~ceinture~ and ~ceinturon~ to the fortress and the hi-fi — and to that one adjective French students learn to reserve for expectancy alone.
en.enchanter:
From Old French ~enchanter~, which English Wiktionary says was “probably borrowed” from Latin ~incantāre~ (“to chant, to enchant, to bewitch”). That Latin verb was built from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) and ~cantāre~, a frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). Because the verb is likely a borrowing and not a direct inheritance, French also has the learned doublet ~incanter~. The Latin verb also gave Italian ~incantare~ and Spanish ~encantar~, and English ~enchant~ is a loan from French.

The development is a simple and striking one: singing over someone became casting a spell on them. French Wiktionary notes how close the link between song and magic is, which is also why ~incantation~ and ~chant~ belong to one family. From “to put under a spell,” ~enchanter~ weakened to “to delight, to charm,” and in modern French it is used both of fairy-tale magic and of ordinary delight, as in ~Enchanté~ (“Pleased to meet you”). The family includes ~enchanteur~ (“sorcerer, charmer”), ~enchantement~, ~désenchanté~ (“disillusioned”), ~chanter~ and ~chant~.
en.enchaîner:
A verb built from the noun ~chaîne~ (“chain”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~. ~chaîne~ comes from Old French ~chaeine~, from Latin ~catena~ (“chain”). The origin of ~catena~ itself is disputed: it is reconstructed from a Proto-Italic *~katesnā~ and sometimes tied to ~cassis~ (“hunting-net”) and a root meaning “to plait,” but several scholars — Martirosyan among them — judge it a borrowing from a Mediterranean substrate rather than an inherited Indo-European word. The deeper source is best left open. The same ~catena~ gives Italian ~catena~, Spanish ~cadena~, and, through Old French, English ~chain~.

Literally ~enchaîner~ means “to put in chains,” and from binding a captive came the figurative senses “to shackle, to subjugate, to enslave.” A further metaphor — links following link — yielded “to link up, to concatenate,” as one ~enchaîne~ ideas or scenes. The French family includes ~chaîne~, ~chaînon~ (“link”), ~déchaîner~ (“to unchain, to unleash”), and the learned ~concaténer~, drawn straight from Latin ~catenare~.
en.enclencher: Built from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and ~clencher~, itself a verb formed from ~clenche~, the latch of a door. French Wiktionary glosses it literally as “to put into the latch.” English Wiktionary parses it slightly differently, as ~en-~ plus ~clenche~ plus ~-er~. Either way, to ~enclencher~ is to engage a latch or a gear, and by extension to set a mechanism, a process or a reform in motion.
en.encombrer:
The origin is debated. French Wiktionary gives Old French ~encombrer~ (“to seize, to hinder”) and says the TLFi derives it from ~combre~ (“barrier”), despite a chronological gap, since ~combre~ is attested only in the fifteenth century. That word would come from a Gaulish word that French Wiktionary writes *~comberos~ (“barrage on a river”). English Wiktionary gives a similar chain through Early Medieval Latin ~incombrāre~ (“to hinder, to burden”) from ~combrus~ (“barricade of felled trees”), possibly from Gaulish *~komberū~, and compares Breton ~kember~, Irish ~comar~ and Welsh ~cymmer~. It traces the Celtic word to *~kombereti~ (“to bring together”), from *~kom-~ (“with”) and the Proto-Indo-European verb *~bʰéreti~ (“to carry”). It also records an alternative: Latin ~cumulus~ (“heap, pile”).

If the Celtic account is right, the picture is vivid: a pile of tree trunks across a river that blocks the way. The sense would then have broadened to any obstruction, then to a burden or a hindrance, and finally to something merely too bulky or too crowded. English ~encumber~ was borrowed from the French verb. The family includes ~encombrement~, ~encombrant~ (“bulky”) and ~désencombrer~ (“to clear”), while the Indo-European root *~bʰéreti~ is the same one that gave Latin ~ferre~ and English ~bear~.
en.encourager:
Formed in Old French from the noun ~courage~ with the prefix ~en-~ (“to put into, to make”) and the verbal suffix ~-er~ — literally “to put courage into.” ~Courage~ derives from ~cœur~ (“heart”), from Latin ~cor~ (“heart”), via a Vulgar Latin ~coraticum~. ~Cor~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱerd-~ (“heart”), source of Ancient Greek ~kardía~, Sanskrit ~hṛ́daya~, German ~Herz~, and English ~heart~ itself. For the medieval French, the heart was the seat of courage, so to embolden someone was, quite literally, to put heart into them.

The metaphor is the same one English keeps in “to hearten” and “take heart,” and it shows how concrete the abstraction once was. To ~encourager~ runs from rousing a wavering soldier to gently spurring a child or backing a worthy cause. Its opposite, ~décourager~, takes the heart back out. From the same root come a cluster of heart-words in French: ~cœur~, ~courage~, ~cordial~, ~accord~, ~courroux~, and ~écœurer~ (“to sicken, to disgust” — literally to turn the stomach, or heart). The medical prefix ~cardio-~, borrowed from Greek, descends from the very same Indo-European root.
en.encourir: Built from the prefix ~en-~ and ~courir~, as a calque of Latin ~incurrere~ (“to run against, run into”), whose ~in-~ the French prefix ~en-~ translates. ~Courir~ itself comes from Latin ~currere~ (“to run”). To ~encourir~ is thus to run into something, usually something unwelcome: ~encourir une peine~, ~un blâme~, ~la colère de quelqu'un~. English ~incur~ comes from the same Latin verb, so the two words are close relatives. The sense is of a risk or penalty one runs into, rather than one imposed from outside.
en.endetter: Formed in French from ~en-~, ~dette~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to put into debt. The noun ~dette~ comes from Old French ~dete~, from Late Latin ~debita~, the neuter plural of ~debitum~ (“what is owed”), from Latin ~debēre~ (“to owe”). English ~debt~ is borrowed from the same French word, and ~débit~ is a doublet of ~dette~. The same pattern gave Occitan and Catalan ~endeutar~, Spanish ~endeudar~ and Portuguese ~endividar~. The reflexive ~s'endetter~, “to get into debt,” is the form used most.
en.endommager:
~Endommager~ appeared around 1165 as ~endamagier~: ~en-~ + ~dommage~, the noun of harm, with the verb ending. ~Dommage~ is Old French ~damage~, from ~dam~ (“loss, hurt”) — Latin ~damnum~, “loss, expense, fine, penalty” — plus the suffix ~-age~. ~Damnum~ continues Proto-Italic *~dapnom~ and is generally linked to the root *~deh₂p-~ of ~daps~, “sacrificial feast,” and Greek ~dapánē~, “expenditure”: at bottom, a loss is what the feast costs. The Romance cousins are Italian ~danno~ and Spanish ~daño~; English, meanwhile, simply took the Old French words whole — ~damage~ is the Old French noun unchanged, and Spenser could still write ~endamage~, borrowed from ~endamagier~, in The Faerie Queene.

~Damnum~ was as much a lawyer’s word as a mourner’s: it covered the fine a court imposed as well as the loss a storm inflicted, and both strands reached French. On the judicial side, ~damnāre~ (“to sentence, to inflict a damnum”) and its compound ~condemnāre~ gave ~damner~ and ~condamner~ — and, through Old French, English ~damn~: the curse is a court sentence in miniature. On the civil side stand ~dommage~, the polite ~C'est dommage~ (“what a pity” — literally “it’s a loss”), ~dédommager~ (“to compensate”), and the legal phrase ~dommages et intérêts~, “damages.” ~Endommager~ itself stayed concrete and material — one endommage a roof, a cable, a painting, not a person. French thus spreads across a whole family what English does with the single word damage: the etymology’s old accounting — feast, expense, loss — still keeps the books underneath.
en.endormir:
~Endormir~ is in the Chanson de Roland (around 1100, as the participle ~endormi~, “asleep”) and continues classical Latin ~indormīre~: ~in-~ + ~dormīre~, “to sleep.” In Latin the compound took the dative and meant “to sleep on or over something” — and so, pointedly, “to be slack, to neglect”: a magistrate could fall asleep over a case the way one nods over a book; Late Latin added “to grow numb,” said of a limb. ~Dormīre~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~drem-~, “to sleep,” with cognates in Greek ~darthánō~, Sanskrit ~drāti~ and Old Church Slavonic ~drěmati~ (“to doze”); Italian ~dormire~ and Spanish ~dormir~ keep the simple verb, where French raised the compound to head of household alongside ~dormir~.

French sharpened a useful division: ~endormir~ puts to sleep, ~s'endormir~ falls asleep. Around the causative, the figurative senses bloomed early and never faded. By about 1175 the verb meant “to lull, to deceive” — to endormir someone’s vigilance is still to talk it to sleep — and Boileau, in 1660, used it for the bore’s special power over an audience. Medicine made it gentle: ~on va vous endormir~ is what French anesthetists still say — “we are going to put you to sleep.” The family includes ~dormeur~, ~dortoir~ (“dormitory”), ~rendormir~, ~endormissement~, and the loveliest title in the language, ~la Belle au bois dormant~ — Sleeping Beauty. English drew on the same Latin stock for ~dormant~ and ~dormitory~: a dormant volcano is simply one that sleeps. Etymologically, then, the verb never strays: whether it numbs a leg, bores a theater, lulls suspicion or soothes a child, ~endormir~ keeps doing the one thing its root has done since *~drem-~ — it makes something sleep.
en.endosser: Formed on the noun ~dos~ (“back”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“on, onto”) and the verb ending ~-er~. No verb *~dosser~ stands behind it, so the prefix and suffix were added together. The noun ~dos~ is inherited from Old French ~dos~, from Latin ~dorsum~ through a Vulgar Latin form ~dossum~, with cousins in Italian ~dosso~ and Catalan ~dors~. To ~endosser~ is literally to put something on one's back, as with a coat or a pack. The sense then shifted to taking on a burden, a task or a responsibility, and to signing the back of a cheque to transfer it, which is the sense behind English “endorse.”
en.enduire:
Inherited from Old French ~enduire~, from Latin ~indūcere~ (“to lead in, to bring in”), formed from ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead”). The Latin verb ~dūcere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to lead, to pull”), which also lies behind English ~tow~ and ~tug~ through Germanic, and behind German ~ziehen~. Italian ~indurre~ and Spanish ~inducir~ continue ~indūcere~ in their own way. ~Enduire~ is a doublet of ~induire~, which was borrowed from the same Latin verb later and in a more learned form.

The two French verbs divided the work. The learned ~induire~ kept the abstract senses of the Latin, to lead into, to induce, to infer, as in ~induire en erreur~. The inherited ~enduire~ developed the physical sense of spreading a layer over a surface: plaster on a wall, varnish on wood, grease on a mould. The noun ~enduit~ (“coating, plaster”), built on its participle, is the commonest everyday survivor. ~Enduire~ conjugates like ~conduire~, one of many French verbs built on ~dūcere~, together with ~produire~, ~réduire~, ~séduire~ and ~déduire~.
en.endurer:
French ~endurer~ comes from Latin ~indūrāre~ (“to harden”), made of ~in-~ and ~dūrus~ (“hard”). English Wiktionary treats it as inherited through Old French ~endurer~, which was already attested around 1050, while the TLFi calls it a semi-learned borrowing. Either way it is an old word, and a later learned borrowing of the same Latin verb gave ~indurer~, so ~endurer~ is its doublet. The adjective ~dūrus~ survives as French ~dur~, Italian and Spanish ~duro~, and the same root stands behind ~durer~ (“to last”), ~durable~ and ~endurcir~. English ~endure~ was borrowed from the French verb.

The meaning moved from the physical to the moral. Latin ~indūrāre~ meant “to make hard,” and to harden oneself against pain is to hold out against it, so French ~endurer~ came to mean “to bear, to suffer patiently.” The step is natural, though the sources do not document it in detail. The modern verb keeps a literary flavor and often governs a hardship: one ~endure~ cold, insults or years of difficulty. The original sense of hardening survives in the relatives ~endurcir~ and ~endurci~, which still describe a hardened heart.
en.enfermer:
From Old French (12th century), formed from ~en-~ (“in”) + ~fermer~ (“to close, shut”). ~Fermer~ comes from Latin ~firmāre~ (“to make firm, fasten, secure”), from ~firmus~ (“firm, steadfast, strong”). ~Firmus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~fermos~ and from PIE *~dʰer-mo-s~ (“holding”), built on the root *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). Through that root it is cognate with Sanskrit ~धर्म~ (~dharma~, “that which holds, law”) and, in the Romance family, with Italian ~fermo~ and Spanish ~firme~; English borrowed ~firm~ from the same Latin word.

The semantic logic is one of fastening: to “make firm” a door is to shut it fast, and so Latin ~firmāre~ gave French ~fermer~, “to close.” Prefix it with ~en-~ and you close someone or something ~inside~ — to ~enfermer~ is to shut in, to lock up, to confine. The word ranges from the literal (a prisoner, an animal, a treasure) to the figurative (to ~s'enfermer~ in silence or in one's certainties). From the same Latin firmness come ~ferme~ (“firm,” and also the farm, once a fixed lease), ~fermeture~, ~affermir~, ~confirmer~, and ~firme~.
en.enfiler: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into,” from Latin ~in-~) and the verb ~filer~, which derives from ~fil~ (“thread”). The verb ~filer~ goes back to Late Latin ~filāre~ (“to spin into thread”), from Latin ~filum~ (“thread”). The sense is concrete: to put something onto a thread, as one threads a needle or strings beads on a cord. By extension the verb came to cover slipping on a garment, and entering a street or passage in a line. Both sources point to ~fil~ and ~filer~, so the formation is plainly French.
en.enflammer:
French ~enflammer~ comes from Old French ~enflamer~, itself from Latin ~inflammāre~ (“to set alight”), a verb built from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) and ~flamma~ (“flame”). The doubled ~m~ of the modern spelling is a Latinizing respelling that brought the word closer to its Latin model. The sources also allow a second reading: seen from inside French, the verb looks like a parasynthetic formation from ~en-~, ~flamme~ and ~-er~. The two accounts give the same verb in practice, and the evidence does not rule either out, so the safest statement is that the word is Latin in origin and French in its present shape and spelling, with the prefix ~en-~ doing the work that Latin ~in-~ once did.

The family around ~flamma~ is large in French and includes ~flamme~, ~flambeau~, ~flamber~, ~inflammable~ and ~inflammation~, the last two being learned borrowings from Latin rather than inherited words. Beside them stands ~enflammer~, which keeps the popular French prefix ~en-~ where the learned words keep the Latin ~in-~. The modern verb thus has two layers in its history: a popular French form that took on the Latin shape in its spelling, and a learned vocabulary of fire that sits close by. Which of the two readings of its formation is the truer one is a question the sources leave open, and either way the word is a descendant of Latin ~flamma~.
en.enfoncer:
French ~enfoncer~ is built from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the verb ~foncer~, which derives from the noun ~fond~ / ~fonds~ (“bottom, depth”). ~fond~ comes from Latin ~fundus~ (“bottom, base, ground”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmḗn~ (“bottom”). That root is cognate with English ~bottom~, German ~Boden~ (“ground”), Ancient Greek ~πυθμήν~ (“bottom, base”), and Sanskrit ~बुध्न~ (~budhna~).

The literal sense is to drive something “to the bottom,” to push it deep in — a nail, a stake, a hand into a pocket. From there the meaning fans out vividly: to ~enfoncer~ a door is to break it in by force; to ~enfoncer~ an enemy line is to pierce and rout it, hence “to defeat”; and intransitively or reflexively, ~s'enfoncer~ is to sink down, to founder, to plunge into water, debt, or darkness. From the same ~fundus~ French keeps ~fond~, ~fonder~ (“to found”), ~fondation~ (“foundation”), ~foncier~ (“pertaining to land”), ~défoncer~ (“to smash in”), and ~profond~ (“deep”) — the whole family circling the idea of a base and what lies at it.
en.enfouir:
From Vulgar Latin *~infodīre~, a reshaping of Latin ~infodere~ (“to bury, to dig in”), formed from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~fodere~ (“to dig”). The simple verb survives in French as ~fouir~ (“to dig”), and the Latin ~fodere~ is generally traced to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to dig.” The Latin verb moved into the ~-ire~ conjugation in popular speech, which is why French ended up with ~enfouir~ and ~fouir~, both in ~-ir~, rather than in ~-re~.

The meaning has stayed close to the Latin: to put something into the ground and cover it, as in ~enfouir un trésor~. It then widened to hiding something deep, as in ~enfouir un secret~ or ~enfouir sa tête dans l'oreiller~. The family of ~fodere~ is rich: French ~fouiller~ (“to search, to dig through”) and ~fouille~ (“excavation”) come from it, as do ~fossé~ (“ditch”) from Latin ~fossa~, a dug trench, and the learned ~fossile~, from Latin ~fossilis~ (“dug up”), which first meant anything unearthed before it was limited to ancient remains.
en.enfourner: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~four~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to put in the oven.” The noun ~four~ goes back to Latin ~furnus~ (“oven”). The verb has relatives across the Romance languages, which built it the same way: Catalan, Occitan and Portuguese ~enfornar~, Italian ~infornare~ and Spanish ~enhornar~. Besides baking, French uses it in familiar speech for swallowing food in great haste, and for shoving something into a place.
en.enfuir: Formed in French from ~fuir~ with the prefix ~en-~, today used almost only in the reflexive ~s'enfuir~, “to run away.” Here ~en-~ carries the sense of “away,” which French Wiktionary ties to Latin ~inde~ (“from there”) and which also lies behind ~s'en aller~. The base ~fuir~ descends from Old French ~fuir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fūgīre~, a reshaping of Latin ~fugere~ (“to flee”), whose root goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰewg-~ and is shared with Ancient Greek ~pheúgō~.
en.engager:
From Old French ~engagier~, derived from ~gagier~ (“to pledge”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”). The base noun is ~gage~ (“pledge, security”), which French took from Frankish *~wadi~, from Proto-Germanic *~wadją~ (“pledge”), in turn from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wedʰ-~ (“to pledge, bind”). The Frankish word also passed into Medieval Latin as ~vadium~. Through this Germanic source, ~gage~ is a doublet of the borrowed English ~wage~, and a cousin of English ~wed~ and German ~Wette~ (“bet, wager”).

To ~engager~ was first to put something “into pledge” — to pawn it, to bind it as security. From this concrete sense of staking a guarantee grew the whole modern fan of meanings: to bind oneself by a promise (to commit), to bind another to oneself by hiring, and to draw a person or thing into an action (to involve, to engage in battle). The reflexive ~s'engager~ kept the strongest flavor of the original pledge — “to commit oneself.” The same family yields ~gage~, ~gager~ (“to wager”), ~dégager~ (“to release, free up”), and the borrowed-back ~engagement~. That a word for emotional and professional commitment began as a banker's word for a pawned object is a fitting reminder that to promise is, etymologically, to put something on the line.
en.engendrer:
From Middle French ~engendrer~, from Old French ~engendrer~ (also ~engenrer~, with an intrusive ~d~ between ~n~ and ~r~, exactly as in ~gendre~ “son-in-law”), from Latin ~ingenerāre~ (“to implant, beget, produce”), itself ~in-~ (“in, into”) plus ~generāre~ (“to beget, bring forth”), from ~genus~ (“birth, race, kind”). The chain reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~genh₁-~ (“to give birth, beget”). The same root surfaces in English ~generate~, ~genus~, and ~kin~, and in Spanish ~engendrar~.

Latin ~ingenerāre~ already carried the sense of bringing a living thing into being, and Old French ~engendrer~ kept that biological core: to father, to procreate. From there the verb spread figuratively to whatever one thing causes another to produce — a fault that ~engendre~ a quarrel, a policy that begets unrest. French still says ~engendrer~ for both senses, biological and causal. The prolific *~genh₁-~ family fills the modern language: ~gendre~, ~genre~, ~génération~, ~gène~, ~génie~, and ~ingénieur~ all descend from the same idea of birth, kind, and inborn capacity.
en.englober: Formed on ~globe~ with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~globe~ was borrowed from Latin ~globus~ (“ball, sphere”), which French Wiktionary links to Latin ~gleba~ (“clod”) and ~glomerāre~ (“to roll into a ball”). To ~englober~ something is thus to put it inside a sphere, and so to treat it as part of a larger whole: a plan that ~englobe~s several measures includes them all in one round shape.
en.engloutir:
French ~engloutir~ is usually traced to Old French ~englotir~, from Late Latin ~ingluttīre~, built with ~in-~ (“in”) on Latin ~gluttiō~ (“to swallow”). French Wiktionary gives only the Latin ~inglutire~ as the source. English Wiktionary adds an alternative: that the verb was formed within Old French from ~en-~ plus ~glotir~, a verb of the same Latin family. Both accounts end at the same Latin ~gluttiō~, so the dispute concerns where the prefix was added, not the root. English ~glutton~, which came through Old French ~gloton~, belongs to the same Latin family.

The literal sense is to swallow greedily, to gulp something down in one go. From there the image widened: the sea can ~engloutir~ a ship, a flood a village, and a spender can ~engloutir~ a whole fortune in a few months. In each case something vanishes whole into a larger appetite. The same root lives on in French ~glouton~ (“glutton”) and ~gloutonnerie~, which share the Latin ~glutt-~ stem, and in ~engloutissement~, the noun for being swallowed up.
en.engranger: Built from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”), the noun ~grange~ (“barn”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so literally “to put into the barn.” The noun ~grange~ comes from Old French ~grange~, from Vulgar Latin *~grānica~, a derivative of Latin ~grānum~ (“grain”): a ~grange~ was a place for storing grain. The verb first described bringing in the harvest, and it extends easily to any gathering and storing: one ~engrange~ crops, but also profits, memories or points. The word keeps a rural picture behind a very general figurative sense.
en.enlever:
Formed within French from the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ~lever~ (“to lift, raise”). ~Lever~ comes from Latin ~levāre~ (“to lift, lighten, relieve”), a verb built on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from the PIE root *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”). Through that root ~enlever~ is distantly cognate with English ~light~ (in weight) and, via Latin borrowings, with ~levity~ and ~elevate~; Italian and Spanish keep the parent in ~levare~ and ~llevar~. The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~inde~ or ~in~, adds a sense of motion away — so the compound means roughly “to lift up and off.”

The core idea is a lifting that becomes a taking-away. To lift a thing off a surface is to remove it, and French let the sense fan out: one can ~enlever~ a stain, a coat, a difficulty, or — more darkly — a person, giving the noun ~enlèvement~ its double life as both “removal” and “abduction.” The same lightening root colors a surprising spread of vocabulary: ~léger~, ~alléger~, ~soulever~, ~élever~, ~prélever~, and ~levée~ all carry the memory of ~levāre~. Even ~levain~ (“leaven”), the agent that lifts dough, belongs to the family — a reminder that to raise and to make light were once one and the same act.
en.ennuyer:
~Ennuyer~ is inherited from Old French ~enoiier~ (also spelled ~enuier~ and ~anoier~), from Late Latin ~inodiāre~. French Wiktionary explains the Latin verb as formed on the phrase ~in odio esse~ (“to be an object of hatred”), from ~odium~ (“hatred”). The sense was therefore “to be hateful to someone.” Related languages took the same verb: Spanish ~enojar~ (“to anger”) and Italian ~annoiare~ (“to bore, to annoy”) descend from it, and English ~annoy~ was borrowed from Old French ~anoier~.

The history of ~ennuyer~ is a long weakening. In Old French it was strong: to make odious, to torment, to cause grief or hatred. By the classical age the noun ~ennui~ could still mean deep distress, as in the tragedies of Racine, and only later faded into the modern sense of boredom. The verb followed, and today ~ennuyer~ means to bore or to bother. Its relatives include ~ennui~, ~ennuyeux~, ~désennuyer~ and, from the Latin noun ~odium~ itself, ~odieux~. English ~annoy~ shows the same path of softening, from “hatred” to mere irritation.
en.enquêter: Formed from the noun ~enquête~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~inquīsīta~ (the feminine past participle of ~inquīrere~, “to look into”), used as a noun in Medieval Latin as ~inquesta~ and giving Old French ~enqueste~. ~Inquīrere~ is itself from ~in-~ + ~quaerere~ (“to seek”), the source of English ~inquire~. French already had an irregular verb for this, ~enquérir~, so speakers made a regular first-group verb from the noun, a pattern fr.Wiktionary compares to ~solutionner~. The result, ~enquêter~, means to carry out an investigation or a survey.
en.enrayer: Formed from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~rai~ (“spoke of a wheel”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The word ~rai~ descends from Latin ~radius~ (“staff, spoke, ray”), which is also the ultimate source of ~rayon~. The picture behind ~enrayer~ is a cart wheel, presumably stopped by jamming something among its spokes. From braking a wheel the verb widened to checking anything in motion, as in halting an epidemic or inflation, and to a firearm that jams.
en.enregistrer:
From the noun ~registre~ (“register, record book”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“to put into”) and the first-conjugation verb suffix ~-er~. The noun ~registre~ comes from Old French ~registre~, from Medieval Latin ~registrum~, an altered form of Late Latin ~regesta~ (“things recorded, a list”), the neuter plural of the past participle of Latin ~regerere~ (“to carry back, record”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~gerere~ (“to carry, bear”). Cognate with English ~register~ and ~registry~, and — through ~gerere~ — with English ~gesture~ and ~digest~.

So to ~enregistrer~ is literally to “put into the record book,” and the surprise lies in that book: the original meaning of ~regerere~ was “to carry back,” a clerk physically carrying entries back to be filed. The doubled ~-r-~ of ~registrum~ is unetymological, picked up in Medieval Latin by analogy with other nouns in ~-istrum~. The verb broadened from formal registration of acts and births to the modern senses of recording sound, capturing data, and saving a file on a computer. From the same ~gerere~ family French inherited ~geste~, ~gérer~, ~digérer~, and ~suggérer~, while ~registre~ itself spread into Dutch, German, and the Scandinavian languages.
en.enrichir:
French ~enrichir~ is a parasynthetic verb — formed in a single stroke from the adjective ~riche~ (“rich”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“to make, to put into”) and the verbal suffix ~-ir~, literally “to make rich.” The adjective ~riche~ is itself a Germanic loan: Old French took it from the Frankish *~rīki~ (“powerful, mighty”), from Proto-Germanic *~rīkijaz~. Through that Germanic family ~riche~ is cognate with German ~reich~, Dutch ~rijk~, and English ~rich~, and with Gothic ~reiks~ (“ruler, mighty one”). The Germanic word was itself borrowed early from Celtic, akin to Gaulish *~rīx~ and Old Irish ~rí~ (“king”), all from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to rule, to direct in a straight line”) — the same root as Latin ~rēx~ (“king”).

The original force of the word was “powerful,” not “wealthy”: in early Old French a ~riche~ man was a mighty one, and only in the thirteenth century did the sense of material prosperity prevail. ~Enrichir~ thus once leaned toward “to make mighty” before settling on “to make wealthy” and, by extension, “to enhance” — one enriches a soil, a language, or a uranium sample. From the same stock French keeps ~riche~, ~richesse~ (“wealth”), and the borrowed ~Reich~, while the deeper root surfaces in ~roi~, ~régir~, and ~royal~.
en.enrouler: Formed from the verb ~rouler~ with the prefix ~en-~, which here has its locative sense of putting something in or around. To ~enrouler~ is to wind something into a roll or around an object. The base ~rouler~ goes back to Old French ~roeler~, built on ~roele~ (“little wheel”), from Late Latin ~rotella~, a diminutive of Latin ~rota~ (“wheel”). Cognates of ~rota~ include German ~Rad~ and Lithuanian ~ratas~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) by way of Old French.
en.enseigner:
From Old French ~enseignier~ (attested around 1050), from Vulgar Latin *~insignare~, an alteration of Latin ~insignire~ (“to mark, to distinguish, to make conspicuous”), compounded from the prefix ~in-~ and ~signum~ (“mark, sign”). ~Signum~ is, by one influential account, traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”) — the standard one follows — though some scholars favor a root meaning “to cut.” Cognate with Italian ~insegnare~ and Spanish ~enseñar~ (“to teach”).

The path from “marking” to “teaching” is the heart of the story: to *~insignare~ was to set a sign upon something, to point it out — and to point something out to a learner is to teach it. French preserves both ends. The original “marking” sense survives in ~enseigne~ (a shop's “sign,” and once a military “ensign” or standard-bearer), while the verb ~enseigner~ moved wholly into instruction. From the same ~signum~ spring ~signe~, ~signal~, ~signaler~, ~désigner~, and ~insigne~, and English ~ensign~, ~sign~, and ~insignia~. A teacher, etymologically, is one who sets up signposts — marking the road so the pupil may follow it.
en.ensoleiller: Formed from ~en-~ and ~soleiller~, which is itself ~soleil~ + ~-er~; English Wiktionary analyzes it directly as ~en-~ + ~soleil~ + ~-er~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and here has its sense of providing with something, so the verb means to fill with sunlight. The noun ~soleil~ descends from Latin ~sōl~ (“sun”), through a Vulgar Latin diminutive form. Today the verb is used literally, for a room bathed in sun, and figuratively, for a face, a day or a mood that is brightened.
en.ensuivre:
From Latin ~īnsequī~ (“to follow closely, to come right after”), in the Vulgar Latin form *~insequere~, which, as the deponent verbs of Classical Latin did, took an ordinary active shape. The verb is ~in-~ + ~sequī~ (“to follow”), and its development in French ran parallel to that of ~sequī~, which became ~suivre~. Words of the same Latin family include ~séquence~, ~suite~ and ~poursuivre~, and English ~sequel~ and ~sue~ are relatives that came through French.

In use, ~ensuivre~ means to follow as a consequence, and it appears mostly in the third person (~il s'ensuit que~, “it follows that”). French Wiktionary notes an interesting wobble. Speakers tend to reanalyse the verb as ~en~ + ~suivre~, so one commonly hears ~il s'en est suivi~ in compound tenses where the older rule would have said ~il s'est ensuivi~. For the same reason ~s'ensuivre de quelque chose~ is rare, because a complement introduced by ~de~ feels redundant next to ~en~. The verb thus shows a fossilised prefix, ~en-~ from Latin ~in-~, being pulled apart again by the speakers' own sense of the language.
en.entamer:
From Late Latin ~intamināre~ (“to soil, to profane”), attested in French from about 1120, with the sense “to begin, to undertake” following by around 1245. The origin is debated. The TLFi connects ~intamināre~ only “probably” to ~tangere~ (“to touch”) — the same touch-root behind ~contaminer~ — so the descent is offered with an explicit hedge rather than as fact. A separate hypothesis sets Latin aside altogether and proposes a Gaulish source, comparing Breton ~tamm~ (“piece”) and ~tennañ~ (“to withdraw, to extract”). The sources present these as competing accounts.

Whatever the root, the development is vivid: from a word meaning “to soil or violate the wholeness of” a thing grew the idea of breaching an intact surface — making the first cut into a loaf, a cask, or a reserve. From that first incision came the abstract “to begin” (to ~entamer~ a conversation or negotiations) and “to eat into, to diminish” (to ~entamer~ one’s savings or someone’s resolve). The French family stays close to the cutting image: ~entame~ (“the first slice”), ~entamure~ (“an incision”) and ~entamable~.
en.entasser: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (“into”), the noun ~tas~ (“heap, pile”) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to put into a heap. The noun's origin is not fully settled. English Wiktionary derives Old French ~tas~ from a Frankish *~tas~ (“mass”), comparing Dutch ~tas~ (“heap”), while French Wiktionary calls the origin obscure and mentions both a Frankish source and, more doubtfully, a link with Latin ~stāre~ (“to stand”). The Germanic account is the one that finds cognates elsewhere. The verb moved from piling up objects to crowding people together and, figuratively, to hoarding money.
en.entendre:
From Old French ~entendre~ (« to pay attention, to understand, to hear »), from Latin ~intendere~ (« to stretch toward, to direct one's attention »), formed from ~in-~ (« toward ») and ~tendere~ (« to stretch »). ~tendere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), the same root behind English ~tend~, ~tension~, and ~thin~, and behind French ~tendre~ and ~tension~. Italian ~intendere~ and Spanish ~entender~ are its close Romance kin.

The original metaphor is bodily: to ~intendere~ was to stretch the mind toward something, as a bow is drawn toward its mark. From « directing attention » the verb split two ways. In medieval usage it came to mean « to understand » — a sense French still keeps in ~entendement~ and the phrase ~bien entendu~ — and then, by a further drift, « to hear », the everyday meaning today. Its noun ~entente~ (« understanding, agreement ») gave English the diplomatic ~entente~. From the same root *~ten-~ spring ~tendre~, ~tendance~, ~attendre~ (« to await »), ~prétendre~, and ~étendre~ (« to spread out »).
en.enterrer:
From the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and a verb on ~terre~ (“earth, ground”), from Latin ~terra~ (“land, earth, soil”). ~Terra~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~terzā~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~ters-~ (“dry”) — so the earth was named, originally, as the ~dry~ land set against the sea. By the same root English has ~thirst~ (the state of being dry), making ~terre~ and ~thirst~ distant cousins. The literal force of ~enterrer~ is exact: to put something into the earth.

The core sense is to bury — a body, a treasure, a bone the dog hides. From there French extends it figuratively: to ~enterrer~ a plan or a project is to lay it in the ground for good, to abandon it; and to ~enterrer~ a rival is to outlive them. From ~terra~ flow a great many words: ~terrain~, ~territoire~, ~terrestre~, ~terrasse~, ~atterrir~ (“to land,” to come to earth), ~déterrer~ (“to dig up”), ~souterrain~ (“underground”), and even ~terrier~ — both the burrow and the dog bred to go down it.
en.enthousiasmer: A verb made from the noun ~enthousiasme~ with the verbalizing ending ~-er~, meaning “to fill with enthusiasm.” The noun is attested in French since at least 1546, in Rabelais, and came through Latin ~enthusiasmus~ from Greek ~enthousiasmós~ (“inspiration, divine possession”). The Greek word rests on ~éntheos~ (“inspired by a god”), formed of ~en~ (“in”) and ~theós~ (“god”). To be enthusiastic was thus, literally, to have a god within.
en.entourer:
A denominal verb formed from ~entour~ (“surroundings, what is round about”), which is ~en~ (“in”) + ~tour~ (“a turn, a going-around”). ~Tour~ comes from Latin ~tornus~ (“a lathe, a turner's tool for tracing circles”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τόρνος~, from Proto-Indo-European *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, bore, turn by twisting”). Cognate, through ~tornus~ and the verb ~tornāre~, with Italian ~tornare~, Spanish ~tornar~, and English ~turn~ and ~tour~.

The image is geometric: to ~entourer~ is to set things all around, as a circle is traced by a turning point. An older form ~entourner~ survived into the 16th century before being smoothed to ~entourer~. From it French draws ~entourage~ (the people round about a person) and ~entour~ in the literary ~à l'entour~ (“round about”). The deeper ~tour~/~tornus~ family is vast: ~tourner~, ~tour~ (both the masculine “turn/circuit” and the feminine “tower” by a different route), ~détour~, ~contour~, ~tournoi~, ~tornade~ (via Spanish), and ~tour~ in ~faire le tour~. All circle back to the carpenter's lathe — a tool that makes roundness by turning, the very gesture of surrounding.
en.entraver:
French has two verbs spelled ~entraver~, and the sources hedge on the first. The common one, “to hobble, to hinder,” is explained in two ways. It may be borrowed from Old Occitan ~entravar~ (“to put a beam on”), from ~trau~ (“beam”), itself from Latin ~trabs~, accusative ~trabem~ (“beam”). Or it may have been built in French from ~en-~ and Old French ~tref~ (“beam”), which has the same Latin source. The two accounts agree that a beam lies at the root of the word. They differ only on whether French took the verb ready-made from Occitan or assembled it from its own parts, and the evidence does not choose between them. That is why the origin of this first ~entraver~ is best told as a possibility rather than a certainty.

The second ~entraver~ is a different word. It descends from Old French ~enterver~ (“to understand”), which goes back to Latin ~interrogāre~ (“to ask, to question”). It is therefore a doublet of ~interroger~, since both go back to the same Latin verb by different routes. English Wiktionary adds that the form of ~enterver~ was influenced by the first ~entraver~, which is why the two verbs now look identical. A verb for blocking movement and a verb for understanding a question thus share one spelling, partly as a result of that influence. Its Old French ancestor already meant “to understand,” a sense that comes from the Latin question and not from beams. For this second verb the hedge falls away, because the evidence traces it plainly to Latin.
en.entraîner:
From Old French ~traîner~ (~traïner~, “to drag, to trail”), prefixed with ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~). The base verb descends from Vulgar Latin *~traginare~, a derivative of *~tragere~, itself reshaped from Classical Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, to draw, to drag”). The deeper origin of ~trahere~ is uncertain — perhaps a Proto-Indo-European *~dʰregʰ-~ — but its past participle ~tractus~ seeded an enormous Latin and English family. Cognate descendants of the same base appear in Italian ~trainare~ and Spanish ~entrenar~ (“to train”).

The literal sense was physical: to drag something along behind oneself, as a current ~entraîne~ a swimmer or a horse drags a cart. From “to pull along” grew the figurative “to lead, to carry away, to bring about as a consequence,” and then the modern athletic sense “to train, to coach” — to repeatedly put someone through their paces, drawing them toward fitness. English borrowed this last sense as ~train~. The shared root ~trahere~ / ~tractus~ underlies a wealth of French words, among them ~traire~ (“to milk”), ~trait~, ~tracter~, ~traction~, ~abstrait~, ~extraire~, and ~portrait~ — all turning on the idea of drawing or pulling.
en.entreposer: Formed from ~poser~ and the prefix ~entre-~, from Old French ~entre-~ and Latin ~inter~ (“between”). It means to put goods into a depot or warehouse, and it is the source of the noun ~entrepôt~ (“warehouse, storage depot”), which English also borrowed. The prefix has no clearly compositional force here, as in many old words with ~entre-~, so the verb is best read as a lexicalized unit. The base ~poser~ goes back to Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to halt, to rest”), which in speech took over the sense “to put, to set down” from Latin ~ponere~.
en.entreprendre:
Formed in Old French from the prefix ~entre-~ (“between, among”), from Latin ~inter~, and the verb ~prendre~ (“to take”). ~Prendre~ descends from Latin ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, seize”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) plus a root ~-hendere~ from PIE *~gʰed-~ (“to seize, take”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~get~ and ~forget~ and with Greek ~khandánō~ (“to hold, contain”). The compound is often read as a calque of the Frankish *~underneman~ (literally “to take among / take under”), the same notion that English keeps in ~undertake~ — to take a task upon oneself.

The image is of reaching in among possibilities and seizing one — taking something on. French let ~entreprendre~ mean to begin a venture, a project, even an effort against someone (~entreprendre quelqu'un~). From it grew the powerhouse noun ~entreprise~ (“undertaking, business firm”) and the agent ~entrepreneur~, which English then borrowed back wholesale for the figure who launches ventures. From the ~prehendere~ root French also keeps ~prendre~, ~apprendre~ (“to take to oneself,” hence “to learn”), ~comprendre~ (“to take together,” hence “to understand”), ~surprendre~, and ~prison~ — a whole web of taking, learning, and grasping.
en.entrer:
From Old French ~entrer~, from Latin ~intrāre~ (“to enter, to go inside”), a denominal verb from ~intrā~ (“within, inside”). ~intrā~ goes back through *~interus~ (“inner,” the source also of ~interior~) to the Proto-Indo-European *~h₁énteros~ (“inner, what is inside”), itself from *~h₁én~ (“in”) — the same little particle behind English ~in~ and Latin ~in~. The Romance cousins all line up: Italian ~entrare~, Spanish ~entrar~, Portuguese ~entrar~.

The verb has stayed close to its plain spatial sense — “to go in” — for two thousand years, which is part of why it remains one of the most common verbs in French. Its figurative reach grew, though: one can ~entrer~ a profession, ~entrer~ data into a machine, or ~entrer~ into a discussion. The ~intrā-~ / ~inter-~ pair seeded a large family in French: the literal ~entrée~ (“entrance,” and the dish that “enters” a meal), ~rentrer~ (“to re-enter, to go back home”), ~entrer~'s causative ~introduire~ (“to lead in”), and the cluster ~intérieur~, ~interne~, ~intime~ — every one of them, at bottom, about being or going “inside.”
en.entretenir:
A compound coined in Old French (12th century) from ~entre~ (“between, mutually”) and ~tenir~ (“to hold”), literally “to hold between” or “to hold together.” ~Entre~ comes from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), and ~tenir~ from Latin ~tenere~ (“to hold, to keep”), which goes back through Proto-Italic to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). That root also yielded Ancient Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”), Sanskrit ~tanóti~, and English ~thin~ — holding conceived as keeping something taut.

The earliest sense was reciprocal: parties who ~entretenir~ one another held together, supported each other. From “holding together” the verb branched in two directions. One leads to material upkeep — to ~entretenir~ a house, a garden, or a car is to keep it in good condition by sustained care; ~entretien~ is its noun, “maintenance.” The other leads to the social and conversational: to ~entretenir~ someone is to keep them in talk, hence ~s'entretenir avec~ (“to converse with”) and ~entretien~ in the sense of “interview.” The same root *~ten-~ underlies a sprawling French family — ~tenir~, ~retenir~, ~contenir~, ~maintenir~, ~tendre~, ~tension~ — all turning on holding, stretching, and keeping.
en.entrevoir: French Wiktionary derives ~entrevoir~ from ~voir~ with the prefix ~entre-~, in the sense of seeing something only partly or briefly, a “glimpse”. English Wiktionary instead treats it as inherited from Vulgar Latin *~intervidēre~, built on ~inter~ (“between”) and ~vidēre~ (“to see”). Either way, the base verb is ~voir~, from Latin ~vidēre~, and the idea is the same: seeing between things or at a half-distance. The sense then extended to foresee dimly, as one glimpses a possibility.
en.entériner:
From Old French ~enterin~ (“entire, whole”), which French Wiktionary derives from a Latin form *~integrīnus~, built on ~integer~ (“whole”). The same Latin word reached French by the inherited route as ~entier~, so ~entériner~ and ~entier~ are close relatives. Latin ~integer~ is ~in-~ (“not”) plus the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), meaning literally “untouched”, hence intact and complete. English holds the same word twice: ~entire~ came through Old French ~entier~, and ~integer~ was taken straight from the Latin.

So ~entériner~ means, properly, “to make whole”. The sense is legal: to give an act or decision its full and definitive validity, hence to ratify or confirm. Today it often describes accepting a done deal, as in ~entériner une décision~. The Latin root is behind a learned family in French: ~intègre~ (“upright, of unbroken integrity”), ~intégral~, and ~intégrer~, which adds a piece to a whole. Its popular cousin ~entier~ kept the old everyday form.
en.envahir:
From Latin ~invadere~ (“to go into, attack, invade”), which compounds the prefix ~in-~ (“into”) with the verb ~vadere~ (“to go, advance, rush”). ~vadere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wāðō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~weh₂dʰ-~ (“to advance, go”). Through that root the Latin verb is cognate with English ~wade~ (from Old English ~wadan~), which kept the older sense of forging ahead on foot, especially through water.

The core image is aggressive forward motion — to ~vadere~ is to stride or rush, and to ~invadere~ is to rush in upon. French inherited it as a verb of overrunning: an army ~envahit~ a country, but so do weeds, water, doubt, or a smell that fills a room. From ~vadere~ and its compounds French also draws ~évader~ (“to escape,” to rush out) and ~s'évanouir~, while the noun side gives ~invasion~ and ~envahisseur~ (“invader”). The same restless “going” sits beneath them all.
en.envelopper:
From Old French ~envoloper~ (also ~anveloper~), by way of Middle French ~enveloper~. French Wiktionary takes it as probably formed from ~veloper~ with the prefix ~en-~, while noting that ~envoloper~ is attested before ~veloper~. English Wiktionary instead derives it from ~en-~ plus Old French ~voluper~ (“to wrap up”), compare Italian ~-viluppare~, from a Vulgar Latin *~vlopp-~. That in turn is traced to Proto-Germanic *~wrappaną~ or *~wlappaną~ (“to wrap, to roll up”), and ultimately to a Proto-Indo-European root *~werb-~ (“to turn, to bend”). The deeper chain is thus a proposal, not a certainty. English ~wrap~ and ~lap~ (“to fold”) are kin to this Germanic stock.

The core sense is to wrap something so that it is entirely covered. The same root gave ~développer~ (originally to unwrap), ~enveloppe~ and, in English, ~envelop~ and ~envelope~. Montaigne uses the verb in the sixteenth century, writing of a man “wrapped and bundled up” whose worth is that of the sheath and not of the sword.
en.envier: Formed in French from ~envie~ + ~-er~, “to feel envy toward.” The noun ~envie~ comes from Latin ~invidia~ (“envy, ill will”), itself from ~invidēre~, “to look at with hostility”, literally to look upon someone (~in-~ + ~vidēre~, “to see”). French Wiktionary also gives a separate account that ties an ~envier~ to Latin ~invitāre~ (“to invite”), which looks like a different, homonymous verb and not the one meaning “to envy.” English ~envy~ comes from the same Latin noun, by way of Old French.
en.envisager:
From ~en-~ + ~visage~ (“face”) + ~-er~, attested from the sixteenth century. The noun ~visage~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~visaticum~, a derivative of Latin ~visus~ (“sight, appearance”), the past participle of ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). The verb thus literally meant “to bring before one's face,” “to look someone in the face.” Through the same root *~weyd-~ it is cognate with English ~vision~ and ~view~, and, more distantly, with English ~wit~ and ~wise~ and Greek ~idéā~.

The development is a tidy metaphor. To ~envisager~ someone was first to gaze at their ~visage~; from “having a face before one's eyes” the verb drifted to the mental sense of “having something in view,” then to “to contemplate, to consider” a possibility — to picture it inwardly as one would a face. English borrowed the word as ~envisage~ with this same abstract meaning. The root *~weyd-~ seeded a large French family, including ~vision~, ~visible~, ~viser~, ~aviser~, ~prévoir~, and ~évident~, all of which turn, one way or another, on the act of seeing.
en.envoler: A compound of the adverb ~en~ (“away, from there”) and ~voler~ (“to fly”), used reflexively: ~s'envoler~ is literally “to fly away.” The adverb ~en~ goes back to Latin ~inde~ (“from there”), and ~voler~ comes from Latin ~volāre~ (“to fly”). The verb is not related to Latin ~involāre~, despite the similar look. From the flight of a bird or a plane, the sense widened to whatever vanishes as if on wings: hopes, time, a stolen purse.
en.envoyer:
From Latin ~inviāre~ (“to send on a journey, to travel over”), ~in-~ (“in, onto”) + ~via~ (“road, way”). ~Via~ comes from Proto-Italic *~wijā~; the PIE source is debated, but it is plausibly a doublet of English ~way~, both descending from a root for travelling or pursuing. To send someone was, literally, to “put them on the road.” Italian ~inviare~ and Spanish ~enviar~ are direct cognates, and ~via~ itself survives unchanged as the English and international preposition ~via~ (“by way of”).

The Latin sense “to set on the way” narrowed in French to “to dispatch, to send” — a letter, a messenger, a signal. A curious wrinkle lies in the conjugation: the future and conditional stems (~enverrai~, ~enverrais~) do not follow the verb's own pattern but were reshaped in the 18th century by analogy with ~voir~ (“to see”), an unrelated verb that merely sounded similar — so ~envoyer~ borrows the future of a stranger. The everyday ~envoyer chercher~ means “to send for,” and the noun ~envoi~ is the act or the parcel sent; the past participle gives the ~envoyé~ (“envoy, dispatched agent”), borrowed into English as ~envoy~. The ~via~ root also yields French ~voie~ (“way, lane”), ~voyage~, ~dévoyer~ (“to lead astray”), ~convoyer~ (“to convey, to escort”), and ~renvoyer~ (“to send back”).
en.errer:
From Old French ~errer~, from Latin ~errāre~ (“to wander, to stray”). The Latin verb lived on in Italian ~errare~ and Spanish ~errar~, and English ~err~ is a learned borrowing of the same word. Latin ~errāre~ already carried two ideas at once: to roam physically and to stray from the truth. The second idea fed the noun ~erreur~ and learned adjectives such as ~erroné~, while ~aberrant~ comes from Latin ~aberrāre~ (“to stray away”).

The history is tangled, because Old French also had an ~errer~ meaning “to travel, to ride,” as in the ~chevalier errant~, the knight-errant who rode from adventure to adventure. According to Wartburg, that sense of going to and fro comes from Latin ~iterāre~, while the sense of making a mistake comes from ~errāre~. The two verbs would then have merged into a single French form. In modern French ~errer~ means only to wander, to drift without a goal, of a person, a gaze or a ghost. The idea of a mistake has passed to ~se tromper~ and survives in ~erreur~ and its learned family. The image of aimless roaming, though, is the one the knight-errant left behind.
en.escompter: The evidence available ties ~escompter~ to ~compter~ (“to count”) and to the noun ~escompte~ (“discount”), without spelling out the intermediate steps, so only the outline can be given with confidence. ~Compter~ comes from Latin ~computāre~ (“to calculate”). The verb first belongs to banking: to ~escompter~ a bill is to pay its holder now, less a deduction for the time still to run. From that financial sense it passed into everyday French, where ~escompter~ means to count on something in advance, to expect it, as in ~escompter un succès~.
en.espacer: Formed in French from the noun ~espace~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to put space between things.” The noun ~espace~ comes from Old French ~espace~, borrowed from Latin ~spatium~, a word that covered a stadium, a racecourse, an extent of ground and a stretch of time. The modern verb keeps both the spatial idea, as in spacing out the letters of a word or the trees in a row, and the temporal one, as in spacing out visits or payments. The same Latin word gave English ~space~, also through French.
en.espérer:
From Latin ~sperare~ (“to hope, to look forward to”), formed from the noun ~spes~ (“hope”). Through Proto-Italic *~spēs~, the word traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~speh₁-~ (“to prosper, to turn out well”), the same root that lies behind Latin ~prosperus~ (“favorable, thriving”), source of French ~prospérer~. Its Romance siblings are everywhere: Spanish ~esperar~, Italian ~sperare~, Portuguese ~esperar~ — though in Spanish the verb has split its labor, also meaning “to wait,” since waiting and hoping are close kin.

The core sense — to look forward to a good outcome — has held remarkably steady from Latin into French. Old French had the form ~esperer~ with an initial vowel that French later dropped in the noun, giving ~espoir~ (the everyday word) beside ~espérance~ (a loftier, more sustained hope, drawn from the present participle). The negative prefix ~dé-~ yields the dark twins ~désespérer~ and ~désespoir~, the loss of all hope. Theological French ranks ~l'espérance~ among the three theological virtues, alongside faith and charity.
