From the same Indo-European root of thriving come ~prospère~, ~prospérité~, and ~prospérer~ — so that to ~espérer~ and to prosper are, far back, the same impulse toward things turning out well.
en.esquisser: Borrowed from Italian ~schizzare~ (“to squirt, to splash,” and so “to sketch quickly”), the verb is attested in French in 1651, after an earlier Middle French form ~esquicher~. The noun ~esquisse~ belongs to the same family. English ~sketch~ is a relative by a parallel route: it came in through Dutch ~schets~ from the Italian noun ~schizzo~. The idea is that of a rapid, rough drawing made in a few strokes, and French extended it to any first outline, as in ~esquisser un sourire~ (“to give a faint smile”).
en.essayer:
A denominal verb from the noun ~essai~ (“a trial, an attempt, an assay”), with Old French forms ~essaiier~ and ~assaier~. The noun ~essai~ comes from Late Latin ~exagium~ (“a weighing”), built on the verb ~exigō~ / ~exigere~ (“to weigh, to measure, to drive out”), which is ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”). That root also gave Greek ~ágō~ (“to lead”) and Sanskrit ~ájati~. From the same ~exagium~ come Italian ~saggio~, Spanish ~ensayo~, and, through Anglo-Norman ~assai~, the English ~assay~ and ~essay~.

The key image is the scale. To weigh a coin or an ore was to ~exigō~ it — to “drive it out” to its exact measure — so ~exagium~ named the test of a metal's purity, and ~essayer~ first meant “to assay, to test.” From testing a thing it broadened to “trying” anything: trying on clothes (~essayer une robe~), trying out a car, or simply attempting a deed. The same family yields French ~essai~ (a trial, and the literary “essay”), ~essayage~ (“fitting,” of garments), ~essayiste~ (“essayist”), and ~essayeur~ (“assayer”) — and, through ~agere~, the immense crop of ~agir~, ~acte~, and ~agent~.
en.essuyer: Inherited from Old French ~essuier~, from Latin ~exsūcāre~ (“to extract the juice from, to dry out”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~sūcus~ (“juice, sap”). The original idea was thus to draw the moisture out of something, and the verb narrowed from drying to wiping a wet surface. French later extended it to enduring, as in ~essuyer un refus~ (“to suffer a refusal”), and the sources I used do not explain that shift. The Latin ~sūcus~ also gave French ~suc~ (“juice”) and ~succulent~.
en.ester:
From Old French ~ester~ (“to stand, to remain”), inherited from Latin ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Italic *~stāō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Latin ~stāre~ lived on as an everyday verb in the Romance languages. Italian ~stare~ (“to stay, to be”) and Spanish and Portuguese ~estar~ (“to be,” of a state or a place) are its direct descendants, and in Spanish ~estar~ shares the work of “to be” with ~ser~. English has the root twice over. Its native cousin is ~stand~, inherited through Proto-Germanic from the same PIE root, like German ~stehen~. Its loan is ~stay~, which entered Middle English from an Anglo-Norman form of ~ester~ itself. French thus lent English a verb that it would all but lose at home.

In Old French, ~ester~ was a full verb meaning “to stand” or “to remain,” and stronger neighbors gradually divided its territory. ~Rester~, which comes from Latin ~restāre~ (~re-~ + ~stāre~, “to stand back, to remain”) and not from ~ester~, took over the sense “to stay.” More surprisingly, ~être~ absorbed part of the conjugation of ~ester~. The past participle ~été~, the present participle ~étant~ and the imperfect ~étais~ descend not from Latin ~esse~ (“to be”) but from forms of ~stāre~, so ~être~ is a suppletive verb, and its “having been” is, etymologically, a “having stood.” Stripped of these roles, ~ester~ survives in modern French only as a defective legal term, in the fixed expression ~ester en justice~ (“to take legal action, to appear in court”), and is used almost only in the infinitive: a fossil of a once-central verb. The same PIE root *~steh₂-~ underlies a vast family of French words, among them ~stable~, ~station~, ~statue~, ~constant~, and ~rester~ itself.
en.estimer:
French ~estimer~ comes from Latin ~aestimāre~ (older ~aestumāre~), “to value, to appraise, to reckon the worth of.” Its origin is debated. The traditional analysis splits it into ~aes~ (“bronze, copper, money”) plus an element meaning “to cut,” glossing it as “one who cuts the bronze” — that is, a minter weighing out coin; the linguist de Vaan instead links it to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eys-~ (“to seek”). Through Old French the word fanned out into doublets: learned ~estimer~ kept the Latin sense, while a popular line gave Old French ~aesmer~, source of English ~aim~ (originally “to estimate, to calculate a target”); English also borrowed ~esteem~ and ~estimate~, and Italian ~stimare~ and Spanish ~estimar~ are cognate.

The semantic arc runs from the marketplace to the heart. At first ~estimer~ meant to set a monetary value — to appraise — and that commercial sense lives on in ~estimer~ un bien (“to value a property”) and in ~estimation~. From “to reckon worth” grew the gentler “to judge, to reckon” (~j'estime que~, “I reckon that”) and finally the warm “to hold in high regard, to esteem” a person. The same root yields ~estime~, ~inestimable~, ~surestimer~, and ~sous-estimer~. If the old etymology is right, a feeling as lofty as esteem began at the mint, with someone literally cutting and weighing metal to fix a price.
en.estomper: Formed from ~estompe~ + the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Estompe~ is a borrowing from Dutch ~stomp~ (“stump, blunt end”), cognate with English ~stump~. In French the ~estompe~ is the stub of rolled paper or leather that artists use to smudge and soften pencil or charcoal lines, and ~estomper~ first meant to shade a drawing with it. The sense then widened, so that ~estomper~ now means to blur outlines, to dim a color or to soften a memory, and its pronominal form says that a shape or a feeling fades away.
en.exagérer:
Learned borrowing from Latin ~exaggerāre~ (“to heap up, to amplify”), which French Wiktionary explains as coming from ~agger~ (“mound, embankment”). French Wiktionary glosses the Latin verb as “to bank up, to increase”, so the physical image comes first: ~ex-~ plus ~aggerāre~ meant to pile up earth into a bank, and ~agger~ named the heap or embankment so built. ~Agger~ is generally linked to ~aggerere~ (“to carry toward”), a compound of ~gerere~ (“to carry”). Italian ~esagerare~, Spanish ~exagerar~ and English ~exaggerate~ are its relatives, all borrowed from the Latin verb. The French verb, like the Latin one, thus rests on a concrete picture of heaping material up before it was used of words and claims. To exaggerate, in this light, is to heap something higher than it stands.

The meaning later became figurative: to heap up came to mean to increase or amplify, and ~exagérer~ now means to represent something as greater than it is, so the old picture of earthworks has faded from view. The Latin root ~gerere~ (“to carry, to bear”) reaches French through ~gérer~ (“to manage”), ~digérer~ and ~suggérer~, so the same carrying verb that sits behind the mound also provides these familiar verbs. French also writes the verb ~exagérer~ with a single g where the Latin spelling had a double one, a simplification that the English ~exaggerate~ did not make. To go from heaping up earth to heaping up words is a short step.
en.examiner:
From Latin ~exāmināre~ (“to weigh carefully”), from the noun ~exāmen~. ~Exāmen~ is a contraction of *~exagmen~, from ~ex-~ (“out”) plus the root of ~agere~ (“to drive, set in motion”) and the instrumental suffix ~-men~ — literally “that which drives out” or “the means of driving.” ~Agere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, lead”), the root behind English ~act~ and ~agent~.

The surprise lies in what ~exāmen~ first named: the tongue or needle of a balance, the slender pointer driven by the weights that shows when the scale is true. To examine, then, was to read the balance-needle — to weigh a thing precisely and judge its worth. From the scales the sense generalized to any careful scrutiny, the testing of a candidate, the inspection of evidence. Curiously, ~exāmen~ also meant a “swarm of bees,” another mass set in motion by the same root. The PIE *~h₂eǵ-~ gives French an enormous family through ~agere~ and its compounds: ~agir~, ~agent~, ~action~, ~exiger~, ~exact~ (a doublet relative of ~examen~), ~rédiger~, and ~naviguer~.
en.excepter:
French ~excepter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~exceptāre~, which French Wiktionary derives from ~excipere~ (“to take out, to pick out”). That verb combines ~ex-~ (“out”) with ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”). The Latin idea is thus one of taking something out of a larger whole, and French kept it as a learned word rather than one passed down through the spoken language.

The image is literal: to ~excepter~ something is to take it out of a group so that a general rule no longer covers it. In modern French the verb is rather formal and survives mostly through its participle ~excepté~, which has hardened into a preposition meaning “except.” The noun ~exception~ and the adjective ~exceptionnel~ belong to the same family, as do many French words built on ~capere~, among them ~accepter~, ~concevoir~, ~recevoir~, ~percevoir~ and ~capable~.
en.exciter:
From Latin ~excitāre~ (“to rouse, to call forth, to wake”), in French use by about 1180. The Latin verb is the frequentative of ~exciēre~ (“to call out, to summon”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~ciēre~ (“to set in motion”), from Proto-Italic *~kieō~, from PIE *~keyh₂-~ (“to set in motion”). Through that root it is cousin to Greek ~κινέω~ (“to move”) — the ancestor of French ~cinéma~ and English ~kinetic~: the cinema and excitement are, at bottom, one and the same idea of setting things moving. Italian ~eccitare~, Spanish ~excitar~ and English ~excite~ all carry the same Latin verb, the English one having passed through French on its way.

The verb began gently: its first French sense, around 1180, was simply “to wake someone up.” From rousing sleepers it moved to rousing feelings — “to spur, to stimulate” (about 1223), “to stir indignation” (1587) — then to bodily reactions (1613), and modern science adopted it wholesale: neurons fire and atoms enter excited states under its name. The richest surprise is the verb's hidden kin: ~ciēre~ bred a clutch of French verbs through its own frequentative ~citāre~ (“to make come, to summon”) — ~citer~ (first to summon before a court, only later to quote), ~réciter~, ~inciter~, ~susciter~ — and above all ~ressusciter~, exciter's solemn near-twin: where ~exciter~ rouses you from sleep, ~ressusciter~ (from ~re-~ and ~suscitāre~, “to raise up again”) rouses you from death. Resurrection and excitement differ, in Latin's bookkeeping, by little more than a prefix.
en.exclamer: ~Exclamer~ is borrowed from Latin ~exclāmāre~ (“to cry out”), built from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~clāmāre~ (“to shout, to call”). The verb is now used almost only in its reflexive form ~s'exclamer~, “to cry out in surprise or admiration.” The Latin ~clāmāre~ also gave many French relatives, including ~réclamer~, ~proclamer~, ~acclamer~, ~déclamer~ and the noun ~clameur~.
en.exclure:
From Latin ~exclūdere~ (“to shut out, to exclude”), which passed through Old French ~excluder~ and Middle French ~exclure~ to reach its modern form. The Latin verb is a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~claudere~ (“to close, to shut”). ~claudere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~klaudō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg, bolt” — the things that lock a door). Cognate, through ~claudere~, with Italian ~escludere~ and Spanish ~excluir~; through the root, with Ancient Greek ~kleís~ (“key, bolt”).

The image is concrete: to ~exclure~ is to shut someone or something out the door, ~ex~ + ~claudere~, and the figurative “to exclude, to leave out, to rule out” grew naturally from that. The Latin ~claudere~ is one of the great hinges of French vocabulary, surviving in a swarm of related verbs: ~clore~ and ~clôturer~ (“to close, to enclose”), ~conclure~ (“to conclude,” to close together), ~inclure~ (“to include,” to shut in), ~reclure~ (whence ~reclus~, “recluse”), and the noun family ~clôture~, ~clé~/~clef~ (“key”), and ~clavier~ (“keyboard”). So an exclusion is, etymologically, a locking-out, and a conclusion a locking-together.
en.excuser:
From Old French ~escuser~, from Latin ~excūsāre~ (“to free from a charge, to excuse”), the exact antonym of ~accūsāre~ (“to accuse”). Both are built on ~causa~ (“cause, legal case, lawsuit”): to ~accuse~ is to put someone ~into~ a case (~ac-~, from ~ad-~), to ~excuse~ is to take them ~out~ of it (~ex-~, “out of”). The deeper origin of ~causa~ is uncertain — en.Wiktionary notes a proposed tie to ~cūdere~ (“to strike”) but adds that some doubt any Indo-European source — so the chain is best traced no further than the Latin noun. Cognate with Italian ~scusare~ and Spanish ~excusar~.

The legal metaphor is the whole story: French ~excuser~ still means to lift the blame off someone, to release them from the “case” pending against them. The same ~causa~ took a startling semantic turn in Late Latin, drifting from “lawsuit” to “matter” to plain “thing” — which is why Italian ~cosa~ and Spanish ~cosa~ both mean “thing,” and why French ~chose~ does too. So ~excuser~ and ~chose~ are quiet cousins. From the same family come ~accuser~, ~causer~ (“to chat,” itself once “to plead a cause”), ~causal~, and the noun ~cause~. The pronominal ~s'excuser~ (“to apologize”) literally has one declare oneself out of the case.
en.excéder: From Latin ~excēdere~ (“to go out, to go beyond”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, to yield”). The verb first meant to go past a limit, as when a sum or a speed ~excède~ a threshold. By extension it came to mean pushing a person past the limit of their patience, hence “to exasperate, to wear out.” The same Latin pair of elements underlies ~excès~ and ~excessif~, and the root ~cēdere~ lives on in ~céder~ (“to yield”), ~procéder~ and ~succéder~.
en.exempter: Formed from the adjective ~exempt~ and the verb ending ~-er~; Italian ~esentare~ is a parallel. The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~exemptus~, the past participle of ~eximere~ (“to take out, to remove”), built on ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~emere~ (“to take, to buy”). To ~exempter~ someone is thus, literally, to take them out of an obligation such as a tax or a duty. The adjective also gave a French noun, ~exempt~, for a kind of police officer, often picked from soldiers who had themselves been exempted from ordinary service.
en.exercer:
From Old French ~essercer~ (attested 1121–34), from Latin ~exercēre~ (“to keep busy, train, practice, work”), a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out, away”) and ~arcēre~ (“to enclose, hold in, keep off”). Latin ~arcēre~ goes back, through Proto-Italic ~arkeō~, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂erk-~ (“to hold, contain, protect”), the same root behind ~arx~ (“citadel”) and ~arca~ (“chest, box”). Italian ~esercitare~ and Spanish ~ejercer~ are its Romance cousins, and English ~exercise~ enters through the same Latin verb.

The inner logic is vivid: if ~arcēre~ means “to hold in,” then ~exercēre~ is literally “to hold out of an enclosure” — to let loose, to put to work — which is exactly what one does when driving penned animals to labor or marching soldiers from camp onto the drill field. From that image of setting energy in motion grew the senses of training, practicing a skill, and wielding a power, all of which ~exercer~ keeps: one exercises a profession, exercises authority, or exercises the body. The same root family yields French ~exercice~, ~exorciser~ (a different ~ex-~ compound, but the Latinate feel is kin), and the more distant ~arche~ and ~coffre~ of the storage sense. The surprising kinship is that a verb of vigorous activity hides, at its heart, a word for shutting things in.
en.exhorter:
~Exhorter~ was borrowed into French from Latin ~exhortārī~ (“to encourage, to urge on”), a deponent verb made of ~ex-~ (“out,” here intensifying) and ~hortārī~ (“to urge, to cheer on”). Latin ~hortārī~ is usually analysed as a frequentative of the older verb ~horīrī~, also “to urge.” The Latin family of encouragement then passed into the Romance languages by learned routes. Italian ~esortare~ and Spanish ~exhortar~ are parallel borrowings of the same Latin verb, not inherited descendants, and English ~exhort~ was taken in the same bookish way.

Because it was a borrowing, ~exhorter~ kept its Latin shape rather than wearing down through sound change, which is why it still carries the silent ~h~ that the Latin spelling preserved. The sense has stayed close to the Latin: to urge someone by speech toward a course of action or a virtue, in a register that is solemn, religious or oratorical (~exhorter à la patience~). The noun ~exhortation~ and the rare adjective ~hortatif~ come from the same Latin family, and all of them keep the idea of spurring someone on with words rather than with force.
en.exiger:
From Latin ~exigere~ (“to drive out, to demand, to exact, to weigh precisely”), compounded from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, to lead, to do”). ~Agere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to set in motion”). Cognate, through ~agere~, with Italian ~esigere~ and Spanish ~exigir~, and — through the root *~h₂eǵ-~ — with Greek ~ágō~ (“I lead”), Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“drives”), and English ~act~ and ~agent~.

The Latin verb carried a striking double sense: literally “to drive out,” but also “to weigh exactly,” from the image of driving a scale's beam level — whence the adjective ~exact~ (“driven to precision”). French ~exiger~ kept the forceful side, “to demand as one's due,” the creditor driving out what is owed. The root *~h₂eǵ-~, through ~agere~ and its participle ~actus~, is among Latin's most productive: French owes it ~agir~, ~agent~, ~acte~, ~action~, ~exact~, ~rédiger~, and ~naviguer~, while English gathers ~act~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~exact~, ~exigent~, and ~ambiguous~ from the same driving root. To exiger a thing is to drive it out of someone, forcefully and to the last measure.
en.exiler: Formed from the noun ~exil~ with the first-group ending ~-er~, though the two Wiktionaries tell it slightly differently. French Wiktionary treats it as a plain derivative of ~exil~, while English Wiktionary describes a semi-learned reshaping of Old French ~essillier~, from Late Latin ~exiliāre~. The noun ~exil~ comes from Latin ~exilium~ (also spelled ~exsilium~), which was linked either to ~exsul~ (“banished, living abroad”) or to ~exsilīre~ (“to leap out”); the choice between them is open. The first French attestation of the noun dates from 1080.
en.exister:
From Latin ~existere~, also written ~exsistere~ (“to step forth, to come into being, to appear”), a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out, forth”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, to set down”). ~sistere~ is a reduplicated form of ~stare~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the great roots of the family. Through it ~exister~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~hístēmi~ (“to make stand”), with English ~stand~ and ~stay~, and with the whole Romance family of standing verbs.

The literal Latin sense was vivid: to ~exsistere~ was to stand out, to step into view, to emerge — existence imagined as a coming-forth from hidden ground into the visible. French borrowed the verb in learned form, keeping the philosophical sense “to be, to have being” while letting the original spatial image fade. The same root *~steh₂-~ gives French an enormous progeny: ~être~ (whose past participle ~été~ comes from ~status~, not from ~esse~), ~rester~, ~stable~, ~station~, ~statue~, ~constant~, ~instant~, ~assister~, ~résister~, and ~consister~ — a vast family in which everything ultimately stands.
en.exonérer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~exonerāre~ (“to unload, to relieve of a burden”), formed from ~ex-~ (“off, out of”) and ~onerāre~ (“to load”), itself from ~onus~ (“burden”). French kept the figurative sense: to release someone from a charge, tax or obligation. English ~exonerate~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb, and the burden root also gives French ~onéreux~ (“costly”) and English ~onerous~.
en.expirer:
Learned borrowing from Latin ~exspīrāre~ (“to breathe out”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe”). Because it was taken straight from Latin and not inherited, the French form is close to the Latin one. Its cousins in the family include ~respirer~ (“to breathe again”), ~inspirer~ (“to breathe in”), ~conspirer~ (“to breathe together”) and ~transpirer~. The noun ~esprit~ is a distant relative as well, from Latin ~spīritus~, “breath”. English ~expire~ and Italian ~espirare~ share the same Latin source.

The verb has had a double life ever since. Its physical sense is to breathe out, as opposed to ~inspirer~, and it still has this meaning in medicine. A figurative sense arose early: to breathe one's last, hence to die, which is the sense of the English verb in the phrase “he expired”. From dying it was an easy step to the ending of things that have a lifespan, so a passport, a contract or a deadline ~expire~. The Latin habit of treating life as a breath, the soul leaving the body in the final exhalation, explains why “to breathe out” could come to mean both dying and running out.
en.expliciter: Formed from the adjective ~explicite~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to make explicit”. The adjective comes from Latin ~explicitus~ (“unfolded, clear”), the past participle of ~explicāre~ (“to unfold, to unroll”), itself ~ex-~ plus ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). The image is of something unrolled so that nothing stays hidden in the folds, which is why ~expliciter~ means to state a thing openly instead of leaving it implied. English ~explicit~ comes from the same Latin participle.
en.expliquer:
From Latin ~explicare~ (« to unfold, to unroll »), formed from ~ex-~ (« out ») and ~plicare~ (« to fold »). ~plicare~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleḱ-~ (“to fold, to plait”). Through this root ~expliquer~ is kin to French ~plier~ (“to fold”) and ~ployer~, and to a crowd of English borrowings — ~ply~, ~apply~, ~deploy~, ~employ~, ~explicit~ — all carrying the buried metaphor of folding and unfolding.

The Latin picture is concrete: a papyrus scroll rolled up, then ~explicare~ — unrolled — so its text lies open to be read. From « unrolling a scroll » the verb moved to « laying a matter open », and so to the modern sense « to make clear, to account for ». A fellow word travelled the opposite way: ~compliquer~ (« to fold together ») describes what is tangled, while ~expliquer~ undoes the tangle. The same root *~pleḱ-~ branches widely in French: ~pli~ (« a fold »), ~plier~, ~appliquer~, ~impliquer~, ~déployer~, ~exploiter~, and ~simple~ itself (« once-folded »).
en.exploiter:
From Vulgar Latin *~explicitāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~explicare~ (“to unfold, unravel, explain”), itself ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~plicare~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~plek-~ (“to plait, fold”). It surfaces in Old French as ~espleitier~ / ~esploitier~ (“to accomplish, carry out”) and shares its root with English ~exploit~ and, through the same Latin ~plicare~, with Spanish ~explotar~.

The path runs from the literal to the figurative: from “unfolding” a thing, to “carrying it out,” to “making it yield a profit.” Early Old French ~espleitier~ meant “to accomplish,” and the related noun gave English its ~exploit~, a notable feat or achievement. By 1560 the modern ~exploiter~ had settled into “to make productive, to turn to account” — a farm, a mine, a resource — and only later acquired the darker, pejorative sense of using a person unfairly. The same ancestral *~plek-~ branches widely in French through ~plicare~ and its kin: ~plier~ (“to fold”), ~ployer~, ~appliquer~, ~compliquer~, and ~expliquer~, that last one the learned doublet of ~exploiter~ — both descend from ~explicare~, one borrowed straight from Latin, the other worn down through popular speech.
en.explorer:
French ~explorer~ comes straight from Latin ~explorare~ (“to observe, examine, scout out, explore”). The verb is transparently ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~plorare~ (“to cry out, weep, wail”). The deepest origin of ~plorare~ is uncertain — etymologists do not assign it a secure Proto-Indo-European root — so we stop, honestly, at the Latin. Through ~explorare~ the word spread across Europe: Italian ~esplorare~, Spanish ~explorar~, and, via French, English ~explore~ and ~exploration~.

The surprising part is buried in ~plorare~, “to cry out.” The ancient — and quite plausible — explanation makes ~explorare~ a hunters' term: to ~explorer~ a region was first to scout it by sending up a shout, the cry that flushed or signalled game. From that very physical sense of beating the bush, the verb climbed to the cool, deliberate “investigate, examine” of the scholar, the surgeon (who ~explore~ a wound), and the geographer. The same tearful root ~plorare~ is hiding in plain sight in two other French verbs: ~déplorer~ (“to deplore, lament,” to weep ~de-~ thoroughly) and ~implorer~ (“to implore,” to weep ~in-~ toward someone in entreaty) — so that ~explorer~, ~déplorer~, and ~implorer~ form a small trio all founded on a cry.
en.exploser:
A back-formation dated to 1801: ~exploser~ was coined in French from the stem of ~explosion~ plus the suffix ~-er~. ~Explosion~ rests on Latin ~explōdere~, from ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~plaudere~ (“to clap, to applaud”). The deep root is given cautiously: ~plaudere~ is tentatively traced to PIE *~pleh₂-~ (“flat, to spread”), but the connection is marked uncertain. Through ~plaudere~, ~exploser~ is cognate with ~applaudir~ and ~plausible~.

The memorable detail lives in the Latin theater. ~Explōdere~ originally meant to drive a performer off the stage by clapping and hooting — to “clap him out.” From this noisy expulsion the word drifted toward the idea of a sudden, forceful bursting-out, and by the time French built ~explosion~ and then ~exploser~, the sense had become the violent release we know: a bomb, a boiler, a temper. The verb arrived only at the turn of the nineteenth century, when chemistry and artillery needed a precise word for it. Modern French relatives include ~explosion~, ~explosif~, and the contrasting ~imploser~ (a twentieth-century coinage on the same pattern).
en.exporter:
~Exporter~ was borrowed from classical Latin ~exportare~ (“to carry out, to carry away”), from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~portare~ (“to carry”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to pass through, to go across”) — the root behind Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbour”) and, on the Germanic side, English ~fare~ and ~ferry~. An isolated medieval form, ~soi esporter~, of obscure sense, appears around 1245; the verb proper, meaning “to carry outside,” surfaces in the early sixteenth century, and the commercial sense in 1756. For that last step the TLFi keeps a prudent hedge: the trade meaning arose perhaps under the influence of English ~to export~ (attested in 1665) — a word England had itself taken from the very same Latin ~exportare~.

If the English influence is real — it is proposed, not proven — then ~exporter~ made a tidy round trip: out of Latin into English commerce, then back across the Channel just in time for the free-trade debates of the eighteenth century, where d'Argenson's journal (1756) shows it at work. Etymologically, every export simply passes through the ~porta~, the gate, on its way to the ~portus~, the port. The carrying family is enormous: ~porter~, ~transporter~, ~importer~, ~déporter~, ~reporter~, ~porte~, ~port~, ~portefeuille~, ~portemanteau~ — and ~opportun~, by the classical account from ~ob portum~, said of the wind that blows a ship toward harbour: the opportune is what carries you safely to port. ~Exporter~ is the same gesture turned seaward: goods, words and ideas carried out through the gate.
en.exposer:
A French compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~poser~ (“to place, to put”), formed to render the Latin verb ~exponere~ (“to set out, to expose”), which had evolved regularly into Old French ~espondre~. The ~poser~ element comes from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to pause, to set down”), whose Romance descendants absorbed the senses of Latin ~ponere~ (“to place”), past participle ~positus~. Through ~positus~ the family is cognate with English ~pose~, ~position~, and ~compose~, and Latin ~ponere~ also gave Spanish ~poner~ and Italian ~porre~.

The literal meaning is to “set out,” to place something where it can be seen — and from this grew several modern senses at once: to ~exposer~ a painting is to display it (whence an ~exposition~), to ~exposer~ an idea is to set it forth, and to ~exposer~ someone to danger is to put them out where the danger can reach them. The construction with ~poser~ rather than the inherited ~espondre~ shows French rebuilding a Latin verb from transparent native parts. The same ~poser~ generated a large family: ~déposer~, ~composer~, ~disposer~, ~proposer~, ~imposer~, and the noun ~position~.
en.exprimer:
French ~exprimer~ comes from Latin ~exprimere~ (“to press out, to squeeze out, to portray vividly”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). ~Premere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to strike, to press”), the same root that, through Latin, gives English ~press~ and ~print~. Italian keeps ~esprimere~ and Spanish ~exprimir~ (“to squeeze”), preserving the very physical core sense.

The metaphor at the heart of the word is wonderfully concrete: to ~exprimer~ is to press something out, the way one squeezes juice from a fruit — and indeed ~exprimer le jus d'un citron~ is still good French. From this literal squeezing the Romans drew the figurative “to press a meaning out into words, to portray,” and that abstract sense, “to express, to convey,” is what dominates modern French. The buried ~premere~ runs through a large family: ~comprimer~, ~imprimer~ (“to print,” literally to press onto), ~opprimer~, ~supprimer~, ~déprimer~, and the nouns ~pression~ and ~expression~. So when one ~exprime~ a feeling, one is, etymologically, wringing it out under pressure until it spills into speech.
en.expulser:
From Latin ~expulsāre~ (“to drive out, to thrust away”), a frequentative of ~expellere~ (“to drive out”), which is ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~pellere~ (“to push, to drive”). The Latin verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pel-~ (“to thrust, to strike”). Frequentatives such as ~expulsāre~ express a repeated or forceful action, so the word carries the idea of driving something out with some insistence. French did not inherit it: ~expulser~ is a learned borrowing, taken directly from Latin, and that is what sets it apart from its cousin ~pousser~.

The two French verbs show how the same Latin family can enter a language by two doors. The plain verb ~pulsāre~ (“to push, to beat”) was inherited and worn down over the centuries into ~pousser~, and the learned ~expulser~ keeps the Latin shape almost intact. English shows the same pattern with ~expel~, from the simple ~expellere~, and ~push~, which is borrowed from French ~pousser~. In use, ~expulser~ is the verb of authority: one expels a pupil from school, a tenant from a flat, a foreigner from a country, or a gas from the lungs. The root also gives ~pouls~, ~impulsion~, ~répulsion~, ~repousser~ and ~propulser~.
en.expédier:
French Wiktionary traces ~expédier~ through Old French ~expedier~ from Latin ~expedīre~, while English Wiktionary instead analyses it as ~expédient~ plus ~-er~; the two accounts disagree. The Latin verb is usually read as a compound of ~ex-~ (“out of”) and the root of ~pēs~, genitive ~pedis~ (“foot”), its literal sense being to free the feet from a snare or from mud, hence to extricate and to make ready. The Indo-European root *~ped-~ (“foot”) is shared with English ~foot~ and Greek ~poús~. The opposite verb was ~impedīre~ (“to entangle the feet”), which gave English ~impede~, and French ~empêcher~ comes from the related ~impedicāre~. English ~expedite~ comes from ~expedīre~ too.

From freeing the feet, the sense moved to clearing an obstacle and getting something out of the way. ~Expédier~ thus came to mean to dispatch: to send off goods or letters, and also to dispatch business quickly, as when one ~expédie~ a task or a visitor. In slang, to ~expédier~ someone can mean to send him packing, or worse. The family includes ~expédition~ (a shipment, or a voyage with a goal), ~expéditeur~ (“sender”), ~expéditif~ (“quick”) and ~expédient~ (“a way out of a difficulty”). More distant cousins from the same root *~ped-~ are ~pied~ and ~pédale~.
en.expérimenter:
From Latin ~experimentare~, a late verb built on ~experimentum~ (“a trial, a proof”), itself from the verb ~experiri~ (“to try, to put to the test”). That verb is ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) joined to a lost simple verb *~periri~ (“to try, to risk”), whose root survives in ~periculum~ (“trial, danger”). The deeper Proto-Indo-European source is debated: it is often traced to *~per-~ (“to go through, to cross”), though some, like De Vaan, prefer *~perh₃-~ tied to ~pario~ (“to bring forth”). Cognate Latin verbs from the same family include ~comperire~ and ~reperire~ (“to find out”). Through the “going through” sense, English ~peril~ and ~experience~ belong to the same web.

The Latin verb meant to know a thing by living through it, so to experiment and to experience were one idea. French long kept both senses in ~expérimenter~, and the noun ~expérience~ still serves for both a scientific trial and lived experience. From the same root grew ~péril~, ~périlleux~, and ~expert~ (one who has been tested). The doubling of meaning is no accident: to the Romans, true knowledge was what you had risked something to learn.
en.externaliser: ~Externaliser~ is borrowed from English ~externalize~, itself built from ~external~ plus ~-ize~, which French spells ~-iser~. The ~-al-~ betrays the English origin, since the French adjective is ~externe~ with no ~-al~. The meaning has also shifted: English ~externalize~ does not mean “to outsource,” whereas French ~externaliser~ does, in the business sense of handing a task to an outside firm. It is a modern word, formed in English and adapted into French.
en.extraire:
From Latin ~extrahere~ (“to draw out, to drag forth”), compounded of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~trahere~ (“to pull, to draw”). The form ~extraire~ shows the regular Old French reshaping of ~-trahere~ on the model of ~traire~ (“to draw, to milk”). The verb ~trahere~ is traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~tragʰ-~ (“to draw, to drag”); it left Italian ~trarre~ and the learned ~estrarre~, Spanish ~traer~, and is held — though the correspondence is debated — to be akin to English ~draw~ and ~drag~.

The sense is wonderfully concrete: ~extrahere~ meant to haul something physically out — a tooth, a thorn, an army from a trap. French kept that literal pull (to ~extraire~ a tooth, ore from a mine, juice from a fruit) and added abstract ones, from extracting a passage out of a book to taking a square root in mathematics. The participle stem ~tract-~ of ~trahere~ seeded a huge family in French: ~trait~, ~traiter~, ~traîner~, ~attirer~, ~abstraire~, ~soustraire~, ~distraire~, and the bookish ~extraction~ and ~extrait~ — all turning on the idea of drawing or pulling.
en.exécuter:
From Latin ~exsecūtus~, the past participle of ~exsequī~ (“to follow out, to pursue to the end, to carry through”), compounded from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and ~sequī~ (“to follow”). Latin ~sequī~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), one of the most fertile roots in the European languages. Italian ~eseguire~ and Spanish ~ejecutar~ are cognates; through the same ~sequī~, French is kin with English ~execute~, ~sequence~, ~pursue~, and ~suite~.

The core image is following a thing all the way through to its end — and from “to follow through” came “to carry out, to accomplish.” The grim sense of “to put to death” is a specialization: to ~exécuter~ a sentence was to carry it out, and the phrase contracted onto the prisoner. The reflexive ~s'exécuter~ keeps the gentler meaning, “to comply, to do what is required.” The root ~sequī~ scatters across French: ~suivre~ (“to follow”), ~suite~, ~conséquence~, ~poursuivre~, ~persécuter~, ~obséquieux~, and ~second~ (“following, the one that follows first”). Modern relatives of ~exécuter~ itself include ~exécution~, ~exécutif~, ~exécutant~, ~exécutable~, and ~inexécutable~.
en.fabriquer:
Attested from the twelfth century, ~fabriquer~ is a learned reshaping of Latin ~fabricāre~ (“to build, to construct, to fashion”), itself derived from ~fabrica~ (“workshop, craft, skilled production”) and ultimately from ~faber~ (“artisan, smith, worker in hard materials”). ~Faber~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fafro-~ and probably to a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰabʰ-~ (“to fit together, to be skilful”). Cognate with English ~forge~ and ~fabric~, and — through that same root — with Armenian ~darbin~ (“smith”).

The popular, inherited descendant of ~fabricāre~ in French is in fact ~forger~ (by way of ~fabrica~ → ~faverge~ → ~forge~): ~fabriquer~ and ~forger~ are doublets, one borrowed from the books, the other worn smooth by centuries of speech. The learned form kept the broad Latin sense of skilled making, which is why ~fabriquer~ today covers honest manufacture as readily as the dishonest kind — one can ~fabriquer~ a chair or ~fabriquer~ a false alibi. The shared workshop root survives across French in ~fabrique~, ~fabrication~, ~fabricant~, ~préfabriqué~, and ~forgeron~, every one of them, at bottom, a thing made by a skilled hand.
en.faciliter:
From Italian ~facilitare~ (“to make easy”), borrowed in the sixteenth century, from Italian ~facile~ (“easy”), from Latin ~facilis~ (“easy, feasible”). The adjective ~facilis~ was built from the verb ~facere~ (“to do, to make”) plus the suffix ~-ilis~ — literally “do-able” — and traces, through Proto-Italic *~fakiō~, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place, to do”). The same root gives Greek ~tithēmi~ (“I place”) and English ~do~ and ~deed~.

The core idea has always been ease: to ~faciliter~ something is to render it ~facile~, to smooth its path. French already had the learned adjective ~facile~ when it reached across the Alps for the Italian verb, Italy being the prestige source of so much Renaissance vocabulary. The fertile root *~dʰeh₁-~ — “to do, to make” — seeded a vast French family far beyond ease: ~faire~ itself, ~facteur~, ~facture~, ~faculté~, ~difficile~ (literally “not easy”), and ~fait~, the bare past participle “done” that became the noun “fact.” Even ~affaire~ (à + ~faire~, “to do”) and the suffix ~-fier~ in countless verbs descend from this same Latin ~facere~. To facilitate, then, is etymologically to make the making easy.
en.facturer: Formed in French from the noun ~facture~ and the ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with an invoice, to bill.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~factūra~ (“a making, a manufacture”), from ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). It is a doublet of the Old French ~faiture~, the form that developed naturally from the same Latin word. In French, ~facture~ came to name the itemized bill for goods supplied, and ~facturer~ is the act of drawing it up or charging an amount on it.
en.faillir:
From Old French ~faillir~ (“to be lacking, to fail, to err”), from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, a remodelling of Classical Latin ~fallere~ (“to deceive, to trick, to escape notice”). The Latin verb is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to stumble, to deceive,” and it is plausibly cognate with Ancient Greek ~σφάλλω~ (~sphállō~, “to make stumble, to trip up”), though the precise reconstruction is disputed. Through Latin ~fallere~, ~faillir~ is kin to Italian ~fallire~ (“to fail, to go bankrupt”) and Spanish ~fallar~, and, by way of Old French, to English ~fail~ and ~fault~.

The sense shifted from deceiving someone to letting them down, then to falling short oneself. French kept a vivid trace of the older meaning: ~il s'en faut~ (“it is lacking”) and the impersonal ~falloir~ (“to be necessary”) spring from the very same Latin ~fallere~, the idea of something missing hardening into the idea of something required. Modern ~faillir~ is now used above all with an infinitive to mean “to nearly do” — ~j'ai failli tomber~, “I almost fell” — a ghost of failure that never quite happened. The same family yields ~faute~, ~faillite~ (“bankruptcy”), ~défaillir~, ~infaillible~, and the borrowed ~fallacieux~.
en.faire:
From Old French ~faire~, from Latin ~facere~ (“to make, to do”), from Proto-Italic *~fakiō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, set”). Romance cousins include Italian ~fare~ and Spanish ~hacer~. Through the same root come Greek ~títhēmi~ (“I place,” source of ~thesis~ and ~theme~), German ~tun~, and English ~do~ and ~deed~ — so the French “to make” and the English “to do” are, deep down, the same word.

The shift from “to put, set” to “to make, do” is natural enough: to make a thing is to set it in place. French ~faire~ swallowed an enormous range of senses, from manufacturing to weather (~il fait beau~) to causation (~faire faire~, “to have done”). A phonetic curiosity hides in its conjugation: the past historic ~fis~, ~fit~ comes not from the infinitive stem but from the Latin perfect ~fēcī~, whose long vowel left the telltale ~-i-~. From ~facere~ and its participle ~factum~ flow a vast progeny: ~fait~, ~façon~, ~facile~, ~facteur~, ~facture~, ~affaire~, ~défaire~, ~satisfaire~, and the learned ~-fier~ verbs (~modifier~, ~simplifier~) — every one a way of making.
en.falloir:
From Old French ~faloir~, an offshoot of ~faillir~ (“to fail, to be lacking”), from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~fallere~ (“to trip up, to deceive, to be wanting”). ~Fallere~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to stumble,” the same source as Greek ~sphallein~ (“to throw down, to make fall”) and Sanskrit ~skhalate~ (“he stumbles”). The impersonal ~falloir~ split off from ~faillir~ under the pull of its third-person form ~faut~ (Latin ~fallit~), remodeled on the pattern of ~valoir~.

The semantic journey is remarkable: from “to be lacking” the impersonal “it lacks” drifted into “it is needed,” and so a verb of deficiency became French's chief verb of necessity, ~il faut~ (“one must”). The notion of falling short survives across its relatives: ~défaillir~ (“to faint, to give way”), ~faillite~ (“bankruptcy,” a merchant who has failed), and ~faute~ and ~défaut~ (“fault, flaw, lack”). English borrowed the same family in ~fail~, ~fault~, ~false~, and ~fallacy~. So the polite ~il faut~ that opens a thousand French sentences is, etymologically, a quiet confession that something is missing.
en.familiariser: ~Familiariser~ is built on ~familier~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make, to render.” French Wiktionary cites the Latin ~familiāris~ (“of the household”) as the source of ~familier~, from ~familia~ (“household”), so the verb says literally “to make someone feel at home with something.” The suffix ~-iser~ itself comes from Greek through Late Latin and is one of the most productive verb-forming endings in French. Used first of making people at ease, ~familiariser~ now mostly means to get someone used to an idea or a skill, as in ~se familiariser avec~ (“to become familiar with”).
en.farcir:
From Latin ~farcīre~ (“to cram, to stuff”), inherited through Old French. Its compound ~infarcire~ (“to stuff into”) has a past participle ~infarctus~, which lies behind the medical term ~infarctus~ (“infarct,” a region of tissue clogged and cut off from its blood supply). English took the same medical word as ~infarct~. The sources give no firmly established deeper root, so the chain stops at Latin.

The French noun ~farce~ (“stuffing”) comes from the same Latin verb, and it gave English ~farce~. The theatrical sense is usually explained as follows: in the Middle Ages, short comic scenes were “stuffed” into the solemn performances of religious plays, and the name of the filling came to name the genre. A farce is thus, etymologically, a stuffing. Other French words from the same source include ~farci~, ~farcissure~ and ~infarctus~. The verb is also used figuratively, as in ~farcir un texte de citations~, to cram a text with quotations.
en.fasciner:
~Fasciner~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fascināre~ (“to bewitch, to cast the evil eye on”), which displaced the inherited Old French form ~fesnier~, the verb that would have developed naturally from the same Latin word. The Latin verb comes from the noun ~fascinum~ (“spell, evil eye”), whose own origin is uncertain. Italian ~affascinare~ and English ~fascinate~ are its relatives. French Wiktionary also gives a second account, a verb formed on ~fascine~ (“bundle, small faggot”); the sources do not reconcile the two, so the origin through ~fascināre~ is the better documented one but not the only one proposed.

The first sense was dark and magical: to fascinate was to harm or paralyze someone with a look, as the evil eye was supposed to do. The harm gradually dropped away, and what stayed was the idea of being held motionless by a gaze, which is how the modern sense, to captivate, was born. The image of a snake that fascinates its prey keeps the old meaning alive. The learned form won out over ~fesnier~, which left no descendant in modern French, and the family continues in ~fascination~ and ~fascinant~.
en.fatiguer:
From Latin ~fatigāre~ (“to weary, to tire, to harass”). Within Latin the verb seems built on an unattested *~fatis~ (“weariness, exhaustion”) plus a suffixal form of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”) — to “drive someone to exhaustion” — and it keeps company with ~affatim~ (“to satiety, enough”) and ~fessus~ (“tired”). Beyond Latin, however, the trail goes cold: the ultimate origin is classed as unknown. De Vaan rejects an older attempt to attach *~fatis~ to a PIE root *~dʰeh₁-~ “to vanish,” faulting it for vague semantics and phonology — so the deep root is genuinely uncertain, not settled.

The sense has held remarkably steady: Latin ~fatigāre~ already meant to wear down, exhaust, or pester, exactly as French ~fatiguer~ does. The figurative reaches are old too — one can ~fatiguer~ the soil by overworking it, or even (in cookery) ~fatiguer~ a salad by tossing it until the leaves go limp. From the same stem French keeps the adjective and noun ~fatigue~, ~fatigant~ (“tiring”), ~infatigable~ (“tireless”), ~défatiguer~ (“to rest, to refresh”), and the medical asthénie is unrelated, but ~fatigabilité~ is kin.
en.fausser:
Inherited from Old French ~falser~, from Late Latin ~falsāre~ (“to falsify”), itself from Latin ~falsus~ (“false, deceptive”). Latin ~falsus~ is the participle of ~fallere~ (“to deceive”). The sound change is regular: an ~l~ before a consonant became a vowel in Old French, so ~falser~ became ~fauser~ and then ~fausser~, the same change that turned ~falsus~ into the adjective ~faux~. Italian ~falsare~, Spanish ~falsear~ and English ~false~ are relatives.

French ~fausser~ means “to make false, to distort”. It applies to a ruling or a result that is skewed, to a key or a lock that is bent, and to a sound that is off pitch, so a ~fausse note~ is a wrong note. In the fixed expression to ~fausser compagnie~ to someone is to slip away, leaving them behind. The learned verb ~falsifier~ (“to falsify”) belongs to the same Latin family.
en.favoriser:
From the noun ~faveur~ (“favor, goodwill”), itself from Latin ~favor~ (“favor, support, applause”), a noun built on the verb ~favēre~ (“to be favorable, to be well-disposed toward”). The verb was coined in French by attaching the productive verbal suffix ~-iser~ to the stem of ~faveur~, on the model of Latin ~favor~. Related Romance forms include Italian ~favorire~ and Spanish ~favorecer~, both expressing the same idea of granting one's favor.

Latin ~favēre~ originally belonged to the language of religion, where it meant to look kindly upon a rite, and the formula ~favēre linguīs~ (“to favor with the tongues”) actually commanded onlookers to keep a reverent silence so as not to spoil a ceremony with ill-omened words. From this notion of benevolent regard the family broadened to mean showing preference, supporting, or advantaging — the senses ~favoriser~ carries today, including a faintly negative one of unfair preferment. The same root nourishes a tight cluster of French words: ~faveur~, ~favorable~, ~favori~ (borrowed back from Italian ~favorito~), ~favoritisme~, and the everyday ~favori~ of a web browser. Even English ~favor~ and ~favorite~ are, through Old French, members of this household descended from a Roman idea of divine and social goodwill.
en.façonner: Formed in French from ~façon~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to give a shape, to work on.” The noun ~façon~ (“way, shape, manner”) comes through Old French and Middle French from Latin ~factiōnem~, the accusative of ~factiō~ (“a making, power of doing”), from ~facere~ (“to make”). French ~faction~ is a learned doublet of the same Latin word. So ~façonner~ is, at heart, “to put into a manner of making.”
en.fermer:
From Old French ~fermer~ (“to close, to fasten, to make firm, to build”), from Latin ~firmare~ (“to strengthen, to make firm, to secure”), a verb built on the adjective ~firmus~ (“firm, steadfast, solid”). ~firmus~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, to support”), the same root that gives Sanskrit ~dharma~ (“that which upholds, law, order”). Through Latin ~firmus~, the French verb is cognate with Italian ~fermare~ and Spanish ~firmar~ (“to sign”), and with English ~firm~ and ~confirm~.

The semantic leap is the surprise here: ~firmare~ meant “to make firm, to secure,” and a door was secured by being fastened shut — so “to make fast” slid into “to close.” In Late Latin the closing sense took hold, and Old French ~fermer~ went on to displace the older ~clore~ (from Latin ~claudere~), which became homonymically tangled with ~clouer~ (“to nail”) and retreated into technical use. A folk etymology once linked ~fermer~ to ~fer~ (“iron”), imagining iron bars, but scholars reject it. The same root *~dʰer-~ underlies ~ferme~ (“firm,” and the noun “farm”), ~fermeté~, ~affermir~, ~confirmer~, and ~fermeture~ — and even the agricultural ~ferme~ traces back through the idea of a fixed, secured holding of land.
en.ferrer:
From Old French ~ferrer~, which goes back to Late Latin *~ferrāre~, known from the participle ~ferrātus~ (“fitted with iron”), itself from Latin ~ferrum~ (“iron”). The sources differ slightly on the route: one has the French verb inherited from the Late Latin form, the other allows that it was formed afresh in Old French from ~fer~ (“iron”). Either way the chain is short. Italian ~ferrare~, Catalan and Portuguese ~ferrar~ and Spanish ~herrar~ (where Latin f- became h-) are its sisters, and English ~farrier~ comes from Old French ~ferrier~, from Latin ~ferrārius~ (“blacksmith”).

The core sense is to fit with iron: to ~ferrer~ a horse is to shoe it, and anglers use the verb for setting the hook in a fish's mouth. Old French already had the ~chemin ferré~, found in Chrétien de Troyes, a road laid with stones on a firm bed so that one did not sink into it. The participle also took a figurative turn: someone ~ferré~ on a subject is solidly armed with knowledge, as in être ferré en histoire. ~Fer~ itself gives ~ferraille~, ~ferronnerie~ and ~maréchal-ferrant~, the farrier.
en.feuilleter: Formed from the noun ~feuillet~ (“leaf of a book, thin sheet”) with the verb ending ~-er~, although English Wiktionary derives it straight from ~feuille~. ~Feuillet~ is a diminutive of ~feuille~ (“leaf”), from Old French ~feuil~, from Latin ~folia~, the plural of ~folium~ (“leaf”). The verb is attested as early as the thirteenth century in a different sense, and it developed two uses from the image of a thin leaf: to turn the pages of a book quickly, and to roll out dough into thin layers, as in ~pâte feuilletée~ (“puff pastry”). English ~folio~ and ~foil~ are cousins from the same Latin word.
en.ficher:
From Middle French ~ficher~ and Old French ~fichier~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~fīg(i)cāre~, a frequentative built on Latin ~fīgere~ (“to fasten, to drive in, to pierce, to nail up”). French Wiktionary lists the Latin verb's senses as running from “to plant” and “to nail” to “to post up” and “to hang”, and adds that the participle of the Latin verb also gave French ~fixer~, ~fixe~ and ~affixe~. Those words are relatives of ~ficher~, not its descendants. French Wiktionary also derives the verb from the noun ~fiche~, whereas English Wiktionary derives all of it from Old French, so the two accounts differ on how much of ~ficher~ comes from ~fiche~.

The most familiar development is the colloquial one. French Wiktionary presents ~ficher~ as a euphemism for ~foutre~, as the reshaping of the participle ~fichu~ on ~foutu~ shows. English Wiktionary likewise calls the “give a damn” sense a minced oath of ~foutre~ (“to fuck”). In phrases meaning “to give a damn” or “to do”, ~ficher~ stands in for the cruder verb. A verb whose Latin source meant to drive things in and fix them in place thus ended up as the polite stand-in for a vulgar one.
en.fidéliser: Formed from ~fidèle~ (“faithful, loyal”) + ~-iser~ (“to make, to turn into”), so “to make loyal,” especially of customers or members. The adjective ~fidèle~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fidēlis~ (“loyal, trustworthy”), from ~fidēs~ (“faith, trust”). It replaced the inherited Old French form ~feoil~, which survives as ~féal~, and it became common only from the sixteenth century. The suffix ~-iser~ reaches French from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself taken from Greek, and is still very productive for coining verbs from adjectives and nouns.
en.fier:
Inherited from Old French ~fier~, from Vulgar Latin *~fīdāre~, a reshaping of Latin ~fīdere~ (“to trust”). The Latin verb belongs to a Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeydʰ-~ (“to trust, to persuade”), which also gave Greek ~peíthō~ (“to persuade”). The Latin word family is large: ~fīdēs~ (“trust, faith”), ~fīdus~ (“faithful”) and ~confīdere~ (“to trust fully”). English ~faith~ and ~fidelity~ are the same family, borrowed through French. Spanish ~fiar~ and Italian ~fidare~ are direct cousins of the French verb.

In French, ~fier~ meant to entrust, to hand something over in confidence, a sense kept in ~confier~ (“to entrust”). The modern verb is nearly always reflexive: ~se fier à quelqu'un~ is to trust someone, and the command ~Ne vous y fiez pas~ means “Don't trust it.” The lone ~fier~ is a trap for learners, because the adjective ~fier~ (“proud”) is an unrelated word that comes from Latin ~ferus~ (“wild, fierce”), and it shares only its spelling. The verb gives ~défier~ (“to defy”, originally to renounce trust) and ~méfier~ (“to distrust”), and the wider Latin family gives ~confiance~, ~fidèle~ and ~foi~.
en.figer:
Where ~figer~ comes from is disputed, and the two accounts run in opposite directions. By the first, which English Wiktionary adopts, the verb comes from Old French ~fegier~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~feticāre~ (“to take on the look of liver”), built on *~feticum~ (“liver”), an alteration of Latin ~ficatum~. French Wiktionary gives this as the view of some authors. By the second account, which French Wiktionary attributes to others, the order is reversed: ~foie~ comes from ~figer~, through a popular form *~figicare~ modeled on Latin ~figere~ (“to fix in the ground, to drive in, to fasten”), whose participle is ~fixus~. English Wiktionary mentions only the first account, while French Wiktionary sets the two side by side.

Because the sources disagree, the question cannot be settled here. If the first account holds, ~figer~ is a cousin of ~foie~, and the verb would originally have meant something like taking on the look of liver. If the second holds, ~figer~ belongs to the family of ~fixus~, the participle of the Latin verb ~figere~, which has to do with fastening something in place. Either way, the modern verb has the sense “to freeze” or “to set,” and in the reflexive ~se figer~ it describes something that stops moving. The sources do not allow a choice between the two origins.
en.figurer:
From Latin ~figurare~ (“to form, to shape, to fashion”), derived from ~figura~ (“shape, form, figure”), itself built on the verb ~fingere~ (“to mould, to shape, especially in clay”). ~fingere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeyǵʰ-~ (“to knead, to form, to build”), the same root that gives Latin ~fictus~ (“shaped, feigned”) and, in the Germanic branch, English ~dough~ and the ~-dy~ of Old English placenames. Cognate with Italian ~figurare~ and Spanish ~figurar~.

The root meaning is hands working clay, and ~figura~ kept that sculptural sense of an outline or moulded shape. From “to give shape to,” French ~figurer~ branched in several directions: to represent or depict (a drawing ~figure~ a scene), to be present in a series — to “appear in a list,” to be included among others — and, reflexively, ~se figurer~, to picture something to oneself, to imagine. The same family is rich in French: ~figure~ (face, figure), ~figuratif~, ~figurine~, ~défigurer~ (to disfigure), ~préfigurer~, and ~configurer~. Through its sibling ~fingere~ come ~feindre~ (“to feign”) and ~fiction~ — a reminder that the line between shaping something and making it up has always been thin.
en.filer:
French ~filer~ comes from Late Latin ~filare~ (“to spin into thread”), from the noun ~filum~ (“thread”); it can equally be felt as a denominal of French ~fil~ (“thread”), its inherited descendant. ~filum~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~gʷʰislo-~ (“sinew, thread”), and is cognate with Lithuanian ~gysla~ (“vein, sinew”), Proto-Slavic *~žila~ (“vein”), and Sanskrit ~jyā~ (“bowstring”) — a web of words for thin, stringy fibers.

The original sense is concrete: to spin fiber into thread, as a spider “spins” its web (~filer sa toile~) or a spinner draws out a thread. From the steady, drawn-out motion of the spindle the verb slid into senses of smooth, continuous movement — to ~filer~ is to glide along quickly, even to “slip away” — and then, by a memorable specialization, to “tail” or follow someone discreetly, paying out one's path behind them like thread. From the same ~filum~ French keeps ~fil~, ~filet~ (“net; thin stream; fillet”), ~ficelle~ (“string”), ~filature~ (“spinning mill; the act of shadowing”), ~défiler~ (“to file past”), and ~profil~ (“profile”).
en.filmer:
~Filmer~ is a denominal verb on the noun ~film~, which French borrowed from English ~film~ in the late 19th century as photography and cinema arrived. The English noun goes back to Middle English ~filme~ and Old English ~filmen~ (« membrane, thin skin »), from Proto-West Germanic *~filmīn~, tied to Proto-Germanic *~felma-~ (« skin, hide ») and ultimately PIE *~pel-~ (« skin, to cover »). So the word for a cinematic ~film~ began as a word for skin.

The sense « thin coating » is recorded by 1577; by 1845 it named the layer of light-sensitive gel on a photographic plate, and by 1895 the celluloid strip itself — and then, by extension, the moving picture recorded on it. French ~filmer~ inherited that final, fully cinematic sense: to ~filmer~ is to record images on film, or now digitally, to shoot a scene. From the same Germanic *~pel-~ « skin » root English keeps ~fell~ (« hide ») and ~film~ itself; French, having borrowed only the noun, built ~filmer~, ~filmage~, and ~cinéma~ around it.
en.filtrer: ~Filtrer~ is formed from ~filtre~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~filtre~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~filtrum~, attested in the eighth century and itself taken, according to French Wiktionary, from Frankish. It is a doublet of ~feutre~ (“felt”), the material the first filters were made of: to filter was originally to pass a liquid through a piece of felt. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and turns the noun into the verb “to pass through a filter,” a sense later extended to sounds, light, news and people.
en.finaliser: Formed from the adjective ~final~ (“last, ultimate”) with the verb suffix ~-iser~, and attested from 1936 in the sense of “to give a final form to, to bring to completion.” The adjective comes from Latin ~fīnālis~, from ~fīnis~ (“end, limit”). The suffix ~-iser~ is the learned French form of Late Latin ~-izāre~, from Greek ~-izein~. A later sense, “to complete,” is probably influenced by English ~finalize~.
en.financer:
Denominal verb from the noun ~finance~, which arose in Old French (around 1280) from the verb ~finer~ (“to bring to an end; to settle, pay”), an altered form of ~finir~ (“to finish”), with the suffix ~-ance~. All of this rests on Latin ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, end”). The early ~finance~ meant the ending or settling of a matter — and since settling an affair so often meant paying it off, Old French ~fin~ itself could mean “money.” Cognate with Italian ~finanza~ and Spanish ~finanza~, and — borrowed — with English ~finance~ and ~final~, all anchored in ~fīnis~.

The slide from “ending” to “money” is the heart of the story: to ~finer~ a debt was to make an end of it by payment, so the noun drifted from “settlement” to “payment,” then by the fifteenth century to “monetary resources,” as in ~trésorier des finances~ (“treasurer of finances”). Medieval Latin ~financia~ even named a tax or levy. The modern verb ~financer~ — to fund, to provide money for — is the natural offspring. From the same ~fīnis~ French keeps a broad family: ~finir~, ~fin~, ~final~, ~définir~, ~confiner~, and ~affiner~ — boundaries and endings everywhere, with money the great settler of ends.
en.finir:
From Old French ~finir~ (with the variants ~fenir~ and ~finer~), from Latin ~fīnīre~ (“to limit, to bound, then to finish”), itself derived from the noun ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, border, end”). The deeper origin of ~fīnis~ is disputed: it is often referred — perhaps from an earlier *~fignis~ — to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, set up”), the root behind Latin ~fīgō~ (“to fix”), a boundary being something “fixed” in the ground; an alternative links it to ~findō~ (“to split”). Cognate verbs are Italian ~finire~ and Spanish ~finir~.

The path of meaning runs from space to time: a ~fīnis~ was first a physical border between fields or peoples — hence the plural ~fīnēs~ for a country's “territory” — and from “to set a limit” the verb slid to “to bring to an end.” The same root spread widely in French: the noun ~fin~ (“end”), ~final~, ~finale~, ~finalité~, ~finir~'s cousin ~définir~ (“to define,” to set the ~fīnēs~ of a meaning) with ~définition~, ~infini~ (“endless”), ~finitude~, and the commercial ~finance~ — originally the “settling, ending” of a debt by payment.
en.fixer:
From Latin ~fixus~, the past participle of ~figere~ (“to drive in, to plant, to fasten”). ~Figere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, to set up”), which also yielded, through Germanic, English ~ditch~ and ~dike~ and German ~Teich~ (“pond”) — all things dug into or stuck in the ground. The Latin participial stem ~fix-~ gave Italian ~fissare~ and Spanish ~fijar~, and the same ~figere~ produced the diminutive ~fibula~ (“clasp, brooch”), a pin that fastens.

The earliest French sense stayed close to the Latin: to ~fixer~ was to make something fast, to set it firmly in place, then to settle the eyes upon it — hence ~fixer du regard~, “to stare at.” From “to make immovable” flowed “to determine, to settle definitively,” as in ~fixer une date~ or ~fixer un prix~. In the twentieth century French re-borrowed the modern repair sense from English ~to fix~, layering a fresh meaning atop the old. From the same root come ~fixe~, ~fixation~, ~fixe~ as a noun (a regular salary), ~préfixe~, ~suffixe~, and ~crucifier~ (literally “to fasten to a cross”). To ~fixer~ something is, at bottom, to plant it where it cannot move.
en.flamber: The verb is formed from the noun ~flambe~ (“tall flame”) and the verb ending ~-er~. It is recorded only once in the twelfth century, and it replaced the older French verb ~flammer~, which came from Latin ~flammāre~ (“to set on fire”), derived from ~flamma~ (“flame”). The verb means “to burn with a bright flame” and, in cooking, “to flambé” a dish with alcohol. By a figurative extension, it also means “to squander,” as in ~flamber son argent~, money going up in smoke.
en.flatter:
French ~flatter~ descends from Old French ~flater~ (“to deceive by hiding the truth, to stroke with the palm”), which English Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~flat~ (“palm, flat of the hand”), from Proto-Germanic *~flatą~ (“palm, sole”) and its relative *~flataz~ (“flat”), from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “flat, broad.” Cognates include Old High German ~flazza~ (“palm of the hand”), Old Saxon ~flat~ (“flat”) and Old Norse ~flatr~ (“flat”), the source of English ~flat~. English also borrowed the verb itself, ~flatter~, from Old French. English Wiktionary points to ~flétrir~ for further reading on the family.

The oldest image is physical: to ~flatter~ was to stroke with the flat of the hand. Already in Old French the verb had slid into a moral sense, to coax or deceive with soft words, and that sense won out: today ~flatter~ means to praise someone beyond what is deserved in order to please. A second line of meaning kept the idea of gentle contact and pleasing effect, as when a dress ~flatte~ the figure or a sound ~flatte~ the ear. Related words include ~flatteur~ and ~flatterie~, and the sense of “stroking” makes the verb a close cousin of ~caresser~ in its earliest use.
en.fleurer: The verb ~fleurer~ (“to give off a smell”) is labeled a derivative of ~fleur~ by French Wiktionary, but the flower may not be involved. English Wiktionary connects it with an old noun ~fleur~ meaning “odour,” now surviving only in dialects, from Old French ~flaour~ (the source of English ~flavour~), ultimately from Latin ~flātus~ (“a blowing, breath”). It also allows that ~fleurer~ may simply be a variant of ~flairer~ (“to sniff out”). The link with the flower noun, from Latin ~flōrem~, is therefore doubtful. Formally, the verb takes the ending ~-er~. The origin remains unsettled.
en.fleurir:
From Latin ~florire~, a Vulgar Latin reshaping of Classical ~florere~ (“to bloom, to flourish”), from ~flos~, stem ~flor-~ (“flower”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰleh₃-~ (“to bloom, to flourish”). The same root, on its Germanic side, gives English ~bloom~, ~blossom~, and ~blade~, and the Gothic ~blōma~ (“flower”) — so the French and English words for flowering are deep cousins.

French kept two strands of meaning side by side. The regular ~fleurir~ means “to flower, to bloom”; but in the figurative sense “to flourish, to thrive,” the older present participle survives as ~florissant~ (and the past ~florissait~), preserving the Latin ~flor-~ rather than the diphthongized ~fleur-~ — a rare doublet within one verb. From the same root grew ~fleur~ (“flower”), ~floraison~ (“blooming”), ~flore~ (“flora”), ~refleurir~, and ~défleurir~. To say a city ~florissait~ was to picture it literally in flower.
en.flotter:
~Flotter~ comes from Middle French ~flotter~, from Old French ~floter~ (“to float”), itself from Frankish *~flotōn~ (“to float, swim”), a Germanic verb that the Franks brought to Gaul. Frankish goes back to Proto-Germanic *~flutōną~ (“to float, swim”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~plew-~ (“to flow, swim”). Its Germanic relatives are Middle Dutch ~vlōten~, Old English ~flotian~ and Old Norse ~flota~ (“to float, to launch”), and English ~float~ is the sibling that never left Germanic ground. The same root also gave Latin ~pluere~ (“to rain”) and Greek ~plein~ (“to sail”), so the rain, the ship and the log on the river share an ancestor.

The verb was first about water: to float, to drift. It then spread to whatever moves like a floating thing. A flag flutters in the wind, a smell or a mood hangs in the air, a crowd mills about, and a hesitating person ~flotte~ between two choices. French Wiktionary links the verb to the noun ~flot~ (“wave”) and, for one of its senses, to ~flotte~, without settling the details; the Frankish descent above comes from English Wiktionary. The family is large: ~flottant~, ~flotteur~ (“float”), ~flottement~ (“wavering”) and ~flotte~ itself, which can mean a fleet or, in slang, water.
en.focaliser: Formed from the adjective ~focal~ plus the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to bring to”), with the stem losing its ending: to bring to a focus, to concentrate on one point, whether light rays or attention. The adjective is a learned formation from New Latin ~focālis~, built on Latin ~focus~ (“hearth, fire”), the same word that gave the inherited French ~foyer~. The optical sense of “burning point” where rays meet explains the shift from fireplace to focal point.
en.foncer:
Derived from ~fons~, an older form of ~fond~ and ~fonds~ (« bottom, base, fund »), which descend from Latin ~fundus~ (« bottom, foundation, estate »). ~fundus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmḗn~ (« bottom »), cognate with English ~bottom~ and German ~Boden~ (« ground, soil »). So ~foncer~ is, at root, « to deal with the bottom of a thing ».

From that base the verb fanned out concretely — « to fit a bottom into » a cask, then « to dig down », and so « to darken », since to deepen a color is to drive it toward its depths. The sense « to charge, to rush at » is explained differently: the sources tie it not to a literal lunge but to the figurative ~fondre sur~ (« to swoop down on ») and the idea of going ~à fond~ (« all the way, full tilt »), so the « charging » ~foncer~ is best read as a variant of that expression rather than as the same word's plain extension. The family includes ~fond~, ~fonds~, ~enfoncer~, ~défoncer~, ~foncé~ (« dark »), and ~fonceur~ (« a go-getter »).
en.fonctionner:
Unlike most verbs in this app, ~fonctionner~ is young and home-grown: it is a denominal coinage, attested around 1787, formed directly on the French noun ~fonction~ (“function, role, duty”). That noun comes from Latin ~functio~ (“a performing, an execution”), the action-noun of the deponent verb ~fungi~ (“to perform, discharge, carry out an office”), whose past participle was ~functus~. Through Latin, ~fonction~ is the close kin of ~défunt~ (“deceased”), literally one who has ~discharged~ life — the ~de-~ marking completion of the duty of living.

The sense development is neat. ~Fonction~ first named a duty or office one performs; the verb ~fonctionner~ then meant “to perform one's function,” and from there spread to machinery and systems — a clock, an engine, an institution that ~works~ by doing what it is meant to do. The word arrives just as the mechanical age does, and it carries that flavour: when a French speaker says ~ça fonctionne~, the metaphor is of a thing duly discharging its office. From the same ~fungi~ / ~functio~ root come ~fonctionnaire~ (“civil servant,” one charged with a function), ~fonctionnel~, ~dysfonctionnement~, and the mathematical ~fonction~.
en.fonder:
From Old French ~fonder~, from Latin ~fundare~ (“to lay a foundation, to establish”), a denominal verb built on the noun ~fundus~ (“bottom, base, the ground of an estate”). ~fundus~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~funðos~ to a Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmḗn~ (“bottom”), the same root that yielded English ~bottom~ and Ancient Greek ~puthmḗn~ (“bottom of a vessel”). The Romance cousins are everywhere: Italian ~fondare~ and Spanish ~fundar~, both “to found.”

To found something is literally to give it a ~fundus~ — to lay its lowest part, its base, before anything can be raised on top. From this concrete sense of laying a footing came the abstract one of establishing an institution, a city, or a doctrine, and figuratively of grounding an argument “on” solid reasons. French kept the underlying noun too, as ~fond~ (“bottom, background”) and ~fonds~ (“fund, capital, a piece of land”), and the doublet relationship there is striking: the financial ~fonds~ and the scenic ~fond~ are the same Latin ~fundus~ wearing two spellings. Other descendants include ~fondation~ (“foundation”), ~fondement~ (“basis”), ~profond~ (“deep,” literally “toward the bottom”), and ~foncier~ (“pertaining to land”). The English ~fund~, ~found~, ~foundation~, and ~profound~ all trace back to the same Latin base.
en.fondre:
~fondre~ comes from Latin ~fundere~ (“to pour, to pour out, to melt”), attested in French from around 1050. Its PIE root is *~ǵʰew-~ (“to pour”), seen in the extended form *~ǵʰew-d-~; the Greek cognate ~khéō~ (“I pour”) and Gothic ~giutan~ belong to the same family. From the molten-metal sense English borrowed ~found~ (as in casting a bell) and ~foundry~, while ~fundere~ also gave ~fuse~ and ~confound~. So the metalworker's foundry and the French verb for melting share one ancient idea of pouring.

The spread of senses is striking. From “to pour” came “to melt” (metal, snow, butter), then “to blend” — colors that ~se fondre~ into one another, giving ~fondu~ in film and ~fondue~ at the table. A separate, vivid branch is ~fondre sur~, “to swoop down on,” as a hawk drops on its prey: the image is of the bird pouring itself down out of the sky. From the same stem French built ~fonte~ (“cast iron; melting”), ~fonderie~ (“foundry”), ~fondation~ and ~fonder~ via the related ~fundus~ family, and ~fusion~. One root, *~ǵʰew-~, runs from a libation poured to the gods to chocolate melting in a pot.
en.forcer:
From Vulgar Latin *~fortiare~, built on Late Latin ~fortia~ (“strength, force”), which was the substantivized neuter plural of the classical adjective ~fortis~ (“strong, brave, firm”). Attested in French since the eleventh century, ~forcer~ is cousin to Italian ~forzare~ and Spanish ~forzar~, and the whole family is kin to the English borrowings ~force~ and ~fort~.

The verb's path follows the noun ~force~, which was carved from that neuter plural ~fortia~ — literally “strong things.” To ~forcer~ originally meant to apply strength, and from there it branched: to force a door, to force a lock, to force someone's hand, to force a plant in a hothouse, even to overstrain (~se forcer~, “to push oneself too hard”). In hunting, ~forcer~ a stag is to run it to exhaustion. The same ~fortis~ underlies a robust French lineage: ~fort~ (“strong”), ~force~, ~forcené~ (“frenzied,” originally “out of one's senses”), ~renforcer~, ~effort~, and ~confort~ (which reached English as ~comfort~ before returning). What began as a Roman soldier's praise — ~fortis~, brave and steadfast — became the verb for any exertion of power, gentle or brutal.
en.forer:
From Latin ~forāre~ (“to pierce, to bore through”), a learned borrowing, as en.Wiktionary calls it. The Latin verb has a noun beside it, ~forāmen~ (“hole, opening”), and the pair belongs to a Proto-Indo-European family of words for piercing and cutting. The Germanic branch of that family gave English ~bore~ and German ~bohren~, so the verb that French uses for drilling a well is a distant cousin of the verb English uses for the same job. Italian ~forare~ continues the Latin verb directly.

In French, ~forer~ is the technical verb of drilling: one drills a well, a tunnel, a hole in a wall, or an oil field. It has produced a small family of its own, with ~forage~ (“drilling”), ~foreur~ (“driller”), ~foret~ (“drill bit”) and ~foreuse~ (“drilling rig”). The compound ~perforer~, from Latin ~perforāre~ (“to pierce through”), shows the same root with a prefix. Because ~forer~ was borrowed from Latin rather than inherited, it kept the Latin shape almost untouched.
en.forger:
Recorded from the twelfth century, ~forger~ comes from Latin ~fabricāre~ (“to fashion, build, construct”), from ~faber~ (“craftsman, smith, worker in hard materials”). The deep origin of ~faber~ is uncertain; it is often referred to a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰabʰ-~ (“to fit together, be fitting”), with proposed cognates including Armenian ~darbin~ (“smith”) and, by some accounts, English ~deft~ and ~daft~. ~fabricāre~ also yielded, by a learned borrowing, the French doublet ~fabriquer~ (“to manufacture”), so French has two reflexes of one Latin verb.

The popular, mouth-worn line of descent narrowed ~fabricāre~ from making in general to the smith's particular making: hammering hot metal. Old French ~forgier~ already meant working iron at the anvil, and from that concrete craft the figurative senses fanned out — to ~forger~ a sword, a chain, but also to forge an alliance, a destiny, or, more darkly, a false document (whence English ~forge~ in the sense “to counterfeit”). The same Latin ~faber~ family gives French ~forge~ (the smithy itself), ~forgeron~ (“blacksmith”), and the archaic ~fèvre~ that survives in the surname ~Lefebvre~ — quite literally “the smith.”
en.formaliser: Two histories share one form. The pronominal ~se formaliser~ (“to take offense”) is formed from ~formel~ and the suffix ~-iser~, while the transitive ~formaliser~ (“to make formal”) is, according to French Wiktionary, a borrowing from English ~formalize~. ~Formel~ comes from Latin ~formālis~, from ~forma~ (“form”), which also gave French ~forme~. The “offense” sense grew from the idea of being scandalized by a breach of form: someone who ~se formalise~ is shocked that the proprieties have not been observed. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~.
en.formater: Formed in French from the noun ~format~ and the suffix ~-er~, probably under the influence of the English verb to format. The base ~format~ has two proposed origins. French Wiktionary derives it either from ~former~ with the suffix ~-at~, or, more likely, from Italian ~formato~, itself from ~formare~. English Wiktionary instead sends it through German ~Format~ from Latin ~fōrmātus~ (“formed”). All the routes lead back to Latin, but their order is unsettled. The verb meant to give a book or sheet its shape, then to prepare a disk for use, a sense that came with computing.
en.former:
From Latin ~formare~ (“to shape, to fashion, to form”), derived from ~forma~ (“shape, figure, mold, beauty”). The deeper origin of ~forma~ is uncertain; one long-standing hypothesis derives it from Ancient Greek ~morphē~ (“shape, form”), perhaps with a swapping of consonants and possibly transmitted through Etruscan, though this remains unproven. Cognate with Italian ~formare~ and Spanish ~formar~.

The verb began concretely — to give matter a shape, to mold — and then climbed into the abstract: to constitute (« former un gouvernement »), to develop a skill, and especially to train or educate a person, so that ~formation~ in modern French means “training” as much as “formation.” The same ~forma~ branched into a remarkably productive family of French words: ~forme~, ~format~, ~formule~, ~formel~, ~uniforme~, ~conforme~, ~déformer~, ~réformer~, and ~transformer~. From a single word for “shape,” French built a whole architecture of forming, reforming, and transforming.
en.formuler:
A denominal verb coined in French (around the late 18th century) from the noun ~formule~ (“formula, set form of words”), itself from Latin ~formula~, a diminutive of ~forma~ (“shape, form, mould”). Latin ~forma~ stands beside the verb ~formāre~, source of French ~former~ (“to form”); a ~formula~ was literally a “little form,” a small fixed pattern. Cognate descendants of ~forma~ include English ~form~ and ~formula~ and Italian ~forma~.
