A ~formula~ began as a legal and ceremonial template — a precise wording you had to follow exactly — and that flavour of fixed, exact expression carried into ~formuler~: to put a thought into a defined, careful form of words. One ~formule~ une hypothèse, a request, an objection — always shaping vague intention into explicit statement. The same ~forma~ root spread widely in French: ~forme~, ~former~, ~formule~, ~formulaire~ (“form, printed template”), ~formel~ (“formal, explicit”), and ~formalité~. Across these the underlying idea is constant — giving a shapeless content a clear, repeatable shape.
en.fortifier:
From Middle French ~fortifier~, borrowed from Late Latin ~fortificāre~ (“to strengthen, to fortify”), a compound of Latin ~fortis~ (“strong”) and a verbal element ~-ficāre~ related to ~facere~ (“to make”). The verb therefore meant, quite literally, “to make strong.” Italian ~fortificare~ and Spanish ~fortificar~ come from the same Latin verb, and English ~fortify~ was borrowed from French. Latin ~fortis~ itself is the ancestor of French ~fort~, and a whole family grew up around it.

In French, ~fortifier~ means to make a place or a person stronger. It is used of a town given walls, towers and ramparts, and equally of bodies and minds, so that one fortifies one's health, one's resolve or an argument. The family includes ~fortification~, ~fortin~ (“small fort”) and ~forteresse~, and other French words are also built on the idea of strength, among them ~réconforter~ (“to put strength back into”) and ~effort~.
en.fouetter: Formed from the noun ~fouet~ (“whip”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to use a whip.” The noun is a diminutive in ~-et~ of Old French ~fou~ (“beech”), from Latin ~fagus~ (“beech”), so a ~fouet~ was originally a little beech switch; it is first found in a thirteenth-century fabliau. French Wiktionary adds that the slang sense “to stink” is a separate matter, from Latin ~foetēre~ (“to stink”), reshaped by the image of a smell that strikes the nose like a lash.
en.fouiller:
French ~fouiller~ comes from Old French ~fooiller~, which goes back to a Vulgar Latin verb reconstructed as *~fodiculāre~ (a contracted *~fodiclāre~ is also cited). That is a diminutive of Latin ~fodicāre~ (“to pierce”), itself a frequentative of ~fodere~ (“to dig”). The same ~fodere~ gave French ~fouir~, which English Wiktionary invites us to compare with ~fouiller~. The chain therefore runs from digging, to repeated piercing, to a diminutive of that piercing, the frequentative and the diminutive each adding a sense of small, repeated action. The Vulgar Latin stage is reconstructed and not attested, so it is a scholarly inference and not a recorded word.

The modern sense is that of searching: to ~fouiller~ is to dig into something, or to rummage through it, in order to find what lies inside. The noun ~fouille~ names the act, in the ~fouilles~ (“excavations”) of archaeologists and in the search of a person or a place by the police. The verb keeps this double character, literal digging and figurative probing, which suits a word whose ancestors were all verbs of digging and piercing. Its relative ~fouir~ shares the Latin source, so the two verbs form a pair, ~fouir~ for plain digging and ~fouiller~ for the searching kind.
en.fournir:
From Old French ~fornir~ (also ~furnir~), borrowed from Frankish *~frumjan~ (“to accomplish, carry out, provide”), from a Germanic base *~fruma~ (“first, foremost; advantage, benefit”). The verb is cousin to Italian ~fornire~ and to the borrowed English ~furnish~ (which English took straight from this Old French verb), and through its Germanic root to German ~fromm~ (“pious, devout,” earlier “useful, upright”). The unexpected nasal ~n~ of the modern stem arose under the influence of the near-synonym ~garnir~ (“to garnish, equip”).

The original idea was “to carry through, accomplish, make ready,” which slid easily into “to provide what is needed, to equip.” From “equipping” came the modern core senses: to supply, to provide, to furnish. The noun ~fourniture~ (“supply, supplies”) and the agent ~fournisseur~ (“supplier”) carry the commercial weight today, while ~fourni~ as an adjective means “well-stocked” or, of hair and beards, “thick, abundant.” It is a tidy irony that English ~furnish~ — which in English narrowed toward outfitting a room with furniture — and French ~fournir~ — which stayed broad, “to supply anything” — are the very same Frankish word, sent down two paths. Kin in French include ~fourniture~, ~fournisseur~, ~fournil~, and ~fourni~.
en.foutre:
From Vulgar Latin *~fŭttĕre~, with expressive doubling of the t, from Classical Latin ~futuere~ (“to copulate with”), infinitive of ~futuō~. The PIE root is uncertain: one proposal connects ~futuō~ to *~bʰew-~ (“to strike, to hit”) and to Latin ~fūstis~ (“club, staff”), but the sources flag this as no more than possible. The Latin verb is the unmistakable ancestor of a whole Romance set — Italian ~fottere~, Spanish ~joder~, Portuguese ~foder~, Romanian ~fute~ — and of French ~foutre~ itself.

Originally crude and sexual, ~foutre~ has had its literal sense largely worn away, surviving today as a vulgar, very general verb of doing, putting and caring — or pointedly not caring. One ~se fout~ of something to mean one does not give a darn about it, and the imperative sends someone away. The register is firmly vulgar and, in the old literal sense, archaic. The French family it spawned is large and idiomatic: ~foutu~ (“done for”), ~foutaise~ (“rubbish”), ~foutoir~ (“shambles”) and the set phrases ~foutre le camp~ (“to clear off”) and ~s’en foutre~ (“to not care a bit”).
en.fragiliser: ~Fragiliser~ is ~fragile~ + the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make fragile, to weaken”. The base ~fragile~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fragilis~ (“breakable, brittle, perishable”), from ~frangere~ (“to break”). The same Latin word had already reached French by popular evolution as ~frêle~, so ~fragile~ and ~frêle~ are doublets. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and forms verbs meaning “to make A”, as in ~fragiliser~ and ~actualiser~.
en.franchir:
French ~franchir~ is formed from the adjective ~franc~ (“free”) with the ending ~-ir~. ~Franc~ comes from Late Latin ~Francus~ (“a Frank”), from the Germanic name of the ~Franks~; in Frankish Gaul only the Franks held full legal freedom, so the ethnic name came to mean “free.” It is thus cognate with English ~frank~, ~Frankish~, and the name ~France~. Old French ~franchir~ / ~franchier~ first meant “to set free,” a literal sense that the parallel ~affranchir~ (“to enfranchise, free”) still preserves.

From “to free” the verb took a striking turn: “to free oneself of a burden,” then “to clear an obstacle by leaping or climbing it,” and finally “to go beyond a limit,” displacing the older Old French ~transir~ in that role. So to ~franchir~ a river, a doorway, or a threshold is, etymologically, to win free of it. The family includes ~franchise~ (“frankness; franchise; exemption”), ~franchissement~ (“crossing”), and ~infranchissable~ (“impassable”), and idioms like ~franchir~ le pas, “to take the plunge.”
en.frapper:
From Old French ~fraper~ (attested 1178), most likely from Frankish *~hrapōn~ (“to snatch, seize quickly”), of Germanic origin. The same Germanic stem ~hrap-~ surfaces in Dutch ~rapen~ (“to gather, seize”), German ~raffen~ (“to snatch up”), and Old Norse ~hreppa~ (“to obtain, reach”), all turning on the idea of grabbing something swiftly and forcefully. Romance absorbed the word too, giving Italian ~frappare~. The initial ~f~ is the telltale mark of a Frankish loan reshaped in Gallo-Romance mouths.

The meaning shifted from a quick snatching to a sudden, forceful blow — the gesture of striking. From there ~frapper~ spread generously: one hits a nail, a clock strikes the hour, a coin is struck (~frapper monnaie~), and, figuratively, a sight or a fact strikes you — ~ça m'a frappé~, “that struck me.” It even yields ~frappé~ for an iced, “shaken” drink. Modern relatives include ~frappe~ (a strike, or typing), ~frappant~ (“striking, remarkable”), and ~frappeur~. The Germanic input here is a reminder that beneath Latinate French runs a strong Frankish current, left by the Germanic people who gave France its very name.
en.fraîchir: Formed from the adjective ~frais~ (feminine ~fraîche~, “cool, fresh”) with the ending ~-ir~, meaning “to turn cooler,” and attested in Old French as ~freschir~. It is used above all of the wind: ~le vent fraîchit~ (“the wind is freshening”). The circumflex of ~fraîche~ stands in for the ~s~ still visible in the Old French spelling. The adjective itself is of Germanic origin, a cousin of English ~fresh~ and German ~frisch~.
en.freiner:
From Latin ~frēnāre~ (“to bridle, to check”), built on ~frēnum~ (“bridle, bit”), the source of French ~frein~. An Old French verb ~frener~ already existed in the sense of bridling or restraining, and English Wiktionary notes that the modern verb can equally be read as ~frein~ plus ~-er~. The Latin verb has sister forms elsewhere: Italian ~frenare~ and Spanish ~frenar~.

The meaning shows how a technology can borrow an image from the stable. The Latin noun ~frēnum~ was the bit that checks a horse, and the verb first meant to bridle or restrain; English Wiktionary gives 1907 as a date for the modern verb, in the early age of the motor car. Figurative uses are easy to find: one ~freine~ spending, ambition or an impulse. The Latin family also gave ~refréner~ (“to hold back”), with English ~refrain~ from the same ~refrēnāre~ by way of Old French, and ~effréné~ (“unbridled”), the opposite of a bridled ardor, as well as ~frein~ itself.
en.friser:
The origin is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries offer different answers. French Wiktionary proposes, with a “perhaps,” that it comes from ~frire~ (“to fry”), the curled, crinkled edges of frying food having suggested the comparison. English Wiktionary instead derives it from a Germanic source, a form like Old Frisian ~frisle~ (“curly hair”), from Proto-Germanic *~frisaz~ (“curly, frizzy”), and links it to English ~frizz~. The hair-curling sense fits either route, so the question stays open.

The literal meaning is to curl hair, and the participle ~frisé~ describes curly hair, curly endive (~chicorée frisée~) and similar crinkly things. From there the verb developed a figurative sense, “to graze, to skim past,” as in ~friser l'accident~ (“to come within a hair of an accident”), and ~friser la quarantaine~ (“to be close to forty”). The family includes ~frisé~, ~frisure~, ~frisette~ and ~frisottis~.
en.frustrer:
Borrowed from Latin ~frūstrāre~ (“to deceive, to disappoint, to make vain”), formed on the adverb ~frūstrā~ (“in vain, to no purpose”). Latin ~frūstrā~ is usually linked to ~fraus~ (“deceit, harm”), though the exact derivation is debated. The verb passed into Italian ~frustrare~ and Spanish ~frustrar~, and English ~frustrate~ comes from the same Latin source.

The Latin verb meant to trick someone's expectations or to leave a plan empty, and French ~frustrer~ carries that idea of depriving someone of what they were counting on. The emotional meaning that dominates today is the sour feeling of being blocked from a goal. That is why ~frustré~ now describes a mood as readily as a deprivation. The same Latin root gives ~frustration~ and ~frustrant~ in French, and the sense of thwarted effort is still visible in the ancestor ~frūstrā~, which meant simply that something was done for nothing.
en.frémir:
From Old French and Middle French ~fremir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fremīre~, an altered form of Latin ~fremere~ (“to roar, to rumble, to murmur”), which shifted to the ~-ire~ conjugation in everyday speech. English Wiktionary traces Latin ~fremō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰrem-~ (“to growl, to roar”). Its cognates include Greek ~brémein~ (“to roar”), and the Greek epithet ~Brómios~ (“the roarer”), a name of Dionysus.

The fascinating shift is from sound to movement. Latin ~fremere~ named a noise, the roar of a crowd, the rumble of the sea, the rustle of a murmur. French ~frémir~ kept that sense for a time and then moved toward what the body does when moved by such sounds: to tremble, to quiver with fear, cold or emotion. A third sense belongs to cooking: water that ~frémit~ is just below the boil, still rippling and murmuring. The noun ~frémissement~ and the adjective ~frémissant~ cover both the trembling and the quiet stir.
en.fréquenter:
First attested around 1190, ~fréquenter~ comes from Latin ~frequentāre~ (“to visit often, to crowd, to celebrate”), a verb built on the adjective ~frequēns~ (“crowded, numerous, repeated”), the same adjective that gives French ~fréquent~, Spanish ~frecuente~, Italian ~frequente~, and English ~frequent~. The deeper origin of ~frequēns~ is disputed: by one account it descends from a Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰrekʷ-~ (“to cram, to stuff”), connected to Latin ~farcīre~ (“to cram”) and Greek ~phrássō~ (“to fence in”), but Beekes judged the Greek comparison quite uncertain, and other scholars propose different roots entirely. The chain back to Latin, however, is secure.

The Latin sense clustered around density and repetition — a ~frequēns~ place was a thronged one — and ~frequentāre~ meant to fill a place by going there again and again. French kept exactly this idea of habitual, repeated presence: one ~fréquente~ a café, a school, or a circle of friends, and by extension the people one keeps company with. The notion of regularity left modern French ~fréquence~ (“frequency”) and ~fréquentation~ (“association”), while the social sense survives in the slightly old-fashioned use of ~fréquenter~ for courting someone.
en.frôler: The origin of ~frôler~ is uncertain. Old French ~froller~ meant “to rub, to thrash”. French Wiktionary derives it from an imitative ~frou~, the sound of something brushing past, and adds that it may be related to ~froisser~ and ~frotter~, comparing Italian ~frullare~ (“to whisk, to beat”). English Wiktionary says only that it is probably imitative. The sense softened from rubbing hard to touching lightly, so ~frôler~ now means to brush against, to graze, or to narrowly miss, and figuratively to come close to something. The rustling ~frou-frou~ is plausibly the same imitation.
en.fuir:
French ~fuir~ descends from Old French ~fuir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fūgīre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~fugere~ (“to flee”), built on the perfect stem ~fūgī~. The root traces to Proto-Italic *~fugiō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰewg-~ (“to flee, run away”). The same Latin verb gave Spanish ~huir~, Italian ~fuggire~, and Portuguese ~fugir~; through the shared root it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~pheúgō~ (“I flee”) and with Latin ~fuga~ (“flight”), source of English ~fugitive~ and ~refuge~.

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: from Latin to modern French, ~fuir~ has always meant “to flee.” French extended it to inanimate subjects, so that a pipe or a roof can ~fuir~ — “leak” — the water escaping as if running away. From the same family come ~fuite~ (“flight, leak”), ~fuyard~ (“runaway”), and the reflexive ~s'enfuir~ (“to flee away”). The learned Greco-Latin branch supplies ~fugace~ (“fleeting”) and the musical ~fugue~, a form in which the voices seem to chase and flee one another.
en.fumer:
From Latin ~fūmāre~ (“to smoke, to steam, to emit vapor”), from the noun ~fūmus~ (“smoke”), from Proto-Italic *~fūmos~, from PIE *~dʰuh₂mós~ (“smoke”). Cognate with Sanskrit ~धूम~ (~dhūmá~), Ancient Greek ~θῡμός~ (~thūmós~, “spirit, breath”), and — from the same root — English ~fume~ and ~dust~.

Latin ~fūmāre~ was first about anything that smoked or steamed: a chimney, a hot dish, a misty field. French ~fumer~ kept all of this — a chimney ~fume~, soup ~fume~ — and only later took on “to smoke tobacco.” A separate homonym ~fumer~ “to manure a field” comes instead from ~fimus~ (“dung”) and should not be confused with it. From ~fūmus~ the language drew ~fumée~ (“smoke”), ~fumeur~, ~fumoir~, and ~parfum~ (literally “through-smoke,” recalling scent rising as incense burned). The deep root *~dʰuh₂mós~ also underlies the borrowed ~fumeux~.
en.fuser: ~Fuser~ is a learned verb built on Latin ~fūsus~, the past participle of ~fundere~ (“to pour, to melt”), and so it is a relative of ~fusion~. Its inherited cousin is ~fondre~, which descends from the same Latin verb through ordinary sound change. The senses “to melt,” “to spread, to gush” and, of laughter or cries, “to ring out” all spring from the idea of liquid flowing. French Wiktionary adds that some senses were influenced by ~fusée~, which probably colored the sense of something shooting off or bursting forth.
en.fusiller: Formed from ~fusil~ and the ending ~-er~, so “to use a ~fusil~ on” someone. The noun comes from Old French ~fuisil~ (also ~foisil~), from Vulgar Latin *~focīlis~ (as in a “fire stone”), from Latin ~focus~ (“hearth, fire”). Italian ~fucile~ is a relative. A ~fusil~ was first a steel for striking sparks from flint, and the name passed to the flintlock gun that used one. The verb came to mean “to shoot with a rifle,” hence “to execute by firing squad.”
en.fusionner:
A denominal verb built on the noun ~fusion~, which French took from Latin ~fusio~ (“a pouring, a melting”), itself from the verb ~fundere~ (“to pour, to melt”), past participle ~fusus~. ~Fundere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~hundō~ and from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰew-~ (“to pour”), the root behind Ancient Greek ~χέω~ (“I pour”) and Gothic ~giutan~. Through that same root, English ~found~ (“to cast metal”) and ~fuse~ are cognates. The verb ~fondre~ (“to melt”) is the directly inherited French outcome of ~fundere~, making ~fusionner~ and ~fondre~ relatives across the learned/popular divide.

The noun ~fusion~ first named the literal melting of metals — pouring molten substances together so they become one mass. ~Fusionner~ generalized that picture: two companies, parties, or files now merge as readily as two metals. The metallurgical sense survives in nuclear ~fusion~ and in ~fusible~ (“a fuse, what melts”). From the same Latin verb come ~fondre~, ~fonte~ (“cast iron, melting”), ~fondue~, ~confus~ (“poured together, muddled”), ~profus~, and ~diffus~ — a whole network turning on the idea of liquid spreading and mingling.
en.fustiger: A learned borrowing from Latin ~fūstīgāre~ (“to beat with a stick”), built on ~fūstis~ (“club, cudgel”). The literal sense was “to cudgel,” and the modern sense, “to criticize publicly and harshly,” is a figurative extension in which words take the place of the stick. The Latin noun ~fūstis~ is also behind French ~fût~ (“shaft, trunk, cask”), which was inherited rather than borrowed, so the two words are distant relatives despite looking unlike. English ~fustigate~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.fâcher:
From Old French ~faschier~ (Middle French ~fascher~). The origin is probably Vulgar Latin *~fasticāre~, an altered form of Late Latin ~fastidiāre~ (“to feel disgust”), from Classical Latin ~fastīdīre~. French Wiktionary points to the Old Occitan noun ~fastic~ (“disgust”) as supporting evidence for the reconstructed Vulgar Latin form, but the intermediate form is reconstructed, not attested, so the chain is a likely one rather than a proven one.

In modern French, ~fâcher~ means “to anger, to annoy”, and the reflexive ~se fâcher~ (“to become angry”) is the main use. Now ~être fâché~ can mean “to be upset” or “to have fallen out” with someone. The Latin source ~fastīdīre~ also lies behind English ~fastidious~, and the French adjective ~fâcheux~ (“annoying”) and the noun ~fâcherie~ (“quarrel”) belong to the same family.
en.fédérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~foederāre~ (“to unite by treaty, to bring together through an alliance”), a verb built on the noun ~foedus~ (genitive ~foederis~, “treaty, league”). The noun is generally linked to ~fidere~ (“to trust”) and ~fides~ (“faith, good faith”), since a treaty was at bottom a pledge of trust between parties; the shared root is reconstructed as Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeydʰ-~ (“to trust, to persuade”). French holds this family on two levels: the inherited branch gave ~foi~ (“faith”), and learned borrowings gave ~fidèle~ and ~fédéral~. Spanish ~federar~ and Italian ~federare~ are sibling borrowings, and English took ~federal~ and ~confederate~ from the same Latin source.

In French the verb is a learned borrowing, and its life is tied to the political words around it. ~Fédéral~ and ~fédération~ carried the charge of the Revolution, whose Fête de la Fédération on 14 July 1790 gathered delegates from across the country to swear union. A sports body ~fédère~ its clubs, and a ~projet fédérateur~ draws people around a shared aim. The Latin diphthong ~oe~ regularly became ~é~ in learned French words, which is why ~foedus~ left ~fédérer~ and ~fédéral~ and not something with an ~oi~. The kinship with ~foi~ is easy to miss, yet the whole family rests on it, since a treaty was a pledge of trust.
en.féliciter:
From Latin ~felicitare~ (“to make happy, to bless”), from ~felicitas~ (“happiness, good fortune”), from ~felix~ (“happy, fortunate”). What surprises here is the original sense of ~felix~: not “glad” but ~fruitful~, ~fertile~. The sources trace it to Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁(y)-~ (“to suckle, to nourish”) — the same nurturing root behind Latin ~femina~ (“woman”), ~filius~ (“son”), and ~fecundus~ (“fertile”). A ~felix~ field was one that bore fruit; only later did fruitfulness become fortune, and fortune become happiness.

So to ~féliciter~ someone is, at the root, to wish them fruitful good fortune. The word keeps purely social company today — congratulations on a success, a marriage, a birth. French relatives include ~félicité~ (“bliss”), ~félicitations~, and the given name ~Félix~; through the same PIE root run ~femme~, ~fils~, and ~fécond~. The bridge from “fertile” to “happy” is the quietly memorable fact of this entry: a word of congratulation that began, far back, in the image of a nursing mother and a fruiting field.
en.fêter:
Inherited from Old French ~fester~, a denominal verb built from the noun ~fête~ (Old French ~feste~) plus the suffix ~-er~. The noun descends from Latin ~festa~, the plural of ~festum~ (“feast day, holiday”), taken as a feminine singular in Vulgar Latin. ~Festum~ goes back through Proto-Italic to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁s-~ (“sacred, religious”), which also yielded Latin ~fanum~ (“temple”) and ~feriae~ (“holidays”). Cognate with Italian ~festa~ and Spanish ~fiesta~, and — through Old French — with English ~feast~ and ~festival~.

The root *~dʰeh₁s-~ belonged to the vocabulary of the sacred, so a ~fête~ was first a religious observance before the word broadened to any joyful celebration. From the same family French keeps ~férié~ (a “jour férié” is a public holiday), ~festin~ (“banquet”), ~festival~, and ~festivité~. The verb today carries the warmth of marking an occasion: one says « on a fêté son anniversaire » or « il faut fêter ça », where the act of celebrating is itself the point. The doublet ~feria~, the Spanish-style fair, re-entered French from Spanish, preserving the older sense of a holy day given over to public rejoicing.
en.gager:
The origin of ~gager~ is Germanic, but the exact path is not fully settled. One account derives it from the noun ~gage~ (“pledge”) or from Old French ~guagier~, which came from ~guage~, a descendant of Frankish *~waddi~, itself from Proto-Germanic *~wadja~ (“pledge”). French Wiktionary traces that further to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wedʰ-~. English Wiktionary says a Vulgar Latin verb *~wadiare~ (from *~wadium~) may have stood in between, but this is only a possibility.

The core idea is a pledge handed over as a guarantee, which fits both senses of ~gager~, “to guarantee” and “to bet.” Walloon ~wadjî~ is a regional relative. English borrowed the same word from Anglo-Norman or Old Northern French in a variant with an initial w, which is why ~wage~ and ~wager~ look different from ~gager~. In French the family includes ~gage~ and ~dégager~. In everyday speech ~gager que~ means “to bet that.”
en.gagner:
From Old French ~gaaignier~ (“to earn, win, cultivate, forage”), from Late Latin *~wadaniāre~, borrowed from Frankish *~waidanjan~ (“to forage, graze, pasture, hunt for food”). This rests on a Germanic base for hunting and pursuit, *~waiþō~ (“pasture, hunting ground”), and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyh₁-~ (“to chase after, pursue, strive for”). Through the same Germanic source come German ~Weide~ (“pasture”) and Old Norse ~veiðr~ (“hunt”), while English ~gain~ was borrowed straight from the Old French verb.

The history is a journey from field to fortune. The earliest sense was agricultural and pastoral — to work the land, to graze animals, to forage — the toil by which medieval people drew sustenance from the earth. From “to get one's living from the land” the meaning broadened to “to earn,” then to “to obtain, acquire,” and finally to the triumphant modern “to win.” The compound ~gagne-pain~ (“breadwinner,” literally “earn-bread”) preserves the older laboring sense beautifully. The French family includes ~gain~, ~gagnant~ (“winner”), ~regagner~ (“to regain”), ~gagne-pain~, and the dialectal ~gagnage~ (“grazing land”) — a quiet memory of the pastures where the word was born.
en.galérer: ~Galérer~ is formed from ~galère~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun, which French took from Catalan ~galera~, comes from Medieval Latin ~galēra~, a variant of ~galea~ and ultimately from Byzantine Greek. It named the oared warship, and by the Renaissance it also meant the sentence of rowing in one as a convict. The modern figurative sense, “an ordeal,” prepared the slang verb: to ~galérer~ is to struggle, to have a hard time, as if chained to the oar.
en.garantir:
From Old French ~garantir~, a denominal verb formed around 1100 from the noun ~garant~ (“warrantor, protector”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ir~. ~garant~ first appears as ~guarant~, of Frankish origin: from ~warand~, related to the Germanic verb ~warjan~ (“to defend, ward off, vouch for”), from Proto-Germanic *~warjaną~, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~wer-~ (“to cover, protect”). The initial Germanic ~w-~ regularly became ~gu-~ then ~g-~ in central Old French, while the northern dialects kept the ~w-~ — which is why English borrowed both ~warrant~ (from Norman ~warant~) and ~guarantee~ (from the southern ~garant~) as a doublet of the same word.

The core idea is standing surety: a ~garant~ is someone who vouches for you and shields you from loss, and to ~garantir~ is to give that protective pledge. From the legal sense of warranting title and quality, the meaning broadened to “to assure, to safeguard, to protect from” — one can ~garantir~ a result, or ~garantir~ oneself from the cold. The same Frankish stem ~warjan~ gave French ~guérir~ (“to heal,” originally “to protect, defend”), and the family includes ~garantie~ (“warranty, guarantee”) and ~garde~. German preserves a relative in ~gewähren~ (“to grant, vouchsafe”).
en.garder:
From Old French ~guarder~ (later ~garder~), from Medieval Latin *~wardare~, itself a borrowing from Frankish *~wardōn~ (“to watch, to guard”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to perceive, to watch out for”). The Frankish initial ~w-~ regularly became ~gu-~ then ~g-~ in central Old French, while the Norman dialect kept the ~w-~ that English borrowed: so French ~garder~ and English ~guard~ are doublets of one and the same Germanic word, and English ~ward~ and ~warden~ preserve the older form. German ~warten~ (“to wait on, to tend”) is a cognate.

The root idea is keeping watch, and from vigilant attention the verb spread to keeping, retaining, and looking after: to guard a fortress, to keep a secret, to look after a child. The reflexive ~se garder de~ (“to beware of”) holds the original sense of wariness. The prefixed ~regarder~ — ~re-~ + ~garder~ — drifted from “to watch over” to simply “to look at,” and gave the noun ~regard~ (“gaze”) and ~égard~ (“consideration”). The Germanic root spreads through French ~garde~, ~gardien~, ~garderie~, ~sauvegarder~, and ~avant-garde~, and feeds back into English as ~reward~ and ~regard~.
en.garer:
From Middle French ~garrer~ and Old French ~garer~, ~warer~ and ~varer~, a word of Germanic origin. It is traced either to Old Frankish *~warōn~ (“to guard, to keep watch”) or to Old Norse ~varask~ (“to be on one's guard”), or to both, and both lead back to Proto-Germanic *~warōną~ (“to watch over, to protect”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to perceive, to heed”). Cognates include Old High German ~warōn~ and Old English ~warian~ (“to guard, to be wary”), and English ~ware~, as in ~beware~. In French the verb is distantly related to ~garder~, ~garde~ and ~garnir~.

The Old French verb meant “to protect, to shelter,” and its reflexive ~se garer~ meant “to take shelter, to step aside out of harm's way,” as in the cry ~garez-vous~ (“mind out”). Pulling a boat into a basin, or a train onto a siding, was likewise a way of putting it out of the way, and the noun ~gare~ is generally linked to this sense before it came to name a railway station. Only later did ~garer~ narrow to its modern main sense, “to park” a vehicle, and ~se garer~ means “to pull over.” The interjection ~gare à toi~ (“watch out”) keeps the older warning sense.
en.garnir:
Inherited from Middle French ~garnir~, from Old French ~guarnir~ (“to protect oneself, arm up”), which English Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~warnijan~ (“to ward, take care of something”). That form is in turn from Proto-Germanic *~warnijaną~ (“to be careful, take heed, refuse”) and ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to close, cover, protect”). The Frankish origin means that the initial ~w-~ became ~gu-~ and then ~g-~ in French, as it did in ~guerre~. Italian ~guarnire~ and Portuguese ~guarnir~ are cognates of the Romance side. On the Germanic side, the same root is found in Middle Dutch ~waernen~, Old English ~wiernan~ (“to withhold, refuse”) and Old Norse ~varna~, and English ~warn~ is related.

The oldest senses of Old French ~garnir~ are of protection: to warn, to fortify a stronghold, to equip and supply it. From there come ~garnison~, the troops that supply a fort, and English ~garrison~. Over time the idea of providing and equipping weakened into that of furnishing, then into that of adorning: you ~garnir~ a dish with parsley or a dress with lace. English ~garnish~ took the same road, borrowed from the Old French stem ~garniss-~. French ~garniture~, ~garni~ (a furnished lodging) and ~dégarnir~ belong to the same family.
en.gaver: Derived from the Old French dialect word ~gave~ (“crop, throat”), the bird's gullet. French Wiktionary links ~gave~ with ~jabot~ (“crop”), while English Wiktionary calls it a doublet of ~joue~ (“cheek”), so the root is not agreed upon. The verb first meant to stuff the throat with food, as in force-feeding geese and ducks (~gavage~). It then widened to “to gorge,” in ~se gaver~, and in slang to “to bore or annoy.”
en.gazer: Two homonymous verbs share this form. One is a denominal of ~gaz~ (“gas”), a word coined in the seventeenth century by the Flemish chemist Van Helmont from Greek ~khaos~; it covers treating with gas, and the colloquial expression for things going well. The other is built on ~gaze~ (“gauze”), a fabric word that is probably borrowed from Arabic ~qazz~ (“silk”). The old idea that the cloth took its name from the city of Gaza is speculative; the CNRTL notes there is no proof that any such industry existed there. Both verbs add the ending ~-er~.
en.geler:
~Geler~ is inherited from Old French ~geler~, itself from Latin ~gelāre~ (“to freeze, to congeal”), a verb built on the noun ~gelū~ (“frost, icy cold”). The Latin noun belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gel-~ (“cold; to freeze”), which also fed the Germanic languages: English ~cold~ and ~cool~ and German ~kalt~ descend from it, with the regular Germanic shift of g to k. Italian ~gelare~ and Spanish ~helar~ are the sibling verbs, so a Romance speaker and an English speaker who complain of the cold are, without knowing it, using relatives.

In French the verb is both impersonal, as in ~il gèle~ (“it is freezing”), and transitive, as in freezing water, a bank account or prices; the figurative uses, to freeze relations or to chill someone's blood, are natural extensions. The Latin noun and verb produced a whole family: ~gel~, ~gelée~ (what has frozen or set, whence English ~jelly~), ~congeler~, ~dégeler~ and ~gélatine~. Italian added ~gelato~, which English borrowed. Even the humble jelly on the table is, etymologically, a frost that has set.
en.germer:
French ~germer~ comes from Latin ~germināre~ (“to sprout, to bud”), the verb of the noun ~germen~ (“sprout, bud, seed”). English Wiktionary describes it as a borrowing, which fits a learned word, and French Wiktionary refers readers to ~germe~ and ~germiner~ as related words. The Latin noun gave French ~germe~ and English ~germ~, and the Latin verb gave English ~germinate~. Italian ~germinare~ is a direct parallel. In Latin, the noun ~germen~ already named the part of a plant from which new growth springs, and the verb ~germināre~ named the act of putting it forth.

The sense stayed botanical for a long time: a seed puts out a first shoot when it germinates. From that picture grew the figurative uses, an idea, a plan or a feeling that begins to take form quietly before it shows. The noun traveled further than the verb. ~Germe~ names the embryo and, by extension, a microbe. The Republican calendar of 1793 named its spring month ~Germinal~ after the same Latin verb, the month when seeds sprout, and Zola took it as the title of his novel of coal miners, an image of hope pushing up through the soil.
en.glacer:
Inherited from Latin ~glaciāre~ (“to freeze, to turn to ice”), a verb formed on the noun ~glaciēs~ (“ice”). French also treats it today as the noun ~glace~ plus ~-er~. The Latin word is generally traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gel-~ (“cold, to freeze”), which also gave Latin ~gelū~ (“frost”) and so French ~geler~, a close relative of ~glacer~. The same root is the source of the Germanic family that includes English ~cold~. Italian has ~ghiaccio~ (“ice”) and the verb ~ghiacciare~.

French ~glacer~ means to freeze something solid or cover it with ice, and it is used figuratively: fear or a cold look can “freeze” a person, and a cold manner chills a conversation. In the kitchen it means to coat with a shiny, smooth layer, as in icing a cake or glazing a roast. The noun ~glace~ covers a whole range from ice to ice cream to a polished mirror, which is why the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles is the Galerie des Glaces. Descendants include ~glaçon~ (“ice cube”), ~glacier~ (a mass of ice) and the learned ~glacial~, along with ~déglacer~ (“to deglaze a pan”).
en.glisser:
Attested in Old French as ~glicier~, ~glisser~ arose from a blend of two verbs: ~glier~ (“to glide”), from the Frankish *~glidan~ (“to glide”), crossed with ~glacer~ (“to freeze, to make slippery”), from Latin ~glaciāre~. The Germanic *~glidan~ is a true cognate of English ~glide~ and is kin to German ~gleiten~; the icy half pulls in the family of ~glace~ (“ice”) and ~glacier~.

The two ancestors merged so neatly because they describe the same sensation — moving smoothly and uncontrollably over a slick surface, as one does on ice. From that core, ~glisser~ fanned out across French: a foot ~glisse~ on a wet floor (to slip), a sled ~glisse~ down a slope (to slide), a hand ~glisse~ into a pocket (to slip in quietly), and a remark can ~glisser~ over a subject without dwelling on it. The reflexive ~se glisser~ means to slip or sneak in. Modern descendants include ~glissade~ (“a slide, a glissade” — borrowed straight into English ballet and mountaineering vocabulary), ~glissant~ (“slippery”), and ~glissement~ (“a sliding, a shift”). It is one of those French words whose Frankish, Germanic blood still shows beneath the Romance surface.
en.glorifier:
From Latin ~glōrificāre~ (“to glorify”), a compound of ~glōria~ (“glory, fame”) and ~-ficāre~, a verb ending that comes from ~facere~ (“to make”). The same Latin verb gave Italian ~glorificare~ and Spanish ~glorificar~, and English ~glorify~ came through Old French. The origin of Latin ~glōria~ itself is unclear, and the sources consulted do not offer a settled root.

The literal meaning is “to make glorious,” and the verb is used to praise or exalt someone, with a slightly lofty tone, as in ~glorifier un héros~. The reflexive ~se glorifier de~ means “to boast of.” The same ending ~-ficāre~ underlies a large number of French verbs in ~-fier~, such as ~magnifier~, ~purifier~ and ~clarifier~, each meaning “to make” something. The noun ~gloire~ and the adjective ~glorieux~ belong to the family, as does ~glorification~.
en.gommer: From ~gomme~ (“gum”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~gomme~ comes from Latin ~gummi~ (also spelled ~cummis~), borrowed directly from Greek ~kómmi~, which French Wiktionary says was itself taken from Egyptian, as the name of a plant exudate. The verb covers two sides: to coat with gum, and the more common modern sense of erasing, presumably through ~gomme~ meaning an eraser. The figurative sense followed, to blur or tone down something, as in ~gommer~ the differences between two things.
en.gonfler:
Inherited from Latin ~cōnflāre~, a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~flāre~ (“to blow”). It meant literally “to blow together”, in practice to fan a fire into life by blowing on it. In French the initial ~c-~ became ~g-~, and Italian ~gonfiare~ shows the same voicing. Two sister compounds of ~flāre~ also survive in French: ~sufflāre~ gave ~souffler~ (“to blow”) and ~inflāre~ gave ~enfler~ (“to swell”). English borrowed the Latin forms directly, as ~conflate~ (“to blow together”, hence to fuse) and ~inflate~.

From fanning a fire, the sense moved to filling something with air and making it swell: one ~gonfler~ a tire, a balloon or a sail, and a river ~gonfle~ when its waters rise. Figurative uses followed, such as inflating figures or puffing up with pride. Two colloquial senses are lively. The adjective ~gonflé~ means “cheeky, daring”, and the slang ~gonfler~ someone means to annoy or bore them. The family includes ~dégonfler~ (“to deflate”, and figuratively to lose one's nerve), ~regonfler~ and ~gonflement~.
en.gorger: Formed from the noun ~gorge~ (“throat”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, literally “to fill the throat,” hence “to stuff with food or drink” and, reflexively, “to gorge oneself.” The noun is inherited from Old French ~gorge~, from Late Latin ~gurga~, related to Latin ~gurges~ (“whirlpool, gulf”). French Wiktionary explains the image as a comparison of the throat to a gaping opening. Compare German ~Gurgel~ (“throat”), which belongs to the same sound-imitating family.
en.goutter: Formed from the noun ~goutte~ (“drop”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to fall drop by drop.” The noun comes through Old French ~gote~ from Latin ~gutta~ (“drop”); the second ~t~ was added back in Middle French to mirror the Latin spelling. Do not confuse ~goutter~ with ~goûter~ (“to taste”), which comes from Latin ~gustāre~ and is a different verb altogether.
en.gouverner:
From Latin ~gubernare~ (“to steer a ship; to direct, to govern”), which Latin borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κυβερνάω~ (~kubernáō~, “to steer”). The pre-Greek origin is unsettled: Beekes assigns ~kubernáō~ to a Mediterranean (Pre-Greek) substrate, while others have tried to link it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷerb-~ (“to turn”) — the safe statement is that the trail goes cold in Greek. Through Latin, the verb gave Italian ~governare~, Spanish ~gobernar~, and English ~govern~.

The original sense was nautical — to hold the tiller — and that maritime image still steers the French family: ~gouvernail~ is the “rudder,” and ~gouverner~ keeps a literal nautical use alongside its political one. The metaphor of guiding a ship became the metaphor of guiding a state, giving ~gouvernement~ (“government”) and ~gouverneur~. The most famous offshoot is indirect: from the same Greek ~κυβερνήτης~ (~kubernḗtēs~, “steersman”) Norbert Wiener coined ~cybernetics~ in 1948 — so the prefix ~cyber-~ of the digital age and the everyday verb ~gouverner~ both descend, through different doors, from a Greek pilot at the helm.
en.goûter:
From Middle French ~gouster~, from Old French ~gouster~, from Latin ~gustāre~ (“to taste, sample”), from ~gustus~ (“a tasting”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵews-~ (“to taste; to choose”). The double meaning of that root — to taste and to choose — is telling: to taste is to try, and to try is to select. Italian ~gustare~ and Spanish ~gustar~ (“to please, to like”) continue the same Latin verb.

The root *~ǵews-~ ranges widely. Through Latin it gives French ~goût~, ~dégoûter~, ~dégustation~, and English ~gusto~ (by way of Italian) and ~disgust~; through Germanic, the “choose” side of the root surfaces in English ~choose~ and ~choice~. In French, ~goûter~ also became the noun ~le goûter~, the afternoon snack — a small tasting between meals. The circle from “taste” to “judgment” closes neatly in the word ~goût~ itself, which, as in English ~taste~, names both the sensation on the tongue and the faculty of aesthetic discernment.
en.grandir:
A French formation rather than a Latin inheritance: ~grandir~ was built on the adjective ~grand~ with the second-conjugation suffix ~-ir~, the same machinery that turns ~rouge~ into ~rougir~ or ~vieux~ into ~vieillir~. The adjective ~grand~ comes from Old French ~grant~, from Latin ~grandis~ (“large, great, grown-up”), with Romance cognates in Italian ~grande~ and Spanish ~grande~; English borrowed ~grand~ from the same Latin word through Anglo-Norman.

The deeper origin of ~grandis~ is genuinely uncertain. It is sometimes connected to a PIE root for “swelling,” *~gʷʰrendʰ-~, a derivation favored by Pokorny but rejected by de Vaan on phonetic grounds; others have tried a root meaning “to grind,” which would make it a distant relative of English ~great~. Because the sources disagree, the chain beyond Latin is best left open. The meaning is transparent throughout: to ~grandir~ is to become ~grand~ — taller, older, more important. From the same adjective French draws ~grandeur~, ~agrandir~, ~grandiose~, and the kinship terms ~grand-mère~ and ~grand-père~.
en.gratter:
From Old French ~grater~, via an attested Medieval Latin ~cratare~, borrowed from Old Low Frankish *~krattōn~ (“to scrape, to scratch”), from Proto-Germanic *~krattōną~. English Wiktionary traces the Germanic verb to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gred-~, with the Albanian noun ~gërresë~ (“rasp”) as a possible cousin. The Germanic relatives are easy to see: German ~kratzen~ (“to scratch”), Swedish ~kratta~ (“to rake”) and the regional English ~scrat~. French then passed the verb on to its neighbors, as Occitan and Catalan ~gratar~ and Italian ~grattare~ show.

The verb is one of the many words that the Franks left in Gallo-Romance. It means “to scrape” a surface with something rough, and also “to scratch” an itch, as in ~se gratter~. A family of everyday words grew from it: ~gratin~, originally the crust scraped from the bottom of a pot, ~grattoir~ (“scraper”), ~grattage~ and ~gratte-ciel~, a calque of English “skyscraper”, which literally scratches the sky.
en.graver:
From Old French ~graver~ (“to dig, to carve”), borrowed from Frankish *~graban~ (“to dig”), from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰrebʰ-~ (“to dig, scratch, bury”). It is therefore a Germanic word, not a Latin one — a cognate of German ~graben~ (“to dig”) and of English ~grave~, the source of ~engrave~, as well as of Old Church Slavonic ~grebǫ~ (“I dig, bury”).

The earliest French sense was the literal “to hollow out” of the Frankish verb; from cutting into the earth it narrowed to cutting into a hard surface — incising stone, metal, or wood with a tool. From that came the figurative “to imprint deeply,” as a memory ~gravée~ in the mind, and in the digital age the curious sense of “to burn” a CD or DVD, where a laser once again cuts a pattern into a hard material. The same Frankish stock yields the French family ~graveur~ (“engraver”), ~gravure~ (“engraving”), and ~regraver~ (“to re-engrave”).
en.greffer:
From ~greffe~, which French Wiktionary derives from Latin ~graphium~ (“stylus”), with the diminutive ~graphiolum~ behind the botanical sense. In Middle French the verb was spelled ~graffer~. Latin ~graphium~ was itself a borrowing from Greek, from the verb ~γράφειν~ (“to scratch, to write”), the same Greek root that underlies English ~graph~ and ~graphite~. English ~graft~ was borrowed from the Old French noun.

The usual explanation is a matter of shape. A stylus was a pointed rod for writing on wax, and the slender cut shoot inserted into a tree is said to have resembled it, so the noun ~greffe~ named the shoot, and the verb ~greffer~ the act of inserting it. French then carried the gardener's term into surgery, for tissue or an organ moved from one body to another, and into figurative use, for one thing attached to another. The same stylus gave a legal sense: the ~greffe~ is a court's registry, kept by the ~greffier~, the clerk who writes. Two worlds, trees and tribunals, thus share one ancestor in the writing tool.
en.greneler: From ~grain~ (“grain, seed, fine granule”), from Latin ~grānum~, with the diminutive suffix ~-el~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~. The verb means to give a surface a grainy texture, as when leather, paper or metal is worked to produce small bumps. The suffix ~-el~ gives the idea of many small grains, so the verb literally sets out to make a surface “little-grained”. French Wiktionary points to ~grenu~ (“grainy”), which shows the same stem spelled with an ~e~ instead of the ~ai~ of ~grain~.
en.grever:
From Old French ~grever~, which English Wiktionary describes as borrowed from Latin ~gravāre~ (“to load”), with influence from the Vulgar Latin adjective *~grevis~ (compare ~grief~), itself from Latin ~gravis~ (“heavy”). French Wiktionary instead gives popular Latin ~gravare~ or ~grevare~, glossed as loading in the concrete sense, causing harm, afflicting. Either way the verb belongs to the family of ~gravis~, “heavy”, and so to the idea of weighing something down.

French Wiktionary describes the classical sense as “to cause harm, to lay a burden on”. By the seventeenth century nobody loaded a cart or a boat with it any longer, and the word survived in figurative use, as of taxes weighing on a country or on the state. It belongs to the same family as ~aggraver~ and ~aggravation~, from popular Latin ~aggrevare~.
en.grignoter:
Built in French from ~grigner~ and the suffix ~-oter~, which makes frequentative and diminutive verbs, as in ~clignoter~ and ~tapoter~. The base ~grigner~ comes from Frankish *~grinan~ (“to grimace”), a Germanic verb cognate with English ~grin~ and German ~greinen~ (“to whine”). ~Grigner~ is nearly gone from modern French but survives in set phrases such as ~grigner des dents~ (“to bare one's teeth”).

The sources do not explain how a verb for grimacing came to mean “to nibble,” and the link is presumably the teeth, in small, repeated bites. The verb has since spread from food to money and territory. One ~grignote~ a savings account, a lead in the polls or a rival's market share, a little at a time. Related words include ~grignotage~ (“snacking, gradual erosion”), and the modern ~grignotine~, a snack food.
en.griller: Formed from ~grille~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~grille~ goes back to Latin ~crāticula~ (“small grill”), a diminutive of ~crātis~ (“wickerwork, hurdle”), and appears in Old French as ~gradilie~, then ~graille~ about 1200. It first meant a lattice of crossed bars used for punishment by fire. The verb originally meant to put someone to death by fire, then to roast, and it weakened to light burning, to toast, and, informally, to smoke a cigarette. Figurative senses followed: to burn out a machine, to run a signal, or to eliminate a competitor.
en.grimper:
Attested in the late 15th century, ~grimper~ is, by the favored account, a nasalized variant of Middle French ~gripper~ (“to grip, to seize, to claw”), reshaped under the pull of ~ramper~ (“to crawl, to creep”), to which it was close in meaning. The hedge is real — fr.Wiktionary marks the derivation as merely ~probable~ — but the source verb is clear: ~gripper~ comes from Frankish *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ (“to grab, to grasp”). It is thus cognate with English ~grip~ and ~gripe~ and German ~greifen~ — a Germanic word that slipped into Romance French.

The semantics fit the proposed origin beautifully: to climb a wall or a tree is to ~grip~ it hand over hand, hauling yourself up by what you can clutch — and the borrowed ~n~ of ~ramper~ left ~grimper~ sounding like its crawling cousin. Modern French keeps both the literal sense (to scale, to clamber) and the figurative (prices that ~grimpent~, “shoot up”). From the same ~gripper~ stem branch French ~gripper~ (now also “to seize up,” of a machine), ~grippe~ (“the flu,” once “a sudden grab” or whim), ~agripper~ (“to grab hold of”), and ~grippe-sou~ (“a skinflint,” one who claws after pennies). The climber and the influenza share, surprisingly, one grasping root.
en.gronder: From Old French ~gronder~, attested around 1230 and preceded by forms such as ~grondre~ and ~grondir~, from Latin ~grundīre~, a variant of ~grunnīre~ (“to grunt”). The Latin verb is probably imitative, an attempt to put the pig's sound into a word. The sense widened from animal noises to any low, deep sound: thunder, a cannon or a crowd ~gronde~. It also took on a human use, “to scold,” when a person grumbles at a child. The related ~grogner~ comes from ~grunnīre~ as well, and the two verbs sit side by side.
en.grossir: Formed from the adjective ~gros~ (“big, thick”) and the ending ~-ir~, in the pattern of deadjectival verbs meaning “to become A,” so ~grossir~ is “to grow big.” ~Gros~ comes from Old French ~gros~ and from Late Latin ~grossus~ (“thick”). The adjective was also borrowed by English as ~gross~. The ending ~-ir~ goes back to Latin ~-ire~, and the same pattern gave ~grandir~ from ~grand~. The verb works both ways, “to become bigger” and “to make bigger,” which is why it serves for people who gain weight, for a magnifying glass, and for a rumor.
en.grouper:
Derived from French ~groupe~ with the suffix ~-er~. ~groupe~ was borrowed in the 17th century from Italian ~gruppo~ (also ~groppo~, “a knot, a cluster, a round mass”), which came through Vulgar Latin *~cruppus~ from a Germanic source — Frankish or Lombardic — going back to Proto-Germanic *~kruppaz~ (“a compressed round mass; lump; the crop of a bird”). So a group is, at heart, a knot or rounded clump of things bunched together.

That Germanic *~kruppaz~ is the same word that, in the native English line, became ~crop~ (originally the rounded pouch in a bird's gullet, then the rounded head of a plant, then a harvest) and German ~Kropf~ (“crop, goitre”). The deeper pre-Germanic root is, by the sources' own admission, uncertain, so the chain is best stopped at *~kruppaz~. From ~groupe~ French built ~grouper~, ~regrouper~, ~groupement~, and ~groupuscule~; English borrowed the noun and verb back as ~group~ — making the bird's crop, the harvest, and the committee all distant relations.
en.gréer:
From Old French ~agreier~ (“to equip”), borrowed from Old Norse ~greiða~ (“to make ready, to equip”). English Wiktionary adds a neat twist: the initial ~a-~ was attached in Old French by analogy with verbs like ~abiller~, then removed again in Middle French, which gave ~greer~ and ~grayer~, in order to avoid confusion with ~agreer~, the ancestor of ~agréer~. The Norse word has a Germanic cousin in English ~ready~, which comes from the same family of words meaning “prepared.”

The sense stayed anchored in the sea: to ~gréer~ a ship is to fit it with masts, yards, sails and ropes, and the noun ~gréement~ names this whole rigging. Modern French keeps the verb almost entirely for ships and, by extension, for boats under sail. The agent noun ~gréeur~ names the person who does it.
en.guetter:
French ~guetter~ is inherited from Old French ~gaitier~ (also spelled ~guaitier~), a Germanic loan taken from Frankish *~wahtōn~ (“to watch, guard”), also given as *~wahtjan~. The Frankish verb was itself a derivative of the noun *~wahta~ (“guard, watch”), which goes back to Proto-Germanic *~wahtwō~ (“guard, watch”). English Wiktionary traces that Germanic noun further to the Proto-Indo-European root *~weǵ-~ (“to be fresh, cheerful, awake”), so the underlying idea is one of being alert and awake. The French verb kept that meaning close to its source: to keep watch, to observe attentively, and by extension to lie in wait for something or someone. The chain thus runs from Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic, then Frankish, Old French and modern French, with the Germanic stage supplying both the sound and the sense.

The shift of Frankish ~w~ to ~gu~ in French is a change also seen in ~gagner~, from Frankish *~waidanjan~ (“to forage, graze”). In an Anglo-Norman or Old Northern French variant the initial ~w~ was kept instead, and that variant is the source of English ~wait~, which therefore descends ultimately from the same origin as the French verb. English ~watch~ is a cousin from the same Germanic family. Two words that look unrelated, ~guetter~ and ~wait~, are thus the same Germanic word that took different forms in different dialects. In ~guetter~ itself, the ~gu~ is simply the French way of writing a Germanic ~w~ sound.
en.guider:
A reshaping, under the influence of the noun ~guide~, of Old French ~guier~ (“to guide, to lead”), which goes back to the Old Frankish ~witan~ (“to show the way, to watch over”). This Germanic verb belongs to a family meaning “to know, to see, to point out”: it is cognate with Old English ~wīsian~ (“to guide, to direct”), German ~weisen~ (“to show, to point”), and, more distantly through the same Indo-European root, with Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”). The reshaped form was reinforced by Italian ~guidare~ and Spanish ~guiar~, which English in turn borrowed as ~guide~.

The Frankish root joins seeing and showing: one who can see the path can point it out, and so ~guider~ means to lead another along a way, whether a road, a course of study, or a moral life. The initial ~gu-~ is the tell-tale Germanic ~w-~ as adapted by Old French, the same shift seen in ~guerre~ (from ~werra~) and ~garder~ (from ~wardōn~). From ~guide~ and ~guider~ French built a tidy family: ~guidage~, ~guidance~, ~guidon~ (the handlebar that steers a bicycle), and the modern ~téléguider~ (“to guide from afar, to remote-control”).
en.guérir:
First attested in the 11th century as ~guarir~, and tellingly its earliest meaning was “to protect, to safeguard,” not “to heal.” It comes from Frankish *~warjan~ (“to defend, ward off, protect”), a Germanic verb whose initial ~w~ regularly became ~gu~ in Old French (compare ~guerre~ from *~werra~, ~garder~, ~guetter~). The Germanic source is cognate with German ~wehren~ (“to fend off, defend”) and with English ~ward~ and ~warn~.

The semantic journey is the memorable part: to “protect” a sick body against its illness, to defend it, slid naturally into “to cure, to heal,” and the protective sense faded, leaving only the medical one. So a French doctor's ~guérir~ still carries, fossilized within it, the older idea of mounting a defense. The same Germanic family gave French ~garantir~ (“to guarantee, vouch for”), ~garnir~ (“to furnish, fortify”), and ~guérite~ (“sentry box, watchtower”) — a cluster all circling protection, watching, and defense, from which ~guérir~ alone slipped over into the gentler work of healing.
en.gâcher:
French ~gâcher~ comes from Old French ~gaschier~, with variants ~guaschier~, ~waschier~ and ~gasser~, a Germanic loan whose first meaning was “to wash, to soak, to dilute with water.” French Wiktionary derives it from Frankish *~waskon~, and English Wiktionary adds an Old Dutch step before Frankish *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~ (“to wash”). English Wiktionary traces that root to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wod-~ (“wet”). The English native cousin is ~wash~, and Old English ~wasċan~ is the same word. Italian ~guazzare~ (“to splash, to wallow”) comes from the same Germanic root. The initial ~w~ became ~g~ or ~gu~ in French, as in ~guerre~ and ~garder~, both Germanic loans too.

The path from washing to wrecking is not fully documented. ~Gâcher~ kept a technical sense in building, “to mix plaster or mortar with water,” and French Wiktionary suggests, with the word probably, that the meaning “to botch” arose because plaster or mortar once mixed and left to harden cannot be reused. This is a plausible explanation rather than a settled one. Old French already had senses like “to soil, to spoil,” which English Wiktionary lists beside “to wash.” The verb gave ~gâchis~, a mess or waste, and ~gâcheur~, and in modern French one ~gâche~ a talent, an evening, or a dish.
en.gâter: From Old French ~gaster~, which meant “to lay waste, to devastate.” English Wiktionary inherits it through Middle French ~gaster~. The Old French verb is usually traced to Latin ~vastāre~ (“to lay waste”), though the shard's sources stop at Old French. The sense softened a great deal over the centuries: a verb for ravaging a country came to mean spoiling a harvest, then spoiling food, a plan, or a child by indulgence. The circumflex of modern ~gâter~ marks the lost ~s~ of ~gaster~, a trace of the older spelling.
en.généraliser:
French ~généraliser~ is formed from the adjective ~général~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to render”). The adjective ~général~ comes from Latin ~generalis~ (“of or belonging to a kind or class”), built from ~genus~, genitive ~generis~ (“kind, race, stock”), plus the suffix ~-alis~. ~Genus~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to give birth, to beget”). That immensely fertile root also yields Greek ~génos~, English ~kin~ and ~kind~, and Latin ~gignere~ (“to beget”) — so to ~généraliser~ is, at root, to speak of a whole begotten family at once.

The semantic move is from “belonging to a genus” to “extend to a whole class”: to generalize is to take what is true of one and apply it to the kind. The verb is attested in the modern abstract sense from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the age of method and classification. The same root *~ǵenh₁-~ saturates French vocabulary: ~genre~, ~général~, ~génération~, ~gène~, ~génie~, ~ingénieux~, and ~gent~ all bear its mark, a sprawling lineage from a single Indo-European word for birth.
en.générer:
From Latin ~generare~ (“to beget, to produce, to generate”), a derivative of ~genus~ (“birth, origin, kind, race”), which descends from Proto-Italic *~genos~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, to produce”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~génos~ (“race, stock”), Sanskrit ~jánas~, and — through Germanic — English ~kin~ and ~kind~. Romance kept the verb alive as Italian ~generare~, Spanish ~generar~, and Portuguese ~generar~.

French borrowed ~générer~ learnedly from Latin rather than inheriting it through ordinary sound change, which is why it keeps its Latin shape so transparently. Its meaning has stayed close to the source — to bring into being, to produce — though modern usage leans heavily on technical and scientific senses: a machine, a reaction, or a computer program may ~générer~ output. The Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ is astonishingly fertile in French, lying behind ~genre~, ~général~, ~généreux~, ~génération~, ~génie~, ~gendre~, and even ~gens~ — a whole family clustered around the ideas of birth, kind, and lineage that the original root named.
en.gérer:
From Latin ~gerere~ (~gestum~) (“to carry, to bear, to produce, to conduct, to manage, to perform”), whose perfect and supine stem in ~gest-~ arose because an older ~s~ became ~r~ between vowels by the regular Latin sound change called rhotacism. According to de Vaan, ~gerere~ goes back through a post-PIE *~h₂ǵ-es-~ to the same Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to lead”) that gave Latin ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), the ancestor of French ~agir~. The verb was a learned borrowing, taken straight from Latin rather than inherited through the slow erosion of everyday speech.

In Latin, ~gerere~ ranged from the concrete “to carry on one's person” to the figurative “to carry out, to administer,” as in ~bellum gerere~ (“to wage war”) and ~rem gerere~ (“to manage an affair”). French kept the administrative sense: to ~gérer~ is to handle, to run, to take charge of. The ~s/r~ split left a rich double family in modern French: from the ~ger-~ side come ~gérer~, ~gérant~, ~ingérer~, ~digérer~, and ~suggérer~; from the ~gest-~ side come ~gestion~, ~geste~, and ~gesticuler~. So a manager who oversees ~la gestion~ of a company and an actor who studies his ~gestes~ on stage are, etymologically, both simply carrying something.
en.gésir:
From Old French ~gesir~ (also ~jesir~), “to lie, to be lying down,” from Latin ~iacēre~ (“to lie, to be stretched out”), from Proto-Italic *~jakēō~, from PIE *~yeh₁-~. This verb of resting belongs beside its causative twin ~iacere~ (short ~e~), “to throw” — what is thrown comes to lie. Cognate with Italian ~giacere~ and Spanish ~yacer~, both still living verbs of lying, and, through the Latin family, with the ~ject~ words English borrowed (~project~, ~reject~) from the throwing branch.

In Old French ~gesir~ was fully conjugated and ordinary, but it withered into one of French's most defective verbs, surviving chiefly in the present, the imperfect, and the participle ~gisant~ — which also became the noun for the recumbent stone effigy carved atop a tomb. Above all it fossilized in the funerary formula ~ci-gît~ (“here lies”), and its plural ~ci-gisent~, still cut into gravestones. The everyday roles of lying and resting passed to other verbs, leaving ~gésir~ a word of the deathbed and the tomb. The same Latin root seeded a wide French vocabulary of lying and location: ~adjacent~ (from ~ad-~ + ~iacēre~, “to lie next to”), the geological ~gisement~ (an ore deposit, where minerals “lie”), the ~gîte~ (a resting-place or lodging), and the learned ~jacent~.
en.gêner:
Denominal verb from the noun ~gêne~, formed with ~-er~. The noun appeared in the 12th century as ~gehine~, from Old French ~gehir~ (“to confess, to avow”), itself from Frankish *~jehhjan~ (“to say, to confess”), with the suffix ~-ine~ (as in ~haine~, ~saisine~). Through Middle French the form ~gehenne~ arose by attraction to ~géhenne~ (“hell, torment”) — a word that travelled from Hebrew ~Gē-Hinnōm~ (the Valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem) through Ancient Greek ~géenna~ into Ecclesiastical Latin ~gehenna~.

The noun first named the torture used to wring out a confession, then weakened to “severe constraint,” then to the everyday “discomfort, embarrassment, awkwardness” of today. The verb ~gêner~ followed the same descent from torment to mere inconvenience: to be ~gêné~ once meant to be racked, now only to feel ill at ease. Mind the homophone: ~gène~ (“gene”) shares the pronunciation but not the history, having entered French much later from scientific English. From the same family come the adjective ~gêné~ and, by the hellish detour, ~géhenne~ itself.
en.habiliter:
French ~habiliter~ entered the language in the fourteenth century as Middle French ~(h)abiliter~, borrowed from Latin ~habilitāre~ (“to make fit, to enable”). The Latin verb rests on the adjective ~habilis~ (“easy to handle, suitable, apt”), which comes from ~habēre~ (“to hold, to have”): what is easy to hold is easy to use. Latin ~habēre~ is also the source of the Romance verbs for “to have,” such as French ~avoir~, Italian ~avere~ and Spanish ~haber~. English ~able~ and ~ability~ belong to the same family and reached English through Old French. French speakers can still see ~habile~ plus a verbal ending inside the word, but the verb was not coined in French.

The meaning moved from “to make capable” to “to give someone the legal capacity to act.” Today ~habiliter~ is chiefly a legal and administrative verb: an authority is empowered, in French ~habilité~, to sign, to inspect or to act for others. French universities even grant an ~habilitation à diriger des recherches~, the qualification that lets a researcher supervise doctoral students. Its relatives show the same root at work: ~habile~ (“skilful”), ~habileté~, ~inhabile~ and ~réhabiliter~, which restores someone's standing, literally making them fit again. The pair ~habile~ and ~habiliter~ separates a personal quality from a conferred status: one is skilled by nature, the other is made fit by a decision.
en.habiller:
French ~habiller~ has one of the most surprising etymologies in the language: it began in carpentry, not in the wardrobe. It comes from Old French ~abillier~, “to prepare a log of wood,” built on ~bille~ (“log, billet of wood”) via ~biller~. The ~h~ and the modern sense arrived later: by the 13th century Middle French ~abiller~ had generalized to “to make ready, to prepare,” and in the 15th century the spelling ~habiller~ and the meaning “to clothe” took hold under the influence of the unrelated noun ~habit~ (“garment”).

So the “dress” sense is a kind of accident: a verb for dressing timber was pulled toward dressing people because it sounded like the word for clothes. The base ~bille~ survives in French in the woodworking and billiard senses, and the false magnet ~habit~ descends instead from Latin ~habitus~, from ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”). From ~habiller~ French built ~déshabiller~ (“to undress”), ~rhabiller~ (“to dress again, to mend”), and ~habillement~ (“clothing”). The same logic of “preparing” still flickers in technical phrases like ~habiller~ a text or a window display.
en.habiter:
From Latin ~habitāre~ (“to dwell, inhabit, occupy”), the frequentative of ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”): to ~habitāre~ is, etymologically, “to keep having,” to hold a place continually. ~Habēre~ descends from the PIE root *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, take hold of”). A common but false intuition pairs Latin ~habēre~ with English ~have~; the two merely resemble each other, for English ~have~ in fact descends from a different root, the one behind Latin ~capere~ (“to seize”). The true Romance heirs of ~habēre~ are French ~avoir~, Italian ~avere~, and Spanish ~haber~; ~habitāre~ itself gave Italian ~abitare~ and Spanish ~habitar~.

The frequentative force — having again and again — is precisely what turns “to hold” into “to dwell”: a home is a place one has and has, steadily, over time. French kept the residing sense, ~habiter une ville~ (“to live in a city”), and extended it to occupation more broadly, even figuratively, as a feeling may ~habiter~ someone. From ~habitāre~ flow ~habitant~, ~habitation~, ~habitat~, and ~cohabiter~; from the parent ~habēre~ come ~habit~ (clothing, once “what one habitually wears”), ~habitude~, and ~avoir~ — the holding, the having, and the dwelling all branches of one grasping root.
en.habituer:
From Old French ~abituer~ (« to clothe, to dress »), from Medieval Latin ~habituare~ (« to accustom »), itself based on Latin ~habitus~ (« condition, bearing, dress, habit »), a noun from ~habēre~ (« to have, to hold »). The deeper origin of ~habēre~ is debated: it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ (« to grab, to take »), but the connection is uncertain, and the once-popular link with English ~give~ is now doubted.

The path of meaning is striking. ~habitus~ named one's outward « bearing » or « dress » — the source, too, of a monk's ~habit~ — and so Old French ~abituer~ first meant « to clothe ». Because a settled way of being shades easily into a settled way of acting, the word slid from outward garb to ingrained custom, giving the modern sense « to get used to ». The same Latin family populates French richly: ~habit~, ~habitude~, ~habituel~, and, through ~habitare~ (« to dwell »), ~habiter~ and ~habitant~.
en.hacher: French ~hacher~ is usually explained as a verb formed from ~hache~ (“axe”) plus the ending ~-er~, as in Old French ~hachier~ (“to chop up”). ~Hache~ itself is a Germanic loan, from Frankish *~happjā~, the same source as Old High German ~happia~ (“hatchet”). English Wiktionary gives a different route: a verb inherited from Old and Middle French, from Frankish *~hakkōn~ and Proto-Germanic *~hakkōną~ (“to chop”), which also gave English ~hack~. Either way the root is Germanic, and the meaning has stayed the same: to cut into small pieces.
en.handicaper:
Derived from the noun ~handicap~, borrowed from English, with the sporting sense attested in French in 1854 and the figurative “to put at a disadvantage” by 1889. The English word, attested from the 1650s, contracts the phrase ~hand in cap~ (also written ~hand i’ the cap~). It named a bartering and wagering game: two parties and a neutral umpire each put forfeit money into a cap, and the players plunged in their hands and withdrew them either full or empty to signal whether they accepted the umpire’s valuation of an uneven exchange. This “hand-in-cap” origin is given as the established account.

By the eighteenth century the umpire’s task of equalizing an unfair match had passed to horse racing, where a superior horse was made to carry extra weight — the ~handicap~. From the racetrack the word spread to any imposed disadvantage, and only around 1890 did it acquire the sense of an encumbrance or disability. French ~handicaper~ thus reaches all the way back to coins drawn blind from a hat. The family in French includes ~handicap~, ~handicapé~ and ~handicapeur~.
en.hanter:
From Middle French ~hanter~, from Old French ~hanter~ (“to frequent, to dwell in a place”). The deeper source is Germanic, and the two Wiktionaries phrase it differently. French Wiktionary derives it from Old Norse ~heimta~ (“to lead home”), from ~heim~ (“home”). English Wiktionary allows Old English ~hāmettan~ (“to bring home, to house”), Old Norse ~heimta~, or both, all from Proto-Germanic *~haimatjaną~ (“to bring home”). Either way the root is the one behind English ~home~ and German ~Heim~, both cognates. The verb is well attested in Normandy and spread from there across the rest of the northern langue d'oïl area.

The original sense was to frequent a place, to visit it often. The ghostly sense is recent: it appears in the nineteenth century, in step with the fashion for English things and the first fantasy novels, probably through a crossing with English ~haunt~, which itself came from Old French ~hanter~. The word may thus have made a round trip through English and come back with spectres. The Norman dialect, however, already had ~hanter~ for “visited by ghosts” and ~hant~ for “ghost, revenant”, so the influence may not have been purely English. Compare also Walloon ~hanter~ (“to court, to go out with”).
en.harceler:
~Harceler~ comes from Middle French ~harceller~ (attested in 1478), a popular variant of ~herseler~. That form was built on ~herser~ (“to harrow”) with the diminutive ending ~-eler~, and ~herser~ in turn comes from ~herse~, the toothed frame dragged over ploughed soil to break up clods. The noun ~herse~ is generally traced to Latin ~hirpex~ (“harrow”). The verb is thus a distant relative of the farmer's harrow, however far the modern sense has traveled from the field.

How the word moved from fields to people is not spelled out in the sources. Today ~harceler~ means to harass, to hound, to hassle, to pester persistently. Modern French uses it in the expressions ~harcèlement moral~ and ~harcèlement sexuel~, which have given the word a legal edge. The related noun ~herse~ survives in French in its own senses, and ~herser~ still means “to harrow a field,” so the agricultural root is still visible beside the figurative verb.
en.harmoniser: Formed from ~harmonie~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which builds verbs meaning “to make or render” something. ~Harmonie~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~harmonia~, itself taken from Ancient Greek ~ἁρμονία~ (~harmonía~, “union, agreement”); it was written ~armonie~ in Old French. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, a form that transcribed Greek verbs, and it remains productive today. So ~harmoniser~ is, literally, “to make harmonious”: to bring things into agreement.
en.hausser:
From Old French ~haucier~, from Vulgar Latin *~altiāre~ (“to raise”), a verb derived from Latin ~altus~ (“high”). French Wiktionary calls *~altiāre~ a collateral form of the Latin verb ~altāre~ (“to raise up”), itself built on the comparative ~altior~ (“higher”). Cognates elsewhere in Romance include Spanish ~alzar~, Italian ~alzare~, Catalan ~alçar~, Occitan ~auçar~ and Romanian ~înălța~. Latin ~altus~ is generally traced to ~alere~ (“to nourish”), so “high” began as “grown.”

The aspirated initial ~h~ of ~hausser~, which blocks liaison, is the same one found in ~haut~ and is usually attributed to Frankish influence on the Latin word. The meaning stayed close to the root: to make something higher, whether literally or figuratively. French speaks of ~hausser les épaules~ (“to shrug”), ~hausser le ton~ (“to raise one's voice”) and ~hausser les prix~ (“to raise prices”). The noun ~hausse~ (“rise”) is derived from the verb, and the prefixed verbs ~rehausser~ (“to heighten, to enhance”) and ~exhausser~ (“to raise up, to grant”) belong to the same family, as does ~haut~ itself.
en.haver: The verb ~haver~ is a mining term meaning to undercut a seam. It matches Old French ~hauwer~ (“to hoe”) and probably comes from Old High German ~hauen~ (“to hew, to cut down”), related to Old Low Frankish *~hauwa~ (“hoe”). German ~Hauer~ (“miner”) comes from the same verb and in turn gave Czech ~havíř~ (“miner”). The origin is given only as probable, so the link to Germanic is likely rather than proven. English ~hew~ is a cousin of German ~hauen~, as is the French ~houe~ (“hoe”) through Frankish.
en.haïr:
From Old French ~haïr~ (also ~hadir~, ~haier~), from Frankish/Old Low Franconian *~hatjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hatjaną~ (“to hate”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kad-~ (“sorrow, hatred”). It is a direct cognate of English ~hate~, German ~hassen~, and Dutch ~haten~ — a rare Germanic intruder among the overwhelmingly Latinate verbs of French, carried in by the Franks who gave their name to France itself.

The meaning has held remarkably steady — to detest — but the conjugation of ~haïr~ is one of the strangest in the language, which is precisely what makes it memorable. The diaeresis (tréma) on the ~ï~ is kept throughout, forcing the disyllabic /a.i/ of ~nous haïssons~ and ~je haïssais~ — except in the three singular persons of the présent and the singular imperative, where it vanishes: ~je hais~, ~tu hais~, ~il hait~, imperative ~hais~, all pronounced as one syllable /ɛ/. The ~h~ is aspirate, so it blocks elision and liaison: one writes ~je hais~, never j'hais, and says ~le haïr~ with an audible gap. In the passé simple and imperfect subjonctif the tréma even usurps the circumflex other verbs take, yielding ~nous haïmes~, ~vous haïtes~, ~qu'il haït~ rather than -îmes/-îtes/-ît. Finally, a living regional variation: in Canadian French the singular keeps the tréma and stays disyllabic — ~je haïs~, ~tu haïs~, ~il haït~ /a.i/ — diverging from the standard monosyllabic ~je hais~. From the same Germanic root spring ~haine~, ~haineux~, and ~haïssable~.
en.heurter:
French ~heurter~ goes back to Old French ~hurter~ (“to collide, to butt”), attested by 1119, but its deeper source is disputed. The account favored by the TLFi derives it from Frankish *~hūrt~ (“ram”), making the verb literally “to butt like a ram”; comparison is drawn with Old Norse ~hrútr~ (“ram”) and Welsh ~hwrdd~ (“ram”). A rival hypothesis posits a Vulgar Latin *~ūritāre~, “to charge like an aurochs,” from Latin ~ūrus~ (“aurochs”) — either way, a large horned beast lurks behind the word. The verb has Germanic kin in Dutch ~horten~ and Middle High German ~hurten~ (“to crash into”), and one famous offshoot in English: ~hurt~ is generally held to be borrowed from Old Northern French ~hurter~, sliding from “knock against” to “injure.”

The form ~hurter~ held the field into the sixteenth century, when the vowel opened before the r and modern ~heurter~ triumphed. The figurative reach came early: by about 1180 the verb could mean “to oppose, to offend,” and modern French still lets sensibilities, colors and interests collide — ~se heurter à~ is “to run up against.” The family is compact and concrete: a ~heurt~ is a clash or a bump, and a ~heurtoir~ is a door knocker — etymologically, if the favored origin is right, a little ram with which every visitor butts the house. English ~hurt~, meanwhile, carries this Old French collision through everyday speech: to be hurt is, historically, to have been struck.
en.hisser: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~hissen~ (French Wiktionary says “German”), and it is of imitative origin according to French Wiktionary. Dutch ~hijsen~, Italian ~issare~ and English ~hoist~ are related. It appears in Rabelais's ~Quart Livre~ as the hauling cry ~inse !~ (“heave!”), with the spelling ~ysser~ recorded in 1573. The reflexive ~se hisser~ (“to haul oneself up”) is recorded in the eighteenth century.
en.hiérarchiser: Formed in French from ~hiérarchie~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, the verb means “to arrange in a hierarchy, to rank by importance.” The noun ~hiérarchie~ was borrowed from Latin ~hierarchia~, which came from Greek ~ἱεράρχης~ (~hierarkhēs~, “hierarch,” the holder of a sacred office). That Greek word joins ~ἱερός~ (“sacred”) and ~ἄρχειν~ (“to rule”), so a hierarchy was first a sacred order of rule, such as the ranks of the Church. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and in French it means “to make, to treat as.” To ~hiérarchiser~ is therefore to give things a rank, as one does with priorities.
en.homologuer:
Borrowed from Latin ~homologāre~ (“to agree, to approve”), which in turn goes back to Greek ~homologeîn~ (“to say the same thing, to agree”), built from ~homós~ (“same”) and a verb of speaking related to ~lógos~ (“word”). The original idea is therefore that of two parties saying the same thing and so being in agreement. The Greek-derived relatives ~homologie~ (“correspondence between parts”) and ~homologue~ (“corresponding, equivalent”) are cited by French Wiktionary as part of the same family.

In French, ~homologuer~ is a legal and administrative verb. A court ~homologue~ an agreement when it confirms it and gives it official force, and the modern uses extend that picture: an authority ~homologue~ a record in sport, a product that has passed a standard, or a decision. The participle ~homologué~ (“officially approved, type-approved”) is common on labels and in sports reports. English has the related ~homologous~ and ~homology~, as well as the rare legal verb ~homologate~.
en.honorer:
French ~honorer~ comes from Latin ~honorare~ (“to honor, to do honor to”), a denominal verb from ~honor~, older ~honos~ (“honor, esteem, public office”). The deeper origin of ~honos~ is unknown: scholars note that a Proto-Indo-European shape like *~ǵʰon-~ would be expected, but there are no clear cognates in other languages, so the root remains obscure — a striking blank for so central a Roman word. Cognate developments survive in Italian ~onorare~ and Spanish ~honrar~, and English ~honor~ / ~honour~ is borrowed from the same Latin family through Old French.
