French preserves the noun directly as ~interprète~. Italian ~interpretare~ and Spanish ~interpretar~ descend from the same Latin verb, as does English ~interpret~.

The original ~interpres~ was a middleman — a negotiator, a broker, then a translator standing between two tongues. From mediating between languages the sense broadened to mediating between a text and its reader: to ~interpréter~ is to draw out a hidden or disputed meaning, whether of a law, a dream, or a difficult passage. A further branch carries the word into performance, where to ~interpréter~ a role or a sonata is to render it, to make its meaning audible. The exact second root remains debated, which is why scholars hedge it; still, the same Latin family yields French ~interprète~, ~interprétation~, and ~interprétariat~.
en.interroger:
From Latin ~interrogare~ (“to ask, to question”), a compound of the preposition ~inter~ (“between, among”) and the verb ~rogare~ (“to ask, to request”). ~rogare~ is usually traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to direct in a straight line”), so that asking may have begun as a figurative “stretching out” of the hand toward someone. The same root gives Latin ~regere~ (“to rule, to keep straight”) and ~rex~ (“king”). Cognate through ~rogare~ with English ~rogation~ and, more distantly through the root, with English ~right~ and ~regent~.

The ~inter~ in ~interrogare~ carries the idea of an exchange passing back and forth between two parties — the to-and-fro of question and answer. From the neutral Latin sense “to ask,” French ~interroger~ specialized toward pointed, official, or insistent questioning: a judge, a teacher, or a police officer ~interroge~, where one merely ~demande~ a favor. The same ~rogare~ surfaces across French in a string of relatives: ~rogatoire~ (as in a ~commission rogatoire~, a judicial request), ~abroger~ (to repeal, literally to “ask away” a law), ~déroger~, ~proroger~, and ~prérogative~ — a cluster in which the original gesture of asking has hardened into the formal vocabulary of law and authority.
en.interrompre:
From Latin ~interrumpere~ (“to break apart, to interrupt”), ~inter-~ (“between”) + ~rumpere~ (“to break”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~Hrewp-~ (“to break, tear”), with a Sanskrit cognate ~lumpáti~ (“breaks, plunders”). The earliest French forms were native re-buildings on ~entre-~ + ~rompre~ (~entrerompre~, around 1160), later re-latinized to match ~interrumpere~.

The literal sense is to “break in between” — to snap the continuity of a speech, an action, or a road. Through ~rumpere~ this verb belongs to a large and vivid family: French ~rompre~ (“to break”), ~corrompre~ (“to corrupt,” literally “to break thoroughly”), ~interruption~, and ~rupture~. English shares the harvest — ~rupture~, ~abrupt~, ~corrupt~, and even ~route~ and ~rout~, both from a Latin ~rupta~ (“a broken-through way, a broken line of soldiers”). To interrupt someone is, etymologically, to break the thread of their words.
en.intervenir:
From Latin ~intervenīre~ (“to come between, intervene, interrupt, occur”), a compound of the prefix ~inter-~ (“between, among”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). ~venīre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”), one of the most widely attested roots in the family: it is cognate with English ~come~, Greek ~baínein~ (“to go, step”), and Sanskrit ~gam-~ (“to go”). To intervene is, literally, “to come between.”

The Latin verb already carried both senses the French keeps: a physical or social one — to step in, to interpose oneself in an affair — and a temporal one, “to happen, to occur in the meantime,” as when an event ~intervient~ unexpectedly. French inherited the prefixed family richly: ~venir~ (“to come”), ~devenir~ (“to become”), ~revenir~ (“to come back”), ~prévenir~ (“to forewarn, to prevent,” literally “to come before”), ~parvenir~, ~survenir~, and ~convenir~ (“to suit, agree”). The same root surfaces in the learned ~avenir~ (“future,” what is “to come”) and in ~événement~ (“event,” something that “comes out”). Even ~aventure~ — what is “about to come” — belongs to this kin. To intervene is thus to insert a coming squarely in the middle of events.
en.interviewer: A verb formed from the noun ~interview~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, and the noun itself comes from English. The route is circular. English ~interview~ was taken from Old French ~entreveue~ (“a meeting”), a noun from ~entreveoir~, which joined ~entre-~ (“between”) to ~veoir~ (“to see”), from Latin ~videre~. French then borrowed the English word back, with its new sense of a journalist questioning a person, and gave it a regular first-group ending. So when a reporter ~interviewe~ someone, the word has crossed the Channel twice.
en.intituler:
From Latin ~intitulare~ (“to give a title to, to inscribe”), a derivative of ~titulus~ (“title, label, inscription, placard”). The origin of ~titulus~ is uncertain — possibly borrowed from Etruscan, the substrate that gave Latin several culture-words of obscure pedigree. From ~titulus~ the Romance languages drew their words for “title”: Spanish ~título~, Italian ~titolo~, and French ~titre~ (via Old French ~title~); English ~title~ and the tiny ~tittle~ (the dot over an i) are doublets from the very same Latin word.

In Roman use a ~titulus~ was an inscribed tablet or notice — the placard naming a thing, even the board nailed above the cross. To ~intituler~ a work is therefore literally to fix a heading on it, to give it its name, and the verb still means “to title, to entitle.” The reflexive ~s'intituler~ means “to be called, to bear the title of.” French keeps a rich family around ~titre~: ~titrer~ (“to give a title, to assay”), ~sous-titre~ (“subtitle”), ~titulaire~ (“holder, titular”), and the verb ~intituler~ itself, all turning on the idea of the name set at the head of a thing.
en.intriguer:
French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~intricāre~ (“to entangle, to embarrass”), while English Wiktionary says it was borrowed from Italian ~intrigare~; the two accounts differ on the route, and the sources do not settle it. Latin ~intricāre~ is built from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~trīcae~ (“hindrances, tangles, trifles”). The verb is a doublet of ~intriquer~. Spanish ~intrigar~ and English ~intrigue~ belong to the same family, the English verb being a borrowing from French.

The Latin sense is the literal one: to tangle someone in difficulties, to put them in a bind. In French the verb covers the tangles of plotting, so that to ~intriguer~ is to weave secret schemes and pull strings, and also a second, everyday sense: to puzzle or to arouse curiosity, as when an odd detail intrigues you. The two senses keep the original image of something knotted and hard to untangle. The family includes ~intrigue~, ~intrigant~ and ~intriqué~, and the learned ~inextricable~ is a distant relative through the Latin verb ~extricāre~, “to untangle.”
en.introduire:
From Latin ~introducere~ (“to lead in, to bring inside”), a compound of the adverb ~intro~ (“inward, within”) and the verb ~ducere~ (“to lead, to conduct”). ~intro~ is itself built on ~in~ (“in”); ~ducere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to lead, to draw”), which in the Germanic branch yields English ~tow~ and ~tug~ and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”). Old French reshaped the inherited form as ~entreduire~ before the learned ~introduire~ prevailed. Cognate with English ~introduce~ and Italian ~introdurre~.

The literal image is of leading something or someone inward — across a threshold, into a room, into a society. French ~introduire~ keeps this concretely physical sense (to insert, to put in: ~introduire une clé dans la serrure~) alongside the social one (to introduce a person, to bring them into a circle) and the abstract (to introduce an idea, a law, a custom). The root *~dewk-~ is one of the great engines of French vocabulary through ~ducere~ and its participle ~ductus~: ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~réduire~, ~séduire~, ~traduire~, plus the nouns ~duc~ (“duke,” a leader), ~conduite~, and ~aqueduc~. To ~introduire~ is, etymologically, simply to lead in.
en.intégrer:
From Latin ~integrāre~ (“to make whole, restore, renew”), a verb built on the adjective ~integer~ (“whole, intact, untouched”). That adjective is itself ~in-~ (“not”) plus a form related to ~tangere~ (“to touch”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~tag-~ (“to touch, handle”): the ~integer~ is literally the “untouched,” the thing left whole. The same root gives Latin ~tangere~, ~tactus~, and ~intāctus~. French ~intégrer~ entered first as a learned, rare word in the 14th century, then was effectively reborrowed in the 19th.

The arc of meaning runs from “to restore to wholeness” to “to make something part of a whole.” That second sense powers all the modern uses: to incorporate elements into a system, to admit a person into a group, to ~intégrer~ a prestigious school (a peculiarly French use meaning to gain admission), and the mathematician's “to integrate.” Because ~integer~ meant “untouched, undivided,” its descendants split between two notions — moral wholeness and numerical wholeness — so that the same root underlies both ~intégrité~ (uprightness) and the English ~integer~ (a whole number). Kin in modern French include ~intégral~, ~intégration~, ~réintégrer~, ~désintégrer~, and, through Old French, the everyday ~entier~ (“entire, whole”).
en.intéresser:
From Latin ~interesse~ (“to be among, to be between, to take part in”), a compound of the preposition ~inter~ (“between, among”) and ~esse~ (“to be”), the latter from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁es-~ (“to be”) that also underlies English ~is~ and German ~ist~. From the impersonal Latin phrase ~interest~ (“it matters, it concerns”) French drew both the noun ~intérêt~ and, in the fourteenth century, the verb ~intéresser~. Italian preserves the parallel ~interessare~ and Spanish ~interesar~.

The semantic thread runs from physical position to mental engagement: what is literally “among” us, what lies “between” the parties, is what concerns them — and what concerns us is what holds our attention. So ~intéresser~ came to mean both “to involve someone, to give them a stake in something” and “to arouse someone's curiosity.” The financial sense survives in ~intéressement~, an employee profit-sharing scheme — a share, quite literally, in what is at stake. The same ~inter~ prefix runs through a crowd of French words such as ~international~, ~intervalle~, ~interrompre~, and ~entretenir~, while ~esse~ surfaces, much disguised, in ~essence~ and in the irregular forms of ~être~. To find something ~intéressant~ is, at root, to feel oneself caught up in the midst of it.
en.inventer:
From Latin ~inventum~, the supine of ~invenīre~ (“to come upon, to find, to discover”), a compound of ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). Latin ~venīre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”) — the very same root, remarkably, that surfaces in the Germanic branch as English ~come~ and German ~kommen~. To ~invenīre~ was literally to “come upon” something. The Spanish ~inventar~ shares the ancestry.

The semantic pivot is the difference between finding and making up: in Latin and early French the word leaned toward discovery — you ~invent~ a thing by coming upon what was already there (a sense fossilized in the legal and archaeological ~invention~, the “finding” of relics or treasure). Only by about 1450 did French ~inventer~ tip toward the modern sense of contriving something that did not exist before, and thence to the pejorative “to make up, to fabricate” (~inventer une excuse~). From the same ~venīre~ come a great crowd of French words — ~venir~, ~avenir~, ~événement~, ~convenir~, ~revenir~, ~souvenir~, ~prévenir~ — all turning on the idea of coming.
en.inverser:
From Latin ~inversare~, a frequentative built on ~inversus~, the past participle of ~invertere~ (“to turn upside down”) — itself the prefix ~in-~ (“in, against”) joined to ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~Vertere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~wertō~ and PIE *~wert-~ (“to turn”). The root is wide-flung: Sanskrit ~vártate~ (“it turns”), and, through Proto-Germanic, English ~-ward~ (as in “toward”) and ~worth~, which began as a verb meaning “to become, to turn into.”

French inherited the popular doublet ~envers~ (“wrong side, reverse”) directly, while ~inverser~ and the adjective ~inverse~ are the more learned, Latinate reborrowings of the same family. To ~inverser~ is to swap two things into each other's place, to reverse an order or a polarity. From ~vertere~ flowed an enormous progeny of French words built on its many prefixes: ~convertir~, ~divertir~, ~pervertir~, ~avertir~, ~revers~, ~version~, and ~vertige~ (the world quite literally “turning”). Few Latin verbs turned out to be so productive.
en.investir:
From Latin ~investīre~ (“to clothe, dress, surround”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) + ~vestīre~ (“to dress, clothe”), itself from ~vestis~ (“garment, clothing”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wes-~ (“to clothe”). Cognate with Italian ~investire~ and Spanish ~investir~, and — through the same ~vestis~ — with French ~vêtir~, ~veste~, and ~vêtement~, and with English ~vest~ and ~vestment~.

The oldest sense was literal then ceremonial: to ~investir~ someone was to robe them in the insignia of an office, hence “to install in a dignity” — the source of ~investiture~, the medieval rite by which a lord clothed a vassal in his fief. From the garment that wraps came the military ~investir~ (“to besiege, to surround a place”), the army girding a town as cloth girds a body. The financial sense — to ~investir~ capital — is the most surprising turn: it arose in the early 1600s, probably through Italian ~investire~ in the East-Indies trade, on the image of giving money a new “dress,” clothing it in a fresh and profitable form. The same root yields ~travesti~ (“cross-dressed”), literally a re-clothing, and ~transvestisme~.
en.inviter:
From Latin ~invītāre~ (“to invite, to summon, to entertain”), attested in French from 1356. The deeper origin is genuinely uncertain: some scholars connect it to ~invocāre~ (“to call upon”), while others reconstruct a Proto-Indo-European base *~weyh₁-~ (“to chase, to pursue”), via a participle *~weyh₁-to-~ (“pursued, sought after”). Because the etymology is disputed, the chain beyond Latin is best left open. The Latin verb passed regularly into Italian ~invitare~, Spanish ~invitar~, and Catalan ~invitar~; English ~invite~ came in through Middle French ~inviter~.

The Latin sense already blended hospitality with enticement — to ~invītāre~ was to summon a guest but also to allure — and French preserves both shades, from ~inviter à dîner~ (“to invite to dinner”) to ~inviter à la prudence~ (“to urge caution”). A striking offshoot survives in card-playing: from the “luring” sense came Spanish and Catalan ~envidar~ (“to stake, to bet”), as a player invites the others to wager. In modern French the family stays compact — chiefly ~inviter~, ~invitation~, ~invité~, and ~invite~ (“an enticement”) — a small but sociable corner of the lexicon.
en.invoquer:
Borrowed from Latin ~invocare~ (“to call upon, to call for help”), from ~in-~ (“upon, toward”) + ~vocare~ (“to call”), the verb of ~vox~ (“voice”). ~Vox~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wekʷ-~ (“to speak, to utter”), through the noun-form *~wṓkʷs~. Cognate with Italian ~invocare~ and Spanish ~invocar~; through the same PIE root, kin to Sanskrit ~vāc~ (“speech”) and, more distantly, to a great family of “voice” words.

The oldest sense is the sacred one: to call a god or higher power by name, to summon aid from above — one still « invoque Dieu » or « invoque les mânes » of the dead. From that solemn act the verb broadened to citing an authority or a text in argument (« invoquer la loi »), and then, more weakly still, to pleading a reason or excuse (« invoquer la fatigue »). The connecting thread is calling something up by naming it. From the same ~vox~ and ~vocare~ French keeps ~voix~ (“voice”), ~vocal~, ~évoquer~ (“to call to mind”), ~provoquer~, ~convoquer~, and ~révoquer~ — a whole family built on the act of the calling voice.
en.irriguer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~irrigāre~ (“to lead water onto, to water”), made of ~in-~ (“onto”), assimilated to ~ir-~ before the following ~r~, and ~rigāre~ (“to water, to moisten”). French kept the agricultural sense of watering land by channels and added a medical one, in which blood ~irrigue~ a tissue. English ~irrigate~ and Italian ~irrigare~ are borrowings of the same Latin verb.
en.irriter: Borrowed from Latin ~irrītāre~ (“to excite, to provoke, to rouse to anger”), a verb whose own origin within Latin is obscure. The same Latin verb gave Spanish and Portuguese ~irritar~ and Italian ~irritare~, and English ~irritate~. In French it covers both the emotional sense, to annoy or anger, and the physical one, to inflame a tissue or skin, as seen in ~irritant~, ~irritation~ and ~irritable~.
en.isoler:
Borrowed in the seventeenth century from Italian ~isolare~ (“to make into an island, to set apart”), itself from ~isola~ (“island”), from Latin ~īnsula~ (“island”). The French adjective ~isolé~ was attested slightly earlier, taken from Italian ~isolato~ (Latin ~īnsulātus~, “made into an island”), and the verb was back-formed from it. Latin ~īnsula~ is also the source of Italian ~isola~, Spanish ~isla~, and — through a different route, with ~île~ — French itself; English ~isle~ and ~isolated~ belong to the same family.

The earliest French use, in 1653, was strictly geographic: a branch of the Nile was said to ~isoler~ a meadow, to cut it off like an island. From there the meaning spread to any setting-apart — a hermit who ~s'isole~, a patient in quarantine, a wire that one must ~isoler~ electrically (hence the English “insulate”). The development was reinforced by the native French ~seul~ (“alone”), which colored the verb toward solitude. The same ~īnsula~ yields a large modern family: ~isolation~, ~isolement~, ~isolant~ (“insulator, insulating”), ~isolateur~, ~isoloir~ (the voting booth), and the geographic ~presqu'île~ (“peninsula,” a calque of Latin ~paene īnsula~, “almost an island”).
en.issir:
From Old French ~issir~ (also ~eissir~, “to go out, to come forth”), from Latin ~exīre~ (“to go out, depart”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~īre~ (“to go”). ~Īre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), one of the great verbs of motion, cognate with Greek ~eîmi~ (“I will go”) and Sanskrit ~éti~ (“he goes”). Romance kin include Italian ~uscire~ (from a related ~ūsciō~) and the Spanish noun reflexes of the same family.

In medieval French, ~issir~ was a fully living verb meaning “to exit.” Then it lost its own battle for survival: in the sixteenth century speakers increasingly preferred ~sortir~, and by the seventeenth ~issir~ had all but vanished as a conjugated verb. Yet it did not die — it fossilized into its participles. The past participle ~issu~ (“descended from, born of”) is thoroughly alive (“~issu~ d'une famille modeste”), and the noun ~issue~ (“a way out, an outcome”) is one of the most common words in French. The same ~exīre~ surfaces in the borrowed ~exit~, and the root ~īre~ underlies a scattered band of French descendants from the verb ~aller~’s suppletive forms to nouns like ~transit~ and ~initiation~ — wanderings, all, of a verb that simply meant “to go.”
en.jaillir:
The origin of ~jaillir~ is uncertain, but the favored account is Celtic. French Wiktionary derives Old French ~galir~ and ~jalir~ from Gaulish *~gali-~ (“to boil, to gush, to well up”), related to a Gaulish noun *~galia~ (“strength”), and compares Irish ~gailim~ (“I boil”). English Wiktionary is more cautious: possibly from a Vulgar Latin verb *~galīre~, itself from Transalpine Gaulish *~gali-~. Both accounts agree on the Gaulish root, so the verb would be one of the few French words surviving from the Celtic language spoken in Gaul, though the intermediate Latin step is a conjecture.

French Wiktionary lists the Old French forms ~galir~, ~jalir~ and ~jaillir~ side by side, and the modern spelling is the last of these. The image is of liquid boiling up and bursting forth: water springs, flames, sparks and light all ~jaillissent~, and the same verb serves figuratively for ideas, cries and truths that burst out. The prefixed ~rejaillir~ (“to spurt back, to splash up”) and the words ~jaillissement~ and ~jaillissant~ continue the family. A Celtic root, if the account is right, would thus be preserved in a verb of sudden, vigorous movement.
en.jalonner: Formed in French from the noun ~jalon~ (“marker stake”) and the suffix ~-er~, so ~jalonner~ means to mark out a line or route with stakes. The base ~jalon~ is attested from 1613 in the spelling ~jallon~, and its origin is uncertain. French sources cite the German dictionary FEW, which proposes a link to ~jaillir~ (“to spurt out”), and Auguste Scheler instead linked it to ~jauger~ (“to gauge”). Both are only suggestions. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~. The verb also works figuratively: a career or a story is ~jalonné~ by its key events.
en.jeter:
From Old French ~jeter~ (“to throw”), from Vulgar Latin *~jectāre~, from Latin ~jactāre~ (“to toss about, to fling repeatedly”), the frequentative of ~jacere~ (“to throw”). A frequentative names a repeated or vigorous action, so ~jactāre~ is “to keep throwing, to hurl about.” ~Jacere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~Hyeh₁-~ (“to throw, to let fly”). Cognate with Italian ~gettare~ and Spanish ~echar~.

That buried ~jacere~ is one of the most productive roots in the learned vocabulary: its past participle ~iactus~ and its compounds gave a long file of French words in ~-jeter~ and ~-jecter~ — ~projeter~ and ~projet~ (“thrown forward”), ~rejeter~ (“thrown back”), ~injecter~ (“thrown in”), ~objet~ (“thrown before”), ~sujet~ (“thrown under”), and ~trajet~ (“a throwing across”). The plain verb keeps the simple gesture of casting away, which is why ~jeter~ ranges from hurling a stone to throwing out the rubbish to “casting” a glance (~jeter un coup d'œil~). Even ~jeton~ — a thrown-down counter — and the cast water of a ~jet~ d'eau trace back to the same Latin act of letting fly.
en.joindre:
From Latin ~jungere~ (“to join, yoke, unite”), descended from the Proto-Indo-European root *~yewg-~ (“to join, yoke”). This is one of the deepest and most widespread roots in Indo-European: it gives Sanskrit ~yoga~ (“union, yoking”), Greek ~zeugnumi~ (“I yoke”), German ~Joch~, and the English ~yoke~ — itself a cognate of the very root, alongside the borrowed ~join~ and ~junction~. Italian ~giungere~ and Spanish ~juntar~ are the Romance kin.

The Latin sense of binding two things together survives intact: one can ~joindre~ two pieces of wood, ~joindre les mains~ (clasp the hands), ~joindre l'utile à l'agréable~ (combine the useful and the pleasant), or — in a thoroughly modern turn — ~joindre~ someone by telephone, that is, reach them. The past participle ~joint~ also names a seal or gasket. The root's reach in French is enormous: ~jonction~, ~adjoindre~, ~rejoindre~, ~conjoint~ (“spouse,” one yoked together with you), ~disjoindre~, ~jointure~, and the borrowed joindre-family aside, even ~joug~ (“yoke”) itself descends from ~jungere~'s noun ~jugum~. From an ox's wooden yoke to a married couple to a phone call, all are, at heart, a yoking-together.
en.jouer:
From Old French ~joer~, ~jouer~ (“to play, jest, frolic”), from Latin ~iocāre~ (“to joke, jest”), a Vulgar-Latin variant of the Classical deponent ~iocārī~, from the noun ~iocus~ (“joke, jest, game”). Cognate with Italian ~giocare~, Spanish ~jugar~, and Portuguese ~jogar~; from ~iocus~ English borrowed ~joke~ and ~jocular~.

A quiet upset hides here: Classical Latin's main verb for playing was ~lūdere~ (the source of ~ludique~ and ~illusion~), while ~iocārī~ meant narrowly to jest with words. Over Late Latin the joking verb broadened to cover all play and amusement and ousted ~lūdere~ from everyday speech, so French inherited ~jouer~ for everything from children's games to performing music and acting a role. From the related noun ~iocus~ came ~jeu~ (“game”), and from ~jeu~ the reduplicated nursery word ~joujou~ and the toy ~jouet~. The word's reach in modern French is remarkably wide — one ~joue~ a sport, an instrument, a part on stage, a card, the stock market, and even, figuratively, with someone's feelings — all descended from a Roman word that meant, at first, merely a good-natured joke.
en.jouir:
Attested at the start of the twelfth century, ~jouir~ comes through Old French ~joïr~ from Latin ~gaudēre~ (“to rejoice, to take inner delight in”), which in Vulgar Latin shifted to ~gaudīre~, joining the productive ~-īre~ conjugation. ~gaudēre~ is thought to derive, by way of an unattested *~gāvidus~, from a Proto-Indo-European root *~geh₂u-~ (“to rejoice”), with Greek cognates such as ~gánumai~ (“to be glad”). From ~gaudēre~ Latin also formed ~gaudium~ (“joy”), source of French ~joie~ and English ~joy~.

The Latin sense was broad, warm delight, and Old French ~joïr~ kept it. French then specialized the verb toward possession and benefit: to ~jouir~ de quelque chose is to enjoy the use of it, hence the legal ~jouissance~ (“usufruct, enjoyment of a right”). Alongside this practical sense the word also narrowed, from the twelfth century onward, toward intense bodily pleasure, and in modern French ~jouir~ used absolutely means to reach sexual climax — a development already plain in eighteenth-century literature. The same ~gaud-~ root surfaces in French ~jouissance~, ~joie~, ~réjouir~ (“to gladden”), and the borrowed ~gaudriole~ — a startling spread from a single Latin verb of rejoicing.
en.juger:
From Latin ~jūdicāre~ (“to judge, to pass sentence”), itself transparently a compound of ~jūs~ (“law, right”) and the verb ~dīcere~ (“to say, to pronounce”) — so that to judge was literally “to speak the law.” Latin ~jūs~ derives, through Proto-Italic ~jowos~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂yew-~ (“right, justice”), while ~dīcere~ goes back to *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”), the root that also gives English ~teach~ and ~token~. Italian ~giudicare~ and Spanish ~juzgar~ are the sister forms; English ~judge~ arrives through Old French ~jugier~.

The agent noun ~jūdex~ (“one who declares the law,” our ~judge~) shows the compound at work: in Roman practice what made law was not the doing of it but the solemn pronouncing of it, and from this act of speech sprang a whole vocabulary — ~iūdicium~, ~iūrisdictio~, and the rest. In French the verb spread from the courtroom into everyday assessment: to judge a distance, to deem something wise, to form an opinion. The same root family flowers richly: ~jugement~, ~juge~, ~préjuger~ and its noun ~préjugé~, ~déjuger~, ~méjuger~, and the legal ~jury~ borrowed back through English. Tucked inside this common verb is a memory of the Roman magistrate gravely speaking the right into being.
en.jumeler: ~Jumeler~ (“to twin, to pair up”) is formed from the noun ~jumeau~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~jumeau~ is a variant of an older form, Old French ~jumel~ or ~gemel~, from Latin ~gemellus~, a diminutive of ~geminus~ (“twin”). The change from ~gemel~ to ~jumel~ is attributed to labialisation, the vowel being rounded next to ~m~. The related Italian ~gemello~ and Spanish ~gemelo~ come from the same Latin word. The suffix ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, here gives the sense “to make into twins,” and by extension to join two things as a pair.
en.jurer:
Inherited from Old French ~jurer~ (“to swear, to take an oath,” and also “to betroth”), from Latin ~iurare~ (also written ~jurare~), “to swear,” the verb of the noun ~ius~ (“law, right, what is binding”). Cognate with Italian ~giurare~ and Spanish ~jurar~; through the noun ~ius~ it belongs to the family that gave English ~jury~, ~just~, and ~judge~, while the act itself parallels English ~swear~.

To ~jurer~ was first to bind oneself by a solemn oath, calling law or the gods to guarantee one's word — « jurer fidélité », « jurer sur la Bible ». From that grave sense the verb developed two everyday descendants. One is to curse or swear profanely — to utter a ~juron~ (“a swear-word”) — as a charretier (carter) was proverbially said to do (« jurer comme un charretier »). The other, more surprising, is a sense of clashing: two colors that « jurent » together are ones that grate against each other, an oath turned into visual discord. From the same ~ius~ French keeps ~juré~ (“juror”), ~jury~, ~juridique~, ~justice~, and ~parjure~ (“perjury”) — the whole vocabulary of law and the sworn word.
en.justifier:
From Latin ~justificare~ (“to make just, to render righteous”), a compound of ~justus~ (“just, righteous”) + the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~Justus~ derives from ~jus~ (“law, right”), from an Old Latin ~iovestos~ resting on the stem of ~jus~, and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂yew-~, denoting binding law or sacred formula. Through ~jus~ the word is cognate with English ~just~, ~jury~, and ~judge~; through ~facere~, from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to set”), it joins a vast Indo-European family.

First a theological and legal word — “to make righteous,” “to clear of a charge” — ~justifier~ then drifted toward the everyday “to give good reason for, to vindicate.” A delightful late detour is the typographer's sense: to ~justifier~ a line of text is to make its margins straight and “right,” spacing the words until the edge is even — the abstract idea of rectitude turned into the literal squaring of a column. The root ~jus~ runs deep in French through ~juste~, ~justice~, ~juger~, ~jury~, and ~juridique~, while ~facere~ surfaces in countless verbs in ~-fier~, among them ~vérifier~, ~modifier~, and ~simplifier~.
en.labelliser: ~Labelliser~ is formed in French from ~label~ + the verbal suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to treat as”), and means to give a product or a service an official label, hence to certify or approve it. The base made a round trip: French ~label~ was borrowed back from English ~label~ (“tag, strip attached to something”), which came from Old French ~lambel~ (“fringe, strip”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is fully productive in technical, administrative and journalistic French. Verbs such as ~moderniser~ and ~numériser~ follow the same pattern.
en.laisser:
French ~laisser~ descends through Old French ~laissier~ — already attested in the ninth-century ~Séquence de sainte Eulalie~, one of the oldest texts in the language — from Latin ~laxare~ (“to loosen, to slacken, to let go”). That verb is built on the adjective ~laxus~ (“loose, slack, wide”), which traces to Proto-Indo-European *~sleg-~ (“to be slack, to be languid”). The same root surfaces in English ~slack~, ~lax~, and ~relax~, and in Latin ~languere~ (“to be faint”), so the verb of letting-go is, at its core, a verb of going loose.

The semantic path is intuitive: to loosen one's grip is to let go, and to let go is to leave behind or to permit. Old French ~laissier~ already spanned “to let, to allow, to abandon,” and modern ~laisser~ keeps all of these — ~laisse-moi~ (“leave me alone”), ~laisser faire~ (“to let happen”). From ~laxare~ French also drew the doublet ~lâcher~ (“to release, to let go”), the noun ~laisse~ (a dog's leash, literally something slackened out), and, more distantly through ~laxus~, the learned ~laxatif~ and ~relâcher~. The economic doctrine of ~laissez-faire~ preserves, fossilized in a slogan, the verb's oldest instinct: loosen your hold and let things run.
en.lancer:
From Old French ~lancier~, from Late Latin ~lanceāre~ (“to wield or hurl a lance”), derived from ~lancea~ (“lance, light spear”), a word the Romans likely borrowed from a Celtic or Iberian source. The throwing weapon gave its name to the act of throwing. Italian ~lanciare~ and Spanish ~lanzar~ are cognate, and English ~lance~ and ~launch~ both descend, through French, from the same ~lancea~.

The verb began as something a soldier did with a spear — to cast it forward — and from that violent gesture generalized to any forceful throw, then to figurative launches: one ~lance~ a rocket, a product, a fashion, or a rumor. English ~launch~ is the same word, borrowed from Old French and specialized into the sense of setting a ship or a venture in motion. The native family is rich: the noun ~lance~, plus ~lancement~, ~lanceur~ (a “launcher,” including a rocket), ~relancer~ and ~relance~ (to throw again, to revive), and ~élancer~ / ~élan~, where the idea of hurling oneself forward yields both a sudden pain and a surge of momentum.
en.larguer: The verb ~larguer~ is formed from the noun ~largue~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~largue~ itself derives from Italian ~largo~ (“wide, broad”). French Wiktionary also allows another route, a direct borrowing from Spanish ~largar~ with the same sense, so the exact path is not settled. The word began as a sailors' term for letting a rope or sail out, giving it slack, which explains the nautical sense “to ease a line.” From there it spread to dropping something, as in ~larguer une bombe~, and finally to the slang sense “to ditch, to dump,” as when one ~largue~ a partner.
en.lasser: Inherited from Latin ~lassāre~ (“to tire, to weary”), a verb built on the adjective ~lassus~ (“tired”). The adjective survived in Old French as ~las~, and it lives on in the exclamation ~hélas~, literally “oh, wretched me” (~hé~ + ~las~). The verb kept its Latin sense of making someone weary, then came to mean getting fed up with something, especially in the reflexive: ~se lasser de~ (“to grow tired of”). The same family gave ~lassitude~, ~délasser~ (“to relax”) and ~inlassable~ (“untiring”).
en.laver:
From Latin ~lavāre~ (“to wash, bathe”), from Proto-Italic *~lawō~, from the PIE root *~lewh₃-~ (“to wash”). The root is widespread: cognate forms include Ancient Greek ~loúō~ (“I wash”) and, through Germanic, Old English ~lēaþor~, the ancestor of English ~lather~. The Romance sisters all preserve the verb plainly — Italian ~lavare~, Spanish and Portuguese ~lavar~ — making it one of the most stable everyday words inherited from Latin.

The sense has scarcely shifted in two thousand years: to cleanse with water, literally and then morally, as in ~laver son honneur~ (“to cleanse one's honor”) or ~laver un affront~. The same root flows through a surprising crowd of French words: ~lavabo~ (literally Latin “I shall wash,” from the priest's washing of hands), ~lavande~ (lavender, named for the bath water it scented), ~lavoir~ (a washhouse), ~lavage~, ~lessive~ and even ~déluge~ — and, borrowed from Italian, ~lave~, the “washing” flood of molten rock from a volcano.
en.lever:
From Latin ~levare~ (“to lift, to raise, to make light”), a denominative verb from the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”). That adjective descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”), the root that also gives English ~light~ and ~lung~. Romance kept the verb everywhere: Italian ~levare~, Spanish ~llevar~ (“to carry”), Portuguese ~levar~, Catalan and Occitan ~levar~.

The core idea is making something rise. From it French grew an unusually large family. The everyday ~lever~ covers raising, lifting, and getting up; with prefixes it yields ~élever~ (“to raise, to bring up”), ~enlever~ (“to remove, to carry off”), ~relever~ (“to lift again, to note”), and ~soulever~ (“to heave up”). The past participle ~levé~ and the action noun ~levée~ gave English ~levee~ (a raised riverbank) and ~levy~ (a raising of troops or taxes), while the tool that raises a load came through Old French as English ~lever~. Even bread remembers the root: ~levure~ (“yeast”) and ~levain~ (“leaven, sourdough”) are what make dough ~lever~ — rise. And the curtain-raising sense survives in ~le lever du soleil~, the sunrise, and historically in ~le lever du roi~, the king's ceremonial rising.
en.libeller: Formed from the noun ~libelle~ and the ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb. ~Libelle~ was borrowed from Latin ~libellus~ (“little book, short writing”), a diminutive of ~liber~ (“book”). The verb first meant to draw up a text in precise, formal terms, the way a clerk words a legal document, and that sense of wording something exactly survives in the modern use for writing out a check or a form. English ~libel~ comes from the same Latin word, and French ~libelle~ also came to mean a defamatory pamphlet.
en.libérer:
French ~libérer~ comes from Latin ~līberāre~ (“to set free”), a verb built on the adjective ~līber~ (“free”). That adjective traces to a Proto-Indo-European *~h₁léwdʰeros~ (“free,” literally “belonging to the people”), from the root *~h₁lewdʰ-~ (“to grow, to rise; people”). The cognates are illuminating: Ancient Greek ~eleútheros~ (“free”) shares the exact formation, while German ~Leute~ and Russian ~ljúdi~ (both “people”) preserve the “people” sense of the same root — freedom, anciently, was the condition of those who belonged to the folk. Notably, Latin ~līberāre~ also descended by the popular route into French ~livrer~ (“to deliver, to hand over”), so ~libérer~ and ~livrer~ are doublets, one learned, one inherited.

~Libérer~ is the relearned, bookish form, restored close to its Latin shape, and it kept the core sense “to set free”: to free a prisoner, to release from an obligation, and — a more mundane modern turn — to vacate, as one ~libère~ a hotel room or a parking space. The adjective ~līber~ and its verb seeded a large French family: ~liberté~, ~libéral~ and ~libéralité~, ~libération~ and ~libérateur~, ~délivrer~ (through ~livrer~), and the borrowed ~libertin~. The motto ~Liberté, égalité, fraternité~ enshrines the noun at the heart of French identity. To liberate, etymologically, is to restore someone to the free condition of the people.
en.licencier:
From Middle French ~licencier~ (also written ~licensier~ or ~licentier~), borrowed from Medieval Latin ~licentiāre~, a verb built on Latin ~licentia~ (“freedom, permission”). That noun comes from ~licēre~ (“to be allowed”), the same verb that gave French ~licite~ and ~illicite~. The family is wide: English ~license~ and ~licentious~ come from the same Latin noun, and Italian ~licenziare~ and Spanish ~licenciar~ are cognate verbs.

The Latin noun covered both freedom and permission. French reached from there the harsher sense of dismissing an employee, now its usual meaning and the source of ~licenciement~ (“layoff”). Related words show the other faces of the root. A ~licencié~ may be a laid-off worker, the holder of a university ~licence~ degree, or a licensed member of a sports federation, all of them tied to a permission granted. And ~licencieux~ (“licentious”) shows freedom pushed too far.
en.lier:
From Latin ~ligāre~ (“to bind, to tie”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). Old French had both the popular form ~lier~ and learned spellings, and the verb passed into English as the borrowed ~liable~ and ~liaison~. Cognates from the same root include Albanian ~lidh~ (“I bind”); within Romance the verb lives on as Italian ~legare~ and Spanish ~ligar~.

The meaning stays close to its root: to ~lier~ is to bind, to fasten, to tie together — ropes, ideas, people. From physical binding grew the abstract senses: ~lier conversation~ (“to strike up a conversation”), to be ~lié~ to someone by friendship, and even a cook's sense, to ~lier~ a sauce by thickening it so the ingredients hold together. The root *~leyǵ-~ produced a dense French family: ~lien~ (“bond, link”), ~liane~ (the binding jungle vine), ~ligament~, ~ligature~, ~ligoter~ (“to tie up”), ~allier~ and ~alliance~, ~obliger~, and ~religion~ — often explained as that which binds the faithful. English ~ally~, ~oblige~, and ~rely~ share the same knot.
en.ligner: From Latin ~līneāre~ (“to draw a straight line”), the verb of Latin ~līnea~ (“line, string”), which gave French the noun ~ligne~. The verb thus has two ties: it descends from the Latin verb, and it is also felt as a verb built on ~ligne~ with the suffix ~-er~. Its senses follow the noun: to rule lines on a page, to mark with lines, and, in angling, to fish with a line. The same family gives ~aligner~ and ~linéaire~.
en.limiter:
From Latin ~līmitāre~ (“to bound, to fix a boundary”), a verb formed on the noun ~līmes~ (genitive ~līmitis~), meaning “a boundary path, a balk between fields, a frontier.” The deeper root is debated: ~līmes~ is sometimes linked to ~līmen~ (“threshold”) and to an idea of a transverse or slanting line, but the connection is uncertain and best left open. Cognate with Italian ~limitare~ and Spanish ~limitar~.

The surprising history lives in the noun. To a Roman surveyor a ~līmes~ was first a balk, the strip of unploughed earth marking off one field from the next; the same word then named the great fortified frontiers of the Empire — the ~Limes~ along the Rhine and the Danube — the very limit of the Roman world. From “the edge as a marked line” the verb ~limiter~ kept both the literal “to mark out, to bound” and the figurative “to restrict, to limit.” French preserves the whole boundary family: ~limite~ (“limit, boundary”), ~limitrophe~ (“bordering, adjacent”), ~illimité~ (“unlimited”), and ~délimiter~ (“to delimit, to mark the bounds of”).
en.liquider: ~Liquider~ is a borrowing from Italian ~liquidare~, itself derived from the adjective ~liquido~ (“liquid”), from Latin ~liquidus~. The Italian verb belonged to the language of commerce and meant “to turn assets into cash,” that is, to make them liquid, and by extension to settle an account. French took over that financial sense and then widened it: to ~liquider~ a stock is to sell it off, to ~liquider~ a debt is to clear it, and in slang to ~liquider~ someone is to get rid of them for good, which is to say to kill them.
en.lire:
From Old French ~lire~, from Latin ~legere~ (“to gather, to collect; to read”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, to collect, to pick up”). The literal Latin meaning was “to gather,” and “to read” developed from the idea of gathering up the letters of a text with the eye, or picking out words one by one. The cognate Greek verb ~λέγω~ (légō) shows the same root branching toward “to pick out” and then “to say, to speak.” Reflexes of ~legere~ survive as Italian ~leggere~, Spanish ~leer~, and Portuguese ~ler~, and the root entered English through Latin borrowings like ~lecture~ and ~legible~.

The semantic journey from “gathering grain or wood” to “reading a page” is one of the most evocative in the Latin vocabulary: the reader is a kind of harvester, going along the line and collecting meaning. The prefixed forms of ~legere~ are everywhere in modern French — ~élire~ (“to elect,” literally “to gather out, to pick out”), ~cueillir~ (“to gather, to pick”), and the learned ~collecter~ and ~sélectionner~. From the same root come ~lecture~ (“reading”), ~lecteur~ (“reader”), ~légende~ (“legend; caption,” originally “things to be read”), ~légion~, and the family of ~-lège~ words such as ~florilège~ (“anthology,” a “gathering of flowers”), and even ~intelligent~ (“choosing between, discerning”).
en.lisser:
The origin of ~lisser~ is debated. French Wiktionary cites the form ~lischier~, in the sense “to iron with a hot iron,” in the glosses of Rashi, and proposes that it arose from a crossing of two Latin words: ~lixāre~ (“to boil in water, to extract by leaching”) and ~allīsus~ (“worn, rubbed down”). Ironing and smoothing were done with hot water, which would explain the first. English Wiktionary prefers another route, a borrowing from Italian ~liscio~ (“smooth, polished”), and lists the crossing only among other theories. Spanish and Portuguese ~liso~ and Catalan ~llis~ show that the family was widespread, but the sources do not settle which way the word traveled.

If the ~lixāre~ account is right, ~lisser~ is a cousin of ~lessive~ (“lye, laundry”) and ~lessiver~, since all of them would rest on Latin ~lixa~ (“lye”), a washing liquid. The word seems to have spread widely only from the 17th century, long after the medieval attestation. Its sense then stayed close to its core idea, making a surface even and free of roughness. If the Italian account is right instead, ~lisser~ is a relatively late loan that joined the French vocabulary of polishing and finishing. Either way, the verb and the adjective ~lisse~ belong together, and only a fuller trail of attestations could say which came first.
en.lister:
Modern French ~lister~ is a denominal verb built directly on the noun ~liste~ (“list”). An older, unrelated-in-sense ~lister~ already existed in Old French around 1165, meaning “to make the border or selvage of cloth,” but the modern verb “to make a list” is a fresh nineteenth-to-twentieth-century coinage (attested 1962) from ~liste~. The noun itself, like Italian and Occitan ~lista~ and Catalan ~llista~, comes from a Germanic word for “strip, border, edge,” reconstructed as Proto-West Germanic *~līstā~. Cognate with German ~Leiste~ (“strip, ledge”), Dutch ~lijst~, and English ~list~, which carries both the “strip/selvage” and “enumeration” senses.

The two meanings of ~liste~ are one image seen twice: a strip of material and a strip of writing. The “enumeration” sense entered French from Italian ~lista~, attested from the fourteenth century, during the Renaissance. By one account the Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~leys-~ (“to trace, to track”), though the sources present this only as a possibility. From the same family French has ~liste~, ~listel~ (an architectural fillet or band), ~lister~, and the calque ~liste noire~ (“blacklist”), borrowed in sense from English.
en.livrer:
From Old French ~livrer~, from Latin ~liberare~ (“to set free, to release”), the verbal derivative of ~liber~ (“free”). Latin ~liber~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~louðeros~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lewdʰero-~, from the root *~h₁lewdʰ-~ (“people, to grow”). The same root produced Greek ~eleutheros~ (“free”) and, through the “people” sense, German ~Leute~ (“people”). The Latin verb itself survives doubly in French: as learned ~libérer~ and as inherited, worn-down ~livrer~.

The semantic drift is remarkable. ~Liberare~ first meant “to free, to release,” then “to release something into someone's hands” — that is, to hand over. From “release into another's keeping” came the everyday sense “to deliver” a parcel or goods, whence the noun ~livraison~ (“delivery”). The darker sense “to betray, to give up to the enemy” is the same gesture turned sinister: to ~livrer~ someone is to hand them over. The reflexive ~se livrer~ means “to give oneself over” to an activity or to surrender. The compound ~délivrer~ keeps the original sense “to set free.” Other descendants of *~h₁lewdʰ-~ include ~libre~, ~liberté~, and ~libéral~.
en.localiser:
Formed within French from the adjective ~local~ plus the suffix ~-iser~. ~local~ comes from Late Latin ~localis~ (“of a place”), a derivative of ~locus~ (“place”). The deeper origin of ~locus~ is uncertain: it appears in Old Latin as ~stlocus~, which would point to a Proto-Italic *~stlokos~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to set, place”), though the etymologist de Vaan is skeptical of this step and leaves the question open. Through ~locus~, French ~local~ is kin to ~lieu~ and to English ~local~ and ~locate~.

The verb's two modern senses both flow from “place.” To ~localiser~ is to determine where something is — to locate it — and also to confine something to one place, to localize it, as one localizes a fire or an infection. From the same ~locus~ French draws ~lieu~, ~local~ (noun and adjective), ~localité~, ~location~, and ~localisation~, the whole cluster organized around the idea of a spot on the map.
en.loger:
Denominal verb from the noun ~loge~ + ~-er~. ~Loge~ comes from Old French ~loge~ (“hut, arbor, shelter”), borrowed from Frankish *~laubja~ (“shelter of foliage, leafy bower”), a Germanic word built on the same root as German ~Laube~ (“arbor, bower”) and ~Laub~ (“foliage”). The same Frankish source, lent into English through Old French, gave English ~lodge~ and ~lobby~.

The earliest ~loge~ was literally a leaf-roofed shelter; from “to provide shelter” the verb ~loger~ broadened to “to house, to accommodate,” then to the everyday “to stay, to be lodged.” Military French kept the older flavor in ~loger les troupes~ (“to quarter the troops”). The noun meanwhile branched into the theater ~loge~ (“box”), the concierge's ~loge~, and the Masonic ~loge~ (“lodge”), this last re-borrowed under English influence. Related French words include ~logement~ (“housing”), ~logis~ (“dwelling”), loger's compound ~déloger~ (“to dislodge, drive out”), and ~logeur~ (“landlord”). The leafy origin survives only as an etymological memory beneath all these tidy modern rooms.
en.longer: From the adjective ~long~ + the verb ending ~-er~. The adjective is inherited from Old French ~lonc~, from Latin ~longus~ (“long”), and is cognate with English ~long~. The ending ~-er~ turns a word into a first-conjugation verb, here with the sense “to go along the length of.” To ~longer~ a wall, a river or a road is to follow it, keeping it alongside, since what one follows is its length. The same adjective gave ~longueur~, ~allonger~ and ~prolonger~, and it is the word that English borrowed in ~chaise longue~, “long chair.”
en.lotir: ~Lotir~ (“to divide into lots”) is formed from the noun ~lot~ with the verbal ending ~-ir~. The noun comes from Old French ~lot~ (also spelled ~loz~), from a Frankish word *~lot~, from the Germanic form *~hlutą~, which also gave English ~lot~. The sense moved from the object used to draw lots to the share each person receives, and that is the share that ~lotir~ hands out: to divide land into portions and assign them. French Wiktionary adds that an older tradition links the Germanic word to Latin ~clāvis~ (“key”); the TLFi-style sources do not rely on it. The ending ~-ir~ is used here in its less common role of forming a verb from a noun.
en.louer:
In the sense “to rent, to lease,” from Old French ~loer~, ~loier~, ~luer~, from Latin ~locāre~ (“to place, to let out, to lease”), a verb built on ~locus~ (“place, spot”). ~locus~ comes from Old Latin ~stlocus~, perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to place, to set”), though de Vaan judges this derivation uncertain and leaves the origin open; the same *~stel-~ would link it, through Germanic, to English ~stall~. To ~locāre~ was literally to put something in a place — and so to place it at someone's disposal for a price.

The leasing sense flows directly from “to place”: letting a field, a house, or one's labour is placing it in another's hands for hire. Modern ~louer~ covers both renting from and renting to, and the root ~locus~ runs through a tidy French family — ~loyer~ (“rent payment”), ~location~ (“rental”), ~locataire~ (“tenant”), ~locatif~, and ~allouer~ (“to allocate”). A famous homonym shadows this verb: the other ~louer~, “to praise,” descends instead from Latin ~laudāre~ (“to praise”) by way of Old French ~loer~, and survives in ~louange~ (“praise”) and ~laudatif~. The two ~louer~s fell together in sound and spelling but were never related — one places a thing for hire, the other lifts a person with praise.
en.louper: Formed from ~loup~ used in the sense of “flaw, defect”, plus the verb ending ~-er~. The word ~loup~ is also the wolf: it comes from Latin ~lupus~ (“wolf”), with the modern spelling shaped by eastern dialects and by the feminine ~louve~, as against the regular central form ~leu~ preserved in ~à la queue leu leu~. From “flaw”, ~louper~ meant to botch a piece of work, and then, more broadly, to miss or fail at something, as in ~louper son train~.
en.lover:
The nautical French ~lover~ (“to coil a rope”) was borrowed around 1678 from Low German ~lofen~ (“to turn, to luff”), a seafarers' term that entered French through the Atlantic and North Sea sailing trade. It belongs to the same Germanic field as the maritime ~lof~ (“luff, windward side”) and English ~luff~ — the act of turning a vessel toward the wind. The Germanic and Dutch nautical vocabulary supplied French with a whole rigging of such loanwords, of which ~lover~ is one neatly coiled example.

From “to turn” the verb specialized into “to wind a rope into neat concentric rings on deck,” the coil itself recalling a turned spiral. Its most vivid modern life is reflexive and figurative: ~se lover~ means “to curl up, to nestle,” as a cat or a snake coils itself into a comfortable spiral — ~le chat se love dans un fauteuil~ (“the cat curls up in an armchair”). A nautical term for stowing rope thus became one of French's most affectionate words for snuggling, the rope's tidy spiral transferred to a sleeping body.
en.luire:
Inherited from Latin ~lūcēre~ (“to shine, to be light”), which belongs to a family built on the Proto-Indo-European root *~lewk-~ (“light, brightness”). The regular Old French outcome was ~luisir~, and ~luire~ is a variant that replaced it under the influence of its future forms, the same shift seen in ~nuire~, ~plaire~ and ~taire~ (from older ~nuisir~, ~plaisir~ and ~taisir~). The stressed Latin ~-ē-~ after a palatal sound gave the ~-ir~ ending, as in ~placēre~ becoming ~plaisir~. The root is also found in Latin ~lūx~ (“light”) and ~lūmen~, in English ~light~ and in German ~Licht~.

The old ~-is-~ stem survives in the present participle and adjective ~luisant~ (“shining”), as in ~ver luisant~, and in the form ~il luisait~. The verb is mostly literary now and appears chiefly in the third person, of stars, eyes, a wet road or a sheen. Related French words include ~reluire~, ~lueur~, ~lumière~, ~lucide~ and ~luciole~ (“firefly”), and even ~lune~, from the same family. Few verbs show the way a Latin verb can slip into a different conjugation class so clearly.
en.lutter:
From Old French ~luitier~ (also ~loitier~, ~luiter~; “to wrestle, to struggle”), attested in the Chanson de Roland around 1080, from Latin ~luctārī~ (“to wrestle, to struggle”). The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~lukto-~ and ultimately to a Proto-Indo-European root *~lewg-~ (“to bend, to twist”) — fittingly, since wrestling is a contest of twisting bodies. Cognate with Italian ~lottare~ and Spanish ~luchar~ (in which Latin ~-ct-~ regularly became ~-ch-~), and, through the prefixed Latin ~reluctārī~ (“to struggle against”), with English ~reluctant~.

The Old French diphthong ~-ui-~ held on for centuries; the reduction to plain ~-u-~ in ~lutter~ is unusual and dates only to the early seventeenth century, paralleling the pairs ~fruit~/~fruité~ and ~nuit~/~nuitée~. The sense has stayed remarkably stable: from the literal grappling of two wrestlers it broadened to any struggle, physical, moral, or political — one may ~lutter~ against an illness, against injustice, or against sleep. Words of the same family in modern French include the noun ~lutte~ (the sport and any struggle), the agent noun ~lutteur~ (“wrestler”), and the adjective ~luttable~. The learned English borrowing ~reluctant~ preserves, etymologically, the image of someone wrestling back against what is asked of them.
en.lâcher:
From Old French ~laschier~ (attested 1080, in the ~Chanson de Roland~), later ~lascher~, from Vulgar Latin *~lassicare~, a dissimilated form of *~laxicare~, itself a frequentative of Latin ~laxare~ (“to loosen, slacken, relax”). ~laxare~ derives from the adjective ~laxus~ (“loose, slack”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)leg-~ (“to be slack, languid”). The same ~laxare~ gave French ~laisser~ (“to let, leave”), and ~laxus~ surfaces directly in English ~lax~, Italian ~lasso~, and Spanish ~laxo~.

The core idea was always one of slackening: to ~lâcher~ a rope is to let its tension go, and from there the verb fanned out into “to release,” “to let go,” “to drop,” and “to abandon.” The familiar sense “to chicken out” (se dégonfler) is a modern figurative extension of the same loosening. From the adjective ~laxus~ French also kept ~lâche~ (“slack” and, of a person, “cowardly”) — a doublet of the verb's own meaning — alongside the learned borrowings ~laxatif~ and ~relâcher~, all turning on the notion of letting tension out.
en.lécher:
French ~lécher~ comes from Old French ~lechier~, which is probably Germanic in origin. French Wiktionary derives it from Old Frankish *~lekkōn~ (“to lick”), attested in the tenth century and continued by Flemish ~lekken~ and German ~lecken~. A variant *~likkōn~, continued by standard Dutch ~likken~, gave a second Old French form, ~lichier~. English ~lick~ belongs to the same Germanic family. English Wiktionary says the word is “probably” from Frankish *~likkōn~, routed through a Vulgar Latin *~liccāre~, ancestor of Italian ~leccare~. Both accounts therefore place a Germanic word at the start, though they differ over whether Vulgar Latin stands between it and French.

The origin is therefore not entirely settled. English Wiktionary offers an alternative: an early contraction of a Vulgar Latin *~ligicāre~, denasalized from *~lingicāre~, which rests on Classical Latin ~lingere~ (“to lick”). The argument runs by analogy with ~ficher~, generally derived from *~fīgicāre~, from ~fīgere~. French Wiktionary gives only the Frankish source and mentions no rival. Neither account is certain, and the sources do not rule one out in favor of the other. The meaning, at least, has barely moved from “to pass the tongue over.” Figurative uses grew around it: ~lécher les vitrines~ is to window-shop, and ~léché~ describes a work polished to excess. The family includes ~lèche-vitrines~ and ~lécheur~.
en.légiférer: Drawn from Latin ~legifer~ (“lawgiver”), a compound of ~lex~, ~legis~ (“law”) and ~ferō~ (“to bring, to bear”), so that to ~légiférer~ is, etymologically, to bear the law. Both halves left many French descendants. ~Lex~ gave ~légal~ and ~législation~, while ~ferō~, which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (“to carry”), gave ~transférer~, ~conifère~ and ~référer~. English ~bear~ is a native cousin of that same root. The verb is a learned word of the legal and political vocabulary, used for the making of laws by a legislature, as in ~légiférer sur un sujet~.
en.légitimer: Formed from the adjective ~légitime~ (“lawful, legitimate”) with the verb ending ~-er~, or possibly borrowed directly from Medieval Latin ~legitimāre~; English Wiktionary gives both routes. The adjective entered French from Latin ~lēgitimus~ (“in accordance with the law”), in Old French as ~legitime~ by the thirteenth century. ~Lēgitimus~ is built on ~lēx~ (“law”), the root of ~loi~ and ~légal~. The verb means to make lawful or to justify, and it has long been used for formally recognizing a child born outside marriage.
en.léguer:
Borrowed from Latin ~lēgāre~, a verb formed from the noun ~lex~ (genitive ~lēgis~, “law”), which also gave French ~loi~. French Wiktionary calls it a denominative of ~lex~ and explains the verb's logic through its two uses. For persons, ~lēgāre~ meant someone “sent by a law,” and for things it described transmission by will. In early Roman law such transmissions also took place by a law, passed in a popular assembly, the ~testamentum calatis comitiis~. The verb was thus tied to law from the start, and the noun ~lex~ stands behind it.

The two uses show how a word built on law could cover both sending someone and handing something down. In modern French the verb is used well beyond wills: one ~lègue~ a house, but also a tradition, a habit or a problem to the next generation. The root idea of a transfer authorised by a rule remains in these uses, although that continuity is an observation about the meanings rather than something the sources state. French Wiktionary treats ~léguer~ as a direct borrowing from the Latin verb, not a French formation on ~loi~, though the two words share the noun ~lex~ as their source.
en.léser:
French ~léser~ comes through Middle French ~leser~ from Latin ~laedere~ (“to hurt, to damage, to offend”), by way of its past participle ~laesus~. Latin ~laedere~ has no secure Proto-Indo-European root. The verb gave Latin a whole family: compounds like ~collidere~ (“to strike together”) and ~ēlidere~ (“to strike out”) lie behind English ~collide~ and French ~élider~, and the noun ~laesiō~ (“an injury”) gave French ~lésion~, English ~lesion~, a term of medicine. The vowel of ~laedere~ shifted in the compounds, which is why they no longer look like their base.

In French, ~léser~ stayed a formal word, used when a person's interests, rights or body suffer harm: ~léser les intérêts de quelqu'un~ is to wrong someone's interests, and the injured party in a lawsuit is the ~partie lésée~. In medicine it describes damage to a tissue or an organ. Its most striking relic is ~lèse-majesté~, from Latin ~laesa maiestas~ (“injured majesty”), the old crime of offending the sovereign, which survives in French as a figure of speech for any insult to a person who expects deference.
en.maigrir: Formed from the adjective ~maigre~ (“thin”) with the verb ending ~-ir~, in the pattern of French verbs that mean “to become” the quality of the adjective, as ~grandir~ comes from ~grand~. ~Maigre~ is inherited from Old French ~megre~, from Latin ~macer~ (accusative ~macrum~), which goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root. The ~-gr-~ spelling of the modern form was perhaps influenced by ~aigre~, or it may be semi-learned, and a dialect form ~maire~ is the regular phonetic result. So ~maigrir~ means to become thin, to lose weight.
en.maintenir:
From Old French ~maintenir~ (“to protect, to defend, to uphold”), from Medieval Latin ~manutenere~, a fusion of the Latin phrase ~manu tenere~ (“to hold in the hand”) — ~manu~, the ablative of ~manus~ (“hand”), plus ~tenere~ (“to hold”). ~manus~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~man-~ (“hand”), while ~tenere~ rests on *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Through this compound the verb is cognate with Italian ~mantenere~, Spanish ~mantener~, and English ~maintain~.

To maintain was first, literally, to keep a thing in hand — hence to support, protect, or defend, the dominant Old French sense. From “to hold up” grew the modern senses “to keep in a given state,” “to assert (an opinion),” and “to keep up, to service.” The last sense, the upkeep of machines and roads, is reinforced in modern French as a calque on English ~maintain~. From ~manus~ French draws ~main~, ~manuel~, ~manier~, and ~manœuvre~; from ~tenere~ come ~tenir~, ~retenir~, ~contenir~, and ~maintenance~ — so that the simple act of holding something in one's hand stands, etymologically, behind a vast machinery of holding, keeping, and managing.
en.majorer: ~Majorer~ is tied to Latin ~maior~ (“greater”), the comparative of ~magnus~ (“big”). French Wiktionary treats it as a French verb formed on ~major~ with the first-group ending ~-er~, while English Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~maiōrāre~ (“to augment”), a verb that was itself built on ~maior~. The two accounts differ on whether the verb was formed in French or inherited from the Latin verb, but they agree on the base. The meaning is “to make greater,” most often a price, a rate or an estimate, and sometimes by extension to overestimate.
en.malmener: A compound of ~mal~ (“badly”) and the verb ~mener~ (“to lead, to drive”). The element ~mal~ comes from Latin ~malus~ (“bad”) and its adverb ~male~ (“badly”), a root that Italian, Spanish and Portuguese share. ~Malmener~ therefore means literally to lead or handle badly, and it came to mean to treat someone roughly, to manhandle. It is used of people who are physically or verbally mistreated and, in sport or politics, of a side that is pushed around by its opponent.
en.maltraiter: Formed in French from ~mal-~ (“badly”) and ~traiter~ (“to treat”), so it means “to treat badly.” The prefix is the adverb ~mal~ fused to the verb, from Latin ~male~ (“badly”), from ~malus~ (“bad”). The base ~traiter~ comes from Latin ~tractāre~ (“to handle, to deal with”), a frequentative of ~trahere~ (“to draw, to pull”), and is related to Italian ~trattare~ and Spanish ~tratar~. Because ~traiter~ covers every kind of handling, from treating a patient to discussing a subject, ~maltraiter~ picks out the negative case: to handle a person roughly or abusively.
en.mandater: Formed in French from ~mandat~ with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, so that ~mandater~ means to give someone a mandate, to commission or appoint them to act. The noun ~mandat~ was borrowed from Latin ~mandātum~ (“commission, order”), from ~mandāre~ (“to entrust, to order”), which English Wiktionary analyzes as ~manus~ (“hand”) plus ~dare~ (“to put, to give”), literally putting something in someone's hand. The same Latin verb gave French ~commander~ and ~demander~, so a mandate shares its ancestry with orders and requests.
en.manger:
From Middle French ~manger~, from Old French ~mangier~, from Late Latin ~manducare~ (“to chew, to eat”), a derivative of ~manducus~ (“glutton”), itself from ~mandere~ (“to chew”). ~mandere~ is traced to Proto-Indo-European *~mendʰ-~ (“to chew”). Cognate with Italian ~mangiare~ and Occitan ~manjar~, both Gallo-Romance reflexes, and — through ~mandere~ — with English ~mandible~ and ~mange~.

The choice of word is itself a small comedy. Where Spanish and Portuguese kept a verb for plain eating (~comer~, from ~comedere~), Gaul preferred ~manducare~, a coarse, popular term meaning roughly “to munch, to champ.” Its source noun ~manducus~ named a glutton, and in Roman farce a ~Manducus~ was a grotesque masked figure with great clacking jaws — so French speakers, etymologically, do not dine so much as chomp. The same root *~mendʰ-~, by way of ~mandibula~, gives the anatomical ~mandibule~ (the jaw), while ~manducare~ itself yielded the learned ~manducation~ and the homely ~mangeoire~, a feeding trough — the very word English borrowed as ~manger~. Modern French ~mâcher~ (“to chew”), by contrast, comes from a different Latin verb, ~masticare~.
en.manier:
The two sources give different routes to one origin. French Wiktionary derives Old French ~maneier~ from ~main~ with the suffix ~-eyer~, while English Wiktionary traces it to Vulgar Latin *~manizāre~. Both rest on Latin ~manus~ (“hand”), so the verb is at bottom “to work with the hand.” Italian ~maneggiare~ is a relative, and French in turn borrowed ~manège~ from it. English ~manage~ is also a loan from the Italian verb, which gives the English word a surprising ancestor in the hand.

The meaning stayed tied to the hand: to handle an object, wield a tool, knead dough, and then by extension to work a language, a concept or a piece of software. The noun ~maniement~ and the adjective ~maniable~ (“easy to handle”) follow the same line. ~Manège~ took a different turn, first the training of horses and then the riding school, and eventually the merry-go-round and the figurative scheme or maneuver. The same hand also lies behind ~manuel~, ~manœuvre~ (from Latin ~manū operāre~, “to work by hand”) and ~main~ itself.
en.manifester:
From Latin ~manifestāre~ (“to make plain, reveal”), from the adjective ~manifestus~ (“caught in the act, evident, palpable”). That adjective opens with ~manus~ (“hand”), but its second element ~-festus~ is genuinely disputed. One long-standing reading links it to a verb of striking, also seen in ~īnfestus~ (“hostile”) and the family of ~dēfendere~ — so ~manifestus~ would picture a wrongdoer literally ~struck~ or ~seized~ by the hand, caught red-handed. ~Manus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~manus~ and continues in French ~main~.

The word entered French around 1100. From “caught in the act” the adjective broadened to “plainly visible,” and the verb ~manifester~ to “make evident, show openly.” Its most public modern sense — to ~demonstrate~ in the streets, to ~protest~ — is a nineteenth-century political development: a crowd makes its will manifest by becoming visible. From the same Latin stock French keeps ~manifeste~ (both adjective and the noun ~manifeste~, a public declaration), ~manifestation~, and ~manifestant~. English ~manifest~, ~manifesto~ (through Italian), and ~manifestation~ are cousins, all carrying that ancient image of something laid bare to the hand.
en.manipuler:
A late verb, formed in the 18th century as a denominal of the French noun ~manipule~, originally a pharmacist's term; Medieval Latin already had ~manipulare~ (“to handle”). ~manipule~ comes from Latin ~manipulus~ (“a handful”), a compound of ~manus~ (“hand”) and the root of ~plere~ (“to fill”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). So a ~manipulus~ is, etymologically, “what fills the hand.”

The word's most vivid life was military: a Roman ~manipulus~ was a tactical unit, said to have first rallied around a bundle of hay tied to a pole — a literal handful raised as a standard before the eagle was adopted. From “handful” the pharmacist's ~manipule~ became a measured handful of ingredients, and the verb meant “to handle” substances by hand; only later did ~manipuler~ acquire the figurative, often pejorative sense “to manipulate” people or facts. Kin in French include ~manipulation~, ~manipulateur~, and — from the same ~manus~ — ~manuel~, ~manœuvre~, and ~manuscrit~.
en.manquer:
Unlike most French verbs, ~manquer~ is not inherited but borrowed, from Italian ~mancare~ (“to lack, to be wanting”), itself from the Latin adjective ~mancus~ (“maimed, crippled, defective”). ~mancus~ originally described a hand maimed or missing, and is connected to ~manus~ (“hand”); both are referred to a Proto-Indo-European *~mh₂nkó-~ (“maimed in the hand”), beside ~manus~ from the root for “hand.” The same adjective survives as Italian ~manco~ and Spanish ~manco~ (“one-handed, maimed”).

From “maimed” the Italian word generalized to “to be missing, to fall short,” and French took it over in the sixteenth century, gradually pushing aside the older native ~faillir~. The most surprising development is grammatical rather than semantic: in the sense “to be missed,” ~manquer~ inverts subject and object, so that ~tu me manques~ literally says “you are lacking to me” yet means “I miss you” — the person felt as absent is the grammatical subject, and the verb agrees with them, as in ~mes amis me manquent~ (“I miss my friends”). The same root gave French the noun ~manque~ (“lack”), the verb ~manquement~ (“a failing, a breach”), and ~manchot~ (“one-armed,” also the name for a penguin), all circling the ancient idea of a defective, incomplete hand.
en.marcher:
From Middle French ~marcher~, from Old French ~marchier~ (“to trample, to tread underfoot”), attested around 1170. The most widely accepted source is Frankish *~markôn~ (“to mark, to press with the foot”), reaching French through Old High German ~marcôn~ — a Germanic verb of the Franks rather than a Latin inheritance. A competing hypothesis, going back to Scheler, instead derives it from Latin ~marcus~ (“a hammer”), through the image of feet hammering the ground; the question is genuinely unsettled.

The oldest sense was “to trample, to tread on,” preserved in the related ~marc~ (“the pressed residue of grapes or olives”), the pulp left underfoot. From that came the ordinary “to walk,” then a remarkable spread of figurative uses: an army on the ~marche~, a plan that ~marche~ (“works, goes well”), and the slangy ~ça marche~ (“all right, it's a deal”). One must not confuse this verb with the noun ~marché~ (“a market,” from Latin ~mercatus~), an unrelated homonym. From the verb the language draws ~marche~ (“a step, a march”), ~démarche~ (“a gait; a course of action”), and ~marcheur~ (“a walker”).
en.marginaliser: Formed from the adjective ~marginal~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which builds verbs meaning “to make A” or “to treat as A.” The adjective ~marginal~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~marginalis~, from Latin ~margo~ (“edge, border”), the source of French ~marge~ (“margin”). To ~marginaliser~ someone or something is therefore to push it to the margin, out of the central part of society, the economy or a debate.
en.marier:
Attested from 1145, from Latin ~maritare~ (“to marry, to give in marriage”), derived from ~maritus~ (“husband, married man”). ~Maritus~ is generally connected to ~mas~ (“male”) and perhaps to an Indo-European element meaning “young woman, bride,” though the deeper derivation is debated and best left open. Italian keeps the noun in ~marito~ (“husband”) and the verb ~maritare~, while Spanish has ~maridar~ beside ~marido~; English borrowed French ~marier~ as ~marry~.

In its earliest French use ~marier~ meant “to give someone in marriage,” the active role of the parent or matchmaker; the reflexive ~se marier~ (“to get married”) appears by around 1170. Beyond the wedding, the verb developed a graceful figurative life: one can ~marier~ colors, flavors, or ideas — that is, blend them harmoniously, as in ~ce vin se marie bien avec le poisson~. The same root gives French ~mari~ (“husband”), ~mariage~, ~marié~ and ~mariée~ (“groom” and “bride”), and ~remarier~. It is worth noting that ~marier~ (“to wed”) and ~Marie~ (the given name) are unrelated despite the resemblance — a coincidence that has confused many a learner, but never the etymology.
en.mariner: Borrowed from Italian ~marinare~, itself from ~marino~ (“of the sea”), which goes back to Latin ~marīnus~, from ~mare~ (“sea”). The verb originally meant to preserve fish or meat in brine, that is, in salted seawater, hence “to pickle.” The modern sense of soaking food in a seasoned liquid before cooking developed from that older preserving technique. The same sea-word underlies French ~marin~ (“sailor”), ~marine~ and ~marinade~.
en.marquer:
French ~marquer~ comes from Old French ~merchier~ (“to make a mark to distinguish something”), an Anglo-Norman and Picard form. Its ancestor is the Germanic noun *~marka~ (“boundary, border, sign set at a limit”), of Frankish origin, from Proto-Indo-European *~merǵ-~ (“boundary, edge”). The modern vowel ~a~ was pulled in by ~marcher~ and by the Italian ~marcare~ and Spanish ~marcar~, themselves from the same Germanic root. Cognate forms abound: English ~mark~, Dutch ~mark~, German ~Mark~, Swedish ~mark~, and even Latin ~margo~ (“edge,” whence French ~marge~).

The oldest sense was territorial: a *~marka~ was a frontier zone, and a ~marquis~ was originally the count of such a borderland, the ~marche~. From “a sign planted at a boundary” the noun ~marque~ generalized to any distinguishing sign, and ~marquer~ to the act of inscribing one — branding cattle, noting down a figure, scoring a goal (this last sense reinforced in the nineteenth century by English ~to mark~). The root spread widely in French: ~marche~ (a border province, as in les Marches), ~marquise~, ~démarquer~, and ~marqueterie~ all belong to it, and through English so do ~demarcation~ and ~marquee~. What began as the line dividing two lands now means simply leaving a trace.
en.marrer: The origin of ~se marrer~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary gives two proposals: the Old French verb ~se marrir~ (“to grieve”), or Spanish ~marear~ (“to bore, to make dizzy”), with ~marearse~ (“to get seasick”). English Wiktionary favors the Spanish source, with the sense shifting from “to get dizzy” to “to be bored” and then, by antiphrasis, to “to be amused.” Whatever the source, the verb first meant “to be bored” and only later came to mean laughing at something that should have been tedious. The noun ~marre~ (as in ~j'en ai marre~) is not the base: French Wiktionary treats it as a back-formation from the verb, and the TLFi rejects any link with ~marrir~.
en.marteler: Inherited from Middle French and Old French ~marteler~, itself formed from Old French ~martel~ (“hammer”, the older form of ~marteau~) and the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Martel~ goes back to Late Latin ~martellus~ (“hammer”). The sense is simply to hammer, to strike repeatedly, whether metal, a door or a rhythm. It then widened figuratively, so that one ~martèle~ one's words, pronouncing each syllable with force, or drives a point home by insistent repetition. Dutch ~martelen~ and the English word ~martel~ are cognates of the Old French noun.
en.masquer:
French ~masquer~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~masque~ (“mask”) with the suffix ~-er~. ~masque~ was borrowed from Italian ~maschera~, and there the trail forks, for the deeper origin is genuinely disputed. By one account it comes from a pre-Romance *~maska~ meaning “black,” recalling that the earliest disguise was simply a blackened face; by another it goes back to Medieval Latin ~masca~ (“witch, specter, nightmare”), itself of uncertain origin; and by a third, much-cited account it derives from Arabic ~مسخرة~ (~masḵara~, “buffoon, mockery”), from a root meaning “to mock.” The TLFi and Littré are wary of the Arabic hypothesis rather than endorsing it, so the question stays open.

Whatever its source, the noun gave French a verb meaning to “mask,” “hide,” or “conceal,” and figuratively to disguise an intention or a flavor. Whichever etymology one favors, the family is broad and international: French ~masque~, ~mascarade~ (“masquerade”), and ~démasquer~ (“to unmask”) sit beside English ~mask~ and ~mascara~ — the cosmetic name itself reflecting that old thread of darkening the face — all converging on the single idea of a covering laid over the true face.
en.massacrer:
French ~massacrer~ is inherited from Middle French ~massacrer~, from Old French ~macecler~ or ~macecrer~. The probable source, though not a certain one, is a Vulgar Latin verb *~matteuculāre~, formed from *~matteuca~, the word that also gave French ~massue~ (“club”). English Wiktionary traces that Vulgar Latin noun further back to *~mattea~ or Late Latin ~mattia~, and ultimately to Latin ~mateola~, glossed there as “hoe.” This last stretch of the chain is a reconstruction, so the origin should be read as likely rather than proven. English ~massacre~ was borrowed from French.

If the chain is right, the verb would have meant “to strike with a club,” which would fit the sense of “to slaughter,” though the sources do not trace that development. The Old French forms ~macecler~ and ~macecrer~ are given as two variants of one word. Today the verb covers the killing of many people and also the careless destruction of things. In everyday French, one can ~massacrer~ a song, a piece of music or a foreign language, which means to perform or speak it so badly that it is ruined, a figurative use of the same violence. The word ~massue~, named above, keeps the memory of that weapon.
en.masser:
The origin of ~masser~ (“to massage”) is debated, and the dictionaries record more than one account. The one English Wiktionary calls probable is a borrowing, around the end of the eighteenth century, from Arabic ~massa~ (مَسَّ, “to touch, to feel”). The same source offers a rival: Portuguese ~amassar~. French Wiktionary lists three accounts for the French verb, among them the Arabic one, a derivation from ~masse~ in the sense of “lump, heap,” and a derivation from another ~masse~, meaning “club.”

Because the accounts conflict, nothing here can be asserted as settled, and the sense that a lump or a club might have given a verb of massage is not explained in the sources. If the Arabic or the Portuguese account is right, the verb is a late borrowing, from around the end of the eighteenth century.
en.mater: Two senses, two stories. The chess and “subdue” sense is a denominal of ~mat~ (“checkmated”) with the ending ~-er~. The chess word ~mat~ comes from ~échec et mat~, which French Wiktionary traces to Arabic ~māt~ (“dead”) and English Wiktionary to Persian ~šâh mât~ (“the king is ambushed”). The slang sense “to eye, to ogle” has an uncertain origin.
