The literal picture is a military one: an army sits down before a town and holds it under siege.

From the idea of being surrounded and hounded by a force, the verb passed to a thought or a worry that will not leave: to be ~obsédé~ by an idea is to be besieged by it. The relatives are many, including ~obsession~, ~obsidional~ (“relating to a siege”), ~siège~, ~assiéger~, ~séance~ and ~présider~.
en.obtenir:
French ~obtenir~ comes from Latin ~obtinēre~ (“to hold firmly, to possess fully, to maintain”), a compound of the prefix ~ob-~ (“against, toward”) and the verb ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). Rather than evolving by regular sound change, it was refashioned in French on the model of the inherited verb ~tenir~ (“to hold”), so that its endings march in step with its everyday relative. The root ~tenēre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch, draw”), the link between stretching and holding being the idea of keeping something taut. That root is cognate with Ancient Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”) and Sanskrit ~tanóti~ (“stretches”).

The sense narrowed from the Latin “hold fast, keep possession of” to the modern French “to get, to come to have,” the result of an effort that secures and keeps something. The prefix ~ob-~ adds the nuance of reaching toward a goal — one obtains by holding on against resistance. French is unusually rich in cousins built on ~tenir~: ~contenir~ (“contain,” to hold together), ~maintenir~ (“maintain,” to hold by hand), ~retenir~ (“retain”), ~soutenir~ (“sustain”), ~détenir~ (“detain”), and ~appartenir~ (“belong”). Even the adverb ~maintenant~ (“now”) hides the root, from Latin ~manū tenendō~ (“holding in the hand”).
en.obéir:
From Old French ~obeir~ (early 12th century, in the Voyage de saint Brendan), from Latin ~oboedīre~ (“to give ear to, hence to submit to”), from ~ob-~ (“toward”) + ~audīre~ (“to hear”). ~audīre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~awizdiō~, a compound of PIE *~h₂ewis~ (“clearly, manifestly” — from *~h₂ew-~, “to perceive”) and *~dʰh₁-~ (“to render”): to hear is “to render clear.” The same perceptual root underlies Greek ~aisthánomai~ (“I perceive”), source of French ~esthétique~ and ~anesthésie~. Cognates of the verb itself: Italian ~obbedire~, Spanish ~obedecer~ — and English ~obey~, lifted from the Old French verb.

Etymologically, obedience is a way of listening: ~oboedīre~ is to turn one's ear toward someone. French keeps the hearing close by. The inherited child of ~audīre~ is ~ouïr~, today almost confined to ~ouï-dire~ (“hearsay”) and to legal memory — English and American courtrooms still open with ~oyez~, “hear ye,” the Old French imperative carried to England by the Normans — while the learned line gave ~audience~, ~auditeur~, ~audition~, ~audible~. Meanwhile obéir widened its empire along dates the TLFi records: people obey wills (12th century), matter obeys forces (1377), passions get obeyed (1550), and by 1671 animals and machines “execute the commanded movement.” Grammar preserves a fossil: the verb now takes its object with à (~obéir à quelqu'un~), yet French still allows the passive ~être obéi~ — a relic of the days when one obeyed someone directly. Family: ~obéissance~, ~obéissant~, ~désobéir~.
en.occasionner: A denominal verb built from ~occasion~ plus the first-conjugation ending ~-er~, meaning “to give rise to, to cause.” The noun was borrowed from Latin ~occāsiō~ (“opportunity, favorable moment”). The learned verb displaced the inherited Old French ~ochoisonner~, which had come down from the same Latin word by regular sound change; the old noun ~ochoison~ (also ~achaison~, reshaped under the influence of Latin ~accūsātiō~) lived alongside it for a time, a reminder that French borrowed the same Latin word twice.
en.occulter: The sources give two routes. French Wiktionary derives ~occulter~ directly from Latin ~occultāre~ (“to hide”), while English Wiktionary analyzes it as the adjective ~occulte~ + the verb ending ~-er~. Both lead to the same Latin family, since ~occulte~ itself comes from Latin ~occultus~ (“hidden, secret”). The core idea is concealment. French uses the verb figuratively, as in ~occulter un problème~ (“to hide a problem, to push it out of sight”), and also in astronomy, where one body blocks another from view, the noun for which is ~occultation~. English ~occult~ comes from the same Latin adjective.
en.occuper:
From Latin ~occupāre~ (“to seize, take possession of, take before others”), an intensive compound of ~ob-~ (“toward, over”) and ~capere~ (“to grasp, seize, take”). ~Capere~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp”), which — perhaps unexpectedly — also gave English ~have~ and ~heave~, and underlies Latin ~captīvus~ and ~capax~. Romance kin include Italian ~occupare~ and Spanish ~ocupar~.

The Latin verb already carried a competitive edge: to ~occupāre~ was to grab something before someone else could, to get there first. That sense of prior seizure survives in the military meaning — an army that ~occupe~ a territory has taken and now holds it. But French let the word soften and spread. Today one can ~occuper~ a seat, ~occuper~ a job, or ~occuper~ an afternoon, and the reflexive ~s'occuper de~ means simply “to busy oneself with, to take care of.” The same ~capere~ seeded an enormous family of French words through its many prefixed forms: ~capter~, ~accepter~, ~concevoir~, ~recevoir~, ~capable~, ~captif~, and the noun ~préoccupation~ — an anxiety that has, quite literally, seized the mind in advance.
en.octroyer:
Inherited from Middle French ~octroyer~, from Old French ~otroiier~, from Early Medieval Latin ~auctōrizāre~ (“to authorize”), a verb built on Latin ~auctor~ (“originator, authority”), itself tied to ~augēre~ (“to increase”). Old French wrote the verb without the Latin ~c~, and the modern spelling with ~c~ is a later restoration after the Latin model: first in writing, then, from Early Modern French, in pronunciation. The same Latin verb thus reached French by two routes, which makes ~octroyer~ a doublet of ~autoriser~, the form that kept closer to the Latin.

To authorize something is to grant it, and the Old French verb meant to grant or concede a request, a favor, a privilege. Modern ~octroyer~ keeps that formal, slightly lofty tone: a power decides, and ~octroie~ a loan, a delay, a right or a charter. The noun ~octroi~ named a tax levied at the gates of a town on goods entering it, and survives in ~octroi de mer~ in the French overseas territories. The pair ~octroyer~ and ~autoriser~ shows two fates of one Latin word, one worn down by speech and later patched up in spelling, the other taken straight from Latin. English ~author~ and ~authority~ come from the same Latin ~auctor~, as does French ~auteur~.
en.officialiser: Formed from ~officiel~ + the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make official”. ~Officiel~ comes from Old French and Latin ~officiālis~, the adjective of ~officium~ (“duty, service, public function”), so something ~officiel~ is literally what belongs to an office. The suffix ~-iser~ is borrowed from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and in French it makes verbs of the type “render A”. ~Officialiser~ thus means to give a fact, a decision or a status an official character, for instance by announcing or recording it formally.
en.offrir:
From Old French ~ofrir~, ~offrir~ (“to offer, present”), from Late Latin ~offerīre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~offerre~ (“to bring before, present, offer”), itself ~ob-~ (“before, toward”) + ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from Proto-Italic *~ferō~, from PIE *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”). Cognate with Italian ~offrire~, Spanish ~ofrecer~, and Catalan ~oferir~; through the same root *~bʰer-~ it is kin to English ~bear~ and ~birth~, and to German ~gebären~ (“to give birth”).

The Latin sense was concretely physical — to carry something forward and set it before another — and the verb early took on a religious coloring, the ~oblātiō~ laid before a god, so that to offer was to present a gift or sacrifice. French kept both the everyday sense of giving a present and the ceremonial one. The root *~bʰer-~ is among the most fertile in Indo-European, and through ~ferre~ it seeded a vast French family: ~offrande~ and ~offre~, but also ~conférer~, ~transférer~, ~souffrir~ (literally “to bear from below”), and the nouns in ~-fère~ such as ~mammifère~ (bearer of breasts). Even ~fertile~ — that which bears — belongs to the same stock.
en.ombrager: Formed from the noun ~ombrage~ (“shade, foliage that casts shade”) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to cover with shade. The noun is either built from ~ombre~ plus the suffix ~-age~, or inherited from Old French ~ombrage~ and ultimately from Latin ~umbrāticus~ (“of the shade”); either way it rests on Latin ~umbra~ (“shade, shadow”). English ~umbrage~ is the same word, and shares the figurative sense of the noun: to take ~ombrage~ is to feel offended, as if a shadow had fallen across one's pride. The verb itself stays largely literal, to shade, and figuratively to cast a shadow over someone.
en.omettre:
Borrowed in Middle French from Latin ~omittere~ (“to let go, to leave out”) and refashioned on the French verb ~mettre~, which is why it ends like its relatives. The Latin verb is usually analysed as ~ob-~ plus ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”), with the ~ob-~ reduced to ~o-~. English ~omit~ was taken from the same Latin verb, and the English noun ~mission~ and French ~mettre~ both come from ~mittere~ as well.

The literal picture is “to let something go by.” In Latin, ~omittere~ covered letting go of a plan, ignoring a point, or skipping over something in a speech, and French kept the sense of leaving out. Because it was reshaped on ~mettre~, ~omettre~ is conjugated like it (~j'omets~, ~omis~). It sits in a large family of ~-mettre~ verbs borrowed from Latin compounds of ~mittere~: ~admettre~, ~commettre~, ~permettre~, ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, along with ~omission~, the noun that preserves the Latin stem unchanged.
en.onduler:
French ~onduler~ is a back-formation from ~ondulation~, not an inherited verb. The pair corresponds to Medieval or later Latin ~undulare~, built on Late Latin ~undula~ (“little wave”), a diminutive of Latin ~unda~ (“wave”). French ~onde~ is the descendant of ~unda~, so ~onduler~ is, at one remove, simply the verb of the wave.

The meaning followed the image. ~Onduler~ describes anything that moves or lies in a wavy line, such as hair, a field of wheat, a flag or a snake, and the related noun ~ondulation~ gives the same idea of gentle repeated rise and fall. The same Latin ~unda~ lies behind several French words that are not obviously waves: ~inonder~ (“to flood”), from Latin ~inundare~, ~abonder~ (“to abound”), from Latin ~abundare~, and ~ondine~ (“water nymph”). English borrowed from the same family: ~undulate~, ~inundate~, ~abound~ and ~redundant~.
en.opposer:
From Latin ~opponere~ (“to set against, to place opposite, to oppose”), refashioned in French after the verb ~poser~. ~opponere~ is a compound of the prefix ~ob-~ (“against, toward”) and ~ponere~ (“to put, to place”), whose past participle ~positus~ supplies the form ~oppositus~. The origin of ~ponere~ is debated — traditionally read as ~po-~ + ~sinere~ (“to set down, to let lie”) — so the deep root is best left open. Through ~opponere~ the verb is cognate with Italian ~opporre~, Spanish ~oponer~, and English ~oppose~ and ~opponent~.

The image inside ~opponere~ is spatial: to set one thing facing another, hence to set them against each other. French ~opposer~ kept this — to place in contrast, to set in conflict, to raise an objection. A neat detail is that French rebuilt the inherited verb on native ~poser~ rather than carrying the Latin stem intact, a common Old French habit that also reshaped ~composer~, ~déposer~, and ~exposer~. From the ~ob-~ + ~ponere~ family French keeps ~opposé~, ~opposition~, ~opposant~, and ~opposable~ (as in the opposable thumb) — a small constellation of confrontation all built on the simple idea of “placing toward.”
en.opter:
Borrowed from Latin ~optare~ (“to choose, to wish for”). ~Optare~ is a frequentative built on a lost verb *~opere~, surviving chiefly in its derivatives, and is connected to ~optio~ (“choice, free choice”) and to ~opinor~ (“to weigh, to suppose”). The same circle of ideas — choosing, seeing, preferring — links it loosely to Ancient Greek ~ὄψομαι~ (“I shall see”), so that to opt was, at root, to fix one's gaze on what one wants.

Latin ~optare~ meant both to wish and to choose, and that double sense survives faintly in French ~opter~, which has narrowed to the act of choosing between alternatives: ~opter pour~ (“to opt for, to plump for”) one option over another. It is a measured, almost administrative word — one ~opte~ for a tax regime or a nationality. The prefixed Latin ~adoptare~ (“to choose to oneself”) gave French ~adopter~, to take a person or an idea as one's own. The ~optare~ family runs through modern French in ~option~, ~optionnel~, ~optant~, ~adopter~, and ~cooptation~ — every one of them turning on the act of deliberate choice.
en.optimiser:
A learned modern coinage. French ~optimiser~ (attested 1906) was modeled on English ~optimize~ (1844, “to make as good as possible”), itself built on Latin ~optimum~, the neuter of ~optimus~ (“best”), the irregular superlative of ~bonus~ (“good”). Latin ~optimus~ is generally connected to ~ops~ / ~opes~ (“wealth, resources, abundance”) — the “best” being, originally, the richest or most resourceful — and so to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, to produce in abundance”), which also gives ~opus~ (“work”) and ~copia~ (“plenty”).

The word’s lineage is more philosophical than most: ~optimum~ entered learned use through Leibniz, who argued that ours is the “best of all possible worlds,” le meilleur des mondes possibles — the seed of ~optimisme~ (1737) and ~optimiste~. From the bare idea of the best, the verb ~optimiser~ generalized to “to make as good as possible,” and has since bred a small family of its own — ~optimisation~, ~optimiseur~, ~suroptimiser~ (“to over-optimize”), and the parallel ~optimaliser~ formed on ~optimal~. Through ~ops~ the same root also stands behind ~copieux~, ~opulent~, and ~œuvre~.
en.opérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~operārī~ (“to work, to labor, to be busy”), itself from the noun ~opus~ (“work, deed, accomplishment”). Latin ~opus~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, to produce in abundance, ability”). It is the scholarly twin of the inherited French ~ouvrer~ and ~œuvrer~, which came down by oral transmission from the same ~operārī~ — a doublet, the bookish form beside the homegrown one. Italian ~operare~ and Spanish ~obrar~ are cognates; English ~operate~ and ~opera~ share the root.

From the plain sense “to work, to act,” ~opérer~ spread to specialized fields: a surgeon ~opère~ on a patient, a process ~opère~ a transformation, a change ~s'opère~ (“takes place”). The same ~opus~ family is everywhere in French: the inherited ~œuvre~ (“work, body of work”) and ~ouvrier~ (“worker”) on the popular side, and on the learned side ~opération~, ~opérateur~, ~opératoire~, ~coopérer~, and the borrowed Italian ~opéra~ (literally “a work”). Even ~opulence~ belongs here, through Latin ~ops~ (“wealth, resources”), kin to ~opus~: at the deepest level, work, abundance, and riches spring from one Indo-European idea of productive power.
en.orchestrer: Formed in French from ~orchestre~ and the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb. The noun ~orchestre~ is a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~ὀρχήστρα~ (~orkhḗstra~), the space between the spectators and the stage where the chorus performed its movements. The word was feminine, like its Greek source, until the 18th century. The name of that space was later transferred to the musicians who played in it, and ~orchestrer~ means to arrange music for such an ensemble, and by extension to organize something, such as a campaign, with a conductor's control.
en.ordonner:
From Latin ~ordināre~ (“to set in order, to arrange, to dispose in rows”), from ~ordō~ (“row, rank, order”). In Old French ~ordināre~ first gave ~ordiner~ and ~ordener~, which by around 1200 had become ~ordonner~, probably reshaped under the influence of ~donner~ (“to give”), as in “donner des ordres.” ~Ordō~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~ordō~ and is plausibly tied to the PIE root *~h₂er-~ (“to fit together”), the same family as Latin ~artus~ (“joint”).

~Ordō~ first named a row of threads on a weaver's loom, so the abstract idea of “order” is woven, literally, from textile work. This double parentage — Latin order plus French ~donner~ — gave the verb its split modern range: to arrange or sort out things, and to command or prescribe (a doctor who ~ordonne~ a remedy issues an ~ordonnance~). From ~ordō~ / ~ordināre~ French keeps a broad family: ~ordre~, ~ordinaire~, ~ordonnance~, ~ordinateur~ (the “orderer” that became the computer), ~coordonner~, ~subordonner~, and ~désordre~.
en.organiser:
A sixteenth-century verb formed from the noun ~organe~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, but resting on a much older base: Medieval Latin ~organizare~ meant “to play a musical instrument,” whence the fourteenth-century Middle French ~organiser~, “to play the organ.” The noun ~organe~ goes back to Latin ~organum~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ὄργανον~ (~órganon~), “tool, instrument, organ of the body,” itself derived from ~ἔργον~ (~érgon~), “work,” from the Proto-Indo-European root *~werǵ-~ (“to do, work”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~work~ and with the Greek-derived ~energy~.

The semantic journey is striking: from a bodily ~organe~ — a part that does its appointed work — to the idea of furnishing a living being with coordinated working parts, and finally to arranging any set of elements into a functioning whole. By the seventeenth century ~organiser~ had shed its musical and purely biological senses for the general meaning “to structure, set in order,” and the modern sense of planning an event followed naturally. The same root and family yield ~organisme~, ~organisation~, ~organe~ itself, and indirectly ~énergie~. To organize, etymologically, is to give something organs — to make it work like a body.
en.orienter:
A denominal verb (around 1485) built on the noun ~orient~ (“the East”), from Latin ~oriens~, the present participle of ~orīrī~ (“to rise, to arise”) — literally “the rising,” the quarter where the sun comes up. ~Orīrī~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~orjōr~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃er-~ (“to stir, to rise”), shared with Ancient Greek ~ὄρνυμι~ (~órnūmi~, “to rouse, set in motion”) and Sanskrit ~ऋणोति~ (~ṛṇóti~).

The word's history is literally a matter of which way you turn. To ~orienter~ first meant to set a building — above all a church — facing ~east~, toward the rising sun and Jerusalem. From that act of physical alignment grew the figurative senses: to position something by the compass, then to ~guide~ a person, to steer choices and careers (~orientation~ scolaire). To lose that alignment is to ~désorienter~, “to disorient.” The same Latin verb yielded ~origine~ (a “rising,” a beginning), ~oriental~, and ~orientation~; English ~orient~, ~origin~, ~original~, and ~abort~ (etymologically “to fail to rise”) all spring from the same idea of rising into being.
en.originer: Formed in French from ~origine~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to originate, to have as a source.” The noun ~origine~ is borrowed from Latin ~orīgō~, ~orīginis~ (“beginning, source, birth”), and it replaced an older popular form ~orine~, inherited from the same Latin word. The Latin noun belongs to ~orīrī~ (“to rise, to arise”), so an origin is literally a rising. The verb is rare compared with ~provenir~ and ~dériver~, which cover the same ground in everyday French.
en.orner:
French ~orner~ comes from Latin ~ornare~ (“to equip, to fit out, to adorn”), present ~orno~. The verb is generally explained as a syncopated form of *~ordnō~, from ~ordo~ (“order, row, arrangement”), making it a doublet of ~ordinare~ (“to set in order”) — to adorn being, at bottom, to set things rightly in their array. ~Ordo~ in turn probably goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂er-~ (“to fit together, to join”), the same root behind Latin ~artus~ (“joint, limb”) and, through Greek, English ~art~ and ~harmony~.

If this account is right, the link between ornament and order is etymological, not just poetic: to ~orner~ is to arrange, to fit each element into a fitting whole. The military Romans first used ~ornare~ for equipping troops and outfitting ships before it settled into “to decorate.” From the same verb French has ~ornement~, ~ornemental~, the past participle ~orné~, and ornière is unrelated despite appearances. The deeper root *~h₂er-~ also feeds ~ordre~, ~ordinaire~, ~art~, and ~harmonie~ — a family in which decoration and right arrangement were never far apart.
en.oser:
From Late Latin ~ausāre~, a verb built on ~ausus~, the past participle of Classical Latin ~audēre~ (“to dare, to be bold”). The classical verb was itself a stative formed on the adjective ~avidus~ (“eager, greedy”), so that to dare was, at root, to be hungry for something. The reconstructed deeper source is a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂weh₁-~ (“to be eager, to desire”). Italian ~osare~, Spanish ~osar~, and Portuguese ~ousar~ are direct Romance cognates.

Late Latin reshaped the irregular ~audēre~ into the regular ~ausāre~, and from this came Old French ~oser~, unchanged in form to this day. The meaning has held firm: ~oser~ is to venture, to have the audacity to act or speak. Because the classical adjective family survived alongside it through learned borrowing, French keeps a striking split: the everyday ~oser~ next to the bookish ~audace~ (“audacity”), ~audacieux~ (“audacious”), and ~avide~ (“eager, avid”) — all ultimately the same Latin nest. Modern French derivatives of ~oser~ include the adjective ~osé~ (“daring, risqué”), the agent noun ~oseur~, and the rare ~réoser~ (“to dare again”). English ~audacious~ reaches the same root by the learned path, through ~audāx~.
en.oublier:
From Old French ~oblier~, ~oublier~ (attested early as ~oblider~, around 980), from Vulgar Latin *~oblītāre~, a verb built in Gaul and Iberia on ~oblītus~, the past participle of Latin ~oblīvīscī~ (“to forget”). Classical Latin had no simple successor that survived into Romance, so the Romance languages reached for the participle ~oblītus~ and forged a fresh verb upon it — a common workaround. The same *~oblītāre~ gives Italian ~obliare~ and the poetic ~oblio~, Spanish ~olvidar~, and Portuguese ~olvidar~, and the learned doublet ~oubli~ / English ~oblivion~ preserves the Latin form more visibly.

The Latin ~oblīvīscī~ is often connected to ~lēvis~ (“smooth”), as though to forget were to let a memory be rubbed smooth, wiped from the surface of the mind — a vivid image whether or not the link is certain. Old French ~oblier~ softened its first vowel under the influence of rounding to become ~oublier~, the modern shape. Alongside the everyday verb the language kept the more literary ~oubli~ (“forgetfulness, oblivion”) and the learned borrowing ~oblitérer~ (“to obliterate, to cancel”), which returns directly to the same Latin root for its sense of effacement.
en.ouvrer:
From Latin ~operārī~ (“to work, labor, be busy”), a verb built on ~opus~, genitive ~operis~ (“work, deed, labor”). The Latin noun descends from Proto-Italic *~opos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₃ep-os~ (“work”), from the verbal root *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, produce”), cognate with Sanskrit ~ápas~ (“work”) and underlying English ~opulent~ and ~opus~. The inherited French verb ~ouvrer~ thus means simply “to work,” and it is the popular doublet of the learned borrowing ~opérer~ (“to operate”).

~ouvrer~ was once an everyday verb but has largely faded, partly because its conjugated forms collided with those of ~ouvrir~ (“to open”); to avoid the confusion it was often refashioned as ~œuvrer~ (“to work, labor at”). The root nonetheless seeded a large French family: the agent noun ~ouvrier~ (“worker”), the adjective ~ouvrable~ (as in ~jour ouvrable~, “working day”), ~œuvre~ (“work, creation”), ~chef-d'œuvre~ (“masterpiece”), and ~main-d'œuvre~ (“labor, workforce”). Through the learned branch come ~opérer~, ~opération~, and ~coopérer~. A single PIE notion of “doing work” thus spans the laborer’s working day and the artist’s finished masterpiece.
en.ouvrir:
French ~ouvrir~ (attested near 980 in the form ~obrirent~, “they opened”) comes from Latin ~aperīre~ (“to open”), by way of a Vulgar Latin *~operīre~. The vowel change from ~a-~ to ~o-~ was no accident: spoken Latin remodeled ~aperīre~ on its antonym ~cooperīre~ (“to cover up,” source of French ~couvrir~), so that the verb for opening and the verb for covering came to rhyme. Latin ~aperīre~ itself is generally traced to a prefix *~ap-~ (“off, away”) plus a root meaning “to cover,” the whole literally “to un-cover.” Through the Romance line it is cognate with Italian ~aprire~ and Spanish ~abrir~, the everyday words for “to open.”

The paired remodeling of ~ouvrir~ and ~couvrir~ is a tidy case of two opposites pulled into the same shape by their very oppositeness — to this day they conjugate alike. The basic sense “to open” has stayed remarkably stable across two millennia, branching into figurative uses (to open a debate, a heart, a road). From ~ouvrir~ French derives ~ouverture~ (“opening, overture”), ~ouvert~ (“open”), and ~ouvre-boîte~ (“can-opener”); the learned Latin stem reappears in ~apéritif~ (a drink that “opens” the appetite), while ~apertura~ lives on in the technical ~aperture~ shared with English.
en.ouïr:
From Middle French ~ouïr~, from Old French ~oïr~, “to hear,” from Latin ~audīre~ (“to hear, to listen”), the present infinitive of ~audio~, from PIE *~au-~ (“to perceive”). Cognate with Italian ~udire~ and Spanish ~oír~, both of which remain the everyday verbs for hearing in their languages — unlike their French sibling, which lost that office. In French the ground was taken over by ~entendre~ (originally “to direct one's attention toward”), which slid from “to attend to” into plain “to hear.”

As ~entendre~ expanded, ~ouïr~ contracted into a defective relic, fossilized in a handful of set phrases: ~ouï-dire~ (“hearsay,” literally “heard-say”), the herald's archaic cry ~oyez~ (“hear ye!”), still echoed in courtrooms, and the perfect ~j'ai ouï dire~ (“I have heard tell”). The adjective ~inouï~ (“unheard-of, extraordinary”) preserves the old participle, and the related noun ~ouïe~ now names the very sense of hearing. The Latin root remains hugely productive in French through later borrowings: ~audience~, ~auditeur~, and the modern ~audio~. Even ~obéir~ belongs here — from Latin ~oboedīre~ (~ob-~ + ~audīre~), literally “to lend one's ear to,” so that to obey is, at root, to listen.
en.pallier:
Borrowed from Late Latin ~palliāre~ (“to cover with a cloak”), a verb formed on Latin ~pallium~ (“cloak, mantle”), a rectangular Greek-style cloak. Italian ~palliare~ and Spanish ~paliar~ are relatives. The same Latin noun gave English ~pall~ (a cloth thrown over a coffin) and the ecclesiastical ~pallium~, a woolen band worn by archbishops.

The literal sense, “to cloak,” is usually thought to have moved to the figurative “to cover up, to disguise” a fault or a wrong, and from there to treating something only on the surface, hiding a problem without curing it. The step is easy to imagine, but the sources do not trace or date it. Modern French ~pallier~ means “to make up for, to compensate for, to remedy,” as in ~pallier un manque~ (“to make up for a shortage”). The medical adjective ~palliatif~ (“that eases symptoms without curing”) and the English ~palliative~ belong to the same family.
en.paralyser: Formed from the noun ~paralysie~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which here means “to cause to suffer N”, with the ending of the noun reshaped. The noun ~paralysie~ was borrowed from Latin ~paralysis~ (“palsy”), from Ancient Greek ~παράλυσις~ (“loosening”). The Greek word is built on the idea of a body or limb loosened and unstrung, so to ~paralyser~ is to strike with palsy, and figuratively to bring a person, a city or a process to a standstill.
en.paramétrer: Formed from ~paramètre~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to set the parameters of something, as in configuring software. The noun ~paramètre~ is itself built on the Greek elements ~παρά~ (“beside”) and ~μέτρον~ (“measure”). The verb is a modern, technical coinage, and its transparent derivation is typical of how French turns a learned noun into an action.
en.paraître:
From Middle French ~paroistre~, from Old French ~paroistre~, ~pareistre~, from Vulgar Latin *~parēscere~, an inchoative (“begin to…”) verb formed on Latin ~pārēre~ (“to appear, to show oneself, to be visible”). ~Pārēre~ traces through Proto-Italic *~pāzēō~ to PIE *~peh₂s-~ (“to watch, to look out for”), an s-extension of *~peh₂-~ (“to protect”). Cognate with Italian ~parere~ and Spanish ~parecer~, both meaning “to seem.”

The inchoative ending *~-ēscere~ is the heart of the story: it turned the plain ~pārēre~ (“to be visible”) into “to come into view, to begin to appear,” capturing the very moment a thing surfaces — which is exactly the nuance modern ~paraître~ keeps in “to appear, to seem, to come out” (a book ~paraît~ when it is published). ~Pārēre~ also combined with prefixes to give ~apparēre~, source of French ~apparaître~ (“to appear”) and the noun ~apparition~, and ~comparēre~, source of ~comparaître~ (“to appear in court”). From the same family French keeps ~apparence~ (“appearance”) and ~transparent~, all turning on the simple idea of being seen.
en.parcourir:
From Old French, a compound of the prefix ~par-~ (from Latin ~per-~, “through, thoroughly”) and the verb ~courir~ (“to run”), modeled on Latin ~percurrere~ (“to run through, traverse”). The base ~courir~ descends from Latin ~currere~ (“to run”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The whole family is mirrored in Italian ~percorrere~ and Spanish ~recorrer~.

The prefix ~par-~ here is intensive and exhaustive: not merely to run, but to run over the whole extent of something. So ~parcourir~ kept a literal sense — to travel across or traverse a region — while developing the figurative one English borrows in “to skim”: to run one's eyes over a page, to ~parcourir~ a book. The same ~currere~ is astonishingly fertile in French, giving ~courir~, ~courrier~ (“mail,” once carried by a running messenger), ~courant~ (“current, running”), ~concourir~, ~secourir~ (“to succour,” literally “to run to the aid of”), and the noun ~cours~. Through Latin it also seeded English ~current~, ~course~, ~corridor~, and even ~car~ — all, at root, things that run.
en.pardonner:
Attested from the end of the 10th century (in the ~Passion~), ~pardonner~ comes from Late Latin ~perdonāre~, a compound of the intensive prefix ~per-~ (“thoroughly, completely”) and ~donāre~ (“to give, to grant”). ~Donāre~ derives from ~donum~ (“gift”), from PIE *~deh₃nom~ (“gift”), from the root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — the same root behind ~donner~, ~donation~, and ~donateur~. The compound is mirrored across Romance: Italian ~perdonare~, Spanish and Occitan ~perdonar~; through Old French ~pardoner~ it also gave English ~pardon~.

The construction is vivid once unpacked: ~per-~ + ~donāre~ means “to give utterly, to remit a debt completely” — to make a clean gift of what one was owed. The earliest French sense was concrete mercy, “to spare, to grant someone their life,” before settling into the modern range of forgiving an offense and excusing a small lapse (~pardonnez-moi~). The shift of ~per-~ to ~par-~ is regular in French (compare ~parfaire~, ~parvenir~, ~parcourir~), where the prefix keeps its sense of completion. The whole family of *~deh₃-~ is one of generosity: ~don~, ~pardon~, ~donateur~, ~condonation~, and the learned ~dot~ (“dowry,” from ~dōs~) — so that to ~pardonner~ is, at root, to give a wrong away entirely.
en.parer:
From Latin ~parāre~ (“to make ready, to prepare, to arrange”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to produce, to procure”). The same root yields English ~prepare~, ~apparatus~, and ~separate~, Spanish ~parar~, and Italian ~parare~. In French, ~parer~ split into senses borrowed back from those neighbors: the defensive “to parry, to ward off” owes to Italian ~parare~ (“to block”), while the equestrian “to halt a horse” echoes Spanish ~parar~ (“to stop”).

Underneath all these meanings lies a single old idea: to get something ready. From “prepare” the verb slid easily toward “arrange attractively,” and so ~parer~ came to mean to adorn or bedeck — a bride is ~parée~ for her wedding, a room ~paré~ for a feast. The fighting sense took a different path through Italy: to make yourself ready against a blow is to fend it off, hence to parry. French keeps both alive at once, and the root *~per-~ blossoms across the language in ~préparer~, ~appareil~, ~séparer~, ~rempart~, ~parade~, and ~parure~ (“finery”). One Latin verb meaning simply “to make ready” thus learned to decorate, to defend, and to bring a galloping horse to a clean stop.
en.parfaire:
From Middle French ~parfaire~, from Old French ~parfaire~, borrowed from Latin ~perficere~ (“to carry through, to complete”) and reshaped by analogy with ~faire~. English Wiktionary instead presents it as ~par-~ + ~faire~, which is the same story seen from French: ~par-~ is the Old French form of Latin ~per-~ (“thoroughly”). Latin ~perficere~ is ~per-~ plus ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to set”), which also gives English ~do~ and German ~tun~.

The meaning has hardly changed: to ~parfaire~ is to bring something to full completion, to finish it off properly, as in ~parfaire son éducation~ or ~parfaire un tableau~. The verb now belongs to a careful, literary register and is mostly met in the infinitive and the participles. Its past participle ~parfait~ became an independent adjective, “perfect.” The learned ~perfectionner~ and ~perfection~ come directly from the Latin family, while ~parfaire~ shows how French reshaped the same Latin verb in popular speech. The long family of ~faire~ includes ~défaire~, ~refaire~, ~satisfaire~ and ~fait~.
en.parfumer: The analysis is disputed. French Wiktionary derives it as ~fumer~ with the prefix ~par-~ (from Latin ~per-~, “through, thoroughly”), first with the sense of fumigating. English Wiktionary instead takes the Middle French verb as probably borrowed from Old Occitan or from Italian ~perfumare~, itself Latin ~per-~ plus ~fūmāre~. Either way the parts are the same: ~fūmāre~ (“to smoke, to steam”) comes from ~fūmus~ (“smoke”). The noun ~parfum~ keeps the picture of a scent that rises through smoke, as from burning incense.
en.parler:
From Old French ~parler~, from Late Latin ~parabolāre~ (“to speak, to converse”), a verb built on Latin ~parabola~ (“comparison, parable; speech”). ~parabola~ was borrowed from Ancient Greek ~παραβολή~ (parabolḗ, “a placing side by side, comparison”), from ~παρά~ (pará, “beside”) and ~βάλλειν~ (bállein, “to throw, to cast”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷelH-~ (“to throw, to reach”). To “speak,” then, is etymologically to “throw words side by side.” Cognate verbs survive as Italian ~parlare~, while Spanish chose a different reflex of the same noun in ~palabra~ (“word”); English took ~parable~, ~parley~, and ~palaver~ from the same Greek source.

The striking detail is that the ordinary French word for talking comes not from Latin's neutral ~loquī~ (“to speak”) but from a churchy, rhetorical word for a “comparison” or “parable” — the speech of sermons and figures. In the mouths of Late Latin speakers ~parabola~ shed its lofty sense and came to mean simply “word, speech,” which is why French ~parole~ means “(the spoken) word” and ~parler~ means “to talk.” From the same root come a large family, including ~parole~, ~parleur~, ~pourparler~ (“negotiation, parley”), and the borrowed ~parabole~ (“parable; parabola”), which kept the geometric and biblical senses the everyday verb left behind.
en.parrainer: Formed from the noun ~parrain~ (“godfather”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to act as a godfather to,” hence “to sponsor.” ~Parrain~ comes from Old French ~parrain~ and from Early Medieval Latin ~patrīnus~, the man who held a child at baptism. English Wiktionary derives ~patrīnus~ from Latin ~pater~ (“father”), whereas French Wiktionary links it to Latin ~patruus~ (“paternal uncle”), so the last step is uncertain. The ecclesiastical sense of spiritual father was later widened to anyone who vouches for or backs a person, a project or an event.
en.parsemer: ~Parsemer~ is ~par-~ + ~semer~. The prefix ~par-~, a variant of Latin ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”), only intensifies the base here: to sow or scatter all over, to strew. The verb ~semer~ comes from Latin ~sēmināre~ (“to sow”), drawn from ~sēmen~ (“seed”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~seh₁-~ (“to sow”), which is also the source of English ~sow~. From the field the verb moved to anything scattered thickly, such as a text dotted with quotations. The prefix ~par-~ no longer forms new verbs, and ~parsemer~ is one of its few survivors.
en.partager:
French ~partager~ is a relatively young verb, coined around 1553 from the noun ~partage~ (“division, sharing”) plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. Behind it stands ~part~ (“share, portion”), from Latin ~pars~, accusative ~partem~ (“a part, a share”), which traces to Proto-Indo-European *~perh₂-~ (“to grant, to allot”). The root is widely fertile, related to Latin ~portiō~ (“portion”) and surfacing in English ~part~, ~portion~, and ~parcel~. Greek ~péprōtai~ (“it has been allotted”) carries the same notion of a share handed out by fate.

The coinage answered a real gap in the language. The older inherited verb ~partir~, from Latin ~partīre~ (“to divide”), had drifted away to mean only “to depart, to leave” — a share of a journey split off, as it were, from the rest. With ~partir~ no longer usable for “to divide,” French built a fresh verb on the noun ~partage~ to recover the lost sense. The root still ramifies widely: ~part~, ~partie~, ~parti~, ~partager~, ~partenaire~ (“partner”), ~parcelle~, ~départ~ and ~répartir~. The fixed phrase ~à part~ (“apart, aside”) and the verb ~partir~ itself remind us that to depart and to share a portion spring from one and the same idea of dividing.
en.participer:
From Latin ~participāre~ (“to share, to take part in”), a compound of ~pars~ / ~partis~ (“a part, a share”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”) — literally “to take a part.” ~Capere~ descends from PIE *~kh₂p-~ (“to grasp, to seize”), through which ~participer~ is cognate with English ~have~ and ~heave~ and with German ~haben~. ~Pars~ also gives French ~part~, ~partie~, and ~partir~.

The Latin verb fused the having of a portion with the act of seizing it, so that to participate is to take one's share of a common thing. From ~capere~ flows an immense French family — ~captif~, ~capter~, ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~, ~accepter~, ~capable~ — while ~pars~ supplies ~partager~, ~parti~, ~partiel~, and ~répartir~. From ~participāre~ itself come the close relatives ~participant~, ~participation~, and the grammatical ~participe~ (the participle, so called because it “takes part” in the natures of both verb and adjective). Thus the dry term of grammar and the lively act of joining in a cause are, etymologically, the very same gesture of taking a share.
en.partir:
From Old French ~partir~ (“to divide, to share, to separate”), from Latin ~partīre~, a variant of Classical Latin ~partīrī~ (“to divide, to share out”), a verb built on ~pars~, ~partis~ (“a part, share, portion”). The noun is generally traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ in the sense “to grant, to allot.” Through ~pars~, ~partir~ is kin to Italian ~partire~ and Spanish ~partir~, and, by way of Old French, to English ~part~, ~party~, and ~depart~.

The modern meaning hides an older one. For centuries ~partir~ meant “to divide” — a sense still alive in the saying ~avoir maille à partir~ (“to have a bone to pick,” literally a tiny coin to split). The notion of leaving grew from the reflexive ~se partir~, “to separate oneself” from a person or place; the reflexive faded but its directional sense stayed, leaving ~partir~ to mean simply “to depart.” The dividing sense lives on in ~répartir~, ~partager~, ~partage~, ~partie~ (“part, match”), ~parti~ (“party, side”), ~partition~, and ~particule~ — and, more distantly through ~pars~, in ~parcelle~ and the borrowed ~portion~.
en.parvenir:
From Latin ~pervenire~ (“to arrive, to reach”), a compound of ~per-~ (“through, all the way”) and ~venire~ (“to come”). ~venire~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷeniō~ and from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”). Cognate with Italian ~pervenire~ and Spanish ~prevenir~ in form, and — through *~gʷem-~ — with English ~come~ and the learned ~advent~.

The prefix ~per-~ supplies the crucial nuance: not merely to come, but to come through, to come all the way to the end — hence “to reach, to attain.” French keeps both the literal and the figurative: a letter ~parvient~ to its addressee, and a person ~parvient~ to wealth or to a goal. From this last sense comes the loaded noun ~parvenu~, literally “one who has arrived,” used scornfully of the newly rich who reached high station from low birth — a social judgment hiding inside a participle. The shared root *~gʷem-~ links ~parvenir~ to the whole French ~venir~ family — ~devenir~, ~revenir~, ~convenir~, ~survenir~, ~prévenir~ — every one of them a different way of coming.
en.passer:
Attested from around 1050, from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~ (“to cross, to step”), derived from Latin ~passus~ (“step, pace”), which is the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread, to stretch out [the legs]”), from PIE *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). A step is, etymologically, a “spreading” of the legs. Cognate with Italian ~passare~ and Spanish ~pasar~; the noun ~passus~ also gave French ~pas~ and, by borrowing, English ~pass~ and ~pace~.

Few French verbs sprawl across so many meanings: one ~passe~ a river (to cross), ~passe~ an exam, ~passe~ the salt, ~passe~ time, and time itself ~passe~. All trace back to the simple image of stepping across a threshold. The same root *~peth₂-~ surfaces in the Latin ~pandere~ family, from which French draws ~expansion~ and ~épandre~, and the ~passus~ branch yields a crowd of everyday words: ~passage~, ~passager~, ~passeport~ (literally a document for “passing a port”), ~dépasser~, ~surpasser~, ~repasser~, and ~trépasser~ — “to pass beyond,” the old, gentle word for dying. To “pass away” is thus, in French as in English, to take a final step across.
en.passionner:
A French formation: ~passionner~ is a denominal verb from the noun ~passion~, which came through Middle French from Latin ~passionem~ (“suffering, enduring”), the action noun of the deponent verb ~patior~ (“to suffer, undergo, be acted upon”). The Latin verb is usually traced to PIE *~peh₁-~ (“to hurt”), though its morphology is irregular and the connection is not beyond debate. From ~patior~ English draws ~patient~, ~passive~, and ~compassion~ — all of them, like ~passion~, originally about being acted upon rather than acting.

The oldest French ~passion~ was Christian: the suffering of Christ, the ~Passion~. From that root sense of strong feeling endured, the word swelled to mean any overmastering emotion or love. The verb ~passionner~ followed: to ~passionner~ someone is to seize them with that intensity, and a debate that ~passionne~ a crowd inflames it. The thread from “to suffer” to “to be impassioned” is the idea of an emotion that takes you over. From the same ~patior~ French keeps ~pâtir~ (“to suffer”), ~patient~, ~passif~, and ~compassion~.
en.patienter: Formed in French from the adjective and noun ~patient~ and the verb ending ~-er~, and meaning “to be patient, to wait.” The base ~patient~ comes from Old French ~patient~, borrowed from Latin ~patiens~ (accusative ~patientem~), the present participle of ~patī~ (“to suffer, to endure”). The family thus rests on the Latin idea of putting up with something, which is also the root of English ~patient~ and ~passion~. In French, ~patienter~ turned that quality into an action, most often an instruction to wait one's turn or to hold on.
en.payer:
From Old French ~paiier~, ~payer~, from Latin ~pācāre~ (“to pacify, to appease”), a verb built on ~pāx~ (“peace”). ~Pāx~ goes back to PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ (“to fasten, to join, to settle”), the root that also gave Latin ~pangere~ (“to fix, to drive in”) and ~pacīscī~ (“to make a pact”); through its Germanic line the same root underlies English ~fang~. Cognate with Italian ~pagare~ and Spanish ~pagar~.

The semantic leap is the memorable part. In Classical Latin ~pācāre~ meant “to make peaceful, to subdue,” but in the money-minded Latin of the Middle Ages it narrowed to a very particular kind of appeasement: to pacify a creditor by settling the debt. To pay was, literally, to make peace with the person you owed. That sense crossed into Old French and crowded out the older one entirely, so that French ~payer~ now means only “to pay.” The peaceful origin is still visible in the cousins of ~pāx~ that French preserves — ~paix~ (“peace”), ~apaiser~ (“to appease”), ~pacifier~, ~pacte~ — a quiet reminder that a settled bill and a settled quarrel were once the same act.
en.peindre:
From Middle and Old French ~peindre~, from Latin ~pingere~ (“to paint, to dye, to embroider, to tattoo, to embellish”), from a nasal-infixed Proto-Indo-European *~pi-n-ḱ-~, from the root *~peyḱ-~ (“to mark, to color; spotted”). The deep sense is marking or cutting a sign into a surface. Through this root ~peindre~ is cognate with Greek ~poikílos~ (“dappled, embroidered”), Sanskrit ~piṃśáti~ (“he cuts, adorns”), and the Old English ~fāh~ (“stained, variegated”).

That the same Latin verb meant both “to paint” and “to embroider” and “to tattoo” recalls a time when all of these were ways of marking a surface with color. French narrowed ~peindre~ to the brush, but kept the figurative reach: one can ~peindre~ a character or a scene in words, “to depict” it. The Latin participle ~pictus~ and noun ~pictūra~ entered French as the learned doublets ~pictural~ and the borrowed ~pictura~ behind ~peinture~, while ~pingere~ itself gave ~peintre~ (“painter”) and ~peinture~. From ~pigmentum~ (“coloring matter”) came both ~pigment~ and, by a worn-down popular route, ~piment~ (“chili pepper”); the same root colors Italian ~pingere~ and Spanish ~pintar~.
en.peiner: Formed on ~peine~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, continuing Old French ~pener~. The noun ~peine~ is inherited from Old French ~peine~, from Latin ~poena~ (“penalty, punishment”), which itself came from Ancient Greek ~poinḗ~ (“penalty, fine, blood-money”). The verb has two uses: intransitive, “to toil, to struggle” (the older sense of suffering effort), and transitive, “to cause pain to, to distress.” The adverb ~à peine~ (“hardly”) is a separate word, from Latin ~paene~ (“almost”).
en.peler: From Old French ~peler~, itself from Late Latin ~pilāre~ (“to remove hair, to depilate”), a verb built on Latin ~pilus~ (“hair”). The original sense was thus to strip hair, then to strip the skin or rind off something, which is how ~peler~ came to mean “to peel” a fruit or a vegetable. English Wiktionary adds that the form may have been influenced by the Old French noun ~pel~, a point French Wiktionary does not mention. The same Latin ~pilus~ gave French ~poil~ (“hair”) by regular sound change, so ~peler~ and ~poil~ are cousins.
en.pencher:
From Old French ~pengier~ (“to be out of plumb”), attested in 1256, from Vulgar Latin *~pendicare~, a derivative of Latin ~pendere~ (“to hang”). The modern form ~pencher~ appears from 1530. ~Pendere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~pendēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, pull, draw”). The root surfaces in Romance ~pendere~ verbs and, more distantly, in English ~pension~ and ~pendant~.

The semantic thread runs from hanging to leaning to inclining: a thing that hangs off true is tilted, and from physical tilt the verb passed to mental tendency — one ~penche pour~ an idea, leans toward it. The related ~pendere~ also meant “to weigh, to pay,” because coins and goods were once weighed in a hanging scale-pan; that image of suspension links the family. From the same root French keeps ~pente~ (“slope”), ~penchant~ (“inclination, leaning”), ~pendre~ (“to hang”), and ~pendule~. To lean, in French, is still quietly to hang at an angle.
en.pendre:
~Pendre~ comes from Old French ~pendre~, itself from Late Latin ~pendĕre~, with a short e, which stands in for Classical Latin ~pendēre~ (“to hang, to be suspended”). Latin had two near-twin verbs: the intransitive ~pendēre~ (“to hang”) and the transitive ~pendere~ (“to make hang, to weigh”). Their conjugations were confused in Late Latin, which is why French ~pendre~ works both ways, “to hang something” and “to hang down”. The Latin verb is traced to Proto-Italic *~pendēō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull; to spin”). Italian ~pendere~ is the direct cousin of the French verb.

Since a pair of scales hangs from its beam, Latin ~pendere~ also meant “to weigh” and so “to pay out”. Its frequentative ~pensāre~ (“to weigh carefully”) gave French ~peser~ and ~penser~, so “to think” is, etymologically, “to weigh in the mind”. Modern ~pendre~ covers hanging a coat, hanging a criminal, and the intransitive droop or sag, as in cheeks that hang. The family is large: ~suspendre~, ~dépendre~ and ~pendule~ (the hanging weight of a clock). English borrowed many of these as ~suspend~, ~depend~, ~pendulum~ and ~pensive~.
en.penser:
From Middle and Old French ~penser~ (also spelled ~panser~), from Latin ~pensāre~ (“to weigh carefully, to ponder”). ~pensāre~ is the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to pull, to spin”) — the image of weights hanging from the arm of a balance. So to “think” is, at root, to “weigh” — to hold ideas in the scales of the mind. ~penser~ is a learned doublet of French ~peser~ (“to weigh”), which descends from the very same Latin verb by the ordinary popular route; the two split apart, one keeping the literal weight, the other the mental one. Cognate reflexes survive as Italian ~pensare~ and Spanish ~pensar~, and the family entered English as ~pensive~ and ~ponder~.

The metaphor of mental weighing is ancient and vivid, and French preserves it throughout the vocabulary of thought. Curiously, the alternate spelling ~panser~ peeled off into a separate verb meaning “to dress a wound, to groom (a horse)” — originally “to take thought for, to attend to” an animal or an injury, the same act of careful consideration applied to care. From ~pensāre~ and ~pendere~ come a wide French family, including ~pensée~ (“thought; pansy”), ~pensif~ (“pensive”), ~penseur~ (“thinker”), and, through the weighing sense, ~dépenser~ (“to spend, to weigh out money”) and ~récompense~ (“reward”).
en.percer:
From Vulgar Latin *~pertusiare~ (“to pierce”), a verb derived from ~pertusum~, the supine of Latin ~pertundere~ (“to thrust through, to bore”) — the prefix ~per-~ (“through”) joined to ~tundere~ (“to strike, to beat”). The same ~pertusum~ gave Old French ~pertuis~ (“a hole, an opening”), a word still found in place-names and in old technical vocabulary, naming the very gap that piercing leaves behind.

To ~percer~ is to make a hole through something, but the verb quickly grew figurative meanings that the English glosses capture: to percer a mystery is to see through it, and a young talent who ~perce~ is one who “breaks through” to success. French keeps several relatives close to the surface: ~perçage~ and ~perceuse~ (the drilling and the drill), ~percée~ (“a breakthrough,” military or otherwise), and ~transpercer~ (“to run through”). The image is consistent across them all — a sharp passage driven clean through a barrier, whether that barrier is a plank, a secret, or an obstacle to fame.
en.percevoir:
French ~percevoir~ comes from Latin ~percipere~ (“to seize wholly, to take in, to perceive”), formed from ~per-~ (“thoroughly, completely”) plus ~capere~ (“to seize, to take”). ~Capere~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp, to seize”), which also surfaces in the Germanic family — English ~have~ and ~heave~ are distant cousins through Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~. The French form was remodeled on ~recevoir~ and ~apercevoir~, all sharing the ~-cevoir~ stem from ~capere~; Italian keeps the more transparent ~percepire~.

The Latin verb already united the physical and the mental: to “take in completely,” whether grasping an object or grasping an idea. French inherited both. ~Percevoir~ still means “to take in through the senses or the mind” — to perceive a sound, to make out a meaning — but it also carries a strikingly concrete administrative sense, “to collect, to levy,” as when the state ~perçoit~ a tax: a literal seizing of money. From this comes ~percepteur~, the tax collector. Around ~capere~ and its compound French clusters ~perception~, ~perceptible~ and ~imperceptible~, ~apercevoir~ and ~apperçu~, plus the wider ~capter~, ~capable~, ~capture~, and ~recevoir~. To perceive, etymologically, is to grasp a thing whole — with the hand, the ear, or the understanding.
en.percher: Formed in French from the noun ~perche~ (“pole”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to set on a perch”, and so “to roost, to settle up high”. The noun ~perche~ comes from Old French ~perche~, from Latin ~pertica~ (“long pole”), probably through a contracted Vulgar Latin form. The fish also called ~perche~ is a separate word, from Latin ~perca~ and Greek ~pérkē~, which means “spotted”. The verb belongs to the pole, since a bird sits on a pole and not on a fish.
en.perdre:
From Latin ~perdere~ (« to destroy, to ruin, to lose utterly »), formed from the prefix ~per-~ (« through, to the end, to destruction ») and the verb ~dare~ (« to give »). ~dare~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”), shared by Ancient Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), Sanskrit ~dádāti~, and — through Latin — English ~donate~ and ~date~. Italian ~perdere~ and Spanish ~perder~ are its Romance siblings.

The literal sense is striking: ~per-~ + ~dare~ is to « give thoroughly away », to give until nothing is left — hence « to destroy » and then « to lose ». The intensive prefix turned the act of giving into the act of losing, a quiet reminder that loss is open-handedness pushed past return. French keeps the whole spread: to ~perdre~ a key, a battle, one's time (~perdre son temps~), or one's way (~se perdre~). From the same verb come ~perte~ (« loss »), ~perdition~, and the adjective ~perdu~, while the root ~dare~ also yields ~donner~, ~rendre~, ~vendre~, and ~pardonner~.
en.perdurer:
From Latin ~perdūrāre~ (“to last, to endure to the end”), a compound of ~per-~ (“through”) and ~dūrāre~ (“to harden, to last”). In this verb the prefix is intensive: it does not add a new direction, it adds the idea of going the whole way. The base ~dūrāre~ comes from the adjective ~dūrus~ (“hard”). Spanish ~perdurar~ and Italian ~perdurare~ are the sister forms, and English has the learned ~perdure~ (“to endure”).

In French, ~perdurer~ is a learned word and a stronger one than ~durer~: it speaks of what continues to exist in spite of time or trouble, as in ~la tradition perdure~ (“the tradition lives on”). Its relatives include ~durer~ (“to last”), ~dur~ (“hard”), ~durable~ and ~endurer~ (“to endure, to bear”), and English has ~endure~, ~duration~ and ~during~ from the same Latin root. Note that ~perdurer~ is formed in Latin, not in French: there is no French verb ~per-~ + ~durer~ in the formation.
en.perfectionner: ~Perfectionner~ is formed from the noun ~perfection~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb: to bring something toward perfection, to refine it. ~Perfection~ came through Middle French from Latin ~perfectiō~ (“complete achievement”), from ~perficere~ (“to finish, to carry through”), itself made of ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and ~facere~ (“to do”). So the idea at the heart of the word is thoroughness: something done all the way through. The verb thus says “to make more complete,” which is why it is used for skills, techniques and tools that are improved step by step.
en.permettre:
From Latin ~permittere~ (“to let pass, to allow, to entrust”), formed from the prefix ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and the verb ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”). French reshaped it on the native model of ~mettre~, giving ~permettre~. Since ~mittere~ rests on a Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, to remove”), ~permettre~ shares its deep ancestry with Italian ~permettere~ and Spanish ~permitir~, and with English ~permit~, borrowed straight from the Latin.

The literal force of ~per-~ + ~mittere~ is vivid: to permit is to “let through,” to send a thing all the way along its path rather than block it. From the same supine stem ~permiss-~ French draws ~permis~ (both the past participle “permitted” and the noun “permit, licence,” as in ~permis de conduire~, “driving licence”) and ~permission~. The verb keeps the company of its siblings built on ~mettre~ — ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, ~transmettre~, ~émettre~ — a tidy set in which a single prefix recolors the shared idea of sending: ~pro-~ forward, ~sub-~ under, ~trans-~ across, ~ex-~ out, and ~per-~ all the way through.
en.perpétrer:
From Latin ~perpetrāre~ (“to carry through, to accomplish”), a learned borrowing, and not a word that passed through the popular sound changes of Old French. The Latin verb is built from ~per-~ (“through, to the end”) and ~patrāre~ (“to bring about, to bring to pass”), whose own origin is unclear. It meant simply to carry something out to completion, with no bad overtones. The same ~patrāre~ gave ~impetrāre~ (“to obtain by request”), borrowed into French as ~impétrer~, a legal term. English ~perpetrate~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb.

The path of the meaning is the interesting part. In Latin, ~perpetrāre~ was neutral, since one could accomplish a good deed as readily as a bad one. In French, as in English, the verb narrowed to the sense it has today: one ~perpètre~ a crime, an outrage, a massacre, an attack, never a good action. Do not confuse it with ~perpétuer~ (“to make perpetual”), from ~perpetuus~, which merely sounds alike. The noun ~perpétration~ and the agent noun ~perpétrateur~ follow the same pattern.
en.perpétuer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~perpetuāre~ (“to make continuous, to cause to last without a break”), attested in French around 1370 in Jean le Fèvre. The Latin verb is built on the adjective ~perpetuus~ (“continuous, unbroken, lasting”), analyzed as ~per-~ (“through”) plus the root of ~petere~ (“to seek, to make for”): what is ~perpetuus~ goes, literally, right the way through. The same formation lies behind the rarer Latin ~perpes~. ~petere~ itself goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, to rush”). Roman institutional language leaned on the adjective in fixed phrases such as ~in perpetuum~ (“for ever”) and ~quaestiones perpetuae~, the standing courts of the late republic, and it is that administrative flavor of permanence that the French verb inherited. Italian ~perpetuare~, Spanish ~perpetuar~ and English ~perpetuate~ are parallel borrowings of the same Latin verb.

French received the adjective long before the verb: ~perpétuel~ was already in medieval use, and the noun ~perpétuité~ supplied the legal formula ~à perpétuité~, which is why a life sentence in French is, literally, a perpetuity. The verb began as a transitive one — to perpetuate a name, a memory, an institution — and acquired its pronominal form ~se perpétuer~ by 1549, the sense in which a species, a custom or an error keeps itself going. That reflexive use carries the modern sting: what ~se perpétue~ today is usually something one would rather see stop, an inequality or a stereotype, so a verb whose Latin ancestor described unbroken duration now most often reports an unwelcome persistence. The ~petere~ family is large in French — ~appétit~, ~compétition~, ~pétition~, ~répéter~, ~impétueux~ — and the ~perpetuus~ branch adds ~perpétuation~, ~perpétuel~ and the musical ~mouvement perpétuel~.
en.persister: Borrowed from Latin ~persistere~ (“to continue steadfastly, to stand firm”), formed from ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and ~sistere~ (“to set, to stand”). ~Sistere~ is a reduplicated present built on the root of ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~, so to persist is, etymologically, to stand through to the end. French has a whole family built on ~sistere~: ~résister~, ~exister~, ~assister~, ~consister~, ~subsister~ and ~insister~. English ~persist~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb.
en.personnaliser:
From the adjective ~personnel~ (“personal”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~ — a modern, regular coinage rather than an inherited verb. ~Personnel~ itself goes back, through Old French, to Latin ~persōnālis~ (“of a person”), from ~persōna~. That noun first meant the ~mask~ worn by an actor on the Roman stage, then the dramatic ~role~ played behind it, and only later the human being who plays a role in life. Its own origin is debated: many trace ~persōna~ to Etruscan ~phersu~, itself perhaps linked to Ancient Greek ~πρόσωπον~ (~prósōpon~, “face, mask”).

The suffix ~-iser~ descends from Latin ~-izāre~, borrowed from Greek ~-ίζειν~ (~-ízein~), the same productive ending behind English ~-ize~. To ~personnaliser~ is thus, etymologically, to stamp something with the ~mask~ of an individual — to make it bear a particular face. The Latin root spread widely in French: ~personne~, ~personnage~, ~personnalité~, ~personnel~ (both the adjective and the noun “staff”), and the legal ~personnalité juridique~. English ~person~, ~personnel~, and ~persona~ share the same theatrical ancestor, a reminder that the modern idea of a unique self began as a hollow wooden face.
en.persuader:
Attested from 1370, borrowed from Latin ~persuādēre~ (“to convince thoroughly”), from ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) + ~suādēre~ (“to advise, urge”). ~suādēre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~swādejō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sweh₂d-~ (“to be sweet, pleasing”) — the very root behind Latin ~suāvis~ (“sweet, agreeable”). So the act of persuading is, at root, a sweetening: to make your view palatable to another.

That same *~sweh₂d-~ gives a surprisingly broad cousinage. Through Germanic it yields English ~sweet~; through Latin ~suāvis~ it yields French ~suave~ and English ~suave~ and ~persuade~; and through Greek it underlies ~hedonism~ (from ~hēdús~, “sweet, pleasant”). French descendants and relatives include ~persuasion~, ~persuasif~, ~dissuader~, and ~suave~ itself. The thread running through all of them — sweetness, pleasantness, persuasion — is one of the tidiest semantic webs in the language: to persuade someone is, etymologically, to make a thing taste good to them.
en.persécuter:
The sources differ slightly. French Wiktionary derives the verb from Latin ~persequor~ (“I pursue”), while English Wiktionary calls it a back-formation from ~persécuteur~, the agent noun, which itself comes from Latin ~persecūtor~. The two accounts agree on the root: Latin ~persequī~ (“to follow through, to pursue relentlessly”), made of ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and ~sequī~ (“to follow”). Latin ~sequī~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), which gave English ~sequel~ and ~sequence~ through Latin, and Latin ~secundus~ (“following, second”).

The Latin verb was neutral and could mean simply to chase or to carry out a plan. Christian Latin gave the noun ~persecūtor~ its dark sense, the one applied to the Roman emperors who hunted believers, and French inherited that sense. From there the verb widened in two directions: to hound a group for its beliefs, and, more lightly, to harass or pester someone, as in ~persécuter~ quelqu'un de questions. The same ~sequī~ underlies French ~suivre~, ~suite~, ~séquence~, ~poursuivre~ and ~second~.
en.perturber:
From Old French ~perturber~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~perturbāre~ (“to throw into confusion, disturb greatly”), from ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) + ~turbāre~ (“to disturb, agitate”), itself from ~turba~ (“turmoil, crowd, disorder”). ~turba~ is probably borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τύρβη~ (~túrbē~, “tumult, disorder”), and the family is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)twerH-~ (“to swirl, whirl”), the same root that, through Germanic, gave English ~storm~. The Latin verb is the ancestor of Italian ~perturbare~ and Spanish ~perturbar~.

The core image is of a crowd thrown into disorder: ~per-~ intensifies ~turbāre~, so to ~perturber~ is to stir something up completely. The same ~turba~ underlies a remarkable spread of French and English words: ~trouble~ (through Vulgar Latin), ~turbine~, ~turbulent~, ~perturbation~, and the murky adjective ~turbide~. Note that the Greek source of ~turba~ is flagged as merely probable in the sources, and the deeper Indo-European connection — though widely cited — is not beyond dispute; the English cognate ~storm~ rests on that proposed root rather than on a settled descent.
en.peser:
From Old French ~peser~ (“to weigh”), from Vulgar Latin *~pesare~, an alteration of Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully, weigh out”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from Proto-Italic *~pendō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). Cognate with Italian ~pesare~ and Spanish ~pesar~, and — through the same Latin verb — with the noun ~poids~ and, more distantly, English ~pension~ and ~pendant~.

The Latin ~pēnsāre~ split into two French verbs that are, etymologically, twins: ~peser~ kept the concrete sense of placing something on a balance, while its learned doublet ~penser~ (“to think”) took up the figurative “to weigh in the mind, to ponder.” To think, in this old image, was to weigh ideas against one another. The metaphor still surfaces in ~peser ses mots~ (“to weigh one's words”) and in the impersonal ~peser~ meaning “to weigh upon, to burden.” From the same root *~(s)pend-~ French inherited a broad family: ~pendre~ (“to hang”), ~suspendre~, ~dépenser~ (literally “to weigh out, to pay out”), ~compenser~, and the noun ~poids~ itself, whose silent ~d~ was added by scribes who wrongly linked it to Latin ~pondus~ (“weight”).
en.peupler:
Denominal verb from the noun ~peuple~ (“people”) + ~-er~. ~Peuple~ descends from Latin ~populus~ (“people, nation, the populace”). The deeper origin of ~populus~ is genuinely unsettled: by one account it goes back to a reduplicated form of the root of ~pleō~ (“to fill”), Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~, making “the people” literally a fullness or a crowd; another hypothesis proposes an Etruscan source, and the standard handbooks flag the further origin as simply unknown. Honest sources keep both options open.

A pointed twist: the Latin verb ~populārī~ did not mean “to populate” but its near-opposite, “to ravage, lay waste” (as an army “peoples” a land with soldiers). French ~peupler~, rebuilt natively from ~peuple~, took the constructive sense “to fill with inhabitants, to populate,” so the French verb and its Latin near-namesake pull in contrary directions. From the same ~populus~ root French inherited ~peuple~, ~peuplade~, ~population~, ~populaire~, ~populeux~, and ~public~ (through ~pūblicus~), alongside the learned ~dépeupler~ (“to depopulate”).
en.photographier: ~Photographier~ is formed from the noun ~photographie~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to take a photograph. ~Photographie~ is a learned compound of two Greek elements, ~φῶς~ (~phôs~, genitive ~phōtós~, “light”) and ~γράφω~ (~gráphō~, “to write, to draw”), so a photograph is literally a “writing with light.” The noun was coined in the 19th century, when the technique itself was invented, and the verb followed from it. English ~photograph~ and German ~fotografieren~ were formed on the same Greek parts.
en.piler: The origin of ~piler~ is given two ways. One account takes it from Latin ~pīlāre~ (“to ram down, to press”), itself from ~pīla~ (“column”); the other treats it as a French verb formed on the noun ~pile~ plus ~-er~. The sources do not settle which is right, and the two may in fact converge. The sense is “to pound or crush,” as in a mortar. Related to it is ~pilon~, the pounding tool, and a colloquial use turned the verb toward braking hard.
en.piller: The origin of ~piller~ is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries differ. French Wiktionary proposes no Latin source and only records how the meaning developed: first “to handle roughly, to harass” (compare Old French ~espillier~ and ~despillier~), then “to strip someone of their belongings, often by trickery”, and in the fourteenth century ~peillier~, “to seize something by force”. English Wiktionary instead derives it, through Middle French ~piller~ and Old French ~pillier~, from Latin ~pilleus~ (“felt cap”), a link the French text does not endorse, so treat it as a proposal. The family includes ~pillage~ and ~pillard~, and English borrowed ~pillage~ from French.
en.piloter:
A denominal verb from the noun ~pilote~ (« pilot, helmsman »), which French borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian ~pilota~. The Italian form is itself an alteration of an earlier ~pedotta~ / ~pedoto~, traced — by a reconstruction the dictionaries mark as unattested — to a Byzantine Greek *~pēdōtēs~ (« steersman »), from Ancient Greek ~pēdon~ (« blade of an oar, steering oar »). The ~pil-~ form is probably owed to influence from the Italian verb ~pileggiare~ (« to navigate »), so even the modern shape rests partly on a proposed crossing rather than a clean line.

From the sea the word climbed into every vehicle: one ~pilote~ a ship, then a plane, a race car, even a company. The verb spread its senses outward — to guide, to steer, to manage, and figuratively to « pilot » a project through to completion. English took the same ~pilot~ from French. Modern relatives include ~pilotage~, ~copilote~, ~télépiloter~ (« to fly a drone »), and the noun ~pilote~ used adjectivally, as in a ~projet~ ~pilote~ (« pilot project »).
en.piquer:
~piquer~ surfaces in the second half of the thirteenth century, and its origin is debated. The explanation favored by the TLFi posits a Vulgar Latin *~pīkkāre~, built on an expressive, onomatopoeic root *~pikk-~ imitating a sharp tap — the high vowel suggesting the point, the crisp consonants the little explosion of the blow. The verb's spread is pan-Romance — Italian ~piccare~, Spanish ~picar~ — which argues for a popular root older than any one language. A rival account, the one French Wiktionary gives, instead derives the verb from ~pic~ (“pick; woodpecker”), whose name goes back to Latin ~pīcus~ (“woodpecker”) — on that reading, nature's own striker of sharp blows would stand behind the verb. Either way, no classical Latin ancestor is attested: piquer is a child of the spoken language.

From “to prick” the verb fanned out into one of the busiest words in French: bees, needles, curiosity and wounded pride all piquent, and the slang sense “to steal” — snatching something with one quick jab — was already in use by the late Middle Ages. The family is everywhere: ~pique~ the weapon (and the card suit French calls by that name), ~piquant~, ~piqûre~, ~piquet~. The most charming member is ~pique-nique~, attested by 1694, from ~piquer~ in the sense “to pick at food” plus ~nique~ (“a little thing of no value”). English borrowed it as ~picnic~, tied the word firmly to eating outdoors, and nineteenth-century French then took that fashion back from English — a word that went on a picnic and came home changed. English ~pique~, the sting of wounded pride, is the same French prick in genteel dress.
en.pirater: Formed from the noun ~pirate~ and the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to act as N.” The noun ~pirate~ was borrowed from Latin ~pirata~, itself taken from Greek ~peiratēs~ (“brigand, sea-raider”). The verb first meant “to practice piracy,” then was applied by analogy to illegally copying software, music or films, and to breaking into computer systems. The figurative sense treats the copier as a sea-robber who takes what belongs to others.
en.pister: Formed from the noun ~piste~ (“track, trail”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to follow a trail,” and then “to tail someone.” The noun was borrowed from Italian ~pista~. French Wiktionary derives that word from the verb ~pistare~ (“to trample, to crush”), from Latin ~pistare~ (“to pound”), the sense still heard in Italian ~pistone~ (“pestle”). English Wiktionary instead treats ~pista~ as a variant of ~pesta~ (“footprint”). Both accounts agree on the picture: a track is what feet leave behind.
en.piéger: ~Piéger~ is formed on the noun ~piège~ (“trap, snare”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and it is already recorded in Old French as ~piegier~, so it is no recent coinage. The noun comes from Latin ~pedica~ (“fetter for the feet, snare”), derived from ~pēs~, ~pedis~ (“foot”): a trap was, at root, something that catches the foot. From “to set a trap for” the verb extended to “to catch in a trap” and, figuratively, “to trick”. Today it also means to booby-trap a car or a parcel. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.placer:
A denominal verb of the 16th century, ~placer~ was formed from the noun ~place~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun ~place~ comes from Old French ~place~, from Vulgar Latin *~plattĕa~, an altered form of Latin ~platēa~ (“a broad street, an open space”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~πλατεῖα~ (~plateîa~, “broad,” in ~plateîa hodós~, “a broad way”). The Greek adjective rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleth₂-~ (“flat, broad, to spread”). Through that root ~place~ is cousin to Italian ~piazza~ and Spanish ~plaza~, and to English ~place~ and ~flat~.

The journey of meaning runs from “a wide road” to “an open square in a town” to, more abstractly, “a spot, a position, a rank.” Once the noun could name any position whatever, French speakers naturally coined a verb for putting something into its position — and so, around 1564, ~placer~ appeared, meaning “to set in a place, to seat.” From the same broad-and-flat root *~pleth₂-~ French gathered ~plat~, ~plateau~, ~platane~ (the plane tree, named for its wide leaves), ~plaine~, and ~aplatir~, while ~place~ itself spun off ~placement~, ~remplacer~, and ~déplacer~.
en.plafonner: Formed in French from ~plafond~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~plafond~ is itself a compound of ~plat~ (“flat”) and ~fond~ (“bottom”), so it first meant a flat surface seen as the bottom of a structure, then a ceiling. The verb originally meant “to fit with a ceiling.” Later it took on a figurative sense, “to reach a ceiling”: of prices, wages or performance, to rise to a limit and go no higher, and hence to cap something at a fixed maximum.
en.plaider: The two Wiktionaries differ slightly on the route. French Wiktionary treats ~plaider~ as a verb formed on the old noun ~plaid~ (“lawsuit, hearing”), while English Wiktionary traces Old French ~plaidier~ from ~plait~, possibly matching a Vulgar Latin verb. Both lead to Latin ~placitum~ (“what pleases”), from ~placēre~ (“to please”), the source of French ~plaire~. In medieval legal Latin that word came to mean a decision, then an appearance before a court, then a lawsuit, and medieval Latin also had a verb ~placitare~ with the sense “to plead”. Courts still say ~plaise à la cour~. English ~plead~ is cognate. The ~plaid~ of Scottish cloth is an unrelated homonym.
en.plaindre:
From Old French ~plaindre~, from Latin ~plangere~ (“to beat, to strike; to beat the breast in grief; to lament”), from Proto-Italic *~plāngō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₂g-~ (“to strike”). The root's striking sense survives in cognates: Latin ~plectere~ (“to beat, punish”), Ancient Greek ~πλήσσω~ (“I strike”), and Old Church Slavonic ~plakati~ (“to weep, beat the breast”).

The memorable detail lies in the root itself: ~plangere~ named the physical gesture of mourning — striking one's own breast — from which the sense of lamenting grew. The Romance descendants split the inheritance: Italian ~piangere~ and Spanish ~plañir~ kept the weeping sense, while French shifted the active verb toward feeling sorrow for another, “to pity,” reserving the reflexive ~se plaindre~ for “to complain.” From the same root come ~plainte~ (“complaint, lament”), ~plaintif~ (“plaintive”), and the legal ~plaignant~ (“plaintiff”). Behind the courtroom complaint and the gentle act of pity alike stands one ancient image: a hand beating against the chest.
en.plaire:
Modern French ~plaire~ comes, through Old French, from Latin ~placēre~ (“to please, to be agreeable, to satisfy”). In Old French the infinitive was long ~plaisir~ (the source of the noun ~plaisir~, “pleasure”), and ~plaire~ is most likely a later analogical reshaping modeled on verbs like ~faire~, working back from forms such as ~il plaît~. The deeper origin is debated: the Latin verb is tied to ~plācāre~ (“to soothe, to appease”), and many trace both to a Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₂k-~ (“flat, to be calm”); De Vaan instead reconstructs *~pleHk-~ (“to please, to permit”), with secure cognates only in Tocharian ~plāk-~ (“to please, to agree”). Romance kept the verb alive everywhere: Italian ~piacere~ and Spanish ~placer~ are its siblings, and English borrowed the family as ~please~ and ~pleasure~.

From the start the sense was “to give satisfaction,” and it never strayed far. A striking trace is the fossilized impersonal ~plaît-il ?~ (“pardon?”) and the courteous ~s'il vous plaît~ (“if it pleases you,” i.e. “please”), where the verb survives in a frozen subjunctive-flavored politeness formula. The same Latin stock seeded a wide family in French: ~plaisir~, ~complaire~ and ~déplaire~, the adjective ~plaisant~, ~complaisant~, and ~placide~ (“placid, calm,” straight from ~plācidus~). Through Latin ~plācāre~ French also gained the learned apaiser's cousin ~placation~ and the verb ~placer~ in its rarer sense. Few verbs so thoroughly stayed put: ~plaire~ has meant essentially the same thing for two thousand years.
en.plaisanter: Formed from ~plaisant~ (“pleasing, amusing”) + ~-er~, “to speak or act in an amusing way.” It is first attested in Middle French, in the sense of “to jest.” The base ~plaisant~ is the present participle of ~plaire~ (“to please”), which comes from Latin ~placēre~. The verb gradually replaced Old French ~gaber~ (“to mock, to joke”), which has since vanished from the language. The sense has remained stable since, from light teasing to saying something not meant seriously.
en.plancher: Formed from the noun ~planche~ and the verb ending ~-er~; the Old French verb ~planchier~ is recorded around 1135. The noun ~planche~ comes from Vulgar Latin ~planca~, a contracted form of *~palanca~, from Greek ~phálanx~ (“log, stout stick”), the same word that gave ~phalange~. The verb first meant “to lay a floor of boards.” The modern sense, “to work hard on a subject, to be quizzed,” is a student slang development from the board of the classroom, and fits the same pattern as ~bûcher~.
