From Latin ~praeparare~ (“to make ready beforehand”), a compound of the prefix ~prae-~ (“before, in advance”) and ~parare~ (“to make ready, to prepare, to furnish”). The verb ~parare~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~perh₃-~ (“to grant, to allot, to provide”), which also yielded Latin ~parere~ (“to give birth, to produce”) and is glimpsed in Ancient Greek ~ἔπορον~ (~époron~, “I furnished”) and Sanskrit ~pṛṇāti~ (“he grants”). Italian ~preparare~ and Spanish ~preparar~ are the sister forms; English borrowed ~prepare~ from the same Latin source.

The kernel is ~parare~, “to get something ready,” and the prefix ~prae-~ simply pulls the readiness ahead in time — to arrange in advance. The bare root ~parare~ survives in French ~parer~, which split into two senses: “to adorn” (to make ready for display) and “to ward off” a blow, the source of ~parade~ and the fencing ~parer~. The same ~parare~ underlies a remarkable spread of French words: ~préparer~, ~réparer~ (“to make ready again,” hence “to repair”), ~séparer~, ~comparer~, ~emparer~, and ~appareil~ — and, through the related ~imperare~, the imperial vocabulary of ~empereur~ and ~empire~.
en.présenter:
From Old French ~presenter~, from Latin ~praesentāre~ (“to place before, to show”), a verb formed on the adjective ~praesēns~ (“present, at hand”). That adjective is itself the present participle of ~praeesse~ (“to be before, to be at the head of”), built from ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”) and ~esse~ (“to be”). The deep root is therefore the Proto-Indo-European verb of being, *~h₁es-~ (“to be”), the same root that gives Latin ~est~ and English ~is~. Cognate verbs survive across the Romance languages, among them Italian ~presentare~ and Spanish ~presentar~, and the family passed into English as ~present~.

The literal image behind ~praesentāre~ is spatial: to make something ~praesēns~ is to set it physically “before” someone, in front of their eyes. From “to place before” the verb naturally acquired the senses of showing, offering, and introducing, and French ~présenter~ still carries all of these — one presents a gift, a person, or an argument. The same adjective ~praesēns~ gave French the noun and adjective ~présent~, covering both “the present moment” and “a present, a gift,” the latter through the old idea of something placed before a recipient. From the prefix ~prae-~ and this same field come many related French words, including ~présence~, ~présentation~, and ~représenter~ (“to represent, to perform again”).
en.préserver:
From Latin ~praeservare~ (“to guard beforehand, keep safe in advance”), formed on ~prae-~ (“before, in advance”) plus ~servare~ (“to keep, guard, watch over, save”). Latin ~servare~ goes back through Proto-Italic to a Proto-Indo-European root *~ser-~ (“to protect, watch over”), with a likely cognate in Avestan ~haraiti~ (“heeds, protects”). The verb is matched by Italian ~preservare~ and Spanish ~preservar~, and English borrowed it as ~preserve~.

The prefix ~prae-~ carries the whole nuance: not merely to keep, but to keep something ahead of harm — to shield it in advance from a danger. Latin ~servare~ should not be confused with its near-homophone ~servire~ (“to serve,” from ~servus~, “slave”); they are distinct roots that French keeps apart. From ~servare~ French inherits and borrows a guarding family: ~conserver~ (“to keep, conserve”), ~observer~ (originally “to watch over, attend to”), ~réserver~ (“to keep back”), and ~préservatif~, which means a protective agent in general but, in everyday French, a condom — a “preserver” in the most literal sense.
en.présider:
From Latin ~praesidere~ (“to sit before, to preside over, to guard”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~sedere~ (“to sit”). ~Sedere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~sedēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”) — one of the great Indo-European roots, cognate with English ~sit~ and ~settle~, German ~sitzen~, and Sanskrit ~sī́dati~ (“sits”).

The image is concrete: the one who presides is literally the one who sits before the assembly, at its head. From this seat of precedence grew the senses of guarding, directing, and chairing a body — to ~présider~ a meeting, a court, a republic. French built a whole institutional vocabulary on the verb: ~président~, ~présidence~, ~présidentiel~, alongside ~coprésider~ and ~vice-présider~. The same root *~sed-~ runs through ~séant~, ~siège~, ~résider~, and ~asseoir~. Beneath the dignity of high office lies a humble physical fact — to preside is to take the foremost seat.
en.présumer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~praesūmere~, a compound of ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~sūmere~ (“to take”): literally “to take beforehand.” The same Latin verb gave English ~presume~, Italian ~presumere~ and Spanish ~presumir~, and the Spanish verb has drifted furthest, since it now usually means “to boast.” Its Latin parent ~sūmere~ also sits inside a whole family of French verbs built on prefixes, such as ~assumer~, ~résumer~ and ~consumer~.

The path from “take beforehand” to “suppose” is short: to take something before it has been proved is to take it for granted. French kept both the neutral sense of “assuming” and a more pointed one, since ~présumer de ses forces~ means to overestimate one's strength, as if one had credited oneself in advance with more than one possessed. The noun ~présomption~ shows the same split. In law, it is a conclusion the court draws from known facts, as in ~présomption d'innocence~, while in everyday speech it is overconfidence, and the adjective ~présomptueux~ describes someone who takes too much for granted about himself. The verb is a good reminder that a ~présumé~ fact is only a fact accepted ahead of its proof.
en.prétendre:
From Latin ~praetendere~ (“to stretch forth, hold out before, allege as a pretext”), formed from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). ~Tendere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~tendō~ and, with a ~d~-extension, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch, draw out”). The kinship reaches far: Ancient Greek ~τείνω~ (~teínō~), Sanskrit ~तनोति~ (~tanóti~), and, through Germanic, English ~thin~ — all stretchings of one ancient thread. French took the verb in the 14th century.

The metaphor at the heart of ~prétendre~ is striking: to hold something stretched out before you, like a screen or a banner. From that came “to put forward as a claim” — to claim a right, to allege a fact, to pretend to (aspire to) a throne or a hand in marriage. English ~pretend~ drifted toward “feign,” but French keeps the older sense of asserting and aspiring; a ~prétendant~ is a suitor or a claimant to power. The *~ten-~ family is vast in French: ~tendre~, ~tension~, ~tente~, ~étendre~, ~intention~, ~attendre~, and ~prétention~ — every one of them, at root, a stretching.
en.prévaloir: A learned borrowing from Latin ~praevalēre~ (“to have greater strength, to be more powerful”), made of ~prae-~ (“before, beyond”) and ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”). French already had ~valoir~, the inherited descendant of that same Latin verb, so ~pré-~ + ~valoir~ is a fair surface reading, but the Latin compound came first. The verb means to hold the upper hand, as an argument or a right does over another. It conjugates like ~valoir~ with one telltale exception, the subjunctive ~prévale~ rather than ~prévaille~. English ~prevail~ comes from the same Latin verb, and ~valid~ and ~value~ come from ~valēre~.
en.prévenir:
From Latin ~praevenire~ (“to come before, anticipate, forestall”), a compound of the prefix ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”) and ~venire~ (“to come”). The verb ~venire~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, go, step”), the same root that, through Germanic, yields English ~come~, and that in Greek gives ~bainō~ (“I go”) and in Sanskrit ~gam-~. Italian ~prevenire~ and Spanish ~prevenir~ are its Romance siblings.

The literal “to come before” spread into several modern meanings that still circle anticipation. To ~prévenir~ can mean to warn or notify someone in advance (~prévenir un ami~), to prevent or forestall something (~prévenir une maladie~ — hence the proverb ~mieux vaut prévenir que guérir~, “prevention is better than cure”), or, in older usage, to favorably or unfavorably predispose someone, surviving in the adjective ~prévenu~ (“biased,” and in law “the accused”). The same ~venire~ powers a huge French family: ~venir~, ~devenir~, ~revenir~, ~convenir~, ~parvenir~, ~survenir~, ~avenir~ (“future,” what is “to come”), and ~événement~. To warn a friend, in this light, is simply to arrive ahead of the trouble.
en.prévoir:
From Latin ~praevidere~ (« to see beforehand, to foresee »), formed from ~prae-~ (« before, in front ») and ~videre~ (« to see »). ~videre~ descends through Proto-Italic *~widēō~ from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”) — a root whose sense slid from seeing to knowing. Through it ~prévoir~ is cognate with English ~wit~, ~wise~, and ~witness~, with German ~wissen~ (“to know”), and, by way of Greek, with ~idea~.

Latin already used ~praevidere~ both literally, « to catch sight of in the distance », and figuratively, « to anticipate ». French inherited only the figurative core: to ~prévoir~ is to see with the mind's eye what has not yet happened. The verb conjugates like ~voir~ except in the future and conditional, where it keeps a regular ~prévoirai~ rather than the irregular ~verrai~ — a small grammatical seam revealing its compound origin. The same root *~weyd-~ underlies a wide French family: ~voir~ itself, ~vision~, ~évident~ (« seen clearly »), ~prévision~, ~prévoyant~, and ~revoir~.
en.prêcher:
Inherited from Old French ~prëechier~, from Latin ~praedicāre~ (“to proclaim in public”), built from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim, to declare”), a verb related to ~dīcere~ (“to say”). The ~d~ between vowels dropped out along the way, which is why Old French ~prëechier~ looks so unlike its source. Regional languages show the spread: Occitan ~predicar~ and Corsican ~predicà~ stay close to the Latin, while Norman ~prêchi~ and Picard ~prêcher~ follow the French pattern. Italian ~predicare~ and Spanish ~predicar~ keep the full Latin shape, and English ~preach~ was borrowed from the Old French verb.

In classical Latin the verb meant to announce something publicly, as a herald does, and also to praise or declare. Christian writers adopted it for proclaiming the Gospel, and that religious sense won out in the Romance languages. French then widened it to any moralizing or advocacy, usually with a faintly ironic edge when the speaker lectures others. The family includes ~prêche~, ~prêcheur~, ~prédicateur~ and ~prédication~, plus the learned ~prédicat~, the grammatical predicate, from the Latin participle for “what is declared” about the subject.
en.prêter:
French ~prêter~ comes through Old French ~prester~ from Latin ~praestare~ (“to stand before, to be at hand, to furnish, to provide”). The verb is ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) plus ~stāre~ (“to stand”), and so reaches the deep Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — making ~prêter~ a distant cousin of ~résister~, ~rester~, and ~stable~. The circumflex in ~prêter~ is a tombstone for a lost ~s~: it marks where the ~s~ of ~prester~ fell silent. Italian ~prestare~ and Spanish ~prestar~ carry the same Latin verb.

The sense-shift is a small drama of generosity. Latin ~praestare~ literally meant “to stand before,” hence “to stand surety, to make good, to supply” — to have something ready ~prae manu~, “at hand.” That readiness is preserved in the adjective ~prêt~ (“ready”), an etymological sibling of the verb. From “to furnish what is ready” the Romance languages narrowed to “to lend,” and French ~prêter~ now means putting something at another's disposal on the promise of return — money, a book, even, figuratively, ~prêter l'oreille~ (“to lend an ear”) or ~prêter serment~ (“to take an oath”). The same root supplies ~prêt~ (“a loan”), ~emprunter~'s partner in finance, and the learned ~prestation~ (“a service rendered, a benefit”).
en.prôner: Formed in French from ~prône~ + ~-er~, “to give the prône,” the Sunday sermon, and from there “to preach, to extol.” The noun has an odd history. Old French ~prosne~ named the grating that separated the nave from the choir, in front of which the priest stood to speak, and the word then passed to the sermon itself. It goes back through Vulgar Latin *~protinum~ and Latin ~prothyra~ to Greek ~próthura~ (“vestibule”), from ~pro-~ (“before”) and ~thura~ (“door”), a cousin of English ~door~. A word for the porch of a house thus ended as a verb for praising something insistently.
en.publier:
From Latin ~pūblicāre~ (“to make public, to bring before the people”), a verb derived from the adjective ~pūblicus~ (“public, belonging to the people”), itself ultimately from ~populus~ (“the people, the populace”). The adjective's form was likely colored by ~pūbēs~ (“adult, grown men”), but its core is the people, ~populus~. Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~pubblicare~ and Spanish ~publicar~; English ~publish~ came through Old French ~publier~ with its characteristic ~-sh~.

To ~pūblicāre~ originally meant to make something the property of the people — including, harshly, to confiscate private goods for the state. From this “to make common/open” the dominant sense narrowed to “to announce openly, proclaim,” and then, with the printing press, to “bring out in print, issue a book.” French ~publier~ now serves both the everyday “to publish” and the formal proclaiming of banns or laws. From ~populus~ and ~pūblicus~ descend a broad family in French: ~public~, ~publication~, ~publicité~, ~république~ (~rēs pūblica~, “the public thing”), ~peuple~, ~populaire~, and ~population~.
en.puer:
From Old French ~puir~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~putīre~, a respelled form of Classical Latin ~pūtēre~ (“to stink, to rot”), the infinitive of ~pūteō~. The shift from ~-ēre~ to ~-īre~ is a change of conjugation class, and the Old French infinitive ~puir~ eventually became modern ~puer~. Behind the Latin verb lies the Proto-Indo-European root *~puH-~ (“to rot, to stink”), which also produced Latin ~pūs~ (“pus”) and, through Proto-Germanic, English ~foul~.

French kept the blunt physical sense of the Latin verb: ~puer~ means to give off a foul smell, and the idea easily turns figurative, as in puer l'argent (“to reek of money,” meaning to flaunt one’s wealth). Its present participle became an adjective, ~puant~, which gave the noun ~puanteur~. Scholars took other words of the family straight from Latin, among them ~putride~, ~putréfier~ and ~pus~. The root *~puH-~ thus ties a bad smell, rot and pus into a single family, and English ~foul~ is its Germanic cousin.
en.puiser:
~puiser~ is a French derivative of ~puits~ (“a well”), which in Old French was written ~puis~; the verb means literally “to draw from a well.” ~puits~ itself descends from Latin ~puteus~ (“well, pit, cistern”), a word whose own origin is uncertain — de Vaan suspects it may be a loanword, while an older proposal tied it to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to cut, strike,” imagining the well as a hole struck into the ground. The Latin ~puteus~ also gave Italian ~pozzo~ and Spanish ~pozo~, and, borrowed into Germanic, lies behind English ~pit~.

From the concrete act of lowering a bucket, ~puiser~ broadened into one of the most graceful metaphors in French: one ~puise~ water, but equally one ~puise~ strength from a friendship, inspiration in a memory, or arguments in a book — drawing up something held in a hidden reserve. The same ~puits~ family yields ~épuiser~ (“to exhaust,” literally to draw a well dry, to ~é-~ /“out” + draw until nothing rises), ~inépuisable~ (“inexhaustible”), ~puisard~ (“a soakaway, sump”), and ~puisatier~ (“a well-digger”) — a whole vocabulary organized around the bucket and the deep cool water it brings up.
en.pulvériser: Learned borrowing, in the late sixteenth century, from Late Latin ~pulverizāre~ (“to reduce to powder”), a verb formed on Latin ~pulvis~, ~pulveris~ (“dust, powder”). The same Latin noun reached French by the inherited route as ~poudre~ and ~poussière~, which makes ~pulvériser~ their learned sibling. The sense was physical at first, grinding something into powder, then spray (~pulvériser un liquide~), and finally figurative: to ~pulvériser~ a record is to smash it to dust. English ~pulverize~ has the same Latin source.
en.punir:
From Old French ~punir~, from Latin ~pūnīre~ (earlier ~poenīre~), a verb built on the noun ~poena~ (“penalty, fine, punishment”) with the fourth-conjugation suffix ~-īre~. ~Poena~ was itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ποινή~ (~poinḗ~, “blood-price, recompense, penalty”), from PIE *~kʷoynéh₂~, from the root *~kʷey-~ (“to pay, to atone”). The same root surfaces in Greek ~timḗ~ (“price, honor”) and Avestan ~kaēnā~ (“punishment”). Cognate Romance verbs include Italian ~punire~ and Spanish ~punir~; English ~punish~ came through Old French ~puniss-~, the stem of the present participle.

The core idea was never mere pain but ~payment~ — a penalty exacted to settle a wrong, a debt of vengeance discharged. That accounting sense explains the rich French family around it: ~punition~, ~punitif~, and the legal ~impuni~ / ~impunité~ (“unpunished,” literally “un-paid-for”). Most telling is the noun ~poena~ itself, which entered French twice: learnedly preserved in this verb, but inherited by ordinary speech as ~peine~ (“pain, trouble, sorrow,” and still “penalty” in ~peine de mort~). Through Old French, that same ~poena~ also gave English ~pain~, so that ~peine~ and ~pain~ are doublets — and a French speaker who takes ~la peine~ to do something is, etymologically, paying a penalty for it.
en.purifier: French ~purifier~ is a borrowing from Latin ~pūrificāre~ (“to make pure, to cleanse”), itself built from ~pūrus~ (“pure, clean”) and the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make”). The same pattern, an adjective followed by ~-ficāre~, gave ~justifier~, ~clarifier~ and ~qualifier~. In Latin the verb often had a religious sense, since purification was a matter of ritual. French also has ~pur~ and ~pureté~ from ~pūrus~, and ~épurer~, a related verb that adds the prefix ~é-~.
en.pécher:
French ~pécher~ is inherited from Old French ~pechier~, which comes from Latin ~peccāre~ (“to make a mistake, to sin”). The Latin verb was sound but not religious: it first meant to go wrong or stumble, and Christian writers made it the standard word for sin. The ending ~-ccāre~ became ~-chier~ in Old French, as in other Latin verbs of the same shape. Italian ~peccare~ and Spanish ~pecar~ are its direct cousins, and the Latin noun ~peccātum~ gave ~péché~ (“sin”).

The family is full of learned words. ~Impeccable~ comes from Latin ~impeccābilis~ (“unable to sin”) and weakened from moral perfection to mere faultlessness, as in an ~impeccable~ suit. ~Peccadille~, a small fault, was borrowed from Spanish ~pecadillo~, a diminutive of ~pecado~. A caution is in order: the verb ~pêcher~ (“to fish”) and the fruit tree ~pêcher~ have a circumflex and unrelated origins, since the fishing verb comes from Latin ~piscāri~ (“to fish”). Only the accent keeps ~pécher~ apart from them.
en.pénaliser: Both Wiktionaries describe ~pénaliser~ as a borrowing from English ~penalize~, though French Wiktionary adds that it matches what French could have built from ~pénal~ and the suffix ~-iser~. ~Pénal~ comes from Latin ~poenālis~, from ~poena~ (“punishment”), which also gave ~peine~. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, and means “to make” or “to subject to.” To ~pénaliser~ is therefore to subject someone to a penalty, whether a legal sanction, a sporting foul or a disadvantage.
en.pénétrer:
From Latin ~penetrāre~ (“to enter, to pierce, to penetrate”), first attested in French around 1314. The verb was built within Latin itself from ~penitus~ (“deeply, inwardly”) and the family of ~penes~ (“within, in the house of”), shaped by analogy with ~intrō~ (“to enter”). The underlying idea is one of the innermost recess of a dwelling — the ~penus~, the household store kept deep inside. Cognate Romance forms descend in parallel: Italian ~penetrare~, Spanish ~penetrar~, Portuguese ~penetrar~. English ~penetrate~ was borrowed from the same Latin source by way of French.

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: to pass into the interior of something, whether a forest, a wall, or a mystery. From the literal “to enter” grew the figurative “to grasp,” so that one can ~pénétrer~ a secret or a person’s intentions, and a person can be pénétré (“filled, imbued”) with an emotion. Modern French keeps a small family from the root, including ~pénétration~, ~pénétrant~ and ~impénétrable~. The shared image throughout is depth — reaching the part of a thing that lies furthest within.
en.pérenniser:
Formed in French from the Latin adjective ~perennis~ and the verb ending ~-er~. Latin ~perennis~ is built from ~per~ (“through”) and ~annus~ (“year”), so it first meant “lasting through the years”, and from there “lasting, unceasing”. The same adjective gave English ~perennial~, and its second element ~annus~ is the source of French ~an~ and ~année~.

The verb takes the Latin idea of lasting through the years and makes it active: to ~pérenniser~ something is to make it durable, to give it a future. It sits among a family of words around ~annus~, including ~annuel~, ~anniversaire~ and ~annuaire~, while the adjective ~pérenne~ and the noun ~pérennité~ come straight from ~perennis~ and ~perennitas~. The “perennial” plant of the garden is the same word again, a plant that lasts year after year.
en.périr:
From Old French ~perir~, passed on through Middle French ~perir~, from Latin ~perīre~ (“to perish, to be lost”). Latin ~perīre~ is a compound of the preposition and prefix ~per-~ (“through”) and the verb ~īre~ (“to go”), so it literally means “to go through,” which can be read as going all the way to the end, and hence to ruin. Latin ~īre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ei-~ (“to go”). Italian ~perire~ is a close cousin. English ~perish~ is itself a French loan, built on the stem ~periss-~ of the Old French verb.

The literal picture of a journey that ends in loss turned ~perīre~ into a Latin word for dying, being destroyed or going to waste, and French kept that range, from people who ~périssent~ at sea to empires and ideas that come to nothing. The same family gave ~périssable~ (“that can spoil”) and ~impérissable~ (“undying”). The simple verb ~īre~ left no infinitive in French, since ~aller~ replaced it, but its stem lives on in learned words such as ~transit~ and ~itinéraire~, and in the stem of the future ~irai~.
en.péter: Formed in French from the noun ~pet~ (“fart”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is inherited from Old French ~pet~, from Latin ~pēditum~ (“a fart”). The verb is therefore literally “to let off a ~pet~”, and its everyday and vulgar register comes with it. By extension ~péter~ took the sense of a sudden sharp noise and then of bursting or breaking: a tire ~pète~, a cable ~pète~, and ~péter les plombs~ is to snap.
en.pétrir:
From Old French ~pestrir~, which comes from a Late Latin form *~pistrīre~, reconstructed rather than attested. English Wiktionary calls it a derivative of Latin ~pistor~ (“baker”); French Wiktionary names instead the feminine ~pistrix~ (“woman baker”) as the base. French ~pétrin~ (“kneading trough”) comes from Latin ~pistrīnum~, so the two words belong to one family. The ~-ir~ ending of ~pétrir~ is therefore inherited from Latin, not added in French to an adjective. The verb has no earlier French base; only the Late Latin form stands behind it.

The ~s~ of ~pestrir~ later fell silent and left an accent behind, as in ~être~ from ~estre~, which gave the modern ~pétrir~. The meaning spread from dough to other soft materials that hands can shape, and then to figurative use: one speaks of someone ~pétri~ d'orgueil or ~pétri~ de talent. ~Pétrin~ gave the familiar idiom ~être dans le pétrin~ (“to be in a fix”), and the family also includes ~pétrissage~, the act of kneading.
en.pêcher:
From Old French ~peschier~ (also spelled ~peskier~), inherited from Latin ~piscārī~ (“to fish”), a verb built on ~piscis~ (“fish”). French Wiktionary adds that in popular Latin the verb became an ordinary active verb, *~piscare~. Latin ~piscis~ has a Germanic cousin in English ~fish~ and German ~Fisch~, from the same Indo-European word for the animal.

The Latin verb was a deponent, one that took passive endings with an active meaning, and popular Latin regularized it into *~piscare~, which is the form French descends from. From the same family come ~pêche~ (“fishing”), ~pêcheur~, ~poisson~ and the learned words ~piscine~ and ~pisciculture~. Beware the homograph ~pêcher~ (“peach tree”), which comes from an entirely different Latin source.
en.qualifier:
From Medieval Latin ~qualificare~, a compound of Latin ~qualis~ (“of what kind, of what sort”) and the verb ~facere~ (“to make”), via the suffix ~-ficare~ — literally “to make of a certain kind.” ~qualis~ derives from the PIE interrogative-relative stem *~kʷo-~, the same pronoun base that lies behind “who” and “which.” The abstract noun ~qualitas~ was famously coined by Cicero as a calque of Greek ~ποιότης~ (“quality”), itself minted by Plato from ~ποῖος~ (“of what nature”). Cognate with Italian ~qualificare~, Spanish ~calificar~, and English ~qualify~.

The original sense was to attribute a quality to something — to say what kind of thing it is. From there ~qualifier~ branched in two directions: grammatically, an adjective ~qualifie~ a noun by describing it; and socially and legally, to ~qualifier~ became to give a title or designation, then to deem someone fit, competent, “qualified.” The sporting sense — a team that ~se qualifie~ for the next round — is a modern extension of that “proving fit” idea. From the same ~qualis~ root spring ~qualité~, ~qualitatif~, and the interrogative ~quel~ itself; the ~-ficare~ ending, meanwhile, recurs across a whole regiment of French verbs such as ~modifier~, ~vérifier~, and ~simplifier~, each one a small act of “making.”
en.quantifier: French ~quantifier~ is a modern borrowing from English ~quantify~, which in turn was built on Latin ~quantus~ (“how much”) and the verb-forming element ~-ficare~ (from ~facere~, “to make”). To ~quantifier~ is thus “to make into a quantity,” to express something as a number or a measure. The English verb gave French a convenient word for the technical and scientific vocabulary of measurement, in which French already had the nouns ~quantité~ and ~quantification~ from the same Latin root. The verb is a reminder that English, for much of its learned vocabulary, borrowed from Latin through French and now sometimes lends it back.
en.questionner: ~Questionner~ is formed from ~question~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to put questions to someone. ~Question~ entered Old French in the 12th century as a learned borrowing from Latin ~quaestiō~ (“a seeking, an inquiry”), from ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask”). Because it was learned, it kept its ~s~ before a consonant, unlike the popular word ~quête~ from the same root. In older French, ~question~ also named judicial interrogation under torture, and ~questionner~ could mean to subject someone to it, before the verb settled on its mild modern sense.
en.quitter:
Modern French ~quitter~ is a verb built from the adjective ~quitte~ (“free of an obligation, even, discharged”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. ~Quitte~ descends from Latin ~quietus~ (“at rest, calm, undisturbed”), the perfect participle of ~quiēscere~ (“to repose”), from the noun ~quies~ (“rest”), all from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷyeh₁-~ (“to rest”). The very same Latin ~quietus~ gives French the doublet ~quiet~ (“calm”) and, through a popular variant ~quētus~, the archaic ~coi~ (“still, hushed”); English ~quiet~, ~quit~, and ~coy~ are cognate, the last borrowed from Old French ~coi~.

The semantic thread runs from “rest” to “release.” In medieval law a person who was ~quitte~ had been left “at peace,” freed from a debt or duty; to ~quitter~ someone was therefore to discharge them, to acquit them of what they owed — a sense still alive in “~quitter~ quelqu'un d'une dette.” From “to release” the verb slid to “to let go of, to part from,” and finally to the everyday “to leave.” The same root produced ~acquitter~, ~quittance~ (“a receipt”), and ~quiétude~, and is buried in English ~acquit~ and ~requite~. A fitting irony hides in the chain: a verb that now means restless departure, “to leave,” was born from a word meaning perfect tranquillity.
en.rabattre: Formed in French from ~battre~ and a prefix, though the sources analyse it differently. English Wiktionary sees ~re-~ added to ~abattre~, while French Wiktionary describes a compound of ~ra-~ and ~battre~; ~ra-~ is an old variant of ~re-~, so the two accounts differ more in bookkeeping than in meaning. Either way the core is ~battre~, from Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, to strike”), probably borrowed from Gaulish. The prefix ~re-~ adds a sense of return or repetition, so the verb meant roughly “to beat down again,” and from there “to fold down, to lower, to reduce, to deduct,” the range of senses it still has.
en.raccorder: Formed in French from ~accorder~ with the prefix ~r-~, a variant of ~re-~ used before a vowel. The base ~accorder~ comes from Late Latin ~accordare~, built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~cor~, ~cordis~ (“heart”): literally “to bring hearts together.” Here the prefix has the sense of joining again or joining up, so ~raccorder~ means to connect two parts so that they fit, whether pipes, roads or the edges of a piece of wallpaper. The image of agreement in ~accorder~ carries over: what is joined must match.
en.raccrocher: Formed from ~accrocher~ and the prefix ~re-~, which loses its vowel and appears as ~r-~ before the initial ~a~ of the base. The base verb is built on ~croc~ (“hook”), a Frankish borrowing cognate with English ~crook~, so the idea is “to put on a hook.” With the prefix, ~raccrocher~ means to hang back up or hang again, then to hang up a telephone receiver, and by extension to catch hold again. The prefix repeats or returns the action, as in many other French verbs. The figurative uses are many: ~raccrocher~ is also to give up a profession, especially in sport, as when an athlete “hangs up” the gloves or the boots.
en.racheter:
~racheter~ is transparently ~r-~ (from Latin ~re-~, “again, back”) prefixed to ~acheter~ (“to buy”), and the interest lies in ~acheter~ itself. That verb comes from Old French ~achater~, from Vulgar Latin *~accaptāre~, a reinforcement with ~ad-~ of ~captāre~ (“to try to seize, to grab at”), the frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take”), from PIE *~kh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). The Romance cognates are everyday verbs: Italian ~accattare~ and, more distantly, Spanish reflexes of the same family. So “to buy” in French is literally “to seek to seize toward oneself.”

The prefix turns acquisition into re-acquisition, and ~racheter~ spans a remarkable range: to buy back what one sold, to buy someone out, to ransom a captive, and — in the theological register — to redeem. That last sense gave ~rachat~ (“redemption, buyout”) and rédempteur's near-synonym in everyday speech. Through ~capere~ the same root reaches a huge family — ~capter~, ~captif~, ~capable~, ~recevoir~ — and even, by other routes, English ~catch~ and ~chase~. A note of caution: some hold that *~accaptāre~ was reshaped from Latin ~acceptāre~; the sources present this as a possibility, not a settled fact.
en.raciner: Formed from the noun ~racine~ (“root”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to take root.” The noun is inherited from Late Latin ~radīcīna~, a diminutive-like form built on Latin ~rādīx~ (“root”) with the suffix ~-īna~. Latin ~rādīx~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European form usually reconstructed as *~wréh₂ds~. The verb is rare today, while its prefixed relatives ~enraciner~ and ~déraciner~, built on the same noun, are common.
en.raconter:
From Old French ~raconter~ (attested c. 1130–40), formed with the prefix ~re-~ on ~aconter~, itself ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~) plus ~conter~ (“to tell, to count”). ~Conter~ descends from Latin ~computare~ (“to calculate, to reckon”), a compound of ~com-~ and ~putare~ (“to reckon, to estimate”). The very same Latin verb gave French its doublet ~compter~ (“to count”), so ~conter~ and ~compter~ are etymological twins, split apart by spelling and sense. Cognates include Spanish ~contar~ and Italian ~contare~, which likewise mean both “to count” and “to tell,” and English ~count~ and ~compute~.

The semantic thread is the link between enumerating and narrating: to “tell” a tale was once to “count off” its events one by one — English preserves the same metaphor in a bank ~teller~, who tells out money. ~Raconter~ adds an intensifying ~re-~ to ~aconter~, yielding “to recount, to relate in full.” Over time ~conter~ specialized toward fiction (a ~conte~ is a tale or fairy story), while ~raconter~ became the everyday verb for telling what happened. From the same ~computare~ flow ~compte~, ~comptable~, ~conte~, ~conteur~, and the learned ~computer~ (“to compute”).
en.raffiner: Formed in French from ~affiner~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base ~affiner~ is itself built in one step from ~a-~ plus the adjective ~fin~ plus ~-er~, “to make fine or pure,” and ~fin~ goes back to Latin ~fīnis~ (“limit, end”), whose sense shifted from “utmost point” to “perfect, delicate.” The prefix ~re-~ here works as an intensifier more than as a strict “again”: ~raffiner~ means to purify or polish further, whether sugar or oil, or manners and taste.
en.raisonner: Formed from the noun ~raison~ with the suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to act or speak with N”: to use reason. In Old French the verb was ~raisnier~ and meant simply “to speak”, so talking and reasoning were one activity. The noun comes from Latin ~ratio~, accusative ~rationem~ (“reckoning, calculation, reasoning”), and ~ration~ is its learned doublet, which is why ~rationner~ is a close parallel. From “to speak” the verb moved to “to argue” and then to “to think logically”.
en.rajeunir: The verb is a French formation from ~ra-~, the adjective ~jeune~ and the verb ending ~-ir~. French Wiktionary treats ~ra-~ as a single prefix, while English Wiktionary reads it as ~r-~ plus ~a-~. The adjective ~jeune~ comes from Latin ~iuvenis~ (“young”). The pattern is the deadjectival ~-ir~ meaning “to become or make A,” here “to become young again” and, with an object, “to make younger.” Old French had its own shorter verb ~jeunir~ and the prefixed ~ajovenir~, so ~rajeunir~ is a later formation.
en.rajouter:
Compound of the prefix ~re-~ and ~ajouter~ (“to add”). ~Ajouter~ comes from Old French ~ajoster~ (“to bring together, place side by side”), built on Latin ~juxta~ (“near, beside”) — the same word behind ~juxtaposer~. So to add was originally to set one thing beside another. ~Juxta~ is related to the family of ~jungere~ (“to join”), from Proto-Indo-European *~yewg-~ (“to join, yoke”), cognate with English ~yoke~ and ~join~.

Old French ~ajoster~ meant to assemble or unite; over time it narrowed to the arithmetic and everyday sense “to add, to put in addition.” Prefixing ~re-~ produced ~rajouter~, which adds again, puts back, or tops up — ~rajouter du sel~ is to add yet more salt. The two verbs coexist with a fine distinction much policed by purists: ~ajouter~ for a first addition, ~rajouter~ for a further one, though in speech ~rajouter~ has spread well beyond that rule. The buried root ~juxta~ also yields French ~juxtaposition~ and the borrowed adverb ~juxta~ in scholarly usage, while the deeper *~yewg-~ underlies ~joindre~, ~jonction~, and ~conjuguer~ — the very act of conjugation being a “yoking together” of forms.
en.ralentir:
~Ralentir~ is a French construction with deep Latin roots: ~re-~ + ~alentir~ (“to slow”), itself built in the twelfth century (attested 1180–90) from ~a-~ + ~lent~ + ~-ir~. The adjective ~lent~ descends from Latin ~lentus~, whose range startles: “flexible, pliant,” “sticky, tenacious,” and only by extension “slow,” even “impassive.” Behind it stands a reconstructed *~lentos~ (“flexible”); some compare the Germanic family of German ~lind~ (“gentle”) and English ~lithe~ (“supple”), though the connection is debated. Within Romance the kinship is plain: Italian and Spanish ~lento~ — and, borrowed from Italian, the ~lento~ of musical scores. ~Ralentir~ itself is a Renaissance refit: Ronsard wrote ~rallenter~ in 1552, Montaigne ~ralentir~ in 1588, and the form in ~-ir~ prevailed, gradually pushing its own parent ~alentir~ into the attic of the language.

The buried picture deserves a pause. For a Roman, a willow switch was ~lentus~ because it bent without breaking; pitch and honey were ~lentus~ because they clung; a sluggish or unmoved person was ~lentus~ too. The senses lived side by side — pliant, sticky, slow, phlegmatic — and French ~lent~ kept only the slowness. ~Alentir~ served the Middle Ages; after the Renaissance preferred ~ralentir~, the parent verb sank into archaism, surviving as a literary rarity. The modern family runs from ~lenteur~ and ~lentement~ to two inventions of the machine age: ~ralenti~ — an engine’s idle, and cinema’s slow motion (~au ralenti~) — and ~ralentisseur~, the French speed bump. And the verb itself stands in capitals on every French road: ~RALENTIR~, an everyday imperative built, far upstream, on the suppleness of willows and the patience of honey.
en.rallier: ~Rallier~ is formed from ~allier~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here carries the sense of doing again or gathering back. ~Allier~ descends from Latin ~alligāre~ (“to bind to”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~ligāre~ (“to bind”). To ~rallier~ is thus to bind together again, first of scattered troops called back to their banner, then of people who join a cause or opinion. English ~rally~ was borrowed from the French verb, and the same Latin ~alligāre~ lies behind both the French ~allier~ and English ~ally~.
en.ramener:
A French compound built from ~re-~ (here marking a return to a starting point) and ~amener~ (“to bring, to lead toward”), which itself is ~à~ (“to”) plus ~mener~ (“to lead, to drive”). The verb ~mener~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~minare~ (“to drive animals along, to herd”), a sense derived from Classical Latin ~minārī~ (“to threaten, to brandish”) — the herdsman drove his cattle forward with shouts and threats. Spanish and Italian preserve the same image in ~menar~ and ~menare~.

The path from “threaten” to “lead” runs through the drover: to threaten an ox into motion is to make it go where you wish, and so *~minare~ slid from menacing to simply conducting. French ~mener~ kept the neutral sense “to lead,” and its prefixed forms map out directions of travel: ~amener~ (lead toward), ~emmener~ (lead away), ~promener~ (lead about, hence “to walk, stroll”). With ~re-~ added, ~ramener~ means to bring someone or something back to where it began — and figuratively to restore, to draw back, or, in slang, to ~ramener sa fraise~ (“to butt in”). The same root underlies ~menace~ and ~ménager~.
en.ramer: ~Ramer~ is a denominal verb, formed from the noun ~rame~ (“oar”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~rame~ comes from Latin ~rēmus~ (“oar”) by way of Old French, and Latin ~rēmus~ is also the source of Italian and Spanish ~remo~. French Wiktionary also lists a different ~rame~, from Middle Dutch or Middle High German, and another, a ream of paper, from Arabic through Catalan, but those words are unrelated to the oar. The literal sense is “to propel a boat with oars.” From the hard, repetitive effort of rowing, informal French drew the figurative sense “to toil, to struggle,” and from there, in computing, “to run slowly” of a lagging machine.
en.randonner: Formed on the noun ~randon~ plus the suffix ~-er~; English Wiktionary describes it instead as coming from Middle French ~randonner~ and Old French ~randonner~ (“to run headlong”). The noun ~randon~ is a derivative of Old French ~randir~ (“to run”), from Old Frankish *~rand~ (“a course, running”), from Proto-Germanic *~randijō~. The headlong gallop gave English ~random~, which shares this ancestry, and French ~randonner~ eventually softened to a long, leisurely walk. French Wiktionary adds that modern ~randon~ may also be a re-Frenchifying of English ~random~, so the word crossed the Channel twice.
en.ranger:
~Ranger~ is derived from the noun ~rang~ (“rank, row”), from Old French ~renc~, from Old Frankish *~hring~ (“circle, ring”), a Germanic word cognate with English ~ring~ and German ~Ring~. To ~ranger~ is thus to put things into a ~rang~ — into their row or rank.

The Germanic origin hides a small surprise: the ancestor *~hring~ meant a circle, not a straight line. Warriors and assemblies once stood in a ring, and the sense of an ordered line of people — a ~rang~ — grew out of that circular formation before flattening into the modern row. From ~rang~ French built a whole household vocabulary of putting-in-order: ~ranger~ (“to tidy, arrange, put away”), ~rangée~ (“a row”), ~rangement~ (“storage, tidying”), ~rangé~ (said of a steady, orderly person), and the prefixed ~arranger~ and ~déranger~ — literally to bring into, or knock out of, the row. To ~déranger~ someone is, at root, to break the tidy ring of their arrangement. The English word ~range~ belongs to the very same family, borrowed back from this French stock.
en.rapatrier:
French ~rapatrier~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~repatriāre~ (“to return to one's country”), built on ~re-~ (“back”) and Latin ~patria~ (“fatherland”), from ~pater~ (“father”). French replaced the Latin prefix ~re-~ with ~ra-~, giving ~rapatrier~ in place of a more regular ~repatrier~. It is a doublet of the Old French verb ~repairer~ (“to return home”), which descended from the same Latin verb by the normal sound changes, whereas ~rapatrier~ was taken in later by scholars. English ~repair~, as in “to repair to a place,” comes from that older French verb, and is thus an unexpected cousin.

The idea of returning to the ~patria~ gave the verb its modern meaning: to send prisoners, refugees or citizens back to their country of origin, and by extension to bring funds back home. The verb also carries a sense “to reconcile.” From the same family come ~patrie~, ~patriote~, ~expatrier~, ~compatriote~ and ~rapatriement~, and ~père~ is the inherited descendant of ~pater~.
en.rappeler:
Built in French from the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”) and the verb ~appeler~ (“to call”). ~Appeler~ descends from Latin ~appellāre~ (“to address, to call by name”), a frequentative-style derivative of ~appellere~, ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~pellere~ (“to push, to drive”), from PIE *~pelh₂-~ (“to approach, to drive”). To call someone was, in the root image, to “drive” your voice toward them. Through Old French ~apeler~, the same Latin verb gave English ~appeal~ and ~appellation~; Romance cousins include Italian ~appellare~ and Spanish ~apelar~.

The literal sense of ~rappeler~ is “to call back”: a general ~rappelle~ his troops, a country ~rappelle~ its ambassador, and one ~rappelle~ a phone caller. From summoning a person back came summoning a thought back — ~rappeler~ now most commonly means “to remind” or, reflexively in ~se rappeler~, “to remember,” literally to call something back into one's own mind. The noun ~rappel~ covers a striking spread of these: a reminder, an encore at a concert, a booster vaccine, a back-payment of wages, and the mountaineer's ~rappel~ (abseiling, “calling oneself back down” the rope). The shared root surfaces across French ~appeler~, ~appel~, ~rappel~, ~interpeller~ (“to call out to, to question”), and the borrowed ~appellation~.
en.rapporter:
Attested from the twelfth century, ~rapporter~ is formed from ~apporter~ (“to bring”) with the prefix ~re-~, marking a bringing back. ~Apporter~ comes from Latin ~apportāre~ (~ad-~ “to” + ~portāre~ “to carry”), and ~portāre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to lead, to pass over, to carry across”). Cognate with Italian ~portare~ and Spanish ~portar~, and — through the same root — with English ~port~, ~portable~, and ~transport~.

The literal core is to carry a thing back to its place, which gives the everyday sense of retrieving or returning. From there the word branched widely: a hunting dog ~rapporte~ the game; a witness ~rapporte~ what was said, hence “to report”; a child who ~rapporte~ on a classmate is a tattletale; and money or land that ~rapporte~ “brings in” a yield — the source of ~rapport~ as “revenue” and, more abstractly, as “relation, connection.” That same carrying root *~per-~ runs through ~porter~, ~apporter~, ~emporter~, ~importer~, ~exporter~, ~port~, and ~portique~ — a whole family built on the simple act of bearing something from one place to another.
en.rapprocher:
A transparent compound of the prefix ~re-~ (here marking repetition and intensification, “again, anew”) and the verb ~approcher~ (“to approach, to bring near”). ~approcher~ itself descends from Late Latin ~appropiāre~ (“to draw near to”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and the adverb ~prope~ (“near”), the same ~prope~ that yields French ~proche~ (“near, close”). The Old French form was ~aprochier~, attested from the twelfth century; English ~approach~ is borrowed from this same Old French verb, so the two languages share the ancestor.

Where ~approcher~ simply brings something near, ~rapprocher~ adds the idea of bringing things near once more or closer together — two people reconciled, two ideas compared, two dates moved nearer. From this comes the rich figurative life of the word: a ~rapprochement~ between former enemies, a diplomatic thaw, is one of the best-known French exports to other languages, English among them. Modern derivatives include the noun ~rapprochement~, the adjective ~rapprochable~, and the military expression ~garde rapprochée~ (“close protection”). At bottom, every use of ~rapprocher~ replays the humble Latin ~prope~: the act of making two things ~proche~ that were not so near before.
en.raser:
French ~raser~ is inherited from Old French ~raser~, which comes from Vulgar Latin *~rāsāre~, a frequentative verb formed on ~rāsus~, the past participle of Latin ~rādō~ (“to shave, to scratch”). A frequentative verb expresses repeated or intensive action. Italian ~rasare~ is a comparable form from the same Latin source. French Wiktionary writes the Latin infinitive as ~rādere~, with the further glosses “to polish” and “to rake.” The chain is short: Latin ~rādō~, its participle ~rāsus~, a Vulgar Latin verb built on that participle, then Old French and modern French. The sources name no other language in this chain, so the word is a plain inheritance from Latin.

In modern French ~raser~ covers three senses glossed for this verb: “to shave,” “to raze,” and “to bore.” The evidence does not say how those senses developed from the Latin sense, so no order of development is claimed here. What the sources do show is the shape of the verb. The stem ~rās-~ of the Latin participle survives in ~raser~, and the ending ~-er~ is the regular French outcome of Latin ~-āre~, as in ~chanter~ from ~cantare~. Because the verb is inherited whole, it has no French base word: ~raser~ was not made by adding ~-er~ to a French noun or adjective.
en.rassembler:
Formed from the verb ~assembler~ (“to assemble, gather”) with the prefix ~re-~, expressing repetition or intensification. ~Assembler~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~assimulāre~ (“to bring together, make alike”), built on ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and a stem related to ~simul~ (“together”) and ~similis~ (“like, similar”). These trace to the PIE root *~sem-~ (“one, together”). Through that root ~rassembler~ is cognate with English ~same~, ~similar~, and ~assemble~ itself, and with Greek ~homós~ (“same”); Italian keeps ~assembrare~. The buried idea is gathering many into a likeness, a oneness.

Where ~assembler~ joins parts together, the ~re-~ of ~rassembler~ adds a sense of pulling scattered things back into one — regathering a dispersed crowd, mustering troops, collecting one's thoughts. Hence its slightly more emphatic, more deliberate ring: ~rassembler ses idées~ (“to collect one's thoughts”), ~rassembler une foule~ (“to gather a crowd”). The political noun ~rassemblement~ (“rally, gathering”) grew from it. The unifying root *~sem-~ runs through a remarkable spread of French: ~sembler~, ~ensemble~, ~assemblée~, ~simple~ (“one-fold”), ~singulier~, and ~simultané~ all descend from the ancient sense of oneness and togetherness that *~sem-~ names.
en.rassurer:
Derived from ~assurer~ with the prefix ~re-~; the verb ~rasseürer~ is attested as early as 1155. The base ~assurer~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~assēcūrāre~, from ~sēcūrus~ (“safe, free from care”), which itself parses as ~sē-~ (“without”) plus ~cūra~ (“care”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷeys-~ (“to heed, observe”). To reassure is thus, at the bottom, to set someone back into a state without care. English ~secure~ and ~sure~, and Spanish ~seguro~, are cognates from the very same Latin source.

The ~re-~ marks restoration: ~assurer~ makes someone confident, ~rassurer~ makes them confident again, calming a fear that had risen. French keeps the “care” at the heart of the family visible in ~sûr~ (sure, safe), ~assurance~ (confidence, and also insurance), ~sécurité~, and ~sécuriser~. There is a quiet etymological irony in the modern insurance industry: ~assurance~ promises freedom from care, yet rests on the careful reckoning of exactly the risks one is paying not to worry about.
en.rater:
Modern French ~rater~ is a denominal verb, coined around 1715 from the noun ~rat~ (“rat”) plus the infinitive ending ~-er~. It grew not directly from the rodent but from the firearm expression ~prendre un rat~, said of a gun that failed to go off: the powder caught but no shot followed. From that misfire, ~rater~ came to mean “to fail to fire,” then simply “to fail” or “to miss.” The noun ~rat~ itself is of obscure, probably imitative Germanic origin, shared with English ~rat~, German ~Ratte~, and Italian ~ratto~.

Why a gun's misfire should be a ~rat~ is itself uncertain, and the sources do not settle it; what is documented is the path from the phrase to the verb. The sense then spread widely: one can ~rater~ a train, an exam, a photograph, or a chance, and a botched thing is ~raté~. From the same noun French also formed mulot-free coinages like ~dératiser~ (“to exterminate rats”) and the noun ~raté~ for an engine's splutter or, of a person, a failure. Few French verbs of such everyday usefulness rest on so homely and so puzzling an image.
en.ratifier:
From Medieval Latin ~ratificāre~, a compound of Latin ~ratus~ (“fixed, established, valid”) and the verb ~facere~ (“to make”), so literally “to make valid”. In compounds ~facere~ took the shape ~-ficāre~, which became French ~-fier~, as in ~vérifier~ and ~modifier~. The adjective ~ratus~ is the past participle of Latin ~rērī~ (“to reckon, to think”): what is ~ratus~ has been reckoned and settled. Italian ~ratificare~ and Spanish ~ratificar~ are parallel forms, and English ~ratify~ is borrowed from the same source.

The verb belongs to the language of law and diplomacy: to ~ratifier~ is to give a finished act its binding force, as when a parliament or a head of state confirms a treaty that envoys have already signed. By extension it came to mean to approve or confirm in general. The root ~rērī~ is fertile. It gave Latin ~ratiō~ (“reckoning, reason”), whence French ~raison~ and ~rationnel~, and English ~rate~, in the sense of a fixed proportion, comes from the same ~ratus~ family. A treaty is thus ratified when it has been, in the Roman sense, reckoned and fixed.
en.rationaliser: Formed from ~rationnel~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make”), with the ending of the base reshaped to ~rational-~. The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~rationalis~ (“endowed with reason”), recorded in French from about 1120 as ~rationel~ and as ~rational~ in 1483. To ~rationaliser~ is to make something rational, whether by explaining it by reason or, in business and administration, by organizing it for efficiency.
en.rattacher:
Derived from ~attacher~ with the iterative prefix ~re-~. The base ~attacher~ comes from Old French ~atachier~, a variant of ~estachier~ (“to fasten, bind”), from ~estache~ (“stake, post”), from Frankish/Gothic *~stakka~ (“stake”). It is therefore a doublet of ~attaquer~ (“to attack”), the two having split from the same Germanic root, and a cognate of English ~attach~ and ~stake~. The literal image is binding something to a post.

The ~re-~ adds the sense of joining back, or joining anew: where ~attacher~ ties a thing on, ~rattacher~ re-ties it or links it to something larger. Modern French stretches this across registers — one can ~rattacher~ a loose page to a binder, a province to a state, a remark to an earlier argument, or, reflexively, a person who feels they belong (se rattacher à une tradition). The Germanic ancestor of the post left a wide family: ~tache~ in some senses, ~attache~ (a fastening, a tie of affection), ~détacher~ (to untie), and the doublet ~attaquer~, which began as a Romance variant of the same fastening verb before veering off into the language of assault.
en.rattraper:
~rattraper~ is a home-grown French formation: ~re-~ (“back, again”) plus ~attraper~ (“to catch”), itself built in the twelfth century from ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad~, “toward”) and ~trappe~ (“trap, snare”). The form ~ratraper~, “to catch again,” already appears around 1280 in Adenet le Roi. ~trappe~ came into Gallo-Romance from Old Low Frankish *~trappa~ (“snare; step”), a Germanic word recorded in medieval Latin as ~trappa~; its cousins are English ~trap~, Dutch ~trap~ (“kick; staircase”) and German ~Treppe~ (“stairs”) — the family seems to join treading and trapping, the snare being something one steps into. So to catch, in French, is etymologically to ensnare: ~rattraper~ is literally “to trap again.”

The meanings unfolded step by step: “catch again” in the Middle Ages, “catch up with” by 1636, “recover, make good” by 1690, and the reflexive ~se rattraper~ — to grab hold, or to make up for a slip — by the nineteenth century. Modern French leans on the verb for every kind of remedial catching-up: a ~rattrapage~ is a make-up exam, a salary adjustment, a recall of defective cars. The trap behind it all had its own adventures: the Germanic word that gave French ~trappe~ also gave English ~trap~, from which North America coined ~trapper~ for the fur hunters of the woods — and in 1827 French borrowed that word back as ~trappeur~. A fitting destiny for a verb of second chances: after centuries away, the language caught its own word again.
en.ravager: From ~ravage~ + ~-er~, “to lay waste.” French Wiktionary treats the verb as formed on the noun ~ravage~ and points to Old French ~revagier~ (“to tear up vine plants”), but it calls that form obscure and suggests it may owe its shape to a change of prefix. The link is therefore only a possibility, and the sources trace the noun no further. What is certain is the modern pattern: a noun of devastation turned into a first-conjugation verb by the ending ~-er~.
en.ravir:
From Popular Latin *~rapīre~, an alteration of Classical Latin ~rapere~ (“to seize, carry off by force”). The Latin verb descends from a PIE root usually reconstructed as *~h₁rep-~ (“to snatch, seize”). The same ~rapere~ gave the learned French doublets ~rapt~ and ~rapide~, while the popular line produced ~ravir~; English borrowed from both branches, taking ~rapid~ and ~rape~ from the Latin and ~ravish~ straight from Old French ~ravir~.

The original violence is plain: to ~ravir~ was to abduct, to plunder, to tear away by force. But French let the sense rise from the body to the soul — to be carried off in rapture, transported by delight — so that the very same verb now means both to kidnap and to enchant. The expression ~à ravir~ (“ravishingly, to perfection”) keeps only the sweetness; ~ravisseur~ (“abductor”) keeps only the menace. From the family come ~ravissement~ (“rapture”), ~ravissant~ (“delightful”), and, through ~rapere~, ~ravage~ and ~rapace~.
en.rayer: Formed from the noun ~raie~ (“line, stripe”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to mark with lines,” hence “to scratch” and “to cross out.” The verb is found in Old French as ~roier~, and ~raie~ comes from Old French ~reye~, a word compared to Welsh ~rica~ and to Late Latin ~riga~. English Wiktionary adds a second possibility, that some forms such as Old French ~raier~ may instead come from Latin ~radiāre~, so the origin is not entirely settled. The most common modern sense is to cancel a word with a stroke, as in ~rayer une mention inutile~.
en.rayonner: Formed from the noun ~rayon~ (“ray”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, in allusion to rays of light or of other kinds. ~Rayon~ itself is built from Old French ~rai~ (“ray”) with the suffix ~-on~. It is a different word from the ~rayon~ meaning “honeycomb” or “shelf”, which comes from a Frankish word through Old French ~ree~, and a third ~rayon~, “furrow”, comes from ~raie~. The verb first meant to shine in rays, and it spread to cheerful faces that radiate joy, to influence that radiates from a centre, and to travelling around a place from a base.
en.rebaptiser: Formed in French from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~baptiser~, so it means “to baptize again.” The base ~baptiser~ goes back to Latin ~baptizāre~, itself from Ancient Greek ~baptízō~ (“to dip, to immerse”), related to ~báptō~ (“to dip”). The verb also took on a lighter sense: to ~rebaptiser~ a street or a company is to give it a new name, as at a christening. The Greek-built ~anabaptiste~ (“one who baptizes again”) names the sixteenth-century movement that rejected infant baptism and rebaptized adults.
en.recadrer:
~recadrer~ is ~re-~ plus ~cadrer~, and ~cadrer~ answers to two masters: the noun ~cadre~ and Latin ~quadrāre~ (“to be square, to fit”). ~cadre~ was borrowed from Italian ~quadro~, from Latin ~quadrum~ (“a square”), from ~quadrus~, from ~quattuor~ (“four”), from Proto-Italic *~kʷettwōr~ and Proto-Indo-European *~kʷetwṓr~ (“four”). Italian ~quadro~ and Spanish ~cuadro~ remain the everyday words for a picture, and the same Latin stem gave English ~quadrant~ and, through a Vulgar Latin *~exquadrāre~, ~square~ itself. ~cadrer~ is attested in French from 1529 in the sense “well-proportioned,” and from 1539 as “to fit exactly” — the sense preserved in ~cela ne cadre pas~.

~cadre~ then went travelling. From “picture frame” it became, in the eighteenth century, the table of posts in a military unit; then the officers who filled those posts; then, in the twentieth century, the salaried manager — ~un cadre~ — of French corporate life. ~cadrer~ followed the concrete sense into the cinema, where it is recorded from 1921 for the framing of a shot, and ~recadrer~ began as the photographer’s word for reframing or cropping an image. It then went abstract twice over: a policy can be ~recadrée~, given a new frame, and so can a person — ~recadrer un employé~ is to call a subordinate back into line. The pleasing consequence is that in a French office one may ~recadrer~ ~un cadre~: re-square a square. The same root supplies ~carré~, ~quatre~, ~quadrilatère~, ~encadrer~ and ~cadrage~.
en.recenser:
From Latin ~recēnsēre~ (“to count again, to review, to survey”), formed from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~cēnsēre~ (“to assess, to give an opinion, to register citizens”). The verb ~cēnsēre~ is the same one that gives ~cēnsus~, the Roman registration of citizens and their property. Its deeper origin is disputed: per De Vaan it perhaps goes back to Proto-Italic *~knsēō~ and to PIE *~ḱens-~ (“to announce, to proclaim”), with a possible cognate in Sanskrit ~śáṃsati~ (“he declares”).

The Roman ~cēnsor~ counted heads and judged morals, and that double sense of “count” and “appraise” runs through the family. French ~recenser~ kept the counting side: to take a census, to make an inventory, to identify and list. From the same Latin stock come ~recensement~ (“census”), ~censeur~, ~censure~, and ~recension~ (a scholarly inventory of manuscript readings). The hedge matters: the leap from *~ḱens-~ “to announce” to “to count” is plausible but not securely proven.
en.recentrer: Formed from ~centrer~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”), so it means to bring back to the centre or to refocus. The base ~centrer~ comes from ~centre~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and ~centre~ from Latin ~centrum~, borrowed from Greek ~κέντρον~ (~kéntron~), a goad or point, and also the fixed leg of a pair of compasses. The Greek word derives from ~kentéō~ (“to prick”). The sense passed from geometry to politics and strategy: to ~recentrer~ a debate or a party is to bring it back to its essentials or to the middle ground.
en.recevoir:
From Old French ~recevoir~, from Latin ~recipere~ (“to take back, to receive”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”). ~capere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, to seize”), through which ~recevoir~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~káptō~ (“to gulp down”) and, on the Germanic side, with English ~have~ and ~heave~ — both, surprisingly, relatives of this Latin verb of taking. The shift from ~recipere~ to French ~recevoir~ follows the regular Latin ~-cipere~ to French ~-cevoir~ pattern.

Latin ~recipere~ meant to take back to oneself, hence to accept what is offered or returned. French kept the core sense of accepting and added social and abstract ones: to ~recevoir~ a guest (to welcome), to ~recevoir~ a blow, to ~recevoir~ a diploma. The root ~capere~ is one of the most fertile in French, surfacing in ~capable~, ~capter~, ~captif~, ~recette~ (a doublet of ~recevoir~'s noun), ~réception~, ~concevoir~, ~décevoir~, ~percevoir~, and ~apercevoir~. The verbs in ~-cevoir~ form a tidy set, all the same Latin ~capere~ taken back, taken up, taken in, or taken away by their prefixes.
en.recharger: ~Recharger~ is formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and the verb ~charger~. ~Charger~ comes from Old French ~chargier~ (“to load, to put in a cart”), attested around 1080, from Late Latin *~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), built on Latin ~carrus~ (“cart”), itself a Gaulish loan. So to ~recharger~ is literally to load again: to refill a weapon, to top up a cartridge, and in the modern age to charge a battery or to reload a page. The sense is plainly repetitive, with nothing fossilized in the prefix.
en.rechercher:
From Old French ~cerchier~ (later Middle French ~chercher~), the source of modern ~chercher~ (“to look for, to search”), with the iterative prefix ~re-~. The base verb descends from Late Latin ~circāre~ (“to go around, to roam in search of”), from ~circa~ (“around”), itself from ~circus~ (“ring, circle”), tied to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, to bend”). The same Latin family gave Spanish ~cercar~ and Italian ~cercare~ (“to look for”), and, through ~circulus~, English ~circle~ and ~circus~.

The path of meaning is geometric at heart: one who searches once “went around” a place, and ~chercher~ originally meant “to roam, to ransack.” In the seventeenth century it displaced the older ~querre~ (which survives as ~quérir~). Prefixed with ~re-~, ~rechercher~ both intensifies and repeats: it can mean “to search thoroughly, to seek out” and “to look for again,” the second loop around the circle. From this productive ~re-~ comes the noun ~recherche~ (“research, inquiry”), borrowed into English as ~research~, and the adjective ~recherché~ (“refined, sought-after”). The underlying *~(s)ker-~ also turns up in ~cercle~, ~cerceau~, and ~recherche~ itself — a whole vocabulary spun from the idea of going round.
en.recommander:
From Old French ~comander~ (“to entrust, to command”), reinforced with the prefix ~re-~, from Late Latin ~commendare~ (a variant of ~commandare~), from ~com-~ (intensive) plus ~mandare~ (“to entrust, to commit to one's charge”). ~mandare~ is itself a compound of ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~dare~ (“to give”), so its literal sense is “to place into someone's hand.” ~manus~ goes back to PIE *~man-~ (“hand”) and ~dare~ to PIE *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~raccomandare~ and Spanish ~recomendar~, and, through ~commendare~, with English ~recommend~ and ~commend~.

The doubled prefix is telling: to ~recommander~ was first to “entrust again” or “entrust earnestly,” and from that idea of warmly committing a person or thing to another's care grew the modern sense of speaking in someone's favor, of endorsing. The military sense of ~commander~ — to give orders — comes from the same root, the commander being the one into whose hand authority is given. The “hand-giving” core of ~mandare~ seeds a wide family in French: ~commander~, ~demander~, ~mander~, ~mandat~, and ~commande~, alongside the learned ~mandataire~. Even English ~mandate~ and ~command~ trace back to that same Latin image of a charge placed, quite literally, in the palm.
en.recommencer:
From ~re-~ (“again”) + ~commencer~ (“to begin”), inherited through Middle French ~commencer~ and Old French ~comencier~ from Vulgar Latin *~cominitiāre~, a compound of ~com-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~initiāre~ (“to begin, initiate”). The latter rests on ~initium~ (“a beginning”), itself from ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”) — so a beginning was once a “going in.” Cognate with Italian ~cominciare~ and Spanish ~comenzar~, and, through the same Old French source, with English ~commence~.

Where ~commencer~ simply marks a first start, ~re-~ adds the idea of doing it once more, so ~recommencer~ is “to begin again.” The buried root ~īre~ (“to go”) runs through a wide French family: ~initial~, ~initier~, ~initiative~, and ~initiation~ all preserve the notion of stepping into something. French has long favoured ~commencer~ over its near-twin ~débuter~, and the prefixed ~recommencer~ remains the ordinary way to say that a thing — a game, a school year, a quarrel — has started over from the top.
en.recomposer: Formed from ~composer~ + the prefix ~re-~, in its sense of “again”: to compose, assemble or put together anew. ~Composer~ is the verb that descends from Latin ~componere~ (~com-~ + ~ponere~, “to put together”), remodeled in French on ~poser~ instead of following the expected ~pondre~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive, so ~recomposer~ can describe rewriting a piece of music or a text, reconstituting a whole from its parts, or reshuffling a political majority.
en.reconduire: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~conduire~, with ~re-~ marking a return to the starting point: to ~reconduire~ someone is to lead them back, to see them to the door or home. ~Conduire~ comes from Latin ~conducere~, a compound of ~con-~ (“together”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to pull, to lead”), the same root as English ~tow~ and ~tug~. A second sense, “to renew,” as in ~reconduire un contrat~, takes ~re-~ in its sense of “again.”
en.reconnaître:
From Latin ~recognoscere~ (“to know again, to recall, to review”), ~re-~ (“again”) + ~cognoscere~ (“to get to know, to learn”), itself ~co(m)-~ (“thoroughly”) + ~gnoscere~ (“to know”), from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know, to recognize”). French passed through Middle French ~recognoistre~, then ~reconnoistre~ and ~reconnoître~, before settling on ~reconnaître~ (and since the 1990 reform, optionally ~reconnaitre~). The root *~ǵneh₃-~ is one of the most fertile in Indo-European, giving English ~know~ and the ~-gnostic~ of ~agnostic~ and ~diagnosis~, Greek ~gignṓskein~, and the Romance cousins Italian ~riconoscere~ and Spanish ~reconocer~.

The Latin idea was iterative: to ~recognoscere~ was to know a second time, to identify something already encountered — which is exactly the modern ~reconnaître un visage~ (“to recognize a face”). From there the verb branched into the moral and social: to ~reconnaître~ a fault is to admit it, to ~reconnaître~ a child or a state is to acknowledge it officially, and a person who shows gratitude is ~reconnaissant~ — for to be thankful is, etymologically, to “acknowledge” a kindness received. The military scout's ~reconnaissance~ (also borrowed into English) is yet another sense: knowing the terrain in advance. The same root threads through French ~connaître~, ~connaissance~, ~reconnaissance~, ~méconnaître~ (“to fail to recognize”), and the learned ~diagnostic~.
en.reconquérir: Formed from ~conquérir~ and the prefix ~re-~, which here carries its ordinary sense of repetition: to conquer again, to win back what was lost. The base ~conquérir~ comes from Old French ~conquerre~, from Latin ~conquīrere~ (“to seek out eagerly”), itself built on ~quaerere~ (“to seek”). The Latin idea of a thorough search narrowed to winning by force, and French then widened it again to winning over a heart or a crowd. ~Reconquérir~ keeps both uses: one can retake a territory or recover someone's trust or a title.
en.reconstituer:
A transparent French formation: ~re-~ (“again”) plus ~constituer~, which French borrowed in the thirteenth century from Latin ~cōnstituere~ (“to set up, establish, fix”), from ~con-~ (“together”) plus ~statuere~ (“to set up, decree”), built on ~status~ and ultimately on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the great PIE root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the same root that produced Italian ~stare~, Spanish ~estar~ and English ~stand~ and ~state~. ~reconstituer~ itself appeared in 1534 meaning “to establish anew,” then came into its own in 1790 in the pages of the Moniteur universel, just as revolutionary France, having dismantled its old institutions, was debating how to build new ones.

The family of *~steh₂-~ through ~statuere~ is among the densest in French: ~constitution~, ~statut~, ~statue~, ~instituer~, ~restituer~, ~destituer~, ~substituer~ — and ~état~ itself, from Old French ~estat~, from Latin ~status~. The nineteenth century then sent ~reconstituer~ in two memorable directions. Medicine produced the ~reconstituant~ (1845–1864), the restorative tonic supposed to rebuild a weakened body. Criminal procedure produced the sense “to piece together exactly how an event unfolded” (attested from the 1850s) — ancestor of the modern ~reconstitution~, in which investigators walk a suspect through the crime scene, and of the historical reenactments staged by enthusiasts in period dress. Italian ~ricostituire~, Spanish ~reconstituir~ and English ~reconstitute~ are its parallel forms — though English speakers may know the idea best from dried soup, reconstituted with hot water.
en.reconstruire:
French ~reconstruire~ is transparently ~construire~ (“to build”) plus the prefix ~re-~ (“again, anew”), thus “to build again.” ~Construire~ descends from Latin ~construere~ (“to heap together, to build”), formed from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~struere~ (“to pile up, to arrange, to build”). ~Struere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~strowō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~strew-~ (“to strew, to spread out”). That root is shared with English ~strew~ and ~structure~, German ~streuen~ (“to scatter”), and Latin ~stratum~ (“something spread out”) — so building was first imagined as a strewing, a laying-out of layers.

The image inside ~construire~ is of piling materials together in arranged courses; ~re-~ simply runs the process again over what has fallen. The verb belongs to a tight Latin family of ~struere~ compounds that all reached French: ~instruire~ (“to instruct,” to build knowledge in), ~détruire~ (“to destroy,” to un-build), and ~obstruer~ (“to obstruct,” to pile up against). From the noun ~structure~ and the root *~strew-~ French also keeps ~construction~, ~reconstruction~, ~structure~, and ~strate~ — all heirs of an Indo-European verb for spreading things out.
en.reconvertir: ~Reconvertir~ is formed from ~convertir~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here means “again” or “back to a former state.” The base comes from Latin ~convertere~ (“to turn around, to transform”), made of ~con-~ and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). So ~reconvertir~ is “to convert again”: to turn something to a new purpose, or back to its earlier one. It is common in economic language, where a factory, a site or a worker is ~reconverti~ for another activity.
en.recopier: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~copier~, so “to copy once more,” as when one makes a clean version of a draft (~recopier au propre~) or transcribes a text by hand. The base ~copier~ comes from Medieval Latin ~copiare~, a verb drawn from Latin ~copia~ (“abundance”): to copy was to multiply the available exemplars. Here ~re-~ expresses plain repetition, and the verb is regularly formed, with nothing hidden in the prefix.
en.recouper: Formed from ~couper~ with the prefix ~re-~ (from Latin ~re-~, “back, again”). The base comes from Old French ~colper~, built on the noun ~colp~ (modern ~coup~, “a blow”), which reaches back through Late Latin ~colaphus~ to Greek ~kólaphos~ (“a slap on the cheek”): to cut was first to separate with a blow. The prefix adds repetition, so ~recouper~ can mean “to cut again.” Its most common modern senses are figurative: pieces of information or accounts that cross one another and thereby confirm each other are said to ~recouper~, as are lines that intersect.
en.recourir:
From Latin ~recurrere~ (“to run back, return”), from ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~currere~ (“to run”). ~Currere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~korzō~ and from PIE *~ḱers-~ (“to run”), the root that, through Latin, gives French ~courir~, ~courant~, ~course~, ~courrier~, and ~secours~, and the English borrowings ~current~, ~course~, ~career~, and ~corridor~.

The verb carries two senses that the prefix ~re-~ pulls in different directions. Transparently, ~recourir~ is “to run again,” the literal repetition a runner or a racer does. But its dominant modern sense is figurative: ~recourir à~ means “to have recourse to, to fall back on” — to run back to something for help. The image is of returning at speed to a source of aid, the same metaphor frozen in the noun ~recours~ (“recourse, appeal”) and in ~secours~ (“help,” literally “running to aid”). So a single Latin verb of running back lives on in French both as the athlete's plain “run again” and as the abstract act of turning to a remedy in need.
en.recouvrer:
French ~recouvrer~ comes from Old French ~recovrer~, from Latin ~recuperare~ (also spelled ~reciperare~, “to regain, to recover”). The Latin verb is linked to ~recipio~ (“to take back, to receive”), itself ~re-~ (“back, again”) plus ~capio~ (“to take, to seize”), and thus to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp, to seize”). From the same Latin source comes the learned doublet ~récupérer~, borrowed later and more directly; ~recouvrer~ is the older, inherited form that passed through the mouths of speakers. English ~recover~ and ~recuperate~ are cousins through this Latin family.

The sense has always centered on getting something back — health, debts, lost property, one's rights. In careful modern French, ~recouvrer~ specializes in formal or financial recovery: one ~recouvre~ a debt, ~recouvre~ one's freedom, ~recouvre~ one's sight. It must not be confused with the homophone-rich ~recouvrir~ (“to cover again”), a different verb from ~couvrir~. The action-noun ~recouvrement~ (“collection, recovery,” as of taxes) belongs to this verb, while ~récupération~ belongs to its bookish twin — two threads spun from one Latin verb of taking back.
en.recouvrir:
~Recouvrir~ is built from ~couvrir~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base verb descends from Latin ~cooperire~ (« to cover completely, to overwhelm »), made of the intensive prefix ~co-~ and ~operire~ (« to cover, to veil »). Italian ~coprire~ and Spanish ~cubrir~ are its Romance siblings; English ~cover~ came through Old French ~covrir~. Note that ~recouvrir~ (« to cover again / completely ») must not be confused with the look-alike ~recouvrer~ (« to recover, regain »), which instead derives from Latin ~recuperare~ — same prefix, different root.

The ~re-~ in ~recouvrir~ carries two readings the French keeps lively: « again » (to cover anew what was uncovered) and « completely » (to cover all over, as paint ~recouvre~ a wall entirely). The figurative « to cover up », hiding or excusing a fault, grew naturally from the literal act of laying something over. The ~operire~ family also yielded ~ouvrir~ (« to open », from ~aperire~, its mirror-twin), ~couvercle~, ~couverture~, and ~découvrir~ (« to dis-cover », to take the lid off and so to find).
en.recruter:
A denominal verb from the late seventeenth century, formed from ~recrue~ (“fresh troops, a new recruit”), the past participle of the older verb ~recroître~ (“to grow again, to grow back”). ~Recroître~ is ~re-~ plus ~croître~, from Latin ~crēscere~ (“to grow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱer-~ (“to grow”). Cognate, through ~crēscere~, with English ~crescent~ and ~increase~ and with the Roman harvest-goddess ~Cerēs~.

The logic is military and botanical at once: a ~recrue~ was the body of men by which an army was made to “grow again” after losses, and ~recruter~ meant to gather such reinforcements. The word's birth was controversial — purists long condemned ~recruter~ as a clumsy denominal coinage, the way ~solutionner~ is mocked today — yet it survived and broadened to any enlisting, from soldiers to volunteers to employees. From the same *~ḱer-~ / ~crēscere~ root French keeps a vigorous family of growth-words: ~croître~, ~croissant~, ~accroître~, ~décroître~, ~accroissement~, and ~crue~ (a river's “rise,” a flood). To ~recruter~ is, at root, to make a force grow once more.
en.recréer: The two Wiktionaries disagree. French Wiktionary traces it to Latin ~recreāre~, while English Wiktionary parses it as ~re-~ + ~créer~ (“to create again”). Latin ~creāre~ (“to make, to bring forth”) is related to ~crescere~ (“to grow”), and the prefix ~re-~ means “again” or “back.” In Latin, ~recreāre~ meant “to make anew, to restore, to refresh,” and that older sense lives on in a separate French verb spelled with an accent, ~récréer~ (“to entertain, to refresh”), the source of ~récréation~. Modern ~recréer~ is the plain “create again”: a copy of a scene, a lost recipe, an atmosphere.
en.rectifier: ~Rectifier~ comes through Old French ~rectifier~ from Late Latin ~rectificāre~ (“to make straight, to put right”). The Latin verb is a compound of ~rectus~ (“straight, right”) and the verbal suffix ~-ficāre~ (“to make”), from ~facere~. The sense “to make straight” was first literal, then moral and technical: to correct an error, to adjust a measurement, to purify a liquid by distilling it again. Related French words include ~rectiligne~, ~correct~ and ~droit~, which all come from ~rectus~ or its family.
en.recueillir:
From Old French ~recoillir~, ~recueillir~, from Latin ~recolligere~ (“to gather again, to collect, to reunite”), formed from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~colligere~ (“to gather together”). ~colligere~ is itself ~com-~ (“together”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”), which descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leg-~ (“to collect, to gather”). The same root gave Greek ~légein~ (“to gather, to say”) and, through Latin ~colligere~, English ~collect~ and ~cull~.
