The primitive sense is the careful picking-up of things one by one — gleaning, harvesting, gathering. ~recolligere~ added the nuance of gathering back together what was scattered, and modern ~recueillir~ ranges over this whole field: one ~recueille~ rainwater, testimony, votes, a stray animal taken in, or — most tellingly — oneself, in ~se recueillir~, “to collect oneself, to gather one's thoughts in meditation or prayer.” From ~legere~ and its compounds French inherited a great harvest of words: ~cueillir~ (“to pick, to gather”), ~accueillir~ (“to welcome”), ~collecte~ and ~collection~, ~recueil~ (“an anthology,” a gathering of texts), ~élire~ and ~élection~ (to “choose out”), and ~lire~ itself, since reading was once the gathering up of letters with the eye.
en.reculer:
Derived from the noun ~cul~ (« rear, backside ») with the prefix ~re-~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~ — literally « to put one's rear backward ». ~cul~ comes from Latin ~culus~ (« buttocks »), from Proto-Italic *~kūlos~ and a Proto-Indo-European *~kuH-l-~, a zero-grade of *~(s)kewH-~ (« to cover »); Old Irish ~cúl~ (« back ») is a relative. The verb is attested in Old French by around 1200.

The blunt anatomical image lies behind a surprisingly genteel modern range. From the basic « to move backward » the verb spread to « to back up » a car, « to back down » or « to give ground » in an argument, and figuratively « to put off » a deadline — French even has the proverb « ~reculer~ pour mieux sauter », « to step back the better to leap ». The family includes ~recul~ (« recoil », as of a gun), ~reculade~, and ~à reculons~ (« backwards »), all preserving, however discreetly, that original picture of moving tail-first.
en.recycler:
A young verb with an ancient wheel inside. ~recycler~ is first attested in 1959 as a refinery term — to send unreacted fluids back through the process — formed in French from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~cycle~; English ~recycle~ had existed since 1926, but the TLFi presents the French verb as a home-grown derivation rather than a borrowing. ~cycle~ was taken from Latin ~cyclus~, from Greek ~kúklos~ (“circle, wheel”), from PIE *~kʷékʷlos~ (“wheel”), a reduplicated derivative of *~kʷel-~ (“to turn”) — the same protoword that became English ~wheel~ and Sanskrit ~cakrá~ (the chakra, and the wheel on India's flag). To recycle is thus, literally, to put something back on the wheel.

The verb's own meaning promptly went around in circles. Born industrial (fluids, 1959), it was applied almost at once to people: French ~se recycler~ means to retrain, to send oneself back through the cycle of studies — the noun ~recyclage~ appears in a 1960 encyclopedia of education — and the usage stays everyday: un comptable qui se recycle dans la pâtisserie. Only later, with the environmental turn of the 1970s, did bottles and paper make it a household word. The Greek wheel rolls through a whole French lexicon: ~bicyclette~, ~cyclisme~, ~cyclone~ (a 19th-century coinage on the Greek, for storms that wheel) and ~encyclopédie~ — from ~enkúklios paideía~, the “circular education” that takes knowledge full circle. A verb meaning “put back on the wheel” that began with refinery fluids, moved on to careers and settled on yogurt pots: ~recycler~ has thoroughly recycled itself.
en.redescendre: Formed in French from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~descendre~, the sense being “to go down again” or “to come back down”. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and marks repetition or a return to a former place. The base ~descendre~ comes from Latin ~dēscendere~, built from ~dē-~ (“down from”) and ~scandere~ (“to climb”), so that the verb is literally a “climbing down”. A verb of ascent thus lies at the root of two layers of downward movement.
en.redessiner:
~redessiner~ is ~re-~ plus ~dessiner~, and ~dessiner~ is an Italian import. French borrowed it from Italian ~disegnare~ (“to draw”), attested from the thirteenth century, which continues Latin ~dēsignāre~ (“to mark out, to designate”), from ~dē-~ and ~signāre~, from ~signum~ (“mark, sign”). The deep root is unsettled: ~signum~ is traced to Proto-Italic *~segnom~ and then to Proto-Indo-European either *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), and the sources do not choose between them. The same Latin verb produced Italian ~designare~ and ~disegnare~, Spanish ~diseñar~, Portuguese ~desenhar~, and English ~design~ and ~designate~.

The French spelling took a long time to settle. The verb surfaces in 1529 as ~designer~ (“to trace the outline of something”), then as ~desseigner~ in 1552 and ~dessigner~ in 1556 — forms probably pulled toward the shape of ~enseigner~ — and reaches ~dessiner~ only in 1664, refashioned on the noun ~dessin~. That noun performed a neat trick of its own: the single Italian word ~disegno~ carried both “drawing” and “plan, intention,” and French ended by splitting the two meanings across two spellings, ~dessin~ for the picture and ~dessein~ for the purpose. Meanwhile Latin ~dēsignāre~ had already been borrowed a second time, straight and learned, as ~désigner~ — so ~dessiner~ and ~désigner~ are doublets, one tracing a shape, the other pointing at a thing. With ~re-~, the verb reaches well beyond the drawing board: the Treaty of Paris ~redessina~ the borders of France. Related French words include ~dessin~, ~dessein~, ~dessinateur~, ~désigner~, ~signe~ and ~enseigner~.
en.redevenir: Formed from ~devenir~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”), which here marks a return to a former state: to ~redevenir~ is to become what one was before. The base ~devenir~ comes from Latin ~dēvenīre~ (“to come down to, to arrive at”), made of ~dē-~ (“down, from”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”), so “becoming” is, at root, arriving at a new state as one arrives at a place. The prefix ~re-~ is Latin in origin and fully productive in French, which is why it attaches so easily to a verb like this one. The double prefix is visible in the word's very shape: a coming that comes back.
en.redimensionner:
~redimensionner~ is built in two steps: ~re-~ on ~dimensionner~, itself a denominal verb from ~dimension~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~dimension~ entered French in the fourteenth century from Latin ~dīmēnsiō~ (“a measuring out”), the noun of action to ~dīmētīrī~ (“to measure out in every direction”), which is ~dī-~ plus ~mētīrī~ (“to measure”). ~mētīrī~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~mētis~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~meh₁-~ (“to measure”), one of the more productive roots in the family: it yields Ancient Greek ~métron~, Old Church Slavonic ~měra~ and — inherited rather than borrowed — English ~meal~, at bottom a measured portion. English ~measure~ and ~dimension~ come from the same Latin verb by way of French.

The noun is medieval, but the verbs are modern and technical. ~dimensionner~ belongs to engineering — sizing a beam, a pipe, a power supply to meet a specification — and ~redimensionner~ followed it, meaning at first to re-specify an installation or scale a project back. Computing then gave it a second life and a far wider public: every window dragged by its corner is ~redimensionnée~, and the verb now competes in technical French with the raw anglicism ~resize~. A third, quieter sense survives in critical prose: to ~redimensionner~ an event is to restore it to its true historical proportions — measuring it out, in the old Latin sense, rather than merely resizing it. The root has been generous to French: ~mesure~, ~mesurer~, ~mètre~, ~immense~, ~commensurable~ and ~mensuration~ all descend from ~mētīrī~, as does the noun ~dimension~ that this verb keeps adjusting.
en.redire: Formed from ~dire~ with the prefix ~re-~, so its basic sense is “to say again”. The base ~dire~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~dīgere~, a reshaping of Latin ~dīcere~ (“to say”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”). A set expression gives the verb a surprising second sense: “trouver à redire” means “to find something to criticize”, and in the negative, “rien à redire” means “nothing to object to”, as if repeating a thing meant answering it back.
en.rediriger:
~Rediriger~ is ~diriger~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”). ~Diriger~ is a learned borrowing of Latin ~dīrigere~ (“to set straight, to steer, to direct”), a compound of ~dis-~ — reinforcing here rather than separating — and ~regere~ (“to rule, to guide in a straight line”), from Proto-Italic *~regō~ and PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to make right”). The root has an unusually visible logic: to rule is to keep a line straight, which is why the same source lies behind a ruler in both senses, the sovereign and the straightedge. Latin ~dīrigere~ gave Italian ~dirigere~, Spanish and Catalan ~dirigir~, Portuguese ~dirigir~ and French ~diriger~, while English took ~direct~ and ~director~ from the same stock. Through ~regere~ and its noun ~rēx~, the root ties French to English ~right~ and ~regal~ and to German ~Recht~ (“law, right”).

French owns this Latin verb twice over. ~Diriger~ is the bookish borrowing, carried in with its consonants intact; but the participle ~dīrēctus~ also travelled the popular route, producing Late Latin *~directiāre~ and from it French ~dresser~. ~Rediriger~ and ~redresser~ are therefore, at bottom, the same instruction — straighten it again — one arriving in a scholar's Latin, the other worn smooth by centuries of ordinary speech. The verb's older meaning is purely spatial: to point something in a new direction, to send a traveller or a letter elsewhere. Then the web arrived, and ~rediriger~ acquired the sense in which it is now most often met — automatically sending a browser or an e-mail on to another address — following English ~redirect~ closely. The same root fills a large corner of the dictionary: ~droit~, ~adroit~, ~direct~, ~dresser~, ~redresser~, ~règle~, ~région~, ~régime~, ~roi~ and ~régner~.
en.redistribuer: Formed in French from the verb ~distribuer~ and the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so ~redistribuer~ means to distribute anew or differently. The base ~distribuer~ was a learned borrowing from Latin ~distribuere~ (“to deal out”), made of ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~tribuere~ (“to assign”), a verb tied to the Roman ~tribus~ (“tribe”) and the sharing of duties and goods among them. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive. The modern sense, as in ~redistribuer les richesses~, is of changing a first allotment.
en.redonner:
Built from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and the verb ~donner~ (“to give”), which descends from Latin ~donare~ (“to make a gift of”), a verb formed on ~donum~ (“gift”) plus the denominative suffix ~-ō~. ~Donum~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~dōnom~ and to PIE *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). The same root is visible across the family: Italian ~donare~, Spanish ~donar~, and the learned English borrowing ~donate~, while the deeper root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”).

The prefix ~re-~ here means both “again” and “back,” which is why ~redonner~ covers two everyday senses: to give once more (~redonner~ de l'espoir, “to restore hope”) and to give back something received. French preserves a rich crop of words from this root, among them ~don~ (“gift”), ~donateur~ (“donor”), ~pardon~ (literally “a giving-through,” hence forgiveness), and ~donnée~ (“a datum,” a thing given). The everyday verb ~donner~ thus carries within it one of the oldest verbs of human exchange, the act of giving, recombined here with a prefix of repetition and return.
en.redoubler: ~Redoubler~ is formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~doubler~. The base ~doubler~ comes from the adjective ~double~, from Latin ~duplus~ (“twofold”), itself ~duo~ (“two”) plus a fold-element related to English ~ply~. The prefix ~re-~, from Latin ~re-~ (“again, back”), here means doing again or intensifying: to ~redoubler~ is to double once more, so to increase greatly, as in ~redoubler d'efforts~. In school French the verb has a special sense, to repeat a year, so that a pupil goes through the same class a second time.
en.redouter:
Inherited from Middle French ~redoubter~ and Old French ~redoter~, formed from ~re-~ and ~douter~. The verb ~douter~ came from Latin ~dubitāre~ (“to waver, to be in doubt”), from the adjective ~dubius~ (“uncertain, wavering”), which is traditionally linked to ~duo~ (“two”), the picture being a mind pulled two ways. Italian ~dubitare~ and Spanish ~dudar~ descend from the same Latin verb, and English took ~doubt~ and ~dubious~ from French and Latin. In Old French, ~douter~ carried both “to doubt” and “to fear,” and it is this second sense that ~redouter~ grew from. The English ~redoubt~ (a small fortification) is an unrelated word.

The prefix ~re-~ in this verb does not mean “again.” It is intensive, so that ~redouter~ means to fear greatly, to dread. The two senses of ~douter~ later separated: the simple verb kept “to doubt,” and the “fear” half survived only in its prefixed offspring. Old French ~douter~ also gave the adjective ~redoutable~, “fearsome,” and the noun ~doute~, still found in ~sans doute~ and ~douteux~. The old link between doubt and fear is not hard to follow: someone who is unsure what will happen often fears the worst. ~Redouter~ is now a fairly literary verb, and the prefix, once a living intensifier, has become a fossil that nobody removes.
en.redresser: Formed from ~dresser~ with the prefix ~re-~, and attested in Old French as ~redrecier~. The base ~dresser~ comes from Late Latin *~directiāre~ (“to straighten”), built on Latin ~directus~ (“straight”), so the idea is straightness. The prefix ~re-~ adds the sense of doing it again or restoring: to set something upright once more, whether a fallen statue or a mistaken course of action. From there come the figurative senses, to put right or to rectify an error or an economy.
en.redécouvrir: Formed from the verb ~découvrir~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here means “again”: to find out or uncover something anew. The base ~découvrir~ is itself ~dé-~ (reversal) plus ~couvrir~ (“to cover”), from Late Latin ~discooperīre~, so its literal sense is “to take the cover off.” From lifting a lid came the figurative “to find out, to reveal.” Adding ~re-~ gives both a literal sense, “to uncover again,” and a figurative one, “to find again something forgotten or neglected,” as when a forgotten author or an old recipe is rediscovered.
en.redéfinir: Formed in French from ~définir~ with the prefix ~re-~ (here in its accented form ~ré-~), meaning “to define again” and, in programming, “to override” an inherited method. The base ~définir~ was borrowed in the 13th century from Latin ~dēfīnīre~ (“to set bounds to, to determine precisely”), itself built on ~fīnis~ (“boundary, end”), the ancestor of French ~finir~ and, through it, of English ~finish~. The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive in French, which makes ~redéfinir~ a transparent modern derivation.
en.redémarrer: ~Redémarrer~ is formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~démarrer~. The base verb ~démarrer~ is a shortened form of an older ~désamarrer~ (“to cast off moorings”), made from ~dé-~ (reversal) and ~amarrer~ (“to moor”), a nautical verb borrowed from Dutch ~aanmarren~ (“to tie, to fasten”). It began as untying a ship from the quay, then came ashore to mean starting a car or an engine, and any undertaking. ~Redémarrer~ adds repetition: to start up again after a stop, as with a stalled motor, a business, or in modern French a computer that is rebooted.
en.refaire:
From the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”) and ~faire~ (“to do, to make”). ~faire~ descends from Latin ~facere~ (“to make, to do”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, to put, to place”). That root is astonishingly widespread: it gives Greek ~tithenai~ (“to put”), German ~tun~ and English ~do~, and within French the vast ~faire~ family — ~défaire~, ~satisfaire~, ~parfaire~, and the suffix in ~confiture~ and ~facile~.

~refaire~ means to do or make again — to redo a calculation, remake a bed, rebuild a wall. But French stretched it cheerfully into the figurative and the slang. One can ~se refaire~ — recoup one's losses at the gaming table, or restore one's health and spirits. More mischievously, ~se faire refaire~ can mean to be swindled, the “re-making” turned against the victim. The deep root *~dʰeh₁-~ originally meant not “do” but “put, set in place” — making was conceived as setting a thing down in the world — and that placing sense survives in cousins like ~thèse~ and ~thème~, both Greek borrowings from ~tithenai~. So ~refaire~, the homeliest of verbs, ultimately reaches back to one of humanity's oldest words for putting something where it belongs.
en.refermer: Formed from ~fermer~ and the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”), in its sense of returning to a former state: to close again what was opened. The base comes from Latin ~firmare~ (“to make firm, to secure”), built on the adjective ~firmus~ (“firm, steadfast”). A door was made secure by being fastened, so “to make fast” slid into “to close.” That sense ended up displacing the older ~clore~ in everyday speech.
en.refléter:
A denominal verb formed from the noun ~reflet~ (“reflection, glint”) plus the suffix ~-er~. ~Reflet~ was borrowed from Italian ~riflesso~, itself from Latin ~reflexus~, the past participle of ~reflectere~ (“to bend back”), from ~re-~ (“back”) + ~flectere~ (“to bend”). The same ~reflectere~ had already descended by the regular sound-changes into French ~réfléchir~, used of light and of thought, so French ended up with two verbs from one Latin etymon. The Latin ~flectere~ is itself of uncertain ultimate origin, lacking secure Indo-European cognates. Cognate forms survive in English ~reflect~ and ~flexible~.

Because ~refléter~ entered through the noun rather than by direct inheritance, it stayed close to the concrete image: a mirror, water, or polished surface that throws back light or likeness — « le lac reflétait le ciel ». ~Réfléchir~, by contrast, drifted toward the mental sense of turning a matter over in one's mind, though it kept the optical meaning too. The shared root ~flectere~ underlies a wide family in French: ~fléchir~ (“to bend, to yield”), ~flexible~, ~réflexe~, ~inflexion~, and ~déflecteur~. The split between ~refléter~ and ~réfléchir~ neatly mirrors, so to speak, the two senses English packs into the single word ~reflect~.
en.reformuler: Formed in French from ~formuler~ and the prefix ~re-~, which here means “again”: to ~reformuler~ is to put something into words a second time, differently or more clearly. The base ~formuler~ is a verb built on the noun ~formule~, from Latin ~formula~, the “little form” that was a diminutive of ~forma~ (“shape, form”). The prefix ~re-~ is fully productive in French and attaches to almost any verb to mean repetition, so the verb is transparent. It is common in teaching, negotiation and customer service, whenever a question or demand is restated.
en.refroidir: Formed in French from ~re-~ + ~froidir~, with ~re-~ here intensive and not a mark of repetition: to refroidir is to grow properly cold, not to grow cold again. The simple verb ~froidir~, from ~froid~ + ~-ir~, has long since dropped out of use and left only the prefixed form. The adjective and noun ~froid~ come from Latin ~frīgidus~ (“cold”), whose Spanish and Italian cousins are ~frío~ and ~freddo~. Slang later gave ~refroidir~ the dark sense of “to bump off”, as though a body were left to go cold.
en.refuser:
From a blend of two Latin verbs. Old French had ~reüser~, regularly descended from Latin ~recūsāre~ (“to object to, to decline”), formed from ~re-~ (“back, against”) and ~causa~ (“cause, legal case”). But the modern form shows an ~f~ that ~recūsāre~ cannot supply; philologists since Diez have explained it as a contamination by Latin ~refūtāre~ (“to drive back, to refute”), built from ~re-~ + ~-fūtāre~ (“to beat”), perhaps from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰau-~ (“to strike”). French ~refuser~ thus carries the ~f~ of one verb and the ~s~ of the other.

The two ancestors are visible across the Romance languages: Italian ~rifiutare~ continues ~refūtāre~, while Spanish ~rehusar~ and Occitan ~refusar~ pattern with the French blend. The meaning has stayed close to its roots — to push back, to decline, to reject a request, an offer, or admittance — and figuratively to deny or withhold (« refuser son aide »). The pure ~refūtāre~ line survives separately in learned French as ~réfuter~ (“to refute”), so the same Latin verb reaches modern French twice: once openly in ~réfuter~, once hidden inside ~refuser~.
en.regagner: Formed from ~gagner~ with the prefix ~re-~, in the sense of doing again or getting back: to win back, to regain, or to return to a place. The base ~gagner~ goes back to Old French ~gaaignier~ (“to earn, cultivate, forage”), from a Late Latin form *~wadaniāre~ borrowed from Frankish *~waidanjan~ (“to forage, graze, hunt for food”), a word tied to the Germanic notion of pasture and the chase (compare German ~Weide~, “pasture”). From working the land for a living, the verb broadened to “to earn” and then to “to win”. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and attaches freely to French verbs. The verb also means to get back to a place, which is why it can be said of reaching home again.
en.regarder:
From Middle French ~regarder~, from Old French ~regarder~ (also ~reguarder~), formed from the verb ~garder~ (“to guard, keep, watch over”) with the prefix ~re-~. ~garder~ comes from Late Latin *~wardāre~, borrowed from Frankish *~wardōn~ (“to watch, keep guard”), from Proto-Germanic *~wardōną~, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to perceive, watch out for”). Through this Germanic line, ~regarder~ is kin to English ~ward~, ~warden~, and ~guard~ (the last itself reborrowed from French), and to German ~warten~ (“to wait”).

The sense moved from “to keep, watch over” toward “to direct one's eyes at.” The prefix ~re-~ here does not mean “again” but adds a sense of attentive, directed looking, so ~regarder~ became “to look at, to watch” — to turn one's guarding gaze onto something. A trace of the older meaning survives in the idiom ~cela ne te regarde pas~ (“that doesn't concern you,” literally “that doesn't watch over you”). From the same root come the noun ~regard~ (“gaze, look”), ~garder~, ~gardien~, ~garde~, and ~égard~ (“regard, consideration”). The shift from guarding to seeing is intuitive: to watch over something, you must keep your eyes on it.
en.regretter:
From earlier ~regreter~ (also ~regrater~), formed with the prefix ~re-~ on a Germanic verb of weeping: Old Norse ~gráta~ (“to weep, lament, bewail”), phonetically reinforced by Old English ~grētan~ of the same sense, rather than from Old Low Frankish *~greotan~. The Germanic root is cognate with Gothic ~grētan~ and survives in modern English dialect ~greet~ (“to weep,” in Scots), all from a Proto-Germanic verb for crying out in grief.

The striking thing about ~regretter~ is that, unlike most French verbs, its core is Germanic, not Latin: the Norse and Scandinavian raiders and settlers who reached the French coasts left behind a word for lamentation. Old French ~regreter~ meant to bewail, especially to mourn the dead — to lament loudly over a loss. From this funerary wailing the meaning softened into the modern range: to miss someone or something, to be sorry, to regret a decision. French still distinguishes ~regretter quelqu'un~ (“to miss a person”) from regretting an act. The Germanic origin left few French relatives; the chief descendant is the noun ~regret~ itself, which English in turn borrowed back — a word that crossed the Channel twice.
en.regrouper:
From ~re-~ (here a prefix of repetition and intensification) and ~grouper~ (“to group, to gather”), a verb attested from the late eighteenth century and formed from the noun ~groupe~. ~Groupe~ itself was borrowed from Italian ~gruppo~ (“knot, cluster, bunch”), which traces back through a Germanic source — Frankish *~kruppa~ — to Proto-Germanic *~kruppaz~ (“rounded mass, lump, body”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~grewb-~ (“to crumple, to bend, to curl up”). Cognate with German ~Kropf~ (“crop, craw, bulge”) and with English ~crop~.

The image at the heart of the word is concrete: a ~groupe~ was first a rounded mass of figures bunched together, a term of painting and sculpture before it became the abstract grouping of people or things. French built the verb ~grouper~ from it, then prefixed ~re-~ to mark a fresh act of gathering — bringing scattered elements back into one mass. The redoubled sense suits its modern uses, from regrouping troops to consolidating data. From the same Italian-Germanic stock French keeps ~groupe~, ~groupement~, ~groupuscule~, and ~regroupement~, while the financial sense of the old Italian word (a “bag of money”) is a reminder that a group was, from the start, simply things bound up together.
en.rejeter:
Attested from the twelfth century, ~rejeter~ comes from Latin ~rejectare~ (“to throw back, hurl back, vomit”), the frequentative of ~rejicere~ — itself the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) joined to ~jacere~ (“to throw”). Latin ~jacere~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~yeh₁-~ (“to throw, cast”). The family includes Italian ~rigettare~ and Spanish ~rechazar~, and through ~jacere~ the English borrowings ~reject~ and ~eject~.

The literal sense — throwing something back — fans out across modern French. The sea ~rejette~ debris onto the shore; a body ~rejette~ a transplanted organ; a plant ~rejette~ new shoots from its base (hence the noun ~rejet~, a sucker or offshoot); a committee ~rejette~ a proposal; and one may ~rejeter~ the blame onto another. The base verb ~jacere~, throw, is astonishingly prolific in French through its participle ~jactus~ / ~jectus~: ~jeter~ itself, ~jet~, ~projet~ and ~projeter~, ~sujet~, ~objet~, ~trajet~, ~injecter~, and ~adjacent~. Whether you reject an idea or skip a stone, you are, etymologically, simply casting something — and in ~rejeter~, casting it right back where it came from.
en.rejoindre:
From ~joindre~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”). ~Joindre~ descends from Latin ~iungere~ (~jungere~, “to join, to yoke, to harness”), from Proto-Italic *~jungō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~yewg-~ (“to join, to yoke”). This is one of the most transparent of all Indo-European roots: it gives Sanskrit ~yoga~ (“union”), Ancient Greek ~ζεύγνυμι~ (zeúgnumi, “to yoke”), English ~yoke~, and German ~Joch~ — and, through Latin, English ~join~ and ~junction~.

The literal image is agricultural: ~iungere~ meant to fit two oxen under a single ~iugum~, a yoke. From joining beasts it generalized to joining anything; ~re-~ then adds the nuance of coming back together. So ~rejoindre~ means to join up with, to catch up to, or to be reunited with — to re-yoke. French keeps a large ~yewg-~ family: ~joindre~, ~jointure~, ~conjoint~, ~adjoindre~, ~disjoindre~, and ~jonction~, alongside the inherited ~joug~ (“yoke”) and the learned ~conjuguer~ — for to conjugate a verb is, etymologically, to yoke its forms together, a fitting root for a verb-learning app.
en.rejouer: ~Rejouer~ is formed from ~jouer~ and the prefix ~re-~, which here carries its ordinary sense of repetition: to play again, as a match, a piece of music or a role. The base ~jouer~ comes from Old French ~joer~, from Latin ~iocāre~ (“to joke”), a verb built on ~iocus~ (“joke, game”). It is a good example of a verb that widened its meaning: Latin ~iocārī~ first meant to jest in words, but the Romance languages extended it to all kinds of play, displacing the Classical verb ~lūdere~. The prefix ~re-~ itself descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.relancer:
From ~lancer~ (“to throw”) with the prefix ~re-~. ~lancer~ descends from Latin ~lanceare~ (« to wield a lance »), a verb built on the noun ~lancea~ (« lance »), which reached French through Old French ~lancier~. The origin of ~lancea~ itself is uncertain: it is generally taken to be a borrowing from a Celtic or Celtiberian source, and is sometimes linked, only tentatively, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₂k-~ (« to strike »). Ancient Greek ~λόγχη~ (« spearhead ») is often compared.

The prefix ~re-~ adds the idea of « again » or « back », so ~relancer~ first meant « to throw back » — to return a ball or a thrown object. From that physical sense the verb branched widely: in hunting it meant « to flush game again », in conversation « to follow up, to press », and in the modern economy « to relaunch, to reboot » a project, a product, or growth. The same family gives French ~lance~, ~lancement~, ~élancer~, and ~s'élancer~, all turning on the image of something hurled or springing forward.
en.relater:
Attested in the 14th century as a denominal verb from Old French ~relat~ (“report, account”), itself from Latin ~relātus~ (“a carrying back, a report”). ~relātus~ is the suppletive past participle of ~referre~ (“to carry back, to report”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry,” from PIE *~bʰer-~, source of English ~bear~). Curiously, ~ferre~ has no participle of its own; Latin borrowed one from a different root — ~lātus~, from older ~tlātus~, from PIE *~telh₂-~ (“to lift, to bear”). So ~relater~ is built on a grafted participle: its stem and its sense of “carrying” come from two separate Indo-European roots.

The metaphor is the reporter's: to ~relate~ an event is to carry it ~back~ to a listener, to bring word of it. French ~relater~ keeps this neutral, almost notarial tone — to set down or recount facts as they occurred — and is cousin to ~relation~ (“account, narrative,” before it ever meant a connection between people) and ~relatif~. That borrowed participle ~lātus~ is astonishingly productive: it gives French ~translater~ and the English family ~translate~, ~relate~, ~oblation~, and ~prelate~, while the ~ferre~ side yields ~référer~, ~offrir~, ~souffrir~, and ~conférer~. Few verbs wear their double ancestry so plainly.
en.relativiser: ~Relativiser~ is formed from the adjective ~relatif~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make relative.” ~Relatif~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~relātīvus~ (“having a relation to”), derived from ~relātiō~ (“relation”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which itself transcribed Greek verbs. To ~relativiser~ is to treat something as dependent on circumstances rather than absolute, and in everyday French it means to put a problem in perspective and play it down.
en.relaxer:
Borrowed from Latin ~relaxāre~ (“to loosen, to release”), formed from ~re-~ and ~laxāre~ (“to loosen”), itself built on the adjective ~laxus~ (“loose, slack”). Spanish ~relajar~ is a cognate. French already had a popular, inherited form of the same verb, ~relâcher~, which developed from the Old French ~relaisser~ family, so ~relaxer~ and ~relâcher~ are two paths from one Latin word: one learned, one worn down by centuries of speech.

The glosses reveal the older, legal life of the learned verb: ~relaxer~ meant to release a prisoner or to acquit. The sense “to relax,” to rest and unwind, is the one most speakers now know, usually in the reflexive ~se relaxer~, and was likely reinforced by English ~relax~, which came from the same Latin verb. The root ~laxus~ left other traces in French: ~lâche~ (“slack, loose,” then “cowardly”) is its popular descendant, while ~laxisme~ and ~laxatif~ are learned ones.
en.relayer:
Attested in the 12th century as ~relaier~, a term of the hunt: by 1240–80 it meant to release fresh hounds against a tiring quarry. It is formed from ~re-~ and Old French ~laier~ (“to leave, to let”), a verb of the north-east — Picardy, Wallonia, Lorraine. There the certainty ends: the origin of ~laier~ is disputed. The TLFi judges it “probably without etymological connection” to ~laisser~ (from Latin ~laxāre~), despite the lookalike meanings, and inclines toward Frankish *~laibjan~ (“to leave behind”). If that Germanic account is right, ~relayer~ is unexpected kin to English ~leave~ (Old English ~lǣfan~, from Proto-Germanic *~laibijaną~, causative of *~bilībaną~ “to remain,” source of German ~bleiben~), the family resting on PIE *~leyp-~ (“to stick, to remain”). A hedged kinship, then — but a vivid one: to relay is, literally, to leave something behind in readiness.

The relay began as a hunting institution: fresh hounds — and from 1573 fresh horses — posted in advance along the expected line of the chase, left waiting to take over. From the hunt it passed to the road: the ~relais~ were the post-houses where couriers changed horses, the heartbeat of travel before the railways. Then the senses multiplied just as the TLFi dates them — workers relieving one another (1636), radio transmission (1933), the ~course de relais~ (relay race, 1939) — and English had long since borrowed the hunting noun as ~relay~. Modern French keeps the verb busy: the press will ~relayer une information~ (pass a story along), satellites relay signals, a colleague ~prend le relais~ (takes over). Another everyday word hides the same ~laier~: ~délai~, from Old French ~deslaier~ (“to put off, defer”) — a deadline is something “left for later.” Every relay, from baton to mast to night shift, keeps the hunting picture: something left along the route, ready to take over.
en.relever:
French ~relever~ is the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back up”) joined to ~lever~ (“to lift, to raise”), and is also continued directly from Latin ~relevāre~ (“to lift again, to lighten, to relieve”). ~Lever~ descends from Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, to make light”), a verb built on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”). The same root surfaces in English ~light~ (the adjective) and ~lever~, and in the family of ~levity~.

The two senses of Latin ~levāre~ — “to lift up” and “to lighten” — both flow into French. ~Relever~ keeps the first vividly: to raise something fallen, to pick up, to stand back up (~se relever~). But the “lighten/relieve” strand survives too, in ~relever la garde~ (“to relieve the watch,” to take over so others may rest) and in nuance, where ~relever~ a dish means to heighten and brighten its flavour. The shared root has been astonishingly productive in French: ~élever~, ~soulever~, ~enlever~, ~prélever~, the noun ~levée~, and ~levain~ (“leaven,” which makes dough rise), alongside the borrowed ~levant~ (the east, where the sun “rises”). To raise, to lighten, to leaven, to relieve — all are one gesture of lifting.
en.relier:
From ~re-~ + ~lier~ (“to tie, bind”), the verb ~lier~ descending from Latin ~ligāre~ (“to bind, tie, fasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind, tie”). Cognate with Italian ~legare~ and Spanish ~ligar~, and — through the same ~ligāre~ — with English ~ligament~, ~liable~, and ~ally~.

The ~re-~ here carries the sense “back together,” so ~relier~ is to bind things one to another — to ~connect~, link, or join. The root threw off a strikingly broad family. From ~ligāre~ directly come ~lier~, ~liaison~, ~lien~, and ~liasse~; with ~ad-~, ~allier~ (“to ally,” to bind to) and its noun ~alliage~; with ~ob-~, ~obliger~ (“to oblige,” literally to bind toward); and the much-discussed ~religion~ — explained already by Roman writers as either a “binding back” of the soul to the gods or a careful “re-reading.” A neat near-pair sits in modern French: ~relier~ also names the craft of ~bookbinding~, in which loose sheets are bound back into a single volume — the etymology made literal on a workbench, gathering scattered leaves into one tied-together whole.
en.relire:
From ~re-~ (“again”) + ~lire~ (“to read”), the latter from Latin ~legere~ (“to gather, choose, read”). ~legere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~legō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”). Cognate, through that root, with Ancient Greek ~λέγω~ (“to gather, say”) and its derivative ~λόγος~ (“word, reason”).

The leap from “gather” to “read” is one of the most quoted in etymology: to read was to gather up the letters of a text, picking out and assembling its signs into sense. ~re-~ adds the loop of repetition, so ~relire~ is “to read again, to read over.” The ancient *~leǵ-~ root spreads widely in French through both inherited and learned channels: ~élire~ (“to choose out, elect”), ~cueillir~ (“to gather”), ~recueillir~, ~collecter~, ~lecture~, ~légende~ (“what is to be read”), and the whole ~-logie~ suffix of the sciences. Every time one ~relire~ a page, one gathers its letters once more.
en.relâcher:
French Wiktionary traces it to Latin ~relaxāre~ (“to loosen again, to slacken”), while English Wiktionary gives Old French ~relascher~, with Latin ~relaxō~ as a comparison, and notes that modern French also reads it as ~re-~ + ~lâcher~. Both views fit: the Latin verb is itself ~re-~ + ~laxāre~ (“to loosen”), from the adjective ~laxus~ (“loose, slack”), and ~lâcher~ is the inherited French form of ~laxāre~. English ~relax~ is a later learned borrowing of the same Latin verb, and French has its own learned doublet, ~relaxer~.

The inherited verb moved along a gentle path from loosening a rope or a muscle to letting go of something held: to release a prisoner, to ease discipline, to let one's attention or effort slacken. The noun ~relâche~ means a pause or respite, and posted outside a theater it still means that there is no performance that day. The adjective ~lâche~ comes from the same Latin ~laxus~ and went from “slack” to “cowardly,” while ~relâchement~ names the slackening of rules or morals. The learned doublet ~relaxer~ narrowed to the sense of resting the body and mind.
en.reléguer:
Borrowed from Latin ~relēgāre~ (“to send away, to banish”), which joins ~re-~ (“back, away”) and ~lēgāre~ (“to send, to dispatch”). The verb ~lēgāre~ is itself derived from ~lēx~ (“law”) and covers the ideas of commissioning, deputing and bequeathing. English ~relegate~ and Italian ~relegare~ come from the same Latin verb, and here the Latin prefix was already in place before the word reached French.

In Roman law, ~relēgātiō~ was a form of banishment generally milder than full exile: a person could be ordered away from Rome or confined to a given place without losing citizenship or property. French kept the idea of sending someone away and softened it into the figurative: to ~reléguer~ is to push a person or a thing into a lesser place, as in reléguer au second plan (“to push into the background”). Sport adopted the noun ~relégation~ for a club demoted to a lower division. The root ~lēgāre~ gives ~léguer~ (“to bequeath”), ~légat~, ~délégué~ and ~collègue~.
en.remarquer:
Formed in French from the prefix ~re-~ (here intensive) and the verb ~marquer~ (“to mark”). ~Marquer~ entered French from Italian ~marcare~, reinforcing an older native ~merchier~, and ultimately rests on a Germanic word — Frankish *~marka~ / Proto-Germanic *~markō~ (“boundary, sign, mark”), the same source as English ~mark~ and ~march~ (a border region) and as French ~marche~ (“frontier march”).

To ~marquer~ is to set a sign upon something; to ~remarquer~ is, etymologically, to “mark it again,” to mark it out a second time so that it stands out to the eye. From this came the two living senses: to ~remarquer~ is both to notice (the thing marks itself out to your attention) and to observe aloud, to remark upon. The noun ~remarque~ followed, and the adjective ~remarquable~ describes precisely what is “worth marking out.” The Germanic root proved astonishingly fertile in French: ~marque~, ~marquer~, ~démarquer~, ~marqueur~, ~démarche~, and ~marquis~ (originally the lord of a border ~marche~) all carry, somewhere within them, the ancient sense of a boundary traced and a sign set down.
en.rembourser:
~rembourser~ is a parasynthetic French verb, built on the noun ~bourse~ (“purse”) with the affixes ~re-~, ~en-~, and ~-er~ — its inner picture is putting money back into a purse. ~bourse~ comes from Late Latin ~bursa~ (“purse, leather bag”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~búrsa~ (“hide, wineskin, leather”), so the purse was first simply a piece of skin. The same ~bursa~ gives Italian ~borsa~, Spanish ~bolsa~, and, through Medieval Latin, English ~purse~ and ~bursar~.

The image is exact and homely: to ~rembourser~ is to refill the purse one had emptied — to give back the money owed, to reimburse a cost. Modern French uses it for refunds, repayments, and reimbursements of every kind: ~rembourser~ un emprunt, une dette, des frais. From the same Greek-by-way-of-Latin ~bourse~ grew a surprisingly large family: ~bourse~ also means a scholarship and the stock exchange (la ~Bourse~), giving ~boursier~ (“scholarship-holder; stockbroker”), ~débourser~ (“to lay out, to spend”), and ~déboursement~ — a whole financial vocabulary unfurled from a single Greek word for an animal’s hide.
en.remercier:
From Old French ~mercier~ (“to thank, to express gratitude”), with the prefix ~re-~ here intensive rather than iterative. ~Mercier~ is built on ~merci~, from Latin ~mercedem~, accusative of ~merces~ (“wages, price, reward”). In late and Christian Latin, ~merces~ slid from “reward” to “favour, grace, mercy” — the heavenly reward — and Old French ~merci~ carried both “mercy” (as in ~à la merci de~, “at the mercy of”) and “grace, favour.”

The path from “mercy” to “thanks” runs through gratitude for a favour granted: to say ~merci~ was to acknowledge a kindness received, and ~remercier~ became the standard verb for rendering that acknowledgment. A pointed modern wrinkle: French uses ~remercier~ as a polite euphemism for sacking an employee — to “thank” someone for their services is to dismiss them, gratitude doubling as the door. The Latin ~merces~ kept its commercial sense in a parallel French family: ~mercenaire~ (“mercenary”), ~commerce~, ~merci~ itself, and ~marché~ — all rooted in the idea of payment, price, and exchange.
en.remettre:
From Old French ~remetre~, from Latin ~remittere~ (“to send back, to let go, to relax”), composed of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, to release, to throw”). ~Mittere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~meitō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”), an extension of *~mey-~ (“to change”). Its Romance reflexes are everywhere — Italian ~mettere~, Spanish ~meter~ — and through Latin ~missa~ it gave English ~mass~, ~mission~, and ~message~.

French ~mettre~ shifted from “to send” to the broad “to put, to place,” and ~remettre~ inherited a remarkable spread of meanings from that base: to put back (~remettre en place~), to hand over (~remettre une lettre~), to postpone (~remettre à demain~), and, echoing the Latin sense of “letting go,” to forgive — ~remettre une dette~ (“to remit a debt”), the very root of English ~remit~ and ~remission~. From the same ~mittere~ family French draws a rich harvest: ~admettre~, ~permettre~, ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, ~émettre~, plus ~message~, ~mission~, and ~messe~ — the Mass, named from the dismissal that closed the service.
en.remonter:
Attested from the twelfth century, ~remonter~ is formed from the verb ~monter~ (“to go up, to climb, to mount”) with the prefix ~re-~, which here marks either repetition (“to climb again”) or a return to a former position (“to go back up”). ~Monter~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~montāre~, derived from Latin ~mōns~, ~montem~ (“mountain”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~men-~ (“to project, to stand up”). Cognate with Italian ~montare~ and Spanish ~montar~, and — through ~mōns~ — with English ~mount~ and ~mountain~.

The striking thing is that to “go up” is, etymologically, to “mountain”: the verb was coined straight from the noun for a peak, the very image of something projecting upward. ~Re-~ then layers on a second motion — climbing anew, going back up a slope or a staircase, but also winding up a clock or watch (remonter une montre), reassembling parts (remonter un moteur), tracing a river or a history upstream (remonter le temps), and reviving someone's spirits (remonter le moral). From ~mōns~ French keeps ~mont~, ~montagne~, ~montée~, ~monture~, ~amont~, and ~surmonter~ — a whole landscape risen from a single word for a height.
en.remplacer:
A French formation rather than an inherited Latin word: ~remplacer~ is built from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~emplacer~ (“to put in place”), itself ~en-~ (“in”) plus ~place~ — so the literal sense is “to put back in the place (of another).” The noun ~place~ descends from Latin ~platea~ (“broad street, open space”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~plateîa~ (“broad way”), the feminine of ~platús~ (“broad, flat”), from a Proto-Indo-European *~pleth₂-~ (“flat, to spread”). Through the same ~platea~ come Italian ~piazza~, Spanish ~plaza~, and English ~place~.

The word thus contains a small history of substitution: to set one thing back into the space another occupied. From this came the sense of standing in for someone — a ~remplaçant~ is a substitute or stand-in — and the abstract notion of one thing superseding another. The deep root *~pleth₂-~ (“flat, broad”) underlies a surprising spread of French vocabulary: ~place~ and ~placer~, ~plat~ (“flat, a dish”), ~plaine~ (“plain”), ~plan~ (“flat surface, plan”), and ~plateau~ all carry the idea of flatness or spreading out, and English ~flat~, ~plate~, and ~plaza~ belong to the same family.
en.remplir:
From the twelfth century, a compound of the prefix ~re-~ and ~emplir~ (“to fill”). ~Emplir~ comes from Latin ~implere~ (becoming ~implīre~ in Late Latin), itself ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~plere~ (“to fill”), related to ~plenus~ (“full”). All trace to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”), which also gave English ~full~ and ~fill~, German ~voll~, Greek ~plērēs~ (“full”), and Sanskrit ~pūrṇa~.

Here ~re-~ does not really mean “again”: it intensifies, so ~remplir~ simply means “to fill completely,” and it has all but replaced the simpler ~emplir~ in everyday French. The verb spans the concrete and the abstract: one fills a glass (~remplir un verre~), fills in a form (~remplir un formulaire~), and fulfills a duty or condition (~remplir une obligation~) — the same metaphor of completion English keeps in ~fulfill~. From ~plenus~ and *~pleh₁-~ comes a broad family of French words: ~plein~, ~plénitude~, ~complet~, ~complément~, ~supplément~, ~plus~, and the borrowed ~plénier~ — a whole cluster turning on the notion of fullness and abundance.
en.remporter:
From ~emporter~ (“to carry away”) with the prefix ~re-~. ~Emporter~ is itself ~porter~ (“to carry”) plus the prefix ~en-~ (Latin ~inde~, “away from there”). ~Porter~ comes from Latin ~portare~ (“to carry”), tied to ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor, passage”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to lead, to pass over”). Cognates from this root include Greek ~poros~ (“passage”) and English ~fare~ and ~ford~.

~Emporter~ means “to carry off, to take away with oneself”; adding ~re-~ gives both “to carry back” and the idiomatic “to carry off again,” but its liveliest modern sense is figurative: ~remporter~ une victoire, un prix, un succès — “to carry off, to win” a victory or prize, as one bears away the trophy. The construction ~l'emporter sur~ (“to prevail over”) belongs to the same image of carrying the day. From ~portare~ flows a vast family: ~porter~, ~porte~, ~port~, ~porteur~, ~portable~, ~apporter~, ~exporter~, ~importer~, ~transporter~, ~comporter~, and ~rapporter~ — all built on the simple act of carrying.
en.renaître:
From the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~naître~ (“to be born”). ~naître~ comes through Old French ~naistre~ from Vulgar Latin *~nascere~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), itself from earlier *~gnāscī~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, to give birth”). That root is one of the most fertile in the family, producing Latin ~genus~ and ~gignere~, English ~kin~, ~kind~, and ~genus~, and the Romance siblings Spanish ~nacer~ and Italian ~nascere~.

~renaître~ means literally to be born a second time, and French uses it with the full weight of that image. A landscape ~renaît~ in spring; hope, courage, or a city ~renaît~ from its ashes — the verb carries an idea of return from apparent death that the plain ~naître~ lacks. It is the everyday word behind the ~Renaissance~, the “re-birth” of art and learning. Defectively, ~renaître~ famously has no past participle in standard use, so one cannot easily say “has been reborn” — a fitting grammatical gap for a verb about endless beginning again. From the same root *~ǵenh₁-~ French draws ~genre~, ~nature~, ~nation~, ~génération~, and ~gendre~ (“son-in-law”), a whole vocabulary of birth, kind, and kinship.
en.rencontrer:
From Old French ~encontrer~ (“to come up against, to meet”), itself derived from ~encontre~ (“an encounter, a meeting”), from Late Latin ~incontrā~, built from ~in-~ (“in, against”) + Latin ~contrā~ (“facing, against, opposite”). The verb ~rencontrer~ adds the prefix ~re-~ to ~encontrer~ and is attested from the 14th century. The base ~contrā~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~komterād~, a feminine form meaning “the opposite one of two,” from PIE *~kom-~ (“with, together”) plus the comparative suffix *~-teros~ — making ~contrā~ a doublet of Latin ~cum~. Cognate with Italian ~incontrare~ and Spanish ~encontrar~.

The oldest French uses were martial: around 1175 ~encontrer~ meant “to clash, to do battle,” for to meet an adversary head-on is to oppose him. The softer sense “to come upon by chance” developed alongside, and once the reinforcing ~re-~ was added, ~rencontrer~ settled into its modern range — to meet a person, to come across a thing, to confront a difficulty. The reflexive ~se rencontrer~ can even mean “to coincide,” two minds meeting on the same thought. The “against” core of ~contrā~ remains visible in the noun ~rencontre~ (“an encounter,” but also “a clash”) and in the fixed phrase ~à l'encontre de~ (“contrary to”). The same root underlies a great brood of French words: ~contre~, ~contraire~, ~contredire~, ~rencontre~, and the borrowed ~contraste~.
en.rendre:
From Vulgar Latin *~rendere~ (“to give back”), an altered form of Classical Latin ~reddere~ (“to give back, to return”). ~reddere~ is itself ~red-~ (“back”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — the same root that gives Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”) and English ~donor~ and ~date~. The irregular ~-nd-~ of the popular form almost certainly arose by contamination from ~prendere~ (“to take, to seize”), so that the verb for “giving back” reshaped itself on the verb for “taking.” Cognate verbs survive as Italian ~rendere~ and Spanish ~rendir~, and the family entered English as ~render~ and ~rent~.

The core idea is restitution — to hand back what one received — and French ~rendre~ still means “to give back” or “to return” something. From there the verb fanned out remarkably: to “render” an account, to “render” a service, to “render” a verdict, and, in the construction ~rendre quelqu'un heureux~, “to make someone happy” — to give them a quality, as it were. The reflexive ~se rendre~ even means “to surrender” or “to go (somewhere),” to take oneself off. From ~reddere~ and ~red-~ come French ~rendement~ (“yield, output”), ~reddition~ (“surrender”), and the noun ~rente~ (“income, annuity”), a sum regularly “given back.”
en.renfermer: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~enfermer~, itself ~en-~ (“in”) and ~fermer~ (“to close”). ~Fermer~ comes from Latin ~firmāre~ (“to make firm, secure”), from ~firmus~ (“firm”), the source of English ~firm~. The literal sense is “to lock up again,” but the prefix often adds only emphasis to ~enfermer~, which is how ~renfermer~ came to mean “to contain, to encompass”: to hold something within oneself or within a text, as in ~renfermer un secret~. The old sense of closing something in, and so of holding it, carries into ~renfermé~, said of someone withdrawn.
en.renforcer:
Derived from Old French ~enforcier~ (“to make strong”), formed with the prefix ~re-~ (here intensive or iterative). ~enforcier~ is itself ~en-~ plus the stem of ~force~, from Vulgar Latin ~fortia~, the neuter plural of Latin ~fortis~ (“strong, sturdy”) taken as a feminine noun. Cognate with Italian ~rinforzare~ and Spanish ~reforzar~, and — through ~fortis~ — with English ~force~ and ~fort~.

The building blocks are transparent: ~fortia~ gave French ~force~, ~en-~ turns the noun into a verb (“to put strength into”), and ~re-~ adds the idea of doing so anew or all the more — to ~renforcer~ is to strengthen what already had some strength. The same ~fortis~ underlies a broad family in French: ~fort~, ~forteresse~, ~fortifier~, ~effort~ (literally a “forcing-out” of strength), ~confort~ (originally a strengthening, a giving of courage), and ~renfort~, the noun of reinforcement. English ~comfort~ borrowed that last sense from Old French before it softened into mere coziness, so that an English ~effort~ and a French ~renfort~ are, at bottom, two ways of summoning the same Latin strength.
en.renier:
From Vulgar Latin *~renegāre~, built on Latin ~re-~ plus ~negāre~ (“to deny”). French Wiktionary adds that, synchronically, French speakers also read the verb as ~re-~ plus ~nier~, since ~nier~ itself descends from ~negāre~. Cognates include Italian ~rinnegare~ and Spanish ~renegar~. The two readings agree on the core idea: a denial, here of a faith, a person or a commitment.

The verb carries a strong religious and moral colour. To ~renier sa foi~ is to abandon one's faith, and ~renier ses amis~ or ~renier son fils~ is to disown them. Through the Romance cognates it also gave English two words. ~Renegade~ came by way of Spanish ~renegado~, from ~renegar~, and ~renege~ was taken from Medieval Latin ~renegare~. French itself has ~renégat~ for the person who has abandoned a faith or a cause, ~reniement~ for the act, and, from the simple verb, ~nier~ and ~dénier~.
en.renommer:
French ~renommer~ is transparently formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~nommer~ (“to name”). ~nommer~ descends from Latin ~nominare~ (“to name”), from the noun ~nomen~ (“name”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”). That ancient root is one of the most widely preserved in the family: it is cognate with English ~name~, German ~Name~, Ancient Greek ~ὄνομα~, and Sanskrit ~नामन्~ (~nāman~).

The prefix ~re-~ pulls the verb in two directions. In its plainest sense ~renommer~ means to “rename,” to give a new name, or to “re-elect,” to name someone again to an office. But ~re-~ also carries an intensive force — to name “again and again,” and so with praise — which yields the older, elevated sense “to glorify, to laud.” That intensive thread is what crystallized in the nouns ~renom~ and ~renommée~ (“renown, fame”): to be much-named is to be famous, exactly as English ~renown~, borrowed from Old French ~renomer~, shows the same drift from repeated naming to celebrity.
en.renoncer:
From Old French ~renoncier~, from Latin ~renūntiāre~, formed from ~re-~ plus ~nūntiāre~ (“to announce, report”), the verb of ~nūntius~ (“messenger, message”). In classical Latin ~renūntiāre~ meant first “to report back, bring word,” and then, by a turn toward formal declaration, “to declare off, refuse, give up.” The Romance line gives Spanish ~renunciar~ and Italian ~rinunciare~, and English ~renounce~ and ~announce~ come through the same ~nūntiāre~ family.

The second Latin sense — a public, official giving-up — is the one French inherited: to ~renoncer~ is to declare formally that one relinquishes a claim, a right, a habit, or a faith. The flavour of solemn announcement still clings to it, which is why one ~renonce~ à un trône, à un héritage, à ses droits — acts of weight, not mere quitting. From the same stem French keeps ~renoncement~ (“renunciation”) and ~renonciation~, the latter especially in legal use. The hidden ~nūntius~ — the messenger bearing word — also lies behind ~annoncer~, ~énoncer~, and ~prononcer~, a small fan of verbs all about the carrying of declarations.
en.renouer: Formed from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~nouer~ (“to tie a knot”). The base ~nouer~ comes through Middle and Old French ~noer~ from Latin ~nōdāre~, built on ~nōdus~ (“knot”), which also gave French ~nœud~. ~Renouer~ first meant to tie a knot again, as in a lace that has come undone. It then moved to human ties: one ~renoue~ a friendship, a conversation or a tradition that had been broken, as if the thread had been taken up again.
en.renouveler:
Formed from Old French ~nouvel~ (“new”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and a verbal suffix, paralleled by Late Latin ~renovellāre~. Behind ~nouvel~ stands Latin ~novellus~ (“young, new”), a diminutive of ~novus~ (“new”), from Proto-Indo-European *~newos~ (“new”) — the very root of English ~new~, German ~neu~, Ancient Greek ~νέος~ (~néos~), and Sanskrit ~náva~.

The verb means literally “to make new again,” and French has spread it across many domains: one ~renouvelle~ a passport or a subscription (extending its validity), ~renouvelle~ the air in a room, ~renouvelle~ a team or a wardrobe, and even ~se renouvelle~ as an artist by reinventing oneself. The reflexive also covers natural recurrence — a phenomenon that ~se renouvelle~ happens again. Note the doubled ~l~ in conjugation (~je renouvelle~), inherited from the ~-ell-~ of ~novellus~. From the same Latin ~novus~ descend a rich crop of French words: ~nouveau~ and ~nouvelle~, ~nouveauté~, ~renouveau~ (“renewal, revival”), ~rénover~ and ~rénovation~ (a learned doublet), ~innover~ and ~innovation~, and ~novice~.
en.renseigner:
French ~renseigner~ is ~enseigner~ (“to teach”) with the prefix ~re-~. ~Enseigner~ descends from Old French ~enseignier~, from Vulgar Latin *~īnsignāre~ (“to mark, point out”), a variant of Latin ~īnsignīre~, from ~signum~ (“sign, mark”). The deeper origin of ~signum~ is uncertain: it is referred either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), and the sources do not settle between them. Through ~signum~ the verb is cognate with English ~sign~, ~signal~, and ~ensign~, and with Italian ~insegnare~ and Spanish ~enseñar~.

The path of meaning is neat: to ~enseigner~ was to “point out by signs,” hence to instruct; ~renseigner~ adds ~re-~ and shifts from teaching a subject to “informing” a person — giving someone the precise sign or pointer they lack. From the same family come the noun ~renseignement~ (“(piece of) information,” and, in the plural, “intelligence” in the espionage sense), ~enseignement~ (“teaching”), and ~enseigne~ (“shop sign, ensign”) — all rooted in the idea of a mark that points the way.
en.rentabiliser: ~Rentabiliser~ is formed from the adjective ~rentable~ (“profitable”) with the suffix ~-iser~, “to make A.” The adjective is itself ~rente~ (“income, annuity”) + ~-able~, attested in Picard in the thirteenth century in ~terre rentable~, land that carried a charge. Before ~-iser~ the base takes the longer form ~rentabil-~, as in ~numériser~ from ~numérique~. The verb means “to make something pay,” by making an investment, a business or a piece of equipment bring in more than it costs.
en.rentrer:
From Old French ~entrer~ (“to enter, to go in”) prefixed with ~re-~, yielding the sense “to enter again, to go back in.” The base verb descends from Latin ~intrāre~ (“to enter, to go into”), itself built on ~inter~ (“among, between, within”) and ultimately on the Proto-Indo-European preposition *~h₁en~ (“in”). Cognates of the underlying family include Italian ~entrare~, Spanish ~entrar~, and — through the same root — English ~enter~ and ~interior~.

The prefix ~re-~ here is doubly productive: sometimes it means “again” (re-enter a room one has left), sometimes simply “back” or “inward,” and in many uses the iterative force has faded entirely, so that ~rentrer~ has become the ordinary verb for “to go home” (~rentrer chez soi~). It also developed transitive senses — to bring something in (~rentrer le foin~, to get the hay in before rain) and to hold something back (~rentrer ses larmes~, to hold back one's tears). From the same stem French built the noun ~rentrée~, used for the return to work or school after the summer holidays, a word with no neat English equivalent. The verb ~entrer~ and its relatives ~entrée~ and ~entremets~ all share the ancestor ~intrāre~.
en.renverser:
From earlier ~enverser~ with the prefix ~re-~; the old verb was later refashioned as ~inverser~. The base ~enverser~ derives from ~envers~ (“the reverse, the wrong side”), from Latin ~inversus~, past participle of ~invertere~ (“to turn around”), built from ~in-~ + ~versus~, from ~vertere~ (“to turn”), Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”). The root is cognate with English ~verse~, ~version~, ~convert~, and ~vertigo~.

The core image is purely physical — to turn something over, onto its ~envers~ — and from it ~renverser~ fanned out into one of French's most versatile verbs: to turn upside down, knock over, spill, run over (a pedestrian), overthrow (a government), and, figuratively, to bowl someone over with astonishment. The added ~re-~ intensified the “turning back/over” rather than meaning “again.” The same *~wert-~ root pervades French: ~vers~, ~verset~, ~version~, ~convertir~, ~divertir~, ~inverser~, ~pervers~, and the noun ~revers~ (“reverse, setback”). Even ~vertige~ belongs here — the world, after all, seeming to turn.
en.renvoyer:
Formed in French from ~envoyer~ (“to send”) with the iterative prefix ~r-~ (a form of ~re-~, “again, back”). ~Envoyer~ itself comes from Latin ~inviare~ (“to set on the way, to travel”), a compound of ~in-~ (“into, onto”) and ~via~ (“way, road”). The future and conditional stems of ~envoyer~ were reshaped in the 18th century under the pull of ~voir~ (“to see”), which is why French says ~enverra~. ~Via~ survives directly in English ~via~ and in Italian and Spanish ~via~ / ~vía~.

If ~envoyer~ is to put someone or something on the road, ~renvoyer~ is to put them back on it — and the prefix's two readings, “again” and “back,” fan out into a remarkable spread of senses. To ~renvoyer~ can mean to send again, to send back, to return (a ball, a favour, a letter), to refer (a reader to a footnote, a case to another court), to postpone, and — pointedly — to dismiss someone from a job or expel a pupil: putting them, so to speak, back out the door. From the same ~via~ come French ~voie~, ~voyage~, ~dévoyer~, ~convoyer~, and ~envoi~.
en.reparler: Formed from ~re-~ (“again”) + ~parler~ (“to speak”). The prefix comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here simply means repetition: to speak again, or to resume a conversation. The base ~parler~ is inherited from Old French and ultimately from Late Latin ~parabolāre~, a verb built on Latin ~parabola~ (“comparison, parable”), itself borrowed from Greek ~παραβολή~. To speak is thus, etymologically, to throw words side by side, and ~reparler~ adds nothing to that history except the second round.
en.repartir:
From ~partir~ prefixed with ~re-~ (“again, back”). ~partir~ comes from Old French ~partir~, from Latin ~partire~ / ~partiri~ (“to divide, share”), a verb on ~pars~, ~partis~ (“a part”). The modern sense “to leave” grew from “to divide”: to ~partir~ was first to part company, to separate oneself from a group — the share-out becoming a departure. Italian ~partire~ and Spanish ~partir~ keep both threads, and through ~pars~ French has ~part~, ~partie~, ~partage~, and the borrowed English ~part~.

French actually holds two close verbs here, distinguished by conjugation. ~repartir~ conjugated like ~partir~ (auxiliary ~être~) means “to set off again, to start up again, to resume.” But ~repartir~ also means “to retort, to reply sharply” — a sense that travels through the idea of “sending back” an answer, the verbal volley returned at once. Care is needed not to confuse this pair with ~répartir~ (“to distribute, apportion”), which carries the accent and stays nearer the original Latin sense of dividing into shares; that one keeps auxiliary ~avoir~. From the same family come ~départ~ (“departure”), ~répartition~, and ~repartie~ (“a quick retort”).
en.repasser: ~Repasser~ is formed from ~passer~ with the prefix ~re-~, “again, back.” The base ~passer~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, built on Latin ~passus~ (“step, pace”), from ~pandere~ (“to spread”). The prefix gives several senses: to pass by again, to retake an exam, to go over something once more, and, by extension, to iron, since an iron is passed back and forth across the cloth. The meanings share the idea of covering the same ground a second time.
en.repenser: From ~penser~ (“to think”) with the prefix ~re-~ in its sense of repetition, so ~repenser~ is “to think again,” to reconsider. ~Penser~ comes from Latin ~pensāre~ (“to weigh carefully”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh”), so to ~repenser~ is, at root, to weigh again. The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive in French, which is why one can rethink a plan, a system or a whole policy.
en.replacer: Formed in French from ~placer~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here marks a return to a former state, “to put back in its place.” The base ~placer~ is a verb of the sixteenth century built on the noun ~place~, from Old French ~place~, from Vulgar Latin *~plattĕa~, an altered form of Latin ~platēa~ (“broad street”), itself from Ancient Greek ~plateîa~ (“broad”). Behind the Greek lies the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleth₂-~ (“flat, broad”).
en.replier:
Formed in French as ~re-~ plus ~plier~ (“to fold”), the prefix here meaning “again” or “back”. The form is old: Old French already had ~replier~ and ~reploier~, which line up with Latin ~replicāre~ (“to fold back”), itself ~re-~ plus ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). The Latin base comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to weave”), which also gave Greek ~plékō~ (“I weave”). The sources do not settle whether the French verb is a pure French formation or in part a continuation of the Latin one; the two readings give the same result. A learned sister, ~répliquer~, was later taken from the same Latin verb, and English ~reply~ came from the Old French ~replier~.

The verb began with the plain gesture of folding something again or folding it back on itself: ~replier~ une carte, ~replier~ ses jambes. The meaning then widened in two directions. Troops that ~se replient~ fall back in order, and the noun ~repli~ names such a retreat. A person who ~se replie sur soi-même~ withdraws into themselves, folded up like the paper. The family splits in two, with ~replier~ for the physical fold and ~répliquer~ for the answer thrown back, in the same way as English ~reply~ and ~replicate~. Related modern French words include ~pli~, ~plier~, ~déplier~, ~repli~ and ~réplique~.
en.replonger: A transparent derivation from ~re-~ and ~plonger~. The base comes from Old French ~plongier~, from Vulgar Latin *~plumbicāre~, a verb built on Latin ~plumbum~ (“lead”): to plunge was first to drop like a lead weight. The prefix ~re-~ descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here carries its two commonest senses, repetition and return to a former state. The verb therefore means both “to dive in once more” and, figuratively, “to sink back” into thought, gloom or a bad habit. The same ~plumbum~ gave French ~plomb~ and ~plombier~, and English ~plumb~ and ~plunge~ are related to it.
en.reporter:
Formed from ~porter~ (“to carry”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”), so first “to carry back, to carry again.” The base ~porter~ descends from Latin ~portāre~ (“to carry, to bear”), ultimately from PIE *~per-~ (“to cross, to go through”), the same root that gave Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor”). Through that root ~portāre~ is distantly kin to English ~fare~ and ~ford~ and to German ~fahren~ — all once about passage and crossing.

The verb fanned out: to carry something back to where it was, to wear a garment again, to transfer (an emotion, a number in arithmetic), and — the sense that flowered later — to put off, to postpone. Beware a false friend within the family: the masculine noun ~reporter~ (“news reporter”) is not this verb at all but a 19th-century borrowing from English ~reporter~, itself from ~report~ + ~-er~ — so French re-borrowed a cousin that had emigrated through ~portāre~ centuries earlier. Native kin include ~report~ (“carryover, postponement”), ~reportage~, ~apporter~, ~emporter~, and ~supporter~.
en.reposer:
In the “rest” sense, from Old French ~reposer~, from Late Latin ~repausare~, from ~re-~ plus ~pausare~ (“to halt, to cease”), itself from Latin ~pausa~ (“a pause”), borrowed from Greek ~παῦσις~ (“a stopping”), from the verb ~παύειν~ (“to cease”). Cognate with Italian ~riposare~ and Spanish ~reposar~, and — through ~pausa~ — with English ~repose~ and ~pause~.

A tangle sits at the heart of this verb. Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to cease, to rest”) became so entwined with classical ~ponere~ (past participle ~positum~, “to place”) that the two fused: French ~poser~ inherits the form of ~pausare~ but much of the meaning of ~ponere~. That confusion is exactly why ~reposer~ today carries both senses at once — “to rest” (one ~se repose~) and “to put back down” (one ~repose~ a glass on the table). From ~pausare~ flow ~repos~, ~pause~, ~poser~, ~reposant~, and ~reposoir~; and the Greek ~παύειν~ behind it all surfaces in learned French through ~menopause~ and the musical ~pause~ — the silence that, etymologically, is simply a rest.
en.repousser:
~Repousser~ is formed from ~pousser~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base verb comes from Latin ~pulsare~ (« to beat, to push repeatedly »), the frequentative of ~pellere~ (« to drive, strike, thrust »), from PIE *~pelh₂-~ (« to drive, to beat »). French ~pouls~, ~pulser~, and ~pulsion~ are kin through the same ~pulsare~; English ~pulse~, ~push~, ~compel~, ~expel~, ~repel~, and ~appeal~ all trace to ~pellere~.

The ~re-~ adds the idea of « back » or « away »: to ~repousser~ is to push something back — an attacker, a temptation, a date on the calendar (one can ~repousser~ a meeting to next week). From physical shoving the senses fan out to repelling an enemy, rebuffing an offer, or turning someone away. Curiously, ~repousser~ also means « to grow back » — hair or grass that ~repousse~ — where ~pousser~ keeps its native French sense of a plant pushing upward. The ~pellere~ / ~pulsare~ root seeds a broad family: ~pousser~, ~poussée~, ~repousser~, ~propulser~, and ~impulsion~.
en.reprendre:
From Old French ~reprendre~ (attested early, “to take back, to blame”), from Latin ~reprehendere~ (“to seize again, to hold back, to reprove”), contracted in Vulgar Latin to ~reprendere~. The word is transparently ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~prendere~, the popular form of ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, to seize”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) + ~-hendere~ (“to grasp”). Latin ~prendere~ displaced classical ~capere~ across the Romance languages; cognate with Italian ~riprendere~ and Spanish ~reprender~.

The prefix ~re-~ carries both “again” and “back,” and ~reprendre~ exploits the whole spectrum: to take an object back, to resume an interrupted task (« reprendre le travail »), to take up a theme anew, to recover (« reprendre des forces »), and — preserving the Latin ~reprehendere~ sense of “to hold back, to check” — to reprimand someone. Commerce kept the literal grasp in ~repreneur~ (one who takes over a business) and ~reprise~ (a buy-back, a resumption, even a darned patch of cloth). The learned doublet ~répréhensible~ (“blameworthy”) descends from the same Latin verb, while ~prendre~, ~apprendre~, ~comprendre~, ~surprendre~, and ~entreprendre~ all share the grasping root.
en.reprocher:
From Old French ~reprochier~ (attested 1132), from a Vulgar Latin *~repropiare~ (« to bring near, set before the eyes »), built on ~re-~ + a verb *~propiare~ (« to approach »), itself from Latin ~prope~ (« near »). The image is concrete: to « reproach » was first to bring a deed right up before someone's face. Romance cognates confirm the line — Spanish ~reprochar~ and, with a different prefix, Italian ~rimproverare~.

The development runs from « to set before the eyes » to « to confront with, » and so to the modern « to hold against, to blame »: one ~reproche~ a fault to a person, putting the misdeed under their nose. French syntax preserves the directional sense — « ~reprocher~ quelque chose à quelqu'un » literally moves the grievance toward the wrongdoer. The same ~prope~ underlies a wide family, including ~proche~ (« near »), ~approcher~ (« to approach »), ~prochain~ (« next, neighbor »), and ~rapprocher~ (« to bring closer »); ~reprocher~ is the one member that turned nearness into accusation.
en.reproduire:
Formed within French from ~produire~ (“to produce”) and the prefix ~re-~ (“again, anew”). ~Produire~ comes from Latin ~prōdūcere~ (“to lead forth, to bring forth”), from ~prō-~ (“forward”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to draw, to pull”). Cognate, through *~dewk-~, with English ~tow~ and ~tug~ and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”), and with the Italian and Spanish counterparts ~riprodurre~ and ~reproducir~.

The core picture is a hand drawing something out into view: to ~produire~ is to “lead forth,” and to ~reproduire~ is to bring it forth again — hence “to copy, to depict faithfully, to breed.” The biological sense (animals that ~se reproduisent~) is a metaphor of repeated bringing-forth. From the same ~dūcere~ French inherited a long ~-duire~ family — ~conduire~, ~traduire~, ~séduire~, ~réduire~, ~induire~ — alongside ~duc~ (“duke,” a “leader”), ~conduit~, and ~aqueduc~. So a faithful ~reproduction~ is, etymologically, the same scene led out before the eyes once more.
en.représenter:
From Latin ~repraesentare~, formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~praesentare~ (“to make present, to present”). That verb derives from ~praesens~, the present participle of ~praesum~ — itself ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”) plus the verb of being, ~esse~ (“to be”). To “present” is thus, literally, to make something “be before” one's eyes; to ~repraesentare~ is to make it present again, to bring it back into view. The Romance descendants line up neatly: Italian ~rappresentare~, Spanish ~representar~, and French ~représenter~.

The Latin verb already carried the double charge that French keeps. In Roman usage ~repraesentare~ could mean “to pay on the spot, to deliver in person,” the sense of literal, physical presence; from there it slid toward “to depict, to portray, to stand for,” a sign standing in the place of an absent thing. Modern ~représenter~ holds both poles at once — an actor ~représente~ a character on stage, a deputy ~représente~ the voters, a painting ~représente~ a landscape. From the same family come ~présent~, ~présenter~, ~présence~, and the noun ~représentation~. To represent is to make the absent present once more.
en.repérer:
Denominal from the noun ~repère~ (“landmark, reference point”), with the verbal suffix. The noun has a tangled history. According to the TLFi, ~repère~ is the same word as ~repaire~ (“lair, den”); its ~-è-~ spelling, attested from 1676 in technical use, is a learned alteration made by associating the word with Latin ~reperire~ (“to find again, to recover”) — so the modern form was reshaped toward a Latin verb it does not actually descend from. ~Repaire~ itself comes from Old French ~repairier~ (“to return home”), traditionally referred to Late Latin ~repatriare~ (“to return to one's homeland,” from ~re-~ and ~patria~, “fatherland,” itself from ~pater~, “father”).

The development is a fine example of folk-etymological respelling. A ~repère~ began as a fixed point to which one returns and orients — a mark on a line, a survey benchmark — and ~repérer~ meant to set such marks. From there grew the modern senses: to locate, to spot, to detect. The “finding” feel of the word owes much to the very ~reperire~ that, the sources stress, shaped only its spelling and not its true descent. From the same ~patria~ family French has ~rapatrier~, ~patrie~, and ~patriote~.
en.requérir:
French ~requérir~ rests on Latin ~requirere~ (“to seek, to ask after, to need”), the prefix ~re-~ (here intensive, “anew, urgently”) joined to ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask, to inquire”). In French the verb was actually rebuilt on the native ~quérir~ (“to fetch, to seek”), modelled on its Latin parent — which is why it keeps the awkward, archaic conjugation of ~quérir~ rather than the smoother shape of a fresh borrowing. ~Quaerere~ is traced to a Proto-Italic *~kʷaizō~ and, more deeply, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷeh₂-~ (“to acquire”). Through ~requirere~, French is cousin to English ~require~ and ~request~.

The sense slid from plain seeking to formal demanding. To ~requérir~ is to call for something with authority or need: a situation ~requiert~ caution, and in court the ~procureur~ (public prosecutor) ~requiert~ a sentence — the technical heart of the word, preserved in the noun ~réquisitoire~ (“closing speech for the prosecution”). Old French ~requerre~ also carried the softer “to entreat, to court,” a shade still felt in ~requête~ (“a request, a petition”). The bare ~quaerere~ seeds a remarkable French harvest: ~quérir~, ~acquérir~ (“to acquire”), ~conquérir~ (“to conquer”), ~s'enquérir~ (“to inquire”), and the nouns ~question~, ~quête~, ~enquête~, and ~conquête~ — a whole vocabulary of seeking radiating from the same root as ~requérir~.
en.respecter:
From Latin ~respectāre~ (“to look back at, to keep in view, to take into account”), the frequentative of ~respicere~ (“to look back, to regard”), itself ~re-~ (“back”) + ~specere~ (“to look”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~spek̑-~ (“to observe, to watch”). The same root, through Latin ~specere~ and its noun ~speciēs~ (“appearance, sort”), gave French ~espèce~, ~spectacle~, and ~inspecter~; through Germanic it surfaces in German ~spähen~ (“to spy”) and English ~spy~.

The metaphor is one of looking: to respect something is, at root, to look back at it and hold it in view. French attests the modern verb only from 1554, in the sense « considérer comme une chose dont on doit tenir compte »; the sense « honorer », to show deference, follows by 1566, and « préserver, ne pas porter atteinte à » by 1573. The deadline sense in English — respecter un délai, « to meet a deadline » — extends the idea of scrupulously observing what is laid down. Older Old French had cousins like ~respitier~ (“to spare”), the ancestor of ~répit~ (“respite”). The same root *~spek̑-~ stands behind a sprawling French family: ~aspect~, ~suspect~, ~perspective~, ~spécial~, and the noun ~respect~ itself.
en.respirer:
Attested from the twelfth century, from Latin ~respirare~ (“to breathe back, to breathe again”), formed from ~re-~ (“again, back”) and ~spirare~ (“to breathe, to blow”). The origin of ~spirare~ is uncertain: De Vaan judges it probably onomatopoeic — an imitation of the sound of breath — while Kroonen would connect it to a PIE *~(s)peys-~ (“to blow, breathe”) and to Proto-Germanic *~fīsaną~. Through the same Latin verb, English gained ~inspire~, ~aspire~, and ~conspire~, all of them, at root, ways of breathing.

The ~re-~ in ~respirer~ suggests a breath drawn back in, the steady rhythm of inhaling once more; figuratively, to ~respirer~ is to take a breather, to feel relief. The root spirals out through French in a remarkable range of words: ~respiration~, ~soupir~ (“a sigh”), ~esprit~ (“spirit, mind” — once a “breath”), ~inspirer~, ~expirer~ (which means both to breathe out and to die), and ~aspirer~. Across this whole family runs the old intuition that breath and spirit are the same thing.
en.responsabiliser: Formed in French from the adjective ~responsable~ and the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make A”: to ~responsabiliser~ someone is to make them responsible, by giving them duties and the trust that goes with them.
