The adjective ~responsable~ comes from Middle French and was built on ~réponse~ (“answer”) plus ~-able~, so a responsible person is one who can be called to answer. French Wiktionary traces it to Latin ~responsus~, a form of the verb for answering. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which had transcribed Greek verbs, and it is highly productive in administrative French.
en.ressembler:
French ~ressembler~ is built within French itself: it is ~sembler~ (“to seem”) plus the intensive prefix ~re-~, formed in Old French. ~Sembler~ descends from Latin ~similāre~ (a variant of ~simulāre~, “to imitate, to copy”), itself from the adjective ~similis~ (“like, similar”). That adjective goes back through Proto-Italic *~semalis~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~sem-~ (“one, together”), the same root that yields notions of sameness and unity. Cognates run wide: Ancient Greek ~homós~ (“same”) and ~homalós~ (“even”), and through Romance, Italian ~rassomigliare~ and Spanish ~semejar~. English borrowed the learned ~similar~ and ~simulate~ from the same Latin stock.

In Old French ~sembler~ meant “to seem, to appear,” and adding ~re-~ pushed it toward “to seem like one another,” hence “to resemble.” The pair drifted apart in sense: today ~sembler~ is about appearance (“Il semble fatigué,” “he seems tired”) while ~ressembler~ is about likeness, and it keeps the telltale preposition à — one resembles ~à~ someone. The root *~sem-~ is astonishingly productive in French through several channels: the native ~sembler~, ~semblable~, ~ensemble~ (“together,” literally “in one”), and ~assembler~; and the learned ~similaire~, ~similitude~, ~simuler~, and ~dissimuler~. Even ~simple~ belongs here, “one-fold.” The humble verb for looking alike thus sits at the heart of a family all about oneness and sameness.
en.ressentir:
French ~ressentir~ was coined within French, around 1190, from ~sentir~ (“to feel, to sense”) plus the prefix ~re-~. ~Sentir~ descends from Latin ~sentīre~ (“to feel, to perceive, to be of an opinion”), which goes back through Proto-Italic *~sentjō~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~sent-~ (“to feel, to go, to head for”). The root's reach is long: Old High German ~sinnan~ (“to strive, to desire”) and modern German ~Sinn~ (“sense, meaning”) are cousins, and through Old French ~sentir~ English drew ~sense~, ~scent~, and ~sentiment~. Italian ~risentire~ and Spanish ~resentir~ mirror the French compound.

The prefix ~re-~ here is intensive rather than repetitive: ~ressentir~ is to feel something deeply, inwardly, often an emotion — ~ressentir de la joie~, ~ressentir de la douleur~. That inward force gave the noun ~ressentiment~ (“resentment”), a feeling re-felt and brooded over, which French lent to English and which philosophers later adopted untranslated. The PIE root *~sent-~, with its double sense of “feeling” and “heading toward,” seeded a remarkably broad French family: ~sentir~, ~sentiment~, ~sensible~, ~sensation~, ~consentir~ (“to feel together,” to agree), ~pressentir~ (“to sense beforehand”), ~assentiment~, and the learned ~sens~ itself. To resent, in French, is simply to feel something all the way through.
en.resserrer: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~serrer~. The base comes from Old French ~serrer~ (“to close, lock fast”), from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to bar”), from Latin ~sera~ (“a bolt or bar for a door”). The prefix ~re-~ (Latin “back, again”) adds the idea of doing it again, or of drawing something tighter still. So ~resserrer~ means to tighten again or further: to narrow a gap, to draw bonds closer. The same bolted door gives French ~serrure~ (“lock”).
en.ressortir:
From ~re-~ + ~sortir~ (« to go out »), literally « to go out again. » The descent of ~sortir~ itself is disputed: Littré derived it from a Vulgar Latin *~surrectire~, from Latin ~surrectus~ (« raised up »), which would make it a doublet of ~sourdre~ (« to well up ») from ~surgere~; the TLFi instead ties it to ~sortiri~ (« to draw lots »), from ~sors~ (« lot, fate »). The sources do not settle the matter, so the prefixed ~ressortir~ inherits that uncertainty.

A separate, homographic ~ressortir~ — « to fall under the jurisdiction of » — comes not from ~sortir~ but from the noun ~ressort~ (« jurisdiction, spring »); the Académie française condemns conjugating that legal sense like a third-group verb. The everyday verb ranges from the literal (to step back outside, to take something out again) to the figurative « to stand out, » as a color ~ressort~ against a background. Kin of the contested base survive in ~sortie~ and, if the ~sors~ account holds, in ~sort~ (« fate ») and ~sorte~ (« kind »).
en.ressourcer: Formed in French from the noun ~ressource~ and the suffix ~-er~, and used today above all in the reflexive ~se ressourcer~, to recover one's strength or energy. The base ~ressource~ comes from Old French ~resource~, the feminine past participle used as a noun of the old verb ~resourdre~ (“to rise again, to be restored”). English Wiktionary traces the same idea to Latin ~resurgere~ (“to rise again”), made of ~re-~ (“again”) and ~surgere~ (“to rise”). A resource was therefore first something that raises one up again. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.restaurer:
From Latin ~restaurare~ (“to rebuild, repair, renew”), formed on ~re-~ (“again”) plus a ~-staurare~ element also seen in ~instaurare~ (“to set up, establish”). The verb passed through Old French and survives in Italian ~restaurare~ and Spanish ~restaurar~; English borrowed it twice over, as ~restore~ and ~restaurant~.

The culinary detour is the surprise. In the eighteenth century a ~restaurant~ was not a place but a thing: a ~restaurant~ was a rich, fortifying broth meant to “restore” the strength of the weak — a restorative. A Parisian bouillon-seller is traditionally said to have advertised such restoratives, and the word for the broth slid to the establishment that served it, then to any eatery, before being re-exported across the world. Meanwhile the older sense thrives: one ~restaure~ a painting, a building, a monarchy. From the same Latin source French keeps ~restauration~ (both “restoration” and “catering”), ~restaurateur~ (“restorer” and “restaurant-keeper” alike), and the doublet ~instaurer~ (“to institute, establish”), its near-twin built on the same root.
en.rester:
Attested from the twelfth century, borrowed from Latin ~restāre~ (“to stay behind, to remain, to be left over”), formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~stāre~ (“to stand, to stand firm”). Latin ~stāre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~stāō~ and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the most fertile roots in the language family. Through ~stāre~, ~rester~ is a sibling of Italian ~restare~ and Spanish ~restar~ and ~quedar~, and, through the same PIE root, a distant cousin of English ~stand~ and ~stay~.

The word's logic is spatial: what ~restāre~ described was standing back, holding one's ground while others moved on — hence “to remain.” Old French already had the inherited ~ester~ from ~stāre~, and ~rester~ (~re-~ + ~ester~) eventually displaced it as the everyday verb of staying. A trace of the “left over” sense survives in arithmetic, where French children say ~il reste~ for a remainder. The root *~steh₂-~ stocks French with a vast family: ~stable~, ~station~, ~statue~, ~constant~, ~rester~ itself, and — surprisingly — the past participle ~été~ of ~être~, which descends not from ~esse~ but from ~status~, the participle of ~stāre~.
en.restituer:
Borrowed in the 13th century from Latin ~restituere~ (“to set up again, put back in place, restore”), from ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~statuere~ (“to set up, establish”), itself built on ~status~, from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), PIE root *~steh₂-~. Cognate with Italian ~restituire~, Spanish ~restituir~ and English ~restitution~, which reached English through French. The verb belongs to the tidy French squad in ~-stituer~, all of them ways of making something stand: ~constituer~ (“set up together”), ~instituer~ (“set in place”), ~destituer~ (“make someone cease to stand in office”), ~substituer~ (“set one thing in another's place”).

The TLFi's record of senses reads like the program of a single idea — making what fell stand again. First the law: to give back what was wrongfully taken (13th century). Then to restore something to its earlier state (circa 1355); to reconstruct a corrupted or missing passage of text (1690); to redraw a ruined monument on paper (1835); to make the past live again in thought (1849); finally to reproduce faithfully — a recording that gives back timbre and detail (late 19th century). All these senses are still alive: philologists restitute lost readings, archaeologists restitute temples, museums debate the restitution of looted art, and sound engineers promise un son fidèlement restitué. Around the verb stand the kin of ~stāre~: ~statue~, ~statut~, ~station~ — and ~état~ itself, from Latin ~status~ via Old French ~estat~: the State, etymologically, is simply “a standing.” To restitute is the root's promise kept: what once stood will be made to stand again.
en.restreindre:
From Middle French ~restraindre~, from Latin ~restringere~ (“to bind back, draw tight”), formed from ~re-~ and ~stringere~ (“to draw tight, bind”). The Proto-Italic ~stringō~ blended two Proto-Indo-European roots: *~strengʰ-~ (“to twist, tie”) and *~streyg-~ (“to stroke, strip off”). Through Old French ~estreindre~ this verb is cognate with English ~strain~, ~strict~, and ~stringent~, and the same family connects to ~strong~.

The Latin sense was physical — to pull something tight — and French kept that grip: to ~restreindre~ is to narrow, limit, or hold in check. The doublet ~étreindre~ (“to embrace, clasp”) preserves the literal tightening, while ~restreindre~ took the figurative path toward restriction. From the same root French gathers a notable cluster: ~restriction~, ~astreindre~, ~contraindre~, and ~étreinte~ — a whole vocabulary of binding, squeezing, and compulsion grown from one idea of drawing a cord taut.
en.restructurer: Formed from ~re-~ and ~structurer~, “to structure again.” The base is a verb built in French on the noun ~structure~, from Latin ~strūctūra~ (“a building, a fitting-together”), the action noun of ~struere~ (“to pile up, to build”), a verb related to English ~strew~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here marks repetition: to give a company, a debt or a text a new arrangement. The family of ~struere~ also gives ~construire~, ~détruire~ and ~instruire~.
en.retenir:
From Latin ~retinere~ (“to hold back, to keep”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back”) and ~tenere~ (“to hold”). Latin ~tenere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), the notion being that to hold is to keep something stretched taut. The same root gave Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), Greek ~teinein~ (“to stretch”), Sanskrit ~tanoti~ (“stretches”), and English ~thin~; the compound parallels Italian ~ritenere~ and Spanish ~retener~.

~Retenir~ fans out across many senses, all from “to hold back”: to retain or keep (~retenir une place~, “to reserve a seat”), to hold someone back (~retenir quelqu'un~), to hold back a feeling (~retenir ses larmes~, “to hold back one's tears”), in arithmetic “to carry” a digit, and — most usefully for a learner — “to remember,” to hold something in the mind. The noun ~retenue~ means both “restraint, reserve” and a school “detention.” From ~tenere~ comes a great family: ~tenir~, ~tenue~, ~contenir~, ~maintenir~, ~obtenir~, ~soutenir~, ~entretenir~, and ~appartenir~ — and, through the kindred ~tendere~, ~tendre~, ~tension~, and ~tente~.
en.retentir:
The verb is formed from the prefix ~re-~ and Old French ~tentir~ (“to give out a sound”), which was built on the participle of Latin ~tinnīre~ (“to ring, to jingle”). The form of that participle is ~tinnitus~, and French Wiktionary notes that ~tentir~ is a lexical doublet of ~tinter~, which developed from the same Latin verb. English preserves the Latin participle almost unchanged in the medical term ~tinnitus~, the ringing in the ears. The Latin verb is imitative: its sound mimics the jingle it describes.

In Old French, ~tentir~ meant to ring or resound, and ~re-~ added the idea of an echo or a sound sent back, so ~retentir~ is to resound, to ring out. Simple ~tentir~ later disappeared, leaving ~tinter~ for the bell and ~retentir~ for the louder, longer noise: a trumpet, a shot, a cry. The verb then took a figurative turn. A word, a piece of news or an event can ~retentir~ in the mind or on a situation, meaning to have repercussions, as in ~retentir sur la santé~ (“to affect one's health”). The family also gave ~retentissant~ (“resounding, far-reaching”) and ~retentissement~ (“echo, repercussion”), both used just as often of fame as of noise.
en.retirer:
A French formation, ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~tirer~ (“to pull, to draw”), built within Old French and gradually displacing the older ~retraire~ (from Latin ~retrahere~, “to draw back”). The base ~tirer~ has a famously disputed origin: many trace it, with Spanish ~tirar~, to a Germanic source, while others derive it from a reanalysis of Old French ~martirier~ (“to torture, to martyr”), from ~martyre~ — the present participle ~martirant~ supposedly re-cut as ~mar~ (“badly”) + a form linked to ~tirant~.

Whatever its root, ~tirer~ supplanted the Latin-derived ~traire~ (from ~trahere~, “to pull”) across much of its territory, and ~retirer~ rode that wave. The literal core is “to pull back”: one ~retire~ a hand, a sword, a candidate from a race. From there spread the senses “to remove, to take off” (clothing), “to withdraw” (money from a bank), and the reflexive ~se retirer~, “to withdraw, to retire from the world.” The same field of ~tirer~ and ~trahere~ yields ~attirer~, ~soutirer~, ~étirer~, ~tiroir~, and — from the Latin side — ~extraire~ and ~soustraire~.
en.retomber: Formed from ~tomber~ and the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”), here in its senses of repetition and return to a former state or place: to fall again, to fall back down. The base verb has a lively history of its own. It comes from an expressive Vulgar Latin *~tumbāre~, which merged in Old French with ~tumer~ (“to tumble”), a verb of Frankish origin. From the fifteenth century ~tomber~ pressed in on the older ~choir~ and eventually ousted it from everyday speech, which left ~tomber~ free to build compounds such as ~retomber~ on its own.
en.retoucher: ~Retoucher~ is formed from ~toucher~ with the prefix ~re-~, “again.” The base comes from Old French ~tochier~, from Vulgar Latin *~toccāre~ (“to knock, to strike”), which is generally held to be imitative of the sound ~toc~. So ~retoucher~ first meant simply “to touch again.” It then took the specialized sense of going back over a finished work to correct it, as a painter does with a canvas, a photographer with a picture or a tailor with a garment.
en.retourner:
From Old French ~torner~, ~tourner~ (“to turn”) prefixed with ~re-~ (“again, back”). The base verb descends from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe, to round off, to fashion”), from ~tornus~ (“lathe”), itself borrowed from Greek ~tórnos~ (“a lathe, a tool for drawing circles”), traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, to turn, to bore”). Through ~tornāre~ the family includes Italian ~tornare~, Spanish ~tornar~, and English ~turn~ and ~tourney~.

The original image is the craftsman's lathe, shaping wood or metal as it spins — so ~tourner~ began as “to turn on a wheel” and broadened to every kind of turning. With ~re-~, ~retourner~ covers both turning over (~retourner une crêpe~, to flip a pancake; ~retourner la terre~, to turn the soil) and going back (~retourner chez soi~, to return home), and reflexively ~se retourner~ is to turn around or, of a sleeper, to toss. The verb can even mean to shake someone emotionally — ~ça m'a retourné~, “it turned me upside down.” The lathe-root spread widely in French: ~tour~ (a turn, a lap, a trick — and, as a feminine noun, a tower by a different route), ~tournoi~ (a tournament, where contestants wheeled about), ~tournevis~ (screwdriver), ~contour~, ~détour~, and ~retour~ (a return) all turn on the same Greek lathe.
en.retracer:
Formed within French from the prefix ~re-~ and ~tracer~ (“to trace, to draw”), itself from Old French ~tracier~, from Vulgar Latin *~tractiāre~ (“to follow a track”), built on ~tractus~, past participle of Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag”). The deeper origin of ~trahere~ is genuinely obscure: some scholars connect it with the Germanic family of English ~drag~ and ~draw~ (Proto-Germanic *~draganą~), but the sound correspondences are irregular, and others prefer to see a loanword from some lost pre-Indo-European language — the question remains open. Cognate with Italian ~tracciare~ and Spanish ~trazar~; English ~trace~ was itself borrowed from the French verb.

The verb's own history runs from the hunt to the memoir. Around 1390, ~retracier~ meant “to follow someone's trail, to pursue”; in the sixteenth century it settled into “to draw anew”; and from the mid-seventeenth century it took on the sense that dominates today — to recount events, to call them back in words. To retrace a life is thus, etymologically, to follow its tracks a second time. The parent ~trahere~ is one of the great providers of French vocabulary: from it descend ~traire~ (“to milk” — to draw the milk), ~trait~, ~portrait~ (a likeness “drawn forth”), ~traiter~ (from the frequentative ~tractāre~, “to handle”), ~traîner~, ~train~, and the learned squad ~extraire~, ~soustraire~, ~distraire~ and ~abstraire~ — to distract someone being, literally, to drag their mind elsewhere. English worked the same vein with ~tract~, ~tractor~ and ~attract~, alongside the French loans ~trace~ and ~train~.
en.retraiter: ~Retraiter~ has two separate formations. In the first, French added ~-er~ to the noun ~retraite~ to make a verb meaning “to retire someone, to pension off.” In the second, it joined ~re-~ (“again”) to ~traiter~, giving “to treat again,” hence “to reprocess,” as with nuclear fuel, waste or data. The base ~traiter~ comes from Latin ~tractāre~ (“to handle, to deal with”), a frequentative of ~trahere~ (“to draw”), and is related to Italian ~trattare~ and Spanish ~tratar~. The prefix ~re-~ here keeps its plain repeating sense.
en.retrancher: Formed in French from ~re-~ and ~trancher~ (“to cut”). The prefix does not mean cutting again here; it points toward removal, so ~retrancher~ means “to cut off, to deduct, to remove.” The base ~trancher~ comes from Old French ~trenchier~, whose Latin source is uncertain: by one account a Vulgar Latin *~trinicare~ (“to cut in three”), by another an alteration of ~truncare~ (“to lop”). English ~retrench~ belongs to the same family of Old French verbs and keeps the sense of cutting back expenses.
en.retransmettre: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~transmettre~, which French reshaped from Latin ~transmittere~ (“to send across”), made of ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~mittere~ (“to send”). Here ~re-~ expresses repetition, so ~retransmettre~ is to transmit again: to pass a message, an order or a signal on a second time, or to relay it onward. The verb is especially common for relaying an event or a broadcast. French ~transmettre~ and English ~transmit~ share the same Latin source.
en.retravailler: Formed from ~travailler~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to rework a text, a piece of metal or a design, or to go back to work. The base comes from Old French ~traveillier~ (“to torment, to cause suffering”), traditionally explained from Vulgar Latin *~tripāliāre~, “to torture with the ~tripalium~,” a device of three stakes. That tidy story is disputed, and some scholars prefer a Late Latin *~trabicula~ (“little beam”) as the source. Whichever is right, the verb travelled from “to torment” to “to toil” to today's neutral “to work,” and ~retravailler~ simply repeats it.
en.retrouver:
From ~re-~ (“again, back”) + ~trouver~ (“to find”), the latter from Vulgar Latin *~tropāre~ (“to compose, invent a melody,” hence “to invent, devise, find”), from Late Latin ~tropus~ (“figure of speech, melody”), borrowed from Greek ~tropos~ (“turn, way, mode”), from ~trepein~ (“to turn”). Cognate with Italian ~trovare~ and Occitan ~trobar~ — the verb that gave ~troubadour~, literally “one who finds (invents) verse.”

The leap from “to compose” to “to find” runs through poetry: to ~trobar~ was to invent a song, to hit upon the right turn of phrase, and from this creative finding came the ordinary sense of coming upon anything. The prefix ~re-~ adds the nuance of recovery — to find what was lost, or to find again — so ~retrouver~ means both “to locate once more” and, of people, “to be reunited”; ~se retrouver~ is to meet up, or to find oneself in a place or a state. The same Greek ~tropos~ surfaces in learned French words far from the verb's everyday warmth — ~trope~, ~tropique~ (the “turning point” of the sun), and ~héliotrope~ (the flower that turns toward the sun) — while ~trouvère~, the northern cousin of ~troubadour~, preserves the medieval poet-finder.
en.revaloriser: Formed from ~valoriser~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”), ~revaloriser~ means “to restore or raise the value of” something, as with a salary, a pension or a profession. The base ~valoriser~ is a twentieth-century coinage built on ~valeur~ with the suffix ~-iser~. ~Valeur~ comes from Latin ~valor~, from the verb ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). English ~wield~ and ~value~ belong to this family. Here ~re-~ expresses a return to a former level, or an increase, rather than a plain repetition.
en.revendiquer:
~Revendiquer~ is a derivative of the noun ~revendication~ and followed the same course: first ~reivendiquier~, it lost its initial ~i~ under the pull of words built with the prefix ~re-~, yielding ~revendiquier~ and then the modern ~revendiquer~. Behind it stands Latin ~vindicare~ (« to lay claim to, to avenge, to set free »), traditionally analysed as ~vim~ (« force ») + a root related to ~dicere~ (« to declare ») — the legal gesture of declaring a claim by force. From the same ~vindicare~ French also drew the doublet ~venger~ (« to avenge »).

The ~re-~ here is intensive rather than truly repetitive: to ~revendiquer~ is to claim something forcefully as one's due — a right, a territory, the authorship of an act. From the Roman courtroom, where ~vindicatio~ asserted ownership of property, the word kept its combative, assertive charge. English ~vindicate~, ~vengeance~, and ~avenge~ all descend from the same Latin verb, as do Italian ~rivendicare~ and Spanish ~reivindicar~.
en.revendre: Formed from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~vendre~, although English Wiktionary adds that it was already Latin ~revēndere~ before reaching Old French, so the prefixed form is inherited and not coined in French. The base ~vendre~ comes from Latin ~vendere~, itself a contraction of ~vēnum dare~ (“to give for sale”). ~Revendre~ means to sell again what one has bought, and so to resell. It gave ~revendeur~ (“reseller, dealer”) and ~revente~ (“resale”).
en.revenir:
Formed in Old French from the prefix ~re-~ (« back, again ») and the verb ~venir~ (« to come »), attested as early as the tenth century. ~venir~ comes from Latin ~venire~, from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”). That root reached English through Germanic as the verb ~come~, and shows up in Ancient Greek ~baínō~ (“I go”) and Sanskrit ~gácchati~ (“he goes”).

The compound is transparent — « to come back » — and stayed close to that sense, but French let it bloom in idiom. ~revenir~ means to return in space, but also « to come to » after a faint, to « amount to » a price (~cela revient cher~), to « come down to » in argument (~cela revient au même~), and, in cooking, to brown lightly (~faire revenir des oignons~). Like its parent ~venir~, it takes the auxiliary ~être~ in compound tenses. The root *~gʷem-~ feeds a whole French clan built on ~venir~: ~devenir~, ~convenir~, ~prévenir~, ~parvenir~, the noun ~avenir~ (« what is to come »), and ~venue~.
en.reverser: From the prefix ~re-~ + ~verser~. The prefix ~re-~ means “again” or “back,” and ~verser~ (“to pour, to pay in”) comes from Late Latin *~versāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~vertere~ (“to turn”). To ~reverser~ is therefore to pour again, to pour back, or, in finance, to pay a sum on to someone else or into another account. A second, modern verb of the same shape exists: ~reverser~ in the sense “to reverse-engineer,” formed from English ~reverse~ + ~-er~. The two words are only homonyms.
en.revisiter: The two sources frame it differently. English Wiktionary gives Old French ~revisiter~, from Latin ~revīsitāre~, while French Wiktionary derives it from ~visiter~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), which is how a modern speaker hears it. ~Visiter~ comes from Latin ~visitāre~ (“to go to see, to visit often”), a frequentative of ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), which also gave English ~wit~. The verb means to visit a place again, and figuratively to look at a familiar subject or work from a new angle.
en.revivre: From Latin ~revīvere~ (“to live again, to come back to life”), built from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~vīvere~ (“to live”). French also treats it as ~re-~ + ~vivre~, and the two analyses give the same meaning. The verb has a literal sense, “to come back to life,” and a looser one, “to feel alive again,” as when relief or good news makes someone ~revivre~. It can also be transitive, meaning “to live through again”: one ~revit~ a memory, an experience or a moment from the past.
en.revoir:
From Old French ~revoir~, ~reveoir~, from Latin ~revidere~ (“to see again, to go back to see”), compounded from the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”) and ~videre~ (“to see”). ~Videre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weid-~ (“to see,” and by extension “to know”). Cognate, through ~videre~, with Italian ~rivedere~ and Spanish ~rever~, and — through the root *~weid-~ — with Greek ~eîdon~ (“I saw”), Sanskrit ~véda~ (“I know”), and English ~wit~ and ~witness~.

~Revoir~ is among the most transparent of French compounds: ~re-~ plus ~voir~, “to see again.” Its substantival use lies hidden inside the everyday farewell ~au revoir~ — literally “until the seeing-again,” a promise of reunion rather than a flat goodbye. The root *~weid-~ is one of the great Indo-European wellsprings, binding sight to knowledge: from it French draws ~voir~, ~vision~, ~évident~, ~prévoir~, ~revue~, and ~vue~, while the same root surfaces in Latin-borrowed English ~vision~ and ~evident~ and in the Germanic ~wise~, ~wisdom~, and ~idea~ (through Greek). To ~revoir~ someone is, etymologically, to let the eyes know them once more.
en.revêtir:
From Old French ~revestir~, from ~re-~ (“again, anew”) + ~vestir~ (“to clothe”), from Latin ~vestire~ (“to dress”), a denominal of ~vestis~ (“garment”). ~Vestis~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~westis~ and to PIE *~wéstis~, from the root *~wes-~ (“to clothe, to be dressed”). The same root surfaces in Gothic ~wasti~ (“garment”), in Tocharian B ~wastsi~, and — most familiarly — in English ~wear~. Through Latin ~vestire~ and ~vestis~ it also yields the learned English borrowings ~vest~ and ~vestment~.

The ~re-~ here is not really “again”: ~revêtir~ does not mean to re-dress but to clothe fully, to robe — hence its use for donning ceremonial or official dress, and figuratively for being “clothed” with authority, dignity, or a title. From clothing a person the sense spread to clothing a thing: a wall ~revêtu~ with marble, a road surface, a coating — whence the noun ~revêtement~ (“cladding, coating, surfacing”). The plain verb ~vêtir~ and its other compound ~dévêtir~ (“to undress”) belong to the same family, as do ~vêtement~, ~veste~, and the borrowed ~investir~ and ~travesti~, all rooted in the idea of putting on a garment.
en.rigoler:
The origin of ~rigoler~ is explained in two competing ways. The first, given by both Wiktionaries, takes it as a blend of ~rire~ (“to laugh”) and Old French ~galer~ (“to have fun, to enjoy oneself”). ~Rire~ is inherited from Latin ~rīdēre~ (“to laugh”), and ~galer~ is of Frankish origin. On this reading the verb joins “laughing” and “making merry” into one jolly word, a pairing that suits its informal register.

The second account, found in French Wiktionary, derives the verb from ~rigole~ (“small channel, drainage trench”), with an initial sense of “to arrange the edges of a ditch or river so that the water can flow freely.” The source does not spell out how channeling water became laughing, so this is best taken as a proposal, not a settled fact. Either way, the verb is colloquial and has produced ~rigolo~ (“funny”), ~rigolade~ (“fun, a lark”) and ~rigoleur~.
en.rimer: ~Rimer~ is formed from the noun ~rime~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, although English Wiktionary treats it simply as inherited from Old French ~rimer~. The origin of ~rime~ itself is uncertain. French Wiktionary mentions Old High German ~rim~ (“number”), modern German ~Reim~ (“rhyme”), and perhaps Latin ~rhythmus~ (“measure, cadence”). Friedrich Diez favored the German source, since ~rhythmus~ could not give Italian ~rima~. English ~rhyme~ owes its spelling to a late learned association with ~rhythm~.
en.rincer:
The origin of ~rincer~ is disputed. It is attested in Old French as ~reinser~ and ~raincer~ (thirteenth century) and as ~raïncier~ and ~recincier~, and Middle French has ~rincer~. One account goes back to Latin ~recentāre~ (“to make fresh”), from ~recēns~ (“fresh, recent”), through a Vulgar Latin *~recentiāre~, giving Old French ~recincier~ (“to rinse, to freshen, to wash”), with a later dissimilation. The rival account, which goes back to Diez, derives it from Old Norse ~hreinsa~ (“to clean”), from Proto-Germanic *~hrainisōną~ (“to purify”), cognate with Gothic ~hrains~ (“pure”) and German ~rein~. Scheler supported the Norse origin with the Picard form ~rinser~, which he said would have become ~rincher~ had it come from Latin, and rejected a third Latin candidate, ~runcāre~ (“to weed”). A further proposal, by Nisard, links it to ~rain~ (“branch”), from Latin ~ramus~, through the paddle used to beat laundry, but the objection is that the verb would then have been *~rainceler~. English ~rinse~ is a cognate.

Whatever its source, the verb is about washing clean. ~Rincer~ is to wash out a glass, a mouth or a piece of laundry in fresh water after the main wash, and the noun ~rinçage~ names the step. Slang also uses the verb for drinking: one can rincer a round of drinks, or rincer one's throat, and to be ~rincé~ is to have been cleaned out of money. In another popular phrase, rincer l'œil, a person feasts the eyes on something. The image is the same each time, a thorough flushing.
en.rire:
From Middle French ~rire~, from Old French ~rire~, from Vulgar Latin *~rīdĕre~, a shift of the Classical Latin verb ~rīdēre~ (“to laugh, to smile, to mock”) from the second to the third conjugation. The change of conjugation class is what kept ~rire~ short and irregular in French. Beyond Latin the trail goes cold: ~rīdēre~ has no securely established Proto-Indo-European etymology, so cautious etymologists decline to reconstruct a deeper root. Within Romance it is cognate with Italian ~ridere~, Spanish ~reír~, and Portuguese ~rir~.

Latin ~rīdēre~ already carried the double edge the French verb keeps — open laughter on one side, derision on the other, as in ~rire de~ quelqu'un (“to laugh at someone”). The smiling sense lived in the derived ~subrīdēre~ (“to smile,” literally “to laugh a little under”), which gave French ~sourire~, where ~sous-~ + ~rire~ still means a laugh held quietly beneath the surface. The same Latin stem furnished ~ridicule~ and ~ridiculiser~ (from ~rīdiculus~, “laughable”), ~dérision~ and ~dérisoire~, and the noun ~rire~ itself. So from one uncertain ancient verb the French language draws its whole vocabulary of mirth: the belly laugh, the quiet smile, and the cutting ridicule alike.
en.risquer:
Attested from the late sixteenth century, ~risquer~ is a denominal verb formed on the noun ~risque~, borrowed from Old Italian ~risco~ (modern ~rischio~). The Italian word's ultimate origin is disputed, but the favoured account derives it from Vulgar Latin *~resecum~, literally “that which cuts,” from ~resecare~ (“to cut off”) — first a rock or reef that could gash a ship's hull, then the peril such hazards posed to seaborne cargo, and at last “risk” in the abstract. Rival proposals invoke Greek ~rhíza~ (“root, cliff”) or Arabic ~rizq~ (“fortune, what providence allots”), but neither is secure.

The maritime stamp is the memorable part: ~risque~ was a merchant's and insurer's word before it was anyone else's, naming the gamble that goods might never reach port. From the concrete cutting edge of a reef the sense broadened to any exposure to loss, and the verb ~risquer~ now ranges from “to endanger” to the everyday “to risk doing.” If the *~resecum~ etymology holds, the noun shares its root with French ~réséquer~ (“to resect, cut away”) and, through ~secare~, with ~scier~, ~section~, and ~sécateur~ — a whole family centred on the act of cutting.
en.rivaliser: Formed in French from the noun ~rival~ and the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to act as a rival”, hence “to compete”. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs. The noun ~rival~ is borrowed from Latin ~rīvālis~, which literally meant a person using the same stream as another, from ~rīvus~ (“brook”). Neighbors who shared a water source, and so quarreled over it, became the model of every competitor. The word is unrelated to ~rive~ (“bank”), despite the resemblance.
en.river: The two sources disagree. French Wiktionary treats ~river~ as formed from ~rive~ in the sense of “edge”: to rivet is to flatten and turn over the end of a nail or bolt so that it holds. ~Rive~ is inherited from Latin ~rīpa~ (“bank”), the source of ~rivage~ (“shore”). English Wiktionary instead points to a Germanic source and compares Danish ~rive~. Neither account is settled here, and the link to the edge of the nail is the one French itself gives.
en.roder:
French ~roder~ comes from Latin ~rōdere~ (“to gnaw, to wear away”). The Latin verb is the parent of a clear family: Italian ~rodere~ and English ~rodent~ (via ~rodens~, the present participle) show it in the same sense of “gnawer.” The same Latin root lies behind French ~éroder~ (“to erode”) and ~corroder~ (“to corrode”), and behind English ~erode~ and ~corrode~.

The Latin sense of wearing something away is the starting point for the French verb. In modern French ~roder~ means “to run in” a new engine so that its parts bed in smoothly, and by extension “to hone” or “to polish”: one can ~roder~ a method, a show or a team, meaning to try it out and smooth it through use.
en.rompre:
From Latin ~rumpere~ (“to break, burst”), which yielded Old French ~rompre~ directly. The Latin verb is a nasal-infixed present built on Proto-Indo-European *~Hrewp-~ (“to break, tear”), the same root that surfaces in Sanskrit ~lumpáti~ (“breaks, plunders”). Through Latin derivatives it is cognate with English ~rupture~ and ~disrupt~.

The core sense “to break” stayed remarkably stable, but French spun it outward into vivid idioms: ~rompre la glace~ (“to break the ice”), ~rompre le silence~, and ~à tout rompre~ (“to bursting point,” of applause). The most surprising descendant of ~rumpere~ is ~route~: a road was originally a ~via rupta~, a “broken way” cut or forced through wilderness, the past participle ~rupta~ standing alone until it became an everyday word. From the same Latin stock French also keeps ~rupture~, ~corrompre~, and ~interrompre~.
en.ronger:
French ~ronger~ comes from Old French ~rongier~, which the sources describe as a crossing of two verbs. One is Old French ~rungier~, from Latin ~rūmigāre~ (“to chew, to ruminate”). The other is a Vulgar Latin *~rodicāre~, built on Latin ~rōdō~ (“to gnaw”). English Wiktionary gives that second ingredient as a reconstructed verb, while French Wiktionary says only that the ~o~ of the nasal syllable comes from ~rōdere~, a verb close in meaning. Either way, ~ronger~ is a hybrid of two Latin verbs of chewing. Latin ~rōdere~ is also the source of English ~rodent~ and ~erode~, and of the learned French ~éroder~.

The oldest sense is physical: mice, rats and worms gnaw at whatever they find. French extended it to any slow wearing away, so that rust, damp and the sea eat at metal and rock, and illness or anxiety eat at a person. The figurative phrases are vivid: se ronger les sangs means “to worry oneself sick,” and ronger son frein means “to champ at the bit,” an image of a horse chewing on its bit. The agent noun ~rongeur~ (“rodent”) gives French its everyday word for mice and squirrels, so an old verb of chewing ended up naming a whole order of mammals.
en.roser: Formed from the noun ~rose~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to turn something pink, to give it a rosy tint.” The noun comes from Latin ~rosa~ (“rose”). English Wiktionary notes that ~rose~ was borrowed from Latin through Old French rather than inherited in the ordinary way, since an inherited word would have taken a quite different shape. The flower gave French its colour word, and the verb simply says “to colour like a rose.”
en.rougir: Formed from the adjective ~rouge~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, with the sense “to become red,” and attested in Old French as ~rogir~. This is the usual job of the ~-ir~ conjugation with colors and qualities, as in ~blêmir~ (“to turn pale”) and ~grandir~ (“to grow”). The base ~rouge~ comes through Middle French and Old French ~roge~ from Latin ~rubeus~ (“red, reddish”). The verb covers everything from a sky or a hot metal turning red to a person blushing from shame or emotion.
en.rouler:
From Old French ~roeler~ (around 1180), a verb built on ~roele~ (“little wheel”) with the ending ~-er~. ~Roele~ comes from Late Latin ~rotella~, a diminutive of Latin ~rota~ (“wheel”), crossed along the way with ~rôle~ (from Latin ~rotulus~, “a little rolled scroll”). ~Rota~ descends from Proto-Italic *~rotā~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~Hret-~ (“to run, roll”). Cognates abound: Sanskrit ~ratha~ (“chariot”), German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), and Lithuanian ~ratas~ (“wheel”).

The verb began concretely — to turn like a wheel, to make something revolve — and then rolled outward in every direction. It came to mean to travel by wheeled vehicle (~la voiture roule~), to coil or wind, and, in vivid slang, to ~rouler quelqu'un~, “to cheat someone,” as if spinning them around. The shared root left French a wheel-shaped vocabulary: ~roue~, ~rouleau~, ~roulette~, ~roulement~, the noun ~rôle~ (originally a rolled-up list of parts), and even ~contrôle~ (from a ~contre-rôle~, a counter-roll kept for checking). English ~roll~, ~rotate~, and ~round~ trace to the same turning root, as does the ~rotary~ motion that names it.
en.rouvrir: Formed from ~ouvrir~ with ~r-~, the form that ~re-~ (“again”) takes before a vowel in older verbs. The base descends from Latin ~aperīre~ (“to open”) by way of Vulgar Latin *~operīre~, reshaped on its opposite ~cooperīre~ (“to cover”). French records the verb first in the reflexive, in 1160, for a heart that opens again. The transitive use appears in 1396, and the concrete sense of reopening a door or a shop, in 1560.
en.ruer:
From Vulgar Latin *~rutāre~, an intensive verb built on ~rutum~, the supine stem of Classical Latin ~ruere~ (“to rush, to hurl, to throw down”). Both Wiktionaries give this chain, and the Vulgar Latin form is reconstructed, not attested. The plain Latin verb ~ruere~ also stands behind the noun ~ruina~ (“collapse, downfall”), which French and English both borrowed as ~ruine~ and ~ruin~. So the kick of a horse and the fall of a city share an ancestor: both start from a violent downward or forward rush.

In French, ~ruer~ first meant “to hurl, to throw with force,” which is the sense of the Latin source, and the reflexive ~se ruer~ (“to rush headlong”) keeps the Latin idea of a sudden onrush. Today the everyday meaning is that of a horse or donkey kicking out with its hind legs, and the figurative phrase ~ruer dans les brancards~ (literally “to kick against the shafts”) means to rebel. Several nouns belong to the family: ~ruade~ (“a kick”) and ~ruée~ (“a rush,” as in ~la ruée vers l'or~, the gold rush).
en.ruiner:
From Middle French ~ruiner~ and Old French ~ruiner~, from Latin ~ruīnāre~ (“to cause to fall down”). Synchronically, French Wiktionary also analyzes it as ~ruine~ + ~-er~, since the noun ~ruine~ comes from Latin ~ruīna~ (“collapse, downfall”), from ~ruere~ (“to rush down, to fall in a heap”). The verb has relatives across the Romance languages: Italian ~rovinare~, Occitan ~arroïnar~ and Spanish ~ruinar~ and ~arruinar~. English ~ruin~ is a loan from the French noun.

The Latin picture is physical: walls and roofs that tumble down. French kept that image and carried it over to fortunes, health and reputations, so ~ruiner~ can describe a house, a harvest or a family. The reflexive form ~se ruiner~ is the usual way to say that someone spends or loses all their money. The family includes the noun ~ruine~ and the adjective ~ruineux~, and the stem ~ruere~ also lives on in learned words such as ~irruption~.
en.rythmer: Formed in French from ~rythme~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense of giving something a rhythm. The noun ~rythme~ is a learned word: it comes from Latin ~rhythmus~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~rhuthmós~ (“regulated, measured movement,” hence “cadence, measure”). French spelled it ~rhythme~ until the spelling reform of 1878. The ending ~-er~ is the everyday way of coining a first-conjugation verb from a noun, here meaning “to provide with or give N.”
en.râler: The earlier form was ~raller~, which the sources trace to Middle French ~rasler~ (“to haggle, to bargain for”). Both Wiktionaries call the verb a doublet of ~racler~ (“to scrape”), meaning that the two are variant outcomes of one source. The sources do not spell out how the senses connect, so no link is claimed here. In modern French ~râler~ covers groaning, the rattling breath of the dying, and the everyday sense of grumbling or complaining.
en.râper:
From Middle French ~rasper~, from Old French ~rasper~, from Vulgar Latin *~raspāre~ (“to scrape, to rake”), a word borrowed from Frankish *~hraspōn~, a Germanic verb meaning “to rake together by scraping.” Frankish *~hraspōn~ comes from Proto-Germanic *~hraspōną~, a derivative of *~hrespaną~ (“to tear”), which English Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)krebʰ-~ (“to turn, to bend, to shrink”). The Romance languages share the verb: Occitan, Catalan, Spanish and Portuguese ~raspar~, and Italian ~raspare~. Cognates in the Germanic family include Old High German ~raspōn~, Dutch ~raspen~ and English ~rasp~, although English borrowed ~rasp~ from the Old French form and did not inherit it from Old English.

So ~râper~ is a Germanic word that entered French through Latin dress. Its circumflex marks a lost consonant: Old French ~rasper~ dropped its ~s~, leaving ~â~ as a scar, in the same way as ~forêt~ or ~hôpital~. The sense is the scraping of a surface against something rough. The verb serves for grating food, as cheese or carrots, and also for wearing away cloth, so that a ~vêtement râpé~ is a threadbare one. The derivatives ~râpe~ (“a grater”) and ~râpé~ keep that rasping motion.
en.réactiver: ~Réactiver~ is formed from ~activer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which here expresses repetition: to activate again. ~Activer~ is built on ~actif~, from Latin ~āctīvus~ (“active, practical”), a derivative of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”). The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive, so ~réactiver~ is a transparent modern formation, used of a switch, an account or a dormant process.
en.réactualiser: ~Réactualiser~ is formed from ~actualiser~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again,” in the sense “to update again” or “to bring back to current relevance.” The form ~ré-~ rather than ~re-~ is the usual one in modern coinages before a vowel, where it keeps the two sounds apart. The base ~actualiser~ is a French creation from the adjective ~actuel~ and the suffix ~-iser~, and ~actuel~ was borrowed from Latin ~actuālis~ (“active, practical”), from ~āctus~ (“act, doing”). The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The result is a verb used of data, texts and ideas that need to be brought up to date.
en.réaffirmer: ~Réaffirmer~ is formed from ~affirmer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again,” which appears in this form before a vowel in modern coinages. The base ~affirmer~ comes from Latin ~affirmāre~, built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~firmāre~ (“to make firm”), from ~firmus~ (“strong, steady”). To affirm is thus to make a statement firm, and to ~réaffirmer~ it is to make it firm once more. The verb is used of principles, commitments and positions that someone restates in order to leave no doubt.
en.réagir:
Attested around 1500, ~réagir~ is a learned formation from Latin ~reagere~ (“to push back, to drive back”), built on the prefix ~re-~ (“back, in return”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, to do, to act”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to lead”). Its sense was later reshaped on the French verb ~agir~ (“to act”), so that ~réagir~ reads transparently as ~ré-~ + ~agir~, “to act back.” Through ~agere~ it is cognate with Italian ~reagire~, Spanish ~reaccionar~, and English ~react~, and through the PIE root with English ~act~, ~agent~, and Greek ~ágein~ (“to lead”).

The word began in the language of physics and chemistry: one substance ~réagit~ upon another, exerting a counter-force or counter-effect. From this technical “acting back” it spread into ordinary life, where to ~réagir~ is to respond — to a remark, a crisis, a provocation — with an action of one's own. The noun ~réaction~ followed the same path and even acquired a political coloring, ~réactionnaire~ naming those who wished to act back against revolutionary change. The fertile root ~agere~ seeds a vast French family: ~agir~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~agiter~, ~action~, ~acte~, and ~rédiger~ — all turning on the idea of setting something in motion.
en.réaliser:
Unlike many commonly used verbs, ~réaliser~ is not a direct inheritance from Latin but a French formation of the fifteenth century, built from the adjective ~réel~ (“real”) and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to render”) — literally “to make real.” ~réel~ descends from Medieval Latin ~reālis~ (“relating to a thing, actual”), from Latin ~rēs~ (“thing, matter, affair”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~reh₁-~ (“property, goods”). So at bottom ~réaliser~ means to turn an idea into a ~rēs~, a real thing. Cognates of ~réel~ survive as Italian ~reale~ and Spanish ~real~, and the verb entered English as ~realize~.

The verb's earliest French sense was the concrete one still central today: to bring a project, a dream, or a sum of money into reality — to “carry out,” to “make happen,” and in cinema to ~réaliser~ a film is to direct it. The mental sense, “to realize, to become aware of,” is a calque of English ~realize~; though long criticized by purists as an anglicism, it was defended by André Gide and has been current since the late nineteenth century. Interestingly, the English meaning echoes an old metaphor already latent in Latin ~reor~ (“to reckon, to think”), where “fixing” a thing in the mind shades into thinking it. From ~rēs~ come a large French family, including ~réel~, ~réalité~, ~réalisme~, ~réalisateur~ (“film director”), and ~république~ (~rēs pūblica~, “the public thing”).
en.réaménager: Built from the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”) and ~aménager~ (“to arrange, to fit out”), so “to arrange anew,” as when a room, a district or a timetable is laid out afresh. The base ~aménager~ is itself ~a-~ + ~ménager~ (“to manage”), from ~ménage~ (“household”), which comes from Old French ~manoir~ (“to dwell”) and Latin ~manere~ (“to remain”). The verb thus rests on the idea of a lived-in space: first a household was kept, then a space was fitted out, and ~réaménager~ does it a second time. The same Latin verb lies behind English ~remain~ and ~mansion~.
en.réapparaître: Formed from ~ré-~ (“again”) and ~apparaître~ (“to appear”), so “to appear again”. The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and has its plain sense of repetition here. The base ~apparaître~ comes from Old French ~aparoistre~, which reshaped Latin ~appārēre~ (~ad-~ + ~pārēre~, “to be visible”) through the Late Latin inchoative ~appārēscere~, a form that stressed coming into view. The modern gloss “to respawn in a video game” is a recent extension of the same repetition, with a character appearing again after being removed.
en.récapituler:
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin ~recapitulāre~ (“to go over the main points again”), built from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~capitulum~, a diminutive of ~caput~ (“head”). The verb thus means, literally, to “re-head”: to run back over the headings. Latin ~caput~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European *~kaput-~ (“head”), and English ~head~ and German ~Haupt~ are its Germanic cousins. Italian ~ricapitolare~ and Spanish ~recapitular~ come from the same Latin verb.

The diminutive ~capitulum~ named a small head, then a heading, and finally a chapter, which is how French got ~chapitre~. Christian writers favored ~recapitulāre~ for summing up a text or a body of teaching under its principal heads, and that learned sense is the one French kept: to ~récapituler~ is to go back over the essentials in order. The family is large. ~Capituler~ originally referred to negotiating terms set out in chapters, hence the sense of surrendering on agreed conditions. ~Capitulation~, ~capital~ and ~chef~ all descend from ~caput~, and ~récapitulation~, shortened in speech to ~récap~, is the noun learners meet first.
en.réceptionner: Formed from the noun ~réception~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~receptio~ (“the act of receiving”), from ~recipere~ (“to receive”), itself made of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to hold”). The verb is a relatively modern coinage of commercial and administrative French, meaning to take delivery of goods and check them on arrival. It is often criticized as a heavy substitute for the plain ~recevoir~, which comes from the same Latin ~recipere~.
en.réciter: Borrowed from Latin ~recitāre~ (“to read aloud, to recite”), a compound of ~re-~ and ~citāre~. In Latin, ~citāre~ meant “to summon, to call forth” and is the source of French ~citer~. To ~réciter~ is therefore to call something forth again, aloud and from memory or text. The sense has changed little: a poem, a lesson or a prayer is ~récité~. French Wiktionary refers readers to ~ré-~ and ~citer~ for the parts.
en.réclamer:
From Old French ~reclamer~, from Latin ~reclāmāre~ (“to cry out against, to protest loudly”), formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“back, against”) and ~clāmāre~ (“to call, to shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, to shout”). Cognate with Italian ~reclamare~ and Spanish ~reclamar~, and — through ~clāmāre~ — with English ~claim~ (itself borrowed from Old French) and, through the same PIE root, with English ~low~ (“to moo”) and Latin ~calāre~.

The Latin verb was originally adversarial: to ~reclāmāre~ was to shout ~re-~, “back,” at a speaker — to clamor in opposition. That confrontational sense survives in modern ~réclamer~ when it means “to protest, to object,” but the dominant modern meaning shifted from crying against something to crying for it: to ~réclamer~ is now above all to demand, to claim, to call insistently for what one is owed — ~réclamer son dû~. A child ~réclame~ its mother; a creditor ~réclame~ payment. From the same ~clāmāre~ French built a loud family: ~clamer~, ~acclamer~, ~proclamer~, ~déclamer~, ~s'exclamer~, and the noun ~clameur~ (“clamor, outcry”) — all of them, like ~réclamer~, rooted in the raised voice.
en.récolter:
French ~récolter~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~récolte~ (“harvest”). That noun was borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian ~ricolta~ (“harvest,” attested from the fourteenth century), the feminine past participle of ~ricogliere~ (“to gather, to collect”). The Italian verb descends from Latin ~recolligere~ (“to gather together again”), formed from ~re-~ plus ~colligere~ (“to collect”), itself ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, to gather”). The French verb ~cueillir~ and the noun ~collecte~ spring from the same Latin ~colligere~.

So ~récolter~ carries inside it the idea of gathering up once more what the field has produced — re-collecting the grain. From the root *~leǵ-~ the Romance languages drew a rich crop: French ~récolte~, ~collection~, ~recueil~ (“anthology,” literally a re-gathering), and ~légende~ (“legend,” from Latin “things to be read”), since the same Latin ~legere~ meant both to gather and to read. Figuratively, French ~récolter~ reaps abstractions too — one can ~récolter~ applause, information, or trouble, just as English speaks of reaping what one sows.
en.récompenser:
Attested in the fourteenth century, ~récompenser~ descends from Late Latin ~recompensāre~, formed with the prefix ~re-~ on Latin ~compensāre~ (“to balance, to weigh one thing against another”). ~compensāre~ is itself ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~pensāre~, the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to weigh”). The same ~pensāre~ underlies an astonishing range of French words and gives English ~compensate~, ~pension~, and ~pensive~.

The original image is a pair of scales: to ~compensāre~ was to set weights against each other until the balance was even. ~recompensāre~ added the sense of weighing back, of giving an equivalent in return — and from there French slid from mere balancing to rewarding. To ~récompenser~ is to give someone their due, but skewed toward the pleasant: a prize, a reward, a deserved good. The neutral metrology survives in the doublet ~compenser~ (“to compensate, to offset”), while the same ~pendere~ family scattered across French in ~peser~ (“to weigh”), ~pensée~ (“thought,” for the mind too weighs ideas), and ~dépense~ (“expenditure”).
en.réconcilier: Borrowed from Latin ~reconciliāre~ (“to restore, to bring back, to reconcile, to re-establish harmony or friendship”). The verb appears in the Roman de Troie (about 1160-1170) in the form ~reconciliier~. It is made of the prefix ~re-~ and the Latin verb ~conciliāre~, whose family also gave French ~concilier~ and ~concile~. The prefix ~re-~ here marks a return to a former state: those who were once friends are brought back together.
en.récupérer:
A learned re-borrowing (around 1495) from Latin ~recuperare~ (“to regain, to recover, to get back”), itself the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) on a stem related to ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”) — recovery being, etymologically, a “taking back.” The same Latin verb had already entered French much earlier by ordinary phonetic descent as ~recouvrer~ (“to recover”), so ~récupérer~ and ~recouvrer~ form a doublet: two French verbs, one inherited and worn down, the other re-cut directly from the Latin. Spanish ~recuperar~, Italian ~recuperare~, and English ~recuperate~ are parallel learned descendants.

Because it was reshaped from the Latin rather than passed down by mouth, ~récupérer~ keeps a transparent, almost technical feel, and its meanings fan out widely: to get back a lost object, to recover one's strength after effort (~récupérer~ after a hard week), to reclaim or recycle materials, and — in a distinctly modern political sense — to co-opt or appropriate a cause or a movement for one's own ends. The noun ~récupération~ covers all of these, from physical recovery to salvage to ideological appropriation. Beside it the older ~recouvrer~ survives in more formal registers, as when one ~recouvre~ a debt or ~recouvre~ one's sight.
en.récuser:
From Latin ~recūsāre~ (“to refuse, to object to”), a learned borrowing built from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~causa~ (“reason, case, lawsuit”). The Latin verb meant, literally, to plead a reason against something, and it belonged both to the courtroom and to everyday refusal. The origin of ~causa~ itself is unknown. Italian ~ricusare~ and Spanish ~recusar~ continue the same Latin verb, and English borrowed it as ~recuse~ in its legal sense.

In French the verb stayed close to its legal home. ~Récuser~ means to challenge the impartiality or competence of a judge, a juror, an expert or a witness, and from there, more broadly, to reject something such as a testimony or an authority. The reflexive ~se récuser~ is what a judge does when he declares himself unfit to hear a case. The older Latin sense of plain refusal faded, while the courtroom sense survived. The same ~causa~ lies behind ~cause~, ~accuser~ (“to bring a case against”), ~excuser~ (“to take out of the case”) and even ~chose~, the popular outcome of ~causa~, whose “thing” began as a “matter in dispute.”
en.rédiger:
From Latin ~redigere~ (“to bring back, drive back, reduce”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, do, act”). ~Agere~ derives from the PIE root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”), source also of Greek ~ágō~ (“I lead”) and, through Latin borrowings, of English ~act~, ~agent~, and ~agile~; Italian and Spanish keep the parent verb in ~agire~ and the like. The literal Latin sense is to “drive back” or “reduce” a thing to some state — to bring it down to order.

The path to “writing” runs through that idea of reduction. Medieval Latin used ~redigere in scriptis~, “to reduce into writing,” to set a matter down in fixed, orderly form — and from this phrase the “write up, compose” sense crystallized. So ~rédiger~ never meant mere scribbling: it means to compose with care, to draft a contract, an article, a report, marshalling loose material into finished prose. Its agent and act are ~rédacteur~ (“editor, writer”) and ~rédaction~ (“drafting; an editorial office; a school essay”). The driving root *~h₂eǵ-~ powers a huge French family beyond it — ~agir~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~action~, ~rédiger~ standing among them as the one that drives words into shape.
en.réduire:
From Old French ~reduire~, from Latin ~redūcere~ (“to lead back, to bring back”), which is ~re-~ (“back”) + ~dūcere~ (“to lead, to draw”). ~dūcere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~doukō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to pull, to lead”). That root reaches far into Germanic: it gives English ~tow~, German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”), and even the ~-zog~ of German ~Herzog~ (“duke,” literally “army-leader,” a calque of Greek ~stratēgós~). Latin built ~dux~ (“leader”) from the same root — the ancestor of ~duke~ and Italian ~duce~.

The meaning traveled a long way. ~redūcere~ first meant simply “to lead back,” and Old French ~reduire~ could mean “to bring back, to restore.” The modern sense “to make smaller” grew from the idea of bringing a thing back to a smaller, simpler, or controlled state — reducing an army, a price, a text, or a rebel “brought back” to obedience. The ~dūcere~ family is one of the richest in French: ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~traduire~, ~introduire~, ~séduire~, ~déduire~, plus the nouns ~duc~, ~conduite~, and ~aqueduc~ (“water-leader”).
en.réfléchir:
From Latin ~reflectere~ (“to bend back, to turn back”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~flectere~ (“to bend, to curve”). The ultimate root of ~flectere~ is uncertain and has no secure Indo-European cognates, though a Proto-Italic *~flektō~ is reconstructed. The verb is cognate with Italian ~flettere~ and survives, through its derivatives, in English ~reflect~, ~flexible~, and ~inflect~. French inherited a popular form ~réflechir~ alongside the learned doublet that gave the noun ~réflexion~.

The metaphor at the heart of this verb is light bending back from a surface. From the optical sense — a mirror ~reflects~ an image — French drew an inward, mental one: to “turn one's thought back” upon itself, to ponder. So ~réfléchir~ means both “to reflect (light)” and “to think hard,” and the two senses illuminate each other — the thinker turns ideas over the way a mirror turns back a beam. A reflexive verb in French is a verbe ~réfléchi~, one whose action bends back onto the subject. From the same ~flectere~ stem descend ~fléchir~ (“to bend, to yield”), ~flexible~, ~réflexe~, and ~circonflexe~ — the accent “bent around” a vowel.
en.réformer:
~réformer~ is formed from ~former~ (“to form, to shape”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“again, anew”), answering exactly to Latin ~reformāre~ (“to form again, restore, transform”). The base ~former~ comes from Latin ~forma~ (“shape, form, mould”), a word of famously uncertain origin: it has long been proposed that ~forma~ is somehow connected to Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape, beauty”) by a metathesis of consonants, but many etymologists reject the idea — there is no evidence ~forma~ ever passed through a stage *~phorma~ — so the link is best presented as disputed rather than settled.

In its earliest French use, ~réformer~ kept the Latin sense of reshaping or restoring to a better state, and that double edge persists. To ~réformer~ a law, an institution, or a habit is to remould it for the better — the sense that gave the religious ~Réforme~ (the Reformation). But French also kept a contrary sense: to ~réformer~ a soldier or a piece of equipment is to declare it unfit and withdraw it from service. The same ~forma~ family fills French with ~forme~, ~former~, ~formation~, ~réforme~, ~conforme~, and ~déformer~ — all variations on shaping and re-shaping.
en.réfugier:
Built in French on the noun ~refuge~ with the infinitive ending ~-er~. ~Refuge~ comes from Latin ~refugium~ (“a place of retreat”), from the verb ~refugere~ (“to flee back, take shelter”), itself ~re-~ (“back”) + ~fugere~ (“to flee”). ~Fugere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fugjō~ and to PIE *~bʰewg-~ (“to flee”), the root that also gives Ancient Greek ~pheugō~ (“I flee”). Through Latin ~fugere~ and its derivatives, the same root yields French ~fuir~, ~fugue~, ~fugitif~, ~refuge~, and ~subterfuge~, and the English ~fugitive~ and the suffix ~-fuge~ in ~centrifuge~.

The verb is almost always reflexive: ~se réfugier~, to take oneself off to safety. The image inside it is precise and slightly counter-intuitive — not merely to flee, but to flee ~back~, to retreat to a refuge, the ~re-~ carrying the sense of withdrawal to a place of shelter. From the physical act of seeking cover the verb extended to the figurative, one can ~se réfugier~ in silence, in work, in memory. The closely related ~réfugié~ (“refugee”) is the same formation frozen as a noun, naming the person who has fled back to safety across a border.
en.réfuter: Borrowed from Latin ~refūtāre~ (“to drive back, to repel”). Roman speakers used the verb in the courtroom and the assembly for pushing back an opponent's claim, and that figure of a blow turned aside is still the core of the French verb. French took it as a learned word, and ~réfuter~ now means to show that an argument or accusation is false. English ~refute~ comes from the same Latin verb, and so does the more formal ~confute~.
en.référencer:
A denominal verb formed in French on the noun ~référence~, which goes back through ~référer~ to Latin ~referre~ (“to carry back, report”), from ~re-~ (“back”) + ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”). ~Ferre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and from PIE *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”) — one of the most widespread of all roots, source of Ancient Greek ~pherō~, Sanskrit ~bharati~, and, in the native Germanic line, English ~bear~. The same Latin verb feeds a large French family: ~référence~, ~référent~, ~conférer~, ~différer~, ~offrir~, and ~transférer~.

The oldest sense of ~référencer~ is bookish — to supply something with references or citations. The verb then drifted into commerce, where it now dominates: to ~référencer~ a product is to enter its reference number in a catalogue and so put it on the shelves; to be ~déréférencé~ is to be dropped from the listing. From that the digital age took ~référencement~ for the listing and ranking of a site, the standard French term for search-engine optimization. Other relatives include ~référenceur~ and ~référençage~, all turning on the idea of carrying something back to a fixed point of reference.
en.référer:
From Latin ~referre~ (“to carry back, report, attribute”), from ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”). ~Ferre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and from PIE *~bʰéreti~ (“to bear, carry”), one of the most widespread Indo-European roots. Through it, ~ferre~ is cognate with English ~bear~, Ancient Greek ~φέρω~ (~phérō~), and Sanskrit ~भरति~ (~bhárati~) — all “to carry.”

The image is one of carrying a matter back to its source. To ~référer~ is to carry a question, a fact, or a name back and lay it before something else: one ~se réfère à~ a text (carries the point back to it for authority), or ~en réfère à~ a superior (carries the matter back up to them for a decision). The same ~ferre~ is astonishingly prolific in French through its prefixed compounds: ~conférer~, ~déférer~, ~différer~, ~offrir~, ~souffrir~, ~transférer~, and the nouns ~référence~, ~rapport~, and ~relation~. English drew the parallel family ~refer~, ~confer~, ~transfer~, and ~offer~ from the very same Latin verb.
en.régaler: French Wiktionary derives ~régaler~ from the noun ~régal~ (“feast, treat”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to treat someone to a feast.” ~Régal~ comes from Old French ~rigale~ (“festivity, entertainment”), which is traced to Old French ~gale~ and the verb ~galer~ (“to enjoy oneself”) with a prefix ~ri-~ borrowed from the same family as ~rigoler~. The family of ~galer~ also gave ~galant~. The sense shifted over time from a festive occasion to the meal itself, and now to anything one relishes: ~régaler~ can mean to delight, and ~se régaler~ to have a feast.
en.régir:
From Latin ~regere~ (« to lead, direct, rule »), from Proto-Italic *~regō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (« to straighten, to direct »). The semantics run straight from the physical to the political: to make straight, hence to set a course, hence to govern. The root is one of the great Indo-European families, cognate with Sanskrit ~rā́jati~ (« he rules »), and — through the same *~h₃reǵ-~ — with English ~right~ and ~rich~ and with the ~-roy~ of ~royal~.

In French ~régir~ holds the formal, abstract sense « to govern, to rule » a state, a set of conditions, or a grammar that ~régit~ which case a verb takes. Its Latin participle ~rectus~ (« straight, right ») and the agent noun ~rector~ seeded a vast family: ~régime~, ~régisseur~ (« stage manager, steward »), ~région~, ~recteur~, ~direct~, ~correct~, and ~droit~ (« right, straight, law »), this last the popular descendant of ~rectus~. Few Latin roots so plainly preserve the metaphor that to rule is to keep things in a straight line.
en.réglementer: Formed from the noun ~règlement~ (“regulation, set of rules”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with” rules: to subject something to a regulation. French Wiktionary dates the verb to 1768. The base ~règlement~ belongs to the family of ~règle~, from Latin ~rēgula~ (“ruler, rule”). The verb is used for laying down official rules, while ~régler~ also covers settling a payment or adjusting a device.
en.régler:
French ~régler~ is a denominal verb, formed in the thirteenth century from the noun ~règle~ (“rule, ruler”), which comes from Latin ~rēgula~ (“straight stick, ruler, rule”). ~Rēgula~ is a derivative of ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct, to rule”), and that verb rests on a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to make right”). The root is one of the great ones: Sanskrit ~rā́jati~ (“to rule, to direct”), Latin ~rēx~ (“king”), and through Germanic the English ~right~ and German ~recht~ all spring from it. Italian ~regolare~ and Spanish ~reglar~ are the Romance cousins of the verb; English borrowed ~regulate~ from the related Latin ~regulāre~.

The oldest concrete sense is wonderfully literal: to ~régler~ a sheet of paper is to rule lines on it with a straightedge — the ruler doing exactly what its name says. From “to draw straight lines” the meaning fanned out to “to set right, to adjust, to put in order”: one ~règle~ a watch, a machine, a thermostat; one ~règle~ a quarrel or a bill (~régler ses comptes~, “to settle one's accounts”). The same root underlies a sprawling French family: ~règle~, ~règlement~, ~régulier~ and ~réguler~, ~régime~ and ~régir~, ~roi~ and ~royal~ (through ~rēx~), and ~rectitude~ and ~direct~ (through ~rectus~, “straight”). To regulate is, at heart, to make crooked things straight.
en.régner:
~Régner~ is attested from the second half of the 10th century, passing through Old French ~regner~ / ~reigner~ and Middle French ~régner~. It descends from Latin ~regnare~ (« to be king, to wield absolute power »), a verb built on the noun ~regnum~ (« kingdom, royal power »). That noun belongs to ~rex~, ~regis~ (« king ») and the verb ~regere~ (« to rule, to guide straight »), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ (« to straighten, to direct »). Italian ~regnare~ and Spanish ~reinar~ are its Romance counterparts; English ~reign~ entered through Old French.

From designating literal monarchy, ~régner~ broadened figuratively: a fashion, a silence, or a mood can now ~régner~ — that is, prevail or hold sway over a place or an age. The synchronic French noun ~règne~ now feels like its source. The same root *~h₃reǵ-~ radiates through a remarkable family touching kingship and straightness alike — ~roi~, ~royal~, ~régir~, ~région~, ~règle~, ~direct~, and ~correct~ — a reminder that to rule, etymologically, was to keep things in a straight line.
en.régresser: ~Régresser~ is a back-formation from the noun ~régression~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~regressiō~ (“a going back”). The verb was carved out of the noun by adding the verbal ending ~-er~, on the model of ~progresser~, which in turn comes from ~progression~. The ending ~-er~ descends from the Latin first-conjugation infinitive ~-are~ and is French's default way of making a verb from another word. The result is a neat pair of opposites, ~progresser~ (“to move forward”) and ~régresser~ (“to move back”), both reached through nouns that Latin supplied first.
en.régulariser: Formed from the adjective ~régulier~ and the suffix ~-iser~, with the stem reshaped on Latin ~regulāris~ (“of a rule”), which comes from ~rēgula~ (“rule, straight rod”). ~Rēgula~ belongs to the family of ~regere~ (“to guide in a straight line, to rule”). The suffix ~-iser~ means to make or bring to a state, so ~régulariser~ is to make regular: to bring a situation, a payment or someone's papers into conformity with the rules, as in régulariser sa situation (“to sort out one's legal status”). English ~regularize~ comes from the same family.
en.réguler: Borrowed from Latin ~rēgulāre~ (“to direct, to regulate”). The verb has an unusual history in French: for centuries it fell out of use, because ~régler~ did its work, and it reappeared only in 1953. Since its return it has sometimes taken on the senses of English ~regulate~, itself a descendant of the same Latin verb, so the word has partly come back to French by way of English usage. It now belongs to the language of biology, economics and engineering, where one ~régule~ a flow, a temperature or a market.
en.régénérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~regenerāre~ (“to bring forth again, to restore”), made of ~re-~ (“again”) and ~generāre~ (“to beget, to produce”). Latin ~generāre~ comes from ~genus~ (“birth, kind”), which belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to give birth, to beget”). That root is very productive: Greek ~génos~ (“race, kind”) and English ~kin~ come from it, as does English ~generate~, borrowed from the Latin verb. Italian ~rigenerare~ and Spanish ~regenerar~ are parallel borrowings of the same Latin word.

In Christian Latin, ~regenerāre~ took on the spiritual sense of being born again, as in baptism, and the religious meaning lingers behind the modern one. French ~régénérer~ now covers everything that is made new: tissue, a forest, a polluted river, a political movement, or a used material put back into service. Its relatives are many. ~Générer~, ~génération~, ~genre~, ~gendre~ and ~engendrer~ all descend from the same Latin family, and ~dégénérer~ is its mirror image, to fall away from one's kind.
en.réhabiliter: ~Réhabiliter~ is formed from ~ré-~ + ~habiliter~. The prefix, from Latin ~re-~, means “back, again”, so the verb means to make someone fit or capable once more: in practice, to restore a person's standing, reputation or legal rights, or to renovate a run-down building. The base ~habiliter~ is a Latin loan, from ~habilitāre~ (“to make fit”), which rests on ~habilis~ (“easy to handle, apt”), from ~habēre~ (“to hold, to have”). The same Latin root gave French ~habile~ and English ~able~.
en.réinstaller: ~Réinstaller~ is formed from ~installer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again,” in the spelling used before a vowel so that the two vowels stay distinct. It means to put back in place, to set up a program or a person once more. The base ~installer~ comes from medieval Latin ~installāre~ (“to put into a stall, to establish in office”), built from ~in-~ and ~stallum~, which was borrowed from Frankish *~stall~. The earliest sense was ceremonial: to seat a canon or bishop in his choir stall. The prefix ~ré-~ descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.réintroduire: Formed from ~introduire~ (“to introduce”) with the prefix ~ré-~, which here expresses repetition: “to introduce again.” The form ~ré-~ rather than ~re-~ is the usual spelling before a vowel in modern coinages. The base comes from Latin ~introducere~ (“to lead in”), made of ~intro~ (“inward”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead”), so the verb means, literally, to lead something inside once more. That same Latin ~ducere~ gave French ~conduire~, ~produire~ and ~traduire~.
en.réintégrer: French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~redintegrāre~ (“to restore, to make whole again”), which became ~reintegrāre~ in Late Latin, while English Wiktionary simply reads it as ~ré-~ plus ~intégrer~. The Latin compound was built on ~integer~ (“untouched, whole”), from ~in-~ (“not”) and the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”). To ~réintégrer~ is therefore to make someone whole again, and so to restore them to a post, a group or a place. English ~integer~, ~entire~ and ~integrity~ share the Latin source.
en.réinventer: Formed in French from the prefix ~ré-~ and the verb ~inventer~, meaning “to invent again” or “to reshape completely”. The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“again”) and is kept apart from the vowel that follows. The base ~inventer~ comes from Latin ~invenīre~ (“to come upon, to find”), built from ~in-~ (“on”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). Early French ~inventer~ leaned toward finding what already existed, and only later toward making something new, so ~réinventer~ is a second invention on top of a first.
en.réinvestir:
~Réinvestir~ is ~investir~ carrying the prefix ~ré-~ (“again, anew”). ~Investir~ was borrowed from Latin ~investīre~ (“to clothe in, to wrap, to cover”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~vestīre~ (“to dress”), itself built on the noun ~vestis~ (“garment, clothing”), from Proto-Italic *~westis~ and PIE *~wes-~ (“to clothe”). The Latin verb spread across Europe by two different routes. A few languages inherited it directly, as Romanian ~învești~ and Catalan ~envestir~ show; most took it back later as a learned borrowing, which is how Italian ~investire~, Spanish ~investir~, German ~investieren~ and — by way of Middle French ~investir~ — English ~invest~ all arose. The underlying noun ~vestis~ is far better represented in everyday French, where it yielded ~vêtir~, ~vêtement~ and ~veste~, while the same root gives English ~vest~ and ~vestment~. Nothing in this ancestry has anything to do with money: at the outset, the entire family is about cloth.

The literal sense came first. To ~investir~ someone was to clothe him, and the ceremony that placed a bishop or a vassal in the robes of his office is still called an ~investiture~; the medieval quarrel over who had the right to perform it set popes against emperors for half a century. From wrapping a person the verb moved to wrapping a place: to ~investir~ a town is to encircle and besiege it, a military sense French keeps to this day. The financial meaning — clothing your capital in a venture — is generally traced through Italian ~investire~ and the vocabulary of banking, with English ~investment~ helping to fix it. Modern ~réinvestir~ inherits the whole spread at once: one reinvests profits, demonstrators reinvest an occupied square, and a politician is reinvested with office. From the same root come ~vêtir~ and ~revêtir~, ~vêtement~, ~travesti~ (“dressed across, disguised”), ~dévêtir~, ~investiture~ and ~investissement~.
en.réitérer: ~Réitérer~ is borrowed from Latin ~reiterāre~ (“to renew, to repeat”), built on ~re-~ (“again”) and ~iterāre~ (“to do a second time”), from ~iterum~ (“again”). English Wiktionary notes that by surface analysis the French verb can also be read as ~ré-~ plus ~itérer~, a learned verb of the same meaning, but the Latin verb already contained both parts. The doubled “again” of ~re-~ and ~iterum~ is what makes ~réitérer~ emphatic: to say or do something once more, often a demand or a promise. English ~reiterate~ is the same Latin verb arrived by another road.
en.réjouir:
From the prefix ~re-~ added to the older verb ~éjouir~ (Old French ~esjoïr~), built on ~joie~ (“joy”) and the verb ~jouir~ (“to enjoy”). The chain leads back to Latin ~gaudere~ (“to rejoice, to be glad”). ~Gaudere~ likely contracts from an earlier *~gāvidēre~ and traces to Proto-Indo-European *~geh₂u-~ (“to rejoice”), the root also behind Ancient Greek ~γάνυμαι~ (“I am glad”). The intensive ~gaudia~ (“joys”) gave Old French ~joie~ directly, while ~gaudere~ itself yielded ~jouir~.

The ~re-~ here is not really “again” but an intensifier: ~réjouir~ is to gladden thoroughly, to fill with delight. Reflexively, ~se réjouir~ means to look forward to something with pleasure — a future-leaning joy the bare ~jouir~ lacks. From the same Latin source come ~joie~, ~joyeux~, ~jouir~, ~jouissance~, ~réjouissance~ (“festivity, merrymaking”), and ~réjouissant~. Through Old French ~joie~, English borrowed ~joy~, ~rejoice~, and ~enjoy~ — so the English and French families of gladness share a single Latin spring in ~gaudere~.
en.rémunérer:
French ~rémunérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~remunerare~ (also deponent ~remunerari~, “to reward, recompense”), formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~munerare~ (“to give, to present”), itself derived from the noun ~munus~ (“gift, service, public office, duty”). ~Munus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~moinos~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~moy-nós~, from the root *~mey-~ (“to exchange”) — the idea being a good or service rendered within a society's web of mutual obligation. The same root surfaces in Latin ~communis~ (“shared, common”) and ~immunis~ (“exempt from duty”), and, by other paths, in the Germanic family behind English ~mean~ (“held in common”).
