French Wiktionary links it to the verb ~siller~ (“to trace a line”) and to ~sillage~, the wake behind a ship, while English Wiktionary analyses ~seillon~ as ~seille~ + ~-on~. The verb then widened from ploughed lines to any lines drawn across a surface: ships ~sillonnent~ the sea, planes the sky, roads and rivers a landscape, and wrinkles a face.
en.simplifier:
French ~simplifier~ formally derives from ~simple~ with the suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make”), modelled on Medieval Latin ~simplificāre~. ~Simple~ comes from Latin ~simplus~ / ~simplex~ (“single, plain”), and the ~-ifier~ ending continues Latin ~facere~ (“to make, do”). ~Simplex~ itself is ~sem-~ (“one, single”) plus ~-plex~ (“-fold”): the first element from Proto-Indo-European *~sem-~ (“one, together”), the second from *~pleḱ-~ (“to weave, fold”). Through those roots ~simple~ is cognate with English ~single~ and ~simple~, and ~-plex~ with English ~plait~, ~ply~, and ~fold~.

So to ~simplifier~ is, etymologically, “to make one-fold” — to reduce a thing folded over on itself to a single layer. The image of folding runs quietly through a whole family: ~double~, ~triple~, ~multiple~, ~complexe~, and ~perplexe~ all carry the same ~-plex~ / ~-pli-~ element, “fold.” Modern French keeps the abstract sense, “to make less complicated,” and built the noun ~simplification~ and intensives like ~ultrasimplifier~ — the latter a quietly ironic word, since over-simplifying rarely makes anything truly single.
en.simuler:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~simulāre~ (“to imitate, to pretend”), a verb built on the adjective ~similis~ (“like, similar”). Latin ~simulāre~ had already reached French once by the popular road, as Old French ~sembler~, so ~simuler~ and ~sembler~ are doublets: one Latin verb that entered the language twice, at different dates and in different shapes. English ~simulate~ is a borrowing of the same Latin verb and English ~similar~ of the adjective behind it, while Italian ~simulare~ and Spanish ~simular~ are its sister learned forms.

The two French descendants then divided the meaning between them. The inherited ~sembler~ drifted from “to look like” to “to seem”, and its participle gave ~semblant~, as in ~faire semblant~ (“to pretend”). The learned ~simuler~ kept the Latin sense of deliberately imitating or feigning, and later added the technical sense of reproducing a process by a model, whence ~simulation~ and ~simulateur~. In sport, especially football, it covers the player who feigns a foul to win a free kick, the “dive” of English. Its mirror image is ~dissimuler~ (“to conceal”), from Latin ~dissimulāre~: to simulate is to pretend to be what one is not, to dissimulate is to hide what one is. The family also includes ~ressembler~ (“to resemble”) and ~simulacre~.
en.situer:
French ~situer~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~situāre~ (“to place in a location, to establish, to assign”), a verb built from the noun ~situs~ (“position, site, location”). That noun is the past participle of the Latin verb ~sinere~ (“to let, to allow, to set down, to leave in place”) — so a ~situs~ is, etymologically, a thing that has been let stand where it is. The same ~situs~ gives English ~site~ and ~situate~, and the legal term ~situs~ survives untouched in English for the place where something legally belongs.

Unlike the battered everyday verbs of French, ~situer~ entered late and bookish, keeping the clean shape of its Latin model. Its meaning has stayed close to the source: to fix a thing in space, and figuratively to place it in a context — ~situer un événement~ (“to date or place an event”), ~se situer~ (“to be located, to position oneself”). The family that grew around it is modern and tidy: ~situation~ (“situation, location, post”), ~situé~ (“located”), ~resituer~ (“to re-place, to put back in context”), and the adjective ~situable~. From a verb of simply letting something stay put, French built its whole vocabulary of placement and circumstance.
en.siéger:
From the noun ~siège~ (“seat, see, siege”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. ~Siège~ descends through Vulgar Latin *~sedicum~ from Latin ~sēdēs~ (“seat”) and the family of ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Italic *~sedēō~, from PIE *~sed-~ (“to sit”). This is one of the most widespread of all Indo-European roots: it gave Latin ~sedēre~, English ~sit~, ~seat~ and ~settle~, German ~sitzen~, Sanskrit ~sī́dati~, and Greek ~hézomai~ — so a senator and a sitting hen share an ancestor.

The verb keeps the literal posture only faintly; mostly it means “to hold a seat,” hence “to sit” on a council or assembly, and by extension “to be located, to have one's seat” — a court ~siège à~ Paris, a company's headquarters ~siège~ somewhere. The noun ~siège~ carries an arresting double life: from “seat” it also became the military “siege,” an army that ~sits down~ around a city until it falls (English ~siege~ borrowed this very word and sense). The root *~sed-~ pervades learned French through Latin compounds — ~résider~, ~présider~, ~posséder~, ~sédentaire~, ~séance~, ~assidu~ (one who ~sits at~ a task), and ~obséder~ (to “sit before,” to besiege the mind) — a vast progeny of a single act: sitting down.
en.soigner:
Of disputed origin, ~soigner~ most likely comes from Frankish *~sunnjōn~ (“to occupy oneself with, to attend to”), borrowed into Low Latin as ~soniāre~ and related to the noun ~soin~ (“care”). The Germanic source *~sunnja~ carried the idea of “need, necessity, care.” A rival hypothesis links it instead to Latin ~somniāre~ (“to dream”), which independently gave ~songer~ (“to think, to muse”); under that view, to care for someone began as thinking attentively about them. Cognate, on the Germanic side, with forms in the older Dutch and German care-words.

Whichever root is right, the meaning settled firmly: to ~soigner~ is to take care of, to look after, to treat — a patient, a garden, a wound, or one's appearance. The reflexive ~se soigner~ means to take care of oneself or to undergo treatment. The verb belongs to a tight French family built on ~soin~: ~soin~ itself (“care”), ~soigneux~ (“careful, painstaking”), ~soigneusement~ (“carefully”), and ~soignant~ (“caregiving,” as in ~le personnel soignant~, “the nursing staff”). The lingering uncertainty between a Germanic “need” and a Latin “dreaming” is itself the memorable detail: French may have built its word for nursing either on duty or on attentive thought.
en.solder: Formed from the noun ~solde~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun has Italian roots, and its sources describe two strands that influenced each other: ~soldo~ (a soldier's pay), from Latin ~soldus~, a contracted form of ~solidus~ (“solid”) and so a doublet of ~sou~ and ~solide~, and ~saldo~ (the balance of an account), from the Italian verb ~saldare~. The verb thus has an accounting sense: to ~solder~ a bill is to settle it so that nothing remains owing.
en.solliciter:
From Latin ~sollicitare~ (“to disturb thoroughly, stir up, agitate”), the denominal verb of the adjective ~sollicitus~ (“thoroughly moved, anxious, troubled”). That adjective is a compound of ~sollus~ (“whole, entire”) and a form related to ~ciere~ / ~citus~ (“to set in motion, rouse”). The two elements trace to PIE *~solh₂-~ (“whole”) and *~keyh₂-~ (“to set in motion”) respectively. Romance cognates include Spanish ~solicitar~ and Italian ~sollecitare~; English ~solicit~ comes from the same Latin verb.

The literal Latin picture is of something “wholly stirred up” — thoroughly shaken, hence anxious or agitated. The verb meant to disturb or rouse, and from rousing someone to act came the sense of urging, then of earnestly requesting. French keeps that progression: to ~solliciter~ is to ask for insistently (a favor, a meeting), to apply for, and, of a thing, to draw on or call upon (one's attention, a muscle). From ~sollus~ (“whole”) French also has ~solennel~ (originally a rite performed “whole,” every year), and from ~ciere~ the family of ~exciter~ and ~inciter~.
en.sombrer:
The origin of ~sombrer~ (“to sink”) is disputed, and the sources give competing accounts. English Wiktionary offers one: the verb comes from Middle French ~soussombrer~, an alteration of ~soussoubrer~ with influence from the adjective ~sombre~, the first part perhaps being taken for a prefix. The word ~soussoubrer~ was probably a loan by a maritime route from Portuguese ~soçobrar~, itself likely from Spanish ~zozobrar~ (older ~sozobrar~), and that from Old Catalan ~sotsobrar~, from ~sotsobre~ (“upside down”), made of ~sots~ (“under”) and ~sobre~ (“over”). Some instead derive the Catalan from a Vulgar Latin *~subsuperāre~, from Latin ~sub~ and ~super~, but that last step is only proposed.

French Wiktionary lists the Iberian account together with two others. One treats ~sombrer~ simply as a denominal verb from ~sombre~. The other presents an Old French verb ~sombrer~ or ~somarer~ (“to plough fallow land for the first time”), from ~sombre~ and ~somart~ (“the season of the first ploughing”), which it links to German ~Sommer~ (“summer”) and to Gaulish *~samo-~ (“summer”), the first ploughing being done on the first fine days. These accounts compete, and the evidence does not settle which is right. Only the Iberian account is given by English Wiktionary. Only the modern sense is secure, that of sinking, whence one can ~sombrer~ into despair or oblivion.
en.sommer:
A denominal verb built on the noun ~somme~ with the suffix ~-er~. The relevant ~somme~ descends from Latin ~summa~ (“the highest thing, the total, the sum”), the feminine of ~summus~ (“highest, topmost”), itself a superlative of ~superus~ (“upper”) and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~upo~ (“up, under”). Cognate nouns survive everywhere: Italian ~somma~, Spanish ~suma~, German ~Summe~, and English ~sum~, ~summary~, and ~summit~.

The two modern senses of ~sommer~ — “to sum up” and “to summon, to call upon” — both spring from ~summa~, by different routes. Roman accountants wrote the running total at the top of a column, the ~summa~ or highest line; to sum was to reach that crowning figure, which gives the arithmetic verb. The other sense passed through the medieval idea of a final, conclusive demand — the upshot of an argument pressed on someone — attested at Douai around 1250 as “to put under obligation, to enjoin,” which is why ~sommer~ today means to formally order someone to act. The same family gives French ~somme~ (“sum”), ~sommet~ (“summit”), ~sommaire~, ~consommer~, and ~suprême~, all reaching, in their way, for the top.
en.sonder:
~Sonder~ is usually explained as formed with the ending ~-er~ on ~sonde~ (“sounding line”), and it appears in Old French as ~sonder~ (“to plumb”). The noun ~sonde~ is probably of Old English origin. It comes from ~sund-~ in compounds such as ~sundġierd~ (“sounding rod”), ~sundlīne~ (“sounding line”) and ~sundrāp~ (“sounding rope”), where the first element, Old English ~sund~ (“sea, water”), came to stand for the whole tool. That word descends from Proto-Germanic *~sundą~ (“a swim, a body of water”), itself from a Proto-Indo-European root *~swem(bʰ)-~ (“to be unsteady, to swim”). Old Norse ~sund~ (“swimming, strait”) is a cognate, and English ~sound~, in the sense of a narrow arm of the sea, belongs to the same family.

French Wiktionary mentions a rival idea, that the verb comes instead from Latin ~subundāre~ (“to plunge”), but it adds that an Old French derivative is not demonstrated, so the origin of the verb is not fully settled. Either way, the meaning is clear: ~sonder~ began as the sailor's act of measuring depth by lowering a weighted line. From the sea it spread to figurative probing, as in sounding out the ground or people's feelings, and to science and medicine, where a ~sonde~ is any instrument pushed into a cavity or sent into the sky. A ~sondage~ is a poll or a survey, and ~insondable~ describes what cannot be fathomed.
en.songer:
From Latin ~somniāre~ (“to dream”), a verb formed on ~somnium~ (“a dream”), itself related to ~somnus~ (“sleep”). ~Somnus~ comes from Proto-Italic *~swepnos~ and PIE *~swépnos~ (“sleep, dream”), from the root *~swep-~ (“to sleep”) — a root with far-flung cousins: Sanskrit ~svápna~ (“sleep, dream”), Lithuanian ~sãpnas~, and, through Germanic, English ~sweven~ (an archaic word for “a dream”). Cognate Romance descendants of ~somniāre~ include Italian ~sognare~, Spanish ~soñar~, and Portuguese ~sonhar~.

The Latin verb meant literally “to dream in one's sleep,” and Old French ~songier~ kept that sense — a ~songe~ is still a dream, especially a portentous one. But French quietly shifted the everyday verb toward waking thought: to ~songer~ is now mostly “to muse, to ponder, to give thought to” (~songer à l'avenir~, “to think about the future”), the sleeping dream having drifted into reverie and reflection. Spanish ~soñar~ kept the literal “to dream,” which makes the French semantic drift the more striking. The root *~swep-~ surfaces elsewhere in French through Latin ~somnus~: ~sommeil~ (“sleep,” the inherited form), ~somnolent~, ~insomnie~, and ~somnifère~ — while ~songe~, ~songer~, and ~songerie~ trace the same root down its dreaming branch.
en.sonner:
From Latin ~sonare~ (« to sound, to resound »), attested in French from the tenth century. ~sonare~ comes from Proto-Italic *~swonaō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~swenh₂-~ (« to sound »). Through that root it is cognate with English ~sound~ and Sanskrit ~svanati~ (« it sounds, resounds »); Proto-Slavic *~zvoniti~ (« to ring ») belongs to the same family.

The core meaning has stayed remarkably steady — to make or give out a sound, especially of bells, clocks, and horns. Around it French grew a wealth of idiom: a clock « strikes » the hour, one « rings » at a door, a boxer's blow « ~sonne~ » its target (« stuns » him), and ~ne pas sonner mot~ means « not to say a word ». From the same root come the nouns ~son~ (« sound ») and ~sonnerie~ (« ringing, ringtone »), the borrowed ~sonnet~ (« little sound, little song »), and learned forms like ~sonore~ and ~résonner~, all still ringing with Latin ~sonare~.
en.sophistiquer: Often explained as a borrowing from Medieval Latin ~sophisticāre~ (“to trick, to falsify, to corrupt”), from Latin ~sophisticus~, itself from Greek ~sophistikós~, from ~sophistḗs~ (“a wise man, a clever expert”). Another analysis treats it as ~sophistique~ + ~-er~, which comes to the same Latin and Greek source. The older meaning was to adulterate or to tamper with, for instance to ~sophistiquer~ a wine, by adding to it. The modern sense “to make more refined or more complex” is probably later, driven by the adjective ~sophistiqué~ and influenced by the shift in English ~sophisticated~.
en.sortir:
French ~sortir~ gathers two senses — to go out and to take out or obtain — under one verb, and its origin is debated. The dominant view derives it from Vulgar Latin *~surctus~, from Latin ~surgere~ (“to rise, to spring up”), itself a contraction of *~surrigere~, from ~sub-~ (“up from below”) and ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to rule”). The literal early meaning was “to spring forth, to gush,” which unifies both senses: what springs out goes out, and what one makes spring forth one obtains. Cognate with Spanish ~surtir~ and Italian ~sortire~.

Around the sixteenth century ~sortir~ displaced the older ~issir~ (from Latin ~exire~) as the ordinary verb for leaving. The transitive sense — ~sortir~ a card, ~sortir~ a result, the legal ~sortir son effet~ (“to take effect”) — preserves the original notion of bringing something forth. A separate Latin verb, ~sortiri~ (“to draw lots,” from ~sors~, “fate, lot”), reinforced the “obtain” branch and may have blended in; from ~sors~ French also kept ~sort~ (“fate, spell”) and ~sorte~ (“kind, sort”). The same root *~h₃reǵ-~ that gave ~regere~ underlies ~régir~, ~direct~, ~roi~, and ~règle~.
en.soucier:
From Old French ~soucier~ (Middle French ~soucyer~), inherited from Latin ~sollicitāre~ (“to stir up, to agitate, to disturb”). The Latin verb comes from the adjective ~sollicitus~ (“agitated, anxious”), usually analyzed as ~sollus~ (“whole”) + ~citus~ (“set in motion”), that is, “wholly stirred.” Italian ~sollecitare~ and Spanish ~solicitar~ are its cousins. What is striking is how heavily French wore the word down. The long Latin shape with its doubled ~ll~ and three syllables before the ending was cut down to a compact ~soucier~, which no longer looks like its source at all.

Because the learned side of French later borrowed the same Latin verb again, ~soucier~ has a doublet: ~solliciter~, which keeps the Latin shape and the sense “to request, to petition” (and, in English, ~solicit~ and ~solicitous~ show the same family). The two verbs share an ancestor but lead different lives, one for worry, the other for asking. The noun ~souci~ (“worry”) was drawn from the verb, and gave ~soucieux~ (“worried”) and ~insouciant~ (“carefree,” literally “not worrying”). The reflexive ~se soucier de~ means to care about something, and is most often met in the negative, as in ~ne pas se soucier de~. The marigold, also called ~souci~, is an unrelated flower whose name only happens to sound the same.
en.souder:
From Old French ~solder~, inherited from Latin ~solidāre~ (“to make solid, to consolidate, to firm up”), a verb built on the adjective ~solidus~ (“solid”). In the move from Old French ~solder~ to ~souder~, the ~l~ before the ~d~ turned into a vowel ~u~, as in many French words. English ~solder~ was borrowed from the Old French verb. The Latin verb has a learned sibling in French, ~consolider~, a borrowing from the prefixed Latin ~consolidāre~, which means the same thing as the plain verb once did.

The path of meaning is short and concrete: to make something solid is, for a metalworker, to fuse two pieces into one firm piece with a molten alloy. French then stretched the verb to any firm joining, and ~souder~ also serves figuratively, as when people are ~soudés~ (“close-knit”) by hardship. From the same Latin adjective ~solidus~ come ~solide~ and ~solidaire~, and the noun ~soudure~ is the direct result of the verb. The old Roman gold coin ~solidus~ is also the ancestor of French ~sou~, though that is a separate trail through the noun.
en.souffler:
From Old French ~sofler~, also ~sufler~ (attested in the early twelfth century), from Latin ~sufflāre~ (“to blow on, to inflate”), composed of ~sub-~ (“from below”) and ~flāre~ (“to blow”), from Proto-Italic *~flāō~, from the PIE root *~bʰleh₁-~ (“to blow”) — the same root that, through its Germanic branch, produced English ~blow~ and German ~blähen~. Cognate with Italian ~soffiare~ and Spanish ~soplar~. The simple ~flāre~ also reached French through other compounds: ~enfler~ (from ~inflāre~) and ~gonfler~ (from ~conflāre~) descend from the same Latin blowing-verb.

In Old French the verb covered everything breath can do: blow, puff, pant, breathe hard. From breathing a word came the sense “to whisper something to someone” (1538) — whence the theater's ~souffleur~, the prompter crouched in his box feeding actors their lines, and the schoolroom sin of whispering answers. The game of checkers gave French the proverb ~souffler n'est pas jouer~ (“blowing is not playing”): under an old rule, a piece that had failed to capture was “blown” — removed from the board. And since the seventeenth century, ~souffler quelque chose à quelqu'un~ has meant to snatch something from under someone's nose — a job, a client, a dance partner — as if stolen with a puff of air. The family is large: ~souffle~ (breath), ~soufflé~ (the dish that is literally “puffed up”), ~soufflet~ (the bellows — and, by extension, a slap), ~souffleur~ (glassblower as well as prompter), ~essouffler~ (to wind, to leave breathless) and ~insuffler~ (to breathe into).
en.souffrir:
From Vulgar Latin *~sufferīre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~sufferre~ (“to bear, to endure, to undergo”), a compound of the prefix ~sub-~ (“under”) and the verb ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). ~ferre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”), one of the most widespread of all roots, giving Ancient Greek ~φέρω~ (~phérō~), Sanskrit ~bhárati~, and — in the Germanic line — English ~bear~. To ~sufferre~ was thus literally to “carry from underneath,” to take a weight on one's shoulders.

That image of bearing a load from below is the whole of the word: the sufferer is the one who carries the burden. French kept both halves of the sense — to ~souffrir~ is to undergo pain, but also, in older and literary usage, to tolerate or permit (~souffrir une exception~, to allow an exception). The root *~bʰer-~ is enormously productive in French through ~ferre~ and its participle ~lātus~: ~offrir~, ~conférer~, ~différer~, ~transférer~, ~préférer~, and the nouns ~relation~ and ~translation~. Note that ~souffrir~ takes a single ~f~ in the infinitive but doubles it across much of its conjugation (~je souffre~) — a fossil of that Vulgar Latin *~sufferīre~ with its geminate from ~sub-~ + ~ferre~.
en.souhaiter:
From Old French ~sohaidier~ (attested 1175, in Chrétien de Troyes), reshaped into ~souhaiter~ by the mid-14th century under the influence of the noun ~souhait~ (which hardened the medial ~-d-~ to ~-t-~). The source is a Gallo-Romance *~subtus-haitare~ (“to promise without committing oneself too far”), a hybrid built from Latin ~subtus~ (“under, beneath”) and Old French ~haitier~. That second element is Germanic: ~haitier~ goes back to a Frankish *~haitan~ (“to call, to command, to vow”), cognate with Gothic ~haitan~ and Old High German ~heizzan~, both “to call, command.”

The blend is a tidy snapshot of how French was made — a Latin preposition welded to a Frankish verb. The ~subtus~ (“under”) lent a shade of reserve, as if a wish were a half-spoken, under-the-breath vow. In Old French ~haitier~ also meant “to gladden, to please,” and the related adjective ~haitié~ meant “cheerful, in good health,” so the family carried a warm sense of well-wishing well suited to its modern descendant. Today ~souhaiter~ keeps the noun ~souhait~ at its side, surviving also in the set phrase ~à souhait~ (“to perfection, as much as one could wish”).
en.soulager:
From Middle French ~soulager~, ultimately from a Vulgar Latin ~subleviare~, an altered ~sublevare~ (~sub-~ + ~levare~, “to lift, lighten”) reshaped on the model of ~alleviare~ (“to relieve”). ~Levare~ derives from ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from PIE *~h₁lengʷʰ-~. By the regular sound-laws ~sublevare~ should have given an Old French ~souléger~ (compare ~alléger~); the modern ~soulager~ instead shows interference. The sources hedge on the source of that interference: the TLFi points to Old French ~assouagier~ (“to soften, soothe”) and to a crossing with ~soulas~ / ~solacier~ (“solace,” from Latin ~solacium~), and notes that some forms may simply be a dialectal ~solacier~ — so the exact path is disputed rather than settled.

The early senses were concrete: an attestation from around 1175 means “to throw cargo overboard in a storm,” i.e. to lighten a ship, before the verb settled on “to unburden” and then “to ease pain.” The same root *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ gives French ~léger~, ~alléger~, ~lever~, ~élever~, and ~soulèvement~, and — through Latin ~levis~ — English ~levity~ and ~lever~. Modern derivatives include ~soulagement~ and ~soulageable~.
en.soulever:
A French formation, ~lever~ (“to raise”) prefixed with ~sous-~ (“under, sub-”); early forms ~soslevar~ and ~suslever~ are attested around 980. ~lever~ descends from Latin ~levare~ (“to lighten, raise”), a denominative of ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from Proto-Italic *~leɣʷis~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”). The root also yields English ~light~ and Ancient Greek ~ἐλαφρός~ (“nimble”); through Latin ~levis~ French keeps ~léger~ and the learned ~lévité~ has an English cousin in ~levity~.

The prefix ~sous-~ pictures lifting a thing from beneath — slipping a force under a load to heave it up. From that physical act French spread the verb outward: to ~soulever~ the lid, to pick up a child, then figuratively to stir up a crowd to revolt, to rouse indignation or enthusiasm, and even to “raise” an objection or a question in argument. The same image of taking a weight off underlies the Latin parent ~levare~, which is why “to lighten” and “to lift” share one verb. From ~levare~ and its kin French also has ~lever~, ~élever~ (“to raise, to bring up”), ~soulèvement~ (“an uprising”), and ~levier~ (“a lever”).
en.souligner:
A transparent compound of ~sous~ (“under,” from Latin ~subtus~) and ~ligne~ (“line”), literally “to put a line under.” The noun ~ligne~ descends from Latin ~linea~ (“a linen thread, a string, a line”), originally the feminine of an adjective meaning “made of flax,” from ~linum~ (“flax, linen”). It is cognate with Italian ~linea~, Spanish ~línea~, and — borrowed through French and Latin — English ~line~ and ~linen~; the carpenter's chalked string that snapped a straight mark gave the word its geometric sense.

The literal meaning is the original one: to draw a line beneath a word on the page. From there the verb rose easily into the figurative, “to emphasize, to stress,” since underlining is how writers point a reader to what matters. French today says ~souligner un mot~ for the pen-stroke and ~souligner un fait~ for calling attention to it, the two senses living comfortably side by side. The flaxen root of ~linum~ runs through a wide field of French words: ~ligne~ and ~aligner~, ~ligature~ and ~linéaire~, and even ~lin~ (“flax”) and ~linceul~ (“a linen shroud”) — a reminder that the humble line began as a thread.
en.soumettre:
From Old French ~suzmetre~, from Latin ~submittere~ (“to lower, put under, yield”), from ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, throw”). In French the verb was remodeled on ~mettre~ (“to put”), with the prefix ~sous-~ (“under”). The Latin ~mittere~ is traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth-~ (“to exchange, remove”). Cognate with Italian ~sottomettere~ and Spanish ~someter~, and — through ~mittere~ — with English ~submit~, ~mission~, and ~commit~.

The literal sense is to “put under,” and the verb still flexes between two directions: to ~soumettre~ a people is to subjugate it, to place it beneath one's power; but to ~soumettre~ a proposal is to lay it before someone for judgment — to “submit” it, deferentially. The reflexive ~se soumettre~ completes the picture, meaning to yield or comply. From the rich ~mittere~ family, whose participle ~missus~ gives the ~-mis~ of so many forms, French draws ~mettre~, ~mission~, ~message~, ~promettre~, ~permettre~, ~admettre~, and ~commettre~ — a whole verbal household built on the idea of sending and placing.
en.soupirer:
From Old French ~souspirer~ (the form Middle French kept), inherited from Latin ~suspīrāre~ (“to draw a deep breath, to sigh”), which is ~sub-~ (“from below”) + ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe”). The Latin verb is the same one that gave Italian ~sospirare~ and Spanish ~suspirar~, and English has taken it back as the literary ~suspire~. English ~spirit~, ~inspire~ and ~expire~ all come from ~spīrāre~.

French extended the verb to the sighs of love, so a ~soupirant~ was a suitor who sighed for a woman, and the word ~soupir~ moved into music, where it names a rest, a silent beat. A more surprising relative is ~soupirail~, a small basement window, which in Old French meant a breathing hole, an air vent. Among the cousins from ~spīrāre~ are ~respirer~ (“to breathe again”), ~aspirer~ (“to breathe toward”), ~conspirer~ (“to breathe together,” hence to plot) and ~esprit~.
en.soupçonner:
~Soupçonner~ is attested around 1200, in the form ~souspecener~; it is built on the noun ~soupçon~, Old French ~sospeçon~ (around 1145, in Wace), from Late Latin ~suspectionem~, a remodelling of classical ~suspicio~ (“mistrust, suspicion”), from ~suspicere~, literally “to look up at,” from ~sub-~ (“from below”) and ~specere~ (“to look”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~speḱ-~ (“to observe”). It was the spoken Latin of Gaul, not the classical language, that French inherited: worn smooth by sound change, ~suspectionem~ collapsed into ~sospeçon~. Spanish ~sospechar~ and Italian ~sospettare~ are its Romance siblings, and English ~suspicion~ a French export; farther afield, English ~spy~ goes back through Germanic to the same root, as do French ~espion~ and ~épier~.

The buried picture is the upward, sidelong glance: in Latin, ~suspicere~ was to eye someone from below — and the very same verb also meant “to look up to, to admire.” Of that double gaze French kept only the wary half: the admiration fell away, the mistrust stayed. The noun then grew a second, daintier life: from 1746 ~soupçon~ could name a barely perceptible quantity — ~un soupçon de lait~ — suspicion shrunk to a trace, as if so little milk could only be suspected, never seen; English borrowed the word in precisely that sense, ~a soupçon of garlic~. The watching family is numerous: ~suspect~, ~spectacle~, ~inspecter~, ~respecter~ (Latin ~respicere~, “to look back at”), ~perspective~. ~Soupçonner~ remains its shadiest member: looking at the world from under lowered lids.
en.sourire:
From Old French ~sourire~ (earlier ~sorire~, ~surrire~), from Latin ~subrīdēre~ (“to smile”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“slightly, somewhat”) and ~rīdēre~ (“to laugh”). The prefix attenuates the action: a smile is, etymologically, a small or under-laugh. French ~rire~ continues ~rīdēre~ directly, as do Italian ~ridere~ and Spanish ~reír~.

The origin of ~rīdēre~ itself is, remarkably, unresolved. Some have linked it to a root meaning “to turn (the mouth),” but De Vaan finds no credible Indo-European source and rejects the once-proposed tie to Sanskrit ~vrīḍate~; Matasović instead floats a connection to Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~ (“to scratch”). So while the French structure of ~sourire~ is perfectly clear — ~sub-~ + ~rīdēre~ — its deepest root is genuinely disputed and best left open. From the same Latin verb come French ~ridicule~, ~dérider~, ~risible~, and ~risée~, alongside English ~ridicule~ and ~deride~ — a whole family branching from laughter, of which the smile is the gentlest member.
en.sous-entendre: A compound of ~sous~ (“under”) and ~entendre~. The preposition ~sous~ comes through Old French ~soz~ and Middle French ~soubs~ from Latin ~subtus~ (“beneath”). The verb ~entendre~ (“to hear, to understand”) goes back to Latin ~intendere~ (“to stretch toward,” hence to direct the mind to something). The literal sense is therefore “to understand underneath”: to give a meaning that is present without being spoken aloud.
en.sous-estimer: Formed from the prefix ~sous-~ and the verb ~estimer~. The prefix comes from the Old French preposition ~sous~, from Latin ~subtus~ (“beneath”), and in verbs like this one it marks insufficiency: to value something below its worth, the opposite of ~surestimer~. The base ~estimer~ descends from Latin ~aestimāre~ (“to appraise, to value”), whose own origin is debated. The traditional account sees a compound of ~aes~ (“bronze, money”) and a verb of cutting, as if appraising began with weighing out metal, while a more recent proposal links it to an Indo-European root meaning “to seek”. English ~esteem~ and ~estimate~ are cognates borrowed from the same Latin word.
en.souscrire:
From Latin ~subscribere~ (« to write underneath, to sign at the foot of »), from ~sub-~ (« under ») and ~scribere~ (« to write »). ~scribere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~, a root meaning « to scratch, to cut, to incise » — writing was first scratching. It is cognate with German ~schreiben~ (« to write »), English ~scribe~ and ~shrive~, and Ancient Greek ~σκάριφος~ (« stylus, scratched outline »).

The meaning follows the Roman gesture exactly: to ~subscribe~ was to write your name at the bottom of a document, and thus to endorse, approve, or commit to it. From that signing of one's assent come all the modern senses — to « subscribe » to a publication, to « take out » an insurance policy or shares, to « subscribe to » an opinion. The same root *~(s)kreybʰ-~ underlies a large French family: ~écrire~, ~décrire~, ~inscrire~, ~prescrire~, ~manuscrit~, and ~scribe~, every one of them an heir to the old act of scratching marks into a surface.
en.soutenir:
From Old French ~sostenir~ (later ~soustenir~), from Vulgar Latin *~sustenīre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~sustinēre~ (“to hold up, bear, endure”). The verb is transparently ~sub-~ (“up from below”) + ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), which descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Through that root it is cognate with Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch”) and ~tenuis~ (“thin”), with Greek ~teínein~ (“to stretch”), and with English ~thin~. Its Romance siblings include Italian ~sostenere~ and Spanish ~sostener~, both still everyday verbs.

The literal Latin sense was physical: to hold something up from underneath, to prop it. From that base the meaning fanned out into nearly every figurative direction in which a weight can be borne — to ~soutenir~ an argument is to uphold it, to ~soutenir~ a friend is to back them, and to ~soutenir~ a siege is to withstand it. The same ~tenēre~ underlies a whole French battalion of compounds built on ~tenir~: ~contenir~, ~détenir~, ~maintenir~, ~obtenir~, ~retenir~. A surprising offshoot is the noun ~souteneur~, literally “one who supports,” which French narrowed to mean a pimp — the man who, with grim irony, “sustains” a prostitute by living off her. The plainer noun ~soutien~ (“support”) and the adjective ~tenace~ (“tenacious”) keep the root’s honest sense of holding firm.
en.souvenir:
From Latin ~subvenīre~ (“to come up, come to one's aid”), formed from ~sub-~ (“under, from below”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). ~Venīre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”), the very root behind English ~come~, Ancient Greek ~βαίνω~ (~baínō~, “to walk”), and Sanskrit ~गच्छति~ (~gácchati~, “goes”). Old French inherited it as ~sovenir~.

The image is wonderfully concrete: a memory ~comes up~ from below into the mind, “se présente à la mémoire.” What in Latin meant “to come to the rescue” narrowed in French to this mental rising — a recollection surfacing unbidden. The verb is normally reflexive, ~se souvenir de~, “to remember,” and its infinitive was nominalized into ~le souvenir~, a memory or a keepsake — the noun English borrowed wholesale as ~souvenir~. The ~venīre~ family is enormous in French: ~venir~, ~devenir~, ~revenir~, ~convenir~, ~prévenir~, ~survenir~, and ~subvenir~ (which kept the older “to provide for, come to aid”). Each is, at heart, a different way of coming.
en.sponsoriser: Formed from the English noun ~sponsor~ with the French verb suffix ~-iser~, giving “to sponsor.” English ~sponsor~ was itself taken from Latin ~spōnsor~ (“guarantor”), so the word has made a loop from Latin through English and back into French. Official French recommendations of 1982 and 1983 favored ~commanditaire~ over ~sponsor~, even though the word is also of Latin origin. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and today builds verbs such as ~moderniser~.
en.spécialiser:
A modern French derivative, formed from the adjective ~spécial~ plus the productive verbal suffix ~-iser~. ~Spécial~ comes from Latin ~speciālis~ (“belonging to a particular kind”), from ~speciēs~ (“appearance, sort, kind”), the noun of ~specere~ (“to look at”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~spek̑-~ (“to observe, to watch”). The suffix ~-iser~ descends through Latin ~-izāre~ from Greek ~-ízein~. English ~specialize~ and Italian ~specializzare~ are parallel formations on the same Latin adjective.

The semantic thread runs through ~speciēs~: a “species” is a particular kind set apart by its appearance, so to specialize is to narrow oneself to one particular kind of thing. The reflexive ~se spécialiser~ means to confine one's training to a single field; the transitive sense — to assign a specialized task, to earmark — keeps the same logic of singling out. Because the root is *~spek̑-~, “to look,” ~spécialiser~ belongs to the great visual family of French: ~espèce~ (the direct descendant of ~speciēs~), ~spécimen~, ~spécifique~, ~spécieux~ (“specious,” fair only in appearance), and — through the looking sense itself — ~spectacle~, ~aspect~, and ~respecter~.
en.spécifier: A learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~specificāre~, built on ~specificus~ (“specific, particular”). That adjective combines Latin ~speciēs~ (“kind, sort”), the source of French ~espèce~, with the verb ~facere~ (“to make”), so ~specificus~ means roughly “making a kind” or “of a particular kind.” To ~spécifier~ is thus to name exactly which kind a thing belongs to, hence “to state precisely.” The same ~speciēs~ gave ~espèce~ by popular descent and ~spécial~ and ~spécifique~ by learned borrowing, a pair of siblings that differ only in how long ago they entered French.
en.stabiliser: Built in French on the stem ~stabil-~ of ~stable~, modeled on Latin ~stabilis~, plus the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make A”): to stabilize is to make stable. Latin ~stabilis~ (“standing firm”) comes from the verb ~stāre~ (“to stand”) and the adjective ending ~-bilis~, and so from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), which also lies behind English ~stand~. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs. Related words include ~stable~, ~stabilité~ and ~établir~, from Latin ~stabilīre~, a cousin of the same family.
en.stagner: Borrowed from Latin ~stagnāre~, “to form a pool, to be still,” a verb built on ~stagnum~ (“pool, standing water”). The sense is physical at the source: water that does not flow becomes a pond. French uses the verb of water that stands still, and by extension of anything that stops moving forward, such as an economy, a career or a conversation. The same Latin noun gave French ~étang~ by inheritance, through Old French ~estanc~, and the same family gave ~étancher~.
en.standardiser: Formed from ~standard~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, a form that transcribed Greek verbs, so “to make conform to a standard”. French ~standard~ is borrowed from English ~standard~, which took it from Old French ~estandart~ (“banner, military ensign”), probably from Old Low Franconian *~standhard~ (“firm, fixed”). A rival theory, defended by the Oxford dictionary, links it instead to medieval Latin ~standardum~, from ~extendere~ (“to stretch out”), so the origin is debated. The sense of a measure or reference is attested from the thirteenth century in Anglo-French, with an obscure origin. It is a doublet of ~étendard~.
en.stationner: ~Stationner~ is formed from the noun ~station~ and the verb suffix ~-er~. ~Station~ comes through Old French ~estation~ from Latin ~statio~ (“a standing still, a post”), from ~stāre~ (“to stand”). The verb meant to stay in one place, to halt, and it now applies above all to vehicles: ~stationner~ is to park, with ~stationnement~ for parking itself. The root ~stāre~ is the same one that lies behind ~ester~ and ~stable~.
en.statuer:
French ~statuer~ comes from Latin ~statuere~ (“to set up, to fix, to establish”), a verb built on the noun ~status~ (“a standing, a position”), itself from ~stāre~ (“to stand”) and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). To ~statuere~ something was to make it stand, to place it firmly. English preserves the same Latin verb in several guises: ~statute~ comes from ~statūtum~, the participle of ~statuere~, and ~statue~ and ~constitute~ come from the same family. The root also underlies English ~stand~ and German ~stehen~.

The physical sense “to set upright” slid into a legal and mental one: to fix a rule, then to settle a question, then to take a decision. That is the meaning French kept, in the phrase ~statuer sur~ (“to rule on”), used of judges, councils and committees that must come to a ruling. The verb stays close to its relatives ~statut~ (a fixed rule), ~statue~ (a figure made to stand), ~constituer~, ~instituer~ and ~destituer~, all of which keep the idea of putting something in place. A court that ~statue~ is, etymologically, one that makes a matter stand firm.
en.stigmatiser:
The sources give two routes. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~stigma~, genitive ~stigmatis~, itself borrowed from Greek ~στίγμα~ (stígma, “prick, mark burned with an iron”). English Wiktionary instead sees a verb taken from Medieval Latin ~stigmatizō~, from Byzantine Greek ~στιγματίζω~ (stigmatízō, “to mark with a stigma”), adding that on the surface it also looks like ~stigmate~ + ~-iser~. The Greek noun comes from ~στίζειν~ (“to prick, to tattoo”), a verb usually linked to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to stick, to pierce,” which English ~stick~ and German ~stechen~ also continue.

The Greek mark was literal: a point pricked or burned into skin, as slaves and criminals were marked so that everyone could see their status. Christian tradition then used ~stigmate~ for the wounds of Christ's Passion said to appear on the bodies of saints, notably Francis of Assisi. The verb kept both strands, and French turned the mark of shame into a figurative one: to ~stigmatiser~ someone is to brand them publicly as guilty or despicable, or to denounce a practice. The family includes ~stigmate~, ~stigmatisation~ and the optical term ~astigmatisme~.
en.stimuler:
From Latin ~stimulare~ (“to goad, prick”), from the noun ~stimulus~, an ox-goad — the pointed stick that drove cattle forward. The deeper root is uncertain: ~stimulus~ is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European *~(s)teyg-~ (“to prick, to be sharp”), source of Greek ~στίζω~ (“to mark by pricking”) and English ~stick~ and ~stitch~; but the etymologist De Vaan is skeptical of that link, and some prefer a base *~(s)tey-~ “sharp object,” which would also lie behind Latin ~stilus~ (“stake, writing-point”). Treat the precise root as disputed.

Whatever its origin, the image is sharp and physical: to stimulate was to jab with a goad, to spur an ox or a soldier into motion. From that literal prick came the figurative “to rouse, excite, whip up,” first in oratory and medicine, now everywhere — one ~stimule~ an economy, an appetite, a nerve. The French family is small and transparent: ~stimulus~, ~stimulant~, ~stimulation~, and the physiological ~stimuline~.
en.stipuler:
From Latin ~stipulārī~ (“to demand a formal promise, to bargain”), a verb of Roman law. The ~stipulātiō~ was a contract concluded by a spoken exchange: one party asked a question in set words (“Do you promise?”) and the other answered with the same verb (“I promise”). No document was needed, only the words said aloud in the right order. French borrowed the verb from Latin, and English ~stipulate~ was borrowed in the same learned way. Italian has ~stipulare~ and Spanish ~estipular~.

The deeper origin of the Latin verb is uncertain, but there is a traditional explanation, going back to Isidore of Seville and repeated in Alain Rey's dictionary. It links the verb to Latin ~stipula~ (“straw, stalk”) and says that, in the old days, a straw was snapped in two to support a promise. Treat this as a tradition and not as an established fact. The same Latin noun ~stipula~ gave French ~stipule~, the botanical term for the small leaf-like appendage at the base of a leaf stalk. From its legal beginning, the modern verb has lost much of its ceremony: to ~stipuler~ is now to state expressly, to specify, as in a clause that ~stipule~ a delivery date, and the related noun ~stipulation~ is the clause itself.
en.stocker:
~stocker~ is a young verb: it is a denominal formed in French from the noun ~stock~, which French borrowed from English ~stock~ in the commercial sense of a reserve of goods. English ~stock~ goes back to Old English ~stocc~ (“tree-trunk, post, stump”), from Proto-Germanic *~stukkaz~ (“tree-trunk”), and is cognate with German ~Stock~ (“stick, cane”) and Dutch ~stok~. The path from “tree-trunk” to “supply of goods” ran through the medieval merchant’s tally — a notched ~stock~ of wood recording debts and stores — though the precise route of that semantic leap is not fully settled.

So the French verb carries, at several removes, the image of a wooden post. Borrowed back into French only in the modern commercial era, ~stocker~ kept its English pronunciation’s hard final consonant and means simply “to keep in reserve, to store up”: on ~stocke~ des marchandises, du carburant, des données. The same English noun seeded a whole family of French business terms — ~stock~, ~stockage~ (“storage”), ~déstockage~ (“clearance, destocking”), ~surstock~ (“overstock”) — a small cluster of Germanic-rooted loanwords sitting, slightly incongruously, among the Latin-descended bulk of French.
en.stopper: Formed in French from the noun and interjection ~stop~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to say stop to, to bring to a halt.” French ~stop~ was borrowed from English ~stop~ in 1792. The French verb is thus a loan noun with a French verb ending attached. In the same family, ~stop~ is also the French word for the road sign, and the clipped ~stop~ for hitchhiking is a pseudo-anglicism, short for ~auto-stop~, that English speakers do not use in that sense.
en.stresser: Formed in French from the noun ~stress~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to cause stress” and, intransitively or reflexively, “to be stressed”. The noun ~stress~ came into French from English, but the English word itself descends partly from Middle French ~destresse~ (“hardship, distress”) and partly from Old French ~estrece~ (“narrowness, oppression”), from Latin ~stringere~ (“to tighten”). It is therefore a word that left French and returned. The psychological sense was studied and popularized by the physician Hans Selye in the 1960s.
en.structurer:
~structurer~ is a denominal verb, formed in French on the noun ~structure~, which comes from Latin ~strūctūra~ (“a building, a fitting-together”), the action noun of ~struere~ (“to pile up, to arrange, to build”). ~struere~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~strowō~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~strew-~ (“to strew, to spread out”), so the deepest image is of strewing or laying things out in order. The same root gives English ~strew~ and, through Latin compounds of ~struere~, English ~structure~, ~construct~, and ~destroy~.

The noun ~structure~ named first a built thing and then, more abstractly, the arrangement of parts within any whole; the verb ~structurer~, more recent, means to give such an arrangement — to organize, to shape into a coherent order: ~structurer~ un texte, une équipe, une pensée. Its negative, ~déstructurer~ (“to break down the structure of”), and the adjective ~structuré~ (“well-organized”) belong to the same modern family, and the root’s Latin relatives crowd French with ~construire~, ~détruire~, ~instruire~, and ~industrie~ — a dense thicket all grown from the idea of piling up and arranging.
en.stériliser: ~Stériliser~ is formed from the adjective ~stérile~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to render A” (as in ~moderniser~). The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~sterilis~ (“barren, unproductive, fruitless”), used first of land, animals and people that bear nothing. French ~stériliser~ extends this idea in two directions: to make a living being unable to reproduce, and to rid an object of living germs, so that nothing can grow on it.
en.subir:
From Latin ~subire~ (“to go under, to approach, to undergo, to submit to”), a compound of the preposition ~sub~ (“under”) and the irregular verb ~ire~ (“to go”). ~ire~ descends from Proto-Italic *~eō~ and ultimately from PIE *~ey-~ (“to go”), a root of remarkable productivity. Cognate with Italian ~subire~ and Spanish and Portuguese ~subir~ — though the Iberian verbs, by a curious twist, came to mean “to go up” while French kept the Latin sense of going under and enduring.

The metaphor at the heart of ~subir~ is bodily: to place oneself beneath a weight and bear it. Latin ~subire~ already covered both the neutral “to undergo” and the heavier “to suffer, to be subjected to,” and French inherited this passive, enduring colour — one ~subit~ a defeat, an interrogation, an operation, rarely anything one would have chosen. The PIE root *~ey-~ behind ~ire~ surfaces all across French through Latin compounds: ~transir~, the noun ~issue~, and learned forms such as ~ambition~, ~initial~, ~transit~, and ~sédition~ all trace to that single small verb “to go.” The closely related ~subit~ (“sudden”) and ~subitement~ preserve another shade of ~subire~ — the abrupt arrival of what “comes up” on us unawares.
en.submerger:
Borrowed as a learned word from Latin ~submergere~ (“to plunge under, to sink”), built from ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~mergere~ (“to dip, to plunge”). The Latin verb ~mergere~ is traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~mezg-~ (“to dip, to dive”). Because French took the word whole from Latin rather than inheriting it, it kept the Latin shape almost intact. English reached the same word the same way, as ~submerge~, and also has ~merge~ from the simple verb ~mergere~, whose older sense was to dip something into a liquid.

In Latin the verb was physical: a ship, a person or a field could be ~submersus~, covered by water. French kept that image and added the figurative sense that the learner sees most often, to be overwhelmed by work, emotion or numbers, as in ~être submergé de travail~. Its relatives show the family at work: ~submersible~ (a vessel that goes under), ~submersion~, and the opposite pair ~émerger~ (“to rise out of the water”) and ~immerger~ (“to plunge in”).
en.subordonner: From Latin ~subordināre~, formed from ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~ordināre~ (“to arrange, to put in order”), which comes from ~ōrdō~ (“row, rank, order”). To ~subordonner~ one thing to another is therefore to place it in a lower rank beneath it, whether a person under an authority or a clause under a main clause. The French verb is thus a close cousin of ~ordonner~ (“to arrange, to command”), and its participle ~subordonné~ gave French the noun for an underling and the grammatical term ~proposition subordonnée~.
en.subsister:
From Latin ~subsistere~ (“to take a stand, halt, endure”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under, up from below”) and ~sistere~ (“to make stand, set”). ~sistere~ is a reduplicated present built on Proto-Italic *~sistō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~stísteh₂ti~, from the root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the same root that gave Latin ~stāre~. Cognate, through that root, with Ancient Greek ~ἵστημι~ (“to stand”) and with the Latin verb-family of ~consistere~, ~resistere~, and ~persistere~.

The literal force is “to stand firm underneath,” hence “to hold out, to keep going.” French ~subsister~ kept this resilient sense: a custom, a doubt, or a person may ~subsister~ — persist, hold on, manage to live. The reduplicated *~steh₂-~ stem seeded a dense thicket of French words: ~consister~, ~résister~, ~persister~, ~insister~, ~assister~, and the nouns ~système~ and ~assistance~. To ~subsister~ is, etymologically, to remain standing when everything around might fall.
en.substituer:
From Latin ~substituere~ (“to put in place of, to set under”), from ~sub-~ (“under, in place of”) + ~statuere~ (“to set up, to establish”). The verb ~statuere~ is built on ~status~, the past participle of ~stāre~ (“to stand”), and so reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the same root behind ~stable~, ~statue~, and the verb ~ester~. Latin ~substituere~ gave Italian ~sostituire~ and Spanish ~sustituir~ as well as the French verb.

The internal picture is precise: ~sub-~ here carries the sense “in the place beneath/instead of,” so to ~substituer~ is to stand one thing in another's stead — to set B where A stood. French preserves a useful grammatical asymmetry: ~substituer A à B~ means to put A in place of B, the new element taking the preposition ~à~. The standing-in-place root spreads through a tidy modern family: ~substitut~ (“substitute, deputy,” and in court a deputy prosecutor), ~substitution~, and ~substituable~ (“interchangeable”). Every one of them, at bottom, is about something taking a stand where another once stood.
en.subventionner: Formed in French from the noun ~subvention~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~subventio~ (“aid”), from Late Latin ~subventiōnem~, a noun of action on ~subvenīre~ (“to come to help”, from ~sub-~ and ~venīre~). To ~subventionner~ is to support a person, a cause or an activity with public money, and the Latin sense of coming to someone's aid remains visible in the word.
en.succomber:
Borrowed into Old French from Latin ~succumbere~ (“to sink down under, to give way”), formed from ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~cumbere~ (“to lie down”), a nasalised relative of ~cubāre~ (“to lie”). The same lying-down element is in other words: ~incomber~ (“to fall to someone”, as a duty does) and ~concubine~ (a woman who lies with someone). English ~succumb~ is the same Latin verb, and Italian ~soccombere~ and Spanish ~sucumbir~ are its relatives.

The Latin image is of someone collapsing under a weight, and French kept that picture: to buckle under a load, or to be overcome by a blow or an enemy. Meanings extended in two directions. One is to yield to something stronger, as in ~succomber à la tentation~ (“to give in to temptation”), where the weight is moral. The other is to die: ~succomber à ses blessures~ means to die of one's wounds, and bare ~il a succombé~ is a gentle way of saying that someone died. In law, ~succomber~ also means to lose a case, so the losing party is the ~partie qui succombe~.
en.succéder:
From Latin ~succēdere~ (“to go under, to come up to, to follow after, to take the place of”), from ~sub-~ (“under, up to”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, to withdraw, to yield”). ~Cēdere~ is of disputed origin, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱe~ (“here”) plus *~sed-~ (“to sit”), giving “to go and sit.” Cognate, through ~cēdere~, with English ~cede~ and the doublets Italian ~succedere~ and Spanish ~suceder~.

The image inside ~sub-~ + ~cēdere~ is of stepping up under someone — moving into the place they vacate — which neatly yields two of the verb's senses: to follow in order, and to inherit a throne or office. From the same ~cēdere~ French built a dense network of motion-and-yielding verbs: ~céder~, ~accéder~, ~précéder~, ~procéder~, and ~succéder~ itself, plus the nouns ~succès~, ~successeur~, ~succession~, and ~procès~. Strikingly, ~succès~ (“success”) is just the past-participle stem of ~succēdere~: a success is literally an outcome that has “followed on,” a “coming-after” that turned out well — the neutral idea of sequence narrowing, over centuries, into the bright modern sense of triumph.
en.sucer:
From Vulgar Latin *~suctiare~, derived from ~suctum~, the supine of Latin ~sugere~ (“to suck”). The Latin verb goes back to PIE *~seu-~ (“to take in liquid”). The root is wonderfully wet across the languages it touched: from it come Latin ~sucus~ (“juice, sap”) and, through Proto-Germanic, English ~suck~, ~sip~, and ~soak~ — even French ~soupe~ (“soup”) belongs, distantly, to the same family of words for drawing in liquid.

To ~sucer~ is to draw something in through pursed lips — a sweet, a thumb, the marrow of a bone. The image of extraction made it naturally figurative: ~sucer~ jusqu'à la moelle, “to suck dry to the marrow,” means to exploit something utterly. The root's French descendants stay close to the body and the kitchen: ~suçon~ (“a love-bite” or a sucked sweet), ~sucette~ (“a lollipop”), ~succion~ (“suction”), and the related ~suc~ (“juice, essence”). What unites them is the oldest gesture of all, the infant's act of drawing in liquid.
en.sucrer:
Denominal verb from the noun ~sucre~ (“sugar”) + ~-er~. ~Sucre~ has one of the great traveling etymologies: from Old French ~sucre~ (also ~çucre~), from Italian ~zucchero~, from Arabic ~sukkar~, from Persian ~šakar~, from Sanskrit ~śárkarā~ — which meant “gravel, grit, ground sugar,” crystalline sweetness named for its resemblance to coarse sand. English ~sugar~ came down the same Mediterranean trade route, as did Spanish ~azúcar~ (which kept the Arabic article ~al-~) and German ~Zucker~.

The verb ~sucrer~ simply means “to add sugar to, to sweeten,” and stays close to its noun. French built a small family around it: ~sucré~ (“sweet,” and figuratively a falsely sweet manner), ~sucrier~ (“sugar bowl”), ~sucrerie~ (“sweet, candy; sugar refinery”), and the slangy reflexive ~se sucrer~ (“to help oneself, take a cut”). The deep Sanskrit sense of grit also surfaces in the scientific ~saccharose~ and ~saccharine~, borrowed through Greek ~sákkharon~ from the very same ~śárkarā~ — so the granular pebble of ancient India hides inside both the kitchen and the laboratory word.
en.suer:
~Suer~ is inherited from Old French ~suer~, which fr.Wiktionary traces to an earlier form ~suder~, from Latin ~sūdāre~ (“to sweat”). The Latin verb comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sweyd-~ (“to sweat”). The Latin ~d~ between vowels dropped out on the way to French, as in many inherited words, which is why ~suer~ no longer shows it. Italian ~sudare~ and Spanish ~sudar~ kept the consonant. English ~sweat~ is a native cousin from the same PIE root, and so is German ~Schweiß~.

Beyond the body, French used ~suer~ for anything that oozes: walls, cheese and cut stone are said to ~suer~. Figurative uses include ~suer sang et eau~ (“to work to the point of exhaustion”) and ~suer à grosses gouttes~. In informal French, ~faire suer~ someone means to annoy them, and ~suer~ may also mean to labor hard. The Latin noun ~sūdor~ (“sweat”) and the verb ~sūdāre~ feed learned and technical vocabulary: ~sudation~, ~sudorifique~, ~exsuder~, along with the inherited noun ~sueur~.
en.suffire:
From Old French ~soufire~, from Vulgar Latin *~suffīcere~ (with a lengthened ~ī~ that drew it into the same class as ~dīcere~, “to say”), from Classical Latin ~sufficere~, a compound of ~sub-~ (“under, beneath”) and ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~Facere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place”), the same root that gives English ~do~ and German ~tun~. The form was later relatinized: the medieval ~soufire~ was reshaped toward its Latin source, isolatedly in the fourteenth century and then regularly from the sixteenth, yielding modern ~suffire~.

The Latin compound first meant “to put under, to set in place of, to supply,” and intransitively “to place oneself beneath” — that is, to be capable of bearing a load, hence “to be enough.” It is this image of standing under a weight without giving way that survives in the French sense “to suffice.” The same Latin ~facere~ underlies an enormous family of French words, among them ~faire~, ~défaire~, ~satisfaire~, and the learned doublet ~fabriquer~; the buried prefix ~sub-~ likewise surfaces in ~souffrir~, ~soutenir~, and ~soumettre~. A small curiosity: ~suffire~ keeps an irregular past participle, ~suffi~, that takes no agreement — a quiet reminder of its tangled Latin pedigree.
en.suggérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~suggerere~ (“to carry up, supply, furnish; to prompt, advise”), formed from the prefix ~sub-~ (“under, up from below”) and the verb ~gerere~ (“to carry, bear, conduct”). ~Gerere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~gezō~; its supine stem ~gestum~ underlies a host of English words. The French verb was taken straight from Latin rather than worn down through Old French, which is why it preserves the Latin shape so cleanly.

The image inside ~suggerere~ is to “carry up” material from below — to supply or feed something to someone, and so to prompt a thought, to put an idea into another's mind without stating it outright. French ~suggérer~ keeps exactly that delicacy: one suggests rather than commands. The root ~gerere~ (“to carry, to carry on”) seeded a remarkably wide family across French and English, including ~geste~ and English ~gesture~, ~gestation~, ~digérer~ (“to digest,” to carry apart), ~registre~, ~congérer~, and the noun ~suggestion~ itself, built on the supine ~suggestum~.
en.suicider: Formed from the noun ~suicide~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, ~suicider~ is mostly met in the reflexive ~se suicider~ (“to kill oneself”). The noun ~suicide~ was built on the model of ~homicide~: French sources explain it from Latin ~sui~ (“of oneself”) and ~caedere~ (“to kill”), and English Wiktionary describes it as borrowed from New Latin ~suīcīdium~, from ~suī~ and ~-cīdium~ (“-cide”). The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default way of coining a verb from a noun. The verb is therefore a late French formation, the noun having come first.
en.suivre:
From Old French ~sivre~, later ~suivre~ — the modern form reshaped on the third-person present ~suit~ (earlier ~siut~) — from Vulgar Latin *~sequere~, a regularized form of Classical Latin ~sequī~ (“to follow”), a deponent verb, from Proto-Italic *~sekʷor~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Cognate with Italian ~seguire~, Spanish ~seguir~, and Occitan ~sègre~; through the same root come Greek ~hépesthai~ and Sanskrit ~sácate~, both “to follow.”

The verb's history is a tangle of irregular forms: the Latin ~q~ produced wildly different dialect outcomes, from Picard ~suire~ to Burgundian ~seugre~ and Norman ~suure~, before standard French settled on the ~-v-~ stem. The PIE root *~sekʷ-~ proved astonishingly fertile in Latin: from the participle ~secundus~ (“following,” hence “second”) French inherited ~second~, while the compounds gave ~poursuivre~, ~ensuivre~, ~exécuter~, ~persécuter~, and ~poursuite~. Even the everyday ~suite~ — a musical sequence, a hotel suite, a retinue “following” a dignitary — is the same root, as is ~conséquence~, literally a “following-together.” A single notion of one thing coming after another thus branches into law, music, logic, and hospitality.
en.superposer: Formed from ~poser~ and the prefix ~super-~, modeled on Latin ~superpōnere~ (“to place on top of”). The prefix is a learned borrowing from Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), a doublet of the inherited ~sur-~, and it is rare on French verbs. The base ~poser~ has a twist of its own: it comes from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to halt”) but took over the sense of placing that belonged to Latin ~ponere~, so the verb for putting one thing over another is built on a word that once meant stopping.
en.superviser:
French borrowed ~superviser~ from English ~supervise~, which in turn comes from Medieval Latin ~supervidere~, formed from ~super~ (“above, over”) and ~videre~ (“to see, to look at”). The Latin verb ~videre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), which also underlies English ~wit~ and German ~wissen~, since seeing and knowing were close neighbors. The prefix ~super~ is the Latin source of French ~sur~, so ~superviser~ is a learned cousin of ~sur~ and ~voir~ put together: to “oversee”.

The journey is a round trip of sorts. A Latin-built verb passed through English before reaching French, and it stayed close to its literal meaning: to watch over work or people from above, in order to direct or check them. The same Latin ~videre~ lies behind the French verb ~voir~ and many learned words such as ~vision~, ~vidéo~, ~évidence~ and ~prévoir~, while ~super~ gave ~superviseur~ and ~supervision~ beside the native ~sur-~.
en.supplier:
From Old French ~souploier~ (also ~sosploier~), from Latin ~supplicāre~ (“to kneel down, to beg humbly”), a verb built on the adjective ~supplex~ (“kneeling, suppliant”). The modern spelling restored the Latin ~sup-~, which the Old French form had worn down. Italian ~supplicare~ and Spanish ~suplicar~ descend from the same Latin verb, and English ~supplicate~ was borrowed from it.

It is tempting to connect ~supplier~ with ~plier~ (“to fold, to bend”), since a suppliant bends the knee. French Wiktionary states clearly that the two have no etymological link, and the deeper origin of Latin ~supplex~ is itself uncertain, so it is safest to say only that the Latin word described someone kneeling in entreaty. The meaning has stayed remarkably stable, from a physical gesture to a spoken request. Related words include ~supplication~, ~suppliant~ and ~supplique~, a formal petition. More dramatically, ~supplice~ (“torture, ordeal”) comes from Latin ~supplicium~, also from ~supplex~.
en.suppléer:
~Suppléer~ goes back to Latin ~supplēre~ (“to fill up, to complete, to make good”), made of ~sub-~ and ~plēre~ (“to fill”). Latin ~plēre~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). The verb entered Old French as ~souploier~ or ~soupleer~, taken from Latin. The root is productive across the family: French ~plein~ (from Latin ~plēnus~) and English ~full~, a native Germanic cousin, belong to it, as do ~complete~ and ~plenty~. English also took ~supply~ from the same Old French verb, so ~suppléer~ and ~supply~ are two forms of one word that went their separate ways.

The central idea is to fill what is missing, and French uses it in two main ways. Transitively or with ~à~, ~suppléer~ means to make up for a lack (~suppléer à un manque~). Of a person, it means to stand in for someone, to take over their place. From the verb came ~suppléant~ (“substitute, deputy”) and ~suppléance~ (“temporary replacement”), while ~supplément~ was borrowed directly from Latin ~supplēmentum~. In each of them, something is added so that the whole is no longer short.
en.supporter:
From Latin ~supportāre~ (“to carry, to bring up, to convey”), a compound of the prefix ~sub-~ (“under, from below”) and the verb ~portāre~ (“to carry”) — literally “to carry from underneath,” the posture of one who bears a load on the back. ~Portāre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~portāō~ and ultimately to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to cross, to pass through”), the same root that gave Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbour”). It is cognate with the Romance family of Italian ~portare~ and Spanish ~portar~, and, through *~per-~, with English ~ford~ and ~fare~.

The Latin sense of physical bearing branched in two directions. One kept the literal idea of holding something up: a beam ~supports~ a roof. The other turned inward and moral — to “bear up under” hardship, hence “to endure, to tolerate.” Modern French keeps both: a wall ~supporte~ a weight, and one ~supporte~ a noisy neighbour, often grudgingly. A curious twist: the sporting sense “to support a team” was re-imported from English ~supporter~, itself a much older loan from French — a word that travelled the Channel and came home with new baggage. From the same root *~per-~ descend a crowd of French words, among them ~porter~, ~porte~, ~port~, ~apporter~, and ~transporter~.
en.supposer:
A French formation modelled on Latin ~supponere~ (“to put under, to substitute, to assume”), reshaped on the native verb ~poser~ (“to place”) under the influence of the prefix ~sub-~ (“under”). Strictly, ~poser~ descends from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to pause, to set down”), which crossed paths with Latin ~ponere~ (“to put”); but the whole ~-poser~ family — ~supposer~, ~composer~, ~proposer~, ~disposer~ — was built in French to answer the Latin verbs in ~-ponere~, so ~supposer~ stands for ~supponere~, literally “to place under.” Cognate in sense with English ~suppose~ and Italian ~supporre~.

The modern abstract meaning — to assume, to conjecture, to take as a premise — grew in scholastic Latin, where ~suppositio~ rendered the logician's notion of a hypothesis, itself a calque of Greek ~ὑπόθεσις~ (~hupóthesis~, literally a “placing under,” a foundation laid beneath an argument). So both the Latin and the Greek term picture an assumption as something set underneath, a support propping up reasoning. French ~supposer~ thus spans the concrete and the mental: to place under, to substitute (~supposer un enfant~, in old law, to pass off a false heir), and to suppose, imply, or surmise. Kin in French include ~supposition~, ~présupposer~, ~suppositoire~ — literally a thing “placed underneath” — and the whole ~poser~ clan.
en.supprimer:
Borrowed from Latin ~supprimere~ (“to press down, to hold back, to stifle”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). ~Premere~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to strike, to press”). It is cognate with Italian ~sopprimere~ and Spanish ~suprimir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~suppress~ and ~press~ itself.

The Latin sense was physical, “to press something down so it cannot rise,” and the French verb keeps that gesture in the abstract: to suppress a revolt, to delete a line, to remove a clause is to push it out of sight. The arrival of computing gave ~supprimer~ a brisk new home as the everyday word for “to delete” a file. The root ~premere~ is one of the most fertile in French, surfacing in ~presser~ (“to press”) and its many kin — ~exprimer~ (“to express,” to press out), ~imprimer~ (“to print,” to press in), ~comprimer~ (“to compress”), ~opprimer~ (“to oppress”), and ~déprimer~ (“to depress”) — a family in which the simple act of pressing has been bent to a dozen meanings.
en.surcharger: Formed from ~sur-~ and ~charger~. The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a worn-down form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), and here carries its common sense of excess. The base ~charger~ goes back to Late Latin *~carricāre~, built on ~carrus~, a wheeled cart borrowed from Gaulish. To ~surcharger~ is thus to load a cart, and by extension a person, a text or a system, beyond what it can bear. It also covers the commercial sense of charging too much.
en.surfer: A French verb formed from the English noun ~surf~ (the breaking waves, then the sport) by adding the French infinitive ending ~-er~, which comes from Latin ~-āre~ and is the default way of making a verb from a borrowed word. Both Wiktionaries agree on this simple chain. The sense “to ride waves” was later stretched to “to browse the web,” the same shift that English made with “to surf the net.” The origin of English ~surf~ itself is uncertain, so it is not traced further here.
en.surgir:
~surgir~ goes back to Latin ~surgere~ (“to rise, to get up”), a contraction of ~surrigere~, from ~sub-~ (“up from below”) plus ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct”), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten”) — the root of English ~right~ and German ~recht~. But French already possessed the verb by inheritance: ~sourdre~, the popular descendant of ~surgere~, said of water welling up, whose old past participle gave ~source~. ~surgir~ is thus a doublet — and it arrived, surprisingly, by sea: it is first attested, as ~sourgir~, in the fifteenth century, as a sailors' term meaning “to cast anchor, to come to port,” probably taken from Catalan ~surgir~, which Mediterranean seamen had used since the thirteenth century. Italian ~sorgere~, Spanish ~surgir~ and English ~surge~ belong to the same Latin family.

So the French verb that now means “to spring up” began its career meaning, of a ship, to drop anchor and stop. Only in the nineteenth century — the figurative sense is attested in 1823 — did the modern meaning take hold, realigned on the classical Latin sense of rising; today memories, crowds and difficulties all surge up without warning. The root's French posterity is rich on both branches: from ~surgere~ come ~sourdre~, ~source~, ~ressource~ (from Old French ~resourdre~, “to rise again,” from Latin ~resurgere~), ~résurrection~ and ~insurrection~ — the insurgent and the resurrected both being, etymologically, people who rise — while ~regere~ supplied ~régir~, ~diriger~ and ~droit~ (from ~dīrēctus~, “made straight”). A word that once anchored ships now names whatever refuses to stay down.
en.surmonter:
Formed in French from ~monter~ (“to climb, to mount”) with the prefix ~sur-~ (from Latin ~super~, “over, above”). ~Monter~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~montāre~, derived from ~mōns~, stem ~mont-~ (“mountain”), from Proto-Italic *~monts~, from PIE *~men-~ (“to stand out, to tower”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~mountain~ and ~mount~.

The literal sense is to “mount over” — to rise above an obstacle — which gives the figurative “to overcome, to surmount, to get over” a difficulty or a fear. ~Surmonter~ can still be physical: a steeple ~surmonte~ a church, sitting atop it. The ~mōns~ family is large and visible on every map: ~mont~, ~montagne~, ~monter~, ~montée~, ~amont~, and ~promontoire~. The same PIE *~men-~ “to tower” also lies behind the borrowed ~éminent~ and ~prominent~ in their idea of jutting up.
en.surnommer:
From ~sur-~ (“over, on top of,” from Latin ~super~) + ~nommer~ (“to name”), reinforced by the noun ~surnom~ (“nickname, surname”). ~Nommer~ descends from Latin ~nōmināre~ (“to name”), from ~nōmen~ (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃nómn̥~. The root is cognate with English ~name~, German ~Name~, Ancient Greek ~ónoma~, and Sanskrit ~nā́man~, and is often linked to the root of “knowing,” a name being how a thing is known.

The layered prefix ~sur-~ originally marked an added or supplementary name laid “over” the given one — a by-name. In medieval usage a ~surnom~ could be an honorific epithet, a descriptive tag, or the hereditary family name (the sense English ~surname~ still carries). The verb ~surnommer~ settled on the playful modern meaning “to nickname.” The same ~nōmen~ root seeded a wide French family: ~nom~, ~prénom~, ~renommée~ (“renown,” literally a re-naming), ~nominer~, ~nommément~, and the learned doublet ~pronom~. Through Latin it also gives ~nominal~ and ~dénomination~.
en.surpasser: Formed in French from the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, beyond”) and the verb ~passer~ (“to pass”). The prefix is the Old French shortening of Latin ~super-~ and here carries the sense of superiority: to go beyond someone or something. The base ~passer~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, from Latin ~passus~ (“step, pace”), so the verb pictures a runner who steps past a rival. It keeps company with ~dépasser~ and ~repasser~, and it has a reflexive use, ~se surpasser~ (“to outdo oneself”).
en.surplomber: Formed from ~sur-~ (“over”) + ~plomb~ + ~-er~. The ~plomb~ here is the lead weight on a builder's line, the plumb line that fixes the true vertical, so ~surplomber~ describes a wall or rock that leans out beyond that line and hangs over what lies below. French Wiktionary treats the verb as formed on the noun ~surplomb~ (“overhang”), itself built on ~plomb~ with ~sur-~, while English Wiktionary derives the noun from the verb; the two accounts point the same way but disagree on which came first. From the physical overhang, the verb extended to any commanding position: to overlook a valley or a town.
en.surprendre:
A French compound of the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, upon”) and the verb ~prendre~ (“to take”), modeled on Latin ~super~ + ~prehendere~. ~Prendre~ comes from the contracted Latin ~prendere~, from ~prehendere~ (“to seize, grasp”), which breaks into ~prae-~ (“before”) and a root ~-hendere~ akin to Ancient Greek ~χανδάνω~ (~khandánō~, “to hold, contain”) and, through Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰend-~ (“to seize”), to English ~get~. Old French had several near-variants — ~sorprendre~, ~sousprendre~ — that later merged.

The literal image is to “take from above,” to overtake. Early on ~surprendre~ meant to seize or attack someone unawares, to take a town by surprise — a military sense of catching the enemy off guard. From this grew the two modern strands: to catch out (to take someone in the act, ~surprendre un secret~) and simply to surprise, to astonish, since the unexpected catches the mind unprepared. The noun ~surprise~ (originally a “taking unawares”) followed the verb into English. Relatives in the ~prendre~ family include ~prise~, ~apprendre~, ~comprendre~, ~entreprendre~, and ~surprenant~ — a whole web spun from the idea of grasping.
en.surveiller:
French ~surveiller~ is a French formation, ~veiller~ (“to keep watch, stay awake”) prefixed with ~sur-~ (“over, above”), attested in 1586 with the sense “to watch over.” The base ~veiller~ comes from Old French ~veillier~, from Latin ~vigilāre~ (“to be awake, keep watch”), from the adjective ~vigil~ (“awake, alert”), from Latin ~vigeō~ (“to be lively, vigorous”). The root is Proto-Indo-European *~weǵ-~ (“to be strong, lively, awake”), which also yielded English ~wake~, ~watch~, and ~vigour~.

The prefix ~sur-~ adds the idea of looking down from above, giving “to oversee, supervise.” The verb sits in a rich Latin family: ~vigilāre~ also gave learned French ~vigilant~ and ~vigile~, and through Spanish the everyday ~vigilar~. From ~surveiller~ itself descend ~surveillance~ (“surveillance”) and ~surveillant~ (“supervisor, monitor”). The English borrowing ~surveillance~ entered around the French Revolution, when the comités de surveillance gave the word its modern overtone of watchful, often suspicious, oversight — a sense already latent in the prefixed French verb.
en.survenir:
French ~survenir~ is built from ~venir~ (“to come”) with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, upon”), literally “to come upon.” ~Venir~ descends from Old French ~venir~, from Latin ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to go, come”). That same root, through different sound laws, produced English ~come~, Ancient Greek ~baínō~ (“I go”), and Sanskrit ~gam~ (“to go”) — one of the clearest demonstrations of how a single PIE root scatters across the family.

The prefix ~sur-~ here conveys suddenness and superposition: something ~survient~ when it comes on top of a situation, unbidden and often unwelcome — an accident, a complication, an unexpected guest. The word thus specialises “to come” into “to occur suddenly, to crop up.” From the same Latin verb the French got an enormous family: ~venir~, ~avenir~ (“future”), ~événement~ (“event,” literally an out-coming), ~revenir~, ~devenir~, ~convenir~, and ~prévenir~ — a reminder that much of what merely “happens” in French is, etymologically, a kind of coming.
en.survivre:
From Old French ~survivre~, attested around 1100 in the conjugated form ~survesquiet~, from Latin ~supervīvere~, a compound of ~super~ (“over, beyond”) and ~vīvere~ (“to live”). Synchronically it reads simply as ~sur-~ + ~vivre~, “to live beyond.” Latin ~vīvere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~gʷīwō~ and the PIE root *~gʷeyh₃-~ (“to live”), one of the great roots of the family: through it ~survivre~ is a cognate of English ~quick~ (in its old sense “alive,” as in “the quick and the dead”), Ancient Greek ~bíos~ (“life”) and Sanskrit ~jīvati~ (“he lives”).

The sense has held firm: to outlive another, or to keep living past some danger or disaster. The compound carries a quiet drama — to ~survivre~ is always to live in relation to something one has outlasted. From the same ~vivre~ stem French draws ~survie~ (“survival”) and ~survivance~, and from the deeper root the whole crowd of ~vif~, ~vivace~, ~viande~, ~convive~ and ~ravitailler~.
en.survoler: The two sources differ on the chain. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~supervolāre~ (“to fly over”), fused from ~super~ (“over”) and ~volāre~ (“to fly”), while English Wiktionary treats it as Middle French ~survoler~, first attested around 1470, formed from ~sur-~ (“over”) + ~voler~ (“to fly”). Either way the sense is clear: to fly over. Italian ~sorvolare~ is the parallel. The figurative sense, to skim over a subject without dwelling on it, follows the same image of passing high above.
en.susciter:
