From Latin ~suscitāre~ (“to rouse, to stir up, to awaken, to revive”), a compound of the prefix ~sub-~ (here “up from under”) and ~citāre~ (“to set in rapid motion, to summon”). ~citāre~ is the frequentative of ~ciēre~ (“to move, to stir, to call”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kei-~ (“to set in motion”). That root also yielded Greek ~kīneîn~ (“to move”), the source of ~cinéma~ and ~kinetic~. French borrowed ~susciter~ as a learned term, so its form stayed close to the Latin.

The literal image is of stirring something up from below — rousing a sleeper, reviving the dead, calling a force into being. Old French already used it for arousing emotions or provoking events, and modern ~susciter~ keeps that abstract reach: one ~suscite~ admiration, curiosity, opposition, or a vocation, always evoking something into existence rather than handling it directly. From the same ~ciēre~ family, French gathered a striking crowd of relatives: ~citer~ (“to cite, to summon”), ~exciter~ (“to excite”), ~inciter~ (“to incite”), ~solliciter~ (“to solicit”), ~ressusciter~ (“to resurrect”), and ~récit~ and ~réciter~ (a tale being something “called back”). The same primal idea of motion even powers ~cinématographe~, so the stirred verb and the moving picture share one ancestral impulse.
en.suspecter:
Borrowed from Latin ~suspectāre~ (“to look at with mistrust, to suspect”), a frequentative of ~suspicere~. That verb joined ~sub-~ (“from below”) and ~specere~ (“to look”), so ~suspicere~ meant literally “to look up at from underneath,” and from there “to look up to” or, with a wary eye, “to mistrust.” The root of ~specere~ is the Proto-Indo-European *~spek-~ (“to observe”), shared with German ~spähen~ (“to scout”) and, by way of Frankish and Old French, with English ~spy~.

The frequentative ending ~-tāre~ marks repeated or intense action. The Latin family reached French by two roads. The popular road, through Old French, produced ~soupçon~ and ~soupçonner~. The learned road produced ~suspect~ and the verb ~suspecter~, which therefore sits beside ~soupçonner~ as a near twin in meaning. Elsewhere the same root underlies a large French family, among them ~spectacle~, ~spécimen~, ~inspecter~ and ~respecter~.
en.suspendre:
French ~suspendre~ descends from Latin ~suspendere~ (“to hang up, hang below”), a compound of the prefix ~sub-~ (“under, up from under”) and ~pendere~ (“to hang, to weigh”). ~Pendere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~pendō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). Through ~pendere~ it is cognate with English ~pendant~, ~pension~, ~ponder~, and ~suspend~ itself, and shares its root with words of weighing and stretching.

The image is concrete — something hung from above, swinging free — and French keeps it: a lamp ~suspendue~ from the ceiling, a bridge ~suspendu~ over a gorge. From there grew the figurative “to interrupt, to leave in abeyance”: to ~suspendre~ a session, a payment, a judgement. The same hanging sense gives ~suspens~ (“abeyance,” as in en suspens) and, borrowed back through English, ~suspense~ — the held breath of a thing not yet resolved. The family also includes ~suspension~ and ~pendule~ (“pendulum, clock”), still literally swinging.
en.symboliser:
~symboliser~ was built on the noun ~symbole~ with the suffix ~-iser~, on the model of medieval Latin ~symbolizāre~, attested from the ninth century in the sense “to agree, to correspond.” The noun goes back through Latin ~symbolum~ to Greek ~σύμβολον~ (~súmbolon~), from ~συμβάλλω~ (~sumbállō~, “to throw together”): ~σύν~ (“with”) plus ~βάλλω~ (“to throw”), the latter from PIE *~gʷelH-~ (“to throw”). And a ~σύμβολον~ was a literal, physical thing: a recognition token — an object such as a knucklebone or a coin snapped in two, each contracting party keeping one half. When the halves were brought together and the break matched, identity and agreement stood proven. Every modern symbol is, etymologically, half of a broken object waiting for its other half.

Strikingly, the verb's first French life followed the medieval Latin sense rather than ours: at its first attestation, around 1512, ~symboliser~ was intransitive and meant “to be in accord, to resemble.” Not until 1615 is it attested as “to represent by a symbol,” and only in 1796 as “to be the symbol of.” The Greek root ~βάλλω~ seeded French with throw-words: ~parabole~ and its astonishing doublet ~parole~ (from Latin ~parabola~ — the comparison “thrown alongside,” which in late Latin came to mean speech itself), ~hyperbole~ (a throw beyond the mark), ~problème~ (a thing thrown forward), ~emblème~ (a thing thrown in, inlaid). English ~symbol~ and ~ballistics~ belong to the same family: matching halves, flying projectiles and figures of speech, all from the art of throwing.
en.synchroniser: Formed in French from the adjective ~synchrone~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make synchronous.” The adjective comes through Latin ~synchronus~ (“contemporary”) from Ancient Greek ~sýnkhronos~, made of ~sýn~ (“with”) and ~khrónos~ (“time”), so it means literally “with the time.” The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Greek-derived verbs in Late Latin and is still very productive for technical verbs. To ~synchroniser~ is to bring two things into the same time, such as clocks, files or dancers.
en.syndiquer: A French formation with the verb ending ~-er~. fr.Wiktionary derives it from ~syndic~, noting the old spelling ~syndicquer~ and a date of 1768 for the modern sense “to form a union,” while en.Wiktionary derives it from ~syndicat~ (“union”), a noun that itself comes from ~syndic~. Either way the root is ~syndic~, a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~syndicus~ (“representative of a town”), from Greek ~sundikos~ (“advocate of a defendant”), built on ~sun-~ (“together”) and ~dikē~ (“justice”). The ~syndic~ was an officer chosen to defend a community's interests, and ~syndiquer~ means to organize workers into such a collective body.
en.synthétiser:
The two Wiktionaries disagree on the route. French Wiktionary derives ~synthétiser~ from English ~synthesize~, attested in the nineteenth century, while English Wiktionary derives it from French ~synthèse~ (“synthesis”). Both go back to the Ancient Greek ~sýnthesis~ (“a putting together”), from ~syn~ (“together”) and the verb ~títhēmi~ (“to put, to place”), the latter from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to do”), which is also the source of English ~do~. The two accounts may not be incompatible, since English could have shaped the verb on French ~synthèse~, but the sources do not settle it.

The idea is the mirror of ~analyse~: to combine elements into a whole rather than to separate a whole into elements. The verb is used in philosophy, in chemistry, where it means to produce a compound by combining simpler ones, and in everyday speech for summarizing. In music the related ~synthétiseur~ (“synthesizer”), an instrument that builds sounds from electronic components, is a twentieth-century word. The Greek verb ~títhēmi~ also gave French ~thèse~, ~hypothèse~ and ~thème~.
en.sécher:
From Latin ~siccare~ (“to make dry, to dry up”), a verb built on the adjective ~siccus~ (“dry”). The same ~siccare~ gives the Romance verbs of drying — Italian ~seccare~, Spanish ~secar~, Portuguese ~secar~ — and the French adjective ~sec~ (“dry”) descends straight from ~siccus~. French keeps a tidy cluster of derivatives around the verb: ~assécher~ (“to drain dry”), ~dessécher~ (“to desiccate”), ~séchage~ (“drying”), and ~sécheresse~ (“dryness, drought”).

From the plain physical sense, French built a vivid metaphor. A student who, faced with a question, knows nothing is said to ~sécher~ — to “dry up,” to run blank, as if the well of memory had gone empty; this is the “see-through” blankness behind the English gloss. From the late nineteenth century, school and military slang extended ~sécher~ to mean skipping a class altogether — ~sécher~ un cours — attested in student argot by the 1890s. The exact path from “to dry up” to “to play truant” is not securely documented, so we note the link without inventing a mechanism for it.
en.sécuriser:
A modern French formation, built from the stem of ~sécurité~ (or ~sécur-~) plus the productive verbal suffix ~-iser~. The ancestor is Latin ~sēcūrus~ (“free from care, untroubled, safe”), a transparent compound of ~sē-~ (“without, apart”) and ~cūra~ (“care, worry”): to be ~sēcūrus~ was literally to be “without a care.” Through Old French this same ~sēcūrus~ also gave the everyday adjective ~sûr~ (“sure, safe”), so that ~sûr~ and the learned ~sécurité~ are doublets, the popular and the scholarly descendants of one Latin word. English ~secure~ and ~sure~ form the very same pair.

The verb itself is strikingly recent: the adjective ~sécurisant~ appeared in the late 1950s, and the transitive ~sécuriser~ followed around 1969, first in a psychological sense — to ~sécuriser~ someone was to set their mind at ease, to free them from anxiety, true to the Latin “without care.” Only later did it broaden to the concrete senses now dominant — to ~sécuriser~ a building, a network, a payment. The same ~cūra~ underlies ~curieux~, ~cure~, ~soin~ via a different path, ~assurer~, and ~procurer~.
en.séduire:
From Latin ~seducere~ (“to lead aside, lead away”), a compound of the prefix ~se-~ (“apart, away”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead, draw”). The verb ~ducere~ descends from PIE *~dewk-~ (“to draw, pull, lead”), the root behind English ~tow~ and the whole ~-duce~ family — ~produce~, ~reduce~, ~conduct~. Romance cognates of the compound include Spanish ~seducir~ and Italian ~sedurre~; English ~seduce~ comes from the same Latin word.

The Latin sense was literal and often political or military: to draw someone aside, to lead troops or followers away from their allegiance. That sense of leading astray darkened in Old French into moral corruption and deception — to ~séduire~ was first to mislead or debauch. Only later did the word soften toward its dominant modern meaning, “to charm, to attract irresistibly,” while keeping an edge of the old “leading astray.” A landscape or an idea can ~séduire~ as easily as a person. From the same ~ducere~ French keeps ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~réduire~, and the noun ~séduction~.
en.séjourner:
From Old French ~sojorner~, whose first vowel became ~é~ in French by dissimilation, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~subdiurnāre~. That verb was built from Latin ~sub-~ (“under, a little over”) and Late Latin ~diurnus~ (“lasting for a day”), so the picture is of staying on for a stretch of days. Latin ~diurnus~ is the adjective of ~dies~ (“day”), and its neuter noun ~diurnum~ gave French ~jour~. English borrowed the verb from the Old French family as ~sojourn~, a literary word for a temporary stay.

The verb thus began as “to spend some days somewhere” and settled into the sense “to stay for a while,” a stay that is longer than a visit and shorter than a residence. French uses it in the language of travel and administration: ~séjourner à l'hôtel~, ~un séjour linguistique~, ~un titre de séjour~ (“a residence permit”). The noun ~séjour~ came from the same Old French verb, and the hidden ~jour~ in the middle is the reason ~séjourner~ also sits beside ~journée~, ~journal~ (originally “a daily thing”) and ~ajourner~ (“to put off to another day”).
en.sélectionner:
A nineteenth-century formation from the noun ~sélection~, from Latin ~selectio~ (“a choosing out”), the action noun of ~seligere~ (“to choose out, to single out, to cull”). ~seligere~ is a compound of ~se-~ (“apart, aside”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”), so its literal sense is “to gather apart.” ~legere~ goes back to PIE *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, to gather”). Cognate, through the same Latin verb, with English ~select~ and Italian ~selezionare~.

The ~legere~ at its core is one of the most generous roots in the language: the act of “picking out” specialized in Latin into reading (picking out letters), and *~leǵ-~ underlies a striking spread of French words — ~lire~, ~élire~, ~collection~, ~légende~ (“things to be read”), and, through the Greek branch of the same root, ~lexique~ and ~dialogue~. ~sélectionner~ itself is the youngest layer: where the older ~choisir~ (a Germanic borrowing) simply picks, ~sélectionner~ carries the cooler, more deliberate flavour of choosing the best from a set — a coach who ~sélectionne~ players, a process of natural ~sélection~. The doublet ~élire~ shows the same ~legere~ worn smooth by centuries of everyday use, while ~sélectionner~ keeps the crisp Latin consonants of a learned, modern coinage.
en.séparer:
Borrowed in 1314 from Latin ~separāre~ (“to pull apart, to divide”), a learned doublet of the inherited French verb ~sevrer~ (“to wean”). The Latin verb joins ~se-~ (“apart, aside”) to ~parāre~ (“to make ready, to procure”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~perh₃-~ (“to produce, to procure”). Cognates abound: Italian ~separare~, Spanish ~separar~, English ~separate~ and its Frenchified doublet ~sever~.

The curious point is that French inherited the same Latin verb twice. The ordinary popular descendant of ~separāre~ is ~sevrer~, which narrowed to the specific sense of separating a child or young animal from the breast — to wean — while the scholarly re-borrowing ~séparer~ kept the broad Latin meaning, to set apart. Such pairs, one worn down by centuries of speech and one taken straight from books, are doublets, and ~séparer~/~sevrer~ is a textbook case. The verb branched into ~séparation~ (including the legal ~séparation de corps~, a separation short of divorce), ~séparé~, ~séparément~, ~séparateur~, and the political ~séparatisme~. The second element ~parāre~ is itself remarkably fertile, lying behind ~préparer~, ~réparer~, ~emparer~, and — through the related ~parere~ (“to give birth, to bring forth”) — the family of ~parent~.
en.sérier: Formed from the noun ~série~ (“series”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to arrange things in a series. ~Série~ is borrowed from Latin ~seriēs~ (“chain, row, succession”), a word tied to ~serere~ (“to join, to link”), so the root image is one of things strung together in a line. The verb is learned and technical, and it describes sorting items into an ordered sequence.
en.sévir:
French ~sévir~ is a borrowing from Latin ~saevīre~ (“to rage, to be furious, to rampage”), the verb of the adjective ~saevus~ (“fierce, savage”). The Latin word described wild animals, storms, soldiers and tyrants in the grip of violence, and French took it over directly as a learned word rather than inheriting it. The same Latin family gave the noun ~saevitia~ (“cruelty”), from which French drew ~sévices~ (“physical abuse”), a legal term still in daily use.

In French, ~sévir~ kept the sense of violence but narrowed it to two main uses. The first is of a disaster or scourge that rages: a storm, an epidemic, a famine, or a drought ~sévit~. The second is of an authority that acts firmly against wrongdoing, as when a government or a school ~sévit~ against offenders, hence “to crack down.” The adjective ~sévère~, which looks like a relative, comes from a different Latin word, ~sevērus~ (“strict, serious”), so the resemblance is partly a coincidence of sound. The verb keeps the ancient Roman picture of raging violence, now applied equally to nature and to discipline.
en.tabler: Formed in French from the noun ~table~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is inherited from Old French ~table~, from Latin ~tabula~ (“board, tablet”), which is also the source of the doublets ~tôle~ and ~taule~. The modern sense of ~tabler sur~, “to count on, to rely on”, is a figurative development of the noun, and the sources I used do not spell out the steps in between.
en.tacher: The usual account makes ~tacher~ a verb built on the noun ~tache~ (“stain”), but English Wiktionary has it inherited from Old French ~tachier~ and Vulgar Latin *~tagicare~, so the direction of derivation is uncertain. The origin of the noun is itself debated. One hypothesis derives it from Gothic ~taikns~ (“sign”), a relative of German ~Zeichen~, though the leap from “sign” to “stain” is hard to follow. Another sees ~tache~ as a back-formation from the verb, with *~tagicare~ built on Latin ~tangere~ (“to touch”) and the variant Old French ~techier~ from *~tigicare~, from ~tingere~ (“to dye”). The sources do not settle the matter.
en.tailler:
From Old French ~talier~ (10th century), from Late Latin ~taliare~ (“to cut, to split”), derived from Latin ~talea~ (“a cutting, slip, scion; rod, stake”) — the slip of wood a gardener slices off to replant. A Vulgar Latin ~taliatura~ (“pruning of trees”) confirms the agricultural cradle of the word. The deeper origin of ~talea~ is disputed: it is traditionally referred to PIE *~teh₂l-~ (“to grow; young shoot”), with a proposed Greek cognate ~tâlis~ (“nubile girl”) whose very existence has been questioned; an alternative ties it to ~tālus~ (“ankle”).

The verb began in horticulture — to cut and prune — then spread to every kind of shaping: cutting stone, tailoring cloth, faceting a gem, dealing cards. The same root yields a rich crop in French: ~taille~ (“cut, size, waist”), ~tailleur~ (“tailor, suit”), ~entaille~ (“notch”), ~détail~ (literally “a cutting up” into small parts), and the compounds ~taille-crayon~ (“pencil sharpener”) and ~tailloir~. Italian ~tagliare~ and Spanish ~tajar~ descend from the very same ~taliare~.
en.taire:
From Latin ~tacēre~ (“to be silent, to hold one's tongue”), from Proto-Italic *~takēō~ and PIE *~tHk-~ (“to be silent”). Old French had the regular form ~taisir~, which by the 12th century was reshaped into ~taire~ along the same path that turned ~plaisir~ into ~plaire~ — the noun-like infinitive yielding to the short verb. ~taisir~ itself faded out by the 15th century. Cognate with Italian ~tacere~ and Romanian ~tăcea~; the Germanic side of the same root shows in Gothic ~þahan~ and Old Norse ~þegja~. Spanish ~callar~ (“to be silent”), despite the matching sense, comes from a wholly different source.

The verb's meaning has stayed remarkably steady: to ~taire~ is to keep silent about something, and the reflexive ~se taire~ (“to fall silent, to shut up”) is one of the commonest verbs in spoken French. Where most Romance languages let the active verb survive, English kept only the adjectival branch: from the Latin participle ~tacitus~ (“silent”) come English ~tacit~ and ~taciturn~, the French ~tacite~ and ~taciturne~, and the legal ~tacitement~. So a ~tacit~ agreement is, at root, one that has kept quiet — the very thing ~taire~ asks you to do.
en.tamiser: ~Tamiser~ is formed from ~tamis~ (“sieve”) with the ending ~-er~. The noun is usually traced through Old French ~tamis~ and Late Latin ~tamisium~ to a Frankish word, *~tamisu~, a source it shares with English ~temse~. French Wiktionary also mentions, as an alternative, an Arabic origin. The verb means “to sift,” and by extension “to filter,” so that one can ~tamiser~ flour, a sound or the light through a curtain, which is how ~lumière tamisée~ came to mean soft, diffused light.
en.taper:
First attested in the 13th century, French ~taper~ rests on an onomatopoeia ~tap~, imitating a short dull knock — the sound itself is the etymology, as the TLFi makes plain, deriving it from an onomatopoeic stem ~tapp-~ evoking a brief muffled noise. Beyond that imitative core the comparisons grow uncertain: the philologist Friedrich Diez linked it to a Germanic family — German ~tappen~ (“to grope, pad”), Dutch ~deppen~, and English ~dab~ — but this kinship is a proposed connection attributed to Diez, not an established line of descent, and is best presented as such rather than as fact.

The meaning fans out from the basic “to strike, knock”: to ~taper~ on the table, to ~taper~ someone (slap them), to ~taper~ dans le ballon (“to kick the ball”), and colloquially “to cadge” money. The most modern branch — “to type” on a keyboard — simply transfers the percussive striking of keys to the older verb of striking. French relatives and offshoots include ~tape~ (“a slap”), ~tapoter~ (“to tap lightly, to pat”), and ~tapette~. Whether any of these ultimately joins a wider Indo-European family remains, on the evidence, an open question rather than a settled one.
en.tapir: Inherited from Old French ~tapir~, which was borrowed from Frankish *~tappijan~ (“to close, to shut in”), from Proto-Germanic *~tappijaną~, itself related to *~tappô~ (“tap, plug”). The original sense was therefore physical, “to stop up, to shut away,” and it moved toward the modern meaning of “to hide, to crouch out of sight,” used mostly in the pronominal form ~se tapir~. The animal called ~tapir~ in both French and English is unrelated: it comes from a language of Brazil.
en.tapisser: Formed from ~tapis~ (“carpet, rug”) and the verb ending ~-er~, with the ~s~ doubled so that it stays pronounced /s/ between vowels. The noun ~tapis~ came through Middle French ~tapiz~ and ultimately from Greek: late Greek ~tapētion~ (“small cover”) is a diminutive of Greek ~tapēs~ (“carpet, rug”), itself an Eastern word of obscure origin, perhaps Iranian. ~Tapisser~ first meant to cover a wall or a floor with fabric, and so it came to mean covering any surface with a decorative layer, as in a wall ~tapissé~ with posters or ivy.
en.tarder:
From Latin ~tardāre~ (“to slow, to delay, to hinder”), derived from the adjective ~tardus~ (“slow, late”). The origin of ~tardus~ is debated: it is sometimes traced to Proto-Italic *~tardo-~ from PIE *~terh₂-~ (“to cross over, to pass through,” hence perhaps “drawn out, long in passing”), but De Vaan judges this uncertain for want of cognates carrying the “slow” sense, and an Etruscan origin has occasionally been proposed instead. So the deep root is genuinely unsettled, not fixed.

The meaning shifted from Latin “to slow, to impede” toward French “to be slow in coming, to be late,” and especially the impersonal turn that voices impatience: ~il me tarde de~ (“I can hardly wait to”), where lateness is felt from the waiting side. From the same family French keeps ~tard~ (“late”), ~tardif~ (“tardy, belated”), ~retard~ (“delay”) and ~retarder~ (“to delay”), ~attarder~ (“to linger”), and the musical ~retardement~. Italian ~tardare~ and Spanish ~tardar~ are its Romance siblings, and English ~tardy~ borrowed the same Latin adjective through Old French ~tardif~.
en.tasser: ~Tasser~ is formed from the noun ~tas~ (“heap”) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to pile up, then to pack down. The origin of ~tas~ itself is uncertain. The most common account traces it to a Frankish word *~tas~ (“heap, mass”), a cousin of Dutch ~tas~ (“heap”) and of Middle English ~taas~. French Wiktionary also notes that Littré and Scheler separated two words, one meaning “heap” and one meaning “anvil, block,” and that another proposal links the heap-word to Latin ~stāre~, but the TLFi does not follow the split. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and turns the noun into an action.
en.tatouer: A borrowing from English ~tattoo~, itself a Polynesian word that English took from the voyages of Captain James Cook, who wrote it down as “tat-tow.” Its precise source is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes either Marquesan ~tatu~ (“marking of the skin”) or Tahitian ~ta tau~, built on ~ta~ (“to incise”). Whichever it was, the word travelled from the Pacific to English ships and then to French, which turned it into an ordinary first-conjugation verb with the ending ~-er~. Tattooing itself is far older than the word; the Pacific name simply displaced earlier terms in the European languages.
en.taxer:
Taken from Latin ~taxāre~ (“to estimate, to rate”, also “to censure”) through Old French ~taxer~, which replaced an older, more popular form ~tausser~. The Latin verb is often explained as a frequentative of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), but that link is only a proposal. French ~taux~ (“rate”) belongs to the same family, and English ~tax~ is the French verb passed on across the Channel.

The core idea is to fix the value or amount of something. From there ~taxer~ came to mean to set a price or duty, and then to impose a tax on goods or people. A second, figurative line developed alongside: ~taxer~ quelqu'un de lâcheté is to charge him with cowardice, that is, to put a label on him as one rates an article. In slang, ~taxer~ also means to cadge or scrounge something from someone. The family includes ~taxe~, ~taxation~, ~surtaxer~ and ~détaxer~, and also ~taxi~, which is a shortening of ~taximètre~, the meter that reckons the fare.
en.teinter: Formed from the noun ~teinte~ (“tint, hue”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to give a tint to.” ~Teinte~ is the feminine past participle of ~teindre~ (“to dye”), used as a noun. Its Latin source is ~tincta~ (“dyed”), from the verb ~tingere~ (“to dye”). Spanish ~tintar~ is a close parallel. The verb stays close to its dyeing ancestor but is gentler in meaning: one ~teinte~ something lightly, and the participle ~teinté~ often describes a mood or a style that carries a hint of another quality.
en.tempérer:
French ~tempérer~ is a learned form of an older verb. Old French had ~temprer~, and the acute accent and full ~e~ were added to bring the spelling closer to Latin ~temperāre~ (“to moderate, to soften”). The TLFi, as English Wiktionary reports, also treats ~tempérer~ as a direct learned borrowing from the Latin verb, in the sense of tempering or soothing. The two accounts are not exclusive, and the sources present both. The same Latin verb had already given the popular form ~tremper~, so French holds two descendants of one word, a doublet.

The two French verbs divided the meaning between them. ~Tremper~ kept the physical sense of soaking or drenching, while ~tempérer~ kept the sense of moderating, softening, bringing something to a measured state: one ~tempère~ an ardor, a climate, or a harsh remark. Learned relatives of the Latin family share the same idea of right measure: ~tempérament~, ~température~ and ~tempérance~. The modern adjective ~tempéré~ (“temperate”) is the most common trace of the verb in everyday French, as in a ~climat tempéré~.
en.tendre:
From Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch, extend, strain, aim, direct oneself toward”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~tendere~ and Spanish ~tender~, with Greek ~τείνειν~ (“to stretch”), and — through the same root — with English ~thin~ (a thing “stretched out”) and, more distantly, ~tend~ and ~tone~.

The physical idea of pulling taut radiates into every sense of the verb: one can ~tendre~ a rope (make it tense), ~tendre~ the hand (stretch it out), or ~tendre~ toward a goal (aim oneself at it). That last, directional sense — straining toward something — is the root of ~tendance~ (“tendency, trend”) and ~tension~. Latin ~tendere~ and the kindred ~tenēre~ (“to hold”) seeded an enormous progeny in French: with prefixes come ~attendre~ (to stretch one's mind toward, hence to wait), ~entendre~ (originally to direct one's attention, hence to hear), ~prétendre~, ~étendre~, ~détendre~, and ~sous-tendre~; the participle gives ~tente~ (a “stretched” canvas) and ~tendon~. Beware the homonym: the adjective ~tendre~ (“soft, tender”) comes instead from Latin ~tener~ — a separate word that merely fell together in spelling.
en.tenir:
French ~tenir~ comes from Latin ~tenēre~ (“to hold, to keep”), which passed through a Vulgar Latin *~tenīre~ before reaching Old French ~tenir~. The Latin verb rests on Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), the same root behind Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch”) and ~tenuis~ (“thin”), Greek ~teínein~ (“to stretch”) and ~tónos~ (“tension, pitch”), Sanskrit ~tanoti~ (“he stretches”), and English ~thin~. The bridge from “stretch” to “hold” runs through the idea of keeping something taut — to hold a thing is to maintain it under tension.

In Romance the verb stayed central: Italian ~tenere~, Spanish ~tener~, Portuguese ~ter~ all live on as everyday words, with Spanish even pressing ~tener~ into service for “to have.” French ~tenir~ is likewise one of the busiest verbs in the language, anchoring countless idioms — ~tenir bon~ (“to hold firm”), ~tenir à~ (“to be attached to”), ~tenir de~ (“to take after”). The root *~ten-~ also yields ~tendre~ (“to stretch, to hold out”), ~tension~, ~contenir~, ~maintenir~ (literally “to hold in the hand,” from ~manu tenēre~), ~obtenir~, and ~teneur~. Even the musical ~ténor~ belongs here: the voice that originally “held” the sustained melodic line.
en.tenter:
From Latin ~temptāre~ (also spelled ~tentāre~), “to feel, to handle, to test, to attempt, to attack.” The verb carries an iterative-frequentative force and rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”); De Vaan, more cautiously, derives it from an extended base *~temp-~ (“to touch, to feel”). Cognates and descendants abound: Italian ~tentare~, Spanish ~tentar~, and — borrowed through French — English ~tempt~, ~taunt~, and ~tentative~.

The meaning travelled from the hand to the soul. To ~tenter~ originally meant to probe by touch, to test the strength of a thing — hence “to put to the test,” a sense kept in the religious ~tenter Dieu~ (“to tempt God,” i.e. to test divine patience) and in ~tenter sa chance~ (“to try one's luck”). From “to test someone” it slid easily to “to entice, to allure,” the dominant modern sense: temptation is, etymologically, a trial. If the root truly is *~ten-~, ~tenter~ belongs to one of the largest Indo-European word-families in French, alongside ~tendre~, ~tension~, ~tente~ (a stretched canvas), ~attenter~, and the borrowed ~tentative~ — all turning on the image of stretching toward something.
en.terminer:
From Latin ~terminare~ (“to set bounds to, to limit, to bring to an end”), a denominal verb built on the noun ~terminus~ (“boundary marker, limit, end”). ~terminus~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~termenos~ to a Proto-Indo-European *~térmn̥~ (“boundary”), and is cognate with Ancient Greek ~térma~ (“goal, finishing post”) and ~térmōn~ (“border”). The Romance siblings include Italian ~terminare~ and Spanish ~terminar~, both “to finish.”

The memorable detail is mythological: ~Terminus~ was also a Roman god, the deity of boundary stones, worshipped each February at the festival of the ~Terminalia~. His shrine on the Capitoline was so sacred that when the great temple of Jupiter was built around it, Terminus alone refused to be moved — a sign, the Romans said, that the bounds of their state would never recede. So at the root of “to finish” lies a stone planted in the earth to say “this far and no farther.” From the same source French has ~terme~ (“term, deadline, word”), ~terminaison~ (“ending”), ~déterminer~ (“to fix the limits of, to decide”), and ~exterminer~ (literally “to drive beyond the boundary”); English ~terminate~, ~term~, and the cinematic ~Terminator~ all share it.
en.terrer: A denominal verb built on ~terre~ (“earth, soil”) with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, so that ~terrer~ means to spread or heap soil onto something. The noun ~terre~ is inherited from Latin ~terra~ (“earth, dry land”), which also gave Italian ~terra~ and Spanish ~tierra~. The verb is a plain French coinage with no older source of its own. The same noun lies behind ~terrain~, ~terrasse~ and ~enterrer~.
en.tester:
The modern French ~tester~ (“to test, to try out”) was formed from the noun ~test~ with the suffix ~-er~, under the influence of English ~to test~. The English noun came, in the fourteenth century, from Old French ~test~ (“an earthen pot”), from Latin ~testum~ and ~testa~ (“earthenware vessel, potsherd, shell”) — the assayer's small cup in which metals were melted to prove their purity. Cognates of that Latin word include Italian ~testa~ and the French inheritance ~tête~, both “head.”

French thus has two unrelated verbs spelled ~tester~. The older, a legal term from Latin ~testārī~ (“to bear witness, to make a will”), means “to make a will” and gives ~testament~ and ~testateur~. The newer ~tester~, our verb, is the metallurgist's pot come full circle: the cup that tested gold lent its name to the noun ~test~, which English turned into a verb of trial and examination, and which French then re-imported. The most surprising relative is ~tête~: in Vulgar Latin the “little pot” ~testa~ was used jokingly for the skull, and that humorous slang ousted the classical ~caput~, so that the ordinary French word for “head” is, etymologically, a clay jug. From the same vessel come ~têt~ (a potsherd), ~tesson~, and the borrowed ~test~ and its newer kin ~tester~, ~retester~, and ~testeur~.
en.tirer:
The origin of ~tirer~ is debated. The leading hypothesis derives it from Gothic *~tairan~ (“to tear, to pull apart”), the same Germanic source that gave Spanish ~tirar~; this fits the kinship felt between ~tirer~, ~tirailler~, and ~déchirer~, and is paralleled by German ~zehren~ (“to consume, destroy”) and ~zerren~ (“to tug”). A rival Latin account (Wartburg) sees a clipping of Old French ~martirier~ (“to martyr, to torture”), from ~martyre~. In any case ~tirer~ largely displaced the older ~traire~, from Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag”).

The spread of meaning is wide: from the core “to pull” come ~tirer~ “to draw out” (~tirer un trait~, “to draw a line”), “to fire, to shoot” (a crossbow being drawn before release), and the printing sense (a ~tirage~ is a press-run, paper pulled off the plate). The torture connection, if true, is grimly apt — medieval racking stretched and dislocated limbs by pulling. Whatever ~tirer~'s own pedigree, the displaced ~traire~ left a productive Latin family in French: ~soustraire~, ~extraire~, ~soutirer~, ~étirer~, ~retirer~, and ~attirer~, all turning on the act of drawing.
en.tisser:
Descended from Latin ~texō~ (“to weave”), by way of Old French ~tistre~. That strong verb was reshaped by analogy into ~tissir~, which then passed into the first conjugation as ~tisser~, so the modern infinitive is a late and regularized form. Latin ~texō~ comes from Proto-Italic *~teksō~, which English Wiktionary derives from the Proto-Indo-European root *~teḱ-~ (“to beget, to produce”), by one of two competing reconstructions, so the exact PIE shape is debated. Related to it are Latin ~textus~ (“fabric, woven thing”) and its French offspring ~texte~, ~textile~ and ~contexte~. Greek ~tekhnē~ (“craft, art”) is usually placed in the same family, though the details of the root are uncertain.

The old strong verb has not entirely vanished. Some northern dialects kept it, such as Norman ~tître~, Gallo ~téstr~ and Walloon ~texhe~, and all of them preserve the older conjugation. The original past participle was ~tissu~, which gave French its word for cloth and, by extension, for living tissue and the social fabric. English ~tissue~ is borrowed from it, a “woven thing”. The verb ~tisser~ itself moved easily from the loom to metaphor: one weaves links, a plot, a web. The word ~texte~ keeps the same picture, a text being a thing woven out of sentences, which is also why ~contexte~ means what is woven together with it.
en.titrer: Formed from the noun ~titre~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~titre~ descends from Latin ~titulus~ (“inscription, label”) and is attested from about 1225. It has two uses that explain the verb's two main senses: a heading or name, so ~titrer~ is “to give a title or headline”, and the fineness of a metal alloy, hence “to determine the strength of a solution or alloy”, the sense behind chemical titration. English Wiktionary also offers a variant account, that the verb is inherited from Old French ~titler~, itself from ~titulus~.
en.tomber:
From an expressive Vulgar Latin *~tumbāre~ (“to fall, to tumble”), built on a root *~tumb-~ that imitates the sound and suddenness of a fall. In Old French this met and merged with ~tumer~ (“to do somersaults, to tumble”), a verb of Frankish origin from *~tūmōn~ (compare Old High German ~tūmōn~, “to turn, to reel”); through that Germanic stock the same idea survives in English ~tumble~. The two near-identical verbs blurred together, and ~tumer~ died out by the sixteenth century, leaving ~tomber~ alone.

What makes ~tomber~ remarkable is that it is an upstart. Old French already had a perfectly good verb for falling, ~choir~ (from Latin ~cadere~), but from the fifteenth century the livelier, half-onomatopoeic ~tomber~ pressed in, and by the seventeenth it had all but ousted ~choir~ from everyday speech. ~Choir~ now survives only in literary corners and in its compound ~déchoir~ (“to decline, to fall from grace”), while its participle lingers in ~échu~ and ~déchet~. ~Tomber~, meanwhile, spread into countless idioms — ~tomber amoureux~ (“to fall in love”), ~tomber malade~, ~laisser tomber~ — and spun off ~tombée~ (“nightfall”) and ~retomber~.
en.tomer: Formed in French from the noun ~tome~ (“volume of a work”) and the suffix ~-er~: to ~tomer~ is to divide a work into volumes. The noun ~tome~ was borrowed from Latin ~tomus~, a word that goes back to Greek ~tómos~ (“a cut, a slice”), the image being of a long text cut into sections. A separate word ~tome~, a variant of ~tomme~, is a cheese and has nothing to do with this one. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~. The verb is rare and technical, used mostly by publishers and librarians.
en.tordre:
Inherited from Old French ~tordre~ (also spelled ~tortre~), from Vulgar Latin *~torcĕre~, itself from Classical Latin ~torquēre~ (“to twist”). The Latin verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~terkʷ-~ (“to twist”). Italian ~torcere~ and Spanish ~torcer~ are its sister continuations. English never inherited the verb, but borrowed a whole family from Latin ~torquēre~ and its participle ~tortus~: ~torture~, ~torment~, ~torque~, ~distort~, ~contort~ and ~retort~ all began as “twistings” of one kind or another.

In French the verb kept its physical sense: one ~tord~ a cloth to wring it out, an arm to hurt someone, a wire to bend it. The reflexive ~se tordre~ is to writhe, and ~se tordre de rire~ is to double up with laughter. The participle ~tortus~ survives in the noun ~tort~ (“wrong, harm”), literally what is twisted, as opposed to what is straight and right. Modern French words from the same root include ~tordu~ (“twisted”, and in slang “crazy”), ~torsion~, ~tortueux~ (“winding, devious”) and ~contorsion~.
en.torturer: A denominal verb: ~torture~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, “to inflict torture on.” The noun comes from Late Latin ~tortūra~ (“a twisting,” then “suffering”), from Latin ~tortus~, the past participle of ~torquēre~ (“to twist, to torture”). French ~torture~ first described a severe penal punishment (1459), then took its modern sense of physical suffering inflicted to extract a confession (1580), and later, by extension, moral suffering (1631). The verb carries all of these senses.
en.totaliser: Formed from the adjective and noun ~total~ with the suffix ~-iser~, a suffix that builds verbs meaning “to make or turn into.” The base ~total~ was borrowed into Middle French in the fourteenth century from Medieval Latin ~tōtālis~, derived from Latin ~tōtus~ (“whole, all”). To ~totaliser~ is to add up into a total, or to reach a total. The stem is unchanged before the suffix, so the formation is a straightforward French one.
en.toucher:
From Old French ~tochier~ (“to touch, to strike, to mention”), from Vulgar Latin *~toccāre~ (“to knock, to strike, as a bell”). This *~toccāre~ is widely held to be of imitative origin, built on the sound ~toc~ — the sharp “knock” made when two hard things meet. It thus replaced the older Latin ~tangere~ (“to touch”). Romance kin include Italian ~toccare~ and Spanish ~tocar~, and through Old French it gave English ~touch~.

The semantic drift is a small marvel of physics: a blow at its very gentlest is nothing more than a touch, so “to strike” slid quietly into “to make contact with.” From bodily contact French ~toucher~ reached for figurative senses — to ~toucher~ a sum of money (to receive it), to ~toucher~ someone (to move them emotionally), and to ~toucher~ a subject (to broach it). The onomatopoeic ~toc~ left other traces: ~toquer~ (“to knock”), the alarm-bell ~tocsin~ (which once literally meant a struck signal), and the noun ~toucher~ itself, the sense of touch. The musical ~toccata~, borrowed into many languages, is from the Italian cousin ~toccare~ — a “touched” keyboard piece.
en.tourmenter: Formed from the noun ~tourment~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes through Old French ~torment~ from Latin ~tormentum~, a word for an instrument of torture or a siege engine, and it is related to ~tordre~ (“to twist”), since such devices worked by twisting. To ~tourmenter~ is thus to put someone through torture, then, more loosely, to harass or to trouble the mind.
en.tourner:
From Old French ~torner~, from Latin ~tornare~ (“to turn on a lathe, to round off”), a verb built on ~tornus~ (“a lathe, a turner's chisel”). That noun was itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τόρνος~ (~tórnos~), a compass or lathe for tracing circles, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, to bore by twisting”). Through the same Latin source come Italian ~tornare~, Spanish ~tornar~, and — by way of Norman and Old French — English ~turn~ and ~tour~.

The earliest sense was thoroughly mechanical: to shape wood or metal by spinning it against a fixed blade, the craft of the ~tourneur~. From this image of rotation the meaning fanned out to cover any circular movement, then a change of direction (~tourner à gauche~), then figurative reversals of fortune and mood (~tourner mal~, “to turn out badly”). The culinary sense of stirring, and the cinematic sense of shooting a film — ~tourner un film~, a memory of the hand-cranked camera — both descend from the same idea of turning. The lathe-sense survives intact in ~tour~ (“lathe”) and ~tournage~. From the Greek-Latin root spring a wide family: ~tour~, ~tournoi~, ~tournevis~, ~contour~, ~détour~, and ~retourner~.
en.tracer:
Attested from the 12th century, from Vulgar Latin *~tractiare~, derived from ~tractum~, the supine of Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, drag”). The deeper origin of ~trahere~ is genuinely unclear: the regular sound laws do not fit a clean Proto-Indo-European source, and scholars variously propose a link to the *~weǵʰ-~ family (“to carry,” as in ~vehere~), a reshaped *~dʰregʰ-~, or — per de Vaan — a non-Indo-European substrate word; the connection to English ~drag~ and German ~tragen~ remains debated rather than proven.

The semantic path is elegant: from “dragging” a stylus came “drawing a line,” then “plotting a route” and figuratively “forging ahead” — hence the colloquial ~tracer~ for “to hurry, race along.” The same Latin ~trahere~ gave French ~trait~, ~traire~, ~portrait~, ~retracer~, and the nouns ~tracé~ and ~traceur~. Whatever its murky deepest root, the idea of dragging something across a surface runs through the whole family.
en.traduire:
From Latin ~traducere~ (“to lead across, to bring over”), from ~trans-~ (“across”) + ~ducere~ (“to lead, conduct”). ~ducere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to draw, to pull”), cognate with English ~tow~ and ~tug~ and with German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”). The Romance siblings are Italian ~tradurre~ and Spanish ~traducir~; French had also inherited the older, properly translation-meaning verb ~translater~, from Latin ~translatare~.

The modern sense rests on a famous misreading. In classical Latin ~traducere~ meant “to lead across, to transfer, to parade” — even “to disgrace,” by leading a culprit publicly across the forum. Around 1400 the humanist Leonardo Bruni, parsing a phrase of Aulus Gellius, took ~traducere~ to mean “to render from one tongue into another,” and the brilliant error spread across Europe, ousting ~translater~ in French by the sixteenth century. A ghost of the old “lead across” sense lingers in the legal ~traduire en justice~ (“to bring before a court”). From the same ~ducere~ French drew a teeming family: ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~réduire~, ~séduire~, ~duc~, and ~aqueduc~.
en.trahir:
~Trahir~ is inherited from Middle French ~trahir~, from Old French ~traïr~, from Latin ~trādere~ (“to hand over, to deliver, to betray”). The Latin verb combines ~trans-~ (“across”) with ~dare~ (“to give”), whose root is the Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). The ~h~ of the modern spelling is a later addition that marks the two vowels as separate syllables. Italian ~tradire~, Portuguese ~trair~ and Occitan ~traïr~ come from the same Latin verb.

The Latin sense “to hand over” was neutral, and it is still visible in ~tradition~, literally “what is handed down.” The meaning “to betray” grew from handing someone over to an enemy, and the agent noun ~trāditor~ gave ~traître~ in French and ~traitor~ in English. English ~treason~ and French ~trahison~ share the same family. In French, ~trahir~ spread from persons to things: ~trahir un secret~ (“to give away”), ~trahir sa pensée~ (“to misrepresent”), and a voice that ~trahit~ emotion (“to reveal”). Related words are ~trahison~, ~traître~, ~tradition~, ~extradition~ and ~traditionnel~.
en.traire:
Inherited from Old French ~traire~ (also ~treire~, “to pull”), from a popular Latin *~tragere~, a reshaping of classical Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag”). English Wiktionary gives the intermediate as Early Medieval Latin ~tragō~. The classical verb is the source of Italian ~trarre~ and of a large learned family in English, including ~tract~, ~attract~ and ~extract~.

In Old French, ~traire~ meant “to pull” in the widest sense, but it was challenged by ~tirer~, a regular verb, and held on only in the narrow sense of pulling on a udder to draw out the milk. It also ousted the old French ~moudre~, which came from Latin ~mulgēre~ and is a cognate of English ~milk~; in a sense, French milks cows with the verb for pulling. The Latin ~trahere~ also gave ~trait~, ~traction~, ~extraire~, ~abstraire~, ~distraire~ and ~soustraire~, all built on the same root.
en.traiter:
From Latin ~tractāre~ (“to handle, to manage, to deal with”), the frequentative of ~trahere~ (“to draw, to pull”), whose past participle is ~tractus~. ~Trahere~ goes back to a PIE root often given as *~tregʰ-~ (“to draw, to drag”); the relationship to Germanic ~drag~ is debated, so it is left aside. Within French itself ~traiter~ is a doublet of the inherited ~traire~ (“to milk,” originally “to draw”). Cognate with Italian ~trattare~ and Spanish ~tratar~.

The frequentative force of ~tractāre~ is “to keep drawing, to handle repeatedly,” and from there “to handle” in every sense — physically, then socially, then intellectually. That spread explains the wide modern range of ~traiter~: to treat a person (well or badly), to treat a patient, to deal with a subject, to process a material or data, and, via ~traité~, to conclude a treaty. The participle ~tractus~ seeded ~trait~ (“line, feature, stroke”), and the same ~trahere~ family gives French ~tracter~, ~traction~, ~extraire~, ~abstrait~, and ~portrait~ — all built on the basic gesture of drawing something out.
en.trancher:
From Old French ~trenchier~ (around 1100), whence also the cognate Romance verbs Catalan ~trencar~ and Italian ~trinciare~. The Latin source is genuinely uncertain, and the sources offer two competing accounts. By one, it comes from a Vulgar Latin *~trinicare~ (“to cut in three”), built on ~tres~ / ~trini~ like ~duplicare~ on ~duplus~; by the other, it is an alteration of Latin ~truncare~ (“to lop, maim”), possibly crossed with a Gaulish *~trincare~. Neither is established, so the chain is best left flagged as disputed rather than forced.

Whatever the root, the meaning is “to cut cleanly through,” and from the literal blade-stroke French drew a rich figurative harvest. To ~trancher~ a question is to settle it decisively — to cut through debate — and an opinion that is ~tranché~ is sharp and unqualified, a metaphor English shares in ~trenchant~. The same Old French verb, borrowed into English, gave ~trench~ (a cut in the ground) and ~retrench~. Native French derivatives are abundant: ~tranche~ (“slice”), ~tranchant~ (“cutting edge”), ~tranchée~ (“trench”), ~trancheur~, and ~trançoir~ — a whole family turning on the clean stroke of a knife.
en.transcender:
Borrowed from Latin ~trānscendere~ (“to climb over, to surpass”), built from ~trāns~ (“across, beyond”) and ~scandere~ (“to climb”). French Wiktionary points to ~descendre~ and ~ascension~ as relatives, which come from the same Latin verb family with other prefixes, so ~transcender~ belongs to a small group of “climbing” words. French took it as a learned word directly from Latin, not through any inherited Old French form.

The French verb keeps the figurative picture of climbing over: to ~transcender~ is to rise above an obstacle, a condition or the ordinary range of experience. Its family in French includes ~transcendant~ and ~transcendance~, while its relatives ~ascension~ and ~descendre~ show the same Latin stem under different prefixes. Like most learned verbs of this kind, it entered French as a ready-made Latin word and was not assembled from French parts.
en.transcrire:
Borrowed from Latin ~trānscrībere~, a compound of ~trāns-~ (“across, over”) and ~scrībere~ (“to write”). The Latin verb meant to copy out, to write over from one place or document to another. Latin ~scrībere~ goes back to a root meaning “to scratch, to cut,” which fits the earliest writing, done by scoring wax or clay with a stylus. The Romance cousins are Italian ~trascrivere~ and Spanish ~transcribir~, and English ~transcribe~ is a learned borrowing of the same Latin verb.

French ~transcrire~ keeps the picture of carrying a text across: to transcribe is to move something from one form to another while changing as little as possible. It can mean copying a document into a register, writing down speech, rendering a language in another script, or putting music in another key or for another instrument. Scientists later borrowed it for biology, where a cell transcribes a gene into RNA. The Latin verb ~scrībere~ yielded French ~écrire~ through the form ~ēscrībere~, and gave a large family: ~décrire~, ~inscrire~, ~souscrire~, ~prescrire~, ~scribe~, ~script~ and ~transcription~.
en.transformer:
From Latin ~transformāre~ (“to change in shape, transform”), a compound of the prefix ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~formāre~ (“to shape, form”), itself from ~forma~ (“form, shape, figure”). The verb entered French around 1295. The origin of ~forma~ is debated: it may be a borrowing from Greek ~morphḗ~ (“form, shape, beauty”) — perhaps via Etruscan — with the consonants transposed, or both words may inherit a common Proto-Indo-European source. The Latin verb also gives Italian ~trasformare~, Spanish ~transformar~, and English ~transform~.

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: to carry a thing “across” into a new form. From that core, French applies it everywhere — from caterpillar into butterfly (a metamorphosis), from raw material into product, and, in rugby, the bonus kick that ~transforme~ a try into added points. ~forma~ seeded an enormous family in French: ~former~ (“to form, train”), ~forme~, ~formule~, ~formel~, ~conforme~, ~réformer~, ~déformer~, ~informer~ (literally “to give shape to,” to put into the mind), and ~uniforme~. The disputed link to Greek ~morphḗ~ means that ~transformer~ may be a distant cousin of ~métamorphose~ — two ways of speaking about a change of shape.
en.transférer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~trānsferre~ (“to carry across, to bear over, to transport”), formed from the prefix ~trāns-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”). That root is one of the most widespread in all Indo-European: it is cognate with English ~bear~, Greek ~phérein~ (“to carry”), and Sanskrit ~bhárati~ (“he carries”). The Latin ~trānsferre~ also gave the past participle ~trānslātus~, source of the English ~translate~ — itself a “carrying across,” of meaning from one tongue to another.

French remodeled the inherited stem on the pattern of regular ~-érer~ verbs, yielding ~transférer~. Its core image is literal transport — carrying a thing from one place to another — and it still serves for moving a prisoner, an employee, a sum of money, or a body from place to place. The figurative ~transfert~ went on to a distinguished career in psychology and law. From the same ~ferre~ French inherited a great convoy of words: ~conférer~, ~déférer~, ~différer~, ~offrir~, ~souffrir~, ~préférer~, and the noun ~fertile~ (“bearing, fruitful”) — every one of them, like ~transférer~, a matter of something carried.
en.transiter: Formed from ~transit~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to pass through”, as goods, travelers or data do. The noun ~transit~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~trānsitus~ (“passage”), which belongs to the verb ~trānsīre~ (“to go across”), made of ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~īre~ (“to go”). The verb is therefore a French coinage on a Latin noun, with no Latin verb behind it in this form.
en.transmettre:
From Latin ~transmittere~ (“to send across, to send over”), reshaped in French on the model of ~mettre~. The Latin verb joins the prefix ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”), which descends from Proto-Italic *~meitō~ and a Proto-Indo-European root *~mey-~ (“to change, to exchange”). The sense traveled from “exchange” to “give, let go” to “send.” English borrowed the same compound as ~transmit~.

The image is one of carrying something across a gap — a message, a disease, an inheritance, a radio wave — and handing it on. ~Mittere~ was one of Latin's most prolific verbs, and through its French heir ~mettre~ (“to put”) and its many compounds it shaped a huge vocabulary: ~admettre~, ~commettre~, ~permettre~, ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, and ~remettre~, alongside the nouns of the ~missus~ / ~missio~ branch — ~mission~, ~message~ (literally “a thing sent”), ~messager~, ~commission~, and ~mise~. So when we ~transmettre~ knowledge from one generation to the next, we are quite literally “sending it across,” performing in the abstract the same act a Roman did when he dispatched a courier over the frontier.
en.transporter:
From Latin ~transportāre~ (“to carry across, to convey”), composed of the prefix ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”). The verb ~portāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to pass through, to cross over”), the root behind Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbour”), and behind English ~fare~, ~ford~, and ~ferry~ — all notions of passage and crossing. Italian ~trasportare~ and Spanish ~transportar~ are the direct Romance parallels.

The literal sense — to carry people or goods from one place to another — has stayed central since antiquity, and it powers a whole modern vocabulary of movement. But French also kept a striking figurative use: to be ~transporté~ is to be carried away by emotion, “transported” with joy, anger, or love, the soul borne off as if bodily. The noun ~transport~ likewise means both “transportation” and a “rapture” or surge of feeling (~un transport de joie~). From the shared ancestor ~portāre~ flows a vast family of French words: ~porter~ itself, ~porteur~, ~apporter~, ~emporter~, ~rapporter~, ~importer~ and ~exporter~, ~portatif~, and ~portable~ — all built on the simple idea of carrying.
en.transposer:
From Latin ~transponere~ (“to transfer, to move across”), itself built from ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~ponere~ (“to put, to place”). The French verb did not keep the Latin shape intact: English Wiktionary says it was altered based on French ~poser~, so that it now looks like ~trans-~ + ~poser~ even though the Latin verb underneath is ~ponere~.

The core sense is “to move something to another place or order,” and the verb has specialized in several directions since. In music, to ~transposer~ a melody is to move it into another key without changing its intervals. In algebra, one can ~transposer~ a term to the other side of an equation. In everyday and literary use, one can ~transposer~ a story into another period or setting, keeping its structure while changing its scenery. The noun ~transposition~ covers all these uses. The verb belongs to a family with ~poser~, ~déposer~, ~composer~ and ~proposer~, all of which share the idea of “placing,” with a different prefix each time.
en.traquer:
The origin of ~traquer~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes that it is probably a verb formed from Middle French ~trac~ (“track, trace”). English Wiktionary gives a fuller chain for that noun: Middle French ~trac~ came from Old French ~trac~ (“track, beaten path, course”), from Middle Dutch ~treck~ or ~treke~ (“a drawing, a pull, a line”), from Old Dutch *~trecken~, and ultimately from Proto-Germanic *~trakjaną~ (“to drag”). If that is right, ~traquer~ shares its Germanic ancestry with English ~track~ and ~trek~, both of which are named as relatives. The hedge matters: the link from ~trac~ to ~traquer~ is a likely derivation, not a documented one.

The verb means “to track, to hunt down, to hound,” and a ~traque~ is a hunt or manhunt in which someone is followed relentlessly. A hunting origin for the sense is natural, since a track is what a hunter follows, but the sources do not spell out the stages, so the story should be taken as plausible rather than documented. In modern French the verb is used both of hunters and police and of the press, which ~traque~ its targets, and the past participle ~traqué~ describes the hunted look of someone who feels pursued. English ~trek~, which has a Dutch and Afrikaans career of its own, is a distant echo of the same Germanic idea of dragging along.
en.travailler:
French ~travailler~ comes from Old French ~traveillier~ (“to torment, to torture, to cause suffering”), from Vulgar Latin *~tripāliāre~ (“to torture with the ~tripalium~”). The ~tripalium~ was, on the most widespread account, an instrument of restraint or torture made of three stakes — ~tri-~ (“three”) plus ~pālus~ (“stake”) — to which slaves were bound for punishment or large animals were tied to be shod. The same source gives Spanish ~trabajar~, Portuguese ~trabalhar~, and Occitan ~trabalhar~, all the ordinary words for “to work.”

The semantic journey is startling: from “to torture” the verb passed to “to suffer, to toil painfully,” then to the neutral “to labor,” and finally to today's “to work” of every kind. The older sense of anguish has not wholly vanished — the noun ~travail~ still names the pains of childbirth, and ~se travailler~ can mean “to torment oneself.” A caution is in order: this tidy ~tripalium~ story, though repeated everywhere, is disputed, and some scholars instead derive the word from a Late Latin *~trabicula~ (“little beam,” a frame for holding animals). Either way the modern ~travailleur~ (“worker”) carries, etymologically, a faint echo of the rack.
en.traverser:
From Old French ~traverser~, from Late Latin ~traversare~, a worn-down form of ~transversare~, itself from the Latin adjective ~transversus~ (“lying across, turned crosswise”). ~transversus~ is the past participle of ~transvertere~, from ~trans~ (“across”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~vertere~ descends from PIE *~wert-~ (“to turn, to bend”), one of the most prolific roots in Indo-European. Cognate with Italian ~traversare~ and Spanish ~atravesar~.

The image is precise: to ~traverser~ is to move along a line “turned across” one's path, to cut from one side to the other. The same *~wert-~ root, through ~vertere~ and its participle ~versus~, fans out across French into ~tourner~, ~version~, ~vers~, ~envers~, ~divers~, and ~convertir~, and even into English ~-ward~, ~worth~, and ~versus~ — all of them carrying some ghost of turning. Closer to home, ~traverser~ has bred a small household of its own: the noun ~travers~ (“breadth, a turning aside”), the adverbial ~à travers~ and ~de travers~ (“askew”), the ~traversée~ (a sea crossing), and the ~traversin~, the long bolster that lies crosswise at the head of a French bed — a humble pillow still quietly “turned across.”
en.traîner:
French ~traîner~ comes from Old French ~traïner~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~tragīnāre~, a verb built on *~tragere~, itself a form of Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull”). The same *~tragere~ gave French ~traire~ (“to milk”). Wiktionary tentatively links ~trahere~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰregʰ-~, but the connection is marked uncertain. Other Romance languages hold close cousins of ~traîner~: Italian ~trascinare~, Catalan ~traginar~ and Spanish ~trajinar~ all descend from related Latin stock. English ~train~ is a loan from the French family.

The verb began as “to pull behind oneself,” as one drags a cart or a long robe. From that came the figurative sense of moving slowly, then of lingering, as in ~traîner dans les rues~ (“to hang around”) or ~ça traîne~ (“it drags on”). The modern circumflex stands where Old French had the diaeresis of ~traïner~. The family also includes ~train~, formed on ~traîner~, and, from ~trahere~, ~trait~, ~traction~, ~attraction~ and ~abstraire~. A railway ~train~ is, etymologically, a thing dragged along behind an engine.
en.trembler:
From Old French ~trembler~ (earlier ~trambler~), from Late Latin ~tremulāre~, a verb built on the adjective ~tremulus~ (“shaking”) and ultimately from Latin ~tremere~ (“to tremble”). That root goes back to the Proto-Indo-European *~trem-~ (“to tremble”), shared with Ancient Greek ~trémō~. The same Latin verb ~tremere~ is also one of the sources of French ~craindre~ (“to fear”), whose initial consonant shifted along the way. English Wiktionary notes that ~trembler~ has a doublet, the learned ~trémuler~, formed on the same Late Latin base. English ~tremble~ is borrowed from French.

The verb began as a physical description of shaking and then gained its emotional uses, since fear and cold make the body shake. Hence ~trembler de peur~ (“to tremble with fear”), ~trembler pour quelqu'un~ (“to fear for someone”), and the colorful ~trembler comme une feuille~ (“to shake like a leaf”). The link with ~craindre~ is a nice trace of the old connection: the Latin verb that gave one verb for shaking and another for fearing. The family includes ~tremblement~ (“tremor”), ~trembloter~ (“to quiver slightly”), ~tremblotant~, and the learned ~trémulation~, a more clinical shaking. English ~tremor~ and ~tremulous~ come from the Latin side.
en.tremper:
Inherited from Middle French ~tremper~, which is a metathesis of Old French ~temprer~ (the ~r~ moving forward a syllable), from Latin ~temperāre~ (“to mix in due proportion, to moderate”). It is a doublet of the learned borrowing ~tempérer~, which took the same Latin verb straight from Latin and so kept its shape. English ~temper~ and Italian ~temperare~ also descend from it, and so does Spanish ~templar~, which is a related form.

The sense progression runs from mixing to dipping. To ~temperāre~ was to blend things in the right measure, for instance wine with water, and the Old French verb kept the idea of mixing a liquid, and then of plunging something into one. In the French of the smith, ~tremper~ means to quench heated steel in water to harden it, and this gave the figurative ~la trempe~ (“quality of one's character”): a person ~de bonne trempe~ is made of strong stuff. Other senses are “to soak” and, in ~tremper dans une affaire~, “to be mixed up in an affair,” which echoes the older mixing sense. Relatives include ~trempette~, ~détremper~ and, through the learned doublet, ~tempérer~, ~tempérament~ and ~température~.
en.tricher:
The origin of ~tricher~ is disputed. French reaches back to Old French ~tricher~ (“to deceive, cheat”), and one account derives it from a Vulgar Latin verb *~triccāre~, from Late Latin ~tricāre~, itself from Latin ~trīcārī~ (“to look for detours, to quibble, to haggle”), a verb tied to the noun ~trīcae~. Support comes from sister languages that have the same verb: Italian ~treccare~, Old Occitan ~trichar~, and Catalan and Occitan ~trigar~.

A rival theory sees a Germanic origin instead, in Middle High German ~trechen~ (as in ~zuotrechen~, “to obtain by deceit”), with Middle Dutch ~treck~ (“ruse, stratagem”) as a relative. English Wiktionary invites a comparison with English ~trick~. It presents the Latin route first and the Germanic one as a further possibility, so neither account can be called settled. What is certain is only that the Old French verb existed; where it came from remains in dispute.
en.trier:
The origin of French ~trier~ is disputed. It is first attested around 1175, as Old French ~trier~ (“to choose, to pick out, to sift, to cull”), and English Wiktionary labels it of uncertain origin; Occitan ~triar~ is a cognate. French Wiktionary reports two rival accounts. By one, ~trier~ is a distortion of ~tirer~ (“to draw out”). By the other, it descends from Late Latin ~trītāre~ (“to grind”), from ~trītum~, the supine of ~terere~ (“to rub, to grind”), and would originally have meant to rub the ear of wheat to separate the grain.

Neither account is settled, so the grain-threshing picture should be taken as a proposal, not a fact. What is certain is the sense of separating good from bad, which gave ~trier~ its modern uses: sorting mail, rubbish or lentils, and picking out candidates. English borrowed the verb as ~try~ by way of Anglo-Norman, where “to sift” gradually became “to test” and then “to attempt”; a ~trial~ is therefore a sorting out. The noun ~triage~, built on ~trier~, came back into English with its medical sense of sorting patients by urgency. If the ~terere~ account is right, ~trier~ would also be kin to ~triturer~ and English ~trite~, but that link remains a hypothesis.
en.triompher:
Borrowed from Latin ~triumphāre~ (“to celebrate a triumph, to triumph”), a verb built on the noun ~triumphus~, the name of the procession that welcomed a victorious Roman general. The noun itself is generally explained as a descendant of Old Latin ~triumpus~, taken from Greek ~θρίαμβος~ (~thríambos~), a hymn to Dionysus; by one account the word reached Rome through Etruscan, but the route is not certain. The verb gave Italian ~trionfare~ and Spanish ~triunfar~, and the noun gave English ~triumph~, which entered English from the same Latin source by way of French.

In Rome, a triumph was a precisely regulated ceremony: the general rode in a chariot along the Sacred Way up to the Capitol, followed by his soldiers and his captives. French ~triompher~ means to win a victory, and more widely to succeed: to triumph over an obstacle, an enemy or one's own fear (~triompher de~), or, of a play or a performer, to be a huge hit. Related words include ~triomphe~ (“triumph”), the learned ~triomphal~, ~triomphant~ and the Parisian monument ~arc de triomphe~, which borrows the Roman image of the victor's procession.
en.tripler: ~Tripler~ is formed from the adjective and noun ~triple~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns a base into a verb: to make something three times as large, or to become so. ~Triple~ comes from Latin ~triplus~ (“threefold”). It is a semi-learned form, reshaped under the influence of Latin from Old French ~treble~, the same ancestor that gave English ~treble~. French thus kept two layers of the word, the older popular one having faded.
en.tromper:
Attested from the late 12th century, ~tromper~ is a denominal verb from the noun ~trompe~ (“horn, trumpet”), and its first meaning was simply “to play the horn,” jouer de la trompe. The noun ~trompe~ is of imitative or Germanic origin, echoing the instrument's blare. How a verb for trumpeting came to mean “to deceive” is one of the small mysteries of French etymology — and the favored explanation is delightfully concrete.

The usual account runs through the reflexive expression ~se tromper de quelqu'un~, literally “to play the horn at someone” — to blare derisively in a person's face, hence “to mock, to make sport of” them. From mockery the sense slid to misleading, then to outright deceiving, and finally the plain ~tromper~ settled into its modern meaning, “to deceive, to fool, to lead astray.” The reflexive ~se tromper~ took the gentler turn “to be mistaken, to make a mistake” — to be, as it were, fooled by oneself. ~Tromper~ also acquired the specific sense of marital infidelity, “to cheat on.” From the same ~trompe~ French keeps ~tromperie~ (“deceit”), ~trompeur~ (“deceiver”), ~trompette~ (“trumpet,” a little ~trompe~), and ~se détromper~ (“to undeceive oneself”).
en.troubler:
From Old French ~trobler~ (also ~trubler~), with the sounds of the “r” swapped from earlier ~torbler~, ~tourbler~ and ~turbler~, themselves from Vulgar Latin *~turbulāre~. That verb is explained in one of two ways: either as a diminutive of Latin ~turbāre~ (“to agitate, to disturb”), or as built on a noun ~turbula~, a diminutive of ~turba~ (“commotion, crowd”). Both routes lead to the same root. Occitan ~trebolar~ and Romanian ~tulbura~ are relatives of the French verb.

The swap of the ~r~ is the telling detail: ~turbler~ became ~trobler~ because the “r” moved forward in the word, and ~trobler~ then settled into modern ~troubler~. The meaning stayed close to its source, the stirring up of something calm. The Latin root also came into French a second time through learned borrowing, giving ~turbulent~, a cousin of ~troubler~ that kept the Latin vowel and the original order of the consonants.
en.trouver:
From Old French ~trover~, from Vulgar Latin *~tropāre~ (“to compose a melody, then to compose verse, then to invent, to find”), derived from Latin ~tropus~ (“a figure of speech, a trope”). The Latin word was borrowed from Greek ~trópos~ (“a turn, a manner, a turn of phrase”), from ~trépein~ (“to turn”), and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~trep-~ (“to turn”). So at its root, to find is to “turn” a phrase.

The path of meaning is unusually beautiful. *~tropāre~ first meant to compose tropes — the sung verses added to liturgical chant — and from “to compose, to invent a song” it widened to “to invent” and then to “to come upon, to find.” The poet who composed such songs was the ~trouvère~ in the north and the ~troubadour~ in the south of medieval France, both literally “finders, inventors.” The same stem gives French ~trouvaille~ (“a lucky find”), ~retrouver~ (“to find again, to meet again”), and ~controuver~ (“to fabricate, to invent falsely”). The learned ~trope~ and ~tropical~ (a zone where the sun “turns”) preserve the original Greek sense of turning, a quiet reminder that, etymologically, every discovery is a turn of phrase.
en.tuer:
From Old French ~tuer~ (“to strike, stun, extinguish”), from Late Latin ~tūtāre~ (“to put out a fire, to smother”), an altered form of Classical Latin ~tūtāri~ (“to protect, to guard against”), the frequentative of ~tuērī~ (“to watch over, protect”), a verb of uncertain deeper origin. The startling thread here is semantic: a verb that once meant “to protect” became the ordinary French word for “to kill.”

The bridge was fire. To “protect” against a blaze meant to ~tūtāre~ it — to smother it, put it out — and from “extinguishing a flame” the sense slid to “snuffing out” more generally: stunning a blow, then dealing a fatal one. By Old French, ~tuer~ already meant “to strike down,” and it eventually crowded out the inherited ~occire~ (from Latin ~occīdere~) as the everyday verb for killing. The protective ancestor ~tuērī~ left gentler descendants in French through its participle ~tūtus~: ~tuteur~ (“guardian, tutor”) and ~tutelle~ (“guardianship”) still mean “one who watches over.” So the same Latin root for watchful protection branches into both the guardian and the killer — a vivid reminder that to “put out” can mean to shield or to slay.
en.typer:
~Typer~ is a denominal verb from the noun ~type~, which French took from Latin ~typus~ (« figure, image, form »), itself a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~τύπος~ (~túpos~, « blow, imprint, mould »). That noun belongs to the verb ~τύπτω~ (~túptō~, « to strike, to beat »): a ~τύπος~ was originally the mark left by a blow, the impression a stamp or seal leaves in wax or clay. The metaphor of the die that stamps identical copies runs through the whole family.

From « imprint » the word drifted toward « model » and then « category », and the verb ~typer~ followed: to ~typer~ someone or something is to stamp them with the marks of a recognizable type, to make them typical or — pejoratively — to stereotype. The printing sense survives in ~typographie~ and ~typo~, the classifying sense in ~type~, ~typique~, and ~stéréotype~ (literally a « solid » printing plate). English ~type~, ~typical~, and ~typist~ spring from the same Greek root.
en.tâcher:
Both French and English sources treat this verb as formed on the noun ~tâche~ (“task”), which comes from Latin ~taxāre~ (“to touch sharply, to estimate”). Latin ~taxāre~ is probably a frequentative of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), and it has two famous offspring in French: ~taxer~ (“to tax, to assess”), borrowed later in learned form, and ~tâche~, the inherited version.

The development is a good example of how a noun of labor gives a verb of effort. A ~tâche~ was a job set for someone; to ~tâcher~ was “to set oneself to a task,” then simply to try or strive. Today it is mostly found in the construction ~tâcher de~ followed by an infinitive (“to try to”), and in the demanding expression ~tâcher que~ with the subjunctive (“to make sure that”). Related words include ~tâche~, ~tâcheron~ (“a piece-work laborer,” and now “a drudge”), ~taxer~ and ~taxe~.
en.télécharger:
A modern French coinage, formed from the prefix ~télé-~ (“at a distance, far off”) and the verb ~charger~ (“to load”). The prefix ~télé-~ comes through scientific Latin from Ancient Greek ~τῆλε~ (~têle~, “far, far off”); ~charger~ descends from Late Latin ~carricare~ (“to load a wagon”), from ~carrus~ (“wheeled cart”), a word the Romans borrowed from Gaulish. So the verb is a hybrid: a Greek adverb of distance bolted onto a Celtic-Latin verb of loading. Cognate with English ~charge~ and ~cargo~, both also from ~carricare~.

Unlike most verbs here, ~télécharger~ has no Roman ancestor: it was minted in French in the early 1980s, in the first age of telematics and computer networks, to name the act of “loading at a distance” — moving a file between a remote machine and a local one. French, unusually, uses the one verb for both directions, distinguishing them as ~télécharger~ for downloading versus ~téléverser~ or ~télécharger vers le serveur~ for uploading. The ~télé-~ element ties it to a whole modern cohort — ~téléphone~, ~télévision~, ~télescope~, ~télégramme~ — while ~charger~ binds it to the older ~charge~, ~chargement~, ~décharger~, and ~surcharger~, the everyday vocabulary of loads and burdens.
en.téléphoner: Formed from the noun ~téléphone~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to use” what the noun names: to telephone. The noun was built from the prefix ~télé-~ and the element ~-phone~, both from Greek: ~τῆλε~ (“afar”) and ~φωνή~ (“voice, sound”). The word therefore means literally “a far voice”, a good description of the device. The verb followed the instrument, as French ~téléphoner~ turned the machine into an everyday action.
en.téléviser:
A modern compound formed on the model of ~télévision~, joining the prefix ~télé-~ — from Ancient Greek ~tēle~ (« far off, at a distance ») — to a base meaning « to see, » ultimately Latin ~videre~ (« to see ») through its participle ~visus~. The whole literally evokes « seeing at a distance, » the very promise the new medium advertised in the early twentieth century.

The verb is a back-formation: ~télévision~ arrived first, and ~téléviser~ was carved out of it to name the act of broadcasting images. Because it echoes ~télévision~ so closely, French keeps ~téléviser~ almost exclusively for that one medium, preferring ~diffuser~ for radio or the internet. The ~télé-~ element is enormously productive, heading a whole family that includes ~téléphone~, ~télégraphe~, ~télescope~, and the clipped ~télé~ for the set itself; the ~-viser~ side links it to ~vision~, ~visible~, ~viser~, and ~visage~, all rooted in the Latin verb of seeing.
en.témoigner:
A denominal verb from the noun ~témoin~ (“witness”), with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. ~Témoin~ descends from Latin ~testimōnium~ (“testimony, evidence”), formed on ~testis~ (“witness”). The etymology of ~testis~ is striking: it goes back to a Proto-Indo-European compound *~tristh₂s~, “a third one standing by” — from *~tréyes~ (“three”) and the root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). A witness, in this ancient image, is the impartial third party who stands beside two disputants. It is cognate with Italian ~testimone~ and Spanish ~testigo~, and with English ~testimony~ and ~testify~.

So to ~témoigner~ is to act as that standing-by third party — to attest, to bear witness. From the legal courtroom the sense broadened: a gift can ~témoigner~ gratitude, and symptoms ~témoignent~ a disease, the verb meaning “to show, to be evidence of.” The path from Latin ~testimōnium~ to French ~témoin~ ran through hard wear — the loss of the medial syllable and the softening of consonants typical of inherited words. From the same ~testis~ root come French ~témoignage~, ~testament~ (a document that “bears witness” to one's will), ~attester~, and ~protester~ (literally “to witness before, to declare publicly”).
en.téter: From Old French ~tetter~, a verb formed on the noun ~tette~ (“teat”) with the verb ending ~-er~. Literally, ~téter~ is “to use the teat,” that is, to suckle. The same noun gave French ~téton~ and ~tétine~, the latter now best known as the rubber teat of a baby's bottle or a pacifier.
en.unir:
From Latin ~unire~ (“to unite, to make one”), from ~unus~ (“one”), from Old Latin ~oinos~, from Proto-Italic *~oinos~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁óynos~ (“one, single”). The same root, through different branches, surfaces as English ~one~ and ~an~, German ~ein~, Greek ~oios~ (“alone”), and Old Irish ~óen~ — a rare case where the kinship is plain to the eye across the whole family.

The meaning has stayed remarkably stable: to ~unir~ is to make things one, to join them into a single whole. Latin ~unus~ poured into French as the bare numeral ~un~, and around it gathered a dense family: ~union~, ~unique~ (“being only one of its kind”), ~unité~, ~unanime~ (“of one mind,” with ~animus~), ~uniforme~ (“of one form”), and the prefixed verbs ~réunir~ (“to bring together again”) and ~désunir~ (“to un-unite”). The English borrowings ~unite~, ~union~, and ~unique~ travel the same path. From “one” as a number grew “one” as togetherness, so that ~les États-Unis~ — the United States — are, etymologically, states made into a single one.
en.urbaniser: Formed from the adjective ~urbain~ (“urban”) and the verb suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make, to turn into.” To ~urbaniser~ is thus to make a place urban. The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~urbānus~ (“of the city”), from ~urbs~ (“city”). Latin ~urbānus~ also meant “refined, polished,” the sense that survives in English ~urbane~.
en.user:
From Vulgar Latin *~ūsāre~, a frequentative formed on ~ūsus~, the past participle of Classical Latin ~ūtī~ (“to make use of, employ, enjoy”) — a verb of uncertain, much-debated Indo-European origin, with no securely reconstructed root. Cognate with Italian ~usare~ and Spanish ~usar~, and — through the same ~ūtī~ — with English ~use~, ~utility~, and ~usual~.

The frequentative shape (“to use repeatedly”) left its mark on the meaning.
