Where ~utiliser~ (a later, learned coinage) simply means “to employ,” the older inherited ~user~ leans toward the consequence of repeated use: things ~usées~ by handling are worn out, and ~s'user~ is to wear away — so ~user~ de patience is to draw it down, and ~usure~ names both wear-and-tear and, by a separate route, the “using” of money for interest. Hence French keeps a telling pair: one ~utilise~ a tool but ~use~ a pair of shoes. The same Latin ~ūtī~ seeded ~usage~, ~usager~, ~usuel~, ~ustensile~, and — with ~ab-~ (“away, amiss”) — ~abuser~ and ~abus~, the “using up” turned into misuse.
en.utiliser:
A late and learned formation, dating from the end of the 18th century, derived from the adjective ~utile~ (“useful”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to render”). Its model was Italian ~utilizzare~. The adjective ~utile~ itself comes from Latin ~ūtilis~ (“useful”), from the verb ~ūtī~ (“to use, to make use of”), whose past participle ~ūsus~ underlies a wide family of words. Cognate in formation with Italian ~utilizzare~ and Spanish ~utilizar~, and through the Latin verb with English ~use~ and ~utility~.

Because ~utiliser~ arrived so late, older French simply said ~user de~ or ~se servir de~; the newcomer's success was so complete that purists once denounced it as a needless neologism. Its ancestor ~ūtī~ — of uncertain deeper origin, with no secure PIE root — was nonetheless prolific in Latin. From the participle ~ūsus~ French draws ~user~, ~usage~, ~usine~ (originally a place put to “use”), ~ustensile~, and ~usure~ (“wear,” and also “usury”), while ~ūtilis~ yields ~utile~, ~utilité~, ~inutile~, and ~utilitaire~. A single notion of putting things to use thus spans tools, factories, wear, and worth.
en.vacciner: Formed in French from ~vaccin~ or ~vaccine~ + ~-er~, “to inoculate.” The noun comes from the learned Latin phrase ~variola vaccina~ (“cowpox”, literally “smallpox of the cow”), where ~vaccina~ is the feminine of ~vaccinus~ (“of a cow”), from ~vacca~ (“cow”). The name records the observation that people who worked with cows, and so caught cowpox, escaped human smallpox. ~Vaccine~ took the sense “inoculation” around 1800, and the masculine ~vaccin~ is attested in 1801, with the verb built on that noun.
en.vaincre:
From Old French ~veintre~ (also ~vencre~, ~veincre~), from Latin ~vincere~ (“to conquer, overcome”), from Proto-Italic *~winkō~, from a nasalized PIE *~wi-n-k-~, built with a nasal infix on the root *~weyk-~ (“to overcome, fight”). The Romance siblings are transparent: Italian ~vincere~ and Spanish ~vencer~ both mean “to defeat.” Through the Indo-European root, Latin ~vincere~ stands beside Gothic ~weihan~ (“to fight”). The modern infinitive ~vaincre~ owes its shape partly to the Latin first-person ~vincō~, which kept the nasal and the ~-c-~ that several Old French variants had worn away.

In Latin ~vincere~ already meant both “to win a battle” and “to prevail” in any contest, and French inherited the full range. One conjugates ~je vaincs~, ~il vainc~ — forms whose silent consonants preserve the Latin cluster on the page. From the same root come the participial noun ~vainqueur~ (“victor”) and, via the Latin supine ~victum~, the learned family ~victoire~, ~victime~, ~convaincre~, and ~invincible~. Note that English ~win~ is a false friend here: it descends from a different PIE root, *~wenh₁-~ (“to strive, desire”), not from *~weyk-~.
en.valider:
From Latin ~validāre~ (“to make strong, to strengthen, to confirm”), built on the adjective ~validus~ (“strong, robust, effective”), which derives from the verb ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”) with the suffix ~-idus~. ~Valēre~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~walēō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). Italian ~validare~ and Spanish ~validar~ share the same Latin source, and the root surfaces in English ~valid~ and ~value~, and even in the name ~Valerie~.

The earliest sense was bodily: a ~validus~ man was hale and vigorous, and to ~validāre~ was to fortify. From physical strength the meaning slid toward the strength of a thing's standing — its soundness, its force in law or logic. To ~valider~ today is to make something hold good: to confirm a ticket, ratify a decision, or certify a result as sound. The same ~valēre~ gave French the everyday ~valoir~ (“to be worth”), and the wider root spread into ~valeur~, ~valable~, ~valeureux~, ~prévaloir~, ~équivaloir~, and ~convalescence~, the last recalling the original sense of returning strength.
en.valoir:
From Latin ~valere~ (“to be strong, be well, be worth”), from Proto-Italic *~walēō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). The kernel of meaning is bodily strength: the Latin farewell ~vale~ was a wish of “stay strong, keep well.” Through this root ~valoir~ is cognate with English ~wield~ (to handle with power) and, by borrowing from the same Latin stem, with English ~value~ and ~valour~.

The slide from “being strong” to “being worth” is the heart of the word: what is robust and sound is what has worth, and so ~valere~ moved from health to value. French kept both edges — se porter bien lingers in ~valétudinaire~, while the worth-sense dominates ~valoir~ today, as in ~cela vaut la peine~ (“that is worth the trouble”) and ~vaille que vaille~ (“come what may”). The verb is also notably irregular, with the present ~je vaux~ and the future ~je vaudrai~ preserving old stem shifts. From the same *~h₂welh₁-~ root flow a rich French family of strength and worth: ~valeur~, ~valable~, ~valide~, ~évaluer~, ~prévaloir~, ~équivalent~, and ~polyvalent~.
en.valoriser:
A modern French coinage (around 1925), formed from ~valeur~ (“value, worth”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~. ~Valeur~ comes from Latin ~valor~, the noun of the verb ~valēre~ (“to be strong, be well, be worth”), from Proto-Italic *~walēō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). That root is robust across the family: it gives English ~wield~, German ~walten~ (“to govern”), and — through Latin ~valēre~ — English ~value~, ~valiant~, and ~valid~.

The primitive idea is strength that translates into worth: to be strong is to be worth something. French ~valoriser~ is the deliberate, almost economic act of making that worth visible — to develop, enhance, or capitalise on something so its value is realised. One ~valorise~ a region's heritage, a waste product, an employee's skills. Being twentieth-century and built on a productive pattern, it spawned a tidy paradigm: ~valorisation~, ~dévaloriser~ and ~dévalorisation~, ~revaloriser~ and ~survaloriser~. Beside them stand older heirs of the same root — ~valoir~ (“to be worth”), ~valeur~, ~valable~ (“valid”), and ~vaillant~ (“valiant”) — all turning on the link between strength and worth.
en.vanter:
From Old French ~vanter~, descended from Late or Vulgar Latin ~vānitāre~. The sources differ on its immediate parent: French Wiktionary treats ~vānitāre~ as a verb drawn from the noun ~vānitās~ (“vanity”), while English Wiktionary says it goes back to Latin ~vānus~ (“empty”) or to ~vānitās~. Either way, the root idea is emptiness, and ~vānus~ is also the source of French ~vain~. Italian ~vantare~ is the sibling form, and English ~vaunt~ is a borrowing from the same French verb.

The reflexive ~se vanter~ means “to boast.” According to French Wiktionary, the transitive use of ~vanter~ (to praise someone or something) appears only in 1580. Today that transitive use is common in the phrase ~vanter les mérites de~ (“to extol the merits of”), and in advertising, where products are praised by those who sell them. The family includes ~vantard~ (“braggart”), ~vanterie~ (“boasting”), ~vanité~ and ~vain~, all pointing back to the Latin idea of the hollow and the empty.
en.varier:
From Latin ~variare~ (“to change, to make different, to diversify”), a verb built on the adjective ~varius~ (“varied, spotted, of different colors”). ~varius~ is perhaps related to ~varus~ (“bent, knock-kneed”), with a notion of things turned different ways; its deeper Proto-Indo-European origin is uncertain and best left unstated. Through ~variare~ the French verb is cognate with Italian ~variare~, Spanish ~variar~, and English ~vary~ and ~various~.

The core idea was diversity of appearance — ~varius~ first described things speckled or many-colored, like a dappled animal — and ~variare~ meant to make such diversity, to alter. French ~varier~ kept both the transitive “to vary, to diversify” and the intransitive “to differ, to change.” A memorable kinsman is ~varicelle~ (“chickenpox”), so named for its spots, a faint diminutive echo of the “speckled” sense; the medical ~varice~ (“varicose vein”), however, belongs to a separate Latin word. From ~varius~ French keeps ~varié~, ~variété~, ~variation~, ~variable~, and ~variante~ — a whole vocabulary of change grown from an adjective that first meant simply “of more than one color.”
en.veiller:
From Latin ~vigilāre~ (“to stay awake, to keep watch”), itself derived from the classical Latin adjective ~vigil~ (“awake, alert, watchful”). The root traces to Proto-Indo-European *~weǵ-~ (“to be strong, lively, awake”). From this same root spring a remarkable set of English cognates: ~wake~, ~watch~, ~vigour~, and even ~vegetable~ (originally “lively, growing”). Italian ~vegliare~ and Spanish ~velar~ are the Romance siblings of ~veiller~.

The verb has always hovered around the idea of holding off sleep. To ~veiller~ is to stay up late, but also to sit up with someone — at a bedside, or beside the dead in a ~veillée funèbre~ (“wake”) — and, more broadly, to keep watch and look after. From the notion of watchfulness comes the construction ~veiller à~ (“to see to, to take care that”) and ~veiller sur~ (“to watch over, to protect”). The same Latin family yields a rich crop of French words: ~vigile~ (“the eve of a feast,” and now a “security guard”), ~vigilant~ and ~vigilance~, ~réveiller~ (“to wake up,” literally “to watch again”), ~surveiller~ (“to supervise, to watch over”), and the noun ~veille~ (“the day before; wakefulness”).
en.vendre:
From Latin ~vendere~ (“to sell, to trade, to praise”), a contraction of ~vēnum dare~ (“to give for sale”) — that is, ~vēnum~ (“sale, that which is for sale”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”). ~Vēnum~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~wesnom~ to PIE *~wes-~ (“to buy, to sell”), the same root behind Sanskrit ~vasna~ (“price”) and Ancient Greek ~ônos~ (“price”); ~dare~ descends from PIE *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~vendere~ and Spanish ~vender~.

The Romans built their word for selling out of two ideas welded together: a thing offered up, ~vēnum~, and the act of handing it over, ~dare~. Latin let the phrase fuse into one verb, and French inherited it whole, so that a sale is etymologically a giving. The buyer's side of the bargain left its own trace: from the same root, through ~vēnum~, French keeps ~vénal~ (“venal, for sale”), the adjective for whatever can be bought, a conscience included. The ~dare~ half seeded a vast family too — ~donner~, ~don~, ~date~, and the learned ~dation~ — while ~vendre~ itself produced ~vente~ (“sale”) and ~vendeur~ (“seller”).
en.venger:
French ~venger~ comes from Old French ~vengier~, attested around 980, which goes back to Latin ~vindicāre~. In Latin the verb meant “to lay claim to, to demand justice,” and then “to avenge,” the legal and the personal sense running side by side. Middle French ~venger~ is the intermediate form. The Latin verb has sisters across the Romance languages, among them Italian ~vendicare~ and Spanish ~vengar~, and English holds two later descendants: ~vindicate~, taken straight from Latin, and ~avenge~, which entered through Old French.

The move from claiming a right to taking revenge is the story of the word. ~Vindicāre~ began in the law courts, where one claimed what was due, and the French verb kept only the avenging half. Related words multiplied: ~vengeance~, ~vengeur~, and ~revanche~, from the verb ~revenger~, which now serves in sport and politics for any return match. Learned vocabulary kept the legal Latin side, for example ~vindicte~, as in the phrase ~vindicte publique~ (“public prosecution”) and the adjective ~vindicatif~. French thus holds the popular verb and the learned family of one Latin word apart, each with a different shade of justice.
en.venir:
From Old French ~venir~, from Latin ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~, from PIE *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”). Cognate with Italian ~venire~, Spanish ~venir~, and Catalan ~venir~ or ~vindre~; through the same PIE root — but down the Germanic line, where *~gʷ-~ became *~kw-~ — come English ~come~, German ~kommen~, and Dutch ~komen~. French ~venir~ and English ~come~ are thus distant cousins despite sounding nothing alike.

The Latin verb's awkward conjugation made for a famously irregular French one: the future stem buckled and shifted, ~venirát~ giving ~venrat~, then ~vendra~, then the modern ~viendra~, an intrusive ~-d-~ wedging itself between ~n~ and ~r~. The root spread widely through Latin compounds, and French inherited a great cluster of them: ~devenir~, ~revenir~, ~prévenir~, ~convenir~, ~parvenir~, ~survenir~, and ~intervenir~. Their Latinate doublets supply ~avènement~, ~convention~, ~revenu~, and ~aventure~ — literally “what is about to come,” ~adventūra~. From a single verb of motion, French built much of its vocabulary of arrival, agreement, prevention, and chance.
en.venter: Formed from ~vent~ (“wind”) and the ending ~-er~. The verb is literally “to wind” and is used impersonally of the weather, as in il vente, “it is windy.” ~Vent~ passed through Middle and Old French from Latin ~ventus~, from Proto-Italic *~wentos~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂weh₁-~ (“to blow”). The same root gave English ~wind~ and German ~Wind~, and Latin ~ventus~ lives on in Italian ~vento~ and Spanish ~viento~. French words built on ~vent~ include ~venteux~ and ~éventail~.
en.ventiler:
Borrowed from Latin ~ventilāre~ (“to toss in the air, to winnow, to fan”), a verb built on ~ventus~ (“wind”). ~Ventus~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂weh₁-~ (“to blow”), which is also the source of English ~wind~ and German ~Wind~. Italian ~ventilare~ and Spanish ~ventilar~ are the same borrowing, and English ~ventilate~ arrived through the same Latin verb.

The first picture is farming: to ~ventilāre~ grain was to toss it in the breeze so the chaff blew away. From there Latin extended the verb to fanning, cooling and stirring up a fire, and even to scattering or divulging something. French uses the airing sense for rooms and buildings, but it also has a quite different modern meaning, to break a sum down and share it among accounts or categories. That sense is probably a figurative extension of the winnowing image of sorting and separating, though the sources do not spell out the path. Relatives include ~vent~, ~ventilateur~, ~éventer~ (“to fan, to expose to the air”) and ~éventail~ (“fan”).
en.verrouiller: Formed in French from ~verrou~ (“bolt”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so to ~verrouiller~ is to fasten with a bolt. The noun ~verrou~ comes from Old French ~veroil~, from a Latin form of ~veruculum~, a diminutive of ~verū~ (“spit, skewer”). The Wiktionaries differ slightly on the exact Latin shape, but both agree on the picture: a bolt is a slim rod, like a small skewer, slid across a door. The verb is used literally for locks and figuratively, for example of a political system or a negotiation that is closed off.
en.verser:
From Old French ~verser~, from Late Latin *~versāre~, a variant of ~versārī~, the frequentative of Latin ~vertere~ (“to turn”). A frequentative names a repeated or intensive action, so ~versāre~ is “to keep turning, to turn over and over.” ~Vertere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to turn, to bend”). Cognate with Italian ~versare~ and Spanish ~verter~, and — through ~vertere~ — with English ~verse~ and ~convert~.

The thread tying the modern senses together is that founding idea of turning. To pour is to tip a vessel and turn its contents out; to capsize (~se verser~, said of a cart or a boat) is to be turned right over; and the financial sense, “to pay in, to deposit,” imagines money being turned out onto the counter — which is why a French salary is ~versé~ and a payment is a ~versement~. English ~verse~ preserves the oldest picture of all: the ploughman ~turning~ at the furrow's end to start the next line, the line of poetry being a “turning.” The same root *~wer-~ feeds a wide French family — ~version~, ~vers~, ~envers~, ~renverser~, ~déverser~, ~convertir~, and ~divers~ — all of them, somewhere, a turn.
en.vibrer: Borrowed from Latin ~vibrāre~, “to shake, to brandish, to quiver.” In Latin the verb could describe a spear being brandished or hurled, a flickering flame or a trembling voice. French kept the idea of rapid back-and-forth motion, first for physical objects such as strings, then for sound and, figuratively, for emotion: to ~vibrer~ is to be stirred, to resonate with a feeling. Derived words include ~vibration~, ~vibrant~ and ~vibreur~. Italian ~vibrare~ and English ~vibrate~ are its relatives; the origin of the Latin verb itself is uncertain, so none is assigned here.
en.vider:
Derived from Old French ~vuidier~, ~voider~, from the adjective ~vuit~ / ~vuide~ (“empty”), modern French ~vide~. ~vide~ goes back through Vulgar Latin *~vocitus~ to the family of Latin ~vacuus~ (“empty”) and ~vacāre~ (“to be empty, vacant”), from Proto-Italic *~wakos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁weh₂-~ (“to lack, be empty”). The modern form arose by generalizing the feminine ~vuide~ and reducing ~vui-~ to ~vi-~.

That PIE root *~h₁weh₂-~ is unexpectedly fertile. Beyond the ~vacuus~ branch — which gives French ~vide~, ~vacant~, ~vacances~, ~évacuer~, and English ~vacant~, ~vacuum~, ~void~ — the same root produced Latin ~vānus~ (“empty”), hence English ~vain~, and, through Germanic, English ~want~ and ~wane~. The verb's range in French is wide and vivid: one can ~vider~ a glass, ~vider~ a room of people, or ~vider~ a fish (gut it) — and, colloquially, be ~vidé~, “wiped out, drained.” In every case the underlying image is the ancient one: to make empty.
en.vieillir: Formed in French from the adjective ~vieil~ (the form of ~vieux~ before a vowel, “old”) plus the verbal ending ~-ir~, with the sense “to become old.” The adjective comes from Old French ~viel~, itself from Latin ~vetulus~, a diminutive of ~vetus~ (“old”). The ~-ir~ ending is the second-conjugation ending, and it is the usual one for verbs meaning “to become” plus an adjective, like ~grandir~ or ~grossir~. The Romance neighbors built the same idea with a prefix: Catalan ~envellir~, Spanish ~envejecer~ and Portuguese ~envelhecer~.
en.violer:
From Latin ~violāre~ (“to treat with force, to profane, to outrage”), in French by about 1100. The Latin verb is traditionally explained as a derivative of ~vīs~ (“force, violence”); the etymologist De Vaan prefers to reconstruct an intermediate adjective *~weyh₁-elos~ — but on either account the base is the PIE root *~weyh₁-~ (“to rush at, to pursue”), which yielded ~vīs~ itself through *~wéyh₁s~ and is cognate with Greek ~ἴς~ (“sinew, strength”) and Sanskrit ~váyas~ (“vigor”). Cognate with Italian ~violare~ and Spanish ~violar~; English ~violate~ is the same Latin verb in scholarly dress.

The French senses unfolded in a revealing order. In the Chanson de Roland, around 1100, what one violated was a sanctuary: the first attested meaning is “to break into and profane a sacred or protected place.” Around 1155 came “to transgress” — laws, oaths, treaties; only around 1170 does the language record the verb applied to the rape of a woman. All three senses flow from the single Latin idea of ~vīs~ — force applied where right forbids it — and all three remain alive: one still violates borders, tombs, secrets and ceasefires. The family stayed close and dark: ~viol~, ~violence~, ~violent~, ~violation~, ~inviolable~. Beware, though, of two innocent lookalikes: ~violette~ goes back to the Latin flower name ~viola~, and ~violon~ to the medieval fiddle ~viole~ — neither the violet nor the violin owes anything to violence.
en.virer:
The origin of ~virer~ is debated. The account both Wiktionaries lead with is that it comes from Late (Vulgar) Latin *~virāre~ (“to turn, to whirl”), probably an alteration of Latin ~vibrāre~ (“to shake, to brandish”), which would make ~virer~ a doublet of ~vibrer~. French Wiktionary adds that the alteration came under the influence of ~librāre~ (“to hurl with a whirling motion”) and ~gȳrāre~ (“to turn”). English Wiktionary mentions as a lesser possibility a form altered from the Greek-derived Latin verb for turning in circles. It also records a Celtic proposal: Gaulish *~viru~ (“to deviate, to veer off”), derived from ~viros~ (“round, crooked”). The Romance relatives are Italian ~virare~ and Spanish ~virar~.

Whatever its source, the verb was first about turning. A ship or a car ~vire~, which gave ~virage~ (“a bend”), and one speaks of ~virer de bord~ (“to tack, to change course”). From a change of direction came a change of state, so something can ~virer au rouge~ (“to turn red”) or ~virer à l'aigre~ (“to turn sour”), and a sudden reversal of opinion is a ~revirement~. The verb is also used for transferring money between accounts and, colloquially, for dismissing someone, but the sources do not say how those uses developed. If the favored account is right, ~virer~ is a distant cousin of ~vibrer~, so to turn and to tremble may share a Latin ancestor.
en.viser:
From Latin ~vīsāre~, a frequentative of ~vīsere~ (“to look at attentively, to go to see”), itself an intensive of ~vidēre~ (“to see”). ~Vidēre~ descends from PIE *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), one of the most fertile roots in the family. Through its Germanic branch the same root gave English ~wit~ and ~wise~, and through Latin ~vīsiō~ it gave ~vision~; the Greek branch yielded ~idéa~. Cognate Romance reflexes include Italian ~visare~ and Spanish ~avisar~.

The progression of sense is tidy: from simply seeing, to looking hard at one thing, to fixing one's eye and weapon upon a target — hence the modern ~viser~ (“to aim at”) and its figurative “to aim for, to have designs on.” A separate, later ~viser~, “to stamp or endorse,” was coined in the seventeenth century from the noun ~visa~ (Latin ~vīsa~, “things seen, verified”), the official's mark that a document had been examined; the travel ~visa~ is the same word. From the rich *~weyd-~ stock French also keeps ~voir~, ~vue~, ~vision~, ~évident~, and ~revoir~, every one of them a way of seeing.
en.visionner: Formed from ~vision~ plus the first-conjugation ending ~-er~, with the sense “to view, to watch closely,” especially a film, a recording or a document, often in a technical or professional setting. The noun ~vision~ is a learned borrowing, through Old and Middle French, from Latin ~vīsiō~ (“sight, appearance”), built on ~vīsus~, the past participle of ~vidēre~ (“to see”). So the verb is a recent practical word resting on one of the oldest Latin verbs of sight.
en.visiter:
From Latin ~visito~ (“to go to see, to visit often”), a frequentative of ~video~ (“to see”), the iterative form built on the participial stem ~vis-~. ~video~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), one of the most productive roots in the family. Through that root ~visiter~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~eîdon~ (“I saw”) and ~oîda~ (“I know”), with Sanskrit ~veda~ (“knowledge”), and with English ~wit~ and ~wise~, where the sense of seeing has shifted entirely to knowing.

The frequentative ~visito~ already implied not a single glance but repeated, attentive looking — the kind of seeing one does when inspecting, calling on, or watching over someone. That nuance survives: a doctor still ~visite~ patients, an inspector ~visite~ a site, and one ~visite~ a city by going round it thoroughly. The same root *~weyd-~ underlies a remarkable spread of French vocabulary: ~voir~ itself, ~vision~, ~visage~, ~visite~, ~visible~, ~évident~, ~revue~, and — through the knowing branch — words like ~idée~ and ~histoire~, both ultimately Greek relatives. Few roots have given French so many ways to talk about looking and learning.
en.visser: In its main sense, “to fasten with a screw,” ~visser~ is formed from the noun ~vis~ (“screw”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~vis~ comes from Latin ~vītis~ (“vine, tendril”), which French Wiktionary links to ~viēre~ (“to twist”): the screw took its name from the spiral of a vine's tendril. A second, unrelated ~visser~ is slang. It is a verlan form of ~servir~ (“to serve”), made by reversing the syllables.
en.visualiser:
Borrowed in 1887 from English ~to visualise~, itself formed on the Latin-derived adjective ~visual~, from Late Latin ~visuālis~, from Latin ~vīsus~ (“sight”), the past participle of ~vidēre~ (“to see”). ~Vidēre~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~widēō~ to Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see; to know”). That double meaning — seeing as knowing — runs through the cognates: English ~wit~ and ~wise~, German ~wissen~ (“to know”), Ancient Greek ~oîda~ (“I know,” literally “I have seen”) and ~idéā~, and Sanskrit ~véda~ (“knowledge”).

The word entered French as a late-19th-century import, riding the era's interest in mental imagery and, soon after, photographic and scientific display. Where older French had ~voir~ and ~vision~ for ordinary seeing, ~visualiser~ specialized in “to form a mental picture of” and later “to render visible, to display” — a screen ~visualise~ data. From the same *~weyd-~ root French holds ~voir~, ~vision~, ~visible~, ~vue~, ~aviser~, ~prévoir~, and ~évident~, while the Greek branch gave ~idée~ and ~idole~ — all, at bottom, things seen.
en.vitrer: ~Vitrer~ is formed from the noun ~vitre~ (“window pane”) and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to fit with glass.” ~Vitre~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~vitrum~ (“glass”), and so a doublet of the inherited ~verre~, which took the ordinary phonetic road from the same Latin word. Spanish ~vidrio~ and Catalan ~vidre~ are related forms. Where ~verre~ names the material and the drinking vessel, ~vitre~ keeps to the glazed surface of a window, and ~vitrer~ is the act of putting that glass in place.
en.vivre:
French ~vivre~ comes straight from Latin ~vīvere~ (“to live”), the present infinitive of ~vīvō~, inherited through Old French ~vivre~ with almost no change of shape. Behind the Latin lies Proto-Italic *~gʷīwō~ and, beyond it, Proto-Indo-European *~gʷíh₃weti~ (“to live, to be alive”). The cognates trace life across the whole family: Greek ~bíos~ (“life,” as in ~biology~), Sanskrit ~jīvati~ (“he lives”), Old Church Slavonic ~žiti~, and — strikingly — English ~quick~, whose old meaning was “alive,” preserved in the phrase “the quick and the dead.”

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: to be alive, and by extension to dwell, to subsist, to experience. French keeps both the bare existential sense and a worldlier one in ~savoir-vivre~ (“good manners,” literally knowing how to live). The root threw off a rich crop of French words: ~vie~ (“life”), ~vif~ (“lively, sharp”), ~vivace~ and ~vivant~, ~survivre~ (“to survive,” to out-live), ~revivre~, ~convive~ (a fellow liver, hence a dinner guest), and the borrowed cheer ~vive !~ (“long live!”). Through the Greek cousin ~bíos~ the same idea returns in ~biologie~, ~microbe~, and ~amphibie~ — so that the science of life and the act of living spring from one ancient verb.
en.voiler:
Derived from the French noun ~voile~ (“veil”), itself from Latin ~vēlum~ (“sail, cloth, curtain”). An earlier form ~veler~ is attested in the twelfth century in the religious sense “to make someone take the veil,” the modern ~voiler~ following around 1380. The origin of Latin ~vēlum~ is debated. The favored account derives it, like its diminutive ~vexillum~ (“banner”), from a Proto-Italic *~wekslom~ and the PIE root *~weg-~ (“to weave, bind”), with which English ~wick~ is connected as a cognate; a rival proposal linking it to *~weǵʰ-~ (“to ride, convey”) is generally judged less attractive.

From the cloth itself, ~voiler~ came to mean to drape, to cover, and so to hide or dim — a sky ~voilé~ is clouded, a voice ~voilée~ is muffled. A separate technical sense, “to warp” (as a bicycle wheel goes out of true), grew from the same image of a flat surface bending like billowing fabric. The root yields ~voile~, ~voilage~, ~dévoiler~ (“to unveil, reveal”) and ~voilette~ (a small hat-veil).
en.voir:
From Old French ~veoir~, earlier ~vedeir~ and ~veder~ (c. 980), from Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see, to perceive, to witness”), the infinitive of ~videō~. The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). Through that root ~voir~ is cognate with Italian ~vedere~ and Spanish ~ver~, and — by the same ancient stem — with English ~wit~ and ~wise~, German ~wissen~ (“to know”), and Greek ~oîda~ (“I know,” literally “I have seen”).

The pairing of seeing and knowing is no accident: across Indo-European languages, *~weyd-~ slid easily from “to perceive with the eye” to “to understand,” a metaphor French still uses when one says ~je vois~ to mean “I understand.” The intervocalic ~d~ of ~vidēre~ softened and then vanished as the word passed through Old French, leaving the smooth modern ~voir~. The root has seeded a large family in French: ~vue~ (“sight”), ~vision~, ~voyant~ (“seer, clairvoyant”), ~évident~ (“evident,” literally “seen out”), ~revoir~, ~prévoir~ (“to foresee”), and ~entrevoir~ (“to glimpse”). The learned doublet ~vidéo~, borrowed back from Latin in the twentieth century, restores the very ~d~ that ordinary speech had worn away centuries before.
en.voler:
From Latin ~volāre~ (“to fly”), attested in Old French as early as 881. The deeper origin is uncertain; De Vaan connects it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷelH-~ (“to throw, to reach”), the flying sense perhaps developing from “to fling (the wings).” It is cognate with Italian ~volare~, Spanish ~volar~, and Portuguese ~voar~, all keeping the plain meaning “to fly.”

French is unusual in that this same verb means both “to fly” and “to steal” — and the bridge between them is falconry. A trained falcon ~vole~, taking its quarry on the wing; the bird seizes the prey in mid-flight. The transitive sense “to seize as a bird of prey does” specialized into “to take what is not yours,” and by the seventeenth century ~voler~ in the sense “to steal” had supplanted the older ~rober~ (“to rob by force,” itself from Frankish *~raubōn~) and ~embler~ (“to steal by stealth”). So the thief and the flier share one verb, joined by the hawk. From ~volāre~ descend French ~vol~ (which means both “a flight” and “a theft”), ~voleur~ (“thief”), ~volée~, ~s'envoler~, and ~volaille~ (“poultry,” the flying farmyard).
en.vomir:
Inherited from Old French ~vomir~, from Vulgar Latin *~vomīre~, the popular form of Classical Latin ~vomĕre~. French Wiktionary traces the Latin verb to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wem-~ (“to vomit”). The same root is found in Ancient Greek ~ἐμέω~ (~eméō~, “to vomit”) and in Sanskrit ~vamati~, which has the same meaning. The Vulgar Latin form differs from the classical one in its long ~ī~ against the short ~ĕ~, which shows the verb passing to a different conjugation on its way into French.

The three ancient languages therefore each keep a form of one old word for the same bodily act, and the meaning of the French verb is the same as that of its Latin ancestor. The evidence records no change of sense along the way. The reconstructed root *~wem-~ is the point of connection: it is not a word anyone wrote down but the shape that Latin, Greek and Sanskrit forms together require. French ~vomir~ is thus one modern outcome of a very old verb, reaching French through Old French and spoken Latin rather than being formed in French.
en.voter:
A late arrival in French, ~voter~ was borrowed in the eighteenth century from English ~vote~. The English word goes back to Latin ~votum~ (“a vow, a solemn pledge, a prayer”), the noun from ~vovēre~ (“to vow, to promise solemnly”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁wegʷʰ-~ (“to promise, to praise solemnly”). Through that root it is cognate with Greek ~eúkhomai~ (“to pray, to vow”) and Sanskrit ~vāghát~ (“one who makes a vow”). English may have built its verb directly on ~votum~ or taken it from Medieval Latin ~votare~.

The path from “vow” to “ballot” runs through religion and parliament: a ~votum~ was an offering pledged to a god, and to vote was first to declare one's solemn wish — the modern ballot is, etymologically, a vow of preference. Because French acquired the word ready-made from English, it sits a little apart from its own learned cousins drawn straight from ~votum~: ~vœu~ (the inherited descendant, “a wish, a vow”), ~votif~ (“votive”), and ~dévot~ and ~dévotion~, where the original sense of solemn pledging to the divine still rings clearly.
en.vouer:
The origin of ~vouer~ is given in more than one way. One account derives it from Old French ~voer~, from Late Latin ~vōtāre~, a verb made from the noun ~vōtum~ (“a vow, a wish”). French Wiktionary instead cites the Latin verb ~voveō~ (“to vow, to promise, to wish”). A further possibility is that French simply formed it from ~vœu~ + ~-er~. In every version the root idea is a solemn promise.

In modern French the verb means “to dedicate, to devote,” as in devoting one's life to something, and a project that seems certain to fail is called ~voué~ à l'échec. Its relatives include ~vœu~, ~dévouer~, ~dévot~ and ~votif~. The verb ~voter~ is a doublet: it reached French from English ~vote~, which came from the same Latin ~vōtum~. Italian ~votare~ and Spanish and Portuguese ~votar~ are comparable verbs.
en.vouloir:
From Old French ~voloir~, from Vulgar Latin *~volēre~, a reshaping of the irregular Classical Latin ~velle~ (present ~volō~, “I want”), from Proto-Italic *~welō~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ (“to choose, to want”). Speakers smoothed the wildly irregular ~velle~ into a regular *~volēre~ built on the stem ~vol-~, already visible in the 8th-century attestation ~si voles~. Cognate with Italian ~volere~ and Romanian ~vrea~; through the same root, by the Germanic line, come English ~will~ and German ~wollen~. Spanish, tellingly, abandoned this verb for ~querer~.

The PIE root *~welh₁-~ meant “to choose” as much as “to want,” and that pairing of desire and selection runs through its descendants — to will something is to single it out. The French verb kept its irregularity to the end, with the curious imperative ~veuille~ and ~veuillez~ used in polite formulas (~veuillez agréer~). Modern French relatives include ~volonté~ (“will”), ~volontaire~ (“voluntary”), ~bienveillant~ and ~malveillant~ (“well-” and “ill-wishing”), and ~velléité~ — a faint, half-formed wish, from the Latin ~velleitās~. The same root even reaches ~voluptas~, “pleasure,” linking what one wants to what one enjoys.
en.voyager:
Denominal from the noun ~voyage~, attested in Old French as ~voiage~, ~viage~, and ~veiage~. The noun descends from Latin ~viaticum~ (“provisions or money for a journey”), the neuter of the adjective ~viaticus~ (“of the road”), from ~via~ (“road, way”). The PIE root behind ~via~ is disputed: it is most often referred to *~weyh₁-~ (“to pursue, drive”), with Lithuanian ~vyti~ (“to chase”) as a relative, while an older account tying it to *~weǵʰ-~ (“to go, convey”) — the root of English ~way~ and German ~Weg~ — is rejected by De Vaan. English ~voyage~ is a borrowing of the same Old French word, and a doublet of the learned ~viaticum~.

The semantic drift is vivid: ~viaticum~ first named the money and supplies you packed for the road, then the journey those provisions paid for, and finally any travel at all. The Church preserved the oldest, most literal sense — ~viatique~ in French still means the Eucharist given to the dying, food for the last journey. From ~via~ also come French ~voie~, ~dévier~, ~trivial~ (from ~trivium~, “a place where three roads meet”), and ~convoyer~. To travel, in this etymology, is simply to spend what you set aside for the road.
en.véhiculer: ~Véhiculer~ was formed in French from the noun ~véhicule~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to carry, to convey.” The noun is borrowed from Latin ~vehiculum~ (“means of transport, carriage, cart”), which is built on the Latin verb ~vehere~ (“to carry”). The meaning is first literal, transporting people or goods in a vehicle. It is extended to things that travel without a body: to ~véhiculer~ an idea, an image or a rumor is to act as the vehicle that carries it from one mind to another.
en.vénérer:
French ~vénérer~ is a borrowing from Latin ~venerārī~ (“to revere, to worship”). French Wiktionary derives the Latin verb from the genitive ~Veneris~ of ~Venus~. In Latin, ~venus~ was first a common noun meaning “charm, desire, love” before it named the goddess, and it is traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wenh₁-~ (“to desire, to strive for”), which also yields English ~wish~ and ~win~. The original sense of ~venerārī~ was therefore to seek the favor of a deity, to court the goodwill of a god.

In Latin the verb was a religious one: one ~veneratur~ the gods with prayers and offerings. It broadened to reverence for anyone worthy of deep respect, and French kept that range: ~vénérer~ a saint, a teacher, a memory. In modern speech it is often used with a hint of exaggeration, for a devotion that is more enthusiasm than worship. Related French words include ~vénération~ and ~vénérable~ and, from the same ~Venus~, ~vénérien~ (“venereal”) and ~vendredi~, the day of ~Veneris~.
en.vérifier:
From Medieval Latin ~verificare~ (“to make true, to prove true”), a compound of ~verus~ (“true”) and ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). Latin ~verus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wēros~ and Proto-Indo-European *~weh₁ros~ (“true, trustworthy”). The same root gave German ~wahr~ (“true”) and English ~very~ (originally “true,” as in “the very man”), while the Italian and Spanish ~verificare~/~verificar~ are direct parallels.

The word is transparent once unpacked: to verify is, etymologically, “to make-true,” to establish that a thing is ~verus~. French inherited it as a learned term, keeping the bookish ~-ifier~ ending from ~facere~ found in a long series of verbs (~modifier~, ~clarifier~, ~justifier~). From the same ~verus~ comes a substantial family: ~vrai~ (the inherited, worn-down form of ~verus~), ~vérité~, ~véritable~, ~vraisemblable~, ~véridique~, and ~vérifiable~. Curiously, the everyday adverb ~voire~ (“indeed, even”) also descends from ~verus~ — a fossil of the Latin for “truly.” So ~vérifier~ and ~vrai~ are doublets of a kind, the learned and the popular reflexes of one Latin word for truth.
en.vêtir:
From Old French ~vestir~, inherited from Latin ~vestīre~ (“to clothe, to dress”), a verb built on the noun ~vestis~ (“garment, clothing”). Latin ~vestis~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wes-~ (“to clothe”), which also yields English ~wear~ through Germanic. The verb has close relatives across the Romance languages: Italian ~vestire~ and Spanish ~vestir~ both preserve the Latin shape. French alone shows the old ~s~ in a different way, as the circumflex of ~vêtir~. In Old French the ~s~ was still pronounced before the ~t~, then fell silent, and the accent mark was left behind as a memorial.

The idea of putting on clothes spread in two directions. One path led to prestige: ~revêtir~ meant to dress again, then to clothe someone with a dignity, which is why a document is ~revêtu~ of a signature or a seal. The Latin compound ~investīre~ (“to clothe in, to confer an office by robing”) gave ~investir~, whose financial meaning came later. Another path led to the wardrobe itself. ~Vêtement~ is the garment, ~dévêtir~ undresses, and the Latin noun ~vestis~ lives on as ~veste~, ~vestiaire~ and ~travestir~, literally “to dress across,” that is, in the clothes of another. English borrowed ~vest~, ~invest~, ~divest~ and ~travesty~ from the same source.
en.zapper: Borrowed from English ~zap~, with the French ending ~-er~. The English word began as an imitative sound of a sudden blow or shot, then came to mean “to destroy, to hit,” and, with the arrival of the television remote control, “to switch rapidly between channels.” French took over the channel-surfing sense first, and then widened it to the figurative uses listed in the app: to skip over something, to drop a subject, to forget. The noun ~zapping~ belongs to the same family and was borrowed with it.
en.éblouir:
French ~éblouir~ comes from Old French ~esbloir~ and ~esbleuir~ (“to dazzle”). English Wiktionary traces these to a Vulgar Latin *~exblaudō~, made of ~ex-~ and *~blaudō~ (“to overwhelm, to make weak”), a verb taken from Frankish *~blōthijan~. That Frankish verb comes from Proto-Germanic *~blauþijaną~ (“to make weak, soften”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰlaw-~ (“weak, timid”). Germanic cousins include Old High German ~blōdi~ (“feeble”), Old English ~blēaþ~ (“timid, gentle”) and Danish ~blød~ (“soft”). The Latin step is attested only by reconstruction.

The path from weakness to dazzle is plausible, since a blinding light overpowers the sight, though the sources do not spell out the development. French then extended the verb from the eyes to the mind, to impress or amaze, and ~éblouissant~ now praises brilliance of any kind. German ~blöde~, from the same family as ~blōdi~, has moved in the other direction: it now means “silly” or “stupid,” a long way from soft or weak. Beyond the French family ~éblouissement~, ~éblouissant~, the verb has no close French relatives.
en.écarter:
The origin of ~écarter~ is debated. French Wiktionary derives the verb of separation from a Latin *~exquartāre~, built on ~quartus~ (“fourth, quarter”) — to ~écarter~ being, on this view, originally to quarter or divide; this ~quartus~ traces back through ~quattuor~ (“four”) to PIE *~kʷetwóres~. The TLFi, however, resists that account, and a distinct ~écarter~ of the card table — “to discard” — is more securely analyzed as ~é-~ + ~carte~ (“card”) + ~-er~, attested from 1611. The two senses are best kept apart rather than forced into one chain.

Whatever the precise root, the lived meaning is to push apart, to set aside, to keep at a distance — ~écarter~ les bras (to spread the arms), ~écarter~ un danger, ~écarter~ une hypothèse. The past participle ~écarté~ names something remote or out of the way. From the same field come ~écart~ (“gap, deviation”), ~écartement~ (“spacing”) and the noun ~écarté~ for the old card game played by discarding.
en.échanger:
A French compound: the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, here intensive) joined to ~changer~ (“to change”). The base ~changer~ comes from Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to barter, to exchange”), a verb of Gaulish origin, from Proto-Celtic *~kambos~ (“crooked, bent”) and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)kh₂emb-~ (“to bend”). Italian ~cambiare~ and Spanish ~cambiar~ are its Romance cousins, and English borrowed the same Gaulish word through Old French as ~change~ and ~exchange~.

The Celtic root meant “bent, crooked,” and the path of meaning ran from “to turn” to “to swap one thing for another” — a fitting image, since an exchange turns goods around between two hands. ~Cambiāre~ is one of the rare everyday Romance verbs that the Romans took from the Gauls rather than from their own Latin stock. The ~é-~ prefix in ~échanger~ underscores the mutual, two-way swap. From the same root French keeps a busy family — ~changer~, ~change~, ~changement~, ~échange~, ~rechange~, ~interchanger~, and the financial ~changeur~ — all turning, in their way, on the idea of exchange.
en.échapper:
From Old French ~escaper~, ~eschaper~ (attested around 1100), from Vulgar Latin *~excappare~, a verb built from the prefix ~ex-~ (“out of”) and Late Latin ~cappa~ (“cape, hooded cloak”). The image is vivid: to ~excappare~ was to slip out of one's cloak, leaving it in a pursuer's grasping hands. Cognate with Spanish and Portuguese ~escapar~, Catalan ~escapar~, Italian ~scappare~, and Romanian ~scăpa~, and with the English borrowing ~escape~.

The same ~cappa~ that lies behind ~échapper~ is one of Latin's most productive garments: it gave French ~chape~, ~chapeau~, ~chaperon~, and ~cape~, and through Italian even ~capot~. Old French ~escaper~ had a doublet ~eschaper~ that hardened into Modern French ~échapper~, while the un-prefixed family kept the cloak's literal sense. A curious relative survives in ~réchapper~ (“to come through, to survive”), and the noun ~échappatoire~ (“a way out, a loophole”) still carries the original gesture of wriggling free. English preserves the cloak-image twice over: ~escape~ from the French verb, and the rarer ~escapade~, a borrowing through Italian and Spanish, for a reckless break for freedom.
en.échauffer:
French ~échauffer~ comes from Middle French ~eschauffer~, from Old French ~eschaufer~ or ~eschalfer~. These go back to a Vulgar Latin verb *~excalfāre~, from Latin ~excalefacere~, built from the prefix ~ex-~ and ~calefacere~ (“to make warm”). The family has a close relative in ~échauder~ (“to scald”), and English ~scald~ is a cognate of that verb.

The core sense of ~échauffer~ is physical: to make something hot, or to warm a body. The verb also carries the figurative senses “to excite” and “to incite”: ~échauffer les esprits~ (“to stir tempers up”) and ~s'échauffer~ in a quarrel (“to grow heated”). Athletes use the reflexive form for warming up before a match, and the noun ~échauffement~ names that warm-up.
en.échelonner: Formed from the noun ~échelon~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is in turn an Old French ~eschelon~ built on ~échelle~ (“ladder”) with the suffix ~-on~, so an ~échelon~ is a “little ladder,” a rung. The verb began in military language: to ~échelonner~ troops was to arrange them in successive lines, one behind another, like the rungs of a ladder. The idea of regular steps then spread to anything set out in stages, such as payments, holidays or tasks spaced over time. English ~echelon~ is a borrowing of the French noun.
en.échouer:
The origin of ~échouer~ is famously obscure, and the sources offer no settled answer. The verb appears around 1559 of galleys run aground, takes the nautical sense “to touch bottom and stop” by 1573, and the figurative “to fail” by 1660. Several competing accounts circulate, none accepted as certain: a derivation from Latin ~cautes~ (“reef”), a variant of ~échoir~, a reshaping of Old French forms of ~escourre~ (“to shake,” from Latin ~excutere~), a development from Latin ~exaquare~ (“to drain dry”), or a shift from ~eschiver~ (“to dodge, slip sideways”). Each runs into phonetic or chronological trouble, so the TLFi leaves the question open.

Whatever its source, the meaning evolved cleanly from the concrete to the abstract: a ship that ran onto a shoal and could go no further became the model for any enterprise that ~échoue~ — that founders, fails, falls through. French keeps the maritime sense alive in ~échouage~ and ~échouement~, while ~déchouer~ means to refloat a stranded vessel.
en.éclaircir: The sources disagree. French Wiktionary derives it from ~claircir~ with the prefix ~é-~, where ~claircir~ comes from ~clair~ (“clear, bright”). English Wiktionary instead gives Late Latin *~exclāricīre~, from Latin ~clāricāre~ (“to make clear”). Either way the prefix ~é-~, from Latin ~ex-~, intensifies the sense, and the base is the idea of clearness. The verb means to make or become brighter, as when the sky clears, and then to make an idea clear, or to solve a mystery.
en.éclairer:
From Old French ~esclairier~, from Latin ~exclārāre~ (“to light up, make bright”), a compound of ~ex-~ (intensive) and the verb ~clārāre~, from the adjective ~clārus~ (“clear, bright, loud”). Latin ~clārus~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, to shout”) — and the link between sound and light is the surprising heart of this word, the spreading of a cry and the spreading of brightness imagined as one. From the same root come ~clamare~ and, in English, ~claim~, ~clear~, and ~declare~.

The earliest French attestations, around the year 980, are of weather: the sky ~esclaire~ when it lightens or flashes. From “to flash, to grow bright” the verb settled into its modern senses — to give light to a room, to illuminate a path, and figuratively to enlighten the mind, to ~éclairer~ a difficult question. The noun ~éclair~ (“flash of lightning,” and hence the glazed pastry, supposedly eaten in a flash) belongs to the same family, as do ~éclaircir~ (“to clarify”), ~clair~, ~clarté~, and ~déclarer~. The verb’s whole career runs along the double track of its root: light that shines and a voice that carries.
en.éclater:
From Old French ~esclater~ (« to burst, splinter, » attested before 1150), from Frankish *~slaitan~ (« to split, tear »), from Proto-Germanic *~slītaną~ (« to tear, slit »). The Germanic line is reconstructed, the dictionaries marking those forms unattested, with the TLFi as the etymology's chief authority. Romance siblings of the Old French form survive in Spanish ~estallar~ and Catalan ~esclatar~, all turning on a core idea of bursting apart.

The semantic core is « to fly into pieces, » and French radiates it in every direction: glass ~éclate~ (« shatters »), thunder and laughter ~éclate~ (« breaks out loud »), a war or a scandal ~éclate~ (« erupts »), and colloquially « s'~éclater~ » means to have a blast. From the same base come the noun ~éclat~ (« a shard, a burst, brilliance »), ~éclatant~ (« dazzling »), and ~éclaté~ (« exploded, » as of a diagram). The journey from a Germanic verb of « tearing » to the French vocabulary of brilliance is a neat case of a violent image — bursting — softening into the language of splendor and radiance.
en.économiser:
~économiser~ was derived in the eighteenth century from ~économie~ with the suffix ~-iser~. The noun had entered French by 1370, as ~yconomie~, in Nicole Oresme's translation of Aristotle's Ethics, meaning the good management of a household — from Latin ~oeconomia~, from Greek ~οἰκονομία~ (~oikonomía~), built on ~οἰκονόμος~ (~oikonómos~, “household steward”): ~οἶκος~ (~oîkos~, “house”) plus ~νέμω~ (~némō~, “to deal out, to manage, to pasture”). Each half has a deep root: ~οἶκος~ goes back to PIE *~wóyḱos~ (“settlement”), cognate with Latin ~vīcus~ (“village”) — whence French ~voisin~, through ~vīcīnus~ — while ~νέμω~ goes back to *~nem-~ (“to allot, to take”), cognate with German ~nehmen~ (“to take”).

For three centuries ~économie~ meant household stewardship rather than national statistics; the sense “thrift, sparing expenditure” is attested only in 1665, in La Rochefoucauld, and it was on that sense that ~économiser~ was minted — the Académie's dictionary traces it to the eighteenth century under the spelling ~œconomiser~, “to administer with thrift.” The family fanned out meanwhile: ~économe~, ~économique~, ~économiste~. And the root ~νέμω~ hides in plain sight elsewhere in French — in the ~-nomie~ of ~astronomie~, ~autonomie~ and ~gastronomie~ (through ~νόμος~, “that which is allotted: usage, law”), and in ~nomade~ (through ~νομάς~, “roaming for pasture,” ~νέμω~ in its herdsman's sense). An economist and a nomad share a root: each, etymologically, manages how resources are dealt out — one over a ledger, the other over grazing land.
en.écosser: Formed from ~cosse~ (“pod, husk”) with the prefix ~é-~, marking removal, and the verbal ending ~-er~: to shell peas is to take them out of their pods. The origin of ~cosse~ itself is debated. The usual account derives it from Late Latin *~coccia~, from Latin ~cochlea~ (“snail, shell”), perhaps crossed with ~coccum~. Littré preferred a Germanic source, compared with Flemish ~schosse~ and German ~Schote~. One French entry even reverses the direction, deriving the verb from Old French ~escosser~ (“to shake out, to strip”), from Latin ~excutere~, and treating ~cosse~ as a back-formation.
en.écouler:
Formed from ~couler~ (“to flow, to run”) with the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out of”), so literally “to flow out, to run off.” The base ~couler~ comes from Latin ~cōlāre~ (“to strain, to filter”), derived from ~cōlum~ (“sieve, strainer, colander”) — flowing liquid was first what a sieve let pass. (This ~cōlō~ “to strain” is distinct from the homonym ~colō~ “to cultivate.”) Italian ~colare~ and Spanish ~colar~ descend from the same straining verb.

The prefix ~ex-~ adds the idea of outward, away: water that ~écoule~ drains off, time that ~s'écoule~ slips away, money that ~s'écoule~ vanishes, a crowd that ~s'écoule~ disperses. By a vivid commercial turn the verb came to mean “to sell off, to clear stock” — goods that pour out the shop door as steadily as water through a strainer. From the same root the language keeps ~écoulement~ (“flow, drainage”), ~découler~ (“to ensue, to flow from”), and, back at the source, ~couloir~ (“corridor,” originally a strainer or channel) and colis is not akin — but ~percolateur~ and ~colature~ are.
en.écouter:
From Middle and Old French ~escouter~ (also ~ascouter~), from Vulgar Latin *~escultāre~, a reshaping of Latin ~auscultāre~ (“to listen attentively, to give ear to”). The Latin verb is built on ~aus-~, the old stem of ~auris~ (“ear”), joined to a second element from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱlew-~ (“to hear”) — so the word is, transparently, “to ear-hear.” Cognates run across Romance: Italian ~ascoltare~, Spanish ~escuchar~, Romanian ~asculta~, and the Picard form ~acouter~, which kept the original initial vowel that standard French dropped.

The first vowel had a turbulent history: the classical ~au-~ weakened, the ~-l-~ vocalized, and ~escouter~ eventually smoothed into ~écouter~, the circumflex marking a vanished ~s~. A surprising side-branch reached English: in Old French an ~escoute~ was a person posted to listen and keep watch, and that noun, borrowed across the Channel, became English ~scout~. From the same Latin source French preserves the learned doublet ~ausculter~ — the physician's verb for listening to the chest through a stethoscope — beside the everyday ~écouter~. The root ~auris~ also surfaces in ~auriculaire~ (the little finger, small enough to fit the ear) and ~oreille~ itself, and the verb yields ~écouteur~ (earpiece, headphone) and ~écoute~ (a listening watch, or telephone tapping).
en.écraser:
Attested from around 1560 and borrowed, with the prefix ~é-~, from Middle English ~crasen~ (“to break, shatter,” source of modern ~craze~), which is itself of imitative origin — by one account from Old Norse *~krasa~ (“to shatter”). Sources mark the Scandinavian source as probable rather than certain. Through that English root, ~écraser~ is a cousin of English ~crash~, ~crush~, and ~craze~.

The word is one of the rarer cases of French borrowing a verb from English (most traffic ran the other way). Its sense is forceful and total: not merely to break but to flatten, squash, obliterate. French built a whole crushing vocabulary on it: ~écrasement~, ~écraseur~, ~écrasant~ (“crushing,” of a defeat or the heat), and the vivid ~écraser comme un ver~ (“to crush like a worm”). The colloquial ~en écraser~ even means “to sleep like a log.” From an imitative Norse-tinged English word for shattering, French forged its strongest verb for grinding a thing to nothing.
en.écrier:
The origin is debated. English Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~escrier~ (“to scream, cry out”), itself a partial blend: in part ~es-~ (“out”) + ~crier~ (“to cry, shout”), and in part Frankish *~skrīan~ (“to yell, call out”), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīhaną~ (“to cry out”), from a Proto-Indo-European root given as *~(s)kerey-~ (“to scream, caw”). French Wiktionary is more hesitant: it calls the origin uncertain, suggests the verb may be a variant of ~écriser~ or ~égriser~, and mentions the simpler analysis ~é-~ + ~crier~.

Whatever its exact descent, the verb has long had a vivid sense: to burst out in a loud cry, usually from emotion. Today it is used almost only reflexively, in ~s'écrier~, to introduce an exclamation (« s'écria-t-il »), which is why it is a staple of narrative prose. The evidence is mixed, so it is safest to say that a native prefix-plus-verb formation and a Germanic contribution have both been proposed. Related French words include ~crier~, ~cri~ and ~récrier~.
en.écrire:
From Middle French ~escrire~, from Old French ~escrivre~ (reshaped to ~escrire~ by analogy), from Latin ~scribere~ (“to write”), the infinitive of ~scribo~. ~scribere~ originally meant “to scratch, to incise,” and descends from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, to carve”), an extension of the root *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). Latin ~scribere~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~skariphâsthai~ (“to scratch an outline”). Notably, it is not related to Greek ~gráphō~ (“to write”), which comes from a different root, *~gerbʰ-~, nor to English ~write~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~ — three unrelated words all born from the act of scratching marks on a surface.

The shift from scratching to writing reflects the ancient technology of the wax tablet and the stylus: to write was to scratch letters into wax or stone. That buried image survives in the modern French family, all built on the ~scrib-~ / ~script-~ stem: ~écrire~, ~écriture~, ~écrivain~, ~décrire~, ~inscrire~, ~prescrire~, ~souscrire~, ~manuscrit~, and ~scribe~. The doublet ~écrire~ (inherited, popular) beside ~scribe~ (learned, borrowed) shows the same Latin verb arriving in French by two different roads.
en.écrouler: Formed in French from the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out, off”) and ~crouler~ (“to give way, to sink”), as in Old French ~acroler~. The verb was first transitive, with the sense of bringing something down, in the early thirteenth century. Modern French uses it almost only in the reflexive form ~s'écrouler~, which means to collapse. The ~é-~ adds the idea of falling completely apart. It is used of walls and buildings, and of hopes, businesses and people who give way under strain.
en.édicter: ~Édicter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēdictāre~, a frequentative of ~ēdīcere~ (“to proclaim, to declare”). French Wiktionary adds that it was taken over to serve as the verb of the noun ~édit~, which comes from the same Latin family. The Latin verb is built on the prefix ~ē-~ (“out”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say”), so the picture is of speaking a rule out loud, with authority. French uses ~édicter~ for a government or an authority that lays down a law, a rule or a penalty, and the sense stays firmly official. English ~edict~ is a cousin from the same Latin source, and ~dire~, ~dicter~ and ~dictature~ belong to the same ~dīcere~ family.
en.éditer:
From Latin ~ēdere~ (supine ~ēditum~, “to give out, put forth, publish”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~dare~ (“to give”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — the same root that gives Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”) and ~dōs~ (“dowry”), and, in French, ~donner~ and ~don~. To ~ēdere~ was literally to “give out” a thing into the world; applied to a book or text, it meant to bring it forth before the public.

French took its bookish vocabulary first from the noun side — ~édition~ (from ~ēditiō~, “a bringing forth”) and ~éditeur~ — and the verb ~éditer~ arose later, around 1784, partly built back from those nouns. The same Latin family yielded ~édit~ (a royal edict, something “given out” by authority) and ~éditorial~. A second, homonymous ~éditer~ entered French in the twentieth century as a computing term, borrowed from English ~edit~; English had clipped that verb from ~editor~, itself ultimately the same ~ēdere~. So the two French ~éditer~ verbs — publishing a book and editing a file — are long-separated descendants of one Latin root meaning “to give out.”
en.éduquer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~ēducāre~ (“to rear, to bring up, to train”), first attested in French in 1385. ~ēducāre~ belongs to the family of ~dūcere~ (“to lead”), but its exact formation is disputed: the CNRTL and the French tradition describe it as a frequentative of ~ēdūcere~ (~ex-~ + ~dūcere~, “to lead out”), while other analyses derive it instead from the noun ~dux~ (“leader”). The two accounts differ in morphology and land on the same root, the Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to pull, to lead”), which also gives, through Germanic, English ~tow~ and German ~ziehen~. In Latin the verb was used as readily of rearing animals and raising plants as of bringing up children, a breadth the French verb never inherited. Spanish ~educar~, Italian ~educare~ and English ~educate~ take up the same Latin verb independently.

The striking thing about ~éduquer~ is how long French resisted it. The everyday verb for raising children was ~élever~, literally to raise up, and lexicographers treated the Latinate newcomer as an affectation. Voltaire mocked the fashion, remarking that people were beginning to ~éduquer~ children instead of ~élever~ them; Féraud disapproved, and as late as the nineteenth century Littré observed that the word appeared in none of the major dictionaries of his day. It climbed all the same: the Académie’s 1842 supplement admitted ~bien éduqué~ and ~mal éduqué~, and the verb is now entirely ordinary. Its Latin relatives arrived earlier and more easily — ~éducation~ and ~éducateur~ were accepted well before the verb they seem to belong to, so for a long stretch French had the nouns without a respectable verb to match. The wider ~dūcere~ family runs through a large share of the modern vocabulary: ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~réduire~, ~duc~, ~conduit~ and ~introduire~.
en.égaler: Formed from the adjective ~égal~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~. The adjective was reshaped in Old French on the model of Latin ~aequālis~ (“even, level, equal”), from ~aequus~ (“level, fair”), replacing older popular forms such as ~evel~. Old Occitan ~egal~ may have been the route by which it came. The verb means to make equal, or to be equal to: one ~égale~ a record, a rival, a performance. The same Latin ~aequus~ lies behind ~équité~, ~équation~, ~adéquat~ and ~équilibre~. The ending ~-er~ makes the adjective a first-conjugation verb.
en.égarer:
The verb comes from Old French ~esgarer~ (“to lose one's way; to be troubled or worried”), through Middle French ~égarer~. English Wiktionary analyzes the Old French as the prefix ~es-~, the ancestor of modern ~é-~, joined to a verb of Frankish origin, from *~warōn~ (“to heed, to pay attention to”). French Wiktionary gives the same analysis, ~es-~ plus ~garer~. The Frankish root belongs to the Germanic family of watching and guarding: German ~wahren~ (“to preserve, to keep”) and English ~wary~ come from the same stock. Frankish, the language of the Franks who conquered Roman Gaul, left French many such words, in particular those of guarding, war and sheltering.

The story of the verb is a shift from losing one's way to losing an object. Old French ~esgarer~ described someone who wandered off course or whose mind was disturbed, and modern French keeps this in ~s'égarer~ (“to go astray”) and in ~égaré~ (“lost, bewildered”), while ~égarement~ names a lapse of judgment or a delusion. The transitive ~égarer~ then came to mean “to mislay”, as in losing one's keys. The base ~garer~ went in the opposite direction, toward safekeeping: it means “to park” a vehicle, and it is also the source of ~gare~ (“station”). So ~égarer~ and ~garer~ are, in a way, opposites built on one Frankish root.
en.égorger:
First attested around 1450, ~égorger~ is a French formation: the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out”) on the noun ~gorge~ (“throat”), the compound meaning something like to bring out through the throat. ~gorge~ comes from popular Latin ~gurga~, a variant of classical ~gurges~ (“whirlpool, gulf, abyss”) — the throat was named after the gaping, swallowing hole it resembles, not the reverse. ~gurges~ is tentatively traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷerh₃-~ (“to devour”), the root behind ~vorāre~, although en.Wiktionary cautions that both the sound correspondence and the morphology are unclear. Sources compare Sanskrit ~gargara~ (“whirlpool”) and Ancient Greek ~górgura~; and Old French ~gort~ (“deep pool”), surviving dialectally as ~gour~, continues the Latin accusative directly. Italian ~gorgo~ continues the Latin noun, and English ~gorge~ and ~regurgitate~ are borrowings from the same stock.

~gorge~ meant the inside of the neck by the early twelfth century, and French built a whole vocabulary on it: ~engorger~, ~dégorger~, ~gorgée~, and the falconers’ ~gorge~, the meal of a bird of prey. ~égorger~ began, and remains, brutally literal — to cut the throat of an animal or a person — and widened to slaughtering and massacring. Its figurative turn is recorded by Furetière in 1690: to ~égorger~ a customer is to ruin him, to charge him a murderous price. That commercial cruelty echoes an older expression on the same noun, ~rendre gorge~ (1598), being forced to give back what one had swallowed. The geographical sense of ~gorge~, a narrow pass between mountains, is later (1675) and was borrowed into English as the ravine ~gorge~. Dictionaries also link the noun to an imitative ~garg-~ group of throat words, among them ~gargariser~ and ~gargouille~, though that connection is presented as a family resemblance rather than a strict line of descent.
en.élaborer:
Borrowed learnedly from Latin ~elaborare~ (“to work out, to take pains over, to produce by effort”), a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and the verb ~laborare~ (“to work, to toil”), from the noun ~labor~ (“work, toil, hardship”). The same ~labor~ underlies French ~labeur~ and ~labourer~ (“to plough”) — the farmer's toil — and was borrowed into English as ~labor~ / ~labour~. Romance kept the learned verb in Italian ~elaborare~ and Spanish ~elaborar~.

The force of the prefix ~ex-~ is “to the finish”: to ~elaborare~ was to work something out fully, to bring it to completion through effort. French ~élaborer~ preserves this exactly — one ~élaborer~ a plan, a theory, a strategy, or a document, building it up carefully piece by piece. Physiology borrowed it too: an organ is said to ~élaborer~ a secretion, working raw material into a finished product. The everyday English ~elaborate~ shares the ancestor but has drifted toward “add detail.” From ~labor~ the French family includes ~laboratoire~ — literally a “place for working” — along with ~collaborer~ (“to work with”) and ~laborieux~ (“laborious, painstaking”).
en.élancer: Formed in French from the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ~lancer~. Here ~é-~ carries the idea of moving out or forth, so ~élancer~ is to hurl something forward, and the reflexive ~s'élancer~ is to hurl oneself, to dash ahead. The base ~lancer~ comes from Old French ~lancier~ and Late Latin ~lanceāre~ (“to wield a lance”), from ~lancea~ (“light spear”), a word the Romans probably borrowed from a Celtic or Iberian source. The same image of a sudden thrust gave the noun ~élan~ (“momentum, surge”) and ~élancement~, a sharp, shooting pain.
en.élargir:
French ~élargir~ comes from Middle French ~eslargir~, formed from the prefix ~es-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out”) and the adjective ~large~ (“wide, broad”), with the inchoative ending ~-ir~. ~Large~ descends from Latin ~largus~ (“abundant, copious, generous”). The deeper origin of ~largus~ is disputed: one account links it to a root meaning “fat, grease,” which de Vaan finds problematic, doubting the long vowel is original; an alternative derives it by metathesis from *~dl̥h₁gʰós~. We give the chain only as far as ~largus~, which is secure. Through Old French ~large~ it is the source of English ~large~ and ~largesse~, alongside Italian and Spanish ~largo~.

The literal sense is “to make broad,” but ~élargir~ long carried a vivid legal meaning: “to release from prison,” to give a prisoner the wide world again. One could say the wrongly jailed man was ~élargi~ — set at liberty. Modern French keeps the spatial and figurative senses (to widen a road, to broaden a debate) and the noun ~élargissement~, used both for an enlargement and, still, for a release.
en.élever:
From Latin ~elevāre~ (“to lift up, to raise”), ~e-~ (a reduced form of ~ex-~, “out, up”) + ~levāre~ (“to lift, to make light”). ~Levāre~ is a verb formed on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from PIE *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light in weight”) — the same root, through Germanic, that gives English ~light~ (not heavy). To raise was, at root, to make something rise by relieving its weight. Through Old French ~lever~, ~levāre~ gave English ~lever~, ~levy~, and ~levee~; Italian ~elevare~ and Spanish ~elevar~ are direct cognates of ~élever~.

French split the simple verb ~lever~ (“to lift”) from the prefixed ~élever~, which specialized toward raising in degree, rank, and especially upbringing. One ~élève~ a wall or a price (raises it), one ~élève~ children (brings them up), and one ~élève~ livestock (rears it) — hence ~élevage~ (“animal husbandry”) and ~éleveur~ (“breeder”). The pupil one brings up educationally is, fittingly, an ~élève~ (“student”). The reflexive ~s'élever~ means “to rise” — a tower, a sum, or a protest. The ~levis~/~levāre~ family is enormous in French: ~lever~, ~levée~, ~élever~, ~élévation~, ~élève~, ~soulever~ (“to lift up”), ~enlever~ (“to take away, to lift off”), ~prélever~ (“to levy, to take a sample”), and ~léger~ (“light”) itself.
en.éliminer:
French ~éliminer~ is a learned borrowing of Latin ~eliminare~ (“to thrust out of doors, to expel”). Its anatomy is vivid: the prefix ~ex-~ (“out of”) plus ~limen~ (“threshold, doorsill”) — literally “to put across the threshold,” to show the door. ~Limen~ is probably bound up with Latin ~limes~ (“boundary, border-path”), the word behind ~limite~, and with ~limus~ (“sideways, oblique”); its ultimate Indo-European root is not securely established. Through ~eliminare~ and ~limen~, French is cousin to English ~eliminate~ and to the modern buzzword ~liminal~ (“on the threshold”).

The original image is almost domestic — sweeping something out over the doorsill, out of the house. From that literal expulsion ~éliminer~ broadened into the abstract “to remove, to do away with”: a candidate is ~éliminé~ from a contest, a hypothesis from an argument, an unknown from an equation. Physiology kept the bodily sense — the kidneys ~éliminent~ waste. Sport made it dramatic, in the ~éliminatoires~ (“qualifying rounds”) that knock teams out. The threshold itself, ~limen~, lurks beneath a small but pointed family: ~préliminaire~ (“preliminary,” what stands before the threshold), ~liminaire~ (an opening note, “on the doorsill”), and, through its sibling ~limes~, the whole field of ~limite~ and ~limiter~.
en.élire:
From Old French ~eslire~, ~eslire~, from Latin ~eligere~ (“to pick out, to choose”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”). ~legere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, to collect”), the same root behind Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”) and the ~-logy~ of countless sciences. Romance cognates include Italian ~eleggere~ and Spanish ~elegir~.

The literal idea is to “gather out” the best from a heap — to single out by careful picking. Old French ~eslire~ covered ordinary choosing as well as formal election, and the past participle ~élu~ still means both “elected” and, in religious language, “chosen, one of the elect.” The plain sense “to choose” narrowed over time toward the political and ceremonial “to elect,” leaving everyday choosing to ~choisir~. A trace of the wider meaning lingers in the formal ~élire domicile~ (“to take up legal residence”). The fertile ~legere~ gave French a whole library of words: ~lire~, ~lecture~, ~élire~'s cousins ~sélectionner~ and ~collectionner~, plus ~légende~, ~collège~, and ~intelligent~ (“choosing between”).
en.éloigner:
From Middle French ~esloigner~, from Old French ~esloignier~ (“to move far off, to send away”), a derivative of ~loing~ (“far”) — modern ~loin~ — with the prefix ~es-~ (from Latin ~ex-~). The adverb ~loin~ descends from Latin ~longē~ (“far, at a distance”), the adverbial form of the adjective ~longus~ (“long, distant”), traced to Proto-Indo-European *~dlongʰos~ (“long”). The Italian ~lontano~ and Spanish ~lejos~ share the same Latin ancestry, while English ~long~ springs from a related branch of the same root.

The core idea is spatial: to ~éloigner~ something is to push it toward the ~loin~, the far horizon. Old French built the verb on the comparative notion of putting distance between things, and the ~es-~ prefix added the sense of separation or removal. Over time the verb gained figurative range — one can ~éloigner~ a suspicion, a danger, or a friend grown cold — so that distance became emotional and abstract as readily as physical. The reflexive ~s'éloigner~ (“to move away, to drift apart”) is now among its commonest uses. From the same Latin ~longus~ French inherited a wide family, including ~long~, ~longueur~, ~allonger~, ~prolonger~, and ~longtemps~, all turning on the measure of length or distance.
en.élucider:
~Élucider~ is borrowed from Latin ~ēlūcidāre~, “to make clear, to illuminate,” formed from ~ē-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and the adjective ~lūcidus~ (“bright, clear”). English Wiktionary adds that, by surface analysis, French speakers can also read it as ~é-~ + ~lucide~ + ~-er~. Latin ~lūcidus~ comes from the verb ~lūcēre~ (“to shine”) and the noun ~lūx~ (“light”). English ~elucidate~ comes from the same Latin verb.

French now uses ~élucider~ for bringing a mystery, a murder, a text or a cause into the clear, and the noun ~élucidation~ follows it. The same Latin family is behind ~lucide~, ~luire~, ~luisant~, ~translucide~ and ~lueur~. The adjective ~lucide~ shows the two senses side by side: a ~lucide~ mind is “clear” in the way a bright room is clear.
en.émailler: Formed from the noun ~émail~ and the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary attests the Old French forms ~esmaillier~ and ~esmailler~, so the verb is old and was built within French on ~esmail~, the ancestor of ~émail~. It means “to coat with enamel,” and by extension “to decorate with bright spots,” as in a meadow enameled with flowers. The gloss “mar” in the app belongs to this figurative family: surfaces dotted or marked with something that stands out.
en.émaner: Learned borrowing from Latin ~ēmānāre~ (“to flow out”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~mānāre~ (“to flow”). The Latin sense was literal, of water or a spring running out. French kept the image but made it figurative: something ~émane~ from a source when it proceeds from it, as an order from an authority or a light from a lamp. English ~emanate~ comes from the same Latin verb, and the noun ~émanation~ is its French relative.
en.émerger:
French ~émerger~ descends from Latin ~emergere~ (“to rise out of, to come forth”), built from the prefix ~e-~ / ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~mergere~ (“to dip, to plunge, to immerse”). The verb ~mergere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~mezgō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~mésgeti~, from the root *~mesg-~ (“to plunge, to dip”). Distant cognates surface in Sanskrit ~majjati~ (“dives under”) and Lithuanian ~mazgoti~ (“to wash”). So ~émerger~ is literally the undoing of immersion: to un-plunge, to break back up out of the water.

The core image is hydraulic — a swimmer or a reef rising above the surface — and from there ~émerger~ spread to anything that comes into view or prominence: a truth that emerges, a leader who emerges from the crowd. Its mirror-twin ~immerger~ (~in-~ + ~mergere~, “to plunge in”) keeps the opposite motion, and the two share the noun pair ~émersion~ and ~immersion~. The modern adjective ~émergent~ (“emerging,” as of nations or technologies) and the borrowed urgence-free term ~émergence~ all trace back to this single Latin verb of dipping and surfacing.
en.émerveiller: Formed on the noun ~merveille~, with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of filling someone with wonder. The Old French verb is recorded as ~esmerveillier~ (and as ~esmerveler~ in English Wiktionary), so the formation is old, with ~é-~ the modern form of Old French ~es-~. The noun ~merveille~ comes from Latin ~mirabilia~ (“wondrous things”), the neuter plural of ~mirabilis~, from ~mirari~ (“to wonder at”). To ~émerveiller~ someone is to make them marvel.
en.émettre:
From Latin ~emittere~ (“to send out, let go, produce”), a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, let go”). The base verb ~mittere~ is of debated origin, plausibly traced to a Proto-Italic *~mitō~ and a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to exchange” or “let go.” It is the same Latin source behind Italian ~emettere~ and Spanish ~emitir~, and behind a swarm of English borrowings in ~-mit~.

The core idea is always a sending-forth, but the object sent has multiplied delightfully. One can ~émettre~ a sound, a light, a banknote, a stamp, a radio signal, an opinion, or a vote — each a thing released into the world. The everyday French verb ~mettre~ (“to put”) descends from the very same ~mittere~, its meaning having drifted from “send” to “place.” The Latin verb is one of the most fertile in French: through it come ~mission~, ~message~, ~admettre~, ~permettre~, ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, and ~remettre~, plus the nouns ~émission~ (a radio or TV broadcast) and ~émetteur~ (“transmitter”). A television program and a postage stamp thus share an ancestor whose single task was simply to let something go.
en.émincer: Formed in French from the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ~mincer~. The prefix ~é-~ comes from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”), and here suggests cutting thin pieces off, hence “to slice thinly.” The base ~mincer~ is from Old French ~mincier~, whose origin is disputed. It is often explained as Vulgar Latin *~minūtiāre~ (from Latin ~minūtus~, “small”), but the sound changes do not fit well, since that source should have given ~menuiser~. A Frankish origin, from *~minnistō~ (“smaller”) or *~minnisōn~ (“to make smaller”), looks more likely, and it would link ~mincer~ to English ~mince~.
en.émouvoir:
~Émouvoir~ is inherited from Middle French ~esmouvoir~ and Old French ~esmovoir~, from Vulgar Latin *~exmovēre~, a reshaping of classical Latin ~ēmovēre~ (“to move out, to remove, to stir up”). Both Latin forms join the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) to ~movēre~ (“to move”). The Old French ~s~ is a leftover of that ~x~, and it was later dropped, the accent on ~é~ being its trace. Italian ~smuovere~ is a close parallel (“to shift, to dislodge”).

The oldest sense of ~émouvoir~ was physical or political: to set in motion, to stir up, as in stirring up a revolt. That sense lives on in ~émeute~ (“riot”), which comes from the old feminine participle of ~esmovoir~, literally something “set in motion.” The verb then turned inward, so that what is stirred is a person's feelings, and ~émotion~ is a close relative. The same Latin ~movēre~ gives ~mouvoir~, ~mobile~, ~moteur~ and ~promouvoir~. To this day, to be ~ému~ is to be, etymologically, “moved,” as in English.
en.énerver:
~Énerver~ is inherited from Middle French ~enerver~, from Latin ~ēnervāre~ (“to cut the sinews of, to weaken”). The Latin verb joins ~ex-~ (“out, away”) to ~nervus~ (“sinew, tendon, strength”), so the original idea is of taking the strength out of someone. Latin ~nervus~ is usually linked to Greek ~neûron~ (“sinew, nerve”), the source of English ~neuron~. French can also read the verb as ~é-~ + ~nerf~ + ~-er~, a surface analysis that matches its form.

The modern meaning reverses the old one. For a long time ~énerver~ meant to enfeeble, to sap, and that sense is still found in literary French.
